I found it hard to slip into Fallout 4's environment at first, but once I did, I was readily greeted by not only the beautiful world and colorful characters, but a story, moulded and changed by your decisions, that delivered the butterflies I expected from Bethesda's newest product. While I would rather not compare it to the previous fallouts, I will say it is the general improvement over the geniuses of Fallout 3 and Fallout: New Vegas that all the fans called upon and hoped for when told of the games release.

Good game, love the action, the shooting aspect has gotten better. You can mod just about anything and make yourself as OP as possible. Being made by Bethesda, it has some bugs and the load times have contributed to around 60 of my hours in the game. Also, there is a hard cap in building for the settlements.  Last thing that is dissapointing is the variation in enemies. Raiders and Ghouls make up around 90% of the things you fight. There are Triggermen, Robots, and Deathclaws, but to a much lesser extent.

It's a good foundation for what could have been an amazing game, but it has some big flaws (like the components grinding or bad dialogues choices).
Still a great game if you are looking for post-apocalyptic Action and Crafting, but the RPG fan should probably pass.

Over 100 hours already and I'm nowhere near finished with my current character. Why is that?
The Good:
Face-sculpting your character - with enough time you can look however you want.
Combat gameplay seems pretty solid, enemy AI can be tricky. No longer can you camp in 1 spot and take out a Raider/Super-Mutant camp - they WILL look for you and they WILL find you.
Making your own settlement(s). Want to build a fortress of death in the middle of the wasteland because now you can.
The enviroment/locations as you travel through the Boston Wasteland is impressive. Everything from a Radiation soaked wasteland to a town built using botched together boats.
Power armour now makes you the tank you're supposed to be with it!
The Bad:
Keyboard layout.. oh gods reworking the keymapping is a pain but it needs to be done.
Your companions will constantly get in the way, but you're going to need them to carry all thta sweet, sweet junk.
Settlement construction (like some other things) is not that intuitive.. mainly because...
The. UI. SUCKS.
The Ugly:
Outside of the main quest line and a few extra bits for the relevant factions there's not much to do from an actual 'questing' stand-point. However there is a huge area to explore.
Summary:
It's well worth investing in. And if you don't, I'm more than happy put more points into being a Cannibal...

No struggling in this game, no learning, no diplomacy, just a straight up shoot em up now.

Fallout 4....whilst a very good idea and a very hyped up game, the game itself had a lot of problems.
For example: We were promised a massive customization system. But the customization system itself is VERY limited, I do not have a problem with having to find the materials in game for my weapons; however I do have a problem with the game itself limiting me. "You can put a silencer on this gun....but only if you have Gunsmith Rank 3" "To achieve Gunsmith Rank 3 you must be level 13 with 5 Intelligence". They ruined the perk system and the S.P.E.C.I.A.L (Strength, Perception, Endurance, Charisma, Intelligence, Agility, Luck) System. Most if not all of the things I liked about the perk system are gone (Terrifying Presence Dialogue, Lady Killer Dialogue, Etc).
Furthermore, I very much enjoyed a melee system in the other Fallout games. In this game however, it is almost nonexistent. Everyone has a gun, and there is maybe one instance where fists are required and it is scripted.
Just like the other games, I do not enjoy the "unconsious" state when you attack an NPC instead of the NPC dieing, except now it is brought to a whole new level where they just fall on their *** and sit on the ground for a moment.
It seems as if the Developers are actually trying to discourage modding, they literally took out three categories from the Nexus Mod sites. Weapons, Quests And Adventures (Voiced Protagonist), and Buildings.
Quests are NOT optional: Walk into an area (Radio signal pops up and a quest to help the BOS is immediately set as active) Or when talking to a person. You can say "Yes I'll do it" or "No" and end up doing it anyway. I tried to haggle MacReady's price and then said that I wanted to cancel and not pay or send Dogmeat back home. So instead, the game takes my money and sends Dogmeat to the Red Rocket Truck Stop.
Settlements...."112 Water, 15 Food, 3 People, 9 Beds, Electricity 100+, Defense 114, Happiness: 29%"- Need I say more?
There are things I enjoy about this.
For Example: Companion customization- I can finally put cosmetic mods on a Dog (Goggles, Bandannas....They need to add hats for our four legged companions)
Settlement customization: I love building my own house.
I like this game, I really do. But I would not reccomend it until the bugs and glitches have been sorted out...and modding is enabled more than it is currently.

I will compare Fallout 4 to New Vegas and Fallout 3, because those are the games that I've played.
Fallout 4 is an awesome game, and due to the way the gameplay is compared to the other games, I think it will be easier for more people to get into the Fallout series.
I like the story, love the character customization, love the gameplay, the companions and how power armor works in this game compared to Fallout 3 and New Vegas.
I do however have some complaints:
I feel like the game didn't let me give my character his/her own personality. You can usually choose to be either nice, rude, or sarcastic, but it seems like you end up being a good person no matter what.
Another thing is that I liked knowing what I would say before saying it (Fallout 3 and New vegas showed you the sentence you would say if you chose the option, whereas Fallout 4 shows a few words that represents the sentence).
I prefered having a bunch of skills+perks, over the perk system in Fallout 4
The endings feel weaker. I'm not a big fan of the endings in Fallout 3, but I loved the endings in New Vegas, because you got to know what the consequences were of what you did in the wasteland. In Fallout 4 the ending just felt kinda ''eh''.
I don't really have anything else to say about this game, except that it was awesome BUT it wasn't the Fallout I fell in love with.
This review probably seems really negative, but it is truly an awesome game, it just lacks a bit in some areas.

I feel like this is the first Bethesda game I've played that worked without a lot of fiddling. It runs pretty well with rare framerate drops on my gtx970 and my i5-4590. I'd say it's in better condition than a typical post-patched bethesda game based on how well it runs.
Speed is tied to framerate so you prolly have to lock it to 60.
The gameplay is probably best described as "Fallout, but more of it" which is more or less what I expected. Some pleasant additions are present (reworked crafting system making it actually fun to do, and it actually feels fun to fight, it's also more difficult, even on normal)
The game's UI has some issues with keyboard controls, that I've personally gotten used to but will probably sour the game for others.  Overall I feel like most of the issues in this game can be sorted out via patch and Bethesda has been pretty eager to send out patches so good on them.
It also kind of simplifies levelling, which is a downer for most people, but I feel like levelling in fallout was needlessly complicated, and most of the skills from other games are still present, even if you don't put stat points directly into them. The progression still feels really good to me. And no arbitrary level cap is present either.
Probably the thing that took the biggest hit was dialogue, since you don't have NEARLY as many options, but it's surprised me from time to time (Finishing a quest before a character tells me about it, so I can immediately report my success and watch them get flustered) and overall I think the characters are written much stronger.
Overall I'd rate this as maybe the best 3D Fallout game, but some issues do need working out. The framerate drops, though rare, seem completely random. I'm excited to see what kind of additions they'll add in DLC and whether they'll be worth it, since DLC is always the best (and worst) parts of these games. I'm hoping for more perks personally.

Like most gamers, I was anticipating this game ever since it was announced at E3 this year. Did it live up to my hype? Well...yes and no. Now, before I begin, I'd like to say that my review will be based on the hours I logged on the Xbox One copy. As it stands, the PC version runs on my rig, it's just the frame-rate that's giving me some issues. With that said, onto the review:
From the moment I started playing to when I made a new character to join with a different faction, I was instantly hooked. Unlike Fallout 3 which took a while before the main story got interesting, here it wastes no time introducing you to the main story. Best thing is, unlike Fallout 3, the main story is actually it's strongest point. Unlike Fallout 3's story of 'Dad leaves Vault and you have to go find him then restore water to the wasteland', here the story is 'Your son is kidnapped and you have to go rescue him' which then evolves from you going to rescue your son to either destroying or joining The Institute. My main issue with the main story actually deals with a faction that comes into play. About half-way through it, the Brotherhood Of Steel show up. Now, yes, it's one of the coolest moments in the game, but when you find out about their true purpose and that they are not like the ones from the Capital Wasteland that you remember, but more..well I guess evil faction.While it's cool that the game presents each faction (Institute, Minutemen, Brotherhood, and The Railroad) each with their own faults and reasons for what they do, you come to realize there's only one GOOD faction to join with and the rest are pretty much evil. Said GOOD faction being the Minutemen as their whole objective is to restore the Commonwealth and help out those in need and it's with them you get to try out new gameplay ideas I'll touch on later.
Onto the other factions now, the Brotherhood do return, as stated earlier, but their whole reasoning for coming is simple: Destroy The Institute and all Synths (Human/Robot). While, yes, when you first meet the Institute, you do learn to hate them, but the lengths the Brotherhood go to show their hatred is just....mind-boggling. Yes, it was cool seeing Liberty Prime back in action and their is a cool quest near the conclusion of the main story but the more I'd talk with the Brotherhood, the more I want to take a FatMan and launch nuke after nuke at them. FAR beyond their old roles from Fallout 3. As for the Railroad...honestly they made a bad impression on me the first time I met them. Mostly, they are there to rescue synths but they, ESPECIALLY their leader, came off as snobbish and...well very ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly. It's worth doing a mission for them just to get the Deliverer Pistol. With The Institute, sadly, I don't have much to say, only that a character from F3 returns and...I might be alone in this one, but I was never a fan of her when she appeared in Fallout 3.
The new gameplay ideas are fun, but I wish they had better tutorials for them, mainly with base-building. Weapon and Armor crafting is fun and I do see alot of subtle improvements to each weapons damage and range (save for one: Anyone else notice that the .50 rounds are a bit weak?) and I do like the new weapons introduced and I love the newer designs of the classic weapons...which leads me to my first real complaint: What the heck happened to the Gauss Rifle?! This badass weapon from Fallout 3 that can easily one shot enemies is not relegated to a weak laser rifle! What happened? Onto the base building and this is where, sadly, the bulk of my complaints are. While it's cool we can build our own settlements and have a community, the way you go about doing it isn't very fun. Building a actual house is a chore (Trust me, stick with prefabs) cause the pieces don't really 'click' together ala Minecraft or Legos (For me on the Xbox One, I don't know if this problem persist on the PC). The BIGGEST issue is this: If you want traders to come into town, you have to be leveled up to a certain point AND have two points in the Local Leader perk AND have enough caps to build them. Heck, you need perks to even do 80% of the crafting and building in the game, with the only things you don't need perks for are building actual houses and defenses (By the way, here's something else the game won't tell you: In order to assign someone to a defense or garden, first you need to be in the Workshop menu, then you highlight a person in the settlement, then you click 'assign', THEN you go to said area you have a defense/garden in and THEN you click 'go' and you'll assign them to it). My only other complaints for Fallout 4 are that caps and bobby pins are harder to come by then usual, the world seems a bit smaller then both Fallout 3 and New Vegas, and that the layered armor system is a bit cumbersome to figure out. Also...
Complaints aside, this is a excellent game and it does live up to the hype. Sure, I kinda wish there was a bit more to do, but hey, that's what DLC is for! If you haven't already, pick this game up, you will not be disappointed (unless your name is Angry Joe then by all means, be disappointed)

7 / 10
Settlements have too many flaws. Way too many. Settlements can't defend themselves unless you're there when its being attacked. Building with a defensive strategy is pointless. The repeat-quests they will start bombarding you with when you have quite a few settlements becomes ridiculously annoying.
The visuals should be better, considering the performance in this game.
Massive problems with shadow performance. If you use anything other than medium-distance shadows, your fps can tank by up to 20 to 25 FPS in certain areas such as the areas in-and-around Fanueil Hall, or any of the large city-areas.
Not enough base-weapons. There's a lot of weapons, but you will generally use whatever hits harder and attacks faster. There needs to be better weapon balance and more base-weapons in this game. Too many of the weapons in this game don't get utilized because they're straight up terrible.
Power armor is overpowered. No reason to beat around the bush. It's just straight up overpowered.
V.A.T.S is a completely useless features unless you specifically build into critical attacks. The reason I feel this way is because V.A.T.S accuracy is absolutely awful compared to using weapons in real-time. The accuracy is so much better in real-time that there's just no reason to use v.a.t.s.
The real-time shooting mechanics are definitely way better than previous fallout games, but that only hurts v.a.t.s because they made the accuracy so much worse when you use v.a.t.s and I don't understand it.
Facial animations are stiff as hell.

Fallout 4, what it is.
Hello. I'm a pompous jerk, and I'm here to tell you what Fallout 4 is. Why am I doing this? Because I feel the inexplicable urge to toss my hat into the ring every time someone makes a broad, untrue (To me, and my oppinion's the only one that matters, right?) generalization about the game. I felt that doing so once, having it on the review page and probably vanish onto page 37 within the first day would do the least harm to everyone.
It's not a deep and complex RPG. This is true, this is fact, don't deny it. There are several quests where things can go differently in minor ways, and the main quest has a fun faction choice element, but the detractors are right. This is not New Vegas, and it's even a little simplified from Bethesda's standards.
It is not an on rails liniar FPS. Pull your heads out of your butts, guys. If I see one more person tell me Modern Warfare 3 offered more exploration freedom than this game I will... do nothing, because we're both on the internet and I'm a wuss, but the fact ramains that it isn't true. You want to complain, feel that Bethesda is dumbing things down from the Obsidian and Black Isle standard? Go ahead. It's true, just don't use hyperbolic nonsense to say it.
The game has optimization issues on certain rigs that outright baffle me. I can't say how large a group of rigs this is, because the groups screaming that the game is a broken, buggy mess and those that say it's running smoother than a baby's bottom are about equally loud, but it's true. Why is this? I don't know. Did Bethesda do too few tests like the infamous Mass Effect 1 three sets of hardware fiasco? Do you just suck at keeping your computer optimized and think that throwing money at it means you're entitled to have it work? I don't know. The fact is that it's unplayably broken for some people and IT WORKS FINE for others. I'm in this latter, lucky group, and it's true. I'm not fanboying out, I'm not lieing. Though I can't tell precisely about the FPS, it at least stays above thirty, I've had two crashes in my hundred someodd hours of play, and it only hits major slowdown when I alt+Tab too much.
Oh, on a miner sidenote about Alt+Tabbing, for those who say the game crashes on startup, One rather obscure cause that a friend of mine ran into is that Bethesda games tend to build their INIs on  initial startup. If any funny business happened during that start up, like, say, alt+tabbing out to answer an IM, the config writer will get confused, not know how big your screen is, and have a massive screaming fit. Solution? Delete your config INI files, and try again. Hope this helps someone.
Is the control scheme broken? Yes, yes, and no. It's obviously a controller friendly scheme, I'm not going to deny that. In fact, I plugged my knock-off X360 controller in and the interface got about 90% easier to use. Not an option for me on the whole, of course, because I SUCK at aiming with an analogue stick, but a thing that's worth noting. Another problem it has is that there are multiple keys for a lot of things, and the game proceeds to tell you the worst possible one. Did you know you can scrap in settlement building by pressing R, then E? You might have, but certainly not through the game telling you because it insists you have to press enter. In fact, E works for ALMOST everything you need to press enter for, and finding this out has made my life a hundred times easier, but again, the tool tips don't help. Also, no in-game rebinding and grenade and bash being on the same key. No, Bethesda, just... no, even if the former has been around since Skyrim or before. I can't remember and research is for motivated people.
Okay, then what is Fallout 4.
I'm kind of torn between "Shooter with heavy RPG elements or RPG with heavy shooter elements. While the system isn't as meaty as previous fallout games, a lot of the perks stand in for old skills. For example, there's no locksmith skill, but there's a locksmith perk that takes four levels to max, (with the level restriction being something I don't feel like getting into.) While in  the old games, it'd take five levels, (4 if you were minmaxing,) and you had the option to grow something else at the same time. Yes, the Perks system in this game is simpler, but it's not 'Baby's first game" simple. You CAN become a god at everything, but that'd take levelling up to about 90, while a full playthrough of the main questline and a good amount of sidequesting's only going to get you up to 40 or so. Up until those very high levels, there's still choice and strategy in what you spend your perks in, and of course looting is always a thing that happens, though the game could do with a bit of variaty. There only really being one armor progression is kind of lame, though I suppose Fallout 1 and 2 pretty much had that, so... yeah.
Is it simpler? Yes. Is it easier? That.. depends. For me? No. I've got the reflexes of a dead cat. Twitch shooting is not a thing I do, and thus Vats, which has been Nerfed  from how godly it previously was, is my life. It's not insanely hard, but on normal or hard it's a challenge. If you're good at FPSes? ...No clue, ask someone else. I heard the mechanics are improved, and they seem to be. (Aside from that grenade hotkey, seriously, go DIE!)
Is it a good fallout game?.
Again, yes and no. Full disclosure. I liked Tactics. It was fun, it had the esthetics, and the story wasn't horrible. I also liked Fallout 3, which was fun, had the esthetics, and the story was... by Bethesda. So a few memerable characters and moments that I love to bits wrapped in a story that's schlock B grade. This is a Bethesda game, which means the story is... there. It does its job, and tries to be inoffensive. The mechanics and setting are great, the in-world story telling is always fun and good for a chuckle. Basically this is a Fallout game, if Fallout 3 was. And I think it's better than 3, with the DLC and mods hopefully improving it still more. Having said all that, this is NOT Fallout 1, 2 or New Vegas. (Have I said that enough?) There are pretty big lore inconsistancies like the omnipresence of neucliar cars, etc, the writing... I'm not going over again, it's a bit goofier, and as mentioned earlier, simpler.
Is it a fun game? Yes, if you like FPS/RPG Hybrids, and aren't cursed with whatever it is that causes some unknown percentage of systems to run like drunk pigs.
It is not an absolutely horrible nightmare that Bethesda should be ashamed or shot for making, as so many enraged people keep screaming. Veterains of the series should know what to expect from a Bethesda title by now, and aside from a baffling refusal to learn certain lessons from Obsidian about gameplay improvements in New Vegas, that's exactly what we got. It's not ground breaking, it's not earth shattering, but given that Fallout 3's engine has not aged well and there's something qualitatively different about playing a Bethesda game from playing New Vegas, (And not always in a bad direction, mind,) it's good to have a new playground to play in, with the upgrades the creation engine has over the old one allowing hopefully for some interesting new mods.
For newcomers with few expectations, play this one if you like the exploration and interesting locations more, plus a neat settlement building feature that's worth a look. If you're into RPGs for their story and your ability to mesh yourself in it, Play New Vegas, but be sure to get the patches.

SPOILER WARNING: I tried to avoid any plot-based spoilers, but it's hard to give a comprehensive review without letting on to anything. I was pretty sure this didn't need a spoiler warning, but wanted to add one just in case. Read at your own risk if you haven't played it yet.
Ah, the latest installment of Bethesda's Fallout franchise: Fallout 4. Right after finishing it, I went back and started playing Fallout: New Vegas, which told me everything that I needed to know about the world of difference that was brought to this latest game. The graphics are leaps and bounds better, which seems obvious with the new console, but is extremely noticeable even on PC. I'm not here to talk about graphics, however, as there is always more to be done in that sense.
This game does what the main line of Fallout games do best -- making you care about your character and those around him or her right out of the starting gate. Death and destruction mesh perfectly with sadness, loss, and lots of other pretty feels. For this reason, the game immersion is on par with Skyrim. While I'm playing, I truly do feel like this is my life, and it takes something big (like having my head blown off by a supermutant) to remind me that it's just a game. The music and atmosphere are impeccable. I can truly feel the heat of the irradiated world on my face when I look up at the sky. I can feel the muggy rain and see it on the skin of my companions.
The formula is similar enough to Fallout 3 in terms of plot, mapping, and items, but the added features make all the difference. Customizing communities, crafting everything from mutfruit plans to turrets, building your own custom house, and modifying weapons/armor in a variety of ways leaves me feeling there's always more to be done in this game. The Fallout series was sorely missing the integration of this kind of RPG crafting element. New Vegas (granted this is Obsidian, not Bethesda) attempted crafting, but it felt confusing and mismanaged. With each installment of the Fallout series, however, it has gotten better. Now, with Fallout 4 finally here (and having finally beaten it), I can say the crafting is on par with the current state of the Elder Scrolls games, and may have even surpassed them.
One place I felt this game shine was in its dialogue choices. Bethesda's games have always had wonderful selection of responses for you to behave as you might in the real world.
This game does continue to fall short in the depth of the quest lines. You get one really great main quest, like in Fallout 3, then everything else is half-baked clique missions and repeating generic quests.
All in all, Jake gives this game a 9.2 out of a total 10.

Like most gamers, I was anticipating this game ever since it was announced at E3 this year. Did it live up to my hype? Well...yes and no. Now, before I begin, I'd like to say that my review will be based on the hours I logged on the Xbox One copy. As it stands, the PC version runs on my rig, it's just the frame-rate that's giving me some issues. With that said, onto the review:
From the moment I started playing to when I made a new character to join with a different faction, I was instantly hooked. Unlike Fallout 3 which took a while before the main story got interesting, here it wastes no time introducing you to the main story. Best thing is, unlike Fallout 3, the main story is actually it's strongest point. Unlike Fallout 3's story of 'Dad leaves Vault and you have to go find him then restore water to the wasteland', here the story is 'Your son is kidnapped and you have to go rescue him' which then evolves from you going to rescue your son to either destroying or joining The Institute. My main issue with the main story actually deals with a faction that comes into play. About half-way through it, the Brotherhood Of Steel show up. Now, yes, it's one of the coolest moments in the game, but when you find out about their true purpose and that they are not like the ones from the Capital Wasteland that you remember, but more..well I guess evil faction.While it's cool that the game presents each faction (Institute, Minutemen, Brotherhood, and The Railroad) each with their own faults and reasons for what they do, you come to realize there's only one GOOD faction to join with and the rest are pretty much evil. Said GOOD faction being the Minutemen as their whole objective is to restore the Commonwealth and help out those in need and it's with them you get to try out new gameplay ideas I'll touch on later.
Onto the other factions now, the Brotherhood do return, as stated earlier, but their whole reasoning for coming is simple: Destroy The Institute and all Synths (Human/Robot). While, yes, when you first meet the Institute, you do learn to hate them, but the lengths the Brotherhood go to show their hatred is just....mind-boggling. Yes, it was cool seeing Liberty Prime back in action and their is a cool quest near the conclusion of the main story but the more I'd talk with the Brotherhood, the more I want to take a FatMan and launch nuke after nuke at them. FAR beyond their old roles from Fallout 3. As for the Railroad...honestly they made a bad impression on me the first time I met them. Mostly, they are there to rescue synths but they, ESPECIALLY their leader, came off as snobbish and...well very ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly. It's worth doing a mission for them just to get the Deliverer Pistol. With The Institute, sadly, I don't have much to say, only that a character from F3 returns and...I might be alone in this one, but I was never a fan of her when she appeared in Fallout 3.
The new gameplay ideas are fun, but I wish they had better tutorials for them, mainly with base-building. Weapon and Armor crafting is fun and I do see alot of subtle improvements to each weapons damage and range (save for one: Anyone else notice that the .50 rounds are a bit weak?) and I do like the new weapons introduced and I love the newer designs of the classic weapons...which leads me to my first real complaint: What the heck happened to the Gauss Rifle?! This badass weapon from Fallout 3 that can easily one shot enemies is not relegated to a weak laser rifle! What happened? Onto the base building and this is where, sadly, the bulk of my complaints are. While it's cool we can build our own settlements and have a community, the way you go about doing it isn't very fun. Building a actual house is a chore (Trust me, stick with prefabs) cause the pieces don't really 'click' together ala Minecraft or Legos (For me on the Xbox One, I don't know if this problem persist on the PC). The BIGGEST issue is this: If you want traders to come into town, you have to be leveled up to a certain point AND have two points in the Local Leader perk AND have enough caps to build them. Heck, you need perks to even do 80% of the crafting and building in the game, with the only things you don't need perks for are building actual houses and defenses (By the way, here's something else the game won't tell you: In order to assign someone to a defense or garden, first you need to be in the Workshop menu, then you highlight a person in the settlement, then you click 'assign', THEN you go to said area you have a defense/garden in and THEN you click 'go' and you'll assign them to it). My only other complaints for Fallout 4 are that caps and bobby pins are harder to come by then usual, the world seems a bit smaller then both Fallout 3 and New Vegas, and that the layered armor system is a bit cumbersome to figure out. Also...
Complaints aside, this is a excellent game and it does live up to the hype. Sure, I kinda wish there was a bit more to do, but hey, that's what DLC is for! If you haven't already, pick this game up, you will not be disappointed (unless your name is Angry Joe then by all means, be disappointed)

Leaving this review makes me quite sad. Here's the bottom line. Unless you are a major fan of the franchise, I can't recommend buying at this time. If you're on the fence, give it around 3-6 months and wait for a sale.
I mean... It says something, when the best Fallout games we've gotten in over the last ten years have been Obsidian's Fallout: New Vegas and Wasteland 2.
Pros:
-The game's graphical update is quite welcome, especially with all the colors.
-The settlement system is a cool idea.
-Animations on some enemies (e.g. The way Feral Ghouls flail about, Mirelurks turtle up and charge, etc.) is phenomenal.
-Running (or, sneaking) around, exploring places and looting things is reasonably enjoyable.
-The additional weapon variety and the crafting to be able to reforge the weapon you've been using into an entirely different role is great.
-The fact that there are populated vaults with something that's capable of talking rather than shooting is nice.
-Your companions will converse with nearby  NPCs, which is a welcome touch.
-The game doesn't restrict you from being polyamorous, if you choose to do so.
That's about all I can think of, in terms of positives. Everything else....where to start.
-What's with the story? I'd accuse it of copying Fo3, but... At least, in Fo3, the father had interesting motivations and was working on harnessing fascinating technologies that would affect the entire wasteland. Here, it's essentially a cutscene that says "here's this person you love that's now dead, here's this other person you love that's now kidnapped, fond slap on the bum, go get 'em tiger".
-The usefulness of ALL items seems great on paper, but it absolutely tanks the pacing, as you inevitably end up spending hours ferrying around endless amounts of trash.
-The game doesn't explain ANYTHING. Which, I wouldn't be an issue, except for how there's a bunch of things implemented in odd ways. For example, there are been functions I learned about only after being told about them by friends. Functions like getting out of your power armor without waiting for the battery to fully drain.
-The traits menu is pretty, but inefficient at communicating information. I prefer the older text interface.
-The PC port is straight-up horrid. Why does leaving the framerate unlocked ♥♥♥♥ with the physics and game speed? Why do are certain functions perma-bound to certain keys? Why does the melee attack and grenade have to share a button? Why are some functions using multiple buttons, but are not usable interchanably? Why are the loading times absolutely abysmal? Why does the game feel like it hasn't been even remotely optimized?
-The AI....oh, man. NPCs taking cover seems great...except, they always leave a large portion of their body exposed. Also, companions are often worse than useless. The number of times my super sneaky character was discovered because a companion would refuse to get out of the open, or would pull everyone by charging into combat as I'm trying to sneak away, or would block my path of escape from a grenade at my feet...AGH.
-One would think that converting a classically silent protagonist into a voiced one would have entailed doing a quality job...apparently not.
-Whatever happened to the whole "role playing" aspect of Fallout? Remember how in the older Fallout games, you could be Sir Benevolent the 3rd or Lord Mc♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the 5th? Here, we'll have none of that lip. You're a good guy locked into the role of being a good guy, fighting for whatever has been pre-determined as being the "good guys". About the most evil thing you can possibly do is request more caps from the NPCs as quest reward....and, even then there are absolutely no consequences, so you have no reason to not do it.
-The conversation system is atrocious. Not only do you have less agency in your decisions than you have in a TellTale game, the game steps on the same rake as Heavy Rain by having one word, vague descriptions that are generally very misleading to what your character actually will say. I suppose, at least, this...thing saved Bethesda a ton of cash (by limiting the dialogue options) after they made the incredibly misguided decision to voice act everything.
-I understand that the karma system from before had its issues, but... The replacement is an utterly useless irritation.
-The settlement interface was built for three-handed mutants. Not only that, Good luck with getting things to line up nicely or not float in mid-air. Also, terrain detection seems to work sparingly, at best (e.g. I've tried planting a melon on a surface, where sometimes the same patch of ground will show that you can, but sometimes, can't plant it).
-The bugs, oh the bugs. I know that the community is going to help out with most of this, but... I think it's an abhorrent practice to have a AAA publisher release a full price title and then outsource the QA to the community. Here are some of my favorite examples:
~Picking a lock, hacking a terminal, checking your PipBoy, or switching weapons has a chance to make it go invisible, leaving you stuck.
~Taking back power armor that was stolen from you leaves it marked as stolen.
~If you die during dialogue, the subtitles will remain on screen and the clip that played during your character's death will continue to play at random intervals.
~Some walls are only solid and present to you. The number of times I've been shot by bandits through a solid brick wall...ugh.
~Floodlights tend to regularly break, nuking the framerate and leaving a massive white void.

So after 100 hours of playing I think I have a clear picture of what I think of this game.
As someone who has spent more than 2000 hours on this franchise I would say that this is a good contender to the fallout series. Not the best but not the worst either.
The story is alright. Don't get me wrong, I throughly enjoyed it while it lasted but there were a few moments which seemed like easy ways out of explaining things. The story will be the same for everyone in the start but after a while you will have to join a faction which has it's own story path and ways to end the game. Each faction has their own ideology which I enjoyed learning more about.
The characters you meet have good voice acting and interesting backstories. Bethesda did a great job on that. The only thing I disliked is when you talk to anyone, your choices what to say are severely limited compared to the vast variety of choices in the previous game, Fallout New vegas.
In that game you could have 9 choices what to say while in this game it's only 4. Due to this you can either way be really mean, really nice or completely natural. Nothing in between which was a let down.
The character building in this game was kinda dissapointing. Sure there were lots of perks to upgrade and it was easy to navigate the perk system but  to actually play the game and enjoy most aspects of it, most of your points will be put into modding perks. You will put around 15 points to upgrade perks so you can even mod weapons to be better which is kinda vital to even survive.You can get all perks if you really put time in it but at that point the story will already be long over and there will be almost no fun new places to explore and use your new abilities.
The map size and content in it has been improved compared to the previous games. The wasteland is vastly colourful, but not enough to drown the dark tone of  it.You will discover something new almost every time you take a step outside in the wasteland. You will have something to do all the time, either it being you trying to build new settlements, to a simple mission where you are supposed to find a cat.
The only real thing I disliked while on the map and it's content is the vaults not being a major part anymore. In the previous games there were multiple vaults, each having their own interesting dark backstory. In this game there are like what? 5 vaults? 1 where you start which spoils the surprise and 4 others, one whom is fully functioning with people in it which completely depletes any fun chance of exploration.
The customization was actually fun. I spent a lot of hours building new settlements and gathering new supplies only to build them. It's a bit buggy but nothing that will ruin your life.
The weapon customization was also fun and finding legendary weapons was a joy however I wish that bethesda still would have put more "one of a kind" weapons like the alien blaster.
As final words I would like to say: This is a game good for newcommers to the Fallout franchise.
It's easy to play and you can have great fun exploring the vast world of the commonwealth. I say "good for newcommers to the Fallout franchise" because of how the previous titles don't look as good and because of how more complex they are. If you enjoy this game then i'm sure you will enjoy all other 5 games.
My recommendation to play after this game if you are new, is Fallout:3, then Fallout:New vegas, Then Fallout 1, Fallout 2 and finally if you really want to(even though I personally don't like it) play Fallout: Tactics.

I just finished the main story and I'm kind of disappointed.
It's a good game and all, but you're forced to wait for mods to fully experience all its potential, and I don't think it's fair at all that the community must work to take care of basic things Bethesda was supposed to work on before releasing the game.
After you're done with the main quest line, you're left with little if not nothing to do. The main quest's end is very anticlimactic, too. You would expect there would be something more after it, or that your "position" in the Commonwealth would change, but no.
It's also very disappointing to see a game so unpolished. Characters often move around hovering over the ground without moving their legs. If you talk with someone, expect the camera to go into their body or point who knows where.
Graphics is not so important, but it's really a shame that so many elements in the world look like they came out from a '90s 3D game. At full quality you still get very bad textures on some elements.
This "settlement building" thing is cool, but nothing more. When you really start using it you find out it's got huge limits, countless bugs, extremely weird and unnatural controls, and no documentation, that makes it frustrating to use. It's supposed to give space to your creativity and give you freedom of building things around, but instead it frustrates you most of the times.
I wouldn't recommend this game in the state it is right now, maybe in the future they'll patch it.

Here, it's essentially a cutscene that says "here's this person you love that's now dead, here's this other person you love that's now kidnapped, fond slap on the bum, go get 'em tiger".
-The usefulness of ALL items seems great on paper, but it absolutely tanks the pacing, as you inevitably end up spending hours ferrying around endless amounts of trash.
-The game doesn't explain ANYTHING. Which, I wouldn't be an issue, except for how there's a bunch of things implemented in odd ways. For example, there are been functions I learned about only after being told about them by friends. Functions like getting out of your power armor without waiting for the battery to fully drain.
-The traits menu is pretty, but inefficient at communicating information. I prefer the older text interface.
-The PC port is straight-up horrid. Why does leaving the framerate unlocked ♥♥♥♥ with the physics and game speed? Why do are certain functions perma-bound to certain keys? Why does the melee attack and grenade have to share a button? Why are some functions using multiple buttons, but are not usable interchanably? Why are the loading times absolutely abysmal? Why does the game feel like it hasn't been even remotely optimized?
-The AI....oh, man. NPCs taking cover seems great...except, they always leave a large portion of their body exposed. Also, companions are often worse than useless. The number of times my super sneaky character was discovered because a companion would refuse to get out of the open, or would pull everyone by charging into combat as I'm trying to sneak away, or would block my path of escape from a grenade at my feet...AGH.
-One would think that converting a classically silent protagonist into a voiced one would have entailed doing a quality job...apparently not.
-Whatever happened to the whole "role playing" aspect of Fallout? Remember how in the older Fallout games, you could be Sir Benevolent the 3rd or Lord Mc♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the 5th? Here, we'll have none of that lip. You're a good guy locked into the role of being a good guy, fighting for whatever has been pre-determined as being the "good guys". About the most evil thing you can possibly do is request more caps from the NPCs as quest reward....and, even then there are absolutely no consequences, so you have no reason to not do it.
-The conversation system is atrocious. Not only do you have less agency in your decisions than you have in a TellTale game, the game steps on the same rake as Heavy Rain by having one word, vague descriptions that are generally very misleading to what your character actually will say. I suppose, at least, this...thing saved Bethesda a ton of cash (by limiting the dialogue options) after they made the incredibly misguided decision to voice act everything.
-I understand that the karma system from before had its issues, but... The replacement is an utterly useless irritation.
-The settlement interface was built for three-handed mutants. Not only that, Good luck with getting things to line up nicely or not float in mid-air. Also, terrain detection seems to work sparingly, at best (e.g. I've tried planting a melon on a surface, where sometimes the same patch of ground will show that you can, but sometimes, can't plant it).
-The bugs, oh the bugs. I know that the community is going to help out with most of this, but... I think it's an abhorrent practice to have a AAA publisher release a full price title and then outsource the QA to the community. Here are some of my favorite examples:
~Picking a lock, hacking a terminal, checking your PipBoy, or switching weapons has a chance to make it go invisible, leaving you stuck.
~Taking back power armor that was stolen from you leaves it marked as stolen.
~If you die during dialogue, the subtitles will remain on screen and the clip that played during your character's death will continue to play at random intervals.
~Some walls are only solid and present to you. The number of times I've been shot by bandits through a solid brick wall...ugh.
~Floodlights tend to regularly break, nuking the framerate and leaving a massive white void.

So after 100 hours of playing I think I have a clear picture of what I think of this game.
As someone who has spent more than 2000 hours on this franchise I would say that this is a good contender to the fallout series. Not the best but not the worst either.
The story is alright. Don't get me wrong, I throughly enjoyed it while it lasted but there were a few moments which seemed like easy ways out of explaining things. The story will be the same for everyone in the start but after a while you will have to join a faction which has it's own story path and ways to end the game. Each faction has their own ideology which I enjoyed learning more about.
The characters you meet have good voice acting and interesting backstories. Bethesda did a great job on that. The only thing I disliked is when you talk to anyone, your choices what to say are severely limited compared to the vast variety of choices in the previous game, Fallout New vegas.
In that game you could have 9 choices what to say while in this game it's only 4. Due to this you can either way be really mean, really nice or completely natural. Nothing in between which was a let down.
The character building in this game was kinda dissapointing. Sure there were lots of perks to upgrade and it was easy to navigate the perk system but  to actually play the game and enjoy most aspects of it, most of your points will be put into modding perks. You will put around 15 points to upgrade perks so you can even mod weapons to be better which is kinda vital to even survive.You can get all perks if you really put time in it but at that point the story will already be long over and there will be almost no fun new places to explore and use your new abilities.
The map size and content in it has been improved compared to the previous games. The wasteland is vastly colourful, but not enough to drown the dark tone of  it.You will discover something new almost every time you take a step outside in the wasteland. You will have something to do all the time, either it being you trying to build new settlements, to a simple mission where you are supposed to find a cat.
The only real thing I disliked while on the map and it's content is the vaults not being a major part anymore. In the previous games there were multiple vaults, each having their own interesting dark backstory. In this game there are like what? 5 vaults? 1 where you start which spoils the surprise and 4 others, one whom is fully functioning with people in it which completely depletes any fun chance of exploration.
The customization was actually fun. I spent a lot of hours building new settlements and gathering new supplies only to build them. It's a bit buggy but nothing that will ruin your life.
The weapon customization was also fun and finding legendary weapons was a joy however I wish that bethesda still would have put more "one of a kind" weapons like the alien blaster.
As final words I would like to say: This is a game good for newcommers to the Fallout franchise.
It's easy to play and you can have great fun exploring the vast world of the commonwealth. I say "good for newcommers to the Fallout franchise" because of how the previous titles don't look as good and because of how more complex they are. If you enjoy this game then i'm sure you will enjoy all other 5 games.
My recommendation to play after this game if you are new, is Fallout:3, then Fallout:New vegas, Then Fallout 1, Fallout 2 and finally if you really want to(even though I personally don't like it) play Fallout: Tactics.
Also I would just like to say that I won the race to 100 hours Plank you salty scrublord. Git dunked on.

No time to read: Fallout 3 in shooter form, but in a wonderful twist actually has the best main storyline(s) and ending(s) in the entire Fallout series.
Let's get this out of the way; a lot of what the other reviews say are right:
- The shooting and combat is better
- The world is HUGE (150 hours in and I haven't seen everything, hell I've completely missed 2 companions)
- The skill/perk system has been streamlined (i.e. 'dumbed down') but still significantly affects how you fight and talk
- The dialogue system is dumbed down and can be downright annoying when an NPC is supposed to handle multiple quests
- The Pipboy inventory system sucks harder than a galactic core black hole.
- The settlement building system can be engrossing but is janky as all hell and is poorly explained.
- It plays a lot like a Bethesda game (glitches, loading screens, robot-like NPCs) but makes up for it with scale and (mostly) improved voice acting.
Now that's out of the way, I want to talk about the story. Fallout 4 has THE best storyline(s) in ALL of the Fallout games. It also has the best 'moral' choice in any video game story I have seen so far, where your relationship with the factions are not dictated by some artificial meter, but by the actions and choices you make in the story. And even in its stilted and robotic way, it has the best portrayal of betrayal in any video game I have seen.

The story starts out slow in Sanctuary, and I must have spent 15 or so hours just exploring and setting up settlements. I started getting bored as I went on the nth mission to help a settlement and finally decided to go to Diamond City. Some more direction during this part of the game, or even just a loot trail to get to Diamond City faster would have probably helped.
The story really gets good once you get to the Institute, the bogeyman of the Commonwealth. As I was descending in the elevator I was expecting a Big MT, full of crazed amoral scientists plotting to take over the world. I got my first surprise when the elevator shaft turned from concrete to glass and what I saw wasn't a dirty industrial lab filled with tesla coils and various animals suspended in transparent tanks, but a scene right out of Star Trek: clean glass and plastic corridors, with normal-looking scientists, technicians and synths going about their business.
At that point I thought to myself, "Oh, so this is like Bioshock Infinite, where the scientist class is able to live in luxury by keeping the synths in slavery and it is my task to expose the system's evil." I cocked my trusty assault rifle and prepared to bust out of this fake utopia with my son Shaun. Then I'm hit with my second surprise: my son Shaun is no longer a child but a 60 year old man, and is in charge of the Institute at that. He welcomes me to the Institute with open arms and even gives me a device to get in and out of the Institute at will.
I immediately called bull**** on that and thought that the Institute was actually all run by the Synths, with some nefarious AI master computer controlling everything from behind the scenes plotting to kill all the humans. But as I explored the Institute and did their quests, I was slowly hit with my third surprise: that the Institute was actually what they said they were. They actually WERE scientists working to save humanity, and their one failing was that they treat synths as machines. And even that was not absolute. From a synth that has completely integrated with her human family to a scientist expressing ethical qualms about creating a child synth that cannot grow up, you get conviced that the Institute is not evil at all, but just another group of people doing what they think is best for all.
And this is when the choices get harder. Because the quests lead up to a point where you have to pick which side to support, and usually the first mission on that path is to go to a faction's HQ and murder all their leaders. In doing so, you usually end up killing EVERYONE in that Faction's HQ. These are not just background NPCs, but quest givers and vendors that you have interacted with for several hours, have their own recognizable personalities and sometimes even a fleshed out backstory. I DIDN'T want to kill these people and actually went out of my way to avoid killing them with my own hands when I invaded their HQ. Though Scribe Haylen may have died in the Prydwen crash, I was at least relieved that I didn't have to shoot her in the head myself.
That is so rare in video games. So often it's just 'kill the bad guys to save the good guys'. Fallout 4 shows so well that in the Wasteland, it's hard to tell who's good and who's bad, good guys die all the time, and sometimes, they die by your hand.
Only a damn Synth wouldn't buy this game... 11/10 would bang.

Fallout 4 is a good game, but it isn't without it's problems.
The Skyrim engine shows it's age. Fallout 4 is not "next gen" by any means. The game is riddled with performance issues and other glitches, while other games that came out this year, like The Witcher 3 and Metal Gear Solid 5, manage to both look AND perform better than Fallout 4, even though graphics and performance is almost always an "either or" scenario.
The game is heavily "streamlined" but this is simply the removal of several key systems from previous Fallout and Elder Scrolls games. There are no skills. The dialog system is ruined. Every conversation now has the same four responses: be nice, be mean, be sarcastic, and ask for information. When you level up, you just take a perk. Again, there are NO SKILLS.
On the flipside of these problems, there are several things the game does right. Looting is now much easier, since you can loot bodies and containers just by looking at them without opening a menu (but this option is still there). Junk items now have purpose, as everything can be used in crafting, either to upgrade weapons and armor or build your base. The weapon and base customization is very extensive and it's very easy to sink hours into building a house. Power Armor is now modular, letting you mix and match suit parts and upgrade them with unique mods.
Despite all of it's problems, there is still a ton of fun to be had with Fallout 4, and I enjoyed my 50 hour playthrough of the game. Hopefully mods will fix most of the game's problems in good time, but if Bethesda waited until next year to release the game, it would be better. It's very evident that Bethesda rushed this title out in an attempt to win a few Game of the Year awards.
I give the game a 7/10 in it's current state.

This is a no spoiler review. So far I have played about 48 hours and really enjoyed this game. It has a lot of elements that have made this series succesful and has made them even better. I have not read any cheats, spoilers, or guides. I have just played this game and have been having a blast. There is so much to do, so much to find, and so many wacky and funny situations.
I have had only a few problems with glithces and have yet to have the game crash. I am able to run high settings with good frame rates with an i5 4670 and a GTX 770 2GB card on the new Windows 10 platform. I think if I had a 4GB card id be able to push the settings much more agressively. As is, it looks good enough for me. I worried needlessly that I would need a 4B card but at 1080p it hasn't been needed. I don't require "ultra" settings, find that the difference is marginal at best in most games and only serves to hog system resources. IF you have a decent 2GB card and an i5 you are good to go. I haven't tested performance on my AMD system yet. I expect that it will run it at medium with lower end settings since it is a of an bit older system.
I really like what they have done to the character building in this game. Perks feel like they mean something, especially at lower levels, which is something that was absent from FO3 and FNV. Decent game, overall, but it completely ♥♥♥♥♥ on anything that the previous fallout games have established. Any RPG elements that characterized the previous games have been torn out and replaced with Shooty-Shooty Bang-Bang mechanics that, while excellent, fail to implement many of the RPG mechanics that Fallout was built on.
Skills are gone, and have been replaced with an emphasized S.P.E.C.I.A.L. system and perk progression. In some ways, I can appreciate the perk system. It feels like a more modern iteration of the core ideas that underlie the skills system. And yet, most of these perks don't feel particularly impactful. Everyone I've talked to who has played this game has followed a near identical character progression, regardless of their special choices. They always go for perks like Gun Nut, Medic, Action Aficionado, and several other perks.
The narrative is SOMEWHAT decent, at least until just about the half-way point. At that point, there are a few paths to choose in terms of what faction you side with. The issue,
, Is that your choice means ♥♥♥♥all. The questlines all follow the same basic outline, destroying the other factions in an almost identical manner. Even the traditional Fallout ending has been completely trashed in exchange for an end-game cutscene that doesn't change based on your actions, except for perhaps a small clip at the beginning that lasts for mere seconds. Choices that managed to FEEL meaningful, even if they aren't in the context of effects in the game world, are gone.
I can't help but feel that the dialogue has been the source of at least SOME of these narrative issues. The game ought to make you at least FEEL you have choice, rather than limiting you to four extremely vauge dialogue options. The traditional Fallout dialogue system succeeded in giving the player more feedback on what their character was going to say, and how they we're going to say it. Because it wasn't limited to four options, there was a lot more room for different dialogue paths to take place. The four-option system fails, to a STUNNING degree, to make the player feel like they're actively engaging in the conversation. When it's time to make a choice, it comes down to Yes/No, "What's the task/More info," or Sarcastic, or something along those lines. Occasionally, you get the option to make a charisma check, which is great and adds at least some degree of depth to dialogue (Even if they only ever give more money or a little bit of extra backstory to a character).
Despite my issues with the game, it's not inherently a bad game. It's got solid gameplay, successfully captures the feeling of the Fallout world, and has a bunch of mechanics that really add a lot to the enjoyment of the game.
In terms of it being a great Fallout RPG game, not really. It's a huge deviation from the Fallout formula, one which I personally didn't particularly like. It's more akin to a Far Cry-esque romp through the Fallout world. That's actually a remarkably accurate reflection of my thoughts on the game.

I've put in over 100 hours in this game, 10x that in skyrim (Bethseda said it was learning from it's successes and failures), and 1/4 of fallout 3.
I clarified this for a very important reason - this game is clearly closer to SKYRIM in scope, atmosphere, and it's focus of mindless exploration and combat with little regard to the story.  In fact, I'd go so far as to say skipping the story will actually ADD to your enjoyment of the game, like Skyrim.  If you're looking for a spiritual successor to Fallout 3 - this is not it.
That being said, I'm almost done and I'm enjoying this game immensely.  The simplfied perk chart that everyone is complaining about, while it strips you of all individualization in what should be a RPG, is a well thought out system that gives you tons of replayability.  Add to that the fact that there's no level cap, and your COMBAT strategies in a playthrough can be very individualized.  Unfortunately, your personality and individual choices are quite the opposite.  Everyone has covered how theres no real choices in conversation, and even more boring if you're not high in charisma, so I won't go into detail with that.  I will add that there is only ONE voice each for each sex, no matter what race, build, or personality u may have.  If you build a 300 pound african american lumberjack cracking jokes with a smile and an axe, he'll have the same voice as a boring as nails nerdy white guy who is nearly anemic from being in an office all his life (both of which I wanted to try btw lol).
The storyline, itself, is EXCELLENT.  The best way I can think to put the problem here is that even when you're contributing heavily to the story, you never seem to leave your mark.  Without you, the story is very well told, voice acted, and planned out.  You're the one messin things up haha.  The companions you can come across in your travels also have good backstories and voice acting (for the most part), and are LOADS better than the ones in skyrim.  Inventory system is a lot cleaner, bugs are already less of a problem than the finished product of Skyrim (but yea, there are bugs) .  That being said, the devs are doing their best to fix everything, as evidenced best by TWO day one patches, and unfortuantely introudcing a visual problem thats been bugging me since pre-patch - apparently someone complained about the visuals to the point where day two changed all NEW characters to a world of mostly sunshine, vbrant colors, and almost no trace of nuclear fallout, whereas the original version was the exact opposite (and looked good that way too I thought).
So to sum up my conflicted thoughts, amazing game, amazing exploration, amazing combat, awful RPG.  Will be an even better game when the game can fully take advantage of the modding tools scheduled for next year.

52 hours in.
Pros:
- atmosphere
- ambient sounds and stock music (not the Radio)
- post apocalyptic setting
- gun customization and modding
- very good sandbox
- quicksave during conversations
- very good gunplay
Cons:
- uninteresting and boring story (no effort done by the game to make me care)
- repetitive quests (kill/fetch/save) without even trying to cover it up with some lore/story fodder
- forced settlement building mechanic
- non-rebindable keys
- no FOV slider
- capped FPS
- .ini files editing almost mandatory for PC players
- lack luster settings
- huge gun models
- power armor is not special anymore
- no Karma system
- no real decisions (basically only Yes/Yes (sarcastic)/No (eventually Yes, 'cause you can't progress without agreeing)/more info)
- annoying main character (at least male version, haven't played the female)
- voiced protagonist
- boring side quests
- glitches (getting frequently stuck after hacking, gun disappearing in 1st person view, regular OOB issues)
- brain-dead companions (thank gods for the Lone Wanderer Perk, Bethesda's trademark stand-in-doorways mechanic is still present, just without the FusRoDah fix)
- Perk system based solely on SPECIALs, no Skills
- long and very frequent loading screens (cannot imagine playing without SSD)
- frustrating console-oriented UI (constant Reloading/Looting issues)
- simplistic and botched dialogues
- PipBoy-oriented everything (almost unusable Map, frustrating inventory)
- no way to know where to put SPECIALs in the beginning, since you can't check the Perk tree
- Survival difficulty no longer special
- VATS is now almost completely useless
TL;DR:
Dumbed down, overhyped, boring and repetitive post-apo sandbox, which is not optimized for the PC. Really not worth the full price of a AAA game. Wait for at least 50% discount, preferably 75% or more.

This is a no spoiler review. So far I have played about 48 hours and really enjoyed this game. It has a lot of elements that have made this series succesful and has made them even better. I have not read any cheats, spoilers, or guides. I have just played this game and have been having a blast. There is so much to do, so much to find, and so many wacky and funny situations.
I have had only a few problems with glithces and have yet to have the game crash. I am able to run high settings with good frame rates with an i5 4670 and a GTX 770 2GB card on the new Windows 10 platform. I think if I had a 4GB card id be able to push the settings much more agressively. As is, it looks good enough for me. I worried needlessly that I would need a 4B card but at 1080p it hasn't been needed. I don't require "ultra" settings, find that the difference is marginal at best in most games and only serves to hog system resources. IF you have a decent 2GB card and an i5 you are good to go. I haven't tested performance on my AMD system yet. I expect that it will run it at medium with lower end settings since it is a of an bit older system.
I really like what they have done to the character building in this game. Perks feel like they mean something, especially at lower levels, which is something that was absent from FO3 and FNV. Companion AI is improved, however I still don't like em. I think this game is more difficult than previous FO series and the early levels can be punishing until you figure out what is going on. There are a LOT of map locations to explore, action is never far away, and I have found that the map respawns much faster in this game. Good things because it keeps things interesting. It is fun to run into a 3 way battle that is already going on between 3 factions.... you can help out your allied faction if they are involved or just wipe all of them out. Sometimes I sit back and watch the fireworks.
IF you like the FO series, this one won't disappoint. This one is not hype that failed to live up to expectations. This one actually surpassed my expectations. I am sure that as expansion content rolls out this game is only going to get even better. Thank you Bethesda! I hope you continue to put out such high quality products.

The narrative is SOMEWHAT decent, at least until just about the half-way point. At that point, there are a few paths to choose in terms of what faction you side with. The issue,
, Is that your choice means ♥♥♥♥all. The questlines all follow the same basic outline, destroying the other factions in an almost identical manner. Even the traditional Fallout ending has been completely trashed in exchange for an end-game cutscene that doesn't change based on your actions, except for perhaps a small clip at the beginning that lasts for mere seconds. Choices that managed to FEEL meaningful, even if they aren't in the context of effects in the game world, are gone.
I can't help but feel that the dialogue has been the source of at least SOME of these narrative issues. The game ought to make you at least FEEL you have choice, rather than limiting you to four extremely vauge dialogue options. The traditional Fallout dialogue system succeeded in giving the player more feedback on what their character was going to say, and how they we're going to say it. Because it wasn't limited to four options, there was a lot more room for different dialogue paths to take place. The four-option system fails, to a STUNNING degree, to make the player feel like they're actively engaging in the conversation. When it's time to make a choice, it comes down to Yes/No, "What's the task/More info," or Sarcastic, or something along those lines. Occasionally, you get the option to make a charisma check, which is great and adds at least some degree of depth to dialogue (Even if they only ever give more money or a little bit of extra backstory to a character).
Despite my issues with the game, it's not inherently a bad game. It's got solid gameplay, successfully captures the feeling of the Fallout world, and has a bunch of mechanics that really add a lot to the enjoyment of the game.
In terms of it being a great Fallout RPG game, not really. It's a huge deviation from the Fallout formula, one which I personally didn't particularly like. It's more akin to a Far Cry-esque romp through the Fallout world. That's actually a remarkably accurate reflection of my thoughts on the game.

Edit - Dec 4 2015 - Wow this blew up, didn't expect 1000+ ratings. Thanks to everybody who rated it helpful or not and thanks to everybody for commenting. I'll respond to any comments posted here or my profile. I also changed my final score of the game in order to clear up some confusion.
Ok, now that I've got 100 hours exactly on this game, I'm going to do an updated thoughts list. This isn't a full review, just a list of observations.
Pros
- The game is really pretty. Compared to the other two 3D Fallout games, it's quite colorful.
- The FPS part of the game is greatly, greatly improved. The guns feel like they have power. The explosives actually work. Melee feels like Skyrim.
- The story is interesting. Certainly not the best, but it had a few twists and turns I didn't see coming.
- Power armor is quite cool. I think they did this really well. It's more like a vehicle that needs fuel and maintenance unlike the last games where it was just an outfit.
- Crafting. You can create many things including mods for your weapons, armor and power armor. You can also craft medicines and drugs.
- All the clutter is useful. Pick up all the junk.
- I loved the updated looks of the various wasteland creatures. Mirelurks, Super mutants, deathclaws etc.
- Common low level enemies pose a threat. Even the lowly bloatfly can have a legendary mutation and will do a lot of damage.
- Generally less buggy. I've only had a few annoying bugs. Less than I imagined for a game of this size and complexity.
- Mods. Bethesda games have always been very moddable and this one is no different.
- Armor layer system. It's pretty cool to have a base outfit, then a piece of armor for every part of the body. However, by about 60 hours playtime I'd already had gotten the best armors and haven't found an upgrade since.
Neutrals
- It runs really well...when you aren't in the city. I get a solid 60fps outside of the city but once I venture in it drops to 30 or less. I've seen a mod that might help with that but I have yet to use it. Also, zooming in with a scope drops my fps as well.
- Voice acting is surprisingly good so most characters. A few feel like they have zero personality while others genuinely feel alive.
- Exploration. There is lots to see and lots to find. You'll be wandering through lots of underground tunnels and ruined buildings. It all starts feeling same-y after a while.
- This game doesn't feel like a true successor to Fallout 3 and NV. It just doesn't have the feeling of a true Fallout game. It feels like a Fallout-themed FPS. What it does, it does well. But I think it's focused to much on the FPS and not enough on the RPG. Todd Howard said it was an RPG with FPS elements but to me it feels like the opposite, an FPS with light RPG elements.
- Removal of skills and casualization. In NV, there were plenty of times where I could use my medicine skill to fix (or kill) a person, use my repair skill to fix machinery or even use my skill level to pass a speech check. None of this is possible in F4, and none of that depth is there. The world feels much less alive.
- Voiced Protagonist. This is the big one for me. I feel as though the game was built around the protagonist having a voice. Because they needed to record so many voice lines, they sacrificed features of the game, mainly skills. If they still had skills, they'd have had to record so much more dialogue for speech checks. Voiced protagonist also limits the amount of variation the story can have, again because that would involve more recording. See where I'm going with this?
- The storyline operates similarly to Mass Effect. You can't be a truly evil ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like in the previous two games, but you can be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ along the way. You will always be a hero.
- Settlement building. I would have put this under pros but it just lacks depth. It's neat but it brings a bunch of hassles. Your settlements need stuff to thrive. They are often being attacked or have some issue. I wanted to build an amazing base, not babysit 50 settlements.
- Removal of the karma system. Sometimes, it was good being bad. In 3 and NV, being good or bad had it's pros and cons. With this game there is no such thing and thus a layer of depth is removed from the game. The closest thing is that your companions may like or dislike certain actions.
- Removal of weapon and armor maintenance. Some people like it. I don't. It removes a layer of depth to the gameplay and makes all those guns and armor you find useless.
- Caps (money) is less useful in this game. You'll find all you need on your adventures, especially if you have the loot perks from the Luck tree. I had over a 1000 .50 sniper rounds before I ever found a .50 rifle for instance. There are a few nice items in shops but they aren't needed.
- Lockpicking is copied from Skyrim. While I'd like to have seen something new, at least I already know how to work this minigame. I've always thought that Oblivion had the best lockpicking system.
- Computer hacking is the same as 3 and NV. I never learned how to properly do it. I just guess words over and over until I get through. At least in this game, you can't be totally locked out.
Cons
- The game is a blatant console port.
- Crappy, controller designed UI. Since there are only 4 options in dialogue, this limits interactions options and removes depth.
- Story spoiler: After the end of the story, you can't lead whatever faction you sided with. They just...exist and call you the leader. They stop advancing their goals.
- After the story, you are just given repetitive settlement babysitting quests. I've stopped caring.
- Little replayability. Because of the lack of depth there aren't many roads to go down and the destinations are all the same.
- Less weapon variety than NV. By about 70 hours I had found all the base varieties of guns and had most of them modded the way I wanted. Haven't picked up a weapon since.
- Non-story quests are just go here, talk to person. Maybe shoot them. There have been a few interesting encounters but it all feels like busywork. This game is actually worse than Skyrim about this since there aren't many different ways to do it because all the depth has been removed.
- Power Armor doesn't work as expected. I expected it to absorb damage, then break. Once a piece breaks, you start taking damage to that area. However how it actually works is just another layer of armor. If you take damage, then you just take less damage, the armor doesn't absorb it all till it runs out of hp.
- But this biggest gripe I have is...
Lack.
Of.
DEPTH!!!!
Seriously, they took 70% of what makes a Fallout game Fallout and threw it away in favor of casualization (to appeal to a bigger audience and thus increase sales) and more SHOOTY ACTION. As a shooter, this game is really good. As a Fallout game, it falls flat on it's face.
My final score: 6.5/10. Fun combat, decent gear and character customization, lots of exploring and collecting. Settlement building. Lack of depth as expected from a Fallout title is the biggest flaw.

The reasons I would recommend this game are for many of the reasons the negative reviewers argue against it.
1 The leveling system is far better in its new form.  Bethesda replaced the skill system were you increased skills to reach a hidden threshold value that would increase ability in a given area.  Instead you now chose a rank in the available abilities, achieving the same goal in a much more transparent way. Mix this with the fact that all of the special stats are useful and you receive fewer points at the beginning of the game, character builds are more important in fo4 than ever. Now can the system be broken? Yes but the old system could be broken just as easily if not more so by min maxing the useful stats.
2 The useless karma system is gone. I've seen so many complaints that the system is gone but it never really did anything but limit what companions would follow you.  It has been replaced by a relationship system with your companions who will react to your actions, building a relationship and letting you in on their back story, taking you on quests and eventually providing unique perks.
3 The Wasteland is as fantastic as ever.  Bethesda has a knack for environmental story telling and it shines in fo4.  Where other games rely on side quests to relay extra story bits Bethesda uses strategically placed terminals and sets to tell stories from before the war and after. It is up to the player to explore, find all the details and then tell the story of what happened.
4. It's different from fo3 and nv.  Many of the complaints I've read are that a player can not be evil. Meaning what? That I can't nuke megaton and join the slavers again. I like that their are 4 factions each having legitimate reasons for their actions and its up to the player to choose their faction and "role play" why they chose said faction and their intentions for amassing so much power.
5 though I agree in some regards the dialog system is not as deep as nv, it is deeper than fo3 imo. I do think the voice acting itself is great and the voiced protagonist is well executed and helped me to role play a woman character which I have avoided in the past.  I liked it and felt that it served its purpose with the style that Bethesda intended it to.
6 The combat in this game is fun and fun and smooth. In fo3 and nv combat was a chore. In fo4 wether using vats or not the combat just works. Partner the improved combat with a focused character build and the new system is incredibly fun and rewarding.
I have been a big fallout fan since the mid 90s and I have truly enjoyed this latest entry to the series.
