It's like Skyrim with guns... literally.
Here's a post-DLC support review:
Disclaimer: I am playing a devil's advocate for Bethesda. Like it or not, I played a lot of Fallout 4 and will continue playing it once I get a better computer because my Alienware is so outdated it can only just barely run this game. I believe that Fallout 4 wasn't a bad game. It's the current Black Sheep of the Fallout Games. If you feel "offended" deal with it. Bethesda ♥♥♥♥ed up, sure, but the community response, both before and after Fallout 4's release with the PS4 mods controversy are things I don't care about. Now onto the review.
I have played Fallout 4 the most out of the Fallout Games I own. Here's my personal gripe with people hating on the game: They literally went in to the Hype. For Bethesda, this was one of the hugest problems with Fallout 4, people expected so much. Too much. What they should've done considering the game was "mostly done" was either release it over the summer or released it when it actually had "Gone Gold" (translations done, game done, some bugs fixed, etc.) but the bugs have been 99% ironed out (I get as many Infinite Loading Screens as I did in New Vegas, which wasn't many, but I've played much more Fallout 4 than New Vegas, so results may vary).
Now the problems with Fallout 4:
-Immersion: Yeah, there wasn't much of it, that's a valuable tool for keeping fans intrested. When I played through New Vegas, I would fail a quest every quest I completed. "We want Mr. House's life preserving technology.", I want to beat him over the head with this golf club and I did, it was worth it. But the problems with some facotrs such as immersion is that too much overwhelms casual players and too little alienates the hardcore players, you'd need an equal amount of immersion to not overwhelm those casual players, and enough immersion to keep your hardcore fanbase happy, it's pretty hard to please both sides without hurting one side even a smidge.
-Dialogue: It could go one way most of the time. Even in some of the DLC's, there would be DLC that ended off with the same statement.
-Voiced Protagonist: Not a huge issue. In about 1-3 years from now, my guess is that people will replace Nate and Nora's dialogue with a text-to-speech program or their own voice. If you do that last one, do a good job. If you use something like Audacity, add a small delay so that if your mouse picks up your mouse clicks or anything keyboard taps, you can just edit the file and there goes that background noise. It's not a huge gripe, but it's one that had some effect on the Fallout Fans. In the future, don't have somebody spend 2 years voices your male and female, even if they're good. I didn't mind in Skyrim when I talked and didn't hear myself, or in Fallout 3, or New Vegas, so I don't think this was necessary, still cool.
-The Dialogue Wheel: Pretty self-explanatory, don't cross the ip's.
-The AI still sucks: Yeah, no comment there.
-The Engine: The Creation Engine is an upgraded Skyrim Engine. You had basically 4 years since Skyrim came out, surely a new engine would've been a good idea. Bethesda, it is with my opinion that before ESO 6 comes to see the light of day, that you should make a new engine, from scrach, or reworked, but upgrade it, by 2020, I'm expecting that games will look like Uncharted 4 at the least, or a little worse than Uncharted 4. After all, if your engine works as well as a car with no wheels, then why use it?
And now my nit picks:
-Named Enemies in Enemy Factions: This was my own gripe. The only person who is a Raider Boss that even bothered to talk to me, was Slag. Only. Slag. I think it would've been intresting to have a dialogue with Red Tourette or Tower Tom and then asking for Food or finding their sister, but then again, they're raiders. And what about the Gunners? Captin Wes would probably like to have Mr./Mrs. Main Character Power on his side.
-Codsworth: Out of the 1k names Codsworth says, he doesn't say a whole bunch that aren't some swear or pop-culture reference. And it's only Codsworth that knows your name. Not Preston, Nick, just Codsworth. Which is both understandable, but considering it sounds like you're giving your life story out, don't you think somebody would be like "Oh, hey, what's your name?"
-Weapon Design Changes: I get this is a new area, but the Flamer looks less like a combat weapon and more like a fancy blowtorch. Or the Gauss Rifle from Fallout 3? Not here either. Instead the Railroad has their own Gauss Rifle cobbled together. Or the Gatling Laser? Different Variant. Combat Rifle? Not even the R91 from 3. Assault Rifle? Different as well. And let's not forget the lack of a Chinese Assault Rifle from Fallout 3. It was in the files. And only until Nuka-World did you get an Ak-styled weapon.
Things I liked about Fallout 4:
-The Combat System: Better. Aiming down the sights isn't like leaing in your head a little closer to see your enemies, or up in your face so close that the recoil from the gun will give you a concussion. ADS was good, and leaning. And everything else, oh, except the AI could've been reworked.
-I could keep coming back to it, even if it was for an hour or two, I loved to come back and continue playing, heck, I am trying to get the rest of the achievements from the main quest specifically in a new playthrough!
-The areas: While Fallout 4 didn't give us 4-5 new areas with differences between them, whether it's how they look or how they were, I liked Far Harbor and Nuka World. Both had their own themes, new or not. Nuka Worlds was Raiders and Rollercoaster, but Far Harbor's theme was much more like Point Lookout.
-The colors: Fallout 4 has lots of color. I like to see that. Sure, it cuts down the grimy perspective that the Captial Wasteland's Wasteland City had, or New Vegas' Desert feeling, but I liked it. It felt like a 50's post apocalypse and not some washed out area where clouds were always in the sky.
And if I forgot to talk about any DLC's I'll put my reviews of them here:
Automatron: Felt very good, liked the armors, liked the robots, gets this if you've got Nuka World, you can put robot mods from that onto Automatron robots.
Wasteland Workshop: Settlement building stuff, was okay, liked concrete stuff, like neon lighting. Still could've been in the base game.
Far Harbor: Take Point Lookout, place it in Maine, throw in some references to older factions, boom. Did a good job with this concept, though.
Contraptions: Take a Rube Goldberg machine and make it in Fallout, could've been better.
Vault-Tec Workshop: Was pretty cool, but Vault Size felt small, I had to disable various debris in order to make it. So in the future, if you do make a vault, make it a huge, open space and allow us to build it as big as we want, no limits, especailly on PC. Also, a molment of silence to Clem, if you had him go back to the power cycle and he died, I'm sorry.
Nuka World: Was probably the best one out of all of them. It's a Disney Land with 2 old-school references thrown in, maybe more. I'm still playing through it, fixed Fallout 4's "You can only be a good guy" issue. You want to be raider, get this, and Automatron, since you know, Robot Parts.
Again, I love Fallout 4, that is my preference. You can say "I did not agree with your opinion." but don't take it as fact. I'm no robot. I'm human, just like you. Bethesda did ♥♥♥♥ up, but I sort-of know why it did ♥♥♥♥ up, and frankly, we're still at fault, as a community, we made so much hype, that it made this game dissappointing. So in the Future, for any game, don't join the Hype train, trust me, hype is what can make or break a game sometimes.

well 116 horus in and i finnally polished off the main story quest.  Not that they took me that long to complete , I just happened to poke around quite a bit, any way  a review is in order  , but where to start.
THE GREAT:
We are back in yet another open world RPG made by bethesda - and boy does it show.  huge land scapes  thousands of places to explore  the fun never stops.
The voice acting-  the VA in this one is superb. There are a lot of returning voice talent that you will recognize if you played any of bethesda's previous games  (such as  the guy that voices Valentine). But lo and behold Bethesda has also hired a lot of new talent that you may have heard in other games.  you'll recognize voices from actors that played parts in the  mass effect series (if you played that series) and the dragon age series . such as the main character's voice  (her name excapes me at the moment) , but she voiced Jack from ME 2 and ME 3. I also heard several characters that were voiced by Garrus' voice actor too.  That said there is a lot of good talent  and all the voice work is top notch.
The setting -  not only is the land scape big but in typical beth fashion the environments ooze character  and atmosphere. (love those radiation storms). also as a move away from previous fallout games  there are actual rain storms in FO 4 too.  I always felt it was stupid that there never was rain in FO games.  a nuclear war would not dry up earth's atmosphere especialy considering that the earth's surface is 70% covered in said water.  so the enviroments and the weather is a big plus in my book.
Weapon crafting -  This is just awesome. there are so many ways to customize a weapon  it's unbeleivable.  I love how the weapon's apperance actually changes to reflect the modifications too. really can't say enough about this aspect of the game.
THE GOOD:
The story -  It's top notch in this game as expected . Bethesda is good at telling a story. it will pull you into the game. not gonna say any thing else about it as i don't want to give any spoilers. however , a few things hold this bacvk from being great. for starters there seems to be less story pathing than say FO NV.  it does offer the same pathing ammount as FO 3 , but after NV I had hoped Bethesda would have upped their game for FO 4.  Suppose I shouldn't have expected that much. after all Skyrim also released after  NV and it's story has next to no actual story branching.
Settlement crafting -  This is awesome too, but you are probably wondering why I only marked this under "the Good"  section and not "the great" section.  while there are many things you can build and many options in the system it has some drawbacks.   first off there is a limit to how many objects you can place in a given settlement. if you try to go crazy detailed with every house, or try to build a large premeter fence (like i did at first), you will hit this limit fast.   Second you can't build every thing from the get go. You have to find those picket fences magazines to ad more stuff. that said the default  stuff you do get is quite extensive.  Overall it was a good addition to an already great game  and i suspect many gamers will just dive into settlement crafting and forget all about the main story.
THE BAD:
The graphics -  are they horrid ugly and festering?  NO.  are the dripping with uber next gen sauce? no there as well.  Do they get the job done and look pretty doing so.  Yeah, but for the experince  they use too many resources.  Don't get me wrong I really LOVE the graphics on this game. and they do have quite a few next gen features  such as tesselation, hair physics, and god rays. but being on the same engine as skyrim with just dx 11 updating  they don't impress as much as they could have. in places some textures are blurry, the hair styles are relatively short to shoulder length despiote having good hair physics in game (why cant they give us some really long hair styles?)  and in general ther are some really odd frame rate drops in odd places.  one minute I could be walking through a dense forest  fighting dogs and bugs at 46-60 fps,  then i would go into a city that had far less shadows casting, far less god rays and next to no enemies to fight in that spot,  but my frames would plummet to the 22-32 fps range. just weird. I did figure out if i turn shadow distance to medium , god rays to high and shadows to high I could keep the dips in the 27-35 fps range , more playable but still odd.
Lack of money and resources- this one was an odd one to me.  the game throws you all the ammo you ever need  constantly. by the end of my play i had 2000 something fusion rounds for laser rifles,  2000 something rounds of .45 weps and qutie a few plasma rounds as well.  what I barely ever had was caps , and building resources. it's an odd mis-balance i felt the devs could have did better with. they should have threw you a  good deal less ammo , and about double the caps they did give you and about 50% more resopurces and the game would have balanced much better.  as it stands , i am never hurting for ammo in the bosston wasteland , but always hurting for caps  which in turn had me hurting for resources a lot.
THE UGLY:
Dumbing down - this came as no suprise , though i had really hoped bethesda was ready to stop dumbing things down. saddly they continue to push the boundaries of "how far can you dumb down a RPG before it is no longer an rpg?".  after a stint in FO4 i give bethesda 2 more games before they just say "screw it, this is not an RPG". Character leveling dumbed down,  Dialouge  dumbed down . really al these things could have their own subject topic  but tyring to compress them here so i'm not writing a novel.     I hate the dialouge wheel. It feels borrowed from bioware's mass effect, yet it offers less options than the game it was borrowed from. the leveling while interstingly approached  after some time i find myself missing the old system. the fact skills are tied into this system makes the game much more limted and less life like than previous outing. want to try to  pick a  lock even if you got fumble fingers?  well too damn bad you haven't picked the perk yet so you can't even attempt it.    just such a  back step from the old special/skill/perk system , now there's just special and perks and they are all blended togehter in one chart. i love the interface but that's about it.
No mods yet -  much of my complaints i could have completely overlooked if the game already had modding. How come it doesn't?   didn't skyrim launch with mod support already  ? corect me if i'm wrong.   that said after having just finished the  main story , i have no intention of firing FO4 up again until bethesda get's offical mod support in the game. And no i'm not looking to graphic mod ♥♥♥♥♥ it up, there are mods out there other than graphic mods, besides the game already pushes my system in certain areas.  Just there is no reason this game shouldn't have launched with mod support already in it. in fact the folks at nexus have already been doing some mods back door via ini file altering.
Don't get me wrong i know i got a lot of bad and ugly  stuff listed in this review. honestly this review barely covers the scope of every thing i wanted to mention and I am loving every minute of this game.  It's not a bad game, I just think it could have been much more than it is.  That said I give it a  80%. if you are a fan of Fallout games or open world rpgs get this game imidiately. if not i'd wait for mod support.  either way you won't be disapointed with the purchase the game is worth every penny it cost.

Ok, so this game gets a thumbs up. I say this because I enjoyed it, despite its numerous flaws. The game is not what New Vegas was, nor is it as good in terms of story or setting. The gameplay is improved considerably, as are the graphics, despite this I did not enjoy it as much as I had New Vegas or even FO3. The reasons for this are simple:
First, you lost all the choice you had in the previous games. You are playing a character that has been made for you, with a preset attittude that can only deviate so far from what is already presented to you. You can do very little in th way of being "Evil" at all in this game short of just murdering everyone you come across, and losing out on a huge amount of the game doing so.
Second, the story was... lackluster. I'd say it was about as good as FO3 and that's about it. Nothing particularly compelling. The major factions, and a fair number of the minor factions were 2D, and lacked any real development aside from the singular facet of their background. The Brotherhood was an exception to this I suppose.
Third, the voice acting of the player character. This one isn't really that big, I just personally don't like it.
Fourth, Dogmeat. This one usually raises some eyebrows. How could Dogmeat be a negative characteristic of the game? Well, let me tell you. This monster would, frequently, "find something" and go running off into rooms filled with traps that he could not set off, but I could. He would frequently run into hordes of enemies alerting them to our position and then run back to me as if to say "Hey guys, aim this way". In the end, the things he finds are never worth the trouble of having him with you, and he was quickly switched out for ANY companion I could get.
The game did have a number of good functions added a well, though some are up for debate. If you like RPGs, choice, gameplay, and of course, Fallout.. avoid this like the plague. Save yourself from depression and disapointment.
Fallout 4 is a pure example of gaming becomming casual, hand holding, copy and paste and overall stupid. They even removed Karma.. Sound familiar..? Yes, as you may fear from reading that, Fallout 4 is like a reincarnation of Call of Duty put into an RPG.
Read this review, it covers everything that's Fallout 4, I had no one else's views effect me, I'm judging this from a true RPG fan and hardcore gamer's view. First, all the upsides, some good news before the horrible news;
+Customization; You can actually set up a base however you want, modify weapons and their bodies, and your suits. Depending on how you dochanges how they work, it's neat, but in a dead no-choice world it's basically butter without bread.
+Better companions; this is probably the highlight of the game, companions are able to be given commands, like looking for items for you, or distracting, etc. Pretty much it though, they're still dumb as rocks because Bethesda's using the same AI from FO3.
+Better combat; All there is to say.. no stupid RNjesus when aiming down sites, and you move around a lot smoother.
I'm very sorry to say.. but that's all the pros. Now for the cons;
-Outdated as heck engine, outdated as heck performance, and forced visuals on outdated engine; they're using the same Creation engine. Not much more should need be said, but if you don't know what this means, it means the game runs like shayt. They forced god rays, atmo fog, reflections, and all kinds of nonsense on an ancient engine, the Engine can't handle these things properly and runs horribly, it's like forcing a ltitle dweeb to bench press a thousand pounds. Or forcing a little remote control toy car's engine to work a Ferrari. It's not possible, it looks good but it's not gonna do good. I have an overkill PC (See on profile) and it dropped to about 9 FPS when just looking at trees.
-Dumbed down to the dirt RPG elements; They removed choice. Yep. Choice. In old fallouts you could tell someone to kill themselves and they would, and it'd effect the story, you become evil, blahblahblah. Fallout 4, though.. you have Yes. Mean, but still Yes. And No, and mean, but still No. And most of the Nos = yes anyway. You have almost no choice, the story is unchangable, almost all sidequests are unchangable. They removed having to think or worry about consequence.
-No Karma; WHAT. THE. ♥♥♥♥. THIS WAS THE MAIN POINT OF FALLOUT; KARMA! This is an extreme example of kid-ifying a game into being some cookie cut copypaste of the original games. There's no denying Bethesda removed it so that there's TRUELY no actual CHOICE or CONSEQUENCE in the game, they removed the last thing that could of kept FO4 as a true RPG. You can slaughter a town and they won't care, and even if you tried, most of them can't die anyway, they're protected by some divine intervention of just falling on their knees and breathing heavy. Depressing.
-Terrible, wretched, billboard character personalities; Remember how in FO3 you had the mysterious murderers. the crack head researcher, the humble roughskin, the majestic vampire? All gone. Everyone is just a depressed do the mission now average joe. If they all wore armor, and they took away all the names, I promise you legitimately can not tell who's who. They all act the same, you will not get attatched to anyone at all. You can kill everyone in this game and not feel bad.
-Outdated visuals; This is hit or miss for some, you can skip this if you don't care abotu visuals. But the graphics suck, screeneis might look good, but in actual gameplay everything's extremely static, the shadows are ugly, textures up close look like Skyrim on medium. Not only does it look horrible, but it runs horrible. Need I say more?
-No factions; there's no factions except for Brotherhood of Steel. And guess what? No weight on your shoudlers for joining them. And no cool quests, just fetch quests. Not even kidding, the first mission you gotta do for BHoS is fetch about 20 blackboxes. And you have to run back and fourth for each one and give it back to the dumb ♥♥♥♥♥.
-Small repetitive world with nothing in it; Oh, there may LOOK like there's a lot, but they all are the same at heart. That rusted down shack? You'll find some caps. That ancient car factory? Some caps in it. All they did was make things look pretty, there's nothing to do. Nothing unique/crazy inside them.
-Your character talks for themselves; This entirely ruins the immersion of an RPG. You can't even actually choose exactly what you want to say. In older Fallouts you could see the dialogue box, and be like "Oh heck yeah that's what I'll say". But in Fallout 4..? Oh boy, you have the choice with Yes. Sarcastic. No. Goodbye. You're not the character anymore, you're controlling someone now. The game isn't about you, but someone else. This is where a game is usually demeed not even an RPG anymore. You won't know what you're-.. sorry, no; the GAME'S character will say.
Fallout 4 truely failed at being Fallout, and not only that it failed at being an actual RPG.
Do I reccommend this game? Depends, actually. I just harped on it hard, but there's still a chance you'll like it. If you like shooters, and Fallout's theme, then go for it. If you like an RPG shooter (RPGs at all for that matter) and what a hard game with choice and story, ignore this game. It's just an arcade shooter with Fallout's world. It's not a true RPG successor.

Fallout 4 seems to be the logical evolution of Fallout 3 and Skyrim, which are alike in many ways. It appears to be the biggest and longest game so far, if you aim to do everything, and not just rush the main story.
In Fallout 3 you had a house, which you could decorate. In Skyrim you had multiple houses, which you could modify somewhat. In this game you can (if you're willing and able) take control of many settlements, even build them from scratch. You can build houses, fences, shops, defense turrets, agriculture and many more things. Electricity is a chapter of its own. Having a generator is a must if you wish to use the more advanced laser turrets, lights, water cleaning machine or one of the many other machines.
Everything has to be connected with copper wires in order to work, which can be extended by power pylons or conduits, which you can attach almost everywhere. You can even build traps, which trigger by pressure or other means.
You will need many materials (some rare) to build the settlements, or to craft armor and weapons. Fortunately you can collect all sorts of junk and then dismantle it in one of your settlements. Which in turn can be used to create new stuff. Remember to pick up the skill that lets you establish supply lines. That way all settlements' ressources can be shared. Weapons and armor, unfortunately, will remain where you put them.
TLDR: Improved version of Fallout 3/Skyrim. Must buy if you liked the predecessors. Also part settlement simulator.

What went wrong with Fallout 4?
Perhaps it was the removal of the skills system, leaving the only form of progression to be the perks system, and adding many uninteresting perks to keep some similarity to the old system. Is it the poorly designed combat system, where the main difficulty is enemies having inflated damage and hp scores?
Bethesda was never particularly good at designing intersting quests since Oblivion, and this shows in FO4, where many quests are simply, go here, kill that thing, or go here, talk to that person, repeat, with no potential for an alternate solution. The situations in which you can solve a quest by talking instead of fighting are few and far between. The speech system is tied purely to the charisma stat, and it's back to being chance based like in Fallout 3.
The characters are the best Bethesda has ever made, which doesn't say much. The companions, while some of them are interesting, are still only as developed as an early Bioware character. Non companions are as paper thin as ever, and I found myself barely caring for most of the major characters.
The voiced main character and simplified dialogue system causes a less roleplayable experience, as your character already has an established background. There's not much choice when it comes to being a nice or mean character, and how you act during a quest usually doesn't change much.
Even siding with the "evil" faction doesn't seem particularly mean, as most of the factions in the game are written with such a gray morality that it almost seems like none of them are a good choice for the game world.
Of course, the game is full of bugs, running what is basically a modified version of the engine from Fallout 3, on the verge of colapsing from it's own unoptimized weight. The game is also not designed well for the PC, as the interface for many things was clearly made with consoles in mind.
This isn't even getting into many of the little problems I have with the design in this game, but overall, Fallout 4 seems like a blatantly unpolished experience by a large developer. If Bethesda is expecting the modding community to fix all their problems for them, this should come as an insult, as they don't care to provide a optimal gaming experience right out of the box.
It's a shame there's no other game quite like this, but in it's current state, Fallout 4 is nowhere near worth the 60$ asking price.

TL;DR: Really Quite Enjoyable, but has bugs and interface issues.
I'll assume if you're reading this, you are at least somewat familiar with the basic premise of Fallout: Large, open world that's set after a nuclear apocalypse. You can go explore the wasteland, help people, kill raiders and muties, get killed by deathclaws, build your own weapons, and even build up and defend settlements. Basically, it's a lot of fun, but it comes with some issues and annoyances. This review pertains to the Steam version of FO4, release version without mods, and was played with keyboard and mouse. You might wonder why this review has so few pros, and so many negatives:
It's Fallout, and everybody is already singing its praises. Its predecessors have been out for years and years, so I can reasonably assume that most people interested in reading my review know the pros of the franchise. As such, I will be focussing on things that were not told to me in any reviews I read (or at least not stressed as much as I would have liked them to).
Pros:
+ Hugely detailed world with tons of things to discover.
+ Gunplay feels better than in previous titles.
+ Client appeares to be more stable than previous titles (Bethesda's games are notorious for their CTD-y nature).
+ The art style manages to perfectly capture the Fallout feel (and I'm talking 1&2 here) while adding new nuances to it.
+ I've seen people criticizing the graphics, but on my old rig, it looks spectacular for the most part. Most graphics settings can only be changed outside the game, however.
0 The perk/skill system has been completely overhauled. There now are no skills any more (such as Energy Weapons or Medicine). I personally do not mind this change per se, as I always preferred perks because of their varied nature, and the importance of skills kind of made INT too good a stat at least in New Vegas (and so made non-int builds considerably less interesting).
Cons:
- The interface was evidently developed for consoles, and is, to put it mildly, frustrating to work with on PC. For example, the perk area has huge tiles and lots of spaces, but only fits half on your screen (the game does not tell you that you have to mouse to the bottom so it begins autoscrolling to the deeper levels). Another example is the system in place to split stacks: There is only a (fiddly) slider. You cannot punch in the numbers. Another would be the arrow keys being bound for conversations and scrolling in
text, but not others (whhere you then scroll by hitting enter, which is never explained).
- The key bindings also appear to be a half-baked port from controllers: Half of the instances for the USE key seem to be hardcoded to pressing the "E" key, even if you've bound the function to another key. So you are able to pick up things from the ground with your assigned key, but if you pick them from a container, only E works. Since many keys are double- and even triple-bound to specific functions in different sections of the interface, this makes navigation and issuing commands a chore that won't soon be learned by your muscle memory. Sure, you alternatively could click most of the commands, but their positioning is very unergonomic and results in a lot of mousework - especially if you work a lot with your inventory. Which you will be doing unless you ignore the main new features (base building and armor/weapon customization).
- The new VATS system is fiddly to control with a mouse (hitting the desired body part when all target options keep switching because the target's animation isn't stopped, but merely slowed down) and confusing. Doubly shameful as VATS was apparently meant to be used regularly (some enemies have very fast, hard-to-predict movement patterns, or impossible-to-hit-in-regular-aim weak spots). I forgo it whenever possible, because it's a
to use on PC.
- Bugs are present, which is kind of unavoidable with a game of this scale. I don't even mind the 'mesh stuck in another mesh, producing looping sound effects because the physics engine is acting up' thing. But I did mind losing all of my 250 stimpaks to... I don't even know. I just know that when I hammered my stimpack key, and nothing happened, I checked to find all of my stimpaks gone. I had not given them to my companion, I had not sold them, I had not stashed them somewhere else. They just vanished from my inventory without a notice or trace. Kind of sucks in a game whose main draw is "collect the loot". If I can't count on the game keeping accurate track of what's in my bags, why collect loot at all?
- Companions are derpy and slightly annoying. They block your path and often enough your shots and they tend to get noticed when trying to stealth. Sometimes they trip up mines and traps. At least you can "level up" their trust in you, which I still don't really count as a positive, because...
- The reputation system of New Vegas is gone. As is the karma system. I don't mind the latter too much, but no reputation with factions? Really? That was one of the best parts of New Vegas!
- The conversation system went from "real choices" and skill checks informing some options to "four flavours of the same dialogue". And this being Bethesda, the dialogue itself is nothing too thrilling, either. Definite downgrade.
All in all, Fallout 4 is a fun game, less prone to crashing than its predecessors, but also hugely lacking in the usability of its PC interface. I'm hoping that something akin to or better than SkyUI for Skyrim is in the making, because as it stands, the interface really diminishes my will to play (and I've spent the entire weekend playing nothing but Fallout 4), because the game *is* genuinely good - it could be a lot better, though. Also, 250 stimpaks gone, and no indication as to how or where they went? Are you kidding me?!

It's like some one made a post-apocalypse themed simulation/action RPG with mechs, but called it Fallout 4 by accident. This game goes right in a lot of places, but also goes horribly wrong in others. There are only 3 features that really stand out for me:
---------------------------------------------
Settlement Building: Something that has been implemented via fan-made mods since Morrowind, Real Time Settler now sees it's official debut in Fallout 4, however it is not perfect, it is plagued by bugs, miniscule population cap, pathetic construction cap, and limitted construction options, fortunately the latter issue is fixed with mods.
Weapon & Armour Customization: Finally, a functioning and in depth weapon/armour customization system in a Fallout game. First seen in Fallout: New Vegas, this rather iffy feature is remade from the ground up. Almost every part of a firearm is customizable, from it's stock/handle right down to the barrel. This is by far the most solid feature.
Power Armour: "But Fallout has always had power armour! That isn't a feature you dumb♥♥♥♥♥" I thought to myself hearing my friend describe the new power armour. I was very wrong. The implementation of Power Armour in previous games has always been lacklustre, but in Fallout 4 it has been perfected. Instead of it just being a regular clothing item, it is now a customizable mech suit. *Almost* every part of a suit of power armour can be upgraded and fitted with mods.
---------------------------------------------
Ah, but now we get to the negative stuff.
Skills & Perks: First I want to say: There are no skills, what-so-ever. They've been removed, cut, thrown away, and I doubt they'll be remaking a return whilst Bethesda Game Studios are under the leadership of Todd Howard. Everything in the RPG department has been butchered and "streamlined". As you level up instead of being able to spend points on skills and put a single perk point into getting a new perk, you'll instead be given the option to unlock a single perk. There are only a handful of useful perks, most of which are related to weapon damage buffs and crafting. All of the rest range from "useless" to "even more useless".
Dialogue Limitations & the BioWare Wheel: Yes, that's right, Bethesda shamelessly ripped off the dialogue wheel from BioWare. Which limits your dialogue options to just four responses, and each response is paraphrased so you never know what you're gonna say next! There are typically four types of responses: Sarcastic Jerk, Good Natured Concerned Parent, Frustrated Concerned Parent, and Questioning Concerned Parent. There's very little in the way of "Bad guy" or "Mercenary" dialogue options.
Story: Good grief what a load of old ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, there isn't much I can say about this waste of time without spoiling the story. There's obvious plot twists, lots of whinging, and lots of things that don't make sense.
Quests: All you need to know summed up into three words: Fetch quests everywhere.
Weapons: Whilst the customization feature is stellar in it's delivery, the amount of *actual* weapons available within the game is, well, nothing to be desired. Whilst the customization options allow for entirely new weapons to be crafted, in actuality there isn't that much diversity in the range of obtainable weapons. A majority of weapons in use tend to be subtle variations on the same pipe\laser gun.
A.I Pathing: Is there anything more comical than a group of raiders trying to chase you, and then running off of a four story building, only to the fall to the ground and die immediately? I think not. That is the quality of A.I pathing we are dealing with here, ladies and gentlemens.
Bugs: Bugs, bugs, bugs galore. Bugs are omnipresent in this game, just like the comically awful A.I pathing. There are countless bugs, I do not even know where to start. Whether it's your current weapon being locked whilst trying to change to something more appropriate for the situation, or it's quests being incompletable due to a specific character vanishing into thin air.
---------------------------------------------
In summary, I recommend this game. Why? It may be a terrible, buggy, lacklustre, broken Fallout game, but you know what, it is a pretty good game on it's own -- Far better than most of the tripe released this year anyway.
If you want a Fallout game, please turn away now, this is not for you. It seldom resembles a Fallout game mechanic wise, and I don't care how many times it references previous installments. However if you are after a post-apocalypse settlement building simulation game, then I highly recommend it for you, the three good features highlighted above are enough to make this game stand out on it's own, however it fails horrifically as a sequal in the Fallout franchise.

TL;DR: Really Quite Enjoyable, but has bugs and interface issues.
I'll assume if you're reading this, you are at least somewat familiar with the basic premise of Fallout: Large, open world that's set after a nuclear apocalypse. You can go explore the wasteland, help people, kill raiders and muties, get killed by deathclaws, build your own weapons, and even build up and defend settlements. Basically, it's a lot of fun, but it comes with some issues and annoyances. This review pertains to the Steam version of FO4, release version without mods, and was played with keyboard and mouse. You might wonder why this review has so few pros, and so many negatives:
It's Fallout, and everybody is already singing its praises. Its predecessors have been out for years and years, so I can reasonably assume that most people interested in reading my review know the pros of the franchise. As such, I will be focussing on things that were not told to me in any reviews I read (or at least not stressed as much as I would have liked them to).
Pros:
+ Hugely detailed world with tons of things to discover.
+ Gunplay feels better than in previous titles.
+ Client appeares to be more stable than previous titles (Bethesda's games are notorious for their CTD-y nature).
+ The art style manages to perfectly capture the Fallout feel (and I'm talking 1&2 here) while adding new nuances to it.
+ I've seen people criticizing the graphics, but on my old rig, it looks spectacular for the most part. Most graphics settings can only be changed outside the game, however.
0 The perk/skill system has been completely overhauled. There now are no skills any more (such as Energy Weapons or Medicine). I personally do not mind this change per se, as I always preferred perks because of their varied nature, and the importance of skills kind of made INT too good a stat at least in New Vegas (and so made non-int builds considerably less interesting).
Cons:
- The interface was evidently developed for consoles, and is, to put it mildly, frustrating to work with on PC. For example, the perk area has huge tiles and lots of spaces, but only fits half on your screen (the game does not tell you that you have to mouse to the bottom so it begins autoscrolling to the deeper levels). Another example is the system in place to split stacks: There is only a (fiddly) slider. You cannot punch in the numbers. Another would be the arrow keys being bound for conversations and scrolling in
text, but not others (whhere you then scroll by hitting enter, which is never explained).
- The key bindings also appear to be a half-baked port from controllers: Half of the instances for the USE key seem to be hardcoded to pressing the "E" key, even if you've bound the function to another key. So you are able to pick up things from the ground with your assigned key, but if you pick them from a container, only E works. Since many keys are double- and even triple-bound to specific functions in different sections of the interface, this makes navigation and issuing commands a chore that won't soon be learned by your muscle memory. Sure, you alternatively could click most of the commands, but their positioning is very unergonomic and results in a lot of mousework - especially if you work a lot with your inventory. Which you will be doing unless you ignore the main new features (base building and armor/weapon customization).
- The new VATS system is fiddly to control with a mouse (hitting the desired body part when all target options keep switching because the target's animation isn't stopped, but merely slowed down) and confusing. Doubly shameful as VATS was apparently meant to be used regularly (some enemies have very fast, hard-to-predict movement patterns, or impossible-to-hit-in-regular-aim weak spots). I forgo it whenever possible, because it's a
to use on PC.
- Bugs are present, which is kind of unavoidable with a game of this scale. I don't even mind the 'mesh stuck in another mesh, producing looping sound effects because the physics engine is acting up' thing. But I did mind losing all of my 250 stimpaks to... I don't even know. I just know that when I hammered my stimpack key, and nothing happened, I checked to find all of my stimpaks gone. I had not given them to my companion, I had not sold them, I had not stashed them somewhere else. They just vanished from my inventory without a notice or trace. Kind of sucks in a game whose main draw is "collect the loot". If I can't count on the game keeping accurate track of what's in my bags, why collect loot at all?
- Companions are derpy and slightly annoying. They block your path and often enough your shots and they tend to get noticed when trying to stealth. Sometimes they trip up mines and traps. At least you can "level up" their trust in you, which I still don't really count as a positive, because...
- The reputation system of New Vegas is gone. As is the karma system. I don't mind the latter too much, but no reputation with factions? Really? That was one of the best parts of New Vegas!
- The conversation system went from "real choices" and skill checks informing some options to "four flavours of the same dialogue". And this being Bethesda, the dialogue itself is nothing too thrilling, either. Definite downgrade.
All in all, Fallout 4 is a fun game, less prone to crashing than its predecessors, but also hugely lacking in the usability of its PC interface. I'm hoping that something akin to or better than SkyUI for Skyrim is in the making, because as it stands, the interface really diminishes my will to play (and I've spent the entire weekend playing nothing but Fallout 4), because the game *is* genuinely good - it could be a lot better, though. Also, 250 stimpaks gone, and no indication as to how or where they went? Are you kidding me?!

Another example is the system in place to split stacks: There is only a (fiddly) slider. You cannot punch in the numbers. Another would be the arrow keys being bound for conversations and scrolling in
text, but not others (whhere you then scroll by hitting enter, which is never explained).
- The key bindings also appear to be a half-baked port from controllers: Half of the instances for the USE key seem to be hardcoded to pressing the "E" key, even if you've bound the function to another key. So you are able to pick up things from the ground with your assigned key, but if you pick them from a container, only E works. Since many keys are double- and even triple-bound to specific functions in different sections of the interface, this makes navigation and issuing commands a chore that won't soon be learned by your muscle memory. Sure, you alternatively could click most of the commands, but their positioning is very unergonomic and results in a lot of mousework - especially if you work a lot with your inventory. Which you will be doing unless you ignore the main new features (base building and armor/weapon customization).
- The new VATS system is fiddly to control with a mouse (hitting the desired body part when all target options keep switching because the target's animation isn't stopped, but merely slowed down) and confusing. Doubly shameful as VATS was apparently meant to be used regularly (some enemies have very fast, hard-to-predict movement patterns, or impossible-to-hit-in-regular-aim weak spots). I forgo it whenever possible, because it's a
to use on PC.
- Bugs are present, which is kind of unavoidable with a game of this scale. I don't even mind the 'mesh stuck in another mesh, producing looping sound effects because the physics engine is acting up' thing. But I did mind losing all of my 250 stimpaks to... I don't even know. I just know that when I hammered my stimpack key, and nothing happened, I checked to find all of my stimpaks gone. I had not given them to my companion, I had not sold them, I had not stashed them somewhere else. They just vanished from my inventory without a notice or trace. Kind of sucks in a game whose main draw is "collect the loot". If I can't count on the game keeping accurate track of what's in my bags, why collect loot at all?
- Companions are derpy and slightly annoying. They block your path and often enough your shots and they tend to get noticed when trying to stealth. Sometimes they trip up mines and traps. At least you can "level up" their trust in you, which I still don't really count as a positive, because...
- The reputation system of New Vegas is gone. As is the karma system. I don't mind the latter too much, but no reputation with factions? Really? That was one of the best parts of New Vegas!
- The conversation system went from "real choices" and skill checks informing some options to "four flavours of the same dialogue". And this being Bethesda, the dialogue itself is nothing too thrilling, either. Definite downgrade.
All in all, Fallout 4 is a fun game, less prone to crashing than its predecessors, but also hugely lacking in the usability of its PC interface. I'm hoping that something akin to or better than SkyUI for Skyrim is in the making, because as it stands, the interface really diminishes my will to play (and I've spent the entire weekend playing nothing but Fallout 4), because the game *is* genuinely good - it could be a lot better, though. Also, 250 stimpaks gone, and no indication as to how or where they went? Are you kidding me?!

Classic RPG's mission design: You need to eliminate a bunch of bandits in a factory. You can either A. go there, gun blazing, kill everyone or B. go there, talk to the leader of the bandits and settle things down. With option B, you can either 1. use charisma if you're a female 2. kidnap his relative and make pressure on him, forcing him and his boys to go away 3. stealthily plant bombs around the factory, tell him to go away or you'll detonate the bombs. In Fallout 4? You can only have one choice: BAM BAM BANG BANG KILL EVERYTHING. Because choices are ♥♥♥♥ing overrated.
In other RPGs, you need to do a lot of things, climb up the power ladder in order to be the master. In Fallout 4, it takes you 2 quests to be the leader of Minutemen. In other RPGs, most of them always save the best for the last, including end game armors, ♥♥♥♥en badass enemies. In Fallout 4, you can get the power armor and fight a Deathclaw in the first 1 hour and 45 minutes. In other RPGs, most of them encourage player to tackle situations by their own way and spice up the experience through each playthrough. In Fallout 4, character buildings boil down to "maxing Strength, Charisma and other crap that affect damage", because 90% of the things you do in this game is killing, blowing ♥♥♥♥♥ up.
In other RPGs, they have complex dialogue trees with a lot of branches that can alter outcomes. In Fallout 4, the dialogue writing is borderline ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, boiling down to 4 options: Yes, No, Sarcastic (what does this mean anyway), Cancel. Why? Because apparently Bethesda thinks players are ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and can't control what their character is going to say. In other RPGs, they tend to deliver complex mechanics (well, because they're RPGs). Here in Fallout 4, Bethestard tripped down the perk system, dumbed down the dialogue, removed Speech check and left a vague Charisma check in some conversations, and they somehow they made the HUD and inventory even worse to look at and navigate. In other RPGs, quests are meaningful. In Fallout 4, 70% in my 30 hours playtime (don't mind the 10 hours line above, I play mostly in offline mode) are fetch quests where my character have to go to point A, kill things, maybe sometimes collect object B. Because the new combat system is too awesome, Bethestard decided to shove a lot of linear shooting gallery sections into the game, the one I hated most in this game where the Minutemen had to go reclaim a fortress plagued with Mirelurks. That. ♥♥♥♥ing. Mirelurk Queen. Is. Too. Bullet. Spongey.
The good things? Aethestic design is better than I initially thought. Crafting is fun. Building settlements is so ♥♥♥♥ing addictive that I consider to reinstall the game just to do that again. But all of them doesn't make a good RPG. I want to play Fallout as a RPG, not a Borderlands-esque shooter with gimmicks. I want branching dialogues, smart writings (not the Planetscape: Torment level, but the Morrowind level, is it too much to ask?), I want complex systems to comeback like perks and traits, I don't want 90% of the game is about gunplay and blowing ♥♥♥♥♥ up, I just want a proper RPG, plays like a RPG, and this is NOT the game I want to play.
So, if you're looking for a post-apocalyptic open-world shooter, then Fallout 4 is the perfect choice. If you're looking for really really good RPGs, then I recommend these games: The Witcher 3 Wild Hunt, The Age of Decadence, Divinity: Original Sin, Wastelands 2, Pillars of Eternity, Underrail, or if you don't mind a bit old school, Avernum: Escape from the Pit, Lords of Xulima, ADOM, Serpent in the Staglands, or if you don't mind old games, Neverwinter Nights, Baldur's Gate, every DnD game released before 2007, or even the original Fallout 1 and 2! or if you don't mind Kickstarter games or unreleased games, Divinity: Original Sin 2, Underworld: Ascendant, my personal anticipate The Dwarves or even the upcoming Mass Effect Andromeda. If you want a post-apocalypse game, then go for Underrail, ♥♥♥♥ing great game.
Why am I even writing this review? What a waste of time. Bethesda created Morrowind, the game that I grew up with that gave me a special passion into videogame, it was a miraculous experience, a one and only gift that none of the followers can deliver the same kind of treatment. When I look at Fallout 4, I only see a shallow title with high production value, a shooter game in the vein of Fallout that I regreted spending time in it. Something SPECIAL has lost. Goodbye Bethesda, you used to be the one I adore, used to.

Growing up I got my hands on Fallout. The original, a top down turned based rpg, and I instantly lost a few months of my life to it. When Fallout 3 came out I preoredered and lost years of afternoons to it. When Fallout New Vegas came out I lost another few years of afternoons to it. When Fallout 4 came out I was excited to play it. For someone who has played Fallout and The Elder scrolls for decades now I would like to inform you that this like all the others in the franchise is both a step up and a step back.
It is a step up in that Power Armor feels meaning full and strong. The guns feel fluid and useable. Every Point into SPECIAL and the Perks feels like it has weight and each one will change how you play. The enemys are terrifying. Nothing says "YOU LOSE" like a mini nuke to the face when you're level ten and unaware that the enemy has it.  The amount of viable play styles and cool things in the world will be enough for almost anyone to get into the game. While certain features feel like they were tacked on at the end or just plained rushed/ignored you don't need them. Modding weapons and armor feels fufilling and usefull. Weapon platforms bring variety while making it so that cool pistol becomes a smg, to a rifle, or to a sniper. Most of the characters feel alive and emotional, and will bring tears and laughs. This game as "game" is a step up.
Where this game is a step back is as an rpg. The choices you make don't feel like they have any impact. The dialogue is the same with only maybe a single line in diffrence for each of your speech choices. The speech choices have been brought down to "info, sarcastic, mean, kind" with a touch of speech challenges for more caps or more info littered in there. The faction system is gone so once you decide you like the gear a group is carrying you can raid their people you find in the waste for no cost. Karma is gone so that means no repercussions for stealing and murdering unless you get caught and then the penalty is death. All the freedom in the world doesn't mean you can slack on the story and interactions. While the companion storys are fleshed out and you can feel for them they just don't feel all that satisfying as other then a quick perk don't add a whole lot to the experience.
Before the final peice of my review I would like to note that it is a BETHESDA game. This means your going to have glitches, bugs, and if you notice them old animations. While not something good it is a standard for them. I have a few visual bugs that happily are not game breaking. I wish everyone the best in starting and playing, but please hold your review for the game. Please if you can't play get a refund or have bethesda support work with you to get it working. First off i would like to say that I have never played NV or Fallout 3. Therfore my review will be written without comparison to previous games. This game is a VERY good game. I'm still much more a fan of the ES series but i had to give this a try from all the hype, and i was not dissapointed. It's map may be a bit small and sometimes a little too easy, but if you are going to complain about a game being too easy or too hard, then I'm afraid you're in the wrong genre. Fallout 4 is a ROLE PLAYING GAME. Not a game that succeeds based on the difficulty of it. This game is designed to give the player an adventure, not a headache. I simply enjoyed the ride, no matter how long or repetitive it was sometime. People need to look at the fact that games arent always going to improve 200% on one of it's predecessors (may have spelled that wrong). It is an entirely new game and will have new aspects to it as well as some previous ones. Without playing the previous games i understand that i don't realize what's missing and what's "all wrong", but as someone who simply enjoys a good RPG i truly believe this game delivers. For all those who say it's too easy or theres not enough map to explore try to take it slower and really take in the beauty of the world. Hell to entertain myself for a bit i put my character (male) in a dress and ran around with a minigun (In screenshots if anyone cares to take a look). If you simply run throgh the world getting all the quests done as quick as possible and trying to get 100% on the game without stopping to actually enjoy the game, it's understandable why some people didn't like it so much. I've heard people say Bethesda has been "simplifying" their games recently and that it makes it much less immersive or that it takes player choices out of the equation. I personnaly found that my choice did not impact the ending at all, but it decided how you got there. It took me about 35 hours to complete the game which is a short play time, and i had completed several side quests i that time as well. But i will conitnue to explore and enjoy the beauty of Fallout, I will conitnue to adventure and enjoy every second of it. My words of advice to anyone thinking about buying this game is that you shouldn't come into it expecting it to be exactly like the older games but 100 times better. Come into it with the attitude that its an entire new system and you can't wait to learn all about the amazing commonwealth, fight deathclaws, run around in a blue sequin dress mowing down raiders with a minigun, and do all the other fun things this game has to offer.
If i must give it a rating based from every other rpg ive played: 7.5/10

Fallout 4 does for the Fallout franchise what Skyrim did for Elder Scrolls. That is, the sacrifice of depth in order to have mass appeal, and that is the most dissapointing part. Longtime fans will be dissapointed with the lack of stat tweaking, now distilled into simple perks, a big let down, at least for me personally. It would seem the narrative suffers also, which may be due in part to the new and limited speach system, a Mass Effect - esque style that generally gives you black and white options with little in between. It does not lack the complexity of titles before it, at this point this is all rather negative, but that is not to say that Fallout 4 isn't a great game.
Fallout 4 is an experience of pure atmosphere and spectacle, never have the wastes felt more alive and dangerous. Enemies feel less rigid, and when something comes♥♥♥♥♥♥bolting at you you feel genuine fear due to the mad sprint or excessive flailing of your adversary.
Weather comes in a variety of flavours, rain, mist or even the forboding radiation storms, once again these add to the atmospere of the Commonwealth as being immersed in the Commonwealth is what Fallout 4 is reliant on.
Gameplay tweaks add to your feeling of survival as much as the weather and the enemies, scavenge the ruins for materials to jury-righ yourself a pretty gun or bit of armour, hell, why not use all those scraps to build a whole damn community for post apocalyptic survivors? It makes the wastes amazing, vibrant and active. It is just a shame that, as much was added to the game, much was also lost.
It lacks much of what made Fallout: New Vegas one of the greats, but makes up for it in different areas, should the DLC give us an impressive narrative, I can see this also becoming one of my favourites.

It's like some one made a post-apocalypse themed simulation/action RPG with mechs, but called it Fallout 4 by accident. This game goes right in a lot of places, but also goes horribly wrong in others. There are only 3 features that really stand out for me:
---------------------------------------------
Settlement Building: Something that has been implemented via fan-made mods since Morrowind, Real Time Settler now sees it's official debut in Fallout 4, however it is not perfect, it is plagued by bugs, miniscule population cap, pathetic construction cap, and limitted construction options, fortunately the latter issue is fixed with mods.
Weapon & Armour Customization: Finally, a functioning and in depth weapon/armour customization system in a Fallout game. First seen in Fallout: New Vegas, this rather iffy feature is remade from the ground up. Almost every part of a firearm is customizable, from it's stock/handle right down to the barrel. This is by far the most solid feature.
Power Armour: "But Fallout has always had power armour! That isn't a feature you dumb♥♥♥♥♥" I thought to myself hearing my friend describe the new power armour. I was very wrong. The implementation of Power Armour in previous games has always been lacklustre, but in Fallout 4 it has been perfected. Instead of it just being a regular clothing item, it is now a customizable mech suit. *Almost* every part of a suit of power armour can be upgraded and fitted with mods.
---------------------------------------------
Ah, but now we get to the negative stuff.
Skills & Perks: First I want to say: There are no skills, what-so-ever. They've been removed, cut, thrown away, and I doubt they'll be remaking a return whilst Bethesda Game Studios are under the leadership of Todd Howard. Everything in the RPG department has been butchered and "streamlined". As you level up instead of being able to spend points on skills and put a single perk point into getting a new perk, you'll instead be given the option to unlock a single perk. There are only a handful of useful perks, most of which are related to weapon damage buffs and crafting. All of the rest range from "useless" to "even more useless".
Dialogue Limitations & the BioWare Wheel: Yes, that's right, Bethesda shamelessly ripped off the dialogue wheel from BioWare. Which limits your dialogue options to just four responses, and each response is paraphrased so you never know what you're gonna say next! There are typically four types of responses: Sarcastic Jerk, Good Natured Concerned Parent, Frustrated Concerned Parent, and Questioning Concerned Parent. There's very little in the way of "Bad guy" or "Mercenary" dialogue options.
Story: Good grief what a load of old ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, there isn't much I can say about this waste of time without spoiling the story. There's obvious plot twists, lots of whinging, and lots of things that don't make sense.
Quests: All you need to know summed up into three words: Fetch quests everywhere.
Weapons: Whilst the customization feature is stellar in it's delivery, the amount of *actual* weapons available within the game is, well, nothing to be desired. Whilst the customization options allow for entirely new weapons to be crafted, in actuality there isn't that much diversity in the range of obtainable weapons. A majority of weapons in use tend to be subtle variations on the same pipe\laser gun.
A.I Pathing: Is there anything more comical than a group of raiders trying to chase you, and then running off of a four story building, only to the fall to the ground and die immediately? I think not. That is the quality of A.I pathing we are dealing with here, ladies and gentlemens.
Bugs: Bugs, bugs, bugs galore. Bugs are omnipresent in this game, just like the comically awful A.I pathing. There are countless bugs, I do not even know where to start. Whether it's your current weapon being locked whilst trying to change to something more appropriate for the situation, or it's quests being incompletable due to a specific character vanishing into thin air.
---------------------------------------------
In summary, I recommend this game. Why? It may be a terrible, buggy, lacklustre, broken Fallout game, but you know what, it is a pretty good game on it's own -- Far better than most of the tripe released this year anyway.
If you want a Fallout game, please turn away now, this is not for you. It seldom resembles a Fallout game mechanic wise, and I don't care how many times it references previous installments. However if you are after a post-apocalypse settlement building simulation game, then I highly recommend it for you, the three good features highlighted above are enough to make this game stand out on it's own, however it fails horrifically as a sequal in the Fallout franchise.

Back in the day, Bethesda were known for janky, unpolished RPGs with a lot of depth and engaging stories. The flaws were largely forgiven, as the game was engaging enough that a horse clipping through the ground, or even the occasional CTD were overlooked by a playerbase looking for a really great RPG experience, and they were the closest thing to it.
What's more, due to the fairly robust nature of the engines, these games became known for the vibrant and varied modding community that sprang up around them. Fans of the game would spend hours of their time to fix and improve all the frequent problems that plagued these games, vastly improving the experience and elevating them from pretty good RPGs to great RPGs.
And then we get to Fallout 4. And man, how quickly things change. From a background of some pretty good stories, we get a watered down shell of an RPG, with the mechanics of a half-dozen other popular games crammed in for mass market appeal. We may not have more than four options during any conversation (Most of which boil down to Yes, Yes but snarky, Give me more information so I can say yes, or No, but really yes though), but we do have janky awkward base building that's pseudo-required for one of the endings!
An event that really sums it up is a point about halfway through, where you've infiltrated the main base of the antagonist faction and are in a room face to face with its leader. Keep in mind, this is a faction that's effectively spent the past 200 years actively ♥♥♥♥ing with the rest of the Commonwealth. Every single decision they make seems to be the most evil, despite the absence of any reasonable motives for it.
And so, you ask them, "Why?". Or rather, that's what any reasonable human being would ask. Your character, however, does not see this as a good use of his time. He's got far more important things to ask, like "How did you come to lead this faction". The antagonist goes on and on about how benevolent the faction is, and how it's truely humanities best hope. Meanwhile, your character has been traipsing around on a surface scarred by their presence. You've seen the damage they've done for no reason, and the fear that the population has of them. And yet, nothing to debate or refute them. Not an option, apparently, to call them out on their hypocritical ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. I think that's a reasonable reaction to have, personally.
And so, with the story tainted, the modders valiantly stepped into the breach, prepared to once again salvage a great experience out of a decent framework. But there's only so much you can do to fix the story. The main character is voiced, so they either have to scavenge around for voice lines that can be repurposed, or go entirely silent, breaking immersion when switching from modded dialog to unmodded. Nevertheless, they made great strides in patching up the gameplay and engine stability, and improving performance that was seriously lacking in the base game. With their hard work, this game became something truely worthy of playing.
Unfortunately, Bethesda decided that this would not do. All these improvements, all this content, and none of it providing income for them. And so, the Creation Club was born. Which is not paid mods, in case you were wondering, mainly because Bethseda says it isn't. It's just small chunks of content, developed by third party coders, that can be added to the base game, for a small fee. So, in ever way except the literal definitions of those words, they aren't paid mods. Promise.
Not only is this particular move scummy, but in usual Bethseda fashion they seem intent on causing it to fail rather than make themselves look bad. So, large story mods that rival DLCs (Which are arguably the best quality mods out there, and might indeed be worth a small amount) are prohibited in order to ensure that they don't "Overshadow the Bethesda developed DLCs". Meaning that, as expected, the Creation Club is full of nothing better than things you can already get for free from Nexus and other places. Certainly, nothing worth the money they're charging for it.
So why, if they are so lacking in value as to not be worth purchasing, am I up in arms? Mostly, as a statement. Years ago, once micro-transactions started making their way into the gaming mainstream, there were those that warned us that, if we didn't fight against them, they would be everywhere. But, they were small, and unimportant, and didn't really hurt the games they were in, so we let them slide. Now many games have some form of microtransactions in them, some worse than others. More recently, Overwatch introduced lootboxes, and after them a bunch of new games have come out with lootboxes in full purchase price games. Content that could once have been enjoyed for free became gated behind a paywall.
I can't stand to see that happen to mods. Mods can add so much value and replayability to the games that support them. Minecraft without mods would never have remained as popular as it is now. Plus, they exist as a testing ground for new ideas. Counterstrike came from a mod. So did DOTA, and from that the whole genre of MOBAs. Day Z wouldn't exist, for better or worse. If developers and publishers start demanding certain content, and only allowing through things that they want, suddenly all that creativity is stamped out. And I can't stand by and see that happen.
EDIT: I'll be damned. I didn't think it possible, but the've actually made this whole paid mods thing even worse. As it turns out, not only are the mods being downloaded directly to your hard drive whether or not you bought them, but they'll keep patching constantly as new mods get added. Not only will this massively bloat the size over time, but it also breaks Fallout 4 Script Extender, a utility that's practically required for modding the game, every time they come up with some more pointless paid mods. Meaning you have to wait for that mod author to come out with an update for that before you can actually go back to playing the game you bought.
Wow. That's bafflingly out of touch. This has now crossed the line by negatively impacting everyone, regardless of whether or not you actually bought into the paid mods. Instead of merely ignoring them, you can now expect a day or so's downtime every few weeks as they add more and more ancilliary and anti-consumer ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to an already mediocre game.

Before I say my opinions on fallout 4 I haven't played any other fallout games, but I have played the Elder Scrolls 3-5, so I had a pretty good idea of what to expect from Bethesda.
This is a very action focused game, which I get doesn't appeal to some rpg gamers, but was always the thing I liked about the Elder Scrolls games rather than boring Final Fantasy style turn based combat for example.
The VATS system is class! and definitely makes the fights varied and less 'shootery'. The rewarding perks system from Skyrim has made it into the game too, which makes leveling up much more satisfying than just getting +1 to a stat.
The much maligned side quests are not too bad. Yes, mostly they tend to be just slaughtering various enemy settlements, but that is still fun.
The voice acting has also copped some flak but I thought it made converations seem like actual conversations and was well performed by the cast. A critisism would be the lack of further conversation after the initial one which reduces companions to Morrowind levels of personality blandness. I kept the dog for company because he at least doesn't judge me!
I haven't played the main quest, because I usually lose a bit of motivation once the main story is done, so I can't comment on it.
For me the biggest issue is the ease of travel on a relatively small map. I'm missing Skyrim's amazing geography!, and I honestly can't see myself playing this for 2 years on one character like I did on that. It has the problem Oblivion had in that you can basically walk in a straight line across the map to your destination which kills some of the great feeling of exploration.
On character development - there really doesn't seem to be any. The Elder scrolls skill system that leveled up a stat as you used it isn't there, so I can't see how you would become a specific type of player ie sniper or close combat. You need all round fighting skills to deal with enemies at various ranges and difficulties. As far as factions go, there just seems to be the 'bad' guys versus you and the group you are currently with. Mass Effect did a much better job of combining a shooter and an RPG than this game.
The settlement building, while totally nonessential to the story, is great fun and really varied and entertaining.
Like the other Bethesda games I've played this is flawed brilliance, every time they edge closer to the perfect game they can't follow through with all their ideas and over-promise and under-deliver. But it's a funny game and I've had a good laugh with friends about things we've done in the game. Would recommend just for the brilliant combat by the way!

--- Revised Edition ---
*Note* I had a longer review previously, but couldn't fit it into the steam review's character limit, so I tried to dumb it down a bit so that the main points would fit.
*Second Note* Please feel free to leave comments, I am new to writing reviews and would love feedback to get better!
---
Pretty much everybody knows what Fallout is, but for those of us who live under rocks and haven't really played a Fallout game before, it is a postapocalyptic first person shooter RPG. I played New Vegas as my first foray into the worlds of steam and Fallout, back when I was focused only on the main story and did little else, so for all intents and purposes this review will be from the point of view of a newcomer to the Fallout franchise.
--- The Good ---
Bethesda games are known for building an immersive world where the player can dive in and be whoever they want for hours on end, and Fallout 4 is no exception. The player can go on a wide variety of paths, from pot shotting with a sniper rifle, to guns blazing with an assault rifle, to charging people with power armor and a baseball bat, to being suave and charming the people and the fauna to fight for you. The world of the Boston area Commonwealth is your oyster, and the main story does a good job of showing the player much of what is available.
Modification and customization are quite extensive in Fallout 4. Every weapon and piece of clothing/armor (including power armor and vault suits) can be modified, from improving recoil to exponentially increasing damage output to rendering certain types of damage nearly useless against you to having super crazy colored power armor that somehow increases your stats (I guess the paint got some kind of "good" radiation). Higher level mods can even change the ammo type of certain weapons, which not only increases damage output, but can be nice when you're running low on your favorite ammo but haven't found a use for your stockpile of .50 caliber rounds yet.
The key cog that makes everything work is the perk tree. There are 10 perks per S.P.E.C.I.A.L. stat, for a grand total of 70 (77 if you include the ability to use a perk to improve a stat), and almost all of them are extremely useful. This is where you are able to make your character really good at creating mods for certain weapons, specialize in certain weapons, reduce or reverse certain negative effects (such as radiation from swimming and eating), get better at cracking passcodes and locks, and so on. Normally things like this can be cumbersome because certain abilities are quite obviously much better than everything else, but FO4 does a good job of making every perk useful in a myriad of situations.
The base building concept is extremely exciting to me. The player can take scrap from any and every item they run across and repurpose it to build settlements where people will live, farm, trade, and fight off raiders, all for you.
The companions make the world really come alive. They are the only people in the game that you really and truly get to know, and can be useful when you need to haul a massive load of scrap back to a base to turn into caps or base improvements. There are quite a few of them (I think 13 but I'm not 100% sure, I only really used 3 but found 8-9), and at least Piper and Nick are quite interesting with their input about the world around them, as well as delving a little into their backstories.
--- The Bad ---
The main story, while not necessarily bad, can be quite annoying. There are 4 main factions vying for power, and while the player is able to join all 4, really only 1 group's questline can be completed. While this means quite a bit of replayability, this is a sandbox game, and there are no other factions to run through and finish their quest lines. You have main faction quests, a ton of side quests that are mostly isolated (there are a few quest chains, like the ones with Jack Cabot), and miscellaneous quests. Morrowind did it best by having 11 total factions, only 3 or 4 of which were really necessary for the plot. Having so few connected quests makes the game feel quite a bit smaller, even though the main quests themselves are quite fun.
The companions, again, are quite interesting, but also make the game somewhat frustrating. For one, there are very few other characters that you interact with at much length, outside of maybe the Brotherhood of Steel and/or the Institute leaders. Now, as the name "companion" implies, you will be spending quite a lot of time with them, and they will generally be the only interesting thing that you aren't shooting or looting or exploring. There is a built in "like" system where each companion either likes, loves, or hates certain actions, from certain conversation choices (which is reasonable) to whether you steal something from somebody (also somewhat reasonable) to opening a lock while exploring areas (like... what?). Seriously, why should I be penalized for opening a lock to get some extra loot? This makes 0 sense (granted I used Piper and she liked it, but the point still stands). I shouldn't have to limit my choice of companion based on whether or not I want to open locked containers in a raider base.
Certain things to do with modification and settlement building are quite rough around the edges. When building settlements, there is no way to redo a landscape (AFAIK), so that destroyed road is going to stay there, and so are those shrubs, and the house that I wanted to build is gonna be all kinds of lopsided because the land isn't even. Meanwhile, making the best water purifier is really bad because it makes too much water to use and exponentially increases the necessary defenses. Some components are also extremely annoying to get (e.g. oil, nuclear material) either because they are scarce (reasonable) or because anything that has them is stupidly heavy and only contains a single unit of said material (thanks, oil).
--- Summary ---
Overall, Fallout 4 is a very fun sandbox to play in for hours on end, and has quite a bit of replayability between the perk tree and how the main factions are split. The variety of weapons, armor, and modifications allows the player to take many different approaches to combat, so if at first you don't succeed, you can try, try again. Companions are quite helpful, but are more trouble than they're worth if they are completely opposite to certain objectives you want to accomplish (like picking locks). Lots of content, but the world can feel small due to a lack of non-main quest faction quests to do.
I give this game a 8.5/10 and would most definitely recommend this to anybody looking for a good game. I personally expect any and all issues to be fixed with either mods or expansions, both of which are pillars of Bethesda games.
