After some hours spent on the game I believe it's time to say something about.
I must say I'm really enjoying this game, the new crafting and upgrade system is brilliant, the new gunplay feels good and smooth the new color palette is beautiful and the models (objects, structures etc.) are really detailed.
However there are good and bad things, and there are some things that I didn't like at all.
To make it all clear I will make the usual  Good/ Bad columns
The good:
-Graphics: one of the less important things imho, for me graphics count at maximum for a 20% of a game but I am really tolerant,  I find Fallout 4's graphics a big improvement from Fallout 3/NV; is it really great? Nope but it's good and does well the job.
-Gunplay: It simply feels good, it's satisfying and responds really well compared to previous titles.
-Crafting/upgrade system: Fresh air, I mean, you can have a full laser-based arsenal (laser pistol, automatic laser pistol, rifle, sniper rifle, shotgun....). It's definitely good and it's a smart thing which fits well in the post-apocalyptic scenario. Ps. the armor upgrades also seem good (especially those of Power Armor), but I didn't really try those so I can't say more.
-Power armor: Simply love it, love the new role it has (no more a powerful armor you can always use), love the models, the UI....LOVE IT. I also understand the lore problems it creates....but we are going to talk about it in a sec.
-Locations: there are a lot of them (as in previous titles), exploration is really encouraged and in some of these areas (some are completely optional) you can find important lore and connections to some smaller story or quests.
-Lore and immersion: If you search it you will find good lore hints and info, some places give you a real Fallout feel. (this is more neutral: you really need to dig a lot to find some)
-Balanced difficulty (Default): the base difficulty is fair, enemies are not so strong but behave better than in F3/NV and some are more aggressive (ghouls for example)
-Great soundtrack (no radio): The base soundtrack is good and immersive, some tracks also reminds me Fallout and Fallout 2 soundtrack...Brilliant!
The Bad:
-Skyrim (or where did the RPG go?): This is BAD for a Fallout game, it isn't even more a real RPG, yes there are some perks, you choose some statistics etc. but that's all.
Stats don't matter anymore: are you stupid as a rock? No problem you won't have some perks...that's all. I remember when you played a low int character in Fallout and Fallout 2: He couldn't even talk, he couldn't do some quests and simple tasks and the dialogues were completely different. Here it doesn't matter.
-Dialogues: Why? Why that stupid, useless, imprevedible dialogue wheel?
-Story: can't say much (I usually do the main quest at the end after playing 70-100h. It didn't seem brilliant to this point and I HATED the fact that I'm not roleplaying, I'm just carrying around the fat♥♥♥♥♥of a character that is not mine. During the main quest I figured out a thing (and I think everyone did) but I could not do anything because "my" character did not, so I had to sit and listen to a stupid dialogue full of bulls**t. THIS IS BAD.
-"Convenience": Some things in the game seem so conveniently placed and simply stupid in the story..."Help us please, take that conveniently placed Power armor..."  "We know each other since yesterday but you helped me in a task I could do by myself...take my personalized and special weapon"   "look! this is the third Fat Man with a bunch of mininukes next to it that I find today, how "lucky"".
-No need to repair weapons: "People of the Commonwealth, from now on you won't need to repair your weapons anymore thanks to MAGIC!". This is stupid...you find weapons 200y old, or weapons made with pipes, wood, screws and other trash, but hey thanks to magic and radiation now every weapon is indestructible.
-Where did all the improvements made in NV go? NV had its downsides but had some great things in it (hardcore mode,bullet diversity, damage threshold...)
-Legendary enemies and loot: Nope...simply nope, don't like it, it's plain stupid. "we could add some special enemies that are stronger..." (bullet sponge yeah)  "great idea, and they should drop some magical piece of gear that makes no sense at all!"
"Woah you are a genius, let's work on it!". Please explain me some of the effects of these drops...I could understand things like that in Skyrim where magic was involved but here is plain nonsense.
-Porting
-BUGS and glitches (to be fair I did not find many game-breaking bugs, but they still are REALLY annoying, and too many)
I like this game but I'm a bit afraid Fallout is becoming too much of a Shooter game than a RPG and this is not good.
I'm tired of games made simplier just to appeal kids and casual gamers to sell more copies; The game however is good but not good as it could (or should if they actually learnt something from Obsidian) be.

After some hours spent on the game I believe it's time to say something about.
I must say I'm really enjoying this game, the new crafting and upgrade system is brilliant, the new gunplay feels good and smooth the new color palette is beautiful and the models (objects, structures etc.) are really detailed.
However there are good and bad things, and there are some things that I didn't like at all.
To make it all clear I will make the usual  Good/ Bad columns
The good:
-Graphics: one of the less important things imho, for me graphics count at maximum for a 20% of a game but I am really tolerant,  I find Fallout 4's graphics a big improvement from Fallout 3/NV; is it really great? Nope but it's good and does well the job.
-Gunplay: It simply feels good, it's satisfying and responds really well compared to previous titles.
-Crafting/upgrade system: Fresh air, I mean, you can have a full laser-based arsenal (laser pistol, automatic laser pistol, rifle, sniper rifle, shotgun....). It's definitely good and it's a smart thing which fits well in the post-apocalyptic scenario. Ps. the armor upgrades also seem good (especially those of Power Armor), but I didn't really try those so I can't say more.
-Power armor: Simply love it, love the new role it has (no more a powerful armor you can always use), love the models, the UI....LOVE IT. I also understand the lore problems it creates....but we are going to talk about it in a sec.
-Locations: there are a lot of them (as in previous titles), exploration is really encouraged and in some of these areas (some are completely optional) you can find important lore and connections to some smaller story or quests.
-Lore and immersion: If you search it you will find good lore hints and info, some places give you a real Fallout feel. (this is more neutral: you really need to dig a lot to find some)
-Balanced difficulty (Default): the base difficulty is fair, enemies are not so strong but behave better than in F3/NV and some are more aggressive (ghouls for example)
-Great soundtrack (no radio): The base soundtrack is good and immersive, some tracks also reminds me Fallout and Fallout 2 soundtrack...Brilliant!
The Bad:
-Skyrim (or where did the RPG go?): This is BAD for a Fallout game, it isn't even more a real RPG, yes there are some perks, you choose some statistics etc. but that's all.
Stats don't matter anymore: are you stupid as a rock? No problem you won't have some perks...that's all. I remember when you played a low int character in Fallout and Fallout 2: He couldn't even talk, he couldn't do some quests and simple tasks and the dialogues were completely different. Here it doesn't matter.
-Dialogues: Why? Why that stupid, useless, imprevedible dialogue wheel?
-Story: can't say much (I usually do the main quest at the end after playing 70-100h. It didn't seem brilliant to this point and I HATED the fact that I'm not roleplaying, I'm just carrying around the fat♥♥♥♥♥of a character that is not mine. During the main quest I figured out a thing (and I think everyone did) but I could not do anything because "my" character did not, so I had to sit and listen to a stupid dialogue full of bulls**t. THIS IS BAD.
-"Convenience": Some things in the game seem so conveniently placed and simply stupid in the story..."Help us please, take that conveniently placed Power armor..."  "We know each other since yesterday but you helped me in a task I could do by myself...take my personalized and special weapon"   "look! this is the third Fat Man with a bunch of mininukes next to it that I find today, how "lucky"".
-No need to repair weapons: "People of the Commonwealth, from now on you won't need to repair your weapons anymore thanks to MAGIC!". This is stupid...you find weapons 200y old, or weapons made with pipes, wood, screws and other trash, but hey thanks to magic and radiation now every weapon is indestructible.
-Where did all the improvements made in NV go? NV had its downsides but had some great things in it (hardcore mode,bullet diversity, damage threshold...)
-Legendary enemies and loot: Nope...simply nope, don't like it, it's plain stupid. "we could add some special enemies that are stronger..." (bullet sponge yeah)  "great idea, and they should drop some magical piece of gear that makes no sense at all!"
"Woah you are a genius, let's work on it!". Please explain me some of the effects of these drops...I could understand things like that in Skyrim where magic was involved but here is plain nonsense.
-Porting
-BUGS and glitches (to be fair I did not find many game-breaking bugs, but they still are REALLY annoying, and too many)
I like this game but I'm a bit afraid Fallout is becoming too much of a Shooter game than a RPG and this is not good.
I'm tired of games made simplier just to appeal kids and casual gamers to sell more copies; The game however is good but not good as it could (or should if they actually learnt something from Obsidian) be.
Overall it's an average shooter game in a post-apocalyptic setting: 6,5/10
As a Fallout RPG game is, sorry to say, Garbage/10 (4/10)

Being new to the fallout series (shame on me) I wasn't at all excited for the release of fallout 4. Having picked up Fallout 3 GOTY and vegas in some steam sale of the past, my vague memory of those games is playing for 10 minutes before turning off.
Probably because I played over the last few years, when those games only looked ok whenever they were released in the distant past.
So fallout 4, best RPG of the year? Yup (sorry witcher 3).
Positive:
-No crashes so far
-Graphics are nice, think GTA V PC first person mode.
-Runs well on a 290x, 1600p
-Building settlements, surprising depth
-Character customisation, weapons, armor, perks, actions.
-Vastness of the game
-Game mechanics will have the obsessive compulsive type living in Nirvana. Everything has *some use
-Grinding doesn't feel like a grind, i just need to play 1 more hour to get this done.......oh just one more hour to fix that.... the game is a time sink, in a good way.
-You really can do your own thing, I spent a lot of time doing settlement parts, only progressing slightly in the story now
-Being unfamiliar with the fallout world it can be a bit daunting at first, but ultimately very satisfying
-Dynamic time and weather is lovely
-Mech Suits
-Pretty tight gunplay for an RPG
Negative:
-Loading times can be a bit longer than one would expect
-Some silly glitches
-Not being able to fast travel when carrying too much gear is a pain
-Some more in depth tutorials on some of the games mechanics would have been nice
-Witcher 3 puts the game to shame graphically
-Performance isn't great considering the graphics but will hopefully improve over time
Overall I will give it a 9/10.

Fallout 4 is probably one of the most amazing games I have ever played. I have put in over 70 hours at this point, and I haven't even finished any quest lines, explored everything, or gotten every weapon or armor piece. I am in love with this game. It is Bethesda's masterpiece thus far, exceding Skyrim for me which is a huge surprise honestly. I love both Fallout and the Elder Scrolls, but Fallout 4 is definitely their best title so far.
-The game runs smooth as butter on my GTX 970 on Ultra settings, coupled with my i5 4690k @ 4.5GHz, and 16GB of RAM.  I dip below 60 FPS occasionally if I'm in a huge battle, or standing atop a tall building, but nothing lower than around 45, and it's only momentarily. It's a consistant 60 FPS all around.
-The gameplay is amazing, with some changes from Fallout 3 as well as some new features. The only con that I have encountered so far is the dialogue system is a bit shallow, offering no real "choice", every option seems to lead to the same result, with a few exceptions. Other than that, this game is a solid 9/10 from me, and that's a big deal coming from me, as I'm usually very harsh on rating games. But this one is a gem, Game of the Year guaranteed, and guaranteed to suck your life from your corpse.

Did I like Fallout3 and New Vegas? Yes.
Do I agree with all of the decisions Bethesda made with Fallout 4? No.
Do I still like Fallout 4? Definitely.
Sure, Bethesda removed some well-established mechanics and I don't like it either, but I still think that the game is definitely good and I'd rather judge the game as a whole than nit-pick about small parts of it. I was hyped for the game, however, I'm not one to expect the game to be a specific way and hold it to that. I'm not required to hate this game because I enjoyed previous ones.
Pros:
+Unlike other open-world games(especially others released this year), there's actually consistantly-good level design here. The better the level design, the funner the world is to explore just for the sake of exploring.
+Combat mechanics are solid and work well.
+Settlements provide for an interesting play experience. You have more customization with building houses than in Skyrim's Hearthfire.
+The games lighting system provides absolutely great atmosphere at times.
+Changes to power armor give more weight(no pun intended) to the decision of using it. Power armor is actually functionally a type of exosuit this time, not just more powerful armor.
+Has the usual areas in Fallout games that have individual stories to them, in which you gradually uncover information about what happened there in the past.
+The ability to customize weapons and armor is a great new feature.
+Filled with easter eggs and secrets.
+Probably the least buggy Bethesda release yet(at least in my experience).
Neutral/Mixed:
~Voiced protagonists aren't bad, but there are only two voices, one for each gender. I would have preferred an approach similar to what Saints Row 3&4 did(three different voices for each gender).
~The ability to upgrade S.P.E.C.I.A.L. stats allows you to do more as one character but negatively impacts replayability.
Cons:
-The Karma and reputation systems are
. I loved these in 3 and NV and I really miss it. Bethesda could have improved these systems and made them greater but, instead, scrapped them.
-Skills are gone and are merged with the perks to make something similar to Skyrim's perk trees. This takes out a layer of character customization and streamlines things a bit much.
-The character creation system is unintuitive. I preferred sliders, where I could keep a mental checklist on what aspects I've changed on my character.
-Dialog system isn't great and you don't get a multitude of options like in previous games. You basically just get options for "explain further", "yes", "no", "maybe"(functionally the same as "no"), and "sarcasm"(good luck trying to predict what your character's going to say there). Sometimes, all four dialog options basically have your character say the same thing in different ways. There also aren't dialog options that are available at certain skill and stat requirements either.
-Your character is no longer a blank slate. Who they are is already there(and "who" they are is boring, too), which takes the fun out of trying to make a character yours.
-The game's engine isn't significantly improved from what was used in Skyrim.
It may have not been the jaw-droppingly great game that some
wanted, and it may not be as good as Fallout 3 and New Vegas, but this was definitely still a good game. Fortunately, I didn't have the same extremely high expectations that a few other players have had.
I'm sure that, once the GECK for Fallout 4 comes out, there will be mods that turn this into a great game.

Overall, I think it's a solid game worth the entertainment value.  I am a fan of the Fallout Lore and I'm always happy to play a game that expands on it.  With that in mind, here are some Pros and Cons;
(Early game spoiler alert)
Pros:
- I think the game looks great graphically and don't really understand why some people are complaining about it.  I have mine set to Ultra settings and everything looks beautiful and runs pretty well.  (with the exception of atleast one location that I know of that has too many graphical glitches to be worth going to)
- The story seems good to me.  Every story can't be the same and this is just a new part of the lore.
- The gun play has been improved and it's noticable.  Since they decided to take the series into an FPS direction, they definitely needed to strengthen that aspect since 3 and NV and I think they did.
- Power Armor... lots and lots of Power Armor.  I love it.
- Good world size
Cons:
- The settlement system is cool at first but begins to feel like it's not complete.  There doesn't feel like there is any incentive to it.  I do love the fact that all that useless junk now has a purpose (since I grab everything) however in the end, you're just building stuff.  I would like to see it have more meaning.  If I'm going to be a faction leader and unite the Commonwealth, well damnit, I want to set up a headquarters and be able to assign local leaders (or elections) to each settlement so they can run it.  I shouldn't have to point to a settler and point to something and say do that, I've got more important stuff to do.  This aspect could definitely add a strategy element to the game that I could run from my headquarters (again, if I was able to establish one).  I would be able to log into a terminal and set up supply routes and check the status of and issue orders to not only my settlements, but my faction military forces.  I'm supposedly a faction leader but I see some of my troops patroling the commonwealth and yet I know nothing about them.  I don't mean on a micro scale, but macro scale.  Just a thought to expand in that direction.  Also, all of this should be optional.  Maybe I could assign and individual to run EVERYTHING so I could go about my RPG ways and play through the story.
- There are also almost too many settlements for not being able to macromanage it.
- I should be able to issue power armor out to my faction (see above)
- The weapons and armor crafting is somewhat cool but it doesn't feel like I can actually create my own stuff.  I shouldn't have to find a base model on the ground somewhere to be able to craft a leather armor piece
- The SPECIAL and Perk system doesn't feel RPGish to me.  I feel like I'm not trying to develop my character but simply wasting Perk skills on crafting stuff.  I'm about level 20 at this point and I don't feel like I've developed my character like a true RPG should be doing.
- The choices you make don't matter.  It's not like SW:KOTOR or ME series.  You're made to be the good guy and that's what you'll be.  This isn't a terrible thing for me because that's what I normally end up doing anyway but maybe someone else wants to create a tyrannical Commonwealth, it's just not going to happen.
In summary, the game and series still has room to improve but this is definitely worth the money in my opinion and I'll definitely put my time into it.  None of the "Cons" are game killers and I still enjoy playing this game.

I wouldn't call myself a huge Fallout fan, but I have played 3 and New Vegas, and I loved both, especially New Vegas. The series has simply amazing worlds for me to explore, and its modding community is virtually unparalleled in the RPG genre (unless you count the Elder Scrolls, made by the same devs with the same engine).
From the start, Fallout 4's story really drives in the point that this one is personal. The first stage actually takes place in 2077, shortly before the nuclear bombs fall during the Great War. You choose to play as either a mother or a father of a young infant, Shaun. You, your spouse, and Shaun are living a quiet and peaceful American dream in a Boston suburb. Suddenly, Vault-Tec comes to your door and informs you that you and your family have been selected to become residents of Vault 111. The timing is perfect, because right afterwards, the bomb sirens sound, and everyone high tails it to Vault 111 in the nick of time, as Boston gets nuked. I should add that I have family in Boston and travel there every once in a while, so the Boston setting felt like a really cool novelty.
Inside Vault 111, you, your spouse, and Shaun enter cryogenic freezing pods, ostensibly to remain preserved until it's safe to get out. But an unknown amount of time later, you briefly regain consciousness long enough to see mysterious people murder your spouse and take Shaun away, before slipping back into cryo-sleep. Sometime after that, you regain consciousness yet again and this time escape the cryo pod, only to discover that all the other cryo pod residents died from malfunctioning systems, and everyone else in the Vault is also dead. You find some weapons and a Pip-Boy, and enter the surface world to face the dangers of wasteland life in 2277, with the ultimate goal of finding Shaun.
Speaking of the Pip Boy, if you have an Android, iOS, or Windows Phone device (which you probably do), GET THE APP! It integrates seamlessly with Fallout 4 (make sure your PC is on the same LAN as your phone or tablet) and you can manage your inventory, switch weapons, use aids, manage quests, and interact with the map, without having to pause the game. I do recommend using a tablet over a phone if possible just for the bigger screen. Also plug in your charger because the app is a serious battery hog. I hope more games include similar features in the future! Every minute of the 60+ hours I've spent in the game has included the use of the Pip Boy on my Android tablet.
The gameplay is not changed much from the older games, which is just as well - if it ain't broke don't fix it. You still have VATS to target your enemies (or you can just treat it like a normal FPS), you still have to worry about carrying too much weight, you can fast travel between discovered places with the Pip Boy map, etc.
The enemies are mostly the same - human raiders, ghouls, super mutants, mirelurks, mole rats, and other mutated wildlife, plus a new group called the Synths (robots who look like humans, aka Terminators). You can give them nice gory deaths (including dismemberment, or the body just plain exploding into pieces, or the body turning into ash and goo) with a sweet variety of melee weapons and firearms (including mini-nuke launchers, laser weapons, plasma weapons, and even a gun that launches balls of radiation!).
There will be many humans and ghouls who are decent enough to not shoot at you on sight, and they will be the ones whom you will befriend (or betray, if you wish), and whom you will perform quests for. You will also come across a few individuals who can be recruited as companions (sadly only one at a time, though you can freely switch between them at will without consequences), and they will provide some nice supporting dialogue, and you can even romance them, Mass Effect style (also romances give you XP bonuses). Speaking of romances, I have to give it to Bethesda for being inclusive of the LGBT community - whether you're male or female, you can romance any companion of either gender (except for robotic ones and the dog). It seems like while society has completely broken down after the nuclear war, people have become completely tolerant of LGBT lifestyles and don't bat an eyelid at same-sex relationships. Maybe the apocalypse isn't so bad after all!
Along the way, you can build settlements - basically safe farming havens for humans and ghouls to just live and work safely. This is a fun addicting minigame that sees you building houses, furniture, and defense systems, and planting crops and building water/power infrastructure, in an effort to keep all settlers happy. You need materials to make all these things, and often they can be acquired by hoarding all the random junk you find in the open world and scrapping it. Now you have a real reason to collect all those glass cups, teddy bears, and other crap. I personally loved this aspect of the game. Building/maintaining settlements is totally optional, so if you don't like it, just don't do it!
A few factions also have "repeatable" quests, where you rescue kidnapped settlers, clear out scum from nearby areas, or find junk for others to use. These quests never "end" - once you finish the objective, another similar one appears in a different location. Completing these quests is not mandatory to advance, but it's a good way to unlock more areas in the open world for fast travel, and also to grind for XP and accumulate bottlecaps and ammo. I spent at least 20 hours grinding XP and hoarding supplies through these missions, which made the main storyline much easier once I got back to it. Again, if you find these repeatable quests annoying, just don't do them.
Sounds great? You bet. But this didn't come without a few flaws.
The most jarring change from previous Fallout titles is the conversation mechanics. In previous games, you had a list of sentences, each sentence containing the exact words to be spoken, and with certain "persuasion" options showing a percent chance of success (higher if you had sufficient intelligence and charisma perks). Now, you get only four options, and you choose from summary words, Mass Effect style, so you may sometimes say something different from what you intended. You also lose the percent chance indicator for persuasion options. There is a mod to replace the summary words with the full text, but it still feels disappointing as having only 4 options makes conversations more limited and predictable. On the bright side, everything your character says includes full audio (unlike previous games) which makes things more immersive.
Dialogue generally feels like it's not that well written, especially compared to the masterpiece that is New Vegas. I guess Obsidian (who handled New Vegas development) is better at writing than Bethesda's internal studio is.
Diplomacy is basically non existent now. Every faction seems to hate one another and there's no way to persuade everyone to cooperate and form a truce - this was something I loved about New Vegas. 3 of the 4 endings are basically the same thing too! It hints at laziness in the writing of the plot. Now, I get that writing different endings for RPGs is a lot of work but hey, you had SEVEN YEARS to make this game, and you basically reused the engine which saved you some work...
On the technical side, things are ok, but not great. Controls reek of console-port and the modding community will no doubt step in for this. Performance on my GTX760 is a solid 60fps on ultra 1080p - note that you HAVE to lock the game to 60fps or else some framerate-dependent mechanics like lockpicking will not work properly. The Gamebryo engine really shows its age with stiff animations, washed out textures, and last-gen lighting, but at least it's mod friendly. Hopefully Fallout 5 will truly be next gen.
Verdict: Fun, worth buying, but don't get your hopes too high.

Fallout meets Borderlands meets Mass Effect. Does it work? Yes it does! While some of the mechanics that made FO3 popular have been simplified or removed, the most important things are still there: superb writing and missions, a huge wasterland to explore and beautiful graphics and music. Combat and crafting have been improved vastly, and while the AI is still as dumb as in any other Bethesda game, the shooting is simply put FUN and never gets tiresome due to the variety of weapons and enemies.
I loved Fallout 3, New Vegas yet still love this game. In my opinion, this is Bethesda's best game. If you liked Mass Effect or Borderlands and restrain from being a "Fallout purist", you will love this.

Simply put, if this game wasn't sold as a Fallout title and instead marketed as a stand-alone title, I would be pleased with it. However, given the linear style that majority of this game adheres to, and the bare-bones representation of the organizations and factions that struggle to survive in the Wastes, I have to say this doesn't do the Fallout franchise much praise.
Karma system is gone, thrown out the window. The Perk system has replaced the Skills system, relying purely on S.P.E.C.I.A.L. and you're able to max out every S.P.E.C.I.A.L. stat in the game. Played long enough, every Sole Survivor will have all the same Perks and S.P.E.C.I.A.L. stats as any other that's played as long as that one. Traits are completely removed, and there's nill to nigh for special, unique perks rewarded based on the adventures your character survives through. The RPG elements that exist are only there so it can claim it's sticking to the roots of Fallout, when in reality it's just cheap makeup thrown over a black-eye.
Quests have basically been gutted out and turned upside-down. Radiant quests are used to replace the variety and creativity that comes with each quest striving to be unique and different. Interactions with NPCs feel boring and lack any stimulation, with no real sense of an economy in this world at all. They attempt to remedy this by letting you build your own seettlements all over, interlink them together, and create your own thriving, wide-spanning community, but this is missing all the vital aspects of the roleplaying element. Just nameless NPCs that do whatever you tell them, wear whatever you want them to, and fight with whatever you give them. Might as well just made everyone into robots.
The only thing that saves this game is the action and combat. It's much better than the previous takes the Fallout franchise has made in the attempt to incorperate a shooting element into the mechanics of the game. They focused on this a great deal and completely removed all the other elements that makes a Fallout game a Fallout game, though. Sure, you can spend hours killing stuff. You can do that in any other game, too.
The atmosphere has the right look. The idea of a dying world, left in the wake of humanity's own demise. Wonders and wastes mingling together from the Pre-War era, creating a brand new kind of Hell-hole. However, the feel is missing. You don't really get the sense that people are living, fighting, and pushing to survive. You don't see the same results that are showing up in the far West of the Wastes, instead every little thing depends on the Sole Survivor. Without this character, only one event would occur in all actuality. Brotherhood of Steel versus the Syndicate. All the other branches, all the other little communities and groups would just be small shadows against these two, and even their own direction and progress seems entirely rooted in the actions of the Sole Survivor.
The game its self is linear in mechanics and action, however the story its self is actually circular. Every route leads to the same result: one major faction on top, the others are ruined and wasted, with one minor group that the Sole Survivor controlls being used as an accessory to the story. There is no impacting difference from the side quests. There's no real hub or community aside from the ones the Sole Survivor creates, besides the one city in the game and one little trading post. The world is barren, and if you ignore every settlement and little side quest, you'll see no impact on the world's end scene what-so-ever as compared to doing a 100% completion.
If this wasn't marketed as a Fallout game, it would've been a good game. However, because it was made to be the a game in a long-standing franchise, it has standards to live up to. It has to adhere to certain principles. It failed to do that for me.

Fallout 4 puts you in the position of being a soldier from before The War, frozen cryogenically and then thawed on a vengeful rescue mission.  On the way, you'll need to save the residents of the Commonwealth (formerly, Boston) again and again - or despoil them for a few extra coin.
Graphics are amazing.  Even if Bethesda decided to use the same engine that they had in Skyrim, they managed to polish it up quite nicely.
Voiced character gives a bit more immersion, and the crafting system allows for plenty of weapons and armor customization.
"Settlement" crafting is strangely addictive.  Modular construction typical for sandbox games (Minecraft, Space Engineers, etc) allows players to build new bases in the Commonwealth wasteland.  In my own experience, and in plenty of others, this is the major time sink for the game; expect to spend hours on hours building a base, then moving to the next and doing it again.  Quests?  What quests?  Oh, right.
Poor optimization and controls, limited music lists, companion AI strangeness, and weirdly out-of-place UI sounds (such as the "Idiot Savant" proc).
UI design focused around consoles, and unchanged for PC users, meaning some limited dialogue responses that restrict the RPG element.
Story was a little lacking compared to previous titles in the series.
Bugs.  And not the giant, radioactive kind.  Expect save game losses, error-message free crashes to desktop, and the occasional bout of major stuttering lag.  Seeing how bad it can get on an i7, with 32Gb RAM and a Radeon 960, I'd expect lower systems may suffer the occasional hernia from the memory leaks.  Major graphics glitches are reported by ATI players.
hosts a bounty of fresh modding for all your enhancing needs; whether you want it to run on older systems with lower graphics, or if you want to get the bug fixes that traditionally Bethesda leaves for their community to patch, that would be the first place to head.

I have played this game for 82 Hours at this point.
Apart from the drastically different skills allocation system and the better melee and attacks, this game is... boring, I find it hard to become the character as I'm forced to take a back seat in this character's story, he talks when I should just be reading my responses and feeling as if I'm telling the NPC the sentence I just read in my head.
Sure it's fun to blow people's faces off with a sawn off shotgun but every quest I've done except the "Find Shaun" quest has had almost no flavour whatsoever. I expected there to be shady dealings with the mayor and synths or something like that, so I looked for a quest, "Go see Abbot at the Wall", I wondered what secrets I might uncover, however the quest was really "Go and get some Green Paint", this is but one of the many, many dissapointing fetch quests. There could have been so, so much more depth to this game, New Vegas always had really deep story plots, like how the White Glove society are really a pack of cannibals, everyone had a story, you could actually fail at a mission in NV and F3.
There is a Mining site, Dunwich Borers, with the Terminals stating the obviously lacking Health and Safety regard for their workers. After you're done murdering the Raiders inside, there's a chained off door you can venture through, suddenly ghouls descend on you and attack you but as you progress, Dmitry Glukhovsky, Metro Style ghost flashbacks start happening. And then you reach a small area with more ghouls except these ones are named, is it going to be some sort of story behind this? Apart from the sometimes well placed objects and the various skeletons in hilarious positions, there's not much substance, the whole game feels like a COD style rail shooter, except you walk from one train track to the next while getting murdered by flying glitchy as ♥♥♥♥ Radscorpions, bullet sponge insects and the molotov throwing raiders and gunners who would put a professional baseball fielder to shame.

Fallout 3 is one of Bethesda's best RPG of all time making the sequel a lot to live up to but it does AS a shooter but not an RPG.
Fallout 4 is still a good game but as a sequel to one of Bethesda's top games it's just short of a masterpiece because it's simply not a good RPG.
What Fallout 4 does right is its shooting mechanics making it feel like a well-polished FPS than Fallout 3 ever was. The Open-World is as good as ever and the many adventures you experience is just as good.
What Fallout 4 does wrong is its RPG elements. Decisions and Outcomes, Simplified leveling system and shorten dialogue. F3 and NV there were many different outcomes to one quest but in Fallout 4 there are barely any, With skills removed as well you barely feel like you're increasing your capabilities in the game, and the dialogue is shortened and limited a lot in this game effecting the questions you probably have about SOME of the unresolved locations, characters and questlines you experience. At the end of the day, you have to ask yourself whether is Fallout 4 a FPS Open-World game? Or a traditional Fallout RPG.
If you're looking for an open-world FPS with some RPG elements you're going to have a good time... but if you're looking for a good Fallout RPG you've come to the wrong place.
Fallout 4 is a good SHOOTER but a terrible RPG. You just can't have both according to Bethesda... maybe next Fallout?

A beta patch has made it so that you can rebind most of your keys and mouse buttons, which is a huge improvement over how it was on release.
There is still the problem of Vsync.  The engine this is built on has a lot of its calculations done based on frame times (this engine was originally used in Morrowind, it was okay back then but not now).  Vsync ruins your mouse input (on top of the game having dodgy mouse settings to begin with, though they can be edited out in the .ini's).  You can disable the Vsync, but this causes a whole heap of bugs in prettymuch every way, from things going too quickly to AI breaking to quests malfunctioning to items and enemies glitching out of maps.
As for the game itself, its really nice.  Its more shooter than any FO game yet (which is kind of wonky with the mouse issues, but kind of playable) but the setting and atmosphere are class, they have gotten rid of the horrible rigid dialogue from older games on the engine, and the item and township customisation are nice.
Its really kind of borderlands-ish, in that you get enchanted drops and grind for them.  This is kind of off putting, but it isnt overbearing like it is in other games with giant purple floating text all over the place and stuff like that.  Or at least thusfar it hasnt been, dont imagine it changing.

The gameplay mechanics. graphics, and audio are all universally improved over previous Fallout games, and while the map is significantly smaller than most, if not all of Bethesda's open-world titles, it feels much better to play through. Bugs and Glitches are fewer than most releases, albeit still present, and unfortunately the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of the Gamebryo engine, tweaked and modified to be called the Creation engine, is still used. Still, in all of these categories it feels like a step in the right direction for Fallout.
Where it falls overwhelmingly short is the story.
Bethesda's storylines are rarely the focus of their games, and are generally expected to fall short of true RPGs. That being said, Fallout 4's story went sideways very quickly. The first half of the story missions are actually gripping and more than enjoyable.
*Minor Spoiler in form of quest name*
It is around the quest "The Molecular Level" where that storytelling begins to fall through.
It is here where it is evident Bethesda looked at Obsidian's handling of Fallout: New Vegas and attempted to mimic the relative success Obsidian had with branching storytelling and choice & consequence, given their(Obsidian's) time and engine constraints.
However, Bethesda failed to properly grasp the correct way to handle these concepts, and ultimately ended up with a complete failure in storytelling. The initially promising choices you are given, are quickly railroaded and result in mindboggling instances of idiocy, where obvious and simple solutions are simply not present, and you are forced into uncomfortable decisions, presumably in an effort to spark emotion and drama, but done in a terrible, terrible way. These instances of the game drastically alter what up to that point had been an incredible experience, and ultimately pollute the remainder of the story.
The first 150 hours of this game were fantastic, it is the last ten where Bethesda♥♥♥♥♥♥the bed. That is an excellent ratio of Time:Enjoyment, and Time:Money Spent, and the reason I give this game a reccomendation. But outside of that, the story brings this down from what would be a solid 9/10 to a 3/10, at best.

People have demonstrated consistently since Fallout 4's release how dangerous expectations can be. To expect great things from the game, and to be disappointed when those expectations are not met, is quite normal. When judgement is rendered solely on the result of those expectations, the fatal mistake is made. It in turn leads to a propensity for jumping to conclusions, and from that point it's a rapid descent into ignorance.
Back when Fallout 4 was released, most of the Steam reviews consisted of incoherent, furious ranting that tarnished the whole title after only a few hours worth of gameplay. After being shocked by the overwhelming amount of negativity, I decided to make my own and openly condemned the bad reviews for what they were: baseless and devoid of perspective. It was quite obvious the authors made that fatal mistake, which is unfair to the many developers who put their soul and passion into creating the game.
In the end, Fallout fans will almost assuredly find disappointments with Fallout 4, as did I. But if the ignorance of the older reviews and reception of previous games ought to teach one thing, it's that those disappointments are no excuse for blind judgement or jumping to conclusions. If an opinion is to be rendered of this game in the form of review, let it be guided by reason and supported by logic. It is in the pursuit of that fairness and clarity that I chose to write this review.
----------------------------------------
Fallout 4 is a deeply enjoyable and well-crafted game.  However, it definitely has its issues. Bethesda tried new things in this title, some more ambitious than others, and not all of them were successful.
It's true that dialogue has been watered down as the devs chose to forgo text conversation choices in favor of a voiced and much more simplified dialogue wheel, which is further hampered by boring choices and weak voice work. Character advancements have been combined into a single perk/SPECIAL sheet. Settlement building, while certainly fun, is mostly aesthetic filler that has little impact on the game world. Side quests far too often amount to just killing some mandatory enemies, particularly with the Minutemen (who are supposed to be the "good guys" of this installment), and can become repetitive.
My most prominent grievance with Fallout 4 is the dialogue overhaul and removal of the karma system, which was completely unnecessary and not desired by a single player in existence. Unlike the previous flaws, this thoroughly irks me. I realized that this ties in to the primary weakness of Fallout 4: its lack of meaningful dialogue in comparison to most Bethesda titles. Far too often, your dialogue choices are short, shallow, meaningless, or all three.
The only choices that have any outcome are blatantly outlined as persuasion options, a lot of which only help you get some extra caps. It's not that you should be making major decisions all the time; the problem is that you, as a speaking character, now have a voice that carries no power. What you decide to say is almost always inconsequential. The dialogue system is highly reminiscent of Mass Effect except watered down; the reason it doesn't work in Fallout is that the two games have totally different approaches to conversation. The previous Fallout games had much better dialogue options because they meant something. Sometimes, your choice of words just made someone hate you, allowed you to entice or inspire others, or developed your reputation through the karma system. Now that karma is gone, your choices are just that much more pointless.
The bottom line is that Bethesda sacrificed a tremendous amount of RPG dialogue elements to accommodate full voice-work. While it was an ambitious attempt, it was an all-around mistake and it sticks out like a sore if you're a fan of Bethesda games or RPG's in general. The dialogue wheel system could have worked out just fine, but Bethesda carried it out in the wrong way.
----------------------------------------
All the aforementioned flaws are some of the most central complaints naysayers have about Fallout 4 and yet not a single one of them has been horrific enough to ruin my experience or let me down. Despite the few bugs I've come across, despite the certain questionable and sometimes idiotic design choices Bethesda made here, this game is still extremely well done. I still feel that incomparable thrill that only Fallout can bring.
Even though Fallout 4 falls extremely short on dialogue and all aspects associated with it, it's still an improvement over its predecessors in almost every other way imaginable. The game suffers some graphical issues like muddy textures and poor lighting at times, like any good Bethesda game, but it's still astoundingly beautiful and even breathtaking at times. Movement, melee, gunplay, and physics are better and smoother than they've ever been.
People were quick to judge the Commonwealth map based on its size and I was prepared to be disappointed as well, but it's surprisingly the best one Bethesda has whipped up thus far. The suburban locations are more organically dispersed and things become more compressed as you near the cities. Streets are narrow, buildings are tall, and locations are absolutely jam-packed alongside a ton of unmarked ruins and buildings you can enter. There are hardly any copy-pasted environments and they all show great attention to detail.
I was also worried that granting access to power armor and a minigun within the first thirty minutes of the game would be a huge balancing issue as well, but it really isn’t. Power armor relies on uncommon fusion cores for power and you’re not an unstoppable god while wearing the suit, especially not at higher difficulties or levels. You can acquire some strong weapons like the minigun or Fatman relatively early but finding sufficient ammo is another matter entirely.
----------------------------------------
Skyrim was a simplification of the Oblivion formula, but it was still a fantastic game. In much the same way, Fallout 4 is a simplification of the Fallout 3/New Vegas formula and is still extremely good. Even in light of its issues, this game has not been a disappointment at all. RPG elements can be enhanced through the wonderful modding community and will eventually make up for some of the game's weaker points, a perk of the PC version. Bethesda has, however, been on a recent trend of simplifying their games too much and I hope they change course.
Truthfully, the negative Steam reviews had me partly worried that I’d be disappointed but I chose to disregard them and arrive at my own opinion. I’ve learned that nearly every point of contention was blown out of context. The few issues that haven’t been redeemed in my eyes still pale in the face of the tremendous work that was done to bring this new and beautiful Fallout world to life. I have no doubt that the naysayers worked up their expectations to heights beyond reason, and it’s therefore no mystery that they hit the ground so hard afterwards. I chose to see Fallout 4 for what it is rather than what I expected or imagined it to be: a lovingly crafted game that, despite being marred by some of its shortcomings, has that same engaging splendor that far supercedes its flaws.
I highly recommend you try the game and approach it with a neutral and reasonable demeanor, and you won’t be disappointed.
----------------------------------------

So, after 140 hours - time to share some thoughts on the newest Bethesda game.
Fallout is, together with Battlefield MY gaming franchise. Most beloved, most played, most dear.
How to approach this, how to keep unbiased...?
Ok, game gets a thumbs up. Barely. Not becasue it's a Fallout game, becasue it's a good, good game. It is however, mediocre Fallout game. I could go on a rant or praise about so many things, that instead of wasting your time I'll just bulletpoint them. Remember, this are the bulletpoints for someone who played Fallout, by someone who played over 10 THOUSAND HOURS in all Fallout games together (mostly F1 and F2, tons of BoS, Lots of F3 and NV and now F4 + Pencil and Paper Fallout). If you have not played previous Fallout games, you will love this game if you like RPG's and open world games. You will love it from start to finish, and I do envy you.
Ok, so let's keep that spoiler free as much as I can.
The Good:
- Crafting system and random weapon drops: great improvement, makes resource gathering and keeping eyes open worth it. Surely the best change in F4.
- Improved Fast Travel system. You can travel from buildings most of the time, unless they are "instance in the instance". Makes life much easier.
- Combat. It works for both VATS and real time. It just works. Weapons have good feeling to them, high cal. weapons gave tons of oomph. There is a tangilbe progres (with a bit of redundancy though as most mods are strict upgrades in ballistic weapons)
- Followers. Although nothing stellar, some of them are quite funny or unique to be a lot of fun to have around.
The Mediocre:
- Main Story. While it's not bad, and even quite interesting at times, with some good space for your wild imagination, it's not anything spectacular. It just... Is. Coule of twitst, some engaging moments but overall did not get close enough to F1 of F2. Fairly in line with F3 and NV.
- NPCs. They are bland. Forget Harold level of awesome. Mundane, not very interesting characters. Yo uare doing quests for random nobodies that you don't give a toss about. NPCs are just a background and they are nowhere previous games colourful bunch. Also, they are quite odd at times - Two russian brothers managing a bar, while hilarious... how they got their russain accents 220 YEARS after the war? Some people act like they all lived before the bombs, while that's impossible in their case. Not speaking about that one particular great quest line.
- Factions. Paper thin and flat. Everyone knows BoS, they are nothing new. Other ones are just that, obvious story choices. No twist, no double sides...
- Base building. It is somewhat fun, but it feels unfinished and tacked on. Clipping issues, snapping issues, no way to say who you assigned to what resource. Mods will possibly fix that, but it does feel unfinished (but it IS addictive and will turn you into a hoarder). Also, it does not have any real impact on the game, it;s essentially a minigame in Fallout, nothing more.
- Character Development. I liked new Perks but all skills are gone. It was easy to just pick up the weapon and play, but it has much more impact. There are no skill based conversation rolls. Charisma is BE ALL END ALL conversation stat. Intelligence is almost only for hacking. No roll in conversation matters if you have 10 charisma - 100% success rate. This is a step backwards, and although it will surely be better for younger players, this is against Fallout nature.
The Bad:
- ENDING. Without spoiling anything I will jsut say they did Mass Effect 3 endings. 4 endings (low number as for a Fallout game) 3 being EXACTLY THE SAME CUTSCENES with different NPCs dependign on player faction choice... one that is different makes the game end so abruptly you're left with "wait, that's it?".
- Post Ending Story. Everyone that played Fallout knows we do paly for that still images with great narration at the end. To see what happens next, how our actions influenced the future. There is nothing like it here. You get a short cutscene with short narrative and NOTHING about the world. Mass Effect 3 all over again.
- Bugs are things that we expect from this series, but the inability of the game to properly function in 120+ FPS due to the fact that physics engine is tied to the framerate (as it always were in this engine) is abosutely unacceptable in 2015. That was ok when Skyrim came out, no one thought of running in in 120+FPS. Today we do. And it ends up breaking exiting the terminals taking away character control and forcing a reload of the save. You have to linit FPS to play the game.
- Textures. I play on Ultra. I have everything maxed - and the game looks ridiculously bad at times. Sure, outsides are great, there is a good atmosphere but look at that (this is not a "slow load" bug...)
There are textures with no bumpmapping, no shading, no tesselation, no NOTHING. Those are bad ported textures from previous Fallout games. This is absolutely sub-par. I can fix that myself, I can wrige my own shader for GMFX and make it look better. But why? What's next? Recording my own sound files?
Well, that's sums it up. If you have not played Fallout and you like RPG/Story/Open World games? This is a clear thimbs up, and a ticket to the amazing world and adventure. You're a fallout veteran? Well you already bought it. So, les just hope leassons of that release will not be lost to Bethesda.

Playing Fallout 4 is a joyous experience. Exploring and collecting loot is more rewarding than in Fallout 3 and the combat is great fun.
An important caveat: it takes time and effort before the game really gets going. Personally I was expecting to be wowed a bit more in the first two hours or so.
The ability to improve and customize weapons plays a big part in the latter. After a few hours of play and some effort, it's easy to create guns that suit a preferred playing style.
The world is filled with locations and quests and there is enough backstory to keep the game intriguing. The general design is interesting and pleasant. Some, if not most, simple side quests offer a lot of action.
The game has a few flaws. The animation isn't very good. This is a problem in conversations. The facial animation is both unconvincing and distracting and doesn't really convey emotion.
The mains story isn't bad in itself, but feels tagged on. After three traumatic experiences in the beginning of the game, experiences that would have broken most people, the protagonist seemingly shrugs any bad feelings of and continues to act as nothing has happened and nothing has changed. There is no sense of urgency and there are no emotional high and low points.
This is also true of relationships within the game. I had some fun flirting with my follower (I chose a female journalist and publisher named Piper) but at some point the relationship reached its conclusion and that was that. Mission accomplished and no consequences.
All this doesn't matter much, Fallout 4 is about exploring and experiencing a sense of wonder. But I do feel that the main story, in part because of poor execution, is a distraction rather than an asset. I would have preferred a character without a backstory. Or a better story that was told in a more convincing way.
The game looks pretty good, but a crisper look would have been appreciated. For various reasons the game looks a bit blurry. The fact that the FOV can't be changed is a bit disappointing.
As mentioned before, the world is filled with content, this is a huge game. But compared to games like The Witcher 3 and Bethesda's own Skyrim, Fallout 4 feels a bit small. It's an odd contradiction.
The optional settlement building is awkward. Yes, it's completely optional, but it feels underdeveloped and some functionality is missing.
Still, for me this is the game of the year. It's a great action RPG and a great open world game. Other games have better stories and tell them better, but the sheer fun I'm having playing Fallout 4 tips the scale for me.

Fallout 4 is definitely a fun game and I certainlyy enjoyed it.  It's not perfect, and I tend to agree with other reviewers who say that it is a simplified version of Fallout 3 or Fallout New Vegas (still my favorite Fallout game in the series to date).
The following observatons are my overall spolier-free feelings about the main aspects of the game:
1.  In all Fallout games I try to hold off as long as possible before ending the main quest.  In this case, I beat the main story line at level 48 and at just under 2 weeks of playing,  The setting, environments, etc were immerseive....Yet, the side quests you are then left with get sort of boring after awhile so my incentive to keep playing is not really that strong (for the record, I've now played it every day for a month since the initial release).  Perhaps earlier games ended for a reason.
2.  This Fallout by far has the most humanizing storyline and engaging moral dilemmas than the previous games.  But at the same time, I really didn't care that much about the main plot - I wanted to just explore more.
3.  Everyone seems to hate the graphics, but I enjoyed them.  I didn't miss the greenish (FO3) or brownish overtones (FO:NV) from the previous ones.  And the fact that my aging nVidia 660Ti plays them on Ultra with only minor stuttering in some places was a pleasant surprise.
4.  The simplified dialogue choices were sort of nice, yet sort of annoying because the generalized summary for each dialogue choice didn't always exactly match what the character said.  For some reason I also found myself clicking the mouse a lot to skip through all the blabbing that took place.
5.  The concept of modding weapons and armor like in Skyrim was fun, but I didn't really feel like the mods were all that excitiing (though I will say a heavily modded shot gun does wonders on a Deathclaw).  The default names given to all items are so generic that it gets confusing - and you  have to strip a weapon of it's parts so you can hot rod another (and that particular process could have been better implemented).
6.  The Power Armor was not that exciting to me and I rarely used it.  The fact that you get it fairly early in the game reduces the overall challenge in my opinion also.
7.  The building system seems more like something that was either put in towards the end of development and not completely finished, or purposely kept simple to the point that I was pretty much uninterested in it.  The game also offers little explanation on how to use it effectively, so I never bothered making anything more than I had to.  Besides - building areas really doesn't amount to that much - it's not like you make an entire city and manage it.  And who plays Fallout to manage a city?
8.  I really missed the Karma system.  It was fun to see how previous games ranked me when I played them.  Some people feel the game really does not let you be a real bad guy/girl, and I tend to agree - there is very little consequence for your actions until you reach the critical parts of the main story line and any choices permenantly affect the rest of the game (even after the main story has ended).  And once that is done?  Ehh, it all just moves on.
9.  The FPS aspect of the game was far improved and felt more like a traditional shooter.  Yet the perks/leveling up was too simplified and not really that interesting....though the map of the perks with the animated Fallout dude were neat.
10.  I didn't need the main character to be voiced and I wasn't sure what the point of that was.  It broke the immersion for me.  Voice acting was generally fine though.
11.  Companions seemed to have a hard time staying with me, and when I needed to dump all my crap into their lap for carrying it home they were often MIA.
So there you have it....I definitely enjoyed it, but it hasn't knocked New Vegas out of the top spot for me.  I'll recommend it for a fun time for sure, but don't expect any super deep RPG elements.

Another winner from Bethesda.
Fallout 4 has made a lot of improvements over its predecessors. The core combat gameplay has been improved in a dramatic way; gone are the days of clunky Fallout 3/NV-style combat, and what we have instead is a competent little shooter that feels consistently satisfying. I expected an improvement in this area, but I wasn't expecting quite as big of a leap as we got in terms of combat, and it feels great. Feels like a proper FPS, although not a perfect one.
Fallout 4 takes place in the Commonwealth, post-apocalyptic Boston. The main quest is a huge step up from Fallout 3 in terms of writing, structure, and gameplay. Without going into spoiler territory, the first two acts of the main quest are a linear progression, and in the third act you can choose one of four factions to side with for the end game. It adds a lot of replayability and the faction dynamics (while not as fully fleshed out as they were in New Vegas) are a lot of fun.
The dialogue system is comparable to Fallout 3's, albeit with a voiced protagonist, but not quite as in-depth as New Vegas's dialogue. I'm not a fan of voiced protagonists so I would have preferred Bethesda have gone the silent route, but what we got isn't a whole lot different than Fallout 3. Very similar player dialogue, just voiced for some reason. Skill checks in dialogue are absent, and we're back to Fallout 3's percentage-based speech system instead of New Vegas's flat number system, which is disappointing. Now, the only stat that matters in persuasion is Charisma.
The new character system is a mixed bag. SPECIAL has been brought to the fore and is more important than the other two modern Fallout games, and skills have been done away with entirely in favor of perks. This system works well for the most part, and leads to a lot of build variety, but there are some questionable decisions on how perks are divided. Instead of dividing weapon proficiency by ballistic/energy/big guns/explosives, it's divided by pistols/semi-auto rifles/automatic weapons/explosives, which just feels strange to me. Furthermore, there are a bit too many perks that do nothing but add 20% effectiveness with a given skill for my taste.
That being said, each SPECIAL's perks have been balanced pretty well, with good perks being found under each attribute, and the player is never made to feel like one stat is essential to their progression with one exception: There's one Charisma perk with a requirement of 6 that is pretty much essential if you plan to spend a lot of time building settlements, which is disappointing. Other than that, lots of variety all around. This new system has some advantages over the old way, and pitfalls of its own, which is to be expected. Overall, not bad, but I think I prefer Fallout 3/NV's way of doing things.
Crafting has been expanded in an absolutely huge way. Every gun and melee weapon has modifications you can craft. A simple machete might only have one modification, but the commonplace pipe weaponry can be customized in dozens of ways. This is not without its drawbacks however, as many, many enemies will be using variants of the same weapons, and some extra base weapons would have gone a long way for variety. This crafting extends beyond weapons, as the player can also craft normal armor and power armor modifications. The player is also able to freely customize settlements, construct buildings from the ground up, attract NPCs to live and tend to your areas, the works. The building interface can be clunky at times but it's easy to pick it up and make a town that feels like you built it with your own two hands. Materials for all types of crafting are scavanged from all the junk you find around the game world. Each item can be broken down into components (duct tape might give you adhesive, or a wrench might give you steel) and those components are used to craft anything and everything. Suddenly all the scrap around the world is valuable, and it really adds to the feeling of scavenging for resources in a post-pocalyptic world.
One strangely absent feature is ammo crafting, which is extremely unfortunate as ammo in Fallout 4 is plainly overpriced. A major gripe I have with the game is that I have a lot of cool weapons I never want to use because ammo for them is scarce to scavenge and expensive to purchase. And it's made even worse because there's no balance: A gun that deals 50 damage might have ammo that costs 2 caps a piece, whereas a gun that deals 80 damage could have ammo that goes for 7-9, so it's still always most prudent to buy the cheap ammo instead. Which ties into another gripe that even with a high Charisma stat and both ranks of the perk that improves prices when buying and selling, things you buy are completely overpriced and you give things away for less than what they're worth. Very disappointing.
One feature I can't fawn enough over is power armor. Power armor, unlike previous games, makes you into a living tank. Very early on in the game you're given your first suit of power armor. It's covered in rust and in bad shape, but it's yours, It's meant to be a pet project throughout the game that you upgrade over time, and it's extremely satisfying. In addition to being far more durable when inside a suit of power armor, you also recieve no falling damage (I will never get tired of jumping hundreds of feet and slamming to the ground unharmed), deal additional melee damage, and can carry considerably more items with you. It even has a snappy Iron Man-style animation when getting in and out, and gathering multiple suits of power armor and working on them is one of my favorite aspects of the game. There's plenty of different modifications and paint jobs to give your armor to make it really feel like yours, and there's five varieties of power armor parts in the game (each variety has a head, left arm, right arm, torso, right leg, and left leg) that you can mix and match with complete freedom. I built myself a power armor bay using the settlement system that I'm quite proud of, and stocked it with various suits of armor.
Now the big one: The game world. Bethesda knocked it out of the park yet again. It's a huge open world with plenty of locations to discover, quests to find, and secrets to uncover. The main quest takes you all around, but the real beauty is getting off the beaten path and exploring Boston and its surrounding area in your own way. There are so many great locations in the Commonwealth, so many areas that are a blast to explore and go through, that it's hard to go wrong even if you just randomly enter any given ruin. I will say that I found it lighter on side content compared to previous Bethesda games. I finished all the unique side quests (save one that my companion wasn't too pleased with doing!), plus the main quest, plus a ton of randomly-generated radiant quests, and still didn't make it to level 50. That said, lighter than previous Bethesda games =/= light, and there's still dozens and dozens of hours worth of content to explore.
And the very best part of the game world? Not a metro tunnel in sight. You're free to explore the ruins of Boston all on the overworld, and it's fantastic.
In short, Fallout 4 is an excellent open-world RPG that like all games, I have some gripes with. But those gripes are heavily outweighed by the massive amount of quality content this game has to offer, and are ultimately small problems in a great game. Easily my game of the year and the best RPG I've played in quite some time. Bethesda did it again.

Fallout 4 is definitely a fun game and I certainlyy enjoyed it.  It's not perfect, and I tend to agree with other reviewers who say that it is a simplified version of Fallout 3 or Fallout New Vegas (still my favorite Fallout game in the series to date).
The following observatons are my overall spolier-free feelings about the main aspects of the game:
1.  In all Fallout games I try to hold off as long as possible before ending the main quest.  In this case, I beat the main story line at level 48 and at just under 2 weeks of playing,  The setting, environments, etc were immerseive....Yet, the side quests you are then left with get sort of boring after awhile so my incentive to keep playing is not really that strong (for the record, I've now played it every day for a month since the initial release).  Perhaps earlier games ended for a reason.
2.  This Fallout by far has the most humanizing storyline and engaging moral dilemmas than the previous games.  But at the same time, I really didn't care that much about the main plot - I wanted to just explore more.
3.  Everyone seems to hate the graphics, but I enjoyed them.  I didn't miss the greenish (FO3) or brownish overtones (FO:NV) from the previous ones.  And the fact that my aging nVidia 660Ti plays them on Ultra with only minor stuttering in some places was a pleasant surprise.
4.  The simplified dialogue choices were sort of nice, yet sort of annoying because the generalized summary for each dialogue choice didn't always exactly match what the character said.  For some reason I also found myself clicking the mouse a lot to skip through all the blabbing that took place.
5.  The concept of modding weapons and armor like in Skyrim was fun, but I didn't really feel like the mods were all that excitiing (though I will say a heavily modded shot gun does wonders on a Deathclaw).  The default names given to all items are so generic that it gets confusing - and you  have to strip a weapon of it's parts so you can hot rod another (and that particular process could have been better implemented).
6.  The Power Armor was not that exciting to me and I rarely used it.  The fact that you get it fairly early in the game reduces the overall challenge in my opinion also.
7.  The building system seems more like something that was either put in towards the end of development and not completely finished, or purposely kept simple to the point that I was pretty much uninterested in it.  The game also offers little explanation on how to use it effectively, so I never bothered making anything more than I had to.  Besides - building areas really doesn't amount to that much - it's not like you make an entire city and manage it.  And who plays Fallout to manage a city?
8.  I really missed the Karma system.  It was fun to see how previous games ranked me when I played them.  Some people feel the game really does not let you be a real bad guy/girl, and I tend to agree - there is very little consequence for your actions until you reach the critical parts of the main story line and any choices permenantly affect the rest of the game (even after the main story has ended).  And once that is done?  Ehh, it all just moves on.
9.  The FPS aspect of the game was far improved and felt more like a traditional shooter.  Yet the perks/leveling up was too simplified and not really that interesting....though the map of the perks with the animated Fallout dude were neat.
10.  I didn't need the main character to be voiced and I wasn't sure what the point of that was.  It broke the immersion for me.  Voice acting was generally fine though.
11.  Companions seemed to have a hard time staying with me, and when I needed to dump all my crap into their lap for carrying it home they were often MIA.
So there you have it....I definitely enjoyed it, but it hasn't knocked New Vegas out of the top spot for me.  I'll recommend it for a fun time for sure, but don't expect any super deep RPG elements.
And now how many years until the next one....??

Leveling up just seems so unsatisfactory now.  You get one perk.  After leveling up a perk, you usually have to wait 10-20 more levels until you can level it up again. Most of them STR perks give you more damage (nothing creative like Skyrim had, like bleed damage on axes, stagger, zoom on arrows, etc), literally none of the charisma perks sound interesting, the luck perks are ok but they barely ever even happen (and this is coming from a maxed luck character), and then there's a bunch of perks littered around that give you access to more crafting or lockpicking or some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Fallout 4 plays upon the exist Bethesda RPG formula quite often for the better, and occassionally for the worse.
TL; DR at the bottom.
+ Boston is big and beautiful. No monotone palette like in Fallout 3 or New Vegas. The city is very open instead of being sectioned off by huge arrays of metro tunnels. Scaffolding and fire escapes introduce a vertical area of exploration. Individual detail in the landscape and diversity of locations make it an even more interesting place than Skyrim for me.
+ Character facial customization is fantastic, yet easy enough to use. I think this is the only game I've ever played where I've been pretty much completely happy with my character's appearance.
+ Combat is tightened up extremely well. Weapons are fluid and effective. Depending on how you tweak your character, enemies are not all bullet sponges and give good visual and audio feedback for damage. VATS is more of a helpful option than an absolute necessity. Small changes like the addition of "sprint" are greatly welcomed.
+ Noticeably more challenging than the previous games. While Stimpak spam is always an option, great armor and weapon choices are needed to survive.
+ Weapon crafting is a great way to introduce variety into a rather limited pool of weapons. Most of the low to mid tier weapons can be customized to any desired function.
+ Story is sufficient. It's hard to pace a game like this well around a single plot, it was definitely more entertaining than the other Fallouts or Skyrim to me. Great vocal performances all around with a seldom-repeating voice pool (*cough* Skyrim *cough*)
+ Armor and Power Armor systems are very neat and dynamic. Most armors are in limb pieces to be individually customized and upgraded (it's a shame they can't be worn atop more clothes.) Power armor suits are an individual entity that can be tweaked to near over-power with the right skills and materials. They feel as hulking and powerful as power armor should have always felt.
+ BOLSTERING with content, not sure if that's a surprise to anyone.
+ So far, very great, memorable quests, at least attributed to the main factions. A lot of illusion of choice when it comes to outcomes, but they're very fun in excecution.
+ Companions STYLISTICALLY are more fleshed out. All companions have their own likes and dislikes, and you earn their trust and admiration through your actions. They have their own backstories to reveal, and amazingly even pipe in during some quest dialogues that never necessarily merited them being there.
+ Licensed and original soundtrack are great.
+- Interesting avenue with skills. Each degree of SPECIAL points unlocks more skills within the SPECIAL tree. Some very useful, some borderline useless. Some hardly seem like they belong on the high tiers that they do or even within their SPECIAL catagory. I favor this skill system to the over Fallouts because perks and flat-out stat buffs are combined (gain a rank in "Gunslinger" to both increase your pistol damage and have a chance of disarming folks), but I much prefered Skyrim's system of "use this skill to upgrade its effectiveness".
- Hardly a loving PC port on the technical side. Criticisms of terrible, muddy textures and overly bright lighting are valid. Running this game on a GTX 960, I had to dumb down the (not in-game, but annoyingly in launcher) graphics options to somewhere between medium and high to maintain 60 frames.
- Hardly a loving PC port on the functionality side. Dialogue UIs are finicky difficult to navigate. The Pip Boy can be clunky at times. Also, let's not forget settlement building. vvv
- Settlement building is an unrewarding chore. To meet the needs of your many, many settlements, all you need to do is haphazardly place a few amenities. Buidling structures, walls, and homes is purely a labor of love. The controls are about as unforgiving and innaccurate as Halo's Forge mode, except you can't fly without cheating in console. Buildings demand a HIGH amount of supplies which ARE NOT SHARED between settlements. It's hard to focus on one settlement, let alone twenty. They yield very little benefit as well.
- Reimplimentations of perks, enemy types, weapons, factions, and story tropes eventually become exhausting fan service. (Justifying some of the "Fallout 3.5" jokes I've seen). It would be nice if Bethesda was a little braver with change.
- I guess I got spoiled for quests from the Obsidian Fallout game and forgot what a Bethesda Fallout is like. After almost 150 hours, I've played about 5 or 6 REALLY interesting side quests that aren't tied into the main story or factions. If you get one of the four factions to hate you early on, you're missing out on a lot of the primary questing in this game. There are few major settlements and towns to find any lengthy, interesting New Vegas-style quests.
- Companions are still largely useless function-wise. They can only use their default; often trashy weapon, unless you give them something WITH ammo which they will expend. Unlike previous games, they don't even serve to tank often for you. They usually get lost or stuck on geometry until the fight is over.
- Yes, the dialogue system is lousy and flawed.
Voice Acting:  I like the idea of a voiced protagonist. I understand some lose the rollplay quality they would have liked, but the CONCEPT of voice acting gives the character a lot more life. However, Bethesda made the mistake of going the Commander Shepard route. There is only one voice actor given to satisfy all builds and races, so they made him a neutral, feminine-sounding♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Instead of the tough Jon Hamm voice I heard in the trailers, he is often a quavery-voiced Chris Parnel-sounding wimp. I haven't spent any time with the female voice to review that.
Dialogue Choice: Most of the limited options lead to the same conclusion. While that was true in the other Fallouts, the illusion of choice feels more prominent here. Be overly nice, overly mean, or neutral. Skills like Barter and Intelligence can't influence your words. Speech challenges are a luck-based percentage gamble like in FO3 and not the flat-out skill challenge like in NV. It's hard to tell what the character is going to say from the brief dialogue sumations given on the wheel. Additionally, you can never tell their tone. What I wanted to say is incorrectly conveyed by the tone.
- It's still a Bethesda RPG. Bugs are apparent (though nowhere near is bad as in something like the NV/Skyrim launch), stealing a cola will cause the whole town to kill you, NPCs repeat the same quips to you every time you pass by, etc.
TL; DR
In summation, it's mostly everything great about the other Fallouts improved with some (though I wish more) new features added. Combat is infinitely more enjoyable, Boston is a great location, the world feels alive and there's tons to do. Technical performance needs improvement, settlement building is a boring chore with a terrible UI. Dialogue isn't quite as free as the previous games. SOME of these flaws are easily obfuscated with mods. Great for a first or a contuation of Bethesda RPG games.
