As with most people who have played it, I love Fallout 4. I was a bigger fan of New Vegas than Fallout 3 and although Fallout 4 is much more of a sequel to Fallout 3 than it is New Vegas, it takes the best of both games and tries to improve them (note I said tries). There's a lot to love about the game but as with any game there are some things that could have been done better.
The S.P.E.C.I.A.L. system has been all but tossed out the window. True you still rely on the traits in the acronym to determine your strength, etc., but the perk system has been extremely dumbed down (read streamlined) and you can no longer invest skill points into your skills which personally I felt was a great part of the older games so I was disappointed. You no longer really have a clear idea of what your chance to sneak or persuade someone is. You just pump as many points as you can into agility and stealth and you'll pretty much always be hidden... same with charisma and persuading people. MOST of the perks from Fallout 3 and New Vegas are gone and replaced with faux perks that really just increase your skill in something like unarmed combat. I dunno. In my opinion this was the worst thing to discover about the game so far. It still works. It just feels like a lot of the RP in RPG has been taken away. That said...
Conversations. Suck. Look, I understand that in order to have the whole game voice acted they had to make things simpler. That doesn't mean what they did is GOOD... and personally I'd rather have had more conversation options to explore the lore of the Commonwealth than fully voice (poorly) acted conversations that amount to 4 choices which once you make one you USUALLY can't go back and choose one of the others to get more info. There's really not much more to say about that, either you love exploring the lore of the world or you would rather play a first person shooter with occasional talking that annoys you because NO SHOOTING.
The combat is better than any of the other two FPS fallout games, hands down. I don't mind that the guns never break because you're constantly upgrading and improving them anyway so you could take that as being maintenance. I don't have a high end PC so the combat can get annoying for me when an enemy teleports across the room and my shotgun blast instead hits my (freaking useless) dog. That's not a problem with the game though... I'm using a $300 PC from Best Buy that I've had for 2 years without upgrading at all. :)
The developers try to trick you into thinking that companions can be more than extra walking backpacks by giving you dogmeat at the beginning of the game, but don't let them fool you. They are just as useless as they are in Fallout 3, New Vegas, Skyrim, etc. The only bonus here is they can't die (thank god because all of my followers would be dead by now after walking in front of my gun too many times). There is a perk you can get to make your followers immune to your weapons... but why waste a perk? If they fall in combat they'll just get up when it's over and most fights aren't difficult enough to need a partner, especially when said partner can't connect any of their shots and stands out in the open while 10 raiders are sniping them. Dogmeat is particularly annoying... either blocking doorways (you can easily tell him to move but jesus christ every 5 minutes) and having to listen to him whine while you're walking around... I don't like dogs.
Lots of people bash the graphics... those people are teenagers so you don't really have to pay any mind to them. The game is beautiful and the animations are light years beyond their last games. Honestly though who cares? I've played much better looking games that were utter crap (Black Ops 3 anyone).
At first glance the map doesn't look very big, but I've been playing for a couple of days and making sure to hit every building / location I come accross and I haven't even made it 1/3rd of the way south. The only reason I've seen Diamond City is because I ran there as soon as I could (it's pretty underwhelming). As such there is a LOT of the world that I haven't seen but that's mainly because I don't like taking my power armor everywhere and super mutants scare me. Oh yeah:
POWER ARMOR! It is no longer a choice of "do I want to go all out and get power armor or do I want to keep my mobility and wear lighter armor?". Power armor is now a tool that you can occasionally use rather than something you wear the entire time. At first it seems like a drag that it needs cells to work correctly but with what little of the world I've explored I already have 10 cells so I'm not worried about their availability. At lower levels the armor is almost essential for some of the missions because without it your armor is pretty pathetic. You can upgrade your suit just like you can upgrade your weapons and armor as well as finding better versions of the suits components. It sort of makes the battles with super mutants more realistic because you can't expect a puny human to go head to head with an army of 10 foot tall super soldiers without some sort of assistance. I'm sure at later levels you can take on super mutants no problem but right now if I'm fighting more than one at a time I'm done...
Because a lot of the guns kind of suck. You begin with the classic 10mm pistol and start collecting an assortment of "pipe" guns which are highly modular home made weapons. If you have the resources and perks to modify them fully they can be almost strong but usually they're pretty pathetic. Once I found a combat shotgun and a hunting rifle I never went back. I haven't messed with energy weapons that much because they require a lot of perks to modify.
If you do buy the game... make sure to create a save right before you leave the Vault. As cool and unique as the intro is... it is way too long to have to play through again.

Review of the game itself;
As a standalone title, I love this game. I have already cleared the main questline once, on my first playthrough. Couldn't put it down!
I decided to restart the game with a brand new character to just start exploring, and pretty much ignore the main story. And honestly this is making me love the game even more.
The side quests and everything around the world is engaging.
The settlement crafting system is actually really great once you get used to it, and I have spent way too much time building my virtual town (feel like I am playing Minecraft sometimes).
As a Fallout sequel, especially compared to Fallout 3 this game falls flat.
Your character is "Good", not matter what you try and do. In Fallout 3 and New Vegas you had options to finish many quests the "good way" or the "bad way". Or sometimes even just the "selfish way", where everyone but you loses (my personal favourite obviously :P).
The story in a nutshell (without spoilers).
You are the Mother/Father of young Shaun.♥♥♥♥♥♥happens and you end up in the post-apocalyptic wasteland, looking for your kidnappped son.
You are now on a mission to find your son, and be the most helpful good/sarcastic good parent you can be while you traverse Boston.
To give it a rating as a standalone game - 9/10 (because I still can't put it down)
To give it a rating as a Fallout sequel - 7-10 (because I still can't put it down, but I am also disappointed the story telling of Fallout 3/Skyrim is gone.)
It's ok, New Vegas is better though.

This is a spectacular game. Lots of people are mad because: Bethesda, and it's not <insert favorite Fallout game here>. Yes, there are bugs. It's a shame Bethesda hasn't worked out more of the kinks with this game and the engine, and they absolutely shouldn't get a pass on that. This also has the worst PC interface I have ever seen in my entire life. It's so completely broken due to unremappable controls for the build mode (which interfere with my movement control setup because I do ESDF, not WASD) that I am forced to play this game with a controller, which is really not something I prefer to do.
Some people also quibble about the voiced main character, and the Mass Effect-style dialog system, failing to realize that such a system give you just as much choice (or very nearly) in conversation as any other system, it merely masks it in a different way. Do the math in terms of the presented options and the way traditional dialog tree setups actually work, and you won't find a substantial difference. Whether you prefer a silent protagonist or not is entirely personal preference, and I can see why some find it somewhat off-putting, but for me, it didn't at all break immersion or make my character feel any less like my avatar in the world, as none of his jabber is so deep or long-winded to make him feel like a separate character. He just now feels like he actually fits into the world better instead of being a walking piece of cardboard that spits out post-it notes for the other characters to read.
It's a different game from its predecessors in some of those details, yet remains largely the same. No, it's not New Vegas. It doesn't need to be. It works well doing what it sets out to do, provides a ton of great content, still gives you a lot of freedom, and does so in a beautiful package that looks gorgeous despite the limitations of what is now a rapidly aging engine.
Thumbs up. Nobody would blame you if you wanted to wait for bug fixes and improved technical stability, which goes for all Bethesda's products, and it definitely takes extremely low marks as far as its interface goes. But rest assured, the content of the game itself is very much worth engaging with. Your mileage will naturally vary depending on what you can or can't accept in the evolution of a franchise, but unless you're a fundamentalist-level purist, there's still a whole lot to love.

If you enjoy the open world, getting to explore a post-apocalyptic environment, making a name for yourself in a fake place, multiple quests, multiple ways to complete the game, then, overall, you should enjoy this game as much as the previous fallouts. In fact, you might even enjoy it more because of the settlement building which allows you to have more of a direct hand in the creation of your wasteland.
Combat, environment, etc. were all very similar to the recent fallout games, although you do get to explore inside buildings more than in the previous games. I remember going through cities in previous games and NO DOORS were open. But, in this game, lots of doors are open in the city. You may also enjoy the more realistic way they did the power armor or enjoy the crafting system, which offers lots of options.
Speaking of crafting, I find a lot of people may be complaining about the dumbed down skill tree. Indeed, I did find this annoying, but only minorly so. However, when you consider the depth of the crafting system, you find that you can edit your character in a much more realistic way - improving/changing a characters weapons/gear to meet your needs. I mean, in the real world, you don't level up, you just get better gear and make it better. So, really, anyone complaining about the skill tree probably doesnt understand crafting and how this can change a character in so many more ways than any of the current or previous skill trees did.
The only major complaint I had was the fact that, although I could potentially join all the factions, I couldn't really rise through the ranks, mess up the infrastructure, etc. like one can in other games.
Edit: In a dialogue, typically, there are only 4 options to choose from. This may be annoying to some. Also, I think they could have provided more options if they had done away if the voice acting. I mean, seriously, save yo money, game developers, and don't give the main character a voice, and put that money to an aspect of the game that matters. Just my 2 cents, though. Because, seriously, the voice does not make it more realistic. I can easily make the character sound however I want them to in my head. This head voice has never detracted from a game for me and I would argue most don't care about their main character having an ingame voice.
But, hey, my character's ingame boyfriend is a ghoul. My life's fallout 4 goal is complete.

It is not as good as New Vegas, plus Bethesda can't seem to fix the same bugs that plague their games for years. However, the mechancs and exploration is enough to interest me. I would recommend it, unless the bugs bother you, then wait awhile for mods to come up.
The character creation is rather through and you can be rather exact in what you make, and as a plus, the skills system is removed in favor of perks. I've always had a problem with the skils, since you weren't likely to need 4-5 combat skills. Plus, some of the perks have interesting effects at higher levels.
The story is better than Fallout 3, but not as good as New Vegas. The major flaw in the story is that you can't be evil. Granted, you can steal and kill, but the story is gated to where the character plays off as a good character. There are a few options for the ending, but it doesn't have a karma system as New Vegas has.
Boston is not as interesting as Vegas, but it isn't as ruined as D.C was in Fallout 3. There's a lot of interesting places to explore and I can't really complain about it.
Weapons are revamped as they handle better first off. Modding allows you to customize your weapons to your liking, plus, thanks the the loot system, some weapons and armor may have some special effects. I think this is a major selling point, as you don't know what you are going to find. The customization of your gear is rather excellent.
Eventually, you will get to settlement building, which adds usefulness to junk that you collect. It is rather interesting concept, but it can be a bit clunky at times. I don't find it as a selling point, but it's competent in what it does.
Along with the tone, the biggest problem I have with the game is the bugs and performance of the game. The game locks the FPS and the mouse acceleration is terrible. FOV doesn't make me sick, but it does seem a bit narrow. Luckily, they can be edited in the ini files. Finally, there are bugs in the Bethesda game, which I would expect bugs in open world games. However, the big problem I have with it is that they are constantly plagued with the same bugs that have been existed since Fallout 3. So your milage may vary depending on what kind of bugs you encounter (have encounter bugs where you can't move in the opening sequence).
Overall, Fallout has improved its mechanics when it comes to weapons and exploring. However, it does fall a little flat in its storytelling and of course the bugs. I've enjoyed my time with the game, but it will depend on what bothers you. If you liked New Vegas, it is not better than that when it comes to choices. Plus if you hate bugs, you will hate this game. But, there is a compelling game here when it comes to exploration and looting. If you dislike any of these things, then wait until the development kit comes out and mods start pouring out in full force.
Update 12/17/15 : I've pretty much explored everything and completed almost all the story lines. The only thing that has changed that it can be argued the writing might be on par with Fallout 3. Hiding dialoge in a wheel may seem nice, but it's also nice to hide the fact that the wheel has the same answers for all four choices. There is only the choice on which faction you help out, other than that, it is a binary yes or no choices, regardless of what is preposed to you. I will recommend this game as an open-world adventure game if you can stand the bugs, but I can't recommend it as an RPG when there is nothing to choose.

Despite a couple of irritating bugs, Fallout 4 manages to live up to Bethesda's claim that the game mark an 'evolution of RPGs'. A decent plot stays consistently interesting, while Bethesda's true talent, creating immersive sandbox-style worlds, will always give you a reason to explore off of the beaten paths. The ability to build and help settlements grow adds to that immersion, while companions and NPCs react to the player and the environment in new and intelligent ways.
The crafting system, which ties into the settlement-building, also deserves seperate mention. The player is able to modify and improve nearly every piece of equipment in the game, from weapons and armor, to buildings and power armor. Most modifications change visual appearance as well as stats, allowing you to shape your character's look in a surprising amount of ways.
I was uncertain whether or not to purchase Fallout 4, as the previous entry did not hook me like it did so many other players. However, I am very glad I gave this entry a chance, as it has become my second favorite game of the year (Second only to the Witcher 3).
HIGHLY Recommended

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I liked Fallout 3, but I wasn't a big fan of it, Fallout New Vegas was even more boring to me. The problem I had with those games was primarily the gunplay, but in New Vegas it was also the really slow movement speed and the long distances you had to travel by foot. Fallout 4 improves on all those aspects but also fails a bit in the areas Fallout 3 did great, however I think many people exxagerate with this, I still think Fallout 4 is a great game which offers tons of exploration. And exploration is the key thing here, the character development isn't that complex, the quests are fine, but don't have that much variety and offer little to no choices most of the time, the characters you meet are fine too, sometimes you meet really interesting characters, but most of the time there is nothing special about them. There are 4 major factions which aren't THAT different to each other and all of them primarily require you to do combat.
All of those things are good, but not great, the exploration aspect however is fantastic, even better than in Fallout 3, because of the new crafting system which makes every little piece of junk useful. It could be even better if ammo was more rare and getting tons of money isn`t that hard too even without the perks which boost your money income. But it is really satisfying just to wander around the world and encounter strange things. One time I entered a random building and a weird quest started, the other time I encountered an old ship in the middle of the town, another time I entered a skyscraper and got ambushed by high security only to get rewarded with the best power armor in the game.
The gunplay is really good now, I would even say better than some pure first person shooters, however the enemy design isn`t that great apart from a few exceptions. The AI is fine, but the way the enemies is designed is classic RPG style which means you can`t dodge attacks and some enemies will have tons and tons of hp. V.A.T.S. is still in the game and before I always ignored VATS, but I realized that if you play with both playstyles combined the game is more fun and has a bit more depth, especially when fighting tougher enemies. There is a good amount of weapons in the game but in my opinion they could easily add more. For example for assault rifles you just have one real assault rifle, then a submachine gun and the pipe rifle maybe. What about an AK or other assault rifles. Without the crafting system the weapon variety would be dissapointed because you quickly find the most weapons in the game except a few really rare ones, but thanks to the crafting system you can keep upgrading the weapons and make them stronger, or you get rewarded with weapons which already have really good upgrades, that motivates you to always keep fighting and searching.
The map is a bit smaller than Fallout 3 I think and definitly smaller than Skyrim, first that was dissapointed to me, but after 45 hours of playtime I still have TONS of things to do so it's fine for me. However the map has the usual Bethesda design, enemies level with you and you will encounter the same enemies in the whole map, except for a few harder areas towards the lower part of the map. The game definitly could use more enemy types and maybe gate the player a bit more from more difficult areas to give an even greater sense of progress apart from the charachter development and weapon crafting. Also the amount of different amor types and clothes you can find is lower than I hoped, in addition to your normal armor you have the power armor though and you also have ot upgrade all of these. I guess it's fine cause this is a singleplayer game, but I really like customizing my character with a unique look in other games, here it is not that easy to do so. Thankfully the character creator is REALLY good.
The quests have the usual Bethesda quality. Writing is a bit better than in previous games I feel, Fallout 3 had better quests, but the big problem of previous Bethesda games was always the main storyline, which still isn`t that spectacular in Fallout 4, but much more interesting. However I don't like the premise of the game, you are a father or mother in search for your son which is still a baby in an extremely dangerous world and you have no clue where he is, but because this is an open world game you will obvioulsy explore a lot and do lots of side missions, if you want, so if you do tons of other things before doing the main storyline it will be really awkward. This is really bad story-telling in my opinion, the story the want to tell doesn't fit in an open world game. They want to tell a traditional 3 act story in a game where the player has complete control over the pacing, that doesn't work, and I don`t understand why they are doing something like this anyway, is it that hard to come up with a story which fits to a game like this? But again, if you don`t wait too long to do the main storyline it still is fun to follow and has a nice twist to it too, but that twist is also a bit artificial.
Not everyone will like this game, if you are a Fallout veteran you might be really dissapointed, I don't know. If you are like me and didn`t like Fallout 3 and/or New Vegas because of the gameplay, then I think you might really like Fallout 4. Oh btw I also really like that your character talks now, I know many people dislike this, but in my opinion it works for Fallout 4, at least with the female character.

Fallout 4 (8.8/10)
(NO MAIN STORY SPOILERS)
Power armor, VATS, Pip-Boy, laser weapons, Dogmeat; yep it’s here folks, finally the game we have all been waiting for. Fallout 4 is finally here and with it comes many new and welcome additions to the Fallout series as well as old ones that we all know and love. Fallout 4 feels like more of a direct sequel to Fallout 3 than a separate game like it did with New Vegas. It has references and characters from Fallout 3 connecting the games in a way as well as dialogue you hear walking through the world with people talking about the Capital Wasteland.
(Your character)
The character creation feels much nicer than the traditional sliders that were present in previous Fallout games and Skyrim. I was quite upset to see that the only hair color you can have is natural colors which made me have to give up my blue haired male and purple haired female. On the topic of characters I am still very much neutral on the idea of having a voiced protagonist, it adds more of an attachment to your character however it limits you in dialogue options. This game also requires multiple playthroughs to get all of the story much like other Fallout games mostly because of the different endings.
(Combat)
The combat is very much improved making it feel like an FPS like call of duty, battlefield, etc. more than a traditional turn based RPG like the earlier Fallout games (Fallout 1, 2, and tactics) Fallout 3 and New Vegas were somewhere in the middle with VATS being your main way of using offense at longer range than a shotgun. In Fallout 4 however, VATS is not necessary. The aiming works well and you can use grenades without having to un-equip your gun. Radiation is more of a concern than ever because now when you take radiation it decreases your max health and you will need to take a rad-away to get that health back.
(Crafting and settlement building)
Fallout 4 allows you to take your weapon crafting further than the others in the series to create truly unique weapons to protect you in the Wasteland. The same goes for armor. Along with weapon crafting and armor we now can make our own settlements. This is an amazing new feature that just feels like it has always belonged in this series. The system is not perfect as things snap together a lot in places you do not want them to be and some items like fences tend to float in certain areas leaving gaps underneath that makes it still functionable but not pleasing to look at. The landscape limits you as to where you can place things as well. All of the crafting requires you to have materials that you can find in the Wasteland. These things can include steel, wood, adhesive, copper, and many more. The fact that you now need to keep your junk makes the weapon “Junk Jet” aka the “Rock-It-Launcher” useless as that weapon uses junk as ammunition. The settlement creation is not a perfect system however, it is a great start and a very welcome addition to the Fallout series.
(Power armor)
The power armor is an icon of the Fallout series and it is back and it finally feels like a big suit of metal should. You have a whole new interface when you have the armor on which makes sense however it is a bit obstructive. Power armor now requires power, this power comes in the form of fusion cores. These can be found in things that look like power generators in industrial buildings. You can also find these on the ground in certain other places and in containers. This power armor is built onto the exoskeleton of the suit which you enter from the back instead of manually putting it on. You can have multiple suits of power armor and mix and match different types of power armor to create a custom suit. There are also many ways of upgrading your power armor to have it specialize in different resistances; for example, one suit could be for radiation resistance and another could be for energy weapon resistance etc. Fallout 4 has made a system of power armor the way it should be, even though I will miss being over powered in a suit of power armor that is worn like clothing.
(Character builds)
Specialization has always been something to keep in mind when playing Fallout games with picking your SPECIAL traits and perks. Fallout 4 allows you (and encourages you) to try different play styles with many perks adding damage to specific types of weapons early on. So I would recommend starting with a generalist build for your first character and trying different play styles to find what you like best then build your second character around that.
(Bugs)
Bugs are the worst and the best of a game. They can range from the game-breaking to the downright hilarious. In Fallout 4, well it is a Bethesda open world game so expect bugs. There are game breaking bugs but there are plenty that you will get a great laugh from which is the kind of bugs I encountered most when exploring the open world of Boston (seriously what is with the flying cars).
(Side quests)
The quests in Fallout 4 have quite a good variety except for the minutemen questline. This series of quests feels very repetitive and actually does repeat after a while having you do the exact same task you did earlier on in the game. Although it is an optional quest line but you do get good rewards further down the quest line.
(Day/Night cycles and weaher)
The weather system is very nice in Fallout 4. There is no specific weather for certain areas, sometimes you will have a rainy night and others you’ll have a radiation storm, it’s like a thunderstorm but whenever lightning strikes you will take a small amount of radiation damage. The night day cycle is as it has always been however night time seems to be quite bright for it being night making your pip-boy light not necessary except in dark buildings.
(AI)
The companion and enemy AI has had a wonderful upgrade and I love it. No longer do enemies run in a straight line to attack you now you’ll see deathclaws running on all fours at time in a winding path to avoid your bullets as they launch a devastating attack. Or feral ghouls that act much more zombie like as you would expect as they run, swarm, and crawl when they lose their legs. The companions no longer follow directly behind you in a straight line, now they will just be generally near you, this is a good thing for the most part however it has led to Dogmeat walking right off of the edge of stairways, cliffs, etc. Companions are also incredibly more useful if not for combat, then for other things. Dogmeat can sniff out enemies, items, and containers. And Nick can hack terminals and pick locks.
Overall Fallout 4 is a great step in the right direction for the Fallout series, although it’s not perfect and leaves out some things from the previous games like hardcore mode from Fallout New Vegas and all the bugs, it is a great game that definitely deserves more than one playthrough. If you like open world games or are a fan of the Fallout series this is a must play. My overall rating is an 8.8/10

I am enjoying the game very much.  I have been following the game through several youtubers and such since it's announcement in june.  Now that I have been playing it for over a week and have experienced a good part of the story, settlements, and side quests, I just wanted to add my thoughts for others to read and consider.
First off, it looks good.  The animations look good.  Are they perfect and bug free? no.  Are they top of the line, blow your mind graphics? no.  But they are a big step up from FO3 and NV, and are still good enough in my opinion.  I don't play FO for the graphics, but I am happy with them.
The gameplay itself.  The gunplay has been overhauled and feels more like a FPS, which I think is good.  It makes VATS a bonus and not a crutch.  Each of the weapons feel unique enough, especially with all the mods.  You are able to tailor guns to your style and build.  The legendary enemies that spawn all over each drop 1 item.  Each of those can be modded so you are not locked into whatever it is when it spawned.  Overall, I am really enjoying the gameplay and much enjoy the upgrades and changes from previous versions.
Settlements: I really like the idea and concept of it, though I think they missed the mark with the execution.  There is very little to no tutorial on it and it can be quite confusing and overwhelming at first.  Especially the "trade routes" you get from the first rank of settlement leader.  It isn't "trade" as much as it is "Share" routes between locations.  All it does is share both resources (Food and Water) and the junk you left is either location with the other.  This is useful, but misleading because trade routes implys earning some sort of bonus or earning caps or something. It is useful for consolidating resources and not requiring a return trip to a single location to drop off junk and such.  You can simply go to the closest location you have linked to your "main" base and drop it there.
Another thing that is very annoying and difficult with settlements is the settler managment.  Assigning them is easy, while in settlement mode, go to them, select them, and assign them to whatever you want them to do.  The issue is finding them, then locating what needs a person assigned to it, and also who is where.  I was hoping for a system simular to Fallout Shelter where there was a menu that would list all your dwellers and their stats and location.  you can then select from there and issue orders from there.  A system simular to this would improve the settlement system several times over.  Maybe someone with make a mod for that (Hint hint, nudge nudge.)
I don't want to provide any story spoilers so I won't add anything other than I am enjoying the story.  I haven't finished it yet because I am doing side quests and such as well.  But so far, it is intriguing and enjoyable.  I have read other reviews that have finished the story and have claimed it was lackluster and boring, but I have yet to encounter that.  I intend to update and/or write another review once I have completed the game, or atleast the main story.  I still have over half the map left to explore and several locations I found but didn't fully explore so I still have much left to do.
In closing, I suggest everyone who is interested, give the game a try.  Just because someone else liked it, or hated it, doesn't you will feel the same.  Maybe you REALLY like the FPS feel of the gunplay, or maybe you hate it.  Maybe there wasn't enough RP in the storyline, maybe you don't like the voiced protagonist.  I personally like it.  Like I said, if your interested, there are several people doing "let's play" videos and such so watch videos and get a feel that way.  Or buy it and try it for yourself.

When i originally wrote my review the game was still just brand new, and in truth my opinion of it hasn't changed all that much. I still think its a fun shooter with RPG elements that deserves a few playthroughs. That being said, i don't like some of the things surrounding the base game.
The DLC is a bit lacking of true playable stories and experiences besides two, but more if you're really into the base-building. Far Harbor i thought was fun, though ive yet to finish it and i haven't played Nuka World; Keep that in mind. I feel Bethesda has a bad habit of only releasing a few DLCs within a year for a game and then dropping all support for them, which is a shame. Games like this, Skyrim and New Vegas would all benefit from a steady development team dedicated to creating extra content for them. Maybe im the only one that thinks that, but all Beth games have something that make them unique from eachother, even if they do borrow from other installments. Oblivion isn't the same as Skyrim, like New Vegas isn't the same as 4; Its not really a negative, but i would love to be able to come back to these games for new experiences without needing overhauls and such, just like 4.
Now, the mods. I don't think this game can be as transformed as Skyrim can be, atleast not right now. Skyrim offers a massive amount of mods that can all drastically enhance and change the experience of the game to be something more then just Skyrim; It can be an immersive, jaw-dropping fantasy that doesn't resemble a bethesda game. I think time will tell with F4, but it just seems to me as it is now, the mods are to support the game's vision rather then offer you new lens to view it through or even change the game completely. Then there is the fact that they're pushing paid mods, microtransactions... and this is where it gets me a bit tiffed. They tried to do it before, and it was universally crapped on; For good reason. Im for supporting people who make huge mods like its their job, but Patreon and other services are better suited for that then forcing someone to buy a costume or sword or whatever. Its the same reason i think of Valve as lazy hacks who don't really care about developing games anymore, because they don't. They let other people develop their content for them, and maybe occasionally they'll patch something or such. This is just an excuse for Bethesda to further make money off of other people's hard work without lifting a finger, and its despicable to say the least.
The Optimization in my mind is the only thing that really bothers me about this game in particular. While i applaud Bethesda for trying to make their game better looking with each installment, they haven't realised the limits of their same engine and how to better use it. This leads to massive frame drops that need mods to fix, mods i hope one day won't be something they can charge you for; It goes back to the lack of a development team to ensure a games longevity. Bethesda is a massive studio, and i realize that they like to make games and then move on. But, that raises the question of why a small team that appreciates their vision, even hiring modders that love your games, doesn't exist. Or heck, even someone who can atleast try and work on some of the issues in the game. Money is an issue, sure, but i don't believe it would be that hard for a multi-million making company. Maybe its because of Zenimax, i may never know.
The actual game. Alot of people don't like the way this game is apparently heading, but in truth its where it needs to go. Do we need actual voice acting for characters? No. Do i like having one? Yeah, kinda. I would love the choice to play with or without it, but i seem to be the only one who appreciates the dialogue camera and actually seeing my character talk, it reminds me of Mass Effect, and something i wish Skyrim had. I play in mainly first person, so getting to see my Character react to things and talk is a welcome addition. Is it less in depth then 3, New Vegas, or even the originals? In ways with some of the RPG mechanics that were removed like Karma/etc, but its just a different play style. Its more of a shooter. 1 and 2 are extremely punishing and have their own reward with figuring out the game, and the atmosphere is daunting to support that, like the original Resident Evils were scary partly because of the controls. Fallout 3 changed the way these games work mostly because it can invoke a different type of immersion when you're actually seeing the world through your character's eyes, and i much prefer it this way. That being said, there are very small and fleeting times where i don't feel like im playing a Fallout game; I feel the same playing Skyrim, and comparing it to the euphoria that i felt at times playing Oblivion. Maybe its age, or maybe because Oblivion and 3 were both my first Bethesda games. Whatever it is, there are glimpses of a different game here, so it doesn't hold the spirit all the way through like the last few installments of the franchise.
A long review for no reason, i still think this is a fun game. Worth 60 bucks? If you have the money, yes. If you have to pick your games because you are on a budget, you might want to torrent it or wait for a sale, and choose carefully what few DLCs to choose from that you get with them, avoid season's pass at all cost. If you're a big fan of Fallout you'll enjoy it, but if you think the originals are a godsend and nothing can ever be good in the franchise again, you probably already haven't purchased it for a reason.

It is definitely better than other new games available right now, but is lacking when compared to FO3. One major issue I found was the map size. It is tiny, nearly unacceptable. I can walk from one end of the map to the other in about a half hour, and that is with fighting enemies along the way. In addition, about 15% of the map is filler. What I mean is that although you can go there, there is nothing to find but massive loads of radiation (to discourage players from realizing how bad it is). There are no structures or landmarks, just trees, patches of highly irradiated water, and the occasional radroach or radscorpian or something of the sorts.
Another issue I found was the amount of size quests. I have logged about 50 hours, and I have already encountered over 60% of the companions (I checked online to see where I could find the best companion, and realized that I already have most of them). Therefore, there must be MANY more new side-quests in order for the game to be playable.
However, fear not, not all is lost. The user interface is fluid and flawless. There are few bugs, and those you do encounter can be fixed within five seconds. The character’s motions are realistic and believable, obviously Bethesda spent a lot of time on what you do see as opposed to what you cannot see (more locations).
Overall, for what it’s worth, it is a good game. However, in my opinion, it fails to live up to the masterpiece that was FO3, but then again, will any game? If you do not mind a small map and few quests, this game is for you. The combat is flawless, and so is everything else you will find in the game.

I liked Fallout 3, but I wasn't a big fan of it, Fallout New Vegas was even more boring to me. The problem I had with those games was primarily the gunplay, but in New Vegas it was also the really slow movement speed and the long distances you had to travel by foot. Fallout 4 improves on all those aspects but also fails a bit in the areas Fallout 3 did great, however I think many people exxagerate with this, I still think Fallout 4 is a great game which offers tons of exploration. And exploration is the key thing here, the character development isn't that complex, the quests are fine, but don't have that much variety and offer little to no choices most of the time, the characters you meet are fine too, sometimes you meet really interesting characters, but most of the time there is nothing special about them. There are 4 major factions which aren't THAT different to each other and all of them primarily require you to do combat.
All of those things are good, but not great, the exploration aspect however is fantastic, even better than in Fallout 3, because of the new crafting system which makes every little piece of junk useful. It could be even better if ammo was more rare and getting tons of money isn`t that hard too even without the perks which boost your money income. But it is really satisfying just to wander around the world and encounter strange things. One time I entered a random building and a weird quest started, the other time I encountered an old ship in the middle of the town, another time I entered a skyscraper and got ambushed by high security only to get rewarded with the best power armor in the game.
The gunplay is really good now, I would even say better than some pure first person shooters, however the enemy design isn`t that great apart from a few exceptions. The AI is fine, but the way the enemies is designed is classic RPG style which means you can`t dodge attacks and some enemies will have tons and tons of hp. V.A.T.S. is still in the game and before I always ignored VATS, but I realized that if you play with both playstyles combined the game is more fun and has a bit more depth, especially when fighting tougher enemies. There is a good amount of weapons in the game but in my opinion they could easily add more. For example for assault rifles you just have one real assault rifle, then a submachine gun and the pipe rifle maybe. What about an AK or other assault rifles. Without the crafting system the weapon variety would be dissapointed because you quickly find the most weapons in the game except a few really rare ones, but thanks to the crafting system you can keep upgrading the weapons and make them stronger, or you get rewarded with weapons which already have really good upgrades, that motivates you to always keep fighting and searching.
The map is a bit smaller than Fallout 3 I think and definitly smaller than Skyrim, first that was dissapointed to me, but after 45 hours of playtime I still have TONS of things to do so it's fine for me. However the map has the usual Bethesda design, enemies level with you and you will encounter the same enemies in the whole map, except for a few harder areas towards the lower part of the map. The game definitly could use more enemy types and maybe gate the player a bit more from more difficult areas to give an even greater sense of progress apart from the charachter development and weapon crafting. Also the amount of different amor types and clothes you can find is lower than I hoped, in addition to your normal armor you have the power armor though and you also have ot upgrade all of these. I guess it's fine cause this is a singleplayer game, but I really like customizing my character with a unique look in other games, here it is not that easy to do so. Thankfully the character creator is REALLY good.
The quests have the usual Bethesda quality. Writing is a bit better than in previous games I feel, Fallout 3 had better quests, but the big problem of previous Bethesda games was always the main storyline, which still isn`t that spectacular in Fallout 4, but much more interesting. However I don't like the premise of the game, you are a father or mother in search for your son which is still a baby in an extremely dangerous world and you have no clue where he is, but because this is an open world game you will obvioulsy explore a lot and do lots of side missions, if you want, so if you do tons of other things before doing the main storyline it will be really awkward. This is really bad story-telling in my opinion, the story the want to tell doesn't fit in an open world game. They want to tell a traditional 3 act story in a game where the player has complete control over the pacing, that doesn't work, and I don`t understand why they are doing something like this anyway, is it that hard to come up with a story which fits to a game like this? But again, if you don`t wait too long to do the main storyline it still is fun to follow and has a nice twist to it too, but that twist is also a bit artificial.
Not everyone will like this game, if you are a Fallout veteran you might be really dissapointed, I don't know. If you are like me and didn`t like Fallout 3 and/or New Vegas because of the gameplay, then I think you might really like Fallout 4. Oh btw I also really like that your character talks now, I know many people dislike this, but in my opinion it works for Fallout 4, at least with the female character.

You got some incremental skill boosts that you choose, and a perk based on your special stats (With FNV being a perk every other level).
This game is more akin to Skyrim than it is to Fallout: New Vegas.
Originally, I was unhappy. But again it's all about embracing change. The crafting is really cool, and I love searching ruins for things I need to build up better guns and strap a jetpack to my power armor.
All in all, I have to give my recommendation. The story is a little simplistic but it is far better than Fallout 3's story. Bethesda is improving their writing little by little with each game they do.

Decided to write this since there are a bunch of jokey reviews at the top of the store page.
Honestly people complain about most the quests being "Go here, shoot/grab this, come back" but the thing is that the actual story and locations behind the quests is what keeps you engaged. The journey you take on these quests (and in general exploration) has some of the best attention to detail I've seen. The level design of this game world has blew me away. For example (keeping it as ambigious as possible to not spoil), I had accessed a police terminal that listed items that had been stolen. The logs told me what the items were and where they were returned. 2 of the items had been returned to a store which I had passed before, so I went to the store and sure enough, the items were there. I love how everything is connected and how you stumble across history about characters you meet in various towns you explore. Another example is of a town where there was this big story unfolded over a series of emails sent by various terminals in the town about some sort of experiment going on. I spent a good hour looking around and piecing everything together and eventually found that they all pointed to a location which I explored and ultimately uncovered a secret area with a unique weapon. Brilliant and well crafted locations to explore, the vertical design is good too, something not seen in previous games and I'm really enjoying exploring the towers.
Enemies are so much better now. I have had to plan a strategy for a lot of encounters now because if I just go running in guns blazing then I'd get slaughtered. My best encounter yet is when I came across a battle between these mercenaries ("Gunners") and the Supermutants. I begin sniping when a vertibird (helicopter) lands and the Brotherhood of Steel appear. They begin shooting the gunners and the supermutants and then two Yao Gui's came in and began tearing them to shreds. I had about 25 enemies to kill and after a long 20 minute battle I had came on top. Then a Mr Gutsy came and killed me.
The gunplay is the tightest it's ever been and it is leagues ahead of its predecessors, do not listen to those that tell you it is lackluster. The gameplay is the best it's ever been. It's not the best out there but it's pretty high up (almost up there with Call of Duty). The settlement building is a nice addition but the limitations (removed with
or tricked with
- beware hits to your FPS though) can really hinder big builders and thinkers. While it's great to build your own town from nothing, it's pretty lackluster in terms of features and mechanics. Placing fences on uneven ground is a massive pain in the backside, it can take a good hour or two to get the walls looking right. It really needs polish and I hope if Bethesda doesn't do this then a mod does. It's a great feeling though once you've made your first settlement, the rewards are pretty good too (I have many industrial water purifiers making water for me to sell. I make around 3000 caps every half hour). The rest of the gameplay and mechanics are great, you'll see complaints about animation but it's silly - the animation is fine and is much better than previous titles).
The story is pretty good so far (I'm loving the approach they're taking this time) and the characters are pretty engaging and interesting. HOWEVER, this game does steer you to being the good guy at some points in the game (definitely in the main story). I have not finished it yet, but it seems that many of the roads you take lead to the same destination. The voice acting is good (I play male but from what I've saw the female voice actor is the better out of the two). Some of the side quests have the distinctive good/evil decisions and outcomes that you'd expect from Fallout, but it is a definite step down from previous titles. I think I would have prefered to have no voice acting and more choices than voice acting and less. Writing lacks in some areas but shines in others.
I had to manually change my FOV using
. Personally this isn't a problem for me - I don't mind the manual work as I do a lot of modding to my Bethesda games, but for the casual gamer this could be a bit of a chew on. The mouse seemed fine for me
Overall I would wholeheartingly recommend this game to anyone wanting to sink hours and hours into a large and deep game world that oozes reward for exploring. It didn't strike that charm that Fallout 3 struck when I first played it (probably because Fallout 3 was my first Fallout game), but I'm beginning to love this world a lot more than the Capital Wasteland and the Mojave Desert now. You can look past the occasional bug and kinks for the massively open experience you receive in return.

Spoiler and length warning! I originally wrote a mostly positive review to Fallout 4, but after sinking almost 100 hours into it, I'd like to recant it. If you just want my recommendation skip the body of text and find the end paragraph at the bottom.
I'm not as happy as I originally was with the game for a variety of reasons. Playing both the original Fallout games as well as 3 & New Vegas, I'd say that the strongest trump for this series is the world building. The lore and history that the game builds and lets you constantly explore simply isn't in Fallout 4 as well as previous titles. The Commonwealth, I feel personally, lacks depth compared to the Capital Wasteland or the Mojave Desert or the entire West Coast. This is due in part to a more limited dialog tree, non-dynamic characters, lacking quests, bothersome & useless gimmicks, and less lore-friendly design. Characters, whether they are companions or not, should be interesting and you should be able to interact with them on multiple occasions to explore different dialogs and quests. The fact the player character has a voice is actually okay, because I feel like they emote and speak the line the way I would have said it. But what made your character YOURS came with perks, stats, and SPECIAL. SPECIAL in the previous games basically set you up for the play style you want; combat focus, stealth, peaceful coversationlist, explorer, hunter, doctor, what have you. Being able to upgrade SPECIAL defeats that because you can eventually become overpower; sure you can not spend that level up point, but that's just idiotic to not level up when you level up. The perks I found were largely combat focused and honestly I feel like a lot were useless or didn't do much at all, as well as they didn't feel like they were giving me an identity. The complete absence of the Karma system also puts a major dent in the creating an identity aspect of the game, because there's not a lot of consequences or edgy decisions. As well, I have found but a few quests and characters that really let some depth come in. Most of the companions I found to be enjoyable and pretty dynamic but all NPCs had some depth in the previous games that I just don't find here. A lot of visual changes and mechanics to things like power armor (still mad they turned it into a useless gimmick), Vertibirds, items, etc. It just doesn't feel the same, and in maybe in a sequel such change would be good, but a series like this needs solidarity or else lots of things are world-breaking. Quests are also very samey; most sidequests usually involve you simply to talk to someone and go kill either raiders, ghouls, super mutants, or synths. More quests like helping roleplaying robots on a jet power sailing ship please! Less quests of going to a place to kill some people because a farmer asked me to. More uncovering the secrets of a mysterious family due to a serum and ancient artifact please! LESS QUESTS of going to a PLACE to kill some PEOPLE because a FARMER ASKED ME TO....PLEASE. Faction quests and the main story are really interesting though, forcing you to make decisions and feel for your character's struggle. I think faction and main quests are really solid. However, I don't like you get accepted into factions easily; most factions in other games had you running through hoops to join, and you earned your position through craftiness and dedication. Random radiant quests are also REALLY annoying. For instance, the first time I was about to get onto a Vertibird to head to the BoS airship? Just as I was about to hop in a message popped up Greentop Nursery needed help, so I had to fast travel there and help kill a tiny band of raiders that were wiped in miliseconds by my missile turrets. As a whole, really hard to feel immersed when you have to stop to go help some dumb farmers. Which brings me to the gimmick of settlements! Utterly useless and bothersome! It's basically that little game Fallout Shelter, or more for a better comparison: the Sims. I don't see the point of building a town for a bunch of unnamed people who don't do anything except run some shops that sell gear I can pretty much get anywhere else eventually? I don't like that I basically have to carry several hundred pounds of garbage around to build these places that are barely about static either. Yay, garbage has a purpose now. The point was to get to a position in the wasteland where you could focus on the real good finds: guns, armor, chems, meds, treasures, and good loot. Not scooping up every tin can. And what's the point of building defenses if they don't work passively? I have defense ratings of over 100 for all my settlements, but if I don't head over when one's in trouble it get destroyed. What's the point of spending all that junk on building turrets and traps if they only work when I'm there? They barely need me when I'm there. It was simple in the previous games; you earn a house, stash your loot, and have a place to call home. Maybe some people get enjoyment from building their own cool fort, and there's nothing wrong with that, but I don't like it as a fan of the series. It's a time waster, as is modding. Lots of folks have said you can go the whole game without wasting time modding weapons, but in my experience, they're wrong. Modding a weapon is the only thing that's going to keep you alive, and making basically essential is silly. I shouldn't have to make the gun awesome, it should already be awesome. Not all previous Fallout weapons were awesome, but everyone had their preference and style. The guns look awful no matter what, they're uninteresting (the shotgun and combat rifle look exactly the same), and the fact that they basically are found unfinish is a load of bull. Why on earth, would a hunting rifle, one of the most iconic weapons of the series, have no stock and a short barrel? Why? That defeats the purpose of a hunting rifle. As a whole the game feels more centered around combat, which was a big part of the previous games, but not the sole factor. Fallout is about exploring, learning, surviving, struggling, earning rewards, and enjoying a unique world in their own way. Running and gunning is the only thing that seems to drive FO4. I think this was to make the game more accessible to new players, and if you're a new player, then I would say start with this game I guess. But you should go back to the other games afterwards and try them on for size. Yeah they might not have the best engine, yes they lack the best graphics, yeah they're buggy, but those games encapsulate what the Fallout series has been about a lot better than Fallout 4. By the way, remember when everyone said New Vegas was buggy as heck? Yeah, I've found Fallout 4 to be way buggier.
I gave Fallout 4 a shot and at first I really liked it, but the more I unwrapped it the less it appealed to me. The game is at its core, functional at best, and has just enough to keep me wanting play a bit  more, but not enough to make me love it like the other games. Maybe I'm just a diehard fan whose projecting their love of the game onto everyone else, but I feel like the game wasn't made for the long time fans. It's like it was made for people who hadn't played Fallout before. Newcomers I think will like the game for its simplified dialog system and straightforward shooter action, so newcomers, give it a go and see what you think, but I also suggest playing one or two of the previous titles first or after to compare. But for long time veteran players, I don't recommend the game because I think you're here for the same reasons I am--the people, the places, the stories, the lore, the challenges, the feelings of accomplishment, and the wide variety interesting, thought-provoking, edgy, and also funny adventures--and you won't find it here like in the previous games aside from a scenarios.

OK, so originally I gave this game a thumbs down.
I was disappointed that the wasteland I knew in Fallout 1,2,3 and New Vegas was different.
Once, I learned to just embrace the changes, I actually ended up loving this game.
There is no longer a skill based system like the other games, but the perk tree is pretty neat. It gives you a lot of different options as far as levelling. I think the thought behind it is that there is a measurable difference in gameplay with every level. Wheras, in Fallout 3, going from level 12 to 13 wasn't a huge deal. You got some incremental skill boosts that you choose, and a perk based on your special stats (With FNV being a perk every other level).
This game is more akin to Skyrim than it is to Fallout: New Vegas.
Originally, I was unhappy. But again it's all about embracing change. The crafting is really cool, and I love searching ruins for things I need to build up better guns and strap a jetpack to my power armor.
All in all, I have to give my recommendation. The story is a little simplistic but it is far better than Fallout 3's story. Bethesda is improving their writing little by little with each game they do.

I don't usually write reviews, but in this case I thought I would. I want to preface this by saying that I love the fallout series of games and the world that was created. That having been said, I have really mixed reviews on fallout 4. The size of the world and general gameplay is all what I would expect from  this series. The new settlement system was an ok idea, but I think it could have been implemented better. The settlements start to get annoying after you have a few running. My largest complaint is the dialog system and general storyline. In fallout 3 you could really go anywhere, do just about anything. You could be a good guy or a really bad guy if you wanted, these options are just not avaialble on fallout 4. Sure, you can say some jerky things to people, but there is no adverse reaction from them and ultimately it makes no difference on the progression of the quest lines. I've completed the game now in record time, which means the storyline was too short in my opinion and offered very little in the way of interesting plot twists and turns. The whole main story line is broken down into just a few decisions and even though I havent gone back to play the other decisions yet, my guess at this point would be that there isn't much difference in the end. All in all I'm still playing it, trying to find any last secrets, and I have recommended it to friends of mine. I'd like to see this game opened to the workshop so modders can enhance some of the games downfalls. Long story short. If you like a shooter without a whole lot of real RPG gameplay and dialog then you'll probably really enjoy this game. If you prefer to play the game because of the story and options, you're probably going to be left disappointed.

After waiting so long for Fallout 4, I am quite happy to say I wasn't disappointed. Far from it, the game exceeded my already high expectations. As usual I won't comment on the graphics because I played on a rig under minimum settings, but the game functioned and looked reasonably well nevertheless. As usual I'll focus on the gameplay and the storyline, and both are excellent. The gameplay features a full weapon modification system that could probably be expanded extensively when they allow mods; the shooting mechanics feel more refined and smooth compared to Fallout 3, and the ability to construct settlements on pre-selected areas (and then having to maintain/defend them) adds some longevity to the game without apparently influencing the mainquest enough to be relevant. Speaking of the mainquest, it combines New Vegas' pick a faction to lead to victory with Fallout 3's more compelling story (IMO). They have removed the Karma system which adds a new layer of ambiguity to the mainquest because each of the factions is anti-heroic, and the lack of a Karma system leaves you wonder which decisions are objectively "right" and "wrong." Whereas Fallout 3 needed Broken Steel just to allow you to play after the ending, Fallout 4 needs an epilogue that brings some closure and catharsis to the decision you make at the end of the mainquest. Besides this, you have an excellent RPG shooter whose contents felt a little slim (compared to Skyrim) but will be expanded in full once the Steam Workshop becomes available. Was considering a 9 out of 10 considering the game feels incomplete without the Steam Workshop, but decided it deserved a 10 out of 10 instead.

I found it was a great game for the first 50 or so hours.  Survival difficulty was initially the perfect level of challenge with some bosses killing me 5 or 6 times before I tried new tactics or used my reasources better.  Thats not for everyone, but for me it was perfect.  The AI is much improved over other open world games, uses cover, grenades, and in some cases will run away from you if you are out of reach, hoping to gain an advantage after you leave your safe spot.  In other ways the AI is still very weak, enemies with stop looking for you eventually even if you snipe one of their friends standing next to them.  Gunplay is substantially better.  If you keep your damage up, even on survival the majority of enemies are not too bullet spongey, outside of the occasional boss or high level monster.
In the end game however I found that things had grown far too easy, even on the hardest difficulty, which is a shame because I know there is a lot of good content and stories in the game that I have yet to experience.  Furthermore, once you have mastered the mechanics and progression system, survival difficulty isn't going to provide much of a challenge on additional playthroughs.
Exploration is just as good or better than previous Bethesda games.  Many of the quests, probably the majority, will be to go a site, clear it out of enemies, loot a particular object, and return.  That is actually strong gameplay as long as the combat remains interesting.  The sites in the game are full of interesting environmental stories, both interesting remains of the world pre-apocalypse and interesting stories of its current inhabitants.  Raiders write about their struggles with the local ghouls or other gangs, and you actually notice them saying some pretty interesting stuff.   There are a handful of quests that stand out as being exceptional, involving real choice in ways that are not obviously presented to the player.  These quests are however rare compared to the standard "kill, loot, return" quests and are its entirely possible to play 20 or 40 hours without experiencing any of them.
The city of Boston is pretty rich in detail.  My first view of it was disappointing, becuase it still is not as big as a modern city.  But moving through three blocks can be quite a trek, with different factions constantly battling each other, gun fire often in the background, and numerous interesting sites around every corner.   Occassionaly I felt like I was playing Battlefield: Fallout, the battles became so big, although this is rare, and obviously the combat is not on the same scale.
New additions such as the modding system and settlements add some additional depth to the game and particularly the looting process.  Every piece of junk is potentially valuable, and I found myself dumping guns I looted to keep additional desk fans or oil cans.  The settlement system isn't polished and can be frustrating to use.  But it is fun when you get the hang of it, and even if it isn't super relevent to the rest of the game, it is a great creative outlet and can a provide a compeling narrative to clearing out sites, even if the game world doesn't change significantly because of your settlements.
Weapon modding has a surprising amount of depth.  When you first figure out the system, it seems like there are obvious choices for range and weapon damage.  However these choices are balanced by two additional important stats that are not immediately apparent in their importance.  Weight actually matters in the handling of the gun, the speed it takes to aim and the speed at which can move while carrying it.   The other stat that is important but not immediately significant is action point cost.   V.A.T.S. is back, and is more interesting because it doesn't pause the game, just slows it.   Some gun mods will allow you to shoot significanlty more often in V.A.T.S. unfortunatley, you would only learn this through trial and error, as the game doesn't make it clear how the different mods impact action point cost.  Unfortunatley this depth is somewhat trivialized but the lack of difficulty as the game progresses.
The dialouge is pretty weak.   Your character has some great lines, but they are few, and the dialouge wheel can really disguise what your character will say.  There are few oppurtunities to resolve situations without fighting but by using dialouge or skill checks instead.     I didn't really identify with my character for a long time, until I had done enough in the world that I felt he had a story.  Your own background story for the character will be inhibited by the protagonist's typically happy and family friend attitude.
The companions were surprisingly awesome.  I usually leave them at home in these kinds of games because i find them annoying, but they are integrated into the storytelling in a meaningful way.  They comment on a wide variety of locations, you can ask them for a opinion on some main quests that you just completed.  They aren't of equal quality of couse.  Their combat AI is pretty weak.
I surprisingly enjoyed the main story, and I felt it created difficult choices and had its share of twists.  Nothing brillant but not bad for a video game story.  The factions are integrated into the main story, and their are a surprising amount of different ways the last few quests can play out, although that might not be immediately apparent until you ask someone else how they did it.
Graphics were weak, but the art style was great.   Preformance was sub optimal with long load times, but there were few crashes or game breaking bugs (4 crashes in 70 hours total).
For me, it was worth a quality 50 hours of gameplay, and I'll come back for more when i can mod it for improved difficulty, more realistic damage, and better stealth.

Ok. Real review time.
I finally got done my first play through and am well in to my second. Fallout 4 is the game I was hoping it would be. I've been a huge fan of the series from back before Bethesda got their paws on it, and while Fallout 3 took some getting used to, I thought I knew what to expect going in to Fallout 4.
For the most part, it delivers solidly on the promise. The time I put through in the first play through was not rushed, but I also didn't stall the advancement of the game. My usual Bethesda gripes were actually low, if barely present. I started playing from the point it unlocked, and played really hard for the first 5 days. I only encountered a handful of crashes and bugs. An amount that I feel is so far the "Bethesda Grace Amount" that it feels like someone else made the game.
The changes to the UI, while a bit hard for me to get used to at first, were welcome and needed. I use a Xbox controller on my PC, and I think that other PC gamers are going to find the changes made wonderful. I've not heard complaints from my friends who play with Keyboards, so I am guessing that the comfort added for Controller users did not take away from ye ole Mouse and Keyboard experience.
Lots of things that I didn't feel mattered in previous Fallout games, matter in this ones. Drugs make the difference in many hard fights, even on Normal difficultly. Compainions are much more usefull (and interesting) than in previous games. But also, perks and advancment paths are made to consider the lone wanderer lifestyle.
Character Creation was charming, but I imagine I'll be installing an "Alternate Start" installation as soon as possible. Advancement is really where the game got me. I'm going to make it somehow comprehensible.
We have Fallout 1 + 2 and then there's Fallout 3, New Vegas...and Fallout4!
Where roleplaying and story aspects were high priority on the first two, things have gone the way that satisfy the newer generation of players, as it seems.
New priorities come in the form of improved shooter elements, easier character developement
and less focus on story telling, diplomacy (no, introducing a perk that befriends npcs while you aim at them isn't what it takes) and even choices.
Were there might be nothing wrong at improving things, it definitely is when other core mechanics (which in this case define the games origin) are dumbed down, replaced (in a worse way) or removed at all.
As many already have mentioned, I'm going to list some pro's and con's I encountered aswell.
pro's:
- "wasteland" feels solid, not too small.
- gunplay seems more polished than before.
- some few interesting side quests.
- some nicely reworked models for creatures like Deathclaws and so on.
neutral:
- crafting system for existing weapons and armors, lets you change parts and values of said things.
Tho there aren't many basic weapons and armor in the game so having tons of different equipment is merely an illusion.
- legendary equipment. There are special values for weapons and armors dropped by legendary critters around the world, which are not craftable.
Seems fine first but of course it's all RNG what you get, weapon or armor and which effect it comes with.
- settlement building. Nice to have your own settlement and build further improvements, like interior decoration, managing food and water supply, turrets and traps for defense
or even construct your own shacks...out of the few parts that are present.
Your settlement can also be attacked by raiders, super mutants and so on...tho in my 70~ hours of gametime I only got attacked once while working on my settlement,
I couldn't even look so fast who attacked as the assailants were steamrolled from settlers and defenses.
Also the bulding controls are quite the challenge.
- graphics are fine, like they were in Fallout 3, NV....with some more fancy lighting.
- performance is solid for the most parts of the game, tho there are places were your framerate will drop significant.
- I haven't crashed once in my playtime, bugs I can't tell either, which doesn't mean there aren't any or I took them for a feature.~
Con's:
- dumbed down S.P.E.C.I.A.L. system, no more skills and skillchecks,
plenty of perks which now have several levels you can choose depending on how high the corresponding special attribute and your character level is.
Which translates to every level you gain a perk point, you can also put that point to increase a spcial attribute, that's it.
There is no max level for a reason now it seems, that said without you could screw your build from the very beginning, quite easily.
Which leads to...
- bad dialogues, even worse as it was in Fallout 3, happy save scamming as you try to see through copypasta choices you get.
- Storyline/Mainquests. As I don't want to spoil here I can only say that choices and outcomings leave much to be desired for.
- Beginning/Vault 111/Tutorial: Way too short, feels unfinished, rushed. Also speaking of tutorial, don't expect one for settlement building.
- Companions. There are plenty but to be honest, besides ♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI that sometimes may even lead to your death, those aren't very special to remember...
I usually had my Dogmeat around me 80% of my playtime.
- voice acting. There's the writing and the voice itself, both are lacking imho, especially the protagonists voice is shallow and feels unfamiliar,
also might be part of the reason dialogue options are that shallow aswell. Too much voice acting altogether.
- RNG loot is through the roof, you're not going to far or dangerous places to receive a bad♥♥♥♥♥gun or something like that, loot isn't hand placed at all as far as I can tell. (excluding companion guns)
- Replay value. I tried a second walkthrough with a different character build but due to reasons above I couldn't even make myself touch the mainquest or settlement again, just ran around killing things and then died of boredom.
- personal gripe. "War, war never changes." ..No♥♥♥♥♥♥I got it the first few times, it's the thing you always get in the ending to make you shiver and think about it but here it's like..oh coo' I can say that too! It's loosing it's meaning, really childish.
- Bethesda. I'm actually asking this to myself...Don't people have any sort of integrity anymore?
- oh yea...UI sucks...again.
Thanks for reading, might have missed stuff but I'm out of fuel.
