The only thing that this game does better than Fallout: New Vegas is graphics, and that can quickly be changed with mods.
Player freedom, one of the most important things in the Fallout series, does not exist. You are stuck in the game's storyline that you can either complete, or ignore, which results in no progression until you do it. Actually that applies to pretty much every quest in the game. There's barely any choice you can make anywhere, with dialogue being the worst case. You can say Yes, No (but you have to say yes eventually), A sarcastic responce (which is a yes), or ask for more info. Where are the interesting conversations about cool♥♥♥♥♥♥that happened in NV?
Speaking of NV, Want to know how many people are immortal in NV? Besides children and companions (unless Hardcore mode), absolutely NO ONE. You can kill the head honcho of ANY OF THE FACTIONS. You can kill the doctor that brought you back from the dead! But in Fallout 4, it is a completly different case. I walked into a small bar in a town, and guess what? 5 PEOPLE IN THAT GOD DAMN BAR WERE UNKILLABLE. HOW DOES THAT MAKE SENSE?!
And on top of it all: ITS TOO. DAMN. EASY. I played 24 hours and I ended up with 114 stimpacks, 50 radaways, and 45 rad-xs. With the Medic perk that increases the effectiveness of stimpacks and radaway, you can practically enter god mode and be unkillable yourself, just like half of the people you meet in the game.
The skill system has been watered down to the point where it doesnt feel like taking certain perks feels worth it anymore. Intelligence sucks levelling-wise because you can just go 1 intelligence (2 if you want Medic) and just abuse Idiot Savant. Where's the cool♥♥♥♥♥♥like the perk in NV that cause people to explode with energy when you kill them with energy weapons? Where are the traits? Where are the ♥♥♥♥ing skills?
This horrible system ties in perfectly with the fact that no matter how you create your character, it doesnt change anything. The only thing that is influenced is how good you are at speech checks, which are pointless in themselves because they just unlock perks for certain companions (that you dont even need cause Lone wanderer exists, on top of the fact that the game is easy) and passes speach checks that earn you slightly more money. In NV, you can either kill the guy that you went against in multiple different ways, OR it could be a battle of words: With a high enough Speech or Barter you can convince the guy to leave without any bloodshed. Now you cant. Aint that fun?
You just feel like you have no impact whatsoever in this entire game. Quite similar to skyrim actually.
Where are the minor faction options anyway? There's this awesome mercenary group in the game that seems pretty badass, and they use millitary callouts and stuff. But there is no option to join them or help them out in something. At all. You either fight them or find them dead. Where are the other cool people in the Wasteland? Where's the NCR? Where's the Legion? Where are the tribes that formed after the great war?
But what really takes the cake is the ending and the weapon customization for me. Weapon customisation flat out SUCKS. That's right: In my opinion the weapon customisation is poorly executed. Why? Because it's incredibly linear. You can choose up to 3 different receivers/charges for guns OR better versions of them, without any other cool things that you can add. You can scavange so much spare parts and extra supplies from areas only to have a set upgrade path for weapons. Melee is even worse, seeing as how the average ammount of upgrades for melee weapons is 1. That single upgrade increases it's damage, or adds more damage of a different type. Guess which one you're gonna get?
And the endings. Oh my ♥♥♥♥ing god. They are all the same ♥♥♥♥ING ENDING, NO MATTER WHICH FACTION YOU PICK. ONE OF THEM STARTS OUT DIFFERENTLY, BUT AFTER THAT IT ENDS UP BEING THE SAME. PLAYER FREEDOM? MORE LIKE A LINEAR *YOU HAVE TO PLAY THE WAY WE WANT YOU TO OR NO STORY PROGRESS* SYSTEM DISGUISED AS PLAYER FREEDOM. IT'S NOT EVEN A GOOD ENDING. IT'S JUST THE PLAYER CHARACTER THAT HAS BEEN PRESET COMPLAIGNING ABOUT HOW HE LIVES IN THIS BORING WASTELAND.
Im sorry if this appears ranty, but there's just so much about this game that I hate.
If you're looking for gameplay and nothing else, then I give the a-ok. Exploration and combat feels great and will give you hundreds of hours of fun. Its just mediocre or worse in every other area, which is a damn shame coming from a Bethesda game, especially a Fallout one.
Dont even try to excuse the game's problems with mods. If you have a crappy sandwitch and add tons of good toppings to make it taste great, all that you're doing is hiding the fact that it's a crappy sandwitch. And you can quote me on that.

I really wish that I could select both yes and no for recommending this game. I've been playing Fallout since the first one came out and while this is the Fallout universe and it is fun to see it in such detail with the beautiful voice acting, it is disappointing to not really interact with it.  Fallout 1 and 2 were tough.  They were unforgiving (and buggy).  You could easily fail a quest because you answered a question wrong or kept asking questions of someone who was obviously becoming irritated with you.  In this game you can't even say "no."  I mean, you can say "no" but for all intents and purposes it is still "yes," they might just act irritated for a second.  You can't be a bad guy, you can't refuse quests and they have completely removed Karma as far as I can tell.
I don't mind the loss of skill points and think they did a good job switching to the perks (there were really too many perks in the newer games anyway).  The combat is hugely improved over Fallout 3 and NV, in my opinion.  And the voice acting is much more engaging and natural.  I wasn't impressed with the textures after other games I've played this year.
Lastly, let me say: I don't want to go back to the hex grid...EVER...or have Vic shooting me over and over point blank in the back of the head.  But as a old school Fallout fangirl, I would rather have the bugs and the clunky fighting and even silent dialogue, over all the polish if it would bring back the accountability you had in the first games.

There's a TL;DR at the bottom of this, unless for some reason you want to read the whole thing.
I've put roughly 150 hours combined of both Fallout 3 and Fallout New Vegas (this review will be mostly making comparisons to those two games.), and I can say with absolute confidence that the combat is
much more satisfying. The guns feel fantastic, each one different than the next. Melee combat has also improved immensely, but I'd have to say that Skyrim's melee is still better. (but that's to be expected, Skyrim doesn't have any guns.) I absolutely adore the new combat system, it makes the game feel so much more like an FPS (which in this game's case is a very good thing), than in 3/NV, which was basically a means to an end.
Now, the Power Armor. If I'm even sort of honest with myself, this is pretty much the biggest reason I pre-ordered the game (and the pip-boy edition at that) a week after it was announced. The Power Armor (from now it will be referred to as 'PA') is such an upgrade from 3 and NV. You feel powerful, as you should be. Raiders just become annoying instead of actual threats, and if you invest heavily into a PA build, eventually so will everything else. There's also the Jet Pack, but I've only just unlocked that. It's honestly the funnest thing to go around stomping in the PA, slaughtering everything that fires back at you. The Deathclaws are also much more scary. In the earlier levels whenever I encountered a deathclaw, I'd panic and pull out my minigun and begin shooting as many bullets as possible before it got close. The removal of fall damage whille in PA is also pretty amazing, because you can just air drop wherever you want, from any height.
The settlement building is definitely an important part of the game, and I enjoy just being OCD as I try and remove any and all useless junk off the workshop sites. But, it can be a bit of a pain to try and find those rarer materials as you try and build your PA garage. It's also fairly challenging, because if you don't leave any defenses, it becomes harder to defend your settlemenst from unwanted raiders. It's not required by the game for you to build settlements, but I highly recommend you do it either way.
I remember a lot of people complaining about the graphics from the E3 trailer. Now, they aren't any Arkham Knight level of detail, but they sure are incredible. I'm able to run most of the settings on Ultra without lag, but occasionally the menu screens act like a slide show, but not the actual game, for some strange reaason. I've yet to figure that out, but the only actual lag I've encountered when in-game is while I'm in a vertibird and looking down on Boston. That causes the most lag whenever I play, but the rest of the time it's a steady 60 FPS.
As well as that, it's also one of the most stable Bethesda games I've ever played. Considering how many times 3, NV, and Skyrim crashed, this game is incredibly stable. I just hope modding it to bits once the modding kit releases doesn't change that.

Normal review:
This game is awesome, and one of the very few games released in the last decade truly worth paying the full $60 for.  You either know what the Fallout experience is or you don't.  You have to make decisions that change the entire game around you, some of these decisions are cut and dried based on how you want to play (righteous, mercenary, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, etc) some of them will leave you wondering if you made the right move... Others will actually haunt you.  There is no right decision it's all shades of grey (not like that other shades of grey, think before that ever existed).  Moral decisions can become so muddy you have to just go as you feel and possibly regret them for a long time.
Pros:
-If you have the hardware this game is stunning, a true example of what modern machines can bring to life.
-Decision based gameplay that will change based on how you play, do a playthrough as a hero and a villian and the game will be substantially different.
-WAY better loot system than previous Fallout games, though some may miss the constant repairing of guns (I do).
-New way to have and use Power Armor, though this is a plus and a minus.
Cons:
-It's a Fallout game, sometimes things happen that make no sense and you just have to live with it.
-Framerates with even the best hardware are inconsistent at best for reasons no one will ever understand at times that will seem strange.
-You have to actually like Fallout to enjoy this, if you didn't like Fallut 3 or New Vegas, you probably won't like this.
-Buy a new GPU when you buy this game.  So far I've measured it taking a steady 8GB RAM and a peak of over 3GB GPU memory everywhere at Ultra.
Bottom line:
Invest the money and play the game, it's cheaper than a drug habit and lasts longer without killing you.  Remember to be  nice to your girlfriend/boyfriend while you play, you won't be seeing much of them.

This is one of the greatest game ive ever played, Fallout 4 is an engrossing game that lures you in with mystery and the promise of adventure. Its wretched wasteland can be captivating, and you never know what odd person or settlement lies around the next bend. Fallout 4 uses its dark world as a canvas for exciting combat and gripping stories, and when you dig deeper into its post-nuclear-apocalypse version of Boston--defending yourself from violent scavengers and using your wits to climb social ladders--you become attached to the new you, and ultimately invested in the fate of your new world.
You transform into an influential wasteland warrior over the course of a multitude of dangerous quests, but this is difficult to imagine at the start when you're a well-to-do citizen of 1950s-esque Boston. The game begins on a peaceful morning at home with your spouse and child; a robot butler provides upbeat banter and a glimpse at what America might have become if the World's Fair era of invention and optimism from the 1930s persisted into the 21st century. Life is pleasant, until a distressful television broadcast. Your family is quickly rushed underground. It's within Vault 111 that you spend the next 200 years, frozen in cryogenic-stasis until your eventual rude awakening in the year 2277.

Improvements over Fallout 3 and New Vegas:
+ Companions have more personality than ever before
+ Combat has been vastly improved
+ Settlements, despite the clunkiness of the controls, are a lot of fun, especially for fans of city building
+ Scavenging feels better than ever, with the game's new crafting system ensuring everything has a use
+ The Dialogue Camera (a la Mass Effect) combined with having a voiced player character makes dialogue more interesting; I find myself less willing to just skip through everything people are saying
+ The skill system has been integrated into the perk tree, which I feel streamlined the gameplay, but not without a cost--more below.
+/- Power armor no longer feels like awkward metal clothing; instead, you feel like a bipedal tank. Now I understand why you always needed training for power armor... but why did they remove power armor training in this game? (New power armor system is a plus, removing the need for training is a minus.)
Tradeoffs, or things that were better in Fallout 3 and New Vegas:
- Dialogue options for your character are very repetitive and linear, offering very little deviation in terms of your character's personality.
- The simplification of character building via removing the Skill system and integrating most of the Skills as perks (hacking, lockpicking, pickpocketing, weapon-category damage, sneak ability) damaged build diversity.
- Between the lack of build diversity and the lack of dialogue variation, the RP aspect of the game has been significantly neutered. While I still feel responsible for what my character has become, it's no where near as immersive or as enjoyable as the prior games.
- The perk tree is horribly balanced. While balance has never been good in Fallout, a good 50% of the perks are borderline useless. Additionally, some SPECIALs are flat out terrible--almost everything in the Endurance line is awful and Endurance itself is negligible, mostly due to how early you gain access to Power Armor, which is head and shoulders above any armor you'll be able to craft at endgame, even with the most basic suit minus upgrades.
- The story--without spoiling anything--is entirely inconsequential. I have never felt so unsatisfied with the ending of an RPG as I did with Fallout 4. This is by far the worst storyline in the entire series, which is a damn shame given how strong the supporting cast of companions is.
tl;dr - The gameplay is almost strictly superior to that of the previous games, but it no longer feels like an RPG. If you are new to the franchise: Fallout is the post-apocalyptic remains of some alternate-timeline 'Happy Atomic 1950s' mixed with B-movie stuff and some more serious themes, never taking itself very serious, though. 200 years after the bombs fell in a conflict with China you wake up in your cryo capsule in one of the few fallout shelters around the Boston area - your partner murdered and your son kidnapped. Trying to piece together what happened and to find your son you venture out into the wasteland encountering super mutants, ghouls, homicidal robots, mutated monsters, and of course the scattered remnants of human civilization.
The world is densely packed with stuff to find and places to explore, several factions to join and many wonderful characters to meet. There's also a lot of passive story telling - by reading logs on surviving computers, finding audio tapes or simply through the arrangement of items in a location, many small side stories are told. If there's one problem with the game, then it's that it is very hard to stay focused on your main goal - finding your son and whoever took him and killed your partner. After all the sidequesting and exploring the final conclusion to the main campaign felt a little bit underwhelming - especially if - like me - you had reached level 60 by that point. Luckily the game isn't over after that - giving you the opportunity to explore all the places you didn't have time to checkout yet. And now the DLC has started pouring in...
Having finished the main game after over 120 hours on my first playthrough when the game was new and having checked out the first DLC I am very satisfied with what Bethesda gave us with this iteration of the franchise. I didn't encounter many bugs even directly after release (a first for Bethesda) -  and nothing game breaking or annoying. Also most bugs that existed then have been fixed by now.
The main story missions in general are good but not on par with the other big open world RPG of 2015 - The Witcher 3. Many sidequest are basically 'go there, kill everyone' or simple fetch quests, and many of the minor faction quests even send you to the same areas repeatedly (aka random side quests). There are great missions (like the big heist), but they are few inbetween - and it's often more the lore around the missions that makes them great, rather than what you actually have to do. That's nothing new for the franchise though, and in my view the Bethesda Fallout games mostly invite you to explore the world - using missions more as a pointer to new areas and then having you discover all those other little things hidden away in the world on your own. The main plot and faction missions mainly prevent you from completely loosing your aim in this large and wonderful world.
Still, a few big changes have been very controversial, like the settlement stuff (building and managing settlements) and the whole crafting system for weapon and armor upgrades (and for robot companions if you own the new Mechanist DLC). Luckily most of this is completely optional. If you don't like crafting just scavenge and steal  (or even buy) weapons and armor - you'll always find enough good gear. If you don't want to build up any settlements, then just limit it to the few bit required if you want to follow the Minutemen or Railroad factions. I personally liked the weapons and armor crafting very much - and didn't care too much for the settlement building stuff.
The biggest change was definitely the way stats (strength, perception, agility, etc. - the base values for all skill checks), skills (like lockpicking, weapon handling, etc.) and perks (modifiers for your skills and extra abilities) work now:
Since the first Fallout your stats were fixed at the start of the campaign and you could only improve them by a little bit throughout the game. You mainly advanced your character by slowly increasing your skills using a small number of points you got at every level up - and by choosing an additional perk at every second level up. Usually you boosted your two or three main skills over the first few levels and only then invested in others. That's the way it's been forever. Even when Bethesda revived the series with Fallout 3 they kept this system almost unchanged.
Now that's completely changed: stats still exists, but skills and perks are all mixed together into abilities. You get one point at each level up, and you can choose to invest it in one of the nine ability slots associated with each stat - or in the base stat itself (unlocking another ability slot and generally improving skill checks based on that stat). Most ability slots can have multiple upgrades, each requiring one point and  - for further upgrades - a minimum level. That means that perks that were formerly available only to high level characters can now - at least in their basic version - be aquired early on, and that higher levels of certain skills (like rifleman, lockpicking or speech) can't be aquired as early as before.
In my opinion this gives more choice right from the start and leads to more rounded characters over the course of the campaign as you don't miss out when investing points in other abilities - you need to wait for the upgrades to your main abilities to unlock at later levels anyways. Also increasing basic stats now allows you to slowly adapt your characters base type (so your guy is too stupid to hack any but the simples terminals? Just raise INT to unlock the Hacking ability). Your choice at the start should still reflect your intended play style and it will take a while - but you now have the option to change that without starting a new game.
If you want a great open world RPG, like the whacky Fallout setting, then there's not much you can do wrong by getting into Fallout 4. It's great game, with the same beloved atmosphere and story telling we know and love from the older parts, but also with some - to me - very welcome changes. I can't wait to explore more of that in the upcomming DLCs - the first one (The Mechanist) already added modding and building your own robots (and boy do they get fancy!).

Firstly, shooting mechanics are really good, probably the best in any fallout game. Lot's of implementation of new, nice mechanics. Shooting a Fat Man at a legendary deathclaw Matriarch has never been so satisfying. Can now stack crits, so no more RNG in that matter, which is something I can really appreciate.
AI is much smarter, theyll take cover, toss grenades and molotovs (a lot, btw). VATS is no longer freeze frame, so you cant just sit in VATS and take your time deciding what to shoot. Health regen is no longer instant, so you cant just "take damage, pipboy, eat a ton of♥♥♥♥♥♥ repeat" anymore "Legendary" (drop uniques) and Higher level enemies now. Really challenging, very rewarding and satisfying. Expect to die a-whole-godamn-lot. Difficulty levelling isnt all that great, lots of bullet sponge; this won't be a probably after early game, since by then you'll have real powerful weapons by then, especially if you build for guns.
Crafting is everywhere, you're probably gonna end up modifying the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of a gun you find rather than buying it from vendors. On a side note, you're probably gonna spend a good amount of the game low on caps, which isn't that big a deal since there's better loot in dungeons and drops (for the most part)
Settlements are a thing, kinda neat. Lotta small nuances with it, though.
A lot of companions.
There are a lot of issues, though:New dialogue system is pretty crap; dialogue options lead to the same outcome, its an illusion of choice... a real step backwards. No more speech checks or barter checks or anything, instead a pretty pathetic persuasion check, which is tied to Charisma (from what I've seen, most persuasion checks dont reward to much at all, usually some meger xp and that's it.)
No more skills, Fallout 4 instead has a retconned system of SPECIAL. Now, each level you are given a point, which you can spend on leveling a SPECIAL or on a perk under each SPECIAL (number of points in a SPECIAL category unlocks certain perks for you to pick). multiple tiers per perk.
No more karma system...if anything, the companions youre travelling with kinda facilitate that though- you're actions are either loved or hated by companions, and they're overall feelings about your behavior can unlock their companion quest... lock you out of their companionship.
TL;DR
Bethesda takes out a BIG portion of the RPG elements and skill system Fallout is famous for, but amps up the combat to a new level. Still a lot of fun

I just want to start off by saying that although I do recommend this game, it's not nearly as good as New Vegas and I am taking off my nostalgia goggles off for this review.
I won't do a summary of the game, that's already covered by 99% of other reviews and the store page.
My biggest problem with the game is that there are no level requirements for any guns and your character just knows how to reload them all proficiently. I feel like all the RPG aspects of the previous Fallout games are missing and my immersion gets broken pretty easily. There is no weapon durability, and you cannot craft ammo (unless I'm missing something here) which in a sense is made up for but I still feel like there should at least be an option to enable weapon durability.
There are no skills in this game like in the previous ones, they are replaced by perks which merge previous perks with skills which makes the game and your character have less variety.
There are so few weapons in this game and this is the part that actually pisses me off the most. Bethesda quality control is a bit bad on the weapon variety and I feel like it's an excuse for all the weapon crafting mods you can add to your weapons which don't count as new weapons! Don't get me wrong, the crafting system and legendary weapon system is pretty cool, but I feel like there's only 3 varients of every weapon type: early game, mid game, and late game. There are very few in-betweens and I feel like I'm using the same damn weapon way too often.
One more thing. YOU CAN'T BE A BAD GUY, HOLY CRAP THIS ANGERS ME. If a baby is drowning in a lake, you have no option other than to say "Yes" to save it. In previous titles, you can just say "No" and lose karma.
As for graphics, meh, looks like a 2007 game using the same old engine. I can't complain because gameplay over graphics but it's still a pet peeve of mine.
I really hate the arguments, "Mods will fix it," "DLC will fix it". It just gives Bethesda an excuse to be lazy.
I recommend this game, however, because it's not a BAD game - it's just missing a lot of features that were on the previous installments and it has some fun locations to look through. The settlement building is fun and I look forward to modding the crap out of that.

A huge improvement over the previous games. People have been whining a lot, but keep in mind they've been developing this game for years, so the graphics are...well, years old! Those who are new to the series (and have apparently crappy graphics cards) will complain the graphics "aren't as good as other games right now." However, those of us loyal fans from at least FO3 era will see a MASSIVE improvement. Things really do look beautiful. Stepping out of the vault for the first time choked me up the same way it did in FO3. (Then again I also cried during the E3 trailer so...)
Please don't complain if your computer (or console) cannot provide you with the high or ultra settings- that's not Bethesda's fault. I'm running it on ultra and it looks fantastic. People's skin actually looks like SKIN! Actual SKIN TEXTURE! My eyes are crying with joy from the improvement over the plastic Barbie Doll people from Skyrim and FO3 who were always way too bright and shiny and blinded me with their stupid ugly faces.
My only complaint is there are some random textures that are oddly low-res, like some walls and decals, and I would like to see an HD texture pack DLC or mod of some kind.
Also, something to be said about the animation. Wow! I really mean, WOW! The animations are so much more fluid. Instead of baddies running at you in one direction like robots, they actually jump around, dive out of then way, tackle you and fall down, zigzag to avoid bullets... it feels much more realistic which affects the gameplay a lot. I'll get to that more later.
I love the new ability to "make" your own gun. You can really pick any weapon and mod the heck out of it. Melee weapons and heavy weapons suffer a lack of variety, but regular old rooty tooty guns have a crazy amount of customization. Same goes for armor.
My complaint is that there are a lot of armors "sets" and clothing you can't actually utlize the modding system for. They don't count for some reason so you can't wear any extra armor on top of them. For example if I want to wear the Greaser Jacket set I cannot put on any arm, leg, chest etc. armor...? Why not? I want to be able to customize myself however I please. I end up ignoring most of the clothes because there's no point.
Oh boy. This is the heaviest section.
So many things have been changed from the previous games. If you haven't played FO4 yet, be prepared for these changes. I was taken by surprise to find that there are no longer ANY SKILLS! How odd to have a Bethesda game without skills.
They also took away the karma system. Boo :( Why would you do this, Bethesda?! From what I understand people LOVED the more in-depth roleplaying of New Vegas. I know I did! I want to be able to make a lasting impact on the world. I want people to either love me or fear me. I want my reputation to carry across the wastes. I want to
Having no karma system, and a very limited dialogue tree, makes me care a lot less.
Speaking of the dialogue tree, I know a lot of people are upset, and I am a bit upset myself. But it's not as bad as I first thought. Yes, the options are limited and kind of... stiff. Yes, I wish there were more options, more personality, and more emotion to what's going on and what I have to say. However it's really not THAT bad. I'm okay with it. If this was the only "bad" change, I wouldn't mind so much. But combined with a lack of karma system and no more skills (meaning no more skill checks in dialogue!) I feel like a large portion of fun has been taken out of the game. I miss the old ways!
The voice acting, though, is nice. I like it. I'm used to games with voice acting- being a fan of Mass Effect I'm used to the main character being voiced. If only there were MORE dialogue options, then the voice acting would have a better chance to shine.
One thing that's bugging me... and I don't know if it's just me... but I don't really give a hoot about the story so far. I never had enough time to form a bond between my game-hubby or my baby. In fact Codsworth is the only one I cared about. In FO3, you were raised in the vault and formed a bond with your dad, so when things went to heck in a handbasket, you cared. In FO4 I'm finding myself just not giving a single damn about my baby and I don't miss my hubby at all. I would have preferred a more open beginning, being able to shape my own story a bit more, since a lot of people dislike being railroaded into things... especially with a game calling itself an RPG!
Combat is now also WAY better. It's faster paced, more fluid, and enemies have personality. Each type of enemy between raiders, feral ghouls, molerats, you name it- they all have their own style of combat. I don't just feel like "Here comes Enemy A" "Now here comes Enemy B" anymore, like I did in previous Fallout games. I highly recommend people play the game on hard difficulty or higher, it really adds extra oomph to combat, and the special weapon rewards are worth it :)
I can't say much about companions yet as I've only used Dogmeat so far. But I have to say he looks f&%$ing adorable in goggles and a bandana. He gets in my way a lot and likes to trip mommy while she's walking, but he's just so darn cute and actually helpful in combat.
I'm not sure if this counts as gameplay but the music is very good. Some new additions that I love, although I hope I get to hear some more of the old tracks from the original games (background music and whatnot from the first Fallout, I believe by Inon Zur) Some of the new tracks are honestly REALLY good and add to the feel of the wasteland.
If I were to give this game a rating, it would be a solid 8/10. This is coming from someone who has spent, and I do mean literally, about 1,000 hours combined in FO3 and NV. In fact I still consider FO3 to be my favorite game of all time. I was very, very hyped for the release of FO4 and I was not disappointed.
(I also want to note, if you have a friend/significant other who likes to watch you play... let them use the Pip-Boy app on your phone. The game becomes instant co-op. They can equip weapons, toggle radio, and eat food while you're in combat! It's very helpful and tons of fun!)
So, from my opinion, the game could stand some improvement, a few hit or miss issues like dialogue, lack of karma, etc. but the rest is turning out amazing so far. And with the promise of DLCs in the near future I know I'll be racking up many hours in this game.

If you are new to the franchise: Fallout is the post-apocalyptic remains of some alternate-timeline 'Happy Atomic 1950s' mixed with B-movie stuff and some more serious themes, never taking itself very serious, though. 200 years after the bombs fell in a conflict with China you wake up in your cryo capsule in one of the few fallout shelters around the Boston area - your partner murdered and your son kidnapped. Trying to piece together what happened and to find your son you venture out into the wasteland encountering super mutants, ghouls, homicidal robots, mutated monsters, and of course the scattered remnants of human civilization.
The world is densely packed with stuff to find and places to explore, several factions to join and many wonderful characters to meet. There's also a lot of passive story telling - by reading logs on surviving computers, finding audio tapes or simply through the arrangement of items in a location, many small side stories are told. If there's one problem with the game, then it's that it is very hard to stay focused on your main goal - finding your son and whoever took him and killed your partner. After all the sidequesting and exploring the final conclusion to the main campaign felt a little bit underwhelming - especially if - like me - you had reached level 60 by that point. Luckily the game isn't over after that - giving you the opportunity to explore all the places you didn't have time to checkout yet. And now the DLC has started pouring in...
Having finished the main game after over 120 hours on my first playthrough when the game was new and having checked out the first DLC I am very satisfied with what Bethesda gave us with this iteration of the franchise. I didn't encounter many bugs even directly after release (a first for Bethesda) -  and nothing game breaking or annoying. Also most bugs that existed then have been fixed by now.
The main story missions in general are good but not on par with the other big open world RPG of 2015 - The Witcher 3. Many sidequest are basically 'go there, kill everyone' or simple fetch quests, and many of the minor faction quests even send you to the same areas repeatedly (aka random side quests). There are great missions (like the big heist), but they are few inbetween - and it's often more the lore around the missions that makes them great, rather than what you actually have to do. That's nothing new for the franchise though, and in my view the Bethesda Fallout games mostly invite you to explore the world - using missions more as a pointer to new areas and then having you discover all those other little things hidden away in the world on your own. The main plot and faction missions mainly prevent you from completely loosing your aim in this large and wonderful world.
Still, a few big changes have been very controversial, like the settlement stuff (building and managing settlements) and the whole crafting system for weapon and armor upgrades (and for robot companions if you own the new Mechanist DLC). Luckily most of this is completely optional. If you don't like crafting just scavenge and steal  (or even buy) weapons and armor - you'll always find enough good gear. If you don't want to build up any settlements, then just limit it to the few bit required if you want to follow the Minutemen or Railroad factions. I personally liked the weapons and armor crafting very much - and didn't care too much for the settlement building stuff.
The biggest change was definitely the way stats (strength, perception, agility, etc. - the base values for all skill checks), skills (like lockpicking, weapon handling, etc.) and perks (modifiers for your skills and extra abilities) work now:
Since the first Fallout your stats were fixed at the start of the campaign and you could only improve them by a little bit throughout the game. You mainly advanced your character by slowly increasing your skills using a small number of points you got at every level up - and by choosing an additional perk at every second level up. Usually you boosted your two or three main skills over the first few levels and only then invested in others. That's the way it's been forever. Even when Bethesda revived the series with Fallout 3 they kept this system almost unchanged.
Now that's completely changed: stats still exists, but skills and perks are all mixed together into abilities. You get one point at each level up, and you can choose to invest it in one of the nine ability slots associated with each stat - or in the base stat itself (unlocking another ability slot and generally improving skill checks based on that stat). Most ability slots can have multiple upgrades, each requiring one point and  - for further upgrades - a minimum level. That means that perks that were formerly available only to high level characters can now - at least in their basic version - be aquired early on, and that higher levels of certain skills (like rifleman, lockpicking or speech) can't be aquired as early as before.
In my opinion this gives more choice right from the start and leads to more rounded characters over the course of the campaign as you don't miss out when investing points in other abilities - you need to wait for the upgrades to your main abilities to unlock at later levels anyways. Also increasing basic stats now allows you to slowly adapt your characters base type (so your guy is too stupid to hack any but the simples terminals? Just raise INT to unlock the Hacking ability). Your choice at the start should still reflect your intended play style and it will take a while - but you now have the option to change that without starting a new game.
If you want a great open world RPG, like the whacky Fallout setting, then there's not much you can do wrong by getting into Fallout 4. It's great game, with the same beloved atmosphere and story telling we know and love from the older parts, but also with some - to me - very welcome changes. I can't wait to explore more of that in the upcomming DLCs - the first one (The Mechanist) already added modding and building your own robots (and boy do they get fancy!).

I just want to start off by saying that although I do recommend this game, it's not nearly as good as New Vegas and I am taking off my nostalgia goggles off for this review.
I won't do a summary of the game, that's already covered by 99% of other reviews and the store page.
My biggest problem with the game is that there are no level requirements for any guns and your character just knows how to reload them all proficiently. I feel like all the RPG aspects of the previous Fallout games are missing and my immersion gets broken pretty easily. There is no weapon durability, and you cannot craft ammo (unless I'm missing something here) which in a sense is made up for but I still feel like there should at least be an option to enable weapon durability.
There are no skills in this game like in the previous ones, they are replaced by perks which merge previous perks with skills which makes the game and your character have less variety.
There are so few weapons in this game and this is the part that actually pisses me off the most. Bethesda quality control is a bit bad on the weapon variety and I feel like it's an excuse for all the weapon crafting mods you can add to your weapons which don't count as new weapons! Don't get me wrong, the crafting system and legendary weapon system is pretty cool, but I feel like there's only 3 varients of every weapon type: early game, mid game, and late game. There are very few in-betweens and I feel like I'm using the same damn weapon way too often.
One more thing. YOU CAN'T BE A BAD GUY, HOLY CRAP THIS ANGERS ME. If a baby is drowning in a lake, you have no option other than to say "Yes" to save it. In previous titles, you can just say "No" and lose karma.
As for graphics, meh, looks like a 2007 game using the same old engine. I can't complain because gameplay over graphics but it's still a pet peeve of mine.
I really hate the arguments, "Mods will fix it," "DLC will fix it". It just gives Bethesda an excuse to be lazy.
I recommend this game, however, because it's not a BAD game - it's just missing a lot of features that were on the previous installments and it has some fun locations to look through. The settlement building is fun and I look forward to modding the crap out of that.
This is for me one of the most awesome games of the year!

This game was not a Fallout game, or even an RPG for that matter. The combat was fine, and the graphics were fine, but do not be mistaken - this is nothing like Fallout 3 or Fallout New Vegas.
Bethesda took every RPG element out of this game - there are no intimidation dialouge options, no intelligence checks, just charisma checks, which are VERY few and far between. Your character either says "yes" or "no" in every dialouge option, they're all just disguised as different dialouge choices. It also seems that, because your character is a parent, they have to be the good guy. There is not a shred gray morality in this game. Every thing your character does makes him/her out as an angel. [SPOILERS AHEAD] Even if you join the Institute, the faction that has (up until the point where you can join), been established as the villans, it will turn out that they are one of the many the good guys. They only faction that made me feel like a villan, and it did so only slightly, was the Brotherhood of Steel, only once I realised they had killed Elder Lions, and only once they commanded me to eliminate the Railroad. Although I have not completed it myself, and have no plans to, I have heard from many that the Minute Men questline is atrocious, and is made up entirely of copy and paste quests.
In conclusion, the game did not have poor fighting mechanics, but the combat is only one part of the formula that made FO3 and FNV great games. And Fallout 4 lacks in every part of that formula, besides the basic combat.

Short Version first followed by a lovely bulleted list.
Fallout 4 is easily one of my favorites of the Fallout series and that is not something I say lightly. I have played through Fallout 1, Fallout 2, Fallout Tactics: Brotherhood of Steel, Fallout 3, and Fallout New Vegas several times over each and while they all definitely have their strengths and weaknesses one thing has always remained the same,
Is it true that their are bugs? Yes. Is it true that this is not the best looking game ever? Yes. Is it true that some features are not implemented perfectly? Yes. However all of these do not detract from the fact that Fallout 4 is overwhelmingly a FUN game. Bethesda will never make a game with amazing graphics, or perfect animations, or even a bug free game. However, they do make games that ooze personality and charm that many major games lack nowadays. Fallout 4 is no exception to this. I've played Witcher 3, Pillars of Eternity, Divinity: Original Sin, and none of them sucked me in like Fallout 4 has. None of them had this addictive feeling of finding out what is just over that hill, what is in that building I can barely make out on the horizon, or the feeling you get from exploring some of the sidequests and hidden little places (like the teddy bears you find posed all over the place) that you just don't find very often in most games nowadays. So yes you should definitely buy this game immediately and discover for yourself what it is like to feel the terror of a legendary deathclaw popping up right in front of you in the Glowing Sea.

This game is fantastic.  A continued journey in the world of the fallout universe and different take on it all the same.  It follows suit with most Bethesda games in the sense that it is an open world RPG that has a lot to complete.  Modding makes more and more possible in this game, and with the release of the SDK coming up, expect a pouring of mods of all varieties that will add to the longevity of an already massive game.  The sound scape is well done, as with most Bethesda.  The graphics, while not cutting edge, and on par with a "Bethesda-esque" type of graphical style.  There are the standard type of "Bethesda" style bugs, such as models twitching and spazzing out, however there are very few serious bugs and they are being patched quickly.  The RPG mechanics are deep and well thought out.  The balance of difficulty in the game is well done and more balanced than most games that you would normally play.  Inventory management, with most Bethesda games, is always a pain in the butt and takes up a lot of time that takes away from the otherwise incredibly enjoyable experience.  The addition of being able to "build" several settlements from scratch like legos is fun and intirguiging.  Already people in the community have been some very incredible things, and I can't way for more of that to come.  The variety of weapons is typical of Bethesda games, where you have a few standard types of weapons, with infinite varieties and customization of each of those types.  Quest types are varied and well thought out.  The story is amazing, and one of the best apolocolyptic stories out there.  Hope this helps you in your purchasing decision.  :)

I got very angry trying to play one of my ALL-TIME favorite game series, when I was frustrated at every aspect. For instance in F3NV, there was a wonderful character interaction wheel; this is dumbed down to arrow keys, one of which is exit...
So I was considerably disappointed at the corruptions of the last game's brilliance. F3NV was just about perfect, and the MODS were incredible. For me, this game is fatally flawed starting with the interface. I simply cannot emmerse into a game that I cannot control. Other games I play with a remapped keyboard without ever thinking about what controls what. My best example is Fallout 3 NEW VEGAS. Perfect example. That is how a game interface should behave; why change it, especially if the change ruins it? In my opinion,the interface is unacceptable, I'm left-handed. ..update...I'm still trying to get my money's worth out of this game; I cn upgrade my review to "average" at best. The interface has improved some, but still is consistently in the way of emmersion. The missions are repetative, boring, predictable, and only sometimes fun, and sometimes advances the story. I still do not understand why so much emphasis on the drudgery of building settlements, as it involves boring, repetative tasks, and uses never-defined requirements to frustrate the player (me) and confuse the process - example - getting settlers to help you select them, but by the time you find what it is they are supposed to do, they wander off, or nothing happens when I click and the next click picks up the item (rendering assignment impossible) and so on. Saving and loading games - how simple can that be - yet you click and nothing happens, you wait and click again and again...
Most games I play through several times. This one just this once and only because I've found some useful console commands that provide 'stuff' in an otherwise impossibly frustrating combat environment.
I had, when it was released, the minimum required system; since then, it is no longer meeting the minimum. I have it all on low, and still in any complex situation (rain, a single combat, crowds, waves, fog, etc., etc,) it grinds from 60fps down to single digits fps. I have never seen so much useless stuff in agame. The environment is loaded with unique and absolutely no purpose whatsoever stuff; it's beyond silly, so much design with no usefull purpose. Repairing power armor always comes down to FAIL because you didn't pick up enough tim cans.. this game is a tin can, and I'm hopingto kick it down the road soon; 180+hours is close to my break-even point for this game, and then Fallout goes on the shelf. I'll start by saying i have played Skyrim, Fallout: NV and Fallout 3, after playing New Vegas i was excited to see what Bethesda had in store for us next and did they ever deliver with Skyrim. Unofortunatly i bought Fallout 3 one month before the release of Fallout 4 and was disappointed in the game.
Once again i am disappointed, i may have expected too much from Bethesda based off of how much i enjoyed F:NV and Skyrim but Fallout 4 lacks the amount of unique content given by both those games.
Wondering what i mean by unique content? well like Fallout 3 there is a severe lack of quest that differ from the rest. Once you beat the main campaign a few times and some unique quests here and there is turns into a repetetive game of go here, kill that.
I find most the content to be doing the exact same thing. For example after a few unique quest with any of the main factions it turns into doing the same thing over and over.
Brotherhood of Steel: Go here kill Ghouls, Go here take Tech.
Minutemen: Go here clear the area, go here defend those guys
Institute: Go here retrieve our robot, go here take out these baddies.
I think to improve this game we need more towns with unique issues it seems as if most of the content is the same old quest given by the same old people.
I will now contrast things i enjoyed and things i didn't about the game
The Good:
V.A.T.S, slowing down vats was an enjoyable edition to the game which made it alittle bit harder.
Improved Voice Acting, i can't say how nice it is to have somewhat lifelike conversations in a RPG
Weapon and Armour Modification Sysem, all im gunna say is epic. It's nice to be able to craft your own weapons rather then HAVING to scavenge the wasteland for hours to look for a reliable and strong weapon
Sprinting, its nice to not have to travel at a light job like in the previous games
Artillery, Synth Grenades and Vertibirds, having artillery support is just down right epic, toss a Smoke Grenade into a bandit camp and watch the bodies fly.  Synth Grenades useful, wish they sent a courser instead and just costed more but owel,  VERTIBIRDS: they need alot of work, i feel as if they're basically a slow fast travel and killing anything with them as you fly by is pretty hard. You should make it so you can send them to places you havn't been and that they come with a gunner. I see no purpose to using them since i can fast travel.
Visuals: I love the landscape and the combat, i've never experienced a scarier moment in a game then when a ghoul jumps out of the pitch black and practically kills you or a deathclaw tries to swallow you.
Traps: Across the wasteland there are many deadly traps waiting for you that make the game alot more intense, as i approached a bridge i noticed one of those explosice canisters and thought man that would be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥if it blew up with all these cars around. Next thing i know theres a frag mine beeping and im jumping into the water as an epic explosion almost kills me.
The Bad:
Lack of Towns: one of the reasons i enjoyed Skyrim and F:NV and hated Fallout 3 was due to the amount of towns and unique quests given in them, travelling through many towns meeting tons of unique characters and completing unique or different quests is alot more intense and fun than going to 1-3 towns meeting a few important people that give you fun and unique quests and being done with it.
Better Settlement System: love the system but it needs work
Overall: Please add more unique quests and towns to make the game more entertaining, grinding levels from going to the same place 3 times and clearing it 3 times for 3 different people isn't enjoyable content
I recommend but it needs work, overall great ideas but needs improvement and unique content.
Also i'd prefer to define a character rather then play as one.

Fallout 4. To be honest, I've never played a Fallout game before. I've played Skyrim, and I love that game, but there was something that never quite caught my full attention. I don't know what it was in the game, whether it was the fact that I wasn't that interested in the story or lore, or whether it was the fact that I always felt too overwhelmed with the vastness and, being completely truthful, emptiness of the land. Within the first few hours of playing Fallout 4 however, I was hooked. Something just intrigued me about every little corner in the game. What's in this building? What's over there? Where did that mini nuke explosion come from? I wasn't expecting much as I never really gave into the hype, no matter how much people raved about Fallout 3. I wanted to distance myself from that so I could get my own opinion. I'm glad I did, as this is one of the best role-playing exploration games there is to date. I'm not going to compare with other Fallouts, but after reading some other reviews whining about how different it is and how it isn't Fallout anymore, I just wanted to say that it's good that this game does things different. Friends who have played Fallout 3 have said how different the games are, but that it doesn't make it worse. If you are looking for a brilliant action-adventure game with a large open world with a lot of verticality, enough to explore for hours on end but not ridiculously big making the game have stupidly boring treks across entire lands before even stumbling upon something even remote as a small settlement, then this is worth picking up. If you want the few flaws this game has, it's the fact that it isn't optimised brilliantly on PC, doesn't have the graphical quality it should do, has a few bugs that can be annoying (though I haven't really had any myself) and the main story is a little dry and doesn't captivate you like it should. However, the side quests and vaults in the game have awesome stories and lore. I am truly in love with this game and can't wait for the future DLC.

Fallout 4 is easily one of my favorites of the Fallout series and that is not something I say lightly. I have played through Fallout 1, Fallout 2, Fallout Tactics: Brotherhood of Steel, Fallout 3, and Fallout New Vegas several times over each and while they all definitely have their strengths and weaknesses one thing has always remained the same,
Is it true that their are bugs? Yes. Is it true that this is not the best looking game ever? Yes. Is it true that some features are not implemented perfectly? Yes. However all of these do not detract from the fact that Fallout 4 is overwhelmingly a FUN game. Bethesda will never make a game with amazing graphics, or perfect animations, or even a bug free game. However, they do make games that ooze personality and charm that many major games lack nowadays. Fallout 4 is no exception to this. I've played Witcher 3, Pillars of Eternity, Divinity: Original Sin, and none of them sucked me in like Fallout 4 has. None of them had this addictive feeling of finding out what is just over that hill, what is in that building I can barely make out on the horizon, or the feeling you get from exploring some of the sidequests and hidden little places (like the teddy bears you find posed all over the place) that you just don't find very often in most games nowadays. So yes you should definitely buy this game immediately and discover for yourself what it is like to feel the terror of a legendary deathclaw popping up right in front of you in the Glowing Sea.

For me, Fallout franchise has always been about the adventure; Meet interesting people and kill them (if you want). Roleplay as the great hero of order, murderous ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, deviant misantrope or anything in between. In comparison to the previous games, I found this one to be insufferable. All I really wanted (at the end of the day) was a new adventure in a new setting, which I kind of got. Happily a friend of mine decided to gift this game to me as a birthday present, which made me very happy indeed.
Too bad the developers decided to make design decisions which are just beyond me. Some positive things I found were improvements to the VADS and better overall gunplay. TBH, despite being Bethesda game and many people experiencing bugs, I was blessed with encountering just few graphical glitches, nothing game breaking.
First big warning sign was the UI... I mean dear lord. Fallout games have never had the best UI, but this one really starts getting in the way. It is just a massive cluster♥♥♥♥ to use the pipboy. Also, why dont the companions show in the compass? More often then not, having the -dog found something- makes me look around just to find the dog, which is out of sight.
As with all Fallouts, the main story seams to be pretty terrible, but that's not why I played the games; I played for the RPG elements and the side stories. Speaking of RPG elements, I dont understand that a developer of predominantly RPGs decided to dumb-down everything in one of their primary series. While I didnt mind the voiced protagonist, the dialogue system is absolutely attrocious; 'yes', 'no', 'sarcastic' and 'whatever-mission-choice-etc'... is all your reply options. Apparently people say that it is Mass Effect-y, but this is even worse; you rarely have any context of what you're about to say and with the quality of dialogue going down like al-qaeda airlines, I stopped caring (for one of the things that I always loved in Fallout).
Then, there is the skill system... or lack there of. At first a little confusing (stats and perks together, what is this?), but pretty nice looking screen none then less. But, all traditional RPG parts are gone. What is the point of even giving the player chance to modify stats at the start if you're going to have pretty much godly stats after a while? Besides, this was one of the great things about the past Fallouts; when you found that single stat point increase in the game, you where at awe. Now, its just boring... as are the perks. I suppose shooting the RPG elements in the head isnt that major thing in this game, as Bethesda basically made the main character what they wanted to be, rather than what the player envisaged. You'll always be forced in to this really tacky caring father looking for his son -role, rather than choosing your own path.
Another thing that really annoyed me about Bethesdas choice was not keeping up with the lore. Yeah, there are pretty titanic inconsistencies within the Fallout universe, but they usually at least have the same style. When I saw the Fallout trailer with power armor + minigun, fighting against Deathclaw, I thought to myself; 'AWESOME!'... then finding out that's pretty much the first thing you do. Then you start to get more power armor stuff... and more. Power armor and deathclaws are suppose to be one of those things that you aspire for, not something you get at level 1. Hour after starting the game I already had the Fat Man... what is going on? Ah, yes - am I the only one to find it weird killing super mutants at level 10 in Fallout? Either the enemies instantly kill you or you can just walk over them.
I found the much vaunted town building to be awful. First problem; do you have three hands? Well then, here is a game for you! WADS + mouse + arrows to build your little fantasy toilet? The entire town building feels too unfinished and tacked-on to the game. While I encourage developers to make changes to their games to keep their respective franchises interesting, this is just so far-off from what Fallout games are; adventure, fighting and roleplaying.
I was looking forwards to the side-quests, but all of the ones I did were always 'go to X and kill raider Y'. Actually, I'd rather do that then the main missions. Yes, main missions in Fallouts are pretty bad, but these were just so uninteresting and uninsipiring that I just couldnt be asked for to continue through (at least side quests didnt force me to go back to settlement and build more beds... seriously). I remember in the past, you could fail/change the quests just by killing quest givers or start working for those who hate the quest giver him/herself, particularly in NV. Its just really disappointing to see quest critical NPC to just fall down and start regaining health.
Finally, some technical issues. As I mentioned, I suffered from relatively few bugs, but there are some other... things. Ok, this is a PC release of traditionally PC game franchise in 2015... and no multi-monitor support? Nice. Secondly, FPS seems to be all over the place, for no particular reason... also, what is up with the mouse acceleration and locked controls? I just dont understand.
This is the first Bethesda game ever that I just gave up. You'd expect me to be angry to the game (and the developers), but I really am not. After five hours or so, I was getting really annoyed with the issues mentioned on above rant, but at one point I realized, while installing another game, that I was playing spider solitaire instead of Fallout 4. It was just too boring to continue.
Perhaps I'll try this later on, but for something worth $60, I felt this was not a good deal at all, despite getting the game as a gift. As far as post-apocalyptic FPS's go, may not be the worst I've played. As a Fallout game, hollow and empty. Better luck next time.

My review recommends the game because I cannot convince myself the game is bad, though if you asked me whether I think it was worth the base price or not I'd tell you it certainly did not. I am only going to list what I found negative, because I almost entirely agree on everyone else as for the positive stuff: the gunplay is awesome, the story is good and so on. I also want to admit I am constantly comparing FO4 with The Witcher 3 because of the following reasons:
I am only going to add that if you know and have played (passionately) both games then you know what FO4 is missing in terms of immersion. Want any details? Facial animations. Voice acting. Please allow me to head on.
So here follows my complaint.
Despite the developers' description of the Commonwealth as the most thriving and advanced former american State, it really looks and feels dead. The reason is as opposed to Washington and New Vegas, there really aren't many other settlements in the proximity of Boston. You'll see for it yourself, I'm just going to say thatI recall Megaton, Rivet City, Little Lamplight (FO3) and Novac, Primm, Goodsprings, New Vegas of course, and all the faction-related settlements. Here... well, there are towns with named characters and all, but you can could count them on the fingers of one hand. A for the just mentioned named npc's - I'm 100% sure if someone bothered doing an accurate list of the ones present in FO3, NV, and FO4 respectively; the ones in the last title would turn out to be one third. I'm also certain there's no need to explain how this 'lack of life' deters to the game experience for anyone who enjoys immersion. Moreover, the game lacks intersting places: the major settlements are incredibly small with limited closed ambients to explore - Diamond City is so much of a letdown, and it appears so ridicolously small that I can't imagine what the game designers and developers were thinking. How could that look realistic? Somebody will come up saying the lack of settlements is made up by the new building feature. I totally disagree, and I see what you did there Bethesda, you saved yourself the assle of projecting secondary settlements, and a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of dialogue scripts and voice recording for each minor character were fed to the wolves with it.
Some were worried about the voice actor, as it could ruin immersion, and dumb down the dialogue choices. I think now that the game's been released and discovered thoroughly that's a secondary issue. As I feel it, the biggest delusion was that the game doesn't really make you feel like your choices have a point in the bigger picture. There is no karma at all, and your reputation with ALL factions can be positive at any time, yes, simultaneously. One of my friends reported being caught in the middle of a firefight between the Institute, the Brotherhood and the Railroad or something and they were all his allies so he didn't get any damage, delving through a myriad of laser discharges. Was choosing between the Enclave and the BOS, between the Legion and the NCR, all that pointless? I won't make any spoiler here, but trust me there's no relevant conflict in which you tie to either of the 2 major groups, for the majority of the game. As for the karma specifically, there's no good or bad, which is positive if you think of that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ biased system found in FO3 (no spoilers again, but the developers think slaughtering so-called 'human bigots' is ok and killing greedy jet-head scum is not). However, Obsidian had done a really good job by converting it into a 'reputation system' connected to what each settlement and each faction thinks of you rather than assuming everything is black and white for everyone. Instead of reasoning upon this new model and understanding the shades of morality within NV, Bethesda just removed the karma thing altogether. You may result as hostile to townfolks or still play as the bad guy - but no particular effects will be a consequence to your actions.
I think this was a very nice addition to the game. In general, personalising weapons and settlements is a very good thing and it fits the Fallout universe quite well. What most people are lamenting, however, is that it was poorly implemented. Being an avid builder myself - whenever a game allows me to be one - I found some stuff really tedious. A perfect example would be how ugly junk fences look when you use them to wall off your settlement, and how much space they 'waste' in your settlement size bar (which imposes you a contruction limit, though there is a workaround for this). You'll be driven nuts trying to construct a  fine chinese wall around your town, for the fence pieces don't attach one to another and leave consistent holes in between. Modding weapons is good, and I like how rifles become basically anything you want depending on your preference and tactics. Why am I listing it as a negative point then? Because like with settlements, Bethesda thought if they removed a lot of content designed on their own it'd be enough to allow the player to (moderately) made up for this by doint it all by him/herself. Wrong.  Most people will disagree with me, but I felt like there was a lack of weapon models. The chinese and classic 'american' assault rifles were removed altogether... Why? Instead we get some odd looking assault rifle that has stats almost identical to the combat rifle. Worth it is to mention the latter also shares the model with the combat shotgun, they look almost the same if you pay attention. I'm not sure I like this, as it feels there are few base weapons justified by the sheer amount of mods. By the way, am I the only one missing the condition system? Being a gun-nut even IRL, I think the perk is much more useful now, but whatever, it's not a reason for scrapping the CND altogether.
I think I felt like somebody had shot me in the belly with rubber ammo when I discovered skill points were removed. Along with the lack of any ethical choice I feel like the character customisation was extremely lowered. Did Bethesda think again that by adding some types of personalisation (namely face modeling and the expanded perks) they could freely remove other content? It took a lot of time to get used to the lack of skill points, and to the modifiable S.P.E.C.I.A.L.'s, though you'll get through it I think. Traits were a goooood addition from Obsidian but Bethesda killed everything good that was done by them. I think the new perk system is good enough to substitute everything that was before.
Sudden deaths for justifiable reasons are frequent, like early level raiders shooting mini nukes in your butt or a bunch of legendary npcs hopping out of nowhere to slaughter you. Also, every (not necessarily consequent) 10 hours of playtime or so the game CTD, and being auto-saves tied to how often you access your Pip-Boy I'd recommend not relying on that. I've lost up to 25 minutes of infight, building, you name it. Hopefully someone will pop up with a new CASM mod, I didn't seem to see it on Nexus.
I don't think the ending of the main story can be rated positively. Whilst I do consider the early plot decent compared to the last 2 FO titles, the ending was so poor and shallow. Continues in the comment section.

For me, Fallout franchise has always been about the adventure; Meet interesting people and kill them (if you want). Roleplay as the great hero of order, murderous ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, deviant misantrope or anything in between. In comparison to the previous games, I found this one to be insufferable. All I really wanted (at the end of the day) was a new adventure in a new setting, which I kind of got. Happily a friend of mine decided to gift this game to me as a birthday present, which made me very happy indeed.
Too bad the developers decided to make design decisions which are just beyond me. Some positive things I found were improvements to the VADS and better overall gunplay. TBH, despite being Bethesda game and many people experiencing bugs, I was blessed with encountering just few graphical glitches, nothing game breaking.
First big warning sign was the UI... I mean dear lord. Fallout games have never had the best UI, but this one really starts getting in the way. It is just a massive cluster♥♥♥♥ to use the pipboy. Also, why dont the companions show in the compass? More often then not, having the -dog found something- makes me look around just to find the dog, which is out of sight.
As with all Fallouts, the main story seams to be pretty terrible, but that's not why I played the games; I played for the RPG elements and the side stories. Speaking of RPG elements, I dont understand that a developer of predominantly RPGs decided to dumb-down everything in one of their primary series. While I didnt mind the voiced protagonist, the dialogue system is absolutely attrocious; 'yes', 'no', 'sarcastic' and 'whatever-mission-choice-etc'... is all your reply options. Apparently people say that it is Mass Effect-y, but this is even worse; you rarely have any context of what you're about to say and with the quality of dialogue going down like al-qaeda airlines, I stopped caring (for one of the things that I always loved in Fallout).
Then, there is the skill system... or lack there of. At first a little confusing (stats and perks together, what is this?), but pretty nice looking screen none then less. But, all traditional RPG parts are gone. What is the point of even giving the player chance to modify stats at the start if you're going to have pretty much godly stats after a while? Besides, this was one of the great things about the past Fallouts; when you found that single stat point increase in the game, you where at awe. Now, its just boring... as are the perks. I suppose shooting the RPG elements in the head isnt that major thing in this game, as Bethesda basically made the main character what they wanted to be, rather than what the player envisaged. You'll always be forced in to this really tacky caring father looking for his son -role, rather than choosing your own path.
Another thing that really annoyed me about Bethesdas choice was not keeping up with the lore. Yeah, there are pretty titanic inconsistencies within the Fallout universe, but they usually at least have the same style. When I saw the Fallout trailer with power armor + minigun, fighting against Deathclaw, I thought to myself; 'AWESOME!'... then finding out that's pretty much the first thing you do. Then you start to get more power armor stuff... and more. Power armor and deathclaws are suppose to be one of those things that you aspire for, not something you get at level 1. Hour after starting the game I already had the Fat Man... what is going on? Ah, yes - am I the only one to find it weird killing super mutants at level 10 in Fallout? Either the enemies instantly kill you or you can just walk over them.
I found the much vaunted town building to be awful. First problem; do you have three hands? Well then, here is a game for you! WADS + mouse + arrows to build your little fantasy toilet? The entire town building feels too unfinished and tacked-on to the game. While I encourage developers to make changes to their games to keep their respective franchises interesting, this is just so far-off from what Fallout games are; adventure, fighting and roleplaying.
I was looking forwards to the side-quests, but all of the ones I did were always 'go to X and kill raider Y'. Actually, I'd rather do that then the main missions. Yes, main missions in Fallouts are pretty bad, but these were just so uninteresting and uninsipiring that I just couldnt be asked for to continue through (at least side quests didnt force me to go back to settlement and build more beds... seriously). I remember in the past, you could fail/change the quests just by killing quest givers or start working for those who hate the quest giver him/herself, particularly in NV. Its just really disappointing to see quest critical NPC to just fall down and start regaining health.
Finally, some technical issues. As I mentioned, I suffered from relatively few bugs, but there are some other... things. Ok, this is a PC release of traditionally PC game franchise in 2015... and no multi-monitor support? Nice. Secondly, FPS seems to be all over the place, for no particular reason... also, what is up with the mouse acceleration and locked controls? I just dont understand.
This is the first Bethesda game ever that I just gave up. You'd expect me to be angry to the game (and the developers), but I really am not. After five hours or so, I was getting really annoyed with the issues mentioned on above rant, but at one point I realized, while installing another game, that I was playing spider solitaire instead of Fallout 4. It was just too boring to continue.
Perhaps I'll try this later on, but for something worth $60, I felt this was not a good deal at all, despite getting the game as a gift. As far as post-apocalyptic FPS's go, may not be the worst I've played. As a Fallout game, hollow and empty. Better luck next time.

Instead of reasoning upon this new model and understanding the shades of morality within NV, Bethesda just removed the karma thing altogether. You may result as hostile to townfolks or still play as the bad guy - but no particular effects will be a consequence to your actions.
I think this was a very nice addition to the game. In general, personalising weapons and settlements is a very good thing and it fits the Fallout universe quite well. What most people are lamenting, however, is that it was poorly implemented. Being an avid builder myself - whenever a game allows me to be one - I found some stuff really tedious. A perfect example would be how ugly junk fences look when you use them to wall off your settlement, and how much space they 'waste' in your settlement size bar (which imposes you a contruction limit, though there is a workaround for this). You'll be driven nuts trying to construct a  fine chinese wall around your town, for the fence pieces don't attach one to another and leave consistent holes in between. Modding weapons is good, and I like how rifles become basically anything you want depending on your preference and tactics. Why am I listing it as a negative point then? Because like with settlements, Bethesda thought if they removed a lot of content designed on their own it'd be enough to allow the player to (moderately) made up for this by doint it all by him/herself. Wrong.  Most people will disagree with me, but I felt like there was a lack of weapon models. The chinese and classic 'american' assault rifles were removed altogether... Why? Instead we get some odd looking assault rifle that has stats almost identical to the combat rifle. Worth it is to mention the latter also shares the model with the combat shotgun, they look almost the same if you pay attention. I'm not sure I like this, as it feels there are few base weapons justified by the sheer amount of mods. By the way, am I the only one missing the condition system? Being a gun-nut even IRL, I think the perk is much more useful now, but whatever, it's not a reason for scrapping the CND altogether.
I think I felt like somebody had shot me in the belly with rubber ammo when I discovered skill points were removed. Along with the lack of any ethical choice I feel like the character customisation was extremely lowered. Did Bethesda think again that by adding some types of personalisation (namely face modeling and the expanded perks) they could freely remove other content? It took a lot of time to get used to the lack of skill points, and to the modifiable S.P.E.C.I.A.L.'s, though you'll get through it I think. Traits were a goooood addition from Obsidian but Bethesda killed everything good that was done by them. I think the new perk system is good enough to substitute everything that was before.
Sudden deaths for justifiable reasons are frequent, like early level raiders shooting mini nukes in your butt or a bunch of legendary npcs hopping out of nowhere to slaughter you. Also, every (not necessarily consequent) 10 hours of playtime or so the game CTD, and being auto-saves tied to how often you access your Pip-Boy I'd recommend not relying on that. I've lost up to 25 minutes of infight, building, you name it. Hopefully someone will pop up with a new CASM mod, I didn't seem to see it on Nexus.
I don't think the ending of the main story can be rated positively. Whilst I do consider the early plot decent compared to the last 2 FO titles, the ending was so poor and shallow. Continues in the comment section.

A much improved version of Fallout 3.
Pros:
- World is much better realized. The map is completely open, unlike Fallout 3 where particularly the city was highly linear.
- Quests, locations and story also much improved. The themepark feel of F3 is mostly improved, with better connection between locations. There are large quest-chains to complete beyond the main story. You can join various factions and complete multiple stories, many linking areas together. Less emphasis on a sort of slapstick feel that F3 had, more serious.
- Crafting. Huge complex crafting mechanics added. Settlements add a bit of spice to the gameplay. Makes it feel more like a world as you can call for aid in the form of artillery and fighters from settlements.
Cons:
- Easy to gimp your character. I wish RPGs with big crafting mechanics would separate crafting and combat. A level up should give you 1 perk to spend on crafting, and 1 for combat. Make the perk sheets separate so we can actually enjoy CRAFTING AND COMBAT in the same game. Instead the game essentially forces you to choose one over the other unless you greatly lower difficulty.
- Bethesda game. In fact F4 is much closer to Skyrim than F3 was to Oblivion.
- VATS is still horrible. Usability improved, but still it is often clumsy.
- Inventory is horrible and clumsy. Particularly as you are picking up far more stuff than you used to.
- Aspects of crafting aren't well realized. Particularly cooking is a mess. Far too many recipes, which make a mess in the inventory. Never used food as it is a pain to sort. Simple usability things like making multiple meat recipes fall under the same category would vastly improve usability. So various creatures meat can be cooked into a generic "cooked fallout steak", instead it separates many of them out, without any particular gain. So many of the recipes give similar effects.
Essentially it is a director's cut version of Fallout 3. If you didn't like that game, it is unlikely F4 will change your mind. The mechanics are very much the same, they have just been improved upon.
