So, this is a wholehearded recommendation if you haven't played any of the previous Fallout games. I can only give a partial recommendation from the position of having only played FO3 (with no DLC) and FNV (with all DLC) because of the places where we've taken a step back.
Let me get the good out of the way. The shooter combat works well. It's fun to use VATS and see heads explode when you nail them repeatedly, it's fun to run and gun, it's fun to get sneaky kills from the darkness. There's still plenty of enemies to drop, and the guns feel like they have impact. Enemies are animated and more "alive" too. If you hit something, unless you're using a little pea shooter, it's going to scream and notice. Crippling arms, legs, and heads of enemies seems to have actual benefit in this entry.
The crafting system is also very good. You can collect anything you find, driving the impulse of your instinct to collect and hoard everything you find. You'll use it to craft not only weapon and armor mods, but furniture and buildings for your own settlements. Building weapon mods, armor mods, chems, and what have you works really well. It feels a lot like crafting in Skyrim did. That is, it's worth some experience, and makes your stuff better.
Settlements deserve their own paragraph. This is a new feature for Bethesda. If you liked having your own house in the Hearthfire DLC for Skyrim, you'll likely love this. Early on, since this is a Bethesda Fallout game, you find you're the "hero of the Wasteland" so you have your main objective, follow your character's motivation, but also fight the evil powers in the Wasteland. One of those, I guess, is the Wasteland itself, because you try to colonize and build towns and defend them from raiders, mutants, and ghouls. You keep them furnished, and have to try to attract new settlers, then have food, water, and other amenities for them. Your reward for this is that you can have settlements that might help you if you get into trouble. It also gives you more locations where you can go get your stuff by having the settlers bring it from town to town. I've seen a lot of really impressive settlements. Not on the level of minecraft megabuilds, but still impressive.
So what's the bad? You're essentially on rails as far as story and roleplaying is concerned. The conversations are limited to 4 options at each time you're allowed to respond, so you get options for yes, no, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and sarcastic. Answering no is usually rejected by the NPCs, so up until a certain point, everyone will have followed the main story quest in mostly the same way. This compared to FNV's branching, twisting story is a huge disappointment.
Also bad: while they've kept the lovely crafting system from Skyrim, they also brought over the homogenization of the skills system. I don't feel like I'm building and roleplaying a character, because no matter where my S.P.E.C.I.A.L. skills are, every character is mostly the same. No matter what, you can still try to convince someone through charisma, though you can get a tiny bit better. You can still carry plenty no matter your strength. Basically, since S.P.E.C.I.A.L. doesn't influence your actual skills, it ends up being more of just sticking points in one skill when you want a certain perk. It just doesn't feel rewarding to try to build a certain way when it doesn't feel like there's a specific advantage or disadvantage for building a certain way.
My last point rolls into how the game railroads you on the main story. It feels like the game is almost balanced for you to have a companion with you 95% of the time, even if there are perks that say you don't need one, and it seems like it's balanced for you to be clad in power armor 95% of the time. It doesn't feel good trying to sneak when you're given so many power cores and stimpacks that you can just facetank everything.
Overall: 7/10. It's still fun, but by the end of it I was rushing through the main story to be done with it. I'd still recommend getting it, but don't expect FNV levels of depth.

The mechanics for weapon and armor modding are solid, the new V.A.T.S. system is a huge improvement over previous games, the voice acting's ranges from good to great, and it includes a lot of mechanics that, in my honest opinion, should have been present to begin with (sprint, grenade hotkey, etc.)
My only real complaints (and minor ones, at that) are these: 1) Why did it seem like a good idea to bind "smash person in face with gun" and "throw grenade" to the same key? There have been a couple occasions where I tried to rifle-bash to create a bit of breathing room only to accidentally throw a grenade point-blank. 2) It would be nice if there was an "align to grid" option when building structures, because as it is you just have to eyeball it (something which I'm not very good at)
Overall, I'd say Fallout 4 is worth your time.

I have only suffered once or twice to the games bugs and crashes, which for a bethesda game is nothing short of impressive, this coupled with the often saving means if the game did happen to crash you really haven't lost much.

Each joinable faction has their own interesting story, none of which are the clean cut good guys. TL:DR - Excellent game, looks great and runs fine, if you liked the previous Fallout and Elder Scrolls games im sure you will enjoy this one.

Having put a decent amount of time into this, I feel secure in saying that Fallout 4 is a strong contender for, if not THE, best Bethesda Fallout game. The mechanics for weapon and armor modding are solid, the new V.A.T.S. system is a huge improvement over previous games, the voice acting's ranges from good to great, and it includes a lot of mechanics that, in my honest opinion, should have been present to begin with (sprint, grenade hotkey, etc.)
My only real complaints (and minor ones, at that) are these: 1) Why did it seem like a good idea to bind "smash person in face with gun" and "throw grenade" to the same key? There have been a couple occasions where I tried to rifle-bash to create a bit of breathing room only to accidentally throw a grenade point-blank. 2) It would be nice if there was an "align to grid" option when building structures, because as it is you just have to eyeball it (something which I'm not very good at)
Overall, I'd say Fallout 4 is worth your time.

I have only suffered once or twice to the games bugs and crashes, which for a bethesda game is nothing short of impressive, this coupled with the often saving means if the game did happen to crash you really haven't lost much.

Good game, great at times. Not best game ever, but a game I would and will play again. This review isn't going to be super long and formatted perfectly, but it will hit most the points and how I feel about them. Some will be a short sentence, others could be a short paragraph, we'll see. I think pros and cons list cause you to focus to much on the aspects out of context, so this is just a list of what comes to mind in the order it comes to mind.
Combat - Fallout quality, nothing special. Weapons are fun and it feels much more immersive, but it's exactly what you would expect. Vats is challenging and can irk me when I am playing on survival and have to wait 3-4 slow motion seconds AFTER killing the enemy and using up my AP. That Vats thing has caused me to die.
Voice Acting - I played a female so I can only speak about her, sue me. Her acting was great. I rarely went hard "renegade" options, but I felt like she did a great job. If you want to play a cold and heartless mother than I'm not sure it will work because she certainly sounds maternal and motherly at times. That said I never felt like her acting was out of place or bad.
Lip syncing - it's laughable, especially when a character forces a smile (dear lord make it stop).
Character customization - Best I have ever used or can think of. The system works really well. It can be a bit annoying to tweak it at times (sometimes having a bunch of sliders is better), but the interface made sense to me.
Controls/User-Interface - Ok, some of this was great and some of it was terrible. I for one like when a game utilizes the alt key because my hand can hit that key thanks to a happy thumb. Alt is how you throw grenades and melee so that helps. The combat and general UI are fine, I like them, nothing special but it doesn't matter much. You can customize the color. Power armor UI is always amber, I don't think you can change it, but the UI looks good and fits the armor. The buiding UI is... manageable, you get used to it. However if we are being fair it shouldn't require us to really stretch and trial and error just to build a basic house, so I consider it bad. The concept is great, the execution is also great, but the process to acheive the greatness can hurt (Why don't the bushes go away?!).
Building/settlements - Covered some of that in the last post. Settlements are unnecessary for the gameplay, which is how it should be. Some people want to roam and explore, others want to build a little homestead. If you build you can get some great benefits, but you don't lose anything by not building. Astetically the walls and stuff can be annoying, but it all works out well enough in the end. I do kind of wish there was more incentive to build proper settlements and connect them.
Plot/Story - Haven't beat it, made a new character as the end was starting to appear on the horizon. It's not bad, nothing stellar, and it's a bit interesting. I wish I was more hooked to it, and it will definitely get really old after one or two playthroughs. ALSO, partial spoiler but I am very very vague, I have some serious ethical issues with what they make you do with the thing you have to build. If anyone follows sci-fi well enough they will understand why that's cruel to make me do that.
What else, what else...
Performance - I meet the reccomended requirements, and the game says I can play on ultra. When I am in the wilderness  or in doors I actually can get 60fps on at least high, sometimes I think even ultra. But when I am in Boston or a town? God now. For obvious reasons the fps tanks as you get near more and more buildings. I doubt it's problematic on upper tier systems, but not everyone has that.
Graphics - If you are basing the game off of graphics then you can go right ahead and leave my review. The graphics are fine, the lighting and character textures are great compared to what I was expecting and even hoping for. Coming over a hill during the morning and gettings a beautiful faceful of morning godray glory is legitametly enjoyable for me.
Bugs/crashes - I had GPU problems where fps would TANK after 30 minutes of playing, but that is gone. No game breaking bugs, a few random things hear and there. It's at par with any game, but beats bethesda standards by a lot.
I'm getting tired...
Levelling - I like the new perks, but each perk point feels less great to spend as compared to new vegas. In new vegas when you spent a new point you got a completely unique perk every time. Where as in this you just kind of bump stats and sometimes get new things. I kind of miss the skill point leveling system
Companions - They function, nothing new. Weird pathing and sometimes, more than I want, I am left fighting alone because my companion won't keep up or follow. There needs to be a menu for marking a companion on the map when you can't freaking find them.
Other things - Can't think of much else, zzzz time. I'll try and come back to add and modify the review.
SHOULD YOU BUY IT?! Yes, I would highly reccomend it. I want more content, but it supports mods and that should go a long way. (That doesn't mean that the mods should be considered a part of Bethesda's work, just that it will allow the community to build off of what bethesda gave us.) This game has a good future and will likely steal at least 20 hours of your life, and that probably won't even be for a properly finished character. I say at least 30 hours for your first character, and that's probably missing a ton of side quests.

Fallout 4 has a great storyline, great graphics, and great attention to detail. Every zone, room, environment tells a story. The game runs great and I have encountered no bugs. It is easy to lose track of time while playing Fallout 4.

The first thing I will say is that Fallout 4 is a good game, therefore I recommend it. While there are many pros and cons, it is not fair for me (everyone has their own opinion) to deem it as sub-par in today's game market.
The first thing I personally noticed is that the world is an interesting place and you come across people and places that catch your eye; this is important in a open-world game. I also noticed that the visuals are great, despite the overwhelming negativity over this subject I heard prior to playing the game. There are certain aspects of visuals and graphics settings that are a little dissapointing, but overall the game looks great visually. The atmospheric music, the music apart from the radio stations, is pretty good and meets the standards of other Fallout games. The radio stations, however, do not. I appreciated the throwback songs, but the lack of variety, annoying voices, and irritating conflicting sounds made me quickly turn my radio off.
The looting, armor, and weapon systems have been completely changed for the better. Customization works well and rewards playing smart and investing time into crafting and conserving. Not much more to say here, but a huge plus.
After the first hour or so of gameplay, some things started to wear on me. The four-button dialogue system, in all honesty, is not only disappointing but degrading in my eyes. Am I so impatient and simple-minded that I don't want to read more than 3 words as my response? This system frequently misleads the player into saying things that they either don't want to say or are forced into saying. As a sidenote, I personally shudder at the introduction of a voiced player in a Fallout game, but that won't affect my assessment of the game. I prefer choice over cinematics, depersonalization, or what Todd Howard calls "hitting emotional beats better". For me, it only withdrew me from the experiences and choices, and broke my immersion a lot of the time. Along with these ideas, the NPCs are very cringeworthy at times. Unsettling facial expressions, talking with no mouth movement, poor mouth movement with dialogue when it does happen, and honestly some poor voice acting all wore down on immersion and eventually made me resist talking to NPCs which is a huge hit to my experience. Also, the dialogue system in general is very flawed. I'm not talking about bugs, though they happen often in this system, but the simplicity in 3 and NV of being locked into conversation worked much better than the live-action conversation in 4. It seems to be an attempt to make dialogue dynamic and more realistic, but ends up a futile attempt that is very unnatural and clunky.
As far as performance goes, I haven't had many issues, but many other have. I personally found a few of the controls to be irritating, but manageable. Key-mapping is a thing even while limited. This game isn't a horrible console port like everyone says.
RPG elements have also been dumbed down. I found myself missing skills and being upset that I felt like a god too quickly. I was never limited to any type of weapon or armor and it felt unsettling. And again, the voiced character made me feel like an outsider rather than like I was immersed in an RPG.
Combat, however, is vastly improved in almost every facet. Dynamic VATS works great and shooting mechanics are amazingly improved. I enjoy using almost every type of weapon and no matter what fight I'm in, I find the experience satisfying. It was disheartening when I realized that I was still playing this game because I really enjoyed taking out Super Mutants and Raiders rather than making difficult decisions or meeting new characters, but it's still a plus.
The primary story isn't great, but it isn't the primary focus. Side-quests' stories are good, but not amazing for the most part. I generally found NPCs to be a bit disappointing both in functionality and depth.
The crafting system is great. It is tedious at times, but rewarding and satisfying. I personally am glad that Bethesda chose to use it as a non-essential activity because those hesitant to use it don't have to, and those that do are still rewarded in the activity itself and also with tangible rewards.
Overall I highly recommend Fallout 4. Don't expect the depth or experience of the previous 3 primary Fallout games, but expect a different yet worthwhile experience.

Mixed feelings about this game so far...  Compared to the games that came before it, Fallout 4 to me definitely feels like more of an "Open World Shooter" and less of a "Role Playing Game".  The experience felt very on-rails and at no point have I really felt that the character I created and the choices I made had much weight or impact on the gameworld.  With 80 hours in the game I've completed the main quest and seen most of the locations throughout the Boston wasteland.
I found the main quest to be fairly terrible, but not entirely unexpected for a Bethesda game.  Still, it isn't like they deserve a pass for poor writing and limited interactions/impact on quest decisions in my opinion; the story should really just be a lot better than it is.  That branches into another point about side questing in Fallout 4, which is also fairly limited when compared to previous games.  There are very few, and none that I've encountered so far of any substantial length or involvement.
Going back to the character him/herself, I feel like much of the potential depth has been stripped away with the inclusion of the voice actors (both are good VA's in my opinion) and the limited dialoge options.  As I said the game forces you down that path of "♥♥♥♥♥ure Protagonist" and there is really no room for deviation on your part as the player.  The 3(4) main quest factions while flavored differently, all feel very similar and the endings are all quite shallow, lending to a samey-feel to everything.
It has been said by many others as well but I think the gameplay system is a regression with the exclusion of skills and simplification into a stat/perk tree.  Most of the perks are uninspirired bonuses and/or rips from Skyrim/fallout 3, with some of the more interesting bonuses only becoming avaliable at final tiers, all leveld in the 30's and 40's... well beyond end-game / content completion for most players.  Itemization is also quite poor in my opinion,   The game has a handful of base guns with a crafting attachment system.  It would seem to expand the # of weapons but in my experience there is a very distinct and linear upgrade path.  Seems about on-par with previous games in the franchise, and certainly mods will expand upon this point particularly.
Speaking on armor however I feel that the system they implemented was poorly thought through.  The modular armor system allowing you to wear (Helmet / R. Arm / L. Arm / Chest / Undergarment / R . Leg / L. Leg severely limimts your asthetic as only a couple of undergarments can be worn under the modular armor peices, of which there are only 4ish sets (leather/metal/combat/synth/uniques).  The customization is nice but again, the choices are usually very linear as to what bonuses are worthwhile to equip.  It creates an illusion of choice as opposed to a host of unique options.  Ultimately armor itself is almost an afterthought as Power Armor is attained 20 minutes into the game and the fusion cores which charge it are extremely abundant to the point where if one was inclined, they could play the majoirty of the game in power armor with very few breaks in use.
I would note that the world in particular feels rather small and compact.  I can tell that the game has a similar size to Skyrim for example, but the way things are laid out in Fallout 4 makes everything seem much closer together.  Another reason is the fact that there are only 2 main NPC cities and both of them are extremely small and, in my opinion, uninspired.  Perhaps the reason for this lack of cities is due to the inclusion of the settlement system, whereby you can recruit settlers and build up your own towns, but I have to say... that this system is lacking any real meaning or purpose in the game.
It reminds me of minecraft in that the settlement system is essentially a vehicle for your own creativiity but where there is ultimately no point or purpose to any of it.  Outside of some specific static quests there does not really seem to be a purpose for building defenses and integrating supply lines and bothering with any of the intracacies of it beyond simply being creative.  This may be enough for some players, but the purposeless-ness quickly wore me down.  This is another area of the game where I can see mods making great strides to add depth and meaning.
In closing I would just say that while I feel I got my money's worth, I am disappointed that Fallout 4 did not have fleshed out roleplaying mechanics and storytelling that were more abundant in New Vegas, 3, even 2 and 1.  There are mods of course, but in the case of Fallout 4 I feel that the game's foundation is lacking to build upon.  We shall see...

I just don't get the hate...
Is it a massive improvement over Fallout 3? Not really, but then Fallout 3 was mind-blowingly frikking awesome, just how much better can you get? It is an evolution of Fallout 3 though, and a very good, very competent one. What more did you want/
Are the graphics next-gen? Perhaps not, but they are still basically great.
Have the RPG elements been dumbed down? Well... sort of, but not really. Yes, they've conflated skills and stats; yes, they've removed level caps. But there are no fewer than seventy skills to be had, each with at least two but more often between 3 and 5 levels... as well as 10 levels of each stat... I long to meet the first person to make that lack of a level cap matter. Only I doubt that I will, they'll probably not spend much time away from their computer...
Fallout 4 is exactly what I wanted from Fallout 4 - another shot at Fallout 3 with a new story and an updated engine.
The world is excellently realised, with backstory all over playing out in snippets of things that you read in desk and drawers and terminals; it's full of little gems like the mall run entirely by robots that are still waiting for their supervisor 200 years later; the supermutants that are convinced of their superiority as a species whilst they scour the wasteland for green salvage because green-ness, not utility, is their determinant for the value of that salvage.
They perhaps shot themselves in the foot with the sheer amount of ♥♥♥♥ing hype they put out months and months before release - the second coming of Santa would have disappointed after that - but after the dust has settled we're left with an utterly absorbing, utterly playable and utterly enjoyable gem of a game. Well done again Bethesda.

Vats is challenging and can irk me when I am playing on survival and have to wait 3-4 slow motion seconds AFTER killing the enemy and using up my AP. That Vats thing has caused me to die.
Voice Acting - I played a female so I can only speak about her, sue me. Her acting was great. I rarely went hard "renegade" options, but I felt like she did a great job. If you want to play a cold and heartless mother than I'm not sure it will work because she certainly sounds maternal and motherly at times. That said I never felt like her acting was out of place or bad.
Lip syncing - it's laughable, especially when a character forces a smile (dear lord make it stop).
Character customization - Best I have ever used or can think of. The system works really well. It can be a bit annoying to tweak it at times (sometimes having a bunch of sliders is better), but the interface made sense to me.
Controls/User-Interface - Ok, some of this was great and some of it was terrible. I for one like when a game utilizes the alt key because my hand can hit that key thanks to a happy thumb. Alt is how you throw grenades and melee so that helps. The combat and general UI are fine, I like them, nothing special but it doesn't matter much. You can customize the color. Power armor UI is always amber, I don't think you can change it, but the UI looks good and fits the armor. The buiding UI is... manageable, you get used to it. However if we are being fair it shouldn't require us to really stretch and trial and error just to build a basic house, so I consider it bad. The concept is great, the execution is also great, but the process to acheive the greatness can hurt (Why don't the bushes go away?!).
Building/settlements - Covered some of that in the last post. Settlements are unnecessary for the gameplay, which is how it should be. Some people want to roam and explore, others want to build a little homestead. If you build you can get some great benefits, but you don't lose anything by not building. Astetically the walls and stuff can be annoying, but it all works out well enough in the end. I do kind of wish there was more incentive to build proper settlements and connect them.
Plot/Story - Haven't beat it, made a new character as the end was starting to appear on the horizon. It's not bad, nothing stellar, and it's a bit interesting. I wish I was more hooked to it, and it will definitely get really old after one or two playthroughs. ALSO, partial spoiler but I am very very vague, I have some serious ethical issues with what they make you do with the thing you have to build. If anyone follows sci-fi well enough they will understand why that's cruel to make me do that.
What else, what else...
Performance - I meet the reccomended requirements, and the game says I can play on ultra. When I am in the wilderness  or in doors I actually can get 60fps on at least high, sometimes I think even ultra. But when I am in Boston or a town? God now. For obvious reasons the fps tanks as you get near more and more buildings. I doubt it's problematic on upper tier systems, but not everyone has that.
Graphics - If you are basing the game off of graphics then you can go right ahead and leave my review. The graphics are fine, the lighting and character textures are great compared to what I was expecting and even hoping for. Coming over a hill during the morning and gettings a beautiful faceful of morning godray glory is legitametly enjoyable for me.
Bugs/crashes - I had GPU problems where fps would TANK after 30 minutes of playing, but that is gone. No game breaking bugs, a few random things hear and there. It's at par with any game, but beats bethesda standards by a lot.
I'm getting tired...
Levelling - I like the new perks, but each perk point feels less great to spend as compared to new vegas. In new vegas when you spent a new point you got a completely unique perk every time. Where as in this you just kind of bump stats and sometimes get new things. I kind of miss the skill point leveling system
Companions - They function, nothing new. Weird pathing and sometimes, more than I want, I am left fighting alone because my companion won't keep up or follow. There needs to be a menu for marking a companion on the map when you can't freaking find them.
Other things - Can't think of much else, zzzz time. I'll try and come back to add and modify the review.
SHOULD YOU BUY IT?! Yes, I would highly reccomend it. I want more content, but it supports mods and that should go a long way. (That doesn't mean that the mods should be considered a part of Bethesda's work, just that it will allow the community to build off of what bethesda gave us.) This game has a good future and will likely steal at least 20 hours of your life, and that probably won't even be for a properly finished character. I say at least 30 hours for your first character, and that's probably missing a ton of side quests.

Fallout 4 is a mixed bag. The voice acting throughout the game was abnormally good for a Bethesda title, but combining a limited 4 option dialogue wheel with a voiced protagonist makes for some vague dialogue responses and answers. I felt like I was not as readily able to learn about the npc I was talking to or say the things I wanted to say as I was in other Fallout games. Another noticable change is the fluidity of the combat in this game when compared to other Fallout titles. Shooting without relying on VATS as a crutch and the slightly upgraded AI makes the game feel like a solid fps. I like perk-based leveling and dislike how it was executed. Ignoring some obvious optimization problems (turn down your shadow distance, helped me alot), some physics bugs, some poor animating on Bethesda's end, the return of OP sneaking, and poor UI, the game is worth a buy on sale to the average person. Most of these issues can/have been fixed by mods but this does not excuse them. I'll recommend the game for now, hoping for a NV/Fo3 throwback DLC.

Now, as a forwarning, I have never played, nor seen, any of the previous Fallout games. This is the first one I've ever tried.
I heard about this game from a friend, who was super hyped about it and wouldn't shut up. Eventually the hype got to me and I preordered it. I've heard a few things from him about Fallout, but I'm mainly blissfully unaware. The game itself is amazing, with graphics to back it up. While this game does have RPG elements, it feels more of a open world FPS, which isn't a bad thing. I quite enjoy the game and all it has to offer.
-Spoilers Below-
Being able to build your own base? ♥♥♥♥. YES. You can make that thing so well defended it isn't funny. Sadly, it's quite rare you're attacked. However, it's still cool to set up a beautiful base and have it attacked only some times. You don't spend too much time at your home base anyways, so it all works out in the end.
Power Armor? ♥♥♥♥. YES. Power Armor within the first hour of gameplay, and that was taking it semi-slow. You even get a minigun AND get to destroy a Death Claw with it. I thought I was king of the world. The Power Armor does require a power source which is rare to find. This makes using the power armor an exotic treat to be used on opponents worthy of your fire power. Don't leave the power source in the armor if you're not in it though. I had mine jacked by a Super Mutant. I had made that power armor so overpowered I ended up having to load into an old save before he took it.
Fat Man Launcher and a Mini Nuke? ♥♥♥♥. YES. First hour of the game as well you can stumble (or look it up and cheat) your way into this beauty. The moment I saw it, I knew I had to try it. The weapon itself is more common than I would expect it to be, but the amount of its ammo that you can collect is. I would use it sparingly with the VATS crit for those special people that just need to stop existing.
Super OP gun? Need I even say it? ♥♥♥♥. YES. First 5 minutes you can get the INCREDIBLY useful weapon in the vault without waiting till your level 18 and have master lockpicking unlocked. That gun is a beast and I would go as far as to say better than the Fat Man, due to it's more available ammo and over powered nature. If you really want it, then I'm certain you can google and figure out how to cheat that way.
Collecting caps wearing you down? Well, there's a way to quicken it by quite a lot using a trader exploit. While I doubt it was intended to exist, it does. Again, google it if you feel like cheating. If not, then :P
-Spoiler End-
All in all, I don't think this game is worth $60. There are still a few major issues, the biggest being crashing after 15mins. Bethesda has released a beta patch for it, but it's upsetting that they didn't catch it before. While I don't think it's worth $60, I don't regret buying it for full price. It's' an amazing game and I intend to spend many more hours playing it. Yes, I'm a hypocrit; lay off!
I know this review was all over the place, but I have very little review writting experience and even less in the Fallout series. Hope you found it semi-helpful.

Edit: Actually let me start by saying ♥♥♥♥ THAT FRIENDLIES DON'T SHOW ON RADAR!
Let me start of by saying my review will contain major spoilers, not that the story's anything to look forward to anyways.
This will probably be the Bethesda game with the fewest hours played in my collection. At the moment I have 87 hours of F4, and 89 hours of F3, and I put probably over 200 hours in F3 on PS3 first.
I have completed the game getting 2 of the 3 possible 'endings', I took my time and did as many quests as I could find. At a certain point I just completely lost interest and started run-n-gunning my way through every main story quest just to get it over with. In short form Bethesda focused on their mechanics, and forgot about everything else, everything that makes Fallout Fallout and not just some open world COD.
Role Playing: There is none. If my review is the first one you're reading somehow then I'll explain it shortly: You have no options in dialogue. You must always go left. You can go a little further to the left or a little less to the left, but in the end you went left, and there wasn't anything you could do about it.
Story: Plot holes, plot holes everywhere. That and weak characters with one sided extremist arguements that end up being hypocritical ♥♥♥♥s. I'll remind you since they're starting, but SPOILERS! When you talk to Father and confront him about using cyborg merc man he basically responds with "It was better than setting him loose on the wasteland." Father doesn't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about the wasteland, and his ♥♥♥♥ing synths are hardwired to shoot anything that moves on sight if it isn't with the institute. Then there's the railroad, who want to set the synths free. Considering the G3 synths legitimately show emotions, I'd naturally ally with them because that seems more my speed than "kill all the stupid humans" and "kill all the stupid robots and mutants and hoarde the tech". However, even the railroad ends up showing their true colors as nutjob extremists that only care about freeing the damn robots. And once the robots are freed they don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥(see raider synths). At the end of their storyline they essentially nuke the most advanced facility on the damn planet FOR NO ♥♥♥♥ING REASON. By the time you reach the damn reactor nearly everyone is dead anyways, so why bother destroying the best equipment for restoring the world while also reducing something like 9 square city blocks to a radioactive crater? This, of course, after killing hundreds of BOS soldiers who (while also extremists in their own stupid way) were killing off feral ghouls and super mutants, essentially making the Commonwealth a safer place to live, with exceptions to the Railroad and the Institute. On the subject of the other two, the Institute does so much shady♥♥♥♥♥♥that Father promises to explain with time but never explains. Examples: Hundreds of violent synths on the surface that claim to kill for them, kidnappings with no records of what happens to the victim, only the solemn fact that they're now replaced with a synth, FEV experiments, records of a violent attack for some pre-war research they weren't even sure existed (University Point computer logs), and the fact they sent a violent merc after a scientist that he himself says he ESCAPED. Last is the Brotherhood who orders you to kill the entire Railroad organization just because they're helping synths, has you heavy hand farmers for crops to fuel their occupation, and just generally treats you like you're a stupid dog made to take orders. Considering one of their highest ranked members turns out to be a synth that was freed and had his memory erased (he doesn't know he's a synth until you do) borderline commits suicide for being a synth (strips naked and asks you to execute him), I'd say they're the epitomy of brainwashing military organizations. Each of the 3 factions orders you to kill the other 2 factions entirely with utterly no other option, even when you're the god damn leader of one (Institute). What the ♥♥♥♥ happened to the diplomatic options of NV??? The only faction not like them is the Minutemen, and they have nothing to do with the storyline unless you teleport into the Institute and proceed to kill Father with them. None of their quests point you in that direction, they're more like the 'Wild Card' option from NV.
Map:
Looks huge! Then you start walking and ou realize, hey, I just crossed half the map from Sanctuary to Diamon City on foot and if you ignored the encounters along the way it only took about 5 minutes... A lot of wasted potential with the ocean, especially with power armor that lets you walk on the bottom of the ocean without drowning (but you can't draw a weapon and the visibility is absolute trash). I hated how so much of NV's map was wasted with impassable terrain, but at least it had a lot of settlements to visit. F4's average location if not a 'key' location is a building overflowing with ghouls/raiders/super mutants, or a settlement you can 'capture' with a quest along the lines of go kill some raiders or some♥♥♥♥♥♥ Skyrim dynamic fetch quests all over again.
Weapon Variety:
There's a handful of weapons. What weapons variety there is, there are clear upper tier weapons that completely outclass lower tier weapons, reducing weapon choices further. The same goes for the mods. It's a cool idea, but top tier mods are the best choice, period. Oh, and scatter lasers are disappointing trash. If every laser hits, then its like +2 damage over a single non-scatter laser (which also has less recoil so you can shoot faster). And the spread is a nightmare compared to shotguns.
Armor Variety:
Same deal with weapons.
Skills:
There are no skills. ♥♥♥♥ your role playing ambitions.
Textures:
On ultra quality and x16 anisotrpic filtering most armors/outfits look like they never fuller rendered and the same goes for any wood that isn't still a tree. It literally makes me think Dragon Age Origins graphics. And honestly, I think those may have been better.
Followers:
Bethesda borrowed directly from a mod for their follower AI that made followers in prior games feel more 'alive'. That's great if you're roleplaying and if it doesn't take away from their usefulness! Except they nuked the RP off the G harder than the filthy commies did to the USA and 90% of the time you can't find your follower cause they're ♥♥♥♥ing around 50 feet away from you, they have some of the worst aim of any NPC I've ever seen, they constantly get in your way in cramped areas, they ♥♥♥♥♥ at your for everything you do that isn't what they'd do, and they can carry so little Lone Wanderer's 100 weight bonus easily outclasses every one of them when factoring in all the other ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Their only use is as bullet sponges since the ♥♥♥♥ers never die. Unfortunately, your bullets too since they LOVE running in front of you.
Bugs:
Yes it's Bethesda, so yes I expected a lot of bugs. But holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ some of them occur so often and so quickly it makes it hard to believe they play tested this thing. Not only the many minor bugs, but I've had 2 game breaking bugs so far. One, when getting out of the cryo pod in the beginning, I couldn't move. I couldn't even save. While I had quick saved before getting in, if I hadn't I'd be back at the character creation screen. The other was on the final mission for the Railroad, I quick traveled into the Institute and the ♥♥♥♥ing game put me in the wrong location. And since everything was on lockdown and I couldn't quick-travel out, I had to no-clip through the roof to get to where I was SUPPOSED to spawn in at. If it had been a console the only way out would have been a prior save.
Positives:
Gunplay
Animations
New twists on enemies (zombie limbs, invulnerable shells)
Fun, if disappointing as all hell
Settlements? (Need a lot of work still, too rough)
Power Armor mechanics & mods
Learned my lesson about pre-ordering, even from my (ex)favorite game studio

Where do I even begin. Well, I'm 20hrs in and feels like I've barley scratched the surface of what this game has to offer.
They've streamlined the leveling system with the skills being removed and the perk system being expanded.  Every level you get a perk point which you use to either bolster a S.P.E.C.I.A.L stat whose level decides what tier of that stats' skills you have access to, (Ie: you need luck 3 to be able to take bloody mess perk) , or you can spend that point on a perk such but not limited to,  bloody mess, incressed lock picking level, increased damage resistance, etc.   Most skills have multiple levels for you to invest your point into increasing their effectiveness.
The Morality system has been stripped out, though you can stil lget in trouble for stealing or attacking civies.
V.A.T.S remains unchanged from previous games
The gunplay is about the same as previous installments as well. Still fun though.
The world has more varried enviroments than previous games with woodlands, ruined cities, ruined beaches, lakes, and suburbs littering the map.
There is also a new settlements mechanic, which is optional,  that requires a good chunk of time and micromanagment
but is strangly relaxing.  you plant crops, manage housing/beds, water and defenses. However you can also form supply lines which pool your resources together and build shops which net your settlement caps (req. charisma 6 and points in local leader perk).
The story is rather engaging, though there are tons of sidequests and diversions to keep you just as busy as the main quest will. The compainions seem more interesting and fleshed out than previous games. Which isn't to say they were bad in previous games, there is just a bit more to them in this one. Actually part of that is that each companion has actions they like or dislike the player making and most are romanceable. you can also have more than one relastionship going if that's your thing. So no need to do multiple playthroughs if you are trying to see all the romance related stories.
Though if you want to play your character differently multple play throughs are still worth the extra effort.
Dunno what else to say. It's a must play. Specially if you enjoyed the prior games. Even if you haven't played them
it's a pretty good jumping on point to the series.

Hello everyone and welcome to my review of Fallout 4.
First i would like to comment on the hate the game is getting for the graphics. I play this game on Ultra Settings with everything maxed out and 1920x1080. It looks beautiful. But there are people who do not have as good as a pc as others. This game looks georgous at Medium graphics settings. There difference in qualtiy is there but barely noticable.
The other thing that people are complainging about is that you get Power Armor and a Minigun at one of the first missions you do in the game. Yeah thats true and i can see why people find it annoying. But then i think about it more and i realise that these people haven't played the game further. They just get to that point and make a review bashing that game. The Power Armor is powered by things called Fusion Cores. These F.C (Fusion Cores) are very hard to find at first in the game, making the use of the Power Armor very limited. I used it for big missions, one's i might have found very difficult and need the Power Armor to give me that extra help. Whent he F.C runs out and you have no more the Power Armor is stuck but shows up on the map.
Now to the actual review.
The game plays very well, as a person who has played the previous Fallout games it does take some getting used to. The VATS is also very different but i feel for the better.  Lets split this review into parts.
Gameplay
The gameplay is very fallout like but with a new movement system. At some points the movement feels very off in a way that is new to the series but is easy enough the get used to.
When you start out the game you are given a Vault 111 jumpsuit as starting armor. As you progress through game you will find armor for different parts of your body which can individually be upgraded and modified with the Armorer and Sciene Perks unlocked. With the different tears ranging from Leather to Combat armor.
Weapons are very strange at first, the 10mm starting pistol is very well made and very strong at the start of the game. As you progress you will find laset musket and other low teir weapons. Like the armor they can all be individually upgraded  with the Gun Nut and Science Perk. I highly recommend upgrading weapons as using the guns without upgrades the further south in the map you get the higher the challenge and the more ammo needed to finish and enemy.
VATS which is the targeting system slows down time and allows you to select a portion the targets body to automatically shoot at. VATS is very inaccurate and seems to be a waste of time until you unlock the perks that improve accuracy. I have been half a metre in front of a supermutant and activated VATS, targeted his head 5 times and missed every single shot. Can be very annoying but i recommend aiming down sight instead until you get those perks.
Story
So i have completed the story with each ending and i will not spoil any of it here. The game doesn't end like the other Fallout games, it will continue after the main story is finished. I like this in a sense that i don't have to worry about leaving the story till i have finished everything beforehand.
There is no level cap so you can unlock all of the perks essentially but it would take way to long. Maybe they could improve this by giving you 3 instead of 1 point towards your perks and then maybe adding a max level so you can unlock 80% of the perks depending on the type of character you are going for. The level cap can then rise when DLC comes out just like in previous Fallout games.
NPC companions are very buggy and you have too keep note of what you say when certain companions are in earshot. As it affects your relationship with them even if you are not accompanied by them. Alot of the companions will have a delay when it comes to shooting a target. As i have been surrounded by ghouls and my companion is standing behind me watching my slaughter.
Overall i would say that this game is worth the buy. It is well made and will have its bugs but thats what makes it a Fallout game. I reccomend adding this game to you steam library as with new mods coming out on the nexus you will be able to improve the base game. I reccomend looking for mods that make the game more enhanced such as better blood textures,
improved animations and darker nights.
Thanks for reading my review and get this game already.
Mods are Free from the Fallout Nexus

Ninety three hours in seven days.
And I haven't even started the main quest line.
What am I doing with my life?
There are so many things you can do in Fallout 4. I've only seen a very small part of it, and yet my obsession has lead me to complete one of the faction quest lines.
Aside from the obvious story line quests, there's so much to do in this game that it would be very difficult for one character to do it all.
Yes, there is no level cap, and the game is open ended. But I feel like the amount of effort required to do, and to see it all in one character would require 300 - 400 hours of gameplay.
My character is at level 54, and I've only a few completed perk trees (out of the dozens).
The settlement building feature, while completely optional, is absolutely phenomenal. Within just a few hours I had already earned enough scrap to build a nice little two story building in which to live and house my things.
The combat is fast and feels incredibly well rounded. The gun play is top-notch and you can only just notice the stat systems in play.
Charging someone full speed with an attack from a combat knife is especially rewarding. Even if you aren't trained to use melee weapons it throws them off balance and staggers them for a few seconds. And they react accordingly.
However, at high levels, some characters can feel unrealistically balanced by taking six shots of .50 BMG right to the face, in order to kill them. And I'm talking about humans, not super mutants. I feel like this unbalanced combat might break immersion for some people if they play on higher difficulty levels.
The voice acting is top notch, as expected with a AAA title. And after 140 hours of gameplay I've yet to hear the same voice actor repeated in major dialog. The conversation system is incredibly deep and immersive, yet the dialog option wheel can be slightly misleading at times.
The world is massive, and if you avoid fast travel you can definitely tell that it's at least on par with Skyrim. However, it's so densely populated with people and things to do and to see that it feels much more expansive.
The world is also historically accurate, filled with tons of actual Boston sights, and even a few Easter Eggs.
The Companion System is acceptable, and it gives you a feeling of getting to know your friends and the people you'll collect in the Wastelands. But I feel like in a game this big, they did an amazing job with it.
But all in all, it really is an amazing game. And if you have the motivation, and the time, I highly recommend getting it.

The game definitely wasn't as lengthy as other games in the series, as I finished in less time than it took me in New Vegas and Fallout 3. It's still a decent length, though. One thing I didn't like was that you could pretty much ONLY play as a good guy. There's no "evil" faction like other games. I always liked being able to do a "good" playthrough and an "evil" playthrough after.

It looks like a lot of people are crapping on this game because it's not just like Fallout 3 or FNV.  If your metric is "I want FNV in a newer game engine" you will probably HATE this game.
That said, I was pretty happily surprised when Fallout 4 didn't turn out to be more of the same.  The world itself in this game is incredibly detailed.  There's so many things in it, and I constantly am getting side-tracked to explore all of the nooks and crannies.  I love how it subtly invites you to do this because you don't have enough ammo or other supplies.  This is the first time playing any video game where I get EXCITED when I find some glue or a typewriter.  Almost everything you see lying around you can pick up and use somehow, it remins me of some of the good Ultima games (like 4 or 7) that way.
Once you finally get the hang of getting settlements going, while this seems tedious at first, it's really not that big a deal to get them operational enough to provide the value you need after you get the hang of it.  And once you get the perk that lets you set up supply lines between settlements, you really start to feel like you're making a difference in the world.
The gun mods are really great.  Like really great.  I love using all the weapons in this game for different reasons at different times.  Sure I use my combat rifle a lot, but the sniper rifle and laser pistol are super useful too.  I did try melee a bit but that seemed pretty non-viable.
Bottom line, if you like games that require crafting and building, and you like that to be combined with combat in a really fun and beautiful setting / sandbox to do it in, Fallout 4 is pretty awesome.
I this game might be more aptly title "Fallout 4: Post Apocalypse Simulator".  When I reset my expectations and evaluate it in that light, I LOVE this game.   When I evaluate it as another iteration of Fallout 3, I HATE this game.
All that said, I think Fallout 4 is a game I'm going to be playing for a while.  I'm already thinking about rolling another char to do things differently with my settlements and perks and I haven't even beaten the game yet.
One final note, I moved the game to load from an SSD and this made a HUGE difference in my enjoyment of the game.  The loading times from a regular HD are pretty much unacceptable right now, and I had it running on 10k RPM drives in RAID 0.

Ninety three hours in seven days.
And I haven't even started the main quest line.
What am I doing with my life?
There are so many things you can do in Fallout 4. I've only seen a very small part of it, and yet my obsession has lead me to complete one of the faction quest lines.
Aside from the obvious story line quests, there's so much to do in this game that it would be very difficult for one character to do it all.
Yes, there is no level cap, and the game is open ended. But I feel like the amount of effort required to do, and to see it all in one character would require 300 - 400 hours of gameplay.
My character is at level 54, and I've only a few completed perk trees (out of the dozens).
The settlement building feature, while completely optional, is absolutely phenomenal. Within just a few hours I had already earned enough scrap to build a nice little two story building in which to live and house my things.
The combat is fast and feels incredibly well rounded. The gun play is top-notch and you can only just notice the stat systems in play.
Charging someone full speed with an attack from a combat knife is especially rewarding. Even if you aren't trained to use melee weapons it throws them off balance and staggers them for a few seconds. And they react accordingly.
However, at high levels, some characters can feel unrealistically balanced by taking six shots of .50 BMG right to the face, in order to kill them. And I'm talking about humans, not super mutants. I feel like this unbalanced combat might break immersion for some people if they play on higher difficulty levels.
The voice acting is top notch, as expected with a AAA title. And after 140 hours of gameplay I've yet to hear the same voice actor repeated in major dialog. The conversation system is incredibly deep and immersive, yet the dialog option wheel can be slightly misleading at times.
The world is massive, and if you avoid fast travel you can definitely tell that it's at least on par with Skyrim. However, it's so densely populated with people and things to do and to see that it feels much more expansive.
The world is also historically accurate, filled with tons of actual Boston sights, and even a few Easter Eggs.
The Companion System is acceptable, and it gives you a feeling of getting to know your friends and the people you'll collect in the Wastelands. But I feel like in a game this big, they did an amazing job with it.
But all in all, it really is an amazing game. And if you have the motivation, and the time, I highly recommend getting it.

Suprisingly stable at release, despite Bethesda's track record. Most of the problems you'll hear about are from people unlocking the framerate to get above 60fps, which causes problems with the physics and simulations. Leave that ini setting alone and you'll more than likely be fine. I've only experience one CTD and one major glitch in 67.5 hrs. (Running Windows 10 Pro, Intel Core i5-2500K, 8GB DDR3 memory,  and my game is installed on an HDD).
As for the game itself, it still feels like Fallout. If you didn't like FO3 or FNV, you won't like this one. However, if you enjoyed one or both of those games, you'll find lots to love in FO4.
The weapon/armor modding system is fantastic. If you enjoy building things at all, you'll probably find yourself spending hours designing  and building settlements. Just fon't forget to play the actual game too!
Improvements over the previous games (in my opinion):
- Aim down sights is far smoother than in FNV (though there is no toggle option in the settings).
- VATS being a bullet-time effect, rather than completely pausing the game, is a vast improvement and makes VATS more of an effective situational tool, rather than a cheap exploit.
-  While skills are removed, the new perks/SPECIAL system is great and a lot more fun to use.
- Karma system has been removed in favor of companion relationships. Doing specific things near companions will affect their relationship with you and may lead to new quests.
I'm sure you can find a list of negatives elsewhere; I just wanted to briefly detail why I enjoy the game and highly reccomend it.

Full review here:
Fallout 4 is a post-apocalyptic First Person Role Playing Game in which you play as a person looking for their son after a nuclear armageddon.
Earth as you know it has been destroyed and know resembles a dangerous wasteland with Ghouls, raiders, Robots, super mutants and generally not very friendly people. You start with a pistol and gather weapons, materials and companions in order to make your city a better and safer place.
Fallout 4 stays loyal to its roots and doens't change the core gameplay aspects of Fallout 3 much. The changes it brought are executed beautifully and expand upon the experience.
This time around, the game takes place in Boston Massachusetts, USA. This means that there are a lot of buildings to explore. Each one has its own story.
The games has a great sense of humor. There is so much irony behind a lot of stuff you do in Fallout. From the Vault Boy posters to the in game dialogs and weapon names, several things are guaranteed to make you smile.
Fallout 4 has a unique, subtle way of telling weird stories. Every building you will ever enter has its own. It's up to the player to uncover it. Look for logs in terminals, clues in dead people's inventory, holotapes and more. The world is filled with them.
It's a world that feels alive. It truly feels like everything happened for a reason, and not simply because "it's a game, they just put that there".
The main story, which we are not going to spoil here, is interesting. Fallout is a franchise where you make important decisions throughout the game and the decisions you made drastically affect the ending. When I finished Fallout 4's main storyline I wasn't sure I made the right decisions. The plot forces the player to form and reform opinions about everything happening in the game. "Did I make the right decision allying with that specific faction, is what they believe actually the right thing?". "Could I have handled that situation any better?". These are questions I caught myself asking while playing.
There are 4 different endings, generally depending on which faction you ally yourself more with. Each ending defers quite a bit from the other in a number of meaningful ways, and it seems they didn't repeat their mistakes with the Fallout 3 ending.
Fallout is known for its great, immersive atmosphere and it never disappoints. The atmophere of Fallout 4 is as gloomy and scary as it should be. The extra colors the developers have added this time around didn't spoil the feeling of a wasteland at all. On the contrary, it gave it the nostalgic perspective of how beautiful the world used to be before the bombs fell.
While playing, make sure to play Diamond City Radio. The 40's and 50's songs are the game's signature music and make Fallout what it is. The game features an amazing soundtrack. You haven't played a Fallout game if you've never blown a Mirelurk Queen's head off with a Mini Nuke listening to “I don't want to set the world on fire” by The Ink Spots
The graphics in Fallout games have never been the best and Fallout 4 is no exception to that. However they have done a good job keeping the game fresh and honestly, nobody complains much about it since there is so much more to the game than just its graphics.
Fallout 4 didn't change the gameplay much. It's a standard FPS RPG that had a small renovation to its perks and stats. The VATS are still here if you want to take your time and have a more relaxed and strategic gameplay. What did change though, is the addition of a whole lot of modifications for your armor and weapons. This is what made me farm for materials, mods and perks for hours in order to perfect a weapon I had found. Every otherwise useless junk you find in the wasteland can be scrapped to materials like steel, rubber, glass, aluminum and many more that you use to modify all of your guns, and armor to find exactly what you need for every situation and enemy.
Bethesda also added a building feature. You can now build houses, stores, defenses, decorations and many others in settlements you are allied with using any materials you find. Settlers come to your settlement depending on a number of factors and if you want, you can keep them happy and occupied. Fallout meets Minecraft? Don't mind if I do!
Fallout 4 is a great game. Its predecessor set the bar high but it turned out to live up to its name. Mods are on their way (at least for PC and Xbox One) that will surely add a lot of stuff to the already rich gameplay. If you're looking for a 50-100 hour post-apocaliptic adventure Fallout 4 is for you.

Full review here:
Fallout 4 is a post-apocalyptic First Person Role Playing Game in which you play as a person looking for their son after a nuclear armageddon.
Earth as you know it has been destroyed and know resembles a dangerous wasteland with Ghouls, raiders, Robots, super mutants and generally not very friendly people. You start with a pistol and gather weapons, materials and companions in order to make your city a better and safer place.
Fallout 4 stays loyal to its roots and doens't change the core gameplay aspects of Fallout 3 much. The changes it brought are executed beautifully and expand upon the experience.
This time around, the game takes place in Boston Massachusetts, USA. This means that there are a lot of buildings to explore. Each one has its own story.
The games has a great sense of humor. There is so much irony behind a lot of stuff you do in Fallout. From the Vault Boy posters to the in game dialogs and weapon names, several things are guaranteed to make you smile.
Fallout 4 has a unique, subtle way of telling weird stories. Every building you will ever enter has its own. It's up to the player to uncover it. Look for logs in terminals, clues in dead people's inventory, holotapes and more. The world is filled with them.
It's a world that feels alive. It truly feels like everything happened for a reason, and not simply because "it's a game, they just put that there".
The main story, which we are not going to spoil here, is interesting. Fallout is a franchise where you make important decisions throughout the game and the decisions you made drastically affect the ending. When I finished Fallout 4's main storyline I wasn't sure I made the right decisions. The plot forces the player to form and reform opinions about everything happening in the game. "Did I make the right decision allying with that specific faction, is what they believe actually the right thing?". "Could I have handled that situation any better?". These are questions I caught myself asking while playing.
There are 4 different endings, generally depending on which faction you ally yourself more with. Each ending defers quite a bit from the other in a number of meaningful ways, and it seems they didn't repeat their mistakes with the Fallout 3 ending.
Fallout is known for its great, immersive atmosphere and it never disappoints. The atmophere of Fallout 4 is as gloomy and scary as it should be. The extra colors the developers have added this time around didn't spoil the feeling of a wasteland at all. On the contrary, it gave it the nostalgic perspective of how beautiful the world used to be before the bombs fell.
While playing, make sure to play Diamond City Radio. The 40's and 50's songs are the game's signature music and make Fallout what it is. The game features an amazing soundtrack. You haven't played a Fallout game if you've never blown a Mirelurk Queen's head off with a Mini Nuke listening to “I don't want to set the world on fire” by The Ink Spots
The graphics in Fallout games have never been the best and Fallout 4 is no exception to that. However they have done a good job keeping the game fresh and honestly, nobody complains much about it since there is so much more to the game than just its graphics.
Fallout 4 didn't change the gameplay much. It's a standard FPS RPG that had a small renovation to its perks and stats. The VATS are still here if you want to take your time and have a more relaxed and strategic gameplay. What did change though, is the addition of a whole lot of modifications for your armor and weapons. This is what made me farm for materials, mods and perks for hours in order to perfect a weapon I had found. Every otherwise useless junk you find in the wasteland can be scrapped to materials like steel, rubber, glass, aluminum and many more that you use to modify all of your guns, and armor to find exactly what you need for every situation and enemy.
Bethesda also added a building feature. You can now build houses, stores, defenses, decorations and many others in settlements you are allied with using any materials you find. Settlers come to your settlement depending on a number of factors and if you want, you can keep them happy and occupied. Fallout meets Minecraft? Don't mind if I do!
Fallout 4 is a great game. Its predecessor set the bar high but it turned out to live up to its name. Mods are on their way (at least for PC and Xbox One) that will surely add a lot of stuff to the already rich gameplay. If you're looking for a 50-100 hour post-apocaliptic adventure Fallout 4 is for you.

Unlike some of the day 1 reviewers I tried to get a little more of the game under my belt before I wrote a review, so here goes.
First - the bad. The game has a large number of bugs and glitches I've encountered so far, which - while not unusual for a Bethesda game - does pull you from the immersion somewhat. Some are mostly innocuous and actually pretty funny to see, others are more insidious, such as an issue I recieved on several accounts where after using a settlements workshop I was unable to access my Pip-Boy until I entered a new zone. Similarly I encountered a bug where I was unable to place items in the workshop despite having ample resources and room in my settlement until I reloaded the game, at which point I was able to place them normally. In some areas of the game (particularly more in the urban Boston area), while playing on the reccomended ultra settings, textures are occasionaly slow to load and framerates drop slightly. Another, more humorous glitch was when I used the scope on my sniper rifle to pick off some mole rats on a distance when, upon entering the scope i was rudely teleported to where the scope was pointing, right into the center of said pack of molerats.
Other than bugs and glitches, I have releatively few complaints. Of them are the removal of the Confirmed Bachelor and Cherez la Femme perks as well as the simplification of the Black Widow and Lady Killer perks, which offered a fair amount of humorous dialogue in older Fallout Games. On that note, the new dialogue wheel takes some getting used to and, while I wasn't very happy with it at first, it did grow on me.
That out of the way - the good. There is just so much game to enjoy. I have spent so much time exploring the map and still feel like I've only scratched the surface. At the time of writing this review I am already more than 25 hours in the game and have hardly touched the main storyline and have only completed a hand full of side quests. More improtantly, it's important to note how much this game feels like a Fallout game. I was worried from Skyrim which featured far too much of the same quest (go to this dungeon that has almost the same exact layout as the last one you did, full of Draugr, and clear it out) the unique layout of most buildings and the quest design going into Fallout 4 has been excellent. The dialogue is funny, the music is wonderful, the armor, weapon, and settlement customization is fantastic. Combat, with the addition of melee attacks on guns and the ability to equip an explosive as well as your main weapon, is far more enjoyable than previous Fallout games and the UI is overall improved, most notably through looting which can now be done without opening each and every container in a room - now you just scroll over it and see it's contents.
Overall I can't reccomend this game enough - it is truly a blast to play. If you're waiting for anything, it should either be for a new computer that can run this game, or for more patches and mods to roll out to help bring you a more streamlined (and possibly more customized) experience. I'll give it an 8/10, rising to a 9/10 when some of the more glaring bugs are patched out.

FOV bugs out often, I've had to enter console and type FOV 90 to fix it a few times and it's never looked like how the game 1st started.
Controls: 5/10
Again no decent remapping, but they are usuable and once you get used to using them your ok. But it's really annoying. Multi function single keys etc.
Bugs: 7/10
They are everywhere but I've not encountered anything game breaking yet. Loading screen doesn't load, CTRL ALT DEL for the cure. Birds stuck on the floor. Enemy stuck on rocks, branches, road dividers, line of sight issues, enemy jumping off great heights to their deaths. etc. And the friend / companion AI! do you get stuck much? I wonder why it has a seriously impressive reset AI programmed in for it ROFL! Village building, I seem to have managed to have bugged my electricity requirement so that it is permanently red, I've removed all generators and then re-built them up to 600 but remains red even though every item has power in the village. Flying stuck animals, enemies which float away, companion whom swims on dry land, companion whom is visually stuck in the wounded position. Power armor getting huge cloud artifacts stuck to your view which can prevent gameplay and you end up guessing what is infront of you or blocking your way. And many many more. The Witcher 3 didn't ship like this...
Summary
The game is not worth £40, it's a AAA game from the past. The open world feeling of open world games is destroyed by the constant loading screens, open a door = loading screen, quick travel = loading screen. I did try to walk the path of stealth and sinper, but you would be more stealthy if you pinned tin cans and wind chimes to your entire body! and, trying to shoot anything at range (till you get a lot of perk perk points in the right areas) is like you just consumed 50 pints of beer and are trying to stand up as soon as you press zoom in to look down your scope. The game just feels, meh, don't know, it's meh, but I will plod on to the end for those momentary surprises and condemn it to the uninstall list. It's like someone whom can use unreal engine 3 had a friend who is a 3d designer and just plopped low poly models in everywhere and added as many light sources as they could without doing any calibration to them other than brightness and that's it.
5/10

I played 10 hour sessions non-stop everyday for 5 days as soon as the game was released. The only reason I didn't play more was because I had college, sleeping, and eating. I'm pretty sure I will get 1000+ hours by next year 11/10/16. If this doesn't win Game of the Year I'd be surprised.

What I do now after I beat the game is I explore the commonwealth, max out my character, and fiddle with settlement building. Some people will hate exploring and settlements and they only want quests which is why they say this game is hollow. These people will just have to wait for DLC or quest mods. All in all, while Fallout 4 could've definitely been better, we have no reason to complain at all with the game Bethesda has given us.
EDIT 2: It's really sad to see that Bethesda will only give us 2 major quest focused DLCs and call it quits after that. Both FO3 and NV had 4 or 5 quest focused DLCs if I remember correctly. Far Harbor was amazing and to know Nuka World is the last DLC for Fallout 4 definitely leaves a bad taste in my mouth. The game and hype was 5 years in the making and to see a game many were hyped for being abandoned after just 1 year of support is just plain disgusting. Bethesda definitely sees FO4 as a failure, but instead of trying to fix their failure they toss it to the side and leave us all to hang. Lost all my respect for Bethesda after this move. Hopefully mods will keep the game alive for a couple more years to come.

I'm not gonna put too much effort into the common gripes with the game. I will go into detail about things that people are not complaining about that I've realized could be much better.
Pros:
- Great character design options (specifically referring to how you design the look of your character); you can truly create a unique looking character.
- FPS aspects are vastly improved from previous installments of the franchise. Battles are ridiculously enjoyable.
- Many of the creatures have been given an intensity to their design and animations. They interact with the environment in exciting ways and the gameplay is brought up a few degrees because of it. The AI is pretty awesome, although there still is clunkiness occurring within it here and there (especially companion AI), but we aren't really existing in a time of I, Robot becoming a reality, now are we?
- Dynamic Volumetric Lighting. DVL looks great, man. Really, though, the game looks fine. The only complaint I have with the game visually is the constant bugging out of textures. That's some kinda bug, because you can see an object one time with horrible textures, look away, and then look back again and see the great looking, intended textures load up.
- The design of the city element of Bostom is fantastic. They put a lot of effort into it and the couple of cities I've discovered within it are great. The expanse of Boston, the metropolis, is very dense and there are plenty of little neat locations to explore. Not so much can be said of the surrounding area (a).
- There are plenty of interesting characters to meet in the game. The companions are, for the most part, pretty cool.
- The crafting system is very nice for weapon/armor modifications. (b) I have one minor complaint about it.
- I actually quite like the perks system, with one gripe (c).
- Speaking as someone with a pretty strong gaming rig, the game has no crashes / bugs that ruin it for me.
- The actual dialog itself is not bad.
- The factions are very nice, with plenty of grey area subject matter to sink your teeth into.
Cons:
- The settlement crafting/building just completely lacks diversity in the elements that you can choose to build. If they simply gave metal the same amount of diverse objects as they did wood, it would be twice as good. And, after that, if they allowed you to build concrete-based stuff, it would be even better! Plumbing? Why not?! Pool tables that the NPC's will play every once in a while? That you could play? Another little mini-game? Darts?
What I'm getting at: they could have easily gave this feature a lot more stuff that the player could mess around with. Right now, people are spending hours to work around its limitations. Conversely, people could be spending hours having FUN doing this♥♥♥♥♥♥ I'm expecting a DLC to vastly expand this aspect of the game, and halfway expecting a free one, at that! Because, as it currently exists, this aspect of the vanilla game is tedious and limited. Add the feature, sure. But do it right!
- The UI leaves much to be desired. Especially for settlement building. It is just very clunky and feels totally unnatural to work with.
- No more skill-related checkpoints in dialogue. You don't need to have a skillpoints-based system to implement this. It could work with the perks-based one that they chose to use, but Bethesda just completely shrugged this possibility off.  Reward people for choosing Medicine or something like that. It's fun to be rewarded, and it is to have fun that we are playing the game for, right?
- The dialogue *options*, as a whole, are pretty limited and repetitive. Distinct and separate from the actual script of lines that the NPC's and main character deliver, there simply aren't many different questions, for instance, that you can ask a given NPC. This also kinda ties together with the aforementioned lack of skill-related checkpoints in dialogue.
- The Side Quests Suck Horribly. I Am Going To Capitalize Every Single Word In This Part Of My Review To Emphasize Just How Much Disappointment I Have With Them. They Are The Same Thing Over And Over: Go To This Place And Kill A Bunch Of♥♥♥♥♥♥And Then Come Back (Or Pick Something Up After Killing A Bunch Of♥♥♥♥♥♥And Then Come Back). Only A Couple Of Side Quests Escaped This Format (Out Of What I've Seen, So Far). Such A Shame, Bethesda.
- The main quest is OK, but not great. Kind of boring, with no real emotional attachment for the first few quests. It gets better, however. This isn't what you play a Bethesda game for, though. They really could fix this, one of these games, but I guess it's just not a priority for them.
- They did away with much of the cool stuff New Vegas brought to the table. It must be pride, I guess. Not implementing different types of ammunition was a big loss, in my opinion.
- No karma system. Even if it isn't displayed everytime you steal something, it would be nice to have it included.
- As far as I can tell, there's no reputation system for the different factions that are present within the game.
- (a) Everything outside of Boston sucks. There is a cool faction to side with if you like being a good guy (I always do), but the main NPC affiliated with it is absolutely dull and boring. The vast emptiness outside of Boston is expected; it *is* the post-apocalypse, after all! But, there are so few quests to be found there. There's no crazy people dressing up as superhumans messing up a town, or cannibal people trying to get people to stay at their camp so that they can eat them, or cave-based settlements run by children, all of which contain awesome side quests. It's just a bunch of empty locations to scavenge for loot or locations with hordes of enemies to clear for your settlements that you can build at. I'm hoping that I have simply not discovered notable locations outside of Boston, but as it stands, it's pretty barren. A friend of mine explored the entire top half of the map and only found two quests and absolutely zero NPC settlements with quests (outside of c_____d; trying to keep this spoiler-free).
- (b) While great, the manner with which one must work to get a specific weapon mod is a little tedious. You need to go and find certain rare materials to build a weapon mod, as an example. Maybe this is just a personal gripe, but I don't really find it fun to scavenge buildings and locations that I've already explored just to find some screws. It gets old quick.
- (c) There really ought to be limitations to your ability to put points into S.P.E.C.I.A.L... Like, once every three levels or something. The game forces you to start pretty low with S.P.E.C.I.A.L. points and it would feel much more rewarding to finally have 6 charisma, for instance, if you have to level up more to reach that point. As it stands, you could just add special points all day and be a badass pretty early in the game.
I would give this game a 7/10, simply because there is so much room for improvement. It could easily become a 10/10 if certain things were fixed (settlement building, a DLC that adds more sidequests and interesting NPC's to the non-Boston parts of the map)... In the end I definitely recommend the game as it is very fun, but I can only truly marvel at its gloriousness once certain things have been added to the base game. THEN, and only then, should Bethesda start adding conventional DLC's that bring you to new maps.
