Absolutely outstanding game! Highly recommended for those who played through and enjoyed Fallout 3. The map is slightly smaller in comparison to other sanbox and RPG games that have been recently released. However this has little effect on the changing environments of the wasteland and the sudden weather changes and random radioactive storms that really change the way you play. The game also seems to drop framerate in the main city (Effect this would have depends on your specs) and also drops occasionally when I use a long range or night vision scope. Overall:

Battles feel much more fluent

Pleasing graphics

Contrary to my expectations, the game turned out all right, and so far it hasn't failed to keep me entertained.
The bad:
* Bugs. Lots of them. Environment interaction (movement) bugs, especially for caravans. Dialog bugs. Mission trigger bugs, even some HUD (playing on Windows 10, and I launched the game when I was on a second desktop, maybe that's why), building large structures causes them to constantly rattle like goats are constantly ramming it.
* There are difficult opponents, which is fine and expected, and there are opponents that come out of nowhere and kill you in 2 seconds (not exagerrating) with some super energy death ray coming out of its head or something, and throw you back to your last saved game which was over an hour ago. It's frustrating and almost made me abandon the game.
* Some items that enhance the HUD should have the option of being turned off, since they really break the graphics in dialogs, turning the characters into red shapes with lots of lines. I can't appreciate the art because of that.
* In a game with multiple factions, there are surprisingly few dialog options that would actually make sense when dealing with those competing factions. The most obvious dialog options are not present.
* Maybe I didn't get the hang of it, but having lead-plated power armor and a lead-plated armor inside gives you the same amount of rads in water as without any lead. If the power armor is waterproof (it is, since I can cross large water bodies without suffocating in it), then how does it not protect you?
* The whole settlement leadership seems very raw. People just stand there like idiots, and interaction is limited, and it seems like I can only assign a single person to a job, and then it doesn't work properly, or I'm doing it wrong. And they aren't even getting assigned, like actually working at that booth I built for selling guns and stuff. They just hang around all over the town.
* You can craft all kinds of furniture, but it's useless. All besides beds. Like I said, this feature feels kinda raw. Like they put it there for marketing purposes, but once you play with it - it doesn't really do anything to you. It doesn't make any sense for you to grow those towns, make them nice, etc. I mean why have all this complex part in the game, if you don't really get anything from it? Maybe there's something later in the game, but for now it seems senseless and utterly useless.
The good:
* weapon and armor modifications crafting. You can take any weapon and modify it to fit your play style, so you can have a long range large caliber sniper rifle, or a short range hip fire, rapid fire rifle with reflex sights, from the same stock weapon.
* Key shortcuts for assigned favorite weapons, so you can put your melee weapon at 1, short range pistol at 2, automated rifle at 3, sniper rifle at 4, plasma something (to kill those scorpions) on 5, and something to throw nukes at Alpha Deathclaw or something, at 6. Also favorites for consumables (Rad-X, RadAway, MedX, Stimpack, Water), so you can quickly heal health and radiation.
The meh.
* Build crafting stations, small towns, if you're into that kind of stuff. It seemed fun at the beginning, but quickly got boring.
The graphics:
Well it's not baaaad. It's better than a lot of games. But it does feel like for a game launched in late 2015, they could've done much, much more to make the game feel more immersive. There are games that came out 2 years ago that provide better face and character animations, better textures, better lighting effects. It's not much different from Skyrim.
Need more hours in the day for this game.

Story: Now I haven't played a lot of the story yet, but so far it seems very interesting and engaging.
Characters: Numerous interesting and unique main characters, aswell as tons of side characters to meet on your journey through the commonwealth.
World: Huge, filled with detail and very atmospheric.
Combat: Vast improvement over Fallout 3 and New Vegas. It feels a lot smoother and features lots of unique, customizable weapons with great designs and sounds.
Graphics: Not the top of the line, but still very beautiful and atmospheric. You really couldn't expect much more from a giant open world RPG without your PC committing suicice.
Base Building: A big, but optional part of Fallout 4. You can build your own settlements at various points in the Commonwealth/Wasteland and have NPCs live there. The ressource management system could use a bit of work since you don't require a lot of the common ressources like wood or steel to build huge fortresses, so you can end up with literal tons of unused wood and steel in your storage, while fighting over every little bit of glue. I can't really say much about raider attacks, as I haven't experienced any so far. The building itself can be quite difficult at times, because the editor doesn't always behave like you want it to. In general it's a very useful and fun addition to the game, even if it has some flaws.
Bugs: I personally have encountered very few bugs. None of them have been irritating and they're usually just small, funny physics glitches.
Overall Fallout 4 is a near perfect game with little flaws.

The things that doesn't work/could be improved for the next game:
- Lots of bugs and performace issues (when ever i go to the central city area - and only there - my game starts to lag alot) this is something that have been in other befesta games, but unlike other devs that gets alot of criticism for it, fans nearly embrace it making jokes about it. - The minecrafing-like feature of settlement building, really needs to be better explained to the player. Better optional tutorials and controls are need for this.

- The dialog option feels contrived and restricts player freedom which is a stable thing of fallout and Befesta games; its nearly always the option of saying no, yes, maybe and the being curious "i would like to know more" that you can say. Great addition to the Fallout series. Exceeded my (realistic) expectations.
The quest structure is pretty much the same, and mechanics like lockpicking and hacking are unchanged. Combat has received a bit of an overhaul, and is much more satisfying due to the weapon modding system. How you craft your gun actually makes a huge difference in how your game is played, and offers more options than simply upgrades. Armor can be upgraded to be more durable, as well as to provide different effects such as greater carry weight. Power armor is now a big lumbering Iron Man-esque suit that you get into, rather than just another piece of normal armor, and can also be modded as well. Legendary enemies help disrupt the normal flow of combat, and being able to store criticals in VATS to use them just when you need them gives it a more dynamic feeling.
Just as you would expect in an apocalyptic wasteland, scavenging is finally a big deal in Fallout 4. Weapon, armor, food, and chem crafting give you a really big incentive (rather: NEED) to scavenge the wasteland for various junk items that can be broken down into raw materials used for crafting. Gone are the days of useless junk thats only purpose is to be sold to a vendor; in fact, I more often welcome a big pack of duct tape as my reward than new guns or armor.
Another way materials can be used is to build settlements: an entirely optional new mechanic that allows you to build your own forts, bases, buildings, and towns. Resources a settlement produces can be used for crafting, and excess resources can be sold to a vendor, giving you a nice reliable bottlecap income. Practical uses aside, building, defending, and managing settlements is just really fun, and allows for a great deal of creativity. An unexpected, but very welcome addition to the game.
Despite other peoples' complaints, I rather enjoy the voiced protagonist. In 3 and NV, say you had 8 dialogue options for a particular conversation. In 4, you'll still have 8 options, they're just presented in a more linear, flowing fashion--more akin to a real conversation. You can still ask questions without progressing the conversation. The voice acting is great, and the dialogue and writing are much better this time around, and much more emotionally charged. Factions feel a lot more organic, and choices are a bit more thought provoking than before. There is less "saint vs mustache-twirling-evil" extremity, but rather more shades of grey. Reminiscent of Mass Effect, companions are actually rather compelling characters, rather than the hollow, mindless zombies that followed you around and occasionally repeated a line or two like in previous games. They also serve as the game's morality/karma system now; different companions will like and dislike different things, and you can build a relationship with them based on your actions. Of course, if you don't want anyone judging you, Dogmeat loves you unconditionally.
The new perks system, in my opinion, only makes character builds even more complex, despite the outcry of the removal of skills being a simplification. Now I must choose: do I put my points into a more traditional "perk" like Critical Banker, into a more skill-like perk like Lockpicking, or into my SPECIAL? Given that your SPECIAL now more directly controls what perks you can take, spending perk points is a much harder decision for me in 4.
Graphics? Not overly detailed, but still aesthetically stunning. Weather effects look particularly nice, as do the new flowing cloth and hair physics. I love the vivid colour pallete. Animations are actually fairly decent for once. Atmosphere and sound design? Simply great. Very eerie at times, and cam be quite immersive. Music and radio? Love 'em. Inon Zur did a spectacular job with the OST, and the radio selection brings back a lot of favourites from FO3 while still mixing in some great new tunes. Absolutely no complaints with any of these. I feel that FO4 takes a bit more after 1&2 than 3/NV, and something the more longer-standing fans of the series will likely appreciate.
Some of my favourite changes in 4 are probably some of the most overlooked or taken for granted. One such example is how looting is much better now, as it's just a little popup menu beside contains and bodies, allowing you to loot in realtime without the need for an extra menu. Cities are now much more functional, and everyone living in them has a home. Level design is magnitudes better than Bethesda's previous titles, and many buildings can be explored in the open world without a loading screen. The map is also far denser than before--it took me over 24 hours to get to Diamond City.
Is the game without problem? Definitely not. There have been some rather major quest bugs, but I'd be surprised if a patch doesn't come out soon to fix them. Some quests have lasting, permanent, irreversible effects on your save (which is honestly pretty awesome), however it's my opinion that some of them don't effectively communicate this to the player prior to having them make a decision. I only found out 10+ hours later that a quest had given me an incurable disease. If I had known this at the time, I likely would've been more careful or simply chosen differently. Additionally, there's a conflict between the new layered armor system and the traditional full-body outfit system. You can use certain clothes as "underarmor" for your layers, but other clothes will occupy all equip slots and are not usable with layered armor. Why not? And of course, the interface could always be better--especially for settlement management. Assigning settlers to different actions in your settlement is a very tedious, frustrating, and confusing process. However, I have had no crashing, significant framerate loss, or any of the usual Bethesda bugginess. These issues are, compared to the rest of the game as a whole, quite trivial, and likely things that can be fixed in future patches, DLC, or mods.
Overall, provided you had realistic expectations, this game should be one to remember. If you're expecting just a reskinned FO3 with better graphics, you'll likely be disappointed. FO4 is very much its own game. I've been having a blast playing this nonstop since release, and I'm not really getting burnt out on it yet. It's absolutely packed full of content and surprises. So far, this is my favourite Bethesda and Fallout game yet.

Hipsters wanna knock this game since it got hype.
Still a damn good game.
Solid 8/10 using a gamepad so no opinion on the "horrible UI"
Game is locked at 60fps but is stable for the most part unless you go to the more dense portions of the map like Cambridge and the Boston Common.
Story is satisfactory with its share of epic fallout moments, not as memorable as FO3's sadly, but DEFINITELY makes up for it with an enumerable amount of awesome and fun and engaging side quests.
I personally loved the dialogue wheel and voiced protagonist, both genders were done insanely well
Combat is 10/10 gratifying, honestly one of the best shooter combat mechanics ive seen in a game so far. Sound design for guns is done superbly, especially in comparison to FO3 and FNV
Settlement building has a learning curve and will honestly be an annoying chore to those who care too much for symmetry and such. After about 45 minutes of learning the mechanics i poured about 3 hours exclusively into it straight afterwards
Crafting is extensive and very personalized, have made some awesome weapons and armor customizations and i havent even discovered all of the base weapons in the game yet. Speaking of, random legendary enemies and legendary loot is a welcomed surprise for people who enjoy the occasional grind for a unique or "enchanted" weapon.
Graphics are passable, can get slightly muddy if you look at individual assets but overall the devs found a way to make this game look beautiful, vibrant, and "next-gen"
Honestly, this game DID meet me expectations, although dissapointing me in a few areas which ive already looked past...first, the skills from previous titles have been stripped away and replaced by the SPECIAL stats, which can be increased from 1 to 10 or choosing a perk of each designated letter. I've found although i can't begin to buff up my medicine, lockpicking, or repair skills anymore, the SPECIAL stats each have their incorporating stats that rise as you progress letters you please. For instance, strength increases your carry weight, but also buffs up your weapon damage in both guns as well as melee, or charisma affects your speech and how well you do in dialogue wheel options that factor in speech level. So yes, in short, this particular game mechanic was simplified to appeal to a broader audience whilst still retaining its merit as an RPG. The other dissapointment is simply the Karma mechanic that actually mattered in FO3 (more so than FNV) is completely gone from the game, and your actions will only affect how your companions see you (by the way, quite a few of them are awesome and well worth the extra hours just to have them at your side.) This dismisses some opportune chances of being a horrible scourge of humanity, as the narrative propogates that you are just a concerned father looking for his son. This option wouldve been nice, although i'm VERY hesitantly willing to forgive it based on how well the story and narrative is driven.
As a final verdict, I'll say i'll definitely recommend this game to newcomers, whilst recommending it to fallout fans if you are aware of the changes i've stated above, i myself do not mind the adoption of nearly all of these new mechanics, but that's for you to decide.
I score this game a very CRITICAL 8.5/10, a great game and well worth your money and hours, dont let some of the unrecommended reviews fool you, although the series has adapted it's still a very true fallout sequel.

Haters....Haters never change....
I am not sure why, but at this point, one week after the Games launch, 21% of the reviews are negative, and the longer I scroll through them, the more I find to laugh at.
This review will destroy 80% of the negatives, read along:
------------
"If you ever played Fallout 3 or Fallout NV, you will be disappointed. Why?
Here is a list of things Bethesda has stripped from the game:
pc control optimization
Karma System
Skill System
Diseases and Injuries system
Dialog Trees"
------------
Lets start with that:
-PC control opitimization-
What kind of reason is that, and what Optimization was there on Fallout 3 or New Vegas? Exactly same launcher, with same easy way to change the Games quality settings to whatever you like. Easy accessible and changeable, turning Fullscreen-Windowed-Borderless, all resolutions, graphic settings etc. with just a few small clicks.
- Karma system -
I can't say that I really liked the Karma system in Fallout 3 or NV, it wasn't bad, but also just didn't seem right. I liked what they did in Fallout 4, the only ones who actually notice you stealing, killing, etc. are your companions and the people who see you doing it. Logical, right? How can the guy in Rivet City know that I just robbed a whole family in Megaton without this family or anyone being present? How can the Brotherhood notice I just killed someone of them, considering this guy was alone, killed by a single headshot? Why can I spend 2000 Bottlecaps in the Rivet City church, gaining Karma, to maximum, but then steal those from the dudes pocket again and still be at almost maximum Karma?
Karma didnt feel like a game mechanic, but more like a obstacle, you have to bend, and it was awfully stressful.
Removing the Karma was just removing a obstacle, now you just will get attacked for stealing/killing when someone sees you or you'll be disliked/liked by your companions.
-Skill System-
I did like the Fallout 3 perk system, but what I didnt like, was to not know what perks come next; "Oh, for this one I would have needed 1 more on strength, ♥♥♥♥! If I had known that I'd..." Fallout 4 gives you a hand on this, instead of slapping you for not knowing. You get the whole list, you even get to see what later levels of a perk can do, no, you cant take the strongest perks to last level right away, everything except the first level of a perk is level bound, so you'd need to be Lvl (im not sure) 23 to learn lockpicking master locks. The skill system isn't ruined, Bethesda turned it more easily to look at and analyze for player that don't want to beforehand look at every perk on a online list.
-Diseases and injuries system-
Not sure what is meant by that anyway. Getting addicted is still a thing, Addictol or a Doctor are expensive, so you always stand between the decision: Boost my power in this situation OR Not take the chance to get addicted. No changes on that, Stimpacks still heal crippled parts, but you don't have to check your "Left legs health" anymore, what was frankly stupid anyway. Also, radiation finally is dangerous. In Fallout 3+NV was ONE, but ONE single spot, where radiation was dangerous, and that was when there was this spot you need to bypass because of the 200+ Rad/s. In Fallout 4, RADs determine how much max life you got, and the more RAD you take, the less max health you got. Now I actually care about swimming through a lake or walking around it, in Fallout 4 I'd rather walk around, Fallout 3 I'd probably take a small nap in the water, maybe drink a sip, and then move on.
-Dialog trees-
You still get Dialog checks based on Charisma, just perks like Child at Heart, that lets you have unique options when talking with childs is out, GOOD. I shouldnt have to take a perk, just hoping that ONE DAY a child or whosoever will appear and I got the right perk for it. If I intent to do a lot of those Dialog checks, I boost my Charisma, DONE. This was a very good change, making it a lot easier to set your character. Do I want to early on focus on doing a lot of damage in fights, talk a lot with people, etc.
----------
This was just one review of which I showed how total meaningless it is.
The truth is, that Fallout is an imense game, that allows you to do what you want, follow the story along, alone or with companions, help people around you, or murder them all or just dont give a damn about anyone and wander off, exploring every whatsolittle corner of the world and just because it isn't exactly like a better Fallout 3, but a completly new Fallout, people start hating without a reason
In the current state, there are bugs, but theres nothing a patch wouldn't fix. This still is a remarkably unique and yet one of the best games out there.
This game doesn't force you anything on, be the type of person you want to be, may it be a father, that just wants his son back, or a mother, that just feels like relaxing on her self build settlements on an island.
War...War never changes, but you can show war who you are.
Have fun!
----------

Review post-Main Quest. NO Spoilers.
Note: The game suffered some performance issues on launch.
I have AMD cards. They released a patch. I no longer have any negative problems with the game.
Onward.
Brief Summary List.
Pros:
Cons:
To detail a few points above,
The main questline really suffers. It's not that its a BAD story, its just that the way they make you go about it makes ZERO sense at times.  I'll try to keep this spoiler free, but there is some basic info you need to know. The commonwealth is occupied by 4 major factions. The main storyline will make you pick 1, and make you enemies with 2 of the remaining 3. The timing of these events will not make total sense. The reaction from these new enemy factions will not make total sense.  It's a mess. The main-quest CREATES massive gaping plot holes before your very eyes. Which is a shame, because the overall premise is very intriguing, and starts off very very strong.
Perk systems. I know i'll catch some flack for saying this. But its better. I know "old school" FO players miss more of the RPG side, but really FO4, pretty much mimicks Skyrims perk/levelings system.  Gain a level, invest a perk. The only real difference being Skyrim made you skill up a base attribute before it could qualify you for the perk, and FO4 lets you rank up base perk trees to qualify you for them. No one complained that Skyrim wasn't RPG enough. So people need to quit complaining. The perks make very significant changes to your character. That's always been the point of an RPG anyway. Shape your character, and give him appropriate skills to roleplay him/her.
Armor. Not Power Armor, just regular clothes you loot. It sucks.  If you want exterior armor pieces like arm guards, chest pieces, leg armor... you're going to be frustrated... Because only a handful of clothing choices let you use those. Heavier armor sets occupy ALL equipment slots, which becomes obsolete, because its always better to have exterior armor mods that give you extra defense, and can be modded to add carrying capacity.  So get used to using your jumpsuit as underwear for the whole thing.  Also the Brotherhood jumpsuits... LOOK STUPID! They look like orange pajamas that kids wear.  Dear Cthulu, someone please mod them to look better...
Weapon Damage and Locations... For the most part, you'll be able to kill things in 1-2 shots, and make headshot kills. But there are plenty of times where you'll unload a .50 cal, or a railgun into a Raiders face, with full Rifleman perk, while stealthed, and he'll survive... It's stupid... I'm not asking to 1-shot behemoths, but it breaks immersion when I see a bald raider take a shot to the eye, and he pulls out his gun and starts searching for me.
Companions and equipping weapons. Its broken. Supposedly you're supposed to be able to give them a weapon, and corresponding ammo, and you hit T to equip them, and they'll use that. WRONG. it doesn't work. I gave one companion a Combat Rifle to upgrade them off their Pipe Rifle, and they SWITCHED TO MELEE... It broke the companions inventory for good.
Settlements. They are broken.  You can add food, water, defense, and beds for days... You can get happiness 80% plus, and things still won't work properly. You'll stop getting settlers randomly. Hooking up lights and electicity doesn't always work properly. Settlers don't always do their job.  There's no good mechanics in place to summarize WHO is doing WHAT, unless you happen to catch them doing their job that second, and have the building menu open to see whats highlighted. There are TOO MANY limitations. I keep having to send my companions to another settlement, because Sancuary is, apparently, too full. Nevermind all the empty beds, buildings, and general wide open space.  And the Size limit? Are you kidding Bethesda? You know someone's going to mod that bull**** away right? Because it is BS.  The game also throws too many unlockable settlesments at you at once.  Even if you fully decked out one, you'd be constantly scavving for junk just to work on the next one.
Finally, Bethesda leaving things unfinished. Mostly what I mentioned above. You'll be playing, and you'll really notice some glaring holes in the game. Whether it be story or function.  Is the game still a step up from FO: NV? Sure. But, barely.  The revamped Power Armor mechanics, graphics, and weapons crafting features are the driving point in that. The Commonwealth is very detailed, and packed dense with greatness, but not enough to hide some obvious missing parts of the game. And EVERYONE knows the modding community will fix it, finish it, and polish it up. It really feels like Bethesda got tired near the end, instead of just toughing it out, and finishing the game, and they went "Ahhhhh, modders will just add more armor anyway. We don't need to add anymore. " Or, "Nahhhh, we don't need to streamline Settlements at all. They'll just re-do this anyway." Its very obvious.
Summary:
Is the game worth getting? It depends. I've dumped an enjoyable 100+ hours into it. It hasn't been perfect. But the game did wow me at many points. I have a lot of fun with gunplay. I love the Power Armor.  I love exploring. Exploration is this games strongest point. If you like that aspect about the Fallout games, then yes, its worth getting.  It is NOT worth getting for the main storyline, nor is it worth getting as a sandbox builder.  One of these issues will likely be fixed by the modding community.  Weapons and Armor modifications will likely have unlimited potential, because of the modding community.  I like this game, but I remember being emphatically blown away by Skyrim, the whole time I did the first-playthrough of it.  This, it blow me away, but at peaks and valleys. It has really big highs, and really ugly, glaring, lows.  It's inconsistent. Which keeps it from being Awesome.
On a scale of 1-10, its stuck at about 7.5.  I'm hoping future DLC and Mods will change my score to a 9.   If you're skeptical DON'T GET IT! ... At least not at retail price. If you want to explore, mods guns, and build a buggy settlement (or not), then go ahead.  All my complaints aside, I've still gotten my moneys worth. I'm still very happy with the game.  But I fully recognize some lost potential, due to laziness on Bethesda's part, is all.
Recommend, but it's not perfect.

Nothing has really changed all that much from Fallout 3 once you are used to the Instagram filters on the graphics.  The world is initially a very pretty place, but ultimately it is a boring environment filled with junk items you are expected to collect.  You require these components because as a hot shot lawyer, as the female protagonist goes, you must build generators and automated machine gun turrets and water purification machines, all things a law degree qualifies you to do.
The story is disjointed with your character sobbing in one moment and then potentially laughing at explosions in the next.  NPC characters are dumb, incredibly dumb, and will frequently get lost or stuck or just vanish entirely.  There are a variety of companions to choose from but none of them are particularly nice people, nor do the ever have anything interesting or entertaining to say.  Plus you can only have one of them with you at a time which means Dogmeat stays home.
The settlement building is atrocious and the user interface with mouse and keyboard is an absolute joke.  What's more, as you progress through the game you end up unlocking even more settlement areas which you must defend and equip with defensive gear and farming equipment, then try to attract settlers from the wasteland and assign them to work each item, without being able to already see who is assigned to what and if there are any free slots - it is infuriating.
The side quests are almost entirely kill quests. Go to X, Kill X. There aren't any options to really negotiate your way in or out of certain situations, Charisma is basically used to beg for 50 more caps for a mission reward.
Power armour is introduced to you 5 minutes in to the actual game itself and you get to keep it.  With the minigun.  After fighting a Deathclaw.  If this sounds like a spoiler, it is.  The game spoils itself in the first 5 mins and effectively blows it's wad early.  Which loops back the the narrative.  It is totally disjointed, a very rushed intro sequence followed up by you being expected to lead a new militia and build a new settlement with this power armer and minigun your time spent at University training to be a lawyer prepared you for!
None of the improvements brought in to New Vegas are here.  In F4 you can craft every part of a weapon but the weapon itself.  You can craft every part of the armour but the armour itself.  Yet I know how to build a fully working artillery.  There is no ammo crafting, but thankfully ammo doesn't cost weight.  There is no requirement to collect or eat any of the food in the wasteland because even on Survival difficulty there is no requirement to eat or drink.  Hacking and lock picking mini games are identical to F3.
The biggest gripe for me personally however is this new dialogue system.  It is terrible.  It is Mass Effect Lite, with four options being presented to you with very little context.  You may get a set of options that say "Diamond City / Sarcastic / No / Yes".  Those are your options.  I have asked 15 people either for directions to Diamond City, or asked what Diamond City is long after I've already visited the place and completed quests there.  At one point my character laughed at another's misfortune, which was entirely not within my character scope and I had no way to tell from the presented options what I was going to say.  It required Quicksaving before selecting each dialogue option so that I could at least try to make my character have a cohesive personality.  The main characters are voiced well, as are some of the NPC's, but the dialogue is frequently dreadfully boring.  In fact, similarly to Fallout 3, the humour and grit of the Fallout world appears lost on Bethesda.
I don't accept "the mods will fix it" is a valid excuse any more.   Bethesda have released buggy rpg-lite's for the past few releases now and it's clear that in the time since F3, yes, the community HAS fixed F3 somewhat.  But we are 7 years on from Fallout 3, and very, very little has changed or improved, and I don't believe Bethesda should get a free pass here when other developers are crucified and hung out to dry over far smaller crimes.

It’s been years since we last stepped foot in the apocalyptic wasteland, and while there certainly is a sense a familiarity in Bethesda’s latest entry in the Fallout franchise, it can’t help but feel like the start of a new era of Fallout. Fans and newcomers alike have plenty to enjoy in this massive game, and it’s there’s plenty game to go around. The only thing that might stop you from enjoying Fallout 4 over the previous entries is how married you are to it’s previous gameplay mechanics.
Fallout 4 brings about a new focus in storytelling with the introduction of a voiced protagonist. Accompanying this is a more personal, stronger main story, as well as a tighter focus on who your character can be. In previous Fallout games, you could be a bumbling idiot, or an evil overlord bent on destruction of everything, this is a bit toned down in F4, the new dialogue system always limits you to just 4 choices, and the ability to have certain dialogue depending on your character’s stats is mostly drawn back with the exception of charisma checks. The absence of skills in favor of a more streamlined leveling system means that your character isn’t going to pick up a gun and not be able to use it, or perform terribly with it. Your character is a concerned parent seeking their son, and you branch out from there. Instead of skills in previous games, most stats are tied to the S.P.E.C.I.A.L system, and extra abilities come from perks, which function as usual, except this time you can find bonus perks in magazines hidden in the world, as well as bonus perks for maxing out your companions relationships. And speaking of those, the karma system is gone as well, replaced with doing actions that your companion will like. That does mean however, that you can be very schizophrenic with your choices without really feel like it’s having the impact it used to, especially if you don’t have a companion with you.
But while we are on combat, it’s worth noting that the shooting mechanics are the best they have ever been, guns feel responsive and the hundreds of mods you can attach to them means that even that early shotgun you found at level 5 can still be a force of nature if you keep it updated. The VATS system returns but no longer freezes time, but instead slows it, again a more grounded choice but it feels more welcome than the changes in dialogue. Power armor is no longer just another piece of armor to equip, but a suit you get into, with the same level of customization as the guns and other armor pieces, it almost encourages you to collect as many as you can, so sure enough, I have a hangar full of power armor suits that would make Tony Stark’s heart melt. But for the first time, power armor really sounds like, well, power armor.
Funding all of these upgrades is an increased focus on finding junk in the wasteland and scrapping it for materials. This is probably the best change from previous entries as it encourages exploration beyond just finding weapons armor and stimpacks. However, scrapping all of your junk in your inventory in the most efficient way possible often times means going to a settlement, dropping all of your junk in the ground, and selecting each and every piece for scrap. A ‘scrap all’ function would be incredibly welcome. Speaking of settlements, Fallout 4 has a bit of a base building mode, where you build houses, power, water, food and defenses for settlements to keep them safe. It can get incredibly addicting but, without the right perks, your resources are exclusive to each base, and while I eventually got the perk that lets me setup supply lines in between the bases, this led to me focusing only on one or two settlements, instead of ones across the map as it was probably intended.
Beyond this, you have the story and quests, and while I did mention the main story as being stronger, the overall world fells as if it’s lacking some truly memorable characters in the world, with the exception of some of your companions. Fetch quests or ones simply boiled down to ‘go here and kill some guys’ are abundant, especially when you might find yourself on a repeating quest chain against your will, with your quest giver not even presenting the option to turn down the next quest, I’m looking at you Preston, you annoying ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I have yet to do all of the side quests in the game, or finish exploring the map in its entirety, so I’m holding my thoughts on the side quest quality until later, but there certainly are some memorable side quests, as well as great rewards for doing them.
Graphically, it won’t blow your computer away from Project Cars, Witcher 3 or Arkham Knight, but it still looks great, using a modified version of the engine that ran Skyrim. Some of the age shows however, because while environments certainly are the best they have ever looked, animations are still a bit stiff and sometimes can just outright break. Speaking of breaking, F4 has significantly less bugs than the last 2 Fallout games did at launch, but that doesn’t mean it got away from them. Some quest bugs, graphical bugs, and the occasional need to restart arise. It’s been a lot worse, but still has room for improvement.
If this is your first Fallout game, dive right in, I guarantee you will have a fantastic time. If you really loved the previous Fallout games, I want you to take a step back for a moment, and ask yourself why you enjoyed them so much. The role playing side is downplayed, but the exploration is as great as ever. The skills and karma are gone, but the moment to moment gameplay feels the best it’s ever been. It’s different, is the point I’m getting at, and with a new console generation typically comes to changes in the formula. Bethesda clearly wanted a tighter focus on character and story this time around, but if that doesn’t bother you, then go crazy.

Now that i have said the good thing - there is the undeniable fact that F4 is, by genre, an ARPG. Weapon upgrades, the new prek tree - everything is far more Diablo than F1&2, with bits of inspiration from COD and Borderlands thrown in. I should have been angry, because i'm, like, old now and have all these fond memories of F1&2, and am generally a RPG type lady with the only straight shooter (COD BOIII) i got recently reserved for the times i need to unwind emotionally. A great game with a lot of fun things to discover. Improved graphics, improved voice acting, and generally cool cinematic dialogue. Like with other Fallout games, the main quest is good, but the fun is in the details. There are lots of weird things to laugh about, lots of ethical dilemmas to consider, and plenty of new weapons, items, and factions to see. Dogmeat is notably improved. The companions and romances are fun, but not nearly as deep as what you would find in Mass Effect. The crafting is fun and optional, and I really enjoy it. The character creator is fantastic, letting you go into as much or a s little detail as you might want. I havent exprienced any game breaking bugs, and only occasionally see something a tiny bit glitchy. At this point, it isn't even annoying, it's just like, "Why is that roach in a trashcan? That's a funny meme!"
Some things that I loved in Fallout 3 and New Vegas are gone, like skills. I really enjoyed the leveling system in previous games, but I found this system to be a little less appealing. It isn't bad by any means, but I wonder why the old way of doing things was scrapped. In addition, morality is gone, which I find somewhat disappointing. While Wild Wasteland is noticably  absent, I still have my other favorite perks: The Mysterious Stranger, Grim Reaper's Sprint, Animal Friend, and Action Girl.
The game is great. It isn't perfect, but it is certainly worth the money. You can asily put a couple hundred hours into this thing and not explore all there is to explore. Is it the game of the year? No. Is it in the top 5 games of the year? Yes.

It’s been years since we last stepped foot in the apocalyptic wasteland, and while there certainly is a sense a familiarity in Bethesda’s latest entry in the Fallout franchise, it can’t help but feel like the start of a new era of Fallout. Fans and newcomers alike have plenty to enjoy in this massive game, and it’s there’s plenty game to go around. The only thing that might stop you from enjoying Fallout 4 over the previous entries is how married you are to it’s previous gameplay mechanics.
Fallout 4 brings about a new focus in storytelling with the introduction of a voiced protagonist. Accompanying this is a more personal, stronger main story, as well as a tighter focus on who your character can be. In previous Fallout games, you could be a bumbling idiot, or an evil overlord bent on destruction of everything, this is a bit toned down in F4, the new dialogue system always limits you to just 4 choices, and the ability to have certain dialogue depending on your character’s stats is mostly drawn back with the exception of charisma checks. The absence of skills in favor of a more streamlined leveling system means that your character isn’t going to pick up a gun and not be able to use it, or perform terribly with it. Your character is a concerned parent seeking their son, and you branch out from there. Instead of skills in previous games, most stats are tied to the S.P.E.C.I.A.L system, and extra abilities come from perks, which function as usual, except this time you can find bonus perks in magazines hidden in the world, as well as bonus perks for maxing out your companions relationships. And speaking of those, the karma system is gone as well, replaced with doing actions that your companion will like. That does mean however, that you can be very schizophrenic with your choices without really feel like it’s having the impact it used to, especially if you don’t have a companion with you.
But while we are on combat, it’s worth noting that the shooting mechanics are the best they have ever been, guns feel responsive and the hundreds of mods you can attach to them means that even that early shotgun you found at level 5 can still be a force of nature if you keep it updated. The VATS system returns but no longer freezes time, but instead slows it, again a more grounded choice but it feels more welcome than the changes in dialogue. Power armor is no longer just another piece of armor to equip, but a suit you get into, with the same level of customization as the guns and other armor pieces, it almost encourages you to collect as many as you can, so sure enough, I have a hangar full of power armor suits that would make Tony Stark’s heart melt. But for the first time, power armor really sounds like, well, power armor.
Funding all of these upgrades is an increased focus on finding junk in the wasteland and scrapping it for materials. This is probably the best change from previous entries as it encourages exploration beyond just finding weapons armor and stimpacks. However, scrapping all of your junk in your inventory in the most efficient way possible often times means going to a settlement, dropping all of your junk in the ground, and selecting each and every piece for scrap. A ‘scrap all’ function would be incredibly welcome. Speaking of settlements, Fallout 4 has a bit of a base building mode, where you build houses, power, water, food and defenses for settlements to keep them safe. It can get incredibly addicting but, without the right perks, your resources are exclusive to each base, and while I eventually got the perk that lets me setup supply lines in between the bases, this led to me focusing only on one or two settlements, instead of ones across the map as it was probably intended.
Beyond this, you have the story and quests, and while I did mention the main story as being stronger, the overall world fells as if it’s lacking some truly memorable characters in the world, with the exception of some of your companions. Fetch quests or ones simply boiled down to ‘go here and kill some guys’ are abundant, especially when you might find yourself on a repeating quest chain against your will, with your quest giver not even presenting the option to turn down the next quest, I’m looking at you Preston, you annoying ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I have yet to do all of the side quests in the game, or finish exploring the map in its entirety, so I’m holding my thoughts on the side quest quality until later, but there certainly are some memorable side quests, as well as great rewards for doing them.
Graphically, it won’t blow your computer away from Project Cars, Witcher 3 or Arkham Knight, but it still looks great, using a modified version of the engine that ran Skyrim. Some of the age shows however, because while environments certainly are the best they have ever looked, animations are still a bit stiff and sometimes can just outright break. Speaking of breaking, F4 has significantly less bugs than the last 2 Fallout games did at launch, but that doesn’t mean it got away from them. Some quest bugs, graphical bugs, and the occasional need to restart arise. It’s been a lot worse, but still has room for improvement.
If this is your first Fallout game, dive right in, I guarantee you will have a fantastic time. If you really loved the previous Fallout games, I want you to take a step back for a moment, and ask yourself why you enjoyed them so much. The role playing side is downplayed, but the exploration is as great as ever. The skills and karma are gone, but the moment to moment gameplay feels the best it’s ever been. It’s different, is the point I’m getting at, and with a new console generation typically comes to changes in the formula. Bethesda clearly wanted a tighter focus on character and story this time around, but if that doesn’t bother you, then go crazy.
8.5/10

I usually save my time not writing reviews about bad, mediocre, or "alright" games but this one really does push a lot of boundaries. Settlements, gunplay on par with Destiny and Call of Duty, a rejuvenated V.A.T.S. system, and literally TONS of weapons and weapon mods make this new Fallout one of the best ones so far. Nay-sayers may complain about the story but that's really to each his/her own. I feel like they blew it out of the water. Every ending to a quest is another god-damn M. Knight Shama-Llama-Ding-Dong twist that keeps you intrigued and playing for hours on end.
The map will feel smaller than Skyrim or the other Fallout games, which is true. In terms of square meters, it definitely is smaller than Bethesda's previous games. But you would not believe how much they packed into the map. With what is commercially available to consumers nowadays, even the most high end computers would have a hard time keeping up with the game if they added in even more things to excavate into this medium sized map. People will also complain about the graphics as well, which is fine. I do agree, they gimped out on us in terms of graphics but again, this goes back to us talking about how much they packed into the map and my computer bugging out every time there is more than one Vertibird in the air nuking anything and everything in its path.
Bug-wise, personally, I've found a handful, but nothing that distracts from the game too much. A game of this scope and magnitude is bound to have a few glitches here and there. Fallout fans will agree that most of these are more funny than they are game-breaking.
This really doesn't need an in-depth analysis. Fallout already has a gigantic fan-base and it's release is proof of that. This may be one of the biggest hyped up releases in a couple of years and in my opinion, nothing released by Bethesda is ever a let-down. They take their time with games and their fans know that their product is up to par.
If you're a Fallout fan, don't second guess yourself. Get it as soon as you can.

It's a mixed bag, I could write a small essay on all the things wrong with this game (and sadly many of them are game design and technical issues that Bethseda has had with their games for so many years now) but the game still can dish out a lot of hours of reasonable content.
My main gripes are:
- The story loses it's momentum c o m p l e t e l y at halfway through the main storyline or so and the story feels underworked and I had a hard time being interested in the story behind my wild goose chase throughout the wasteland.
- Which faction you end up choosing to stay loyal will decide the fate of the commonwealth and who you side with will depend on a premise which you can't know if true or not. Many of your encounters with people in the game exist to sell you on that premise but because you still can't know if it's true or not the choice is thus a blind one and as such feels meaningless and unsatisfying.
- Expect a lot of unnecessary quicksaving and reloading, pickpocketing and dialogue option checks are still chance based and a failed one will typically result in the player reloading.
- Plenty of the content is lacking, especially settlements with the poor interface and lack of proper explanation as well as tedious micromanagement and resource gathering.
- If you're new to Bethseda games, do not expect a polished experience, there WILL be lots of bugs, weird AI behavior and odd stuff will happen, for me it's a big reason why I enjoyed this game actually but it can also be frustrating at times when quest NPC's disappear or you take the elevator to an entirely different building. Make sure to save often.
FInal Verdict: This game will disappoint many fans but most players should be able to get a fair amount of hours worth exploring the vast wasteland, there are plenty of things to do and plenty of places to go. The game can be scary at times for those of you who can't stomach that it may not be a good investment, although the ability to have an npc companion with you at near all-times can help make the world feel less intimidating.

54 hrs into Fallout 4, my impressions:
+ Non VATS combat is much better than earlier games, I'm having a ton of fun shooting things
+ Crafting my own custom weapons is my JAM, love doing that in games
+ Settlement building is weirdly interesting and I genuinely enjoy making safe, warm, defended places to live for all these nameless NPCs
+ World is varied and really dense with places to explore. Most of my time in the game has just been wandering the commonwealth and stumbling on new places
+ Graphics are actually quite nice, definitely an improvement over previous Bethesda games
+ Enemy ai patterns are much improved from previous fallout FPS games and enemies are more interesting to fight
- Main quest is hot, steaming trash
- There's no sense of progression in faction quests. Within the first 2 quests your already a Brotherhood of Steel KNIGHT. Same problem with the Minutemen
- Related to the last one: Faction questlines are super short
- There's a poverty of bespoke side quests. I've spent almost FIFTY hours and I've found a dozen or so genuine, non repeatable side quests
- Dialogue system is laughably bad (getting in and out of conversations is a PAIN), roleplaying anything other than a good guy is nearly impossible
- This is very much a Gamebryo Bethesda game, and as such has all the annoying jank that previous entries did. Fortunately I haven't had any gamebreaking bugs and only one CTD, but the jank is palpable
Basically, if you wanted a loot based, Fallout flavored, STALKER-esque shootbang with RPG elements, you'll love Fallout 4, just try not to think about the story too much.

This is very much a sequel to 2008's Fallout 3, with its emphasis on exploration and scavenging, rather than 2010's Fallout: New Vegas, where character development and storylines were handled better.
Compared directly to Fallout 3 there have been improvements in graphics, gunplay, AI... almost everything. Are there seven years worth of improvements here though? I don't think so.
On the plus side, this world is absolutely massive yet isn't filled with huge stretches of deserted wasteland. It is also often a vertical landscape where a single building can take an hour to explore, fight enemies, scavenge for goodies, etc. There are probably hundreds of buildings like this, some which aren't even quest related.
In such a big world containing so much to loot it is commendable that there is now a real purpose to scavenging, with the new weapon and armour crafting and settlement building.
In short, this is Fallout 3.5, which is great if you were a fan of that game and yet also a little underwhelming and disappointing, even more so if you preferred the RPG elements of New Vegas.

There was were so many complains on the Witcher 3 when it first got released and guess what, Witcher 3 is a nominee for the best game of the year. Real gamers were too busy to complain.  I'm running F4 on a MAC and guess what, so far, no huge bugs/issues at all. I seriously have no idea what people are complaining about.

The amount to customiztion is extremely high. Same goes for the weapons. It appears no two weapons are exactly the same anymore, which correctly reflects the situation of a post atomic world, where everyone is making their own thing. In order to upgrade your weapons/armor, youll need to hoard huge amounts of supplies. Some haters hate this but hey, in a post nuclear world, how else are you going to produce your stuff? Back in F3/NV, I would scream if i accidentally pressed E and let junk in my inventory, but now it's different junk is treasure.  Power armor is also something that needs to be managed as they run on fuel and have health points so they will break (you can still repair them).

I am a long time Fallout and Bethesda fan, I've played Fallout 3 and NV (3 is better in imo) and recently played Fallout 1. Fallout 4 is DEFINITELY the best game in the series. It takes all the things we know and love from 3 and improves them to an excellent game worthy of the Fallout name.
Pros-
Combat is 1000% better, did you REALLY enjoy 3's clunky mechanics
Graphics are superior, but not bar setting.
Drugs like RadX, Jet etc actually have a purpose. I completed 3 multiple times without using any drugs
Power Armour feels like it should - essentially an enclosure that makes you a tank, and you feel more like a badass wearing it. It also is a limited resource so you cant simply get the winterised T-51b armour like in Fallout 3 and hog it for the rest of the game.
Armour in general is improved with specific body parts that you attach to your chartacter
Dialogue system is more cinematic and is an improvement.
Story depth and characters including followers are superior
Quite a steep difficulty curve which I enjoyed
Crafting system is completely new to fallout and a godsend
Cons-
Bugs, opbviously. Not game breaking however
Follower AI has been essentially the same for Skyrim and Fallout 3, and this really needs to stop. Last of Us and Bioshock Infinite has clearly demonstrated that followers dont need to be absolute morons.
Dialogue options are slightly less deep
You can't really make a purely 'evil' character.
No karma system (not really a big deal, but a negative to some)
Enemy AI could be improved
More music could have been added.
The radio station host is such an extremely poor downgrade from Three Dog.
The game has next to no tutorial about 90% of the mechanics
Overall, excellent fun game. Sure to give you hundreds of hours of fun

I usually save my time not writing reviews about bad, mediocre, or "alright" games but this one really does push a lot of boundaries. Settlements, gunplay on par with Destiny and Call of Duty, a rejuvenated V.A.T.S. system, and literally TONS of weapons and weapon mods make this new Fallout one of the best ones so far. Nay-sayers may complain about the story but that's really to each his/her own. I feel like they blew it out of the water. Every ending to a quest is another god-damn M. Knight Shama-Llama-Ding-Dong twist that keeps you intrigued and playing for hours on end.
The map will feel smaller than Skyrim or the other Fallout games, which is true. In terms of square meters, it definitely is smaller than Bethesda's previous games. But you would not believe how much they packed into the map. With what is commercially available to consumers nowadays, even the most high end computers would have a hard time keeping up with the game if they added in even more things to excavate into this medium sized map. People will also complain about the graphics as well, which is fine. I do agree, they gimped out on us in terms of graphics but again, this goes back to us talking about how much they packed into the map and my computer bugging out every time there is more than one Vertibird in the air nuking anything and everything in its path.
Bug-wise, personally, I've found a handful, but nothing that distracts from the game too much. A game of this scope and magnitude is bound to have a few glitches here and there. Fallout fans will agree that most of these are more funny than they are game-breaking.
This really doesn't need an in-depth analysis. Fallout already has a gigantic fan-base and it's release is proof of that. This may be one of the biggest hyped up releases in a couple of years and in my opinion, nothing released by Bethesda is ever a let-down. They take their time with games and their fans know that their product is up to par.
If you're a Fallout fan, don't second guess yourself. Get it as soon as you can.

This is very much a sequel to 2008's Fallout 3, with its emphasis on exploration and scavenging, rather than 2010's Fallout: New Vegas, where character development and storylines were handled better.
Compared directly to Fallout 3 there have been improvements in graphics, gunplay, AI... almost everything. Are there seven years worth of improvements here though? I don't think so.
On the plus side, this world is absolutely massive yet isn't filled with huge stretches of deserted wasteland. It is also often a vertical landscape where a single building can take an hour to explore, fight enemies, scavenge for goodies, etc. There are probably hundreds of buildings like this, some which aren't even quest related.
In such a big world containing so much to loot it is commendable that there is now a real purpose to scavenging, with the new weapon and armour crafting and settlement building.
In short, this is Fallout 3.5, which is great if you were a fan of that game and yet also a little underwhelming and disappointing, even more so if you preferred the RPG elements of New Vegas.

The dialogue choices are so limited there's now way to play your own character.
The problem isn't with the dialogue wheel itself but the limited nature of choices. Mass Effect handled this way better. Here your choices are essentially boiling down to tone rather than actual choices. You're already set as a paladin of the wasteland, the only player choices is how sarcastic you choose to be about it.

This game is a great addition to the series of games Bethesda has released. It has its pros and cons, of course.
Pros:
-Easily the least buggy game they've put out I can remember. Sure, there's the occassional issue, but nothing gamebreaking and no crashes (as of this review)
-Excellent controls* (Keybinding cons, however)
-Rather engaging story, even if I detest voice-acted protagonists.
-The customization is amazing, from the power armor, to the weapons, to the settlements.
-As it is a Bethesda game, and my being only 14+/- hours in, I still have a lot to experience with this one.
Cons:
So, these may be more preference than anything, but hopefully the actual issues will come through.
-Dialogue options. I'm not happy with the 'cutscene-esque' way in which its presented, or how the PC is voiced, or the 4 options given, which is usually: 1. Yes, 2. No, 3 Sarcastic comment, 4. Persuasion. Personally I'd have prefered a multitude of options and no voice acting.
-Keybinding. This is a seriously stupid nitpick due to the fact it shouldn't even have been messed up. Say you want to rebind E (activate/do most anything) to right Shift key. You can do that, but there's no option to rebind looting, which is by default also E. It's seems like an oversite that they'll fix in a patch, who knows.
-Placing items with the settlements feature can be extremely frustrating on inclines. Youll end up with a great looking outer defense with a great big hole under the flat base of your makeshift barricade.
-Survival Setting. This is a con because I expected the need to eat and sleep like in New Vegas, but that was Obsidian. I dunno, seems stupid to label it survival and not have included that.
-Dogmeat. I love the little guy, I really do, but all he would do was sneak up on me, open doors, give away my position or just scare me and almost make me shoot him. So he stays home.
-Getting certain things. Now, I'm not that far into the main quest, but within the first couple hours, you get several... things, I'll say to avoid spoilers, that seem like they're obtained too hastily. Now, some may argue that's for the better, but eh.
Final verdict:
It's honestly a fantastic game, and all the people saying its not fallout, or it's got this issue and that are grasping at straws. Have the recommended system requirements and you'll be fine. Is it game of the year? Eh, maybe. I haven't played Witcher 3 but for a few minutes and most people say that is, so I have no way to claim one way or another. Compared to Fallout 3 and New Vegas? It improves on so much. So very much. And let's be honest, if you're getting it on PC, the amount of mods thet'll be made will give you a fine assortment of options to tailor it to specifally what you'd be after.
8/10 (thus far, may go up once I get more into quests)

Writing a new review for Fallout 4 as I've put more time into the game.
First of all, this game is very much in the same style as Fallout 3. It has the same grindy feel to it...going from site to site clearing it out...looking for that hidden magazine or bobblehead or secret room with phat loot. In a way this game is as grindy as an mmo, but it's single player.
I do recommend this game. It's using the same engine as Skyrim so there are a lot of similarities. There are some really annoying things though.
For one, dumping all your loot is a bit tedious. And there's no way to lock the items you are wearing so if you're just mashing left click and E to dump everything and accidentally dump all your armor...you have to go through a massive list of items to find it and put it back on. Usually if I do this it's such a pain that I just reload the game.
Quick saving and reloading this game is literally the only way to play. This kind of means that you can easily kill a very difficult fight by just reloading and reloading and reloading until the stars align and everything goes right. Because of this, if you run around clearing out everything in the game you're going to end up way over powered even on the greater difficulties...unless you pick some ridiculous skills and suck.
While there are not a lot of choices to be made in this game....and the ones you do have are either pseudo choices or one choice is CLEARLY better than another...there is a fair bit of story and content in this game about what happened and what is happening.
I do have fun hacking terminals and reading all the personal emails. There seems to be a lot more talk about what happened right before the war than in previous fallouts (with the exception of fallout 2 where you hacked into some super ai in a vault and found out that China and the US got into a nuclear war over resources, specifically oil, as the US blew up some of China's oil wells and then started drinking their milkshake)
The game is pretty smooth. VATS is better in this than in Fallout 3. There are a TON of unique weapons. All the old classics are here (fatboy, junk jet, etc). Being able to mod your weapons gives you a bit of a bonus (although it takes a fair bit of skills to get the good stuff and you may be better off not using those points and instead putting them somewhere more effective).
The whole building up your town thing is an interesting thing to waste a ♥♥♥♥♥on of time on. It might be fun to build up your towns as you wait for expansion content, etc.
The game is just massive though. It is just like Skyrim..literally has a lot of parallels. Everything is high quality.
It's just rather linear. You get overpowered pretty easily (just like in Fallout 3). There's very few choices in the game (so far). Your followers are OP...since they don't die they just kneel down for a minute then get right back up again. So you can use them as distraction/fodder when fighting Deathclaws or something early on.
And since you can turn any item into salvage...UNLIKE Fallout and Skyrim, you pick up EVERY LITTLE ♥♥♥♥♥♥ COFFEE MUG because you can build your town with it later so who cares.
My current build is a stealth melee weapon str/agi build. Lockpicking is a must. Hacking is great for story. And some boosts to bartering are okay. Occassioanlly I need to use a long range weapon in certain situations, but for the most part I can just stealth in or run in and slaughter everything / run and hide around corners, etc.
The power armor is pretty fun, too. I've already collected 6 suits and I'm not sure what I'm going to do with them all. I'm maybe 30% through the content of this game...and USUALLY (though not always) a site tells you when you 'complete' it (kill everything inside).
Really this game is not hard. It's just tedious. If you grind and clear areas and carry loot back home long enough you will beat everything. It's not like you need to attain a level of skill at the game before you can beat it...just keep clearing sites and grinding and getting xp and carrying loot and everything will be completed. That's kind of annoying but I guess it makes it massively appealing.

When I first played through this game, I was very disapointed. While it is a fairly good single player shooter, it lacks a lot of the RPG elements you would expect. Immersion was also not the games strong point. The story was very forced and by the mid game the ammount of shots it took for me to kill an enemy (and for an enemy to kill me) was crazy. For example, in the middle of a fight, me and a super mutant used up all our ammo shooting point blank into eachother before reloading and kept shooting point blank at eachother. I ended giving up on the game.
I have come back 2 years later and have found myself having a hugely more postive experience to the point where it has become one of the best experiences I have come across in gaming. Why? Two reasons.
The first of which is the release of the survival mode. While I know this mode is not for everyone, it can lead to immense frustration. However, this high risk and high reward gameplay has brought in so much more immersion into the gameplay and additionally the RPG elements really shine through. The actions you make really have weight to them! One wrong move can spell doom and you have to load a save at the last time you slept. Some things about this mode seem so tedious such as the inability to fast travel (However, this can be corrected with mods).
Mods are the second reason why my experience with the game has improved so much. While the creation club is a poor money grabbing move by Bethesda, mods outside this can easily be added to the game to change your experience in many ways. For example, I got a mod which allowed me to build cars, which allowed me to fast travel between my settlements (However, these are VERY expensive to make). You can customise your experience in so many ways, that it fixes so much of the original game and caters it to how YOU play.
Overall, I would recommend this game to any one who is a bethesda fan who played Skryim, or in need of a casual or hardcord game in the post nuclear war setting. Mods and survival mode allow all types of people to have a good time with this game.

I'm now 84 hours into Fallout 4, and I'm starting to form cogent opinions.  First and foremost, I have to give this game a strong positive recommendation.  It's immersive and fun, and one of those games that you can easily sit down to play after the kids go to bed and not look up at the clock again until two or three in the morning.  Combat has made some very superior strides over its predecessors, as has crafting.  It is so much more fun to customize and mod your weapons and armor than in earlier iterations, where it seems like you just had to horde a stockpile of your favorite weapon so you could use the extras to repair as the gun inevitably broke down.  The random pieces of junk that had little use beyond selling to a vendor in previous iterations now all have some use with the new crafting system.  It makes the concept of scavenging much more relavant to the actual game experience.  You have a real reason to grab everything that isn't nailed down beyond waiting at a vendor for his caps to respawn so you can unload more of your junk.
That being said, I have a major criticism to make, and that's my character's dialogue being fully voiced yet woefully under-represented in dialogue options.  You tend to get four options in every dialogue point, and they are represented with a pithy one to three word phrase that leaves you guessing as to the actual content of your statement.  "Sarcastic," is my least favorite of these.  Sarcrasm is a nuanced thing; it can be biting and harsh, or it can be lighthearted and fun.  I'm sorry, but I need to know exactly what kind of sarcasm my character is going to use.  Staying in character matters to me.  "Ask for more money" is another really frustrating option.  I want to know what my character is going to say before I make a dialogue choice; these options simply aren't enough information for me to effectively do that.
Another issue that hits even closer to home to me as a long time fan of Bethesda's RPG's on the PC platform is how this is going to tie the hands of mod developers.  Some of my favorite mods have been fully voiced companions that have been masterfully crafted to fit seamlessly into the game's quests and adapt with your character regardless of what choices you make - top notch examples include John Jarvis' and Christina Slagman's "Sofia" companion for Skyrim, Emma Lycanthrop's "Vilja" companion for Oblivion and Skyrim, and "Willow" companion by llama for New Vegas.  These fan created characters all enhanced my immersion into their respective worlds greater than any of Bethesda's characters, and I look forward to seeing what the modding community creates for Fallout 4.  Unfortunately, in terms of NPC interactions, modders are going to be left with two bad options - either use only game assets for your character's dialogue with the companion, which will result in a generic and sometimes awkward experience, or to voice your character's responses themselves, which will at least triple the amount of work and resources when you account for the need to voice both a male and a female response in dialogue.  Additionally, this will kill immersion because as you pop in and out of mod content and game content, your character's voice will noticeably change.
This leads into my second major complaint, and that is the companion characters Bethesda has given us.  They are interestingly written and good characters for the most part.  But they tend to not fit into the game very well at all.  One really frustrating example if you play a sneak/rogue character character is that the characters have scripted moments in most areas where you cross the threshold of a room and if you aren't in combat, the companion strolls into the center of the room and makes a comment about it.  This would be an awesome thing for immersion, if it wasn't for the fact that the room is filled with wandering ferals that I haven't shot yet and now you just blew our cover.  I'm looking at you, Piper.  Another complaint is that "Thoughts" option on the dialogue wheel rarely has any relevance to what is actually happening in the story.  One really game breaking example for me was at a crucial point in the story where I had to leave Piper to go do something dangerous on my own that I might not come back from, there wasn't any kind of a goodbye.  Mind you we were dating at this point and she was supposedly crazy about me.  I wanted that interaction; it seemed too important to the story to not occur.  So before I was about to leave I pulled up the chat wheel and selected "Thoughts" which was the closest option to what I really wanted to talk about.  All she wanted to talk about is how successful a reporter she is and offered me some gum drops.  So I left, and when I came back, I didn't get any kind of, "I didn't think I'd ever see you again!" or "I was so worried!" or even a "Hey cool you didn't die."  Just more generic lines that had no relevance to what was actually going on.  Now I guarantee you a great mod writer like the ones I mentioned above would script something into a pivotal story moment like this that would really add to the immersion.  I've got to say, I'm just experiencing a slight twinge of disappointed at this point.  I expected better.  It's a great game, and I can tell it's got plenty of more miles to go for me, but the dialogue change has destroyed an important aspect of immersion that the genre possessed previously.  My hope is in the sheer creativity of the modding community.  I just know that they will come up with great content despite the limitations and after I've played the game out completely, I look forward to coming back in a few months and starting a new playthrough with some mods.

I found this game to be quite fun.  It is a puzzle solving game that is EXTREMELY similar to the Professor Layton series.  Don't be deceived by the game's childish art style, the puzzles can be quite challenging for adults.
I believe there are over 250 puzzles in this game, including optional ones.  Only about 80 of them are required to beat the game.  Most of the puzzles can be solved with critical thinking, but there were a few that I admit I had to use a walkthrough to solve.  I really liked the hidden objects and written answer puzzles, just because I could usually solve them myself.  The rhythm puzzles were a bit tedious, and the sliding and the hidden picture puzzles were just really boring and difficult for me.  Luckily there is only 1 required hidden picture puzzle, and only 2-3 sliding puzzles that weren't that bad.  The rhythm puzzles are commonly used, with 3-4 in each chapter, all of them required.  If you find them difficult or, like me, too tedious, you can always use hints that you gain from solving bonus puzzles.  I'm really glad they put this in, as the hints saved me so much time and effort, and got me out of many tight spots.
The story is quite simple.  You are May, a girl who got into a balloon accident and has landed in a strange town.  To top it off, your brother is missing.  Sucks to be you.  You must go out into Dragonville and try to find your brother and what is up with the citizens of Dragonville.  One of the main problems I have with this game is its use of characters.  Most of the characters in the game only serve to be used for 1 or 2 puzzle, and then they are never seen again.  In fact, only about 5 characters are in more than one of the four acts.  The ending contained a plot twist that I pretty much saw coming from a mile away.  I'm really just glad they bothered with a coherent story.
Overall, I would suggest this game if you are interested in a puzzle solving game, or if you just want to think a little.  While it is worth the full price of $10, I would suggest waiting until it is on sale, mainly since the steam summer sale is just around the corner.

As many of the other commenters have said, this is a game that aspires to be a Professor Layton game. Except, of course, there are a number of giant flaws that make the game completely unpalatable, unlike Professor Layton.
1. Puzzles are rather easy for the first three chapters ("Find the gigantic name scrawled on the wall and input it into the answer box.") and suddenly spike up to "lots of brute force required"-difficulty ("Which of these four hands of cards has the best chance of winning a game of Variant Poker?") during the last chapter. It's as if the developers had no idea who their target audience would be, so they just mashed up a bunch of random puzzles and riddles and called it a game.
2. Puzzles are ambiguously worded in many cases (The bug spray can't be "next to" the bugs? Is that "orthogonally" or "orthogonally and diagonally"?), thus making it impossible to determine which solution was intended. In some cases, multiple solutions are accepted, but in others, they are not.
3. The rhythm "puzzles". The game asks you to repeat the rhythm of a certain tune it plays. That's it. No puzzle elements in it whatsoever, so I'm really not sure what it's doing here. If I wanted a rhythm game, I would have bought a rhythm game, not a puzzle game. On this note [pun not intended], the tune always plays twice, save for one exception right in the middle of the game, which only plays once. This is unnecessarily annoying and time-consuming in the first instance, and disorienting in the second.
4. Completely unbalanced hint system. Either the hint system is useless (in that the information it gives you is information you already know), or that it gives you information you yourself couldn't work out (which defeats the whole purpose of a puzzle). In one particular case; namely, a puzzle asking you to count the number of mate-in-ones on a chessboard; the hint itself gives completely false information (a king moving out the path of a rook can only give discovered check in six ways, not seven).
5. No explanations for your answer's truth value. It only tells you whether your answer is right or wrong. Normally, this wouldn't be a problem. However, given the problems noted above, this just makes the game ridiculously unplayable, and turns the game into one of "Guess what the person who made this puzzle was thinking when he came up with an incorrect answer which we won't hint at!"
6. The puzzle resets itself if you get it incorrect (which, during the last few chapters, is practically inevitable). You got it incorrect due to a slightly misplaced piece? Have fun placing them back in.
7. Sliding puzzles. There are at least 40 of them in the game. However, as far as I dare to check, they are all of the same size (3x3), and there is a trivial method for solving sliding puzzles, making these pure timewasters.
8. Plot holes everywhere. What happened to the balloonist? Did Lukatello make it out alive? Is Doyle really completely incompetent at this whole "keeping one's intentions secret", and is May TRULY so stupid that she doesn't suspect a thing until Doyle meets Uter (yet is apparently intelligent enough to be able to solve brute-force 4-piece dissection puzzles in her head)?! How do we even know that that person IS Uter (and not one of Uter's lackeys), and that Doyle isn't merely Uter in disguise?!
The key difference between this "puzzle game" and any game from the Professor Layton series is that this game seems to want to be at odds with puzzle-solving immersion, as if the creators of the game hated puzzles with all their fortunes and wanted to intentionally ruin peoples' puzzle-solving experiences while raking in money for a garbage product.
All in all, it is an absolutely horrible game with no respect whatsoever for the player's time. Your £6.99 would be far better spent on, say, Braid, QUBE, or Sokobond; where the creator has actually test-solved all the puzzles and verified that they aren't completely outrageously impossible or broken. Don't even bother getting this game unless it's to verify my observations, in fact; I wouldn't even take it for free.
