With the popularity of Nintendo's
series, it is expected that other will try to copy the formula.  Wanting to get into it, software maker V5 decided to make their first game in the same style.  While their software programs are great products, their first video game leaves something to be desired.
While the game tries to make the game seem logical through a story, it is a weak one at best.  The art style clearly point towards a kid's appeal with simple design and button eyes.  However, as various point, the story feels like it is really for adults.  One part asks the player to give medication to make someone fall unconscious.  Such questionable material should not be in a game that would be appealing for kids.  Even when it the game is squarely in the children area, walking fishwomen and birdmen just keeps the story from getting even slightly believable.  With the game's bipolar story, it makes you wonder if the story was written by one person or by committee.
At the heart of the game, the puzzles also feel as juvenile as the story.  Most of the puzzles have such a dated feel, they seem like something that came from an old puzzle book.  Such a dated feeling make it that only kids will not have heard at least a variation to the puzzle.  Even if the player cannot figure out the puzzle, the hints make it so easy, they all but say "This is the answer."  It is one thing to make an easy game, but to make it that thinking is not required for a puzzle game defeats the purpose of a puzzle game.  When making a puzzle game, being able to solve it using your own brain and logic makes it a rewarding experience.  Without it, it is not worth playing at all.
One thing that they try to do to mix things up is adding music levels into the mix.  Just like the puzzles, the music is also lacking in appeal or personality.  Every song has a simple pattern, many of which sound like they could be from a single-tone like a foghorn or whistle.  As for playing the songs, the player simply has to repeat the pattern of the music.  Once again, unlike other games like
or
, it does not take much skill to do enough to clear a song.  Additionally, if the player does enough to reach the quota, then they can just let the song run without doing anything else to finish.  Since they put seemingly no sought towards the music, it hardly worth having them in there in the first place.
Despite their efforts to be original, the game ends up being a poor man’s
.  Even for those areas that are different, they just feel like bad versions of other, better games.  Even with the questionable story, the game has a childlike feel, and children are the ones that will clearly like this game.  For everybody whose age is in double digits, they are better places to look.

Broken Sword: The Angel of Death is the prime example of how to not do a Broken Sword game.
The gameplay is cluncky and a complete frustration to control at times, where the previous game used a control scheme for gaming consoles but still made it work somehow this one failed miserably, making it frustrating to play regardless of you using the keyboard or mouse when controling your character.
The facial animations are downright creepy and hilarious, and in my playthrough I came across multiple instances where the player character's left leg would twist into weird positions.
Like many old Point and Click Adventure games sometimes there isn't a lot of direction on what you have to do, with you having to play the "guess what the developer has in mind" game in order to progress. The inventory is a complete mess with it being presented as a line at the top of the screen that you scroll through and with the game not clearing out items you will never need again it will end up being a convoluted mess. In my playthrough I also came across a bug that made the game unbeatable, this bug taking the form of a key item that somehow vanished from my inventory and I do remember having that item at some point during the game.
The story is very in style with the Broken Sword series and one of the few good aspects of the game however, the ending comes pretty abruptly without giving the game an epilogue to the events. The voice acting for the most part is pretty good as well, sometimes the dialogue comes off as being a bit cheesy but works well within the Broken Sword series.
In the end I could only recommend this game to anyone only and only if they are die hard fans of the franchise, and even then I would caution them to only play it if they can't fathom skipping a game in the series. For every one else, stay away! This game is not worth your time, I am sure there are countless other games you would rather be playing.

I bought this during the last Steam Winter Sale. Which is to say, I've entered No Man's Sky after the Atlas Rises patch.
I, just like many others saw how the game was originally hyped and marketed. I watched from a distance, excitedly and then, disappointed that it had turned out that much of the marketing had been an outright lie. I wasn't glad I didn't purchase on day one. I was upset that something totally possible wasn't real.
Now, I still wanted the game. Mostly for the infinite universe, the ability to hop on and off planets seamlessly and explore procedurally generated lands. This game gives you that! And it's awesome!
But as many others stated, it doesn't give you a fully realized, living and breathing universe with characters and races and politics and such. It honestly gives you 3 races to interact with. They're all stationary, sitting at ports, stations and bases and they're always on their smartphones (just like real life! lol fml) But interaction with them does have depth in the fact that you have to learn their languages, learn what they want and need. You have to watch your standing with each race. I don't know why yet, I've only got 17 hours in the game right now.
Piloting your ship is pretty good and easy to pick up and learn. I don't know why you can't invert the Y axis so it pilots like a typical aircraft but I got used to it.
But honestly, if you want to know what this game plays like, I'll put it to you this way. If they advertised this game as a SPACE BIOLOGIST/ARCHEOLOGIST SIMULATOR then EVERYONE would have had the right idea and people wouldn't have been so angry about it. You go from planet to planet analyzing flora and fauna getting money out of that. Then you can pick up quests at space stations which involve discovering locations, flora and fauna, mining, killing fauna, collecting bounties... oh yes, about that...
Collecting bounties and combat in general in this game is a clear afterthought. It's why I say the game is better marketed as a space biologist sim. You have a multitool that can act as a firearm but the only thing you'll ever get in fights with is flying drones or 4 legged drones or aggressive animals. You won't ever get in a shootout or a gunfight with another alien. No, that only happens in the form of dogfights in space. Which, isn't bad.
So why did I still buy this game? Because Hello Games literally caused the most infamous ♥♥♥♥ up in game release history and I believe they're sincerely regretful about it. I believe that with that regret, they have true incentive to update the game until it is what they originally dreamt it to be. And I want to be there for that.
The Atlas Rises update really gives the game a lot. And I find myself driven to keep playing. I don't feel this sense of loneliness in the universe that others keep talking about. I do see remnants of other players leaving messages and naming stuff. Honestly, the universe in this game is how many planets large? 18 Quintillion? Why the hell would anyone EXPECT to see another player in a universe that big? I think Hello Games should consider shrinking it if anything. Especially if they intend to add TRUE multiplayer to the game eventually, and they must plan to as they said as much in the Atlas Rises update. But yeah, with a universe that large, it doesn't feel weird not to see anyone.
Anyways, get this one on sale. I don't know why they have it at full 59.99 all the time even after that release disaster.

This is an excellent, well-made, laid-back puzzle platformer, with a minimalistic style to its look, feel, and gameplay.
Everything about this seems a bit cliched, but it carries a very charming appeal to it, giving it its own unique personality.  BOOR is the name of the world you're in, taken over by an A.I. sentience akin to SKYNET in Terminator.  The game is divided into four acts.  Each act introduces some new element to the puzzling, and carries its own boss to beat.  Every boss is different, and the way to beat them is different also.  Almost every puzzle level is contained in a single screen.  The game states there are 85 levels.  Some level areas scattered throughout the game have no puzzles, just a sight-seeing walk, which is truly a nice breather in the overall scheme.  Other level areas have character engagement with NPCs, either scripted conversations, or the characters are simply present and you can interact with them if you wish.   They are survivors of this hostile takeover and extermination of the AI sentience.  They mainly provide you with story background and current events in the story.  One act contain levels where you need to escort an NPC safely through.  There are even terminals with logs and diary pages you can read if you choose to, which will give more background to the story.  These you'll find in non-puzzle areas.  Lastly, there is one room that contains three arcade machines, salvaged from BOOR and repaired to working order, and each of these contain a different game to play, within BOOR.
All in all, truly, for the cheapest game I purchased this Steam winter sale, this was one of the best I've played of all those winter sale purchases.  Only sixty cents; I kind of feel like I short-changed the developer on this one.   I wasn't expecting such a robust and well-crafted little game that carried a good and fair challenge amidst an enriched story with a charming personality.  The way it ended opened a door for a sequel of a whole other kind... isometric rpg squad-based action akin to knights of old republic gameplay elements but more action... in this devasted world of BOOR, post this story.  Dev, are you hearing me?  The ending of BOOR kicked a mighty door open to explore this world in different ways... even Borderland style, if you wish to imagine extremes...

May’s Mysteries is a shining example of how to create a good port from a handheld game for PC. Sadly it’s not as good at balancing puzzle difficulty or at distributing said puzzles in a storyline. It’s a decent and– more importantly– quite long game.
May’s Mysteries: The Secret of Dragonville is actually a port of a Nintendo DS game called May’s Mystery: Forbidden Memories. Naturally the display and control of the DS don’t translate at all to PC, so the developer essentially created an entirely new game from the same content.
At first look it seems like an educational cartoon in the form of a video game: something one buys for little children to keep them occupied while teaching them problem solving. The fairly straightforward story, visual design and simple characters also confirm this.
Yet, as the story progresses, the puzzles gradually leave the difficulty range suited for children, and reach the point where even an adult may think about using the Skip button. Chess puzzles, riddles that require practical experience, elaborate geometric conundrums… there are 271 brain-twisters in 14 categories, so don’t expect to finish anytime soon.
This huge number and the difficulty curve also means that you get a really long game for a low amount of money, making May’s Mysteries one of the best puzzle games available on Steam.

I loved all Professor Layton's games and naturally thought I would enjoy this clone. However, it is not the case. The puzzles which I have gone through do not make sense and are not logical. Either because they are poorly worded and, resultantly, there are more than one choice which might fit. Either there are parameters missing to make sense of them. Either because the answer is not in the puzzle itself but somewhere else in the game.
Very few puzzles in the Layton's series have resisted me more than a few minutes because they were well designed, logical and contained all the elements required to solve them. But this game's logic is "puzzling" and, worse of all, at no point is the solution explained, so you get no feedback as to why this answer was the correct one.
Good game, would recommend!

Recommended only if you're already a fan of the Professor Layton games, or games of that style, and are craving a similar experience on PC, rather than a portable device. Unfortunately it pales in comparison to the Professor Layton games, namely in feel, story and puzzle design, but for a cheap imitator it does the job good enough.

I think this is ok for children. (They might also have more patience to sit through the pointless delays before and after the puzzles.)
The story is definitely for children (but interesting enough that I wanted to see the end, and not just solve all puzzles). The puzzles seem aimed at kids too.
I don't know how bright children are these days, and of course they don't all have the same grasp of puzzles, so my vague guess would be somewhere between age 8 and 12.
If you're relatively old and fuzzyheaded like me, always liked varied puzzles but just aren't up to the tough stuff anymore, this might entertain you too. There's plenty to do, and you can return to all the puzzles (skipped, solved, as well as unlocked bonus) at any time, including after the end.
I turned off sound (and thus skipped all rythmic puzzles), so I can't say anything on either.
The interface is easy.

This is a game which desperately wants to be Professor Layton.  I am disappointed that it fails to get close.  (Layton fan who has puzzle 100% completion on all the games)
One of the great elements of the Layton games is the personality of the characters.  They are approachable, friendly and are great catalysts for adventure.   The support characters are introduced at times which are relevent to the story and not in waves of people.  Although the story in the Layton games is key to it's success, it manages to play on a level field with the puzzles.  The puzzles themselves don't just reflect the story, but with frequency, they tell and enhance it.
This game fails to unite these three elements.  The characters are fairly hollow, the story is convoluted and the puzzles (all too frequently) are driven not by difficult design, but instead by difficult phrasing.  Couple this with a hint system which generally fails to explain what the puzzle is actually asking this game creates frustration not stimulation.
Having said that, there are puzzles which are suitibly challenging as a consequence of good design.  It is a pity that they are so few and far between.
Combining the poor story and poor puzzle design with the poor options (including limited sound and video options) I cannot recommend this game very strongly.
The grain of salt that must come with this review is that I am a Layton fan and those games are the very best the genre has to offer.  For all my criticism, this is not a bad game.  It is just that compared to the leading game in the genre it is not as good.
I would love to see this game simplified.  Limit the story and focus on the puzzles.  It needs to find something that makes it different to the competition, and at the moment it is nothing more than a Layton clone.
Do I recommend it?  I think that people who like Layton may find it ok.  It is no replacement though.  If this had a demo which I had been able to play, I would not have purchased it.

This is the fourth game in Broken Sword series and... uhm... Oh, for god’s sake! No. Just no. Plain and simple. This game isn't worthy of the Broken Sword name. What have you done to the beloved franchise??? Sorry for blurting my frustration out but
is a complete disappointment for any fan of the series, and would be most certainly a wrong choice to introduce someone to it. I'll try to be very brief about what's been done in this game and why it just didn't fit with the rest of the series, neither with tone nor with the gameplay. Oh, and there is one thing that I've never dreamt of telling about a Broken Sword game to begin with: the scenario is bad!
After the events of the
, George is back in New York and running a bail bonds office with his partner Virgil. Aside constant indigence due to the lack of decent clients, life has been quiet for Mr. Stobbart... that is until an attractive blonde named Anna Maria shows up on his door step, asking for help about another manuscript! That is the moment the Italian mafia takes a hit on George's shop, leaving the place wrecked and Virgil pretty much♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ From that point onwards, George is yet again sucked into another adventure "vaguely" involving Templar lore. Ready for the Ark of Ashdod? Because that was one Christian legend not trifled by the series. They must have thought "Hey, we didn't include the Arc on any previous games. Wanna arrange an appearance for that?" and the response was this, I guess "Sure, let's make it Indiana Jones style with church thrown in as bad guys!"
Don't get me wrong, I'm not even Christian and I wouldn't be offended on religious matters to begin with. This is fiction. But the lore is so mismatched, the story gives you a headache in its short lived lifespan. Okay, here is the start of my actual complaints, so if you intend to play this game for the sake of completion, and would like to avoid spoilers, skip the rest of this paragraph. It is already customary to Broken Sword games to include interconnection for obscure political/religious groups but it's been done elaborately until now. Here, we have the mafia and the Vatican as core power players - and Mafia are the good guys! And there will be no decent explanation to the heartfelt (!) sacrifices (!!!) they've been doing to protect humankind! Weird, huh? Add to this already weird display the Arc of Ashdod, a scientist obsessed with monatomic gold, nuns working at a wafer factory and Turkish secret service. Frustrated yet? And surprise, there is no satisfying story explanation when you come to end. Just a bunch of needless NPC deaths and sacrifices, added with every good natured side character showing up in the catacombs of Vatican (???) to help our characters. That is plain lousy writing.
Another major disappointment is that we have a new protagonist to accompany George instead of Nico: Anna Maria. You heard it right. Nico isn't a protagonist in this story. She's been replaced by an Italian blond whose loyalty will be the primary concern of debate for the remainder of the whole game. Nico herself won't be appearing till way past the middle of the game to share some snarky remarks to display cheap jealousy, take under a brief and mostly irrelevant adventure in Arizona to “help” George investigate, and play the part of a damsel in distress by the ending. That's it. Nico is not relevant in this game. That is one tradition broken alright with much frustration attached to it. It was a decent idea to present some competition for Nico as a romantic interest, but this is badly done. Anna Maria is shallow and needy until the end of the game, and there, she serves as a traumatizing element for George. That's all.
Yes, I said traumatizing. Yes, in a Broken Sword game. The tone of the game is very slow pacing and somewhat dark compared to previous installations. It's as if there was a shortage of decent humor in the department when people were writing the script. It's always dark and moody, starting with the opening cinematic. That's specifically why this shouldn't be called a Broken Sword game. Even everything else were to fail, you could always count on humor in Broken Sword series. It seems not anymore. Whatever your take for this whole mess would be though, it will come to an end soon. The whole game consists of 4 places: New York, Istanbul, Arizona and Rome. Yup, that's it, and every story arc is so badly rushed you understand not a thing aside that there was an Arc and evil church was trying to assemble it.
The game already continues the 3D style of the 3rd game, but the art style made a fast transition from cartoony to robotic realism. Sure, layering seem decent and it is a fitting art choice for the already moody undertone but I wish characters would attain
facial expressions. There is no feeling left. They look clucky, they move clunky and they mostly seem like everyone is badly constipated. The gameplay is a hybrid between WASD controls and mouse, and it mostly doesn't work properly - especially on time bound game sequences. Cameras are as hellish as the third game too.
Let's talk puzzles btw. Now, gameplay logic is somewhat inferior and obscure, sure. This is not unheard of from adventure games anyhow. But some puzzles are not only ill-prepared and time consuming, some are plain irrelevant to common sense. There is a scene that George is tied down at the back of an Italian massage parlor and has to escape, for example. Now that was some enforced ACME logic if I've ever seen some! One positive thing that can be said is that hacking puzzles are a decent addition and they are somewhat fun.
At the end of the day, you'll play this game to say that you've played it if you are a Broken Sword fan anyhow. You'll get annoyed, you'll curse, you'll be fed up half way through but you'll play. If you are not though, spare yourself some pain and just find something better to do.

George Stobbart is back, but not of his will. Troubles always look for him anytime, anywhere.
George is working as Lawyer again in his own office... With lack of clients. A girl called Anna Maria will come in his office seeking for his help as she's found a manuscript that might lead to a treasure and she's being followed by some thugs. And the moment those thugs break into the office our adventure begins.
The previous chapter has kind of changed into a thrid person puzzle as the mouse was not used and a 3d engine was introduced, but this chapter reintegrate the use of mouse pointer both for movement and inventory/dialogue options. You can still move with keyboard and maybe it's more comfortable in some "platform" situations. And in those same situations mouse might not be optimized as it should because some hot zones, as ledges you might want to grab onto, are not adequately covered as they should.
Some riddles and puzzles are interesting and tough, I personally love the sections of "hacking" where you have to direct a beam from a point to another by deviating its trajectory with a determined number of elements and at the same time avoiding other elements. Other puzzles might be not so logical as it may look forcing some sessions of trial and error without any idea of what you're doing.
While some characters are well defined or just ok, many others are kind of... caricatures which after a while might result being funny... In some cases.
The engine is again 3d, and this time looks smoother and more realistic than the cartoon-style engine from the previous chapter, and, honestly, I appreciate this news.

Rating:  10/10  Great Game!
Lighting Returns is by far the best RPG I've experienced. Your first playthrough will be difficult and slightly frustrating. The game doesn't hold your hand. It throws you into the world giving you five days to complete the five main quests and tells you to Have Fun!
Discovery is up to the player. After the initial quest tutorial, the game opens up and allows you to go where you please. You can begin anyone of the main quests in any order. This game offers so much freedom. It's not linear. Take on any challenge when you feel ready. Because the game doesn't hold your hand, I'd recommend studying a LR:XIII Guide or Youtube if you get stuck. If you're the type of player who wants to figure out things through discovery, you'll love this game. It tells you nothing. So it's up to the player to find answers.
Lighting Return is fully customizable. Complete quests in any order you like. Customize Lighting's attack & defense skill as you like. You can even customize Lighting's look and color scheme to fit you individual liking. Change her outfits, colors, and/or add adornments. She is 'your' Lighting. Make her look how you want her to look. You can also customize Lighting to your playstyle. You can build Lighting as a Mage, Melee, Tank, or anything in-between.
The world is beautiful. Each area is filled with detail and immersive. Lots of NPC's to talk with and each area is filled with quests. There is always something to do when not doing the main missions. Unfortunately, Side Quests are somewhat required if you want to increase your attack/defensive levels. On this note, the game gets much harder as time continues.
Lighting Returns is the best PS4 to PC port I've seen to date. Much better than Final Fantasy XIII-2 port. FF XIII-2 is a train wreck on PC. So if you're coming off the sequel, Lighting Returns will run like a dream PC rigs. My rig can comfortably play Lighting Returns at 60 fps. On another side note: the game doesn't offer a full range of pc customization option. I'd say most players with decent pc specs will be able to run this game at full settings, 60 fps. The game run really well and doesn't hog any system resources.
Lighting Returns story is a Hot Mess. You'll need to have played Final Fantasy XIII-2 to "somewhat" understand what the hell is going on. The only thing holding the story together are the voice acting and presentation. Character Development and narrative are the strongest points of the game.
TL;DR Overall: Great game. Great Characters. Wonderful narrative, horrible story. Great combat. Lots of customization. Lots to do in the way of side quests & upgrade system. Best PC port in the FF XIII series. Lighting is best waifu.  The most OVERLOOKED Final Fantasy.  10/10

BOOR is a unique puzzle game that has a very familiar feel to some others.
While the idea isn't original, the gameplay is fluent and polished!

A really nice and well designed game. Simple but effective art and mechanics, decent music and animation. The puzzles require thought but not obnoxious stop-and-think-for-five-minutes-then-spend-another-five-trying-to-get-it-to-work; in general it is just a swell game.
The only real problem with the puzzles of the main game itself is that some of them do not kill the player if they make a mistake, but the puzzle doesn't reset on its own. So players have to get themselves killed or reset the level through the menu to try again which is both repetitious and immersion breaking. There also isn't any way to tweak the audio levels, and controller vibration also has no off-switch.
It is cool that the game has boss fights, but they are the weak point of the game as a whole. The bosses are just survival gauntlets, they attack in the same sequence everytime, and they aren't very challenging. They are thus just about staying alive, and if the player gets hit once they have to restart the whole thing. And since the bosses sometimes throw out unexpected new changes in their pattern, and they get more difficult as the fight goes on, it makes it very hard to beat most of the bosses without mandatory repetitious resets. It is too the point where most of the bosses require the player to know ahead of time what to do. It also isn't very great that the primary gimmick the player has really is useless in most of the boss fights, and trying to use it often actually makes things more complicated.
The final area of the game and the final boss are also so, ridiculously unenjoyable that honestly the player should just stop after the fourth boss. The final area is basically the classic L33T puzzle-platforming game. Trial and error, everything gets reset if you make one mistake, everything requires tedious amounts of accuracy, players need to learn the specific ways and quirks of the mechanics without any direction or teaching, there's no leniency at all and players are expected to get through several minute long screens without failing once or it's all reset. The final boss is also everything the other bosses are, but worse. Lengthy, repetitious attack patterns that are always the same; the attacks either aren't challenging at all or are too challenging. The boss throws out attacks that require the player to already know what the attack is otherwise they'll likely die because the player needs to get ready preemptively to respond to it, which means almost mandatory failure. And for some reason the entire game frozen for several minutes and became inoperable in the middle of the fight as well.
Great well priced and well designed game, save for the bosses but it isn't too bad with them, it's mostly just unfortunate that the developer thought that amping the difficulty to absurd heights in the final area and boss what you're supposed to do for the climax of the game. The game would have been infinitely more memorable and enjoyable if it retained it's moderate, fair difficulty up until the end instead of throwing out straight up throat punches every second of the final section and boss to the point where it's honestly better to just not play it. That entire portion of the game really ruins the overall image and memory of it.
Basically, stop playing after the fourth boss. It seriously isn't worth it.

After I beat BOOR, I thought long and hard about how to write this review.
I personally believe that a game should be judged by its own merit. On the flip side of that, there are MANY puzzle/platformers that BOOR is rubbing shoulders with. Now depending on which side you find yourself landing on may affect your decision to purchase this game.
BOOR is a Puzzle/platformer along the same lines as the famous Limbo/Braid. Taking visual queues from one of my favorite games, Monochroma. You play a small child in a futuristic paradise called Eden. A colony of sorts, where things have gone terribly wrong thanks to an artificial intelligence that calls itself BOOR. Our heroic girl has an amazing ability that she can multiply herself for a limited time. She will have to use this gift as she awakens in a mysterious place filled with lasers/robots and assorted death traps.
Gameplay itself is rather simple. Not too many buttons to fuss with and simple responsive controls. You will find yourself wishing that the little girl could move a bit faster, but I never found there was an issue of delay. You can jump, and multiply. That’s about it. Occasionally you will find a door or switch that requires you to flip by pressing one of the directional buttons. Basic goal is just keep going right until the end.
Moving on to the meat of the game, lets talk about the puzzles. BOOR has an incredible and addictive flow to how the game progresses. You complete puzzle rooms and get tidbits of story all the while progressing towards a boss.  I have played quite a few of these types of games, so I didn’t have any trouble with the puzzles. Mostly they are simple and logical and do lean on the easy side. While the ability to multiply is a rather simple mechanic, BOOR does use it to a great extent in many different ways. Having you sacrifice clones, press multiple switches, and fool your enemies as to where you are.
BOOR does a solid job of raising the ante and introducing different environmental hazards. From robots with giant laser rifles or turrets with heat seeking rockets. You may only have one power but you use your enemies as a power against themselves. This idea is highly prevalent throughout the game. There is even an achievement for having enemies shoot each other. You must be aware of your own character, the clone, and what your enemies are doing, which leads to some tricky moments.
Then you have the boss fights. These I had a bit of a love/hate relationship with, as they are super simplistic. All the bosses have a pattern that they follow to be defeated. The only reason you find yourself dying is because the pattern changes little by little as the fight progresses. It’s more about just standing in the right spot at the right time then anything skill related. Which means you might just die simply cause you didn’t know what was going to happen next.
Throw in the fact you die in one shot and have to repeat every boss fight from the beginning and it can lead to some repetitive moments. Nonetheless, they are a welcome aspect that does break things up from being a slog of puzzle after puzzle. As a side objective there are hidden collectibles in the levels as well. The collectibles are just that, and don’t really change or add anything to the game.
Lastly, the developer on the Steam page says the game has eighty levels, which I can’t really comment on. The game doesn’t number the rooms you are in and to be honest I didn’t feel like there was really eighty puzzles more than just eighty rooms to the game in total. I could be wrong mind you. You are welcome to count.
The visuals of BOOR are perhaps what impressed me most about this title. BOOR has a minimalist approach using shades of grey, black and red. It uses these colors to create an impressive tone and startling scenes. Quite a bit of detail can be seen in most areas of the game and even in the backgrounds. While certain areas of the game are beautiful and majestic, others are industrial, cold, full of robots, sprockets, and steel. I would’ve like to seen more open areas for the art to truly shine but most of the time you’re plunged in the depths of a factory setting, solving puzzles.
Overall character design and level design are done well especially for its simple aesthetics. Despite the puzzles leaning on the easy side they are designed well. I didn’t find any bugs, mistakes, or issues of any kind during my time with BOOR. Graphically, I have very little complaints other than it is disturbing no human being has pupils in this game. Makes it seem like everyone is wearing glasses. This is especially odd given that all the robots have pupils. Another minor detail is that death is always the same no matter what hits you. Some of the fun of puzzle/platformers is watching the main character die in a horrific ways. BOOR just has you fly back on to the ground even if a missile hits you.
Another area that I do have a bit of gripe with is BOOR’s soundtrack. It is very repetitive and did begin to grate on my ears especially during boss fights. This could be chalked up to personal preference but there is an option to turn it off. It just becomes super hectic during boss fights and very distracting. In other areas of the game the music is just fine.  Certain sound effects were way super loud for some reason as well. Anytime you would read dialogue I had to remove my head phones as the noise became overwhelming. Sound sliders would’ve been very welcome for these types of situations but unfortunately there are none.
You are looking at about a four to five hour game in total. Perhaps longer or shorter depending on your skill with these types of games. Sadly, the game lacks a bit of replay value as it is a once and done type of deal. This is why I suspect there is only one save file for you in the game. I am fine with this as the game doesn’t overstay its welcome. BOOR is rather fast paced and I liked that aspect. The game does have controller support but for XBOX controllers only, as my Logitech wasn’t detected. The game does also feature Steam Achievements/Cards.
By the time I finished BOOR I had more questions than I did answers. Whats with the cat jacket? How did I survive that crash? Why can I multiply? The developer definitely leaves it open to the idea of a sequel. I would recommend relaxing when it comes to the story as it is a rather light aspect. Nothing is super concrete other than evil robots. Go.
Like I said at the beginning, based off its own merits BOOR does exactly everything it needs in this genre of games. It’s fun and addictive but there are moments I wish BOOR thought outside the box. There is no stand out feature here that is innovative and makes this a must buy. It’s a solid well made game if you enjoy the genre. It doesn’t re-invent the wheel essentially. Coming in at €4.99/$4.99/£3.99 I can easily say it’s a safe purchase, coming far below the usual indie standard. This is more than a fair price and I recommend this game to anyone who loves the aforementioned games.

It's got good gameplay, but the busy visuals get in the way.
Rather than the graphic design complementing the gameplay by offering useful information in a stylish way, you have a psychedelic blur that exists only to be colorful. Because of this, the gameplay, which is designed to be challenging in a good way, ends up being combined with the additional challenge of deciphering the locations, speeds, and hitboxes of the actual game elements from amidst all of the colorful noise. It's like if someone made a WMP visualization and then someone else separately made a game and they put them together without discussing anything.
To put it another way, if Tetris were made in the same way as Dyad, the falling "blocks" would be indestinct bubbles without definied edges, the background would be a visualization of colors similar to those of the "blocks", the blocks wouldn't snap to a grid, and the whole playing area would have a constant rippling visual effect so that even if the tiles did have columns, you wouldn't be able to tell quite which column they were in at any given time.
And here's a video demo of me explaining this:
All that said, Dyad isn't bad, and there's fun to be had here if you can get used to mentally separating the gameplay bits from the pretty color bits. But I wouldn't recommend it either.

This is a challenging Choplifter clone, with wonderfully simple controllers.
Nowadays, voxel graphics are pretty generic but in this game, the art style lends itself to the game. Stylistically, this is a super simple game. You pilot a helicopter, you save POWs and lost soldiers, and sometimes haul equipment back to the base. You only need two button: left and right keys on a keyboard, and left bumper and right bumper on a controller.
As far as challenge is concerned, there's a lot. Apart from 25 levels of rescues, you need to finesse your way through trees, water, and caves. And if you really want to be hardcore, you can collect 5 dog tags that are littered through each level.
One big highlight of this came, though, is the low spec requirements. I've been able to play this on the lowest end hardware I have at an output of 1080p, and that's on an 3-year-old HP Stream 11 running on a Celeron processor with integrated graphics and 2GB of RAM.
Some people might want more of a story, but this is really just an arcade game that would have, in another era, gleefully eaten your coins. If you're an older gamer who wants to instantaneouly pick up and play, but still want a challenge, than Dustoff Heli Rescue is the game for you.

WazHack is a traditional roguelike. What does that mean?
-You can only save the game for the sole purpose of stopping now and continuing later. You can't load a save if things go south.
-If your character dies, it stays dead. Your only option is to start over.
-The dungeons are built randomly. Each run is subtly different.
-The game is
. You will die. A lot. A whole lot.
-The game doesn't hold your hand at all. It won't ask questions if you tell it you want to cast fireball where you're standing. It'll let you, and then it'll kill you with your own fireball.
For better or worse, WazHack makes no effort to disguise the fact that it takes heavy inspiration from NetHack, the roguelike that put roguelikes on the map (if Rogue itself didn't, anyway). A lot of mechanics are shared between the two, so Nethack players should feel mostly at home.
That said, there are subtle differences as well, which NetHack veterans will pick up on and perhaps promptly get killed by. If you're one of the elite few that actually
NetHack, and yearn for the days when you didn't know every single trick in the game, definitely give WazHack a try.

When I saw that this game received mixed reviews, I still kept my hopes high. After all, Broken Sword 3 got mixed reviews, and I enjoyed it, despite being trampled by boxes ;).  Then I played it. I will say this: I'm glad I played it. I'm a Broken Sword fan; therefore, I must play the whole series. If you are a Broken Sword fan, you probably should play it. It doesn't get everything wrong, it just doesn't get enough right. I feel that Broken Sword 3 was much stronger in terms of story and graphics. Anyhow, lets get to the positives of this game before I load you with the negatives.

First of all, the characters are still great. George Stobbart is still wonderful. We have the same voice actor, and his delivery is great. We get to see some "guest star" characters from previous Broken Sword games, which I always enjoy. There are a few new characters that are amusing, and well done all around. Also (slight spoiler, but good grief she's on the cover), we have a new heroine! Her name Anna Marie and I personally wish she wasn't there because Nico Collard is the best. However, she is there, and she does a good job at keeping you guessing about character loyalties, overrall game plot, etc. I love the sountrack. There are portions that sound like the regular Broken Sword standard soundtrack (which is great), and then there are the special portions. There is a stage in the game where Nico is in Phoenix, Arizona. Yeah...more on that later. While she is there, there is a great guitar soundtrack that really enhances the atmosphere. There is a spy soundtrack in a section where George is doing a covert operation. Very cool. Also, the controls are much better. I didn't like how BS3 only used the keyboard. Here, you use both mouse and keyboard, pointing where you want to go or look at with mouse and hold control to run. So the positives are the characters, the music, and the script. Now the negatives.

First of all, the story is horrible. For me, it boarders on heresy. In each BS game, we are dealing with an ancient artifact or technology that will bring about the end of the world. This time around, the ancient artifact is The Ark of the Covenant. Now, if your mind jumped to Indiana Jones and Raiders of the Lost Ark...you would be on the right track. (Spoiler!) (Spoiler!) George Stobbart is our Indiana Jones, the "good guys" are the Mafia, and the Nazis are played by...high officials in The Catholic Church. Nico Collard and Anna Marie take turns being Marion.  If this plot doesn't sound absurd, I don't know what does.
.  Horrible isn't it? The game really doesn't look finished either. There are instances where you look on a large area map, and there are indentations in the map that make you think that you will go to said place once the story opens up to that area. Some of the places show up, and some don't. Seriously, the look and feel of this game is like Nico's hair: messy and unfinished. The ending is incredibly rushed and depressing. The ending sequence throws logic out the window, since all the characters you helped in the game somehow find the secret entrance and come to your aid, and it's never explained how. Apparently its easy to find the secret chambers in the Vatican. You know how you had so many places to visit in the first three games, not to mention hidden temples and stuff? Even in Broken Sword 3? Well, here you get to start in NY, go to Syria, then Phoenix, Arizona, then lastly, a small section of Rome including supposed hidden offices of The Vatican. Thats it. Four. There are no cut scenes. The game just puts widescreen bars into view, which lets you know this is a cut scene, with no change in graphics. I'm not a stickler on graphics, but they should be at least on par with the previous 3D title. This takes a step backwards. Now the character gripe. While Anna Marie is not a pointless character, Broken Sword has always been about George and Nico. Nico doesn't show up till halfway through the game. She is a side character in her own game series, which ticks me off. I'm sorry if the negatives seem to be disjointed. To sum it up: The story is ridiculous, the game looks unfinished and ends rather sadly (trust me when I say that it was not necessary).

So should you buy it? If you are a BS fan, I think you should still play it. If the storyline strikes you with  the "its so bad its funny" vibe, or if you don't think it a ridiculous premice, then you should play it. The script works well within the plot. For all my complaints, I'm glad I played it. It would have annoyed me if I hadn't. Also, I got this game on sale. Knowing what I know now, I'm really glad I did. This is definitely the weakest game in the series. I hope for a better time with Broken Sword 5: The Serpent's Curse.

This game seems to be receiving a lot of hate.
Is it well deserved? Well... yes... and no.
This is definitely the worst of all series. But it is still quite interesting and atmospheric.
The one thing, that massively lets thie game down is its puzzles. You would think, that difficult puzzles in a game, dedicated to puzzle-solving is a good thing. And you would be 100% right.
But in this game, puzzles can be hard to slove not due to their intended complexity, but due to them being illogical, due to the unclear goals that should be achieved, lack of information or downright stupidity.
Sometimes the most unobvious actions need to be completed, to progress with the story. Like showing one guy an object, which you found much earlier in the game and which has no connection whatsoever to this particular guy - not even a hint that it should be shown to anyone. And this is just one example of many - I could go on all night, but don't want to post spoilers.
Let's just say, that in previous three games, I got hopelesly stuck and needed to use walkthrough only once. That's ONCE in THREE games. In this game, I am about half way through and already had to google the solutions to quests about 5 times. And they not even difficult quests - just one tiny extra bit of information would make them fun and enjoyable to solve. But the game does not give you this info and you're getting stuck - going back and forth between locations, talking to everyone, clicking on everything and getting p****d off - because you still can't find the solution.
Also - the game feels unfinished and/or unpolished. There are random locations on the map, that you never able to unlock and travel to and random objects in the world, that are there for no reason. They don't give you info, they don't help you solve puzzles, they not even there for laughs (like some objects in previous titles) - they are just there, so your protagonist can approach... let's say - book on a table, and say in loud monotonous voice - "It's the book"... Wow - thanks, Captain Obvious! I would have never guessed, if you had not told me... So yeah - in comparison to other titles in the series, this game sucks harder, than any German actress I've ever seen.
Why do I still recommend it then? Well - because it's the Broken Sword game and I am a bit of a fan.
Also because:
- The atmosphere is still there. Alike Broken Sword 3 - it's in 3D, so world does feel a bit empty, but somehow it still manages to be quite charming.
- George, Nico and some of the old characters return, bringing back the memories.
- The usual dark/ridiculous sence of humour is still there.
- Story isn't that bad.
- Those quests that have any logic to them are still quite interesting to solve.
That about sums it up.
So... In general, the verdict is as follows:
If you are fan of the Broken Sword, then by all means get this game for your collection (wait for sale). And if you are not, you are much better off playing the first two games, becoming a fan and only then getting Broken Swords 3 and 4 (wait for big sale).
It's not bad a deal if you're following the story from the beginning and spend 2-3 bucks on this one.

Let's just put this out there: this is a super flawed gem of a game. I wouldn't recommend buying this at regular price, unless you are a big fan of exploration and can look past some flaws. At $25 or less, it is worth the purchase as there is a good game in there.
At the point of this review, I've put right at 12 hours into the game so there us a lot i haven't experienced yet. But I have had a good time overall. I really like the aesthetics of the game. It looks great and runs smoothly (although, I have read the game had performance issues at first launch). There is plenty to keep you entertained if you like exploring and like to do things at your own pace. There are points of interest all over the place to check out, most of which reward you in some way. For example, finding a crashed ship that is a big upgrade in inventory space has been a highlight of the game so far for me.
That, unfortunately, leads to one of my annoyances with the game. Inventory management is, at least st this point, a central focus. There are items and materials to collect literally everywhere, nearly alk of which is usefully or valuable. Juggling your inventory was a driving force for me to find more space. Not a game killer, but needlessly annoying and clunky.
Another issue I've had is the game does a poor job tipping you off to some basic mechanics of the game. A prime example is massage popup to tell you what button to hit to execute certain actions. Let's say you're in position to hit your hyperdrive. A message will appear in the corner saying "hit (x) to activate hyperdrive." Unforunately (x) is not the actual button you need to high. Instead, it has the hyperdrive symbol and yoj gave to go into the control options to find the corresponding button. Again, not a game killer, but you can see the trend. And I would also recommend reading tips online before getting started so you can get a better handle on what the game forgets to mention.
So, let's break it down:
Pros
Explorer's dream
Lots of rewards for doing stuff (talk to every NPC)
Looks nice!
Runs smoothly
No shortage of things to keep you occupied
Cons:
Irritating inventory management early on
Poor job of teaching game mechanics
Bad in-game tutorial
Overall, I've really had a good time with this game. I can see a lot to enjoy and suck my time. I just wish I didn't have to scrape the tarnish off to enjoy.

Great 2D platform game with puzzles. The game is not intended to tell you a very deep story, but i don't think it will take advantage of its utensils: BOOR is left in a tiny attempt of what could have become.

A human colony built away from Earth seems like a nice place to live. Where nothing goes wrong as everyone lives to better the colony. But what happens when you add something nonhuman.
You play a little unnamed girl who wakes up while a security system, Boor, starts to eliminate the humans in the colony. Tasked to save the people, travel through Eden to find and defeat Boor as you encounter twists and turns. Maybe along the way, you can hear the background of Eden and Boor by interactions between you and other characters.
BOOR plays like any other puzzle platformer. Platform your way through the puzzles imbedded within each level through a total of 85 sectioned off to four acts. As you continue, bits of information about Eden or Boor will be relayed to you by others between key levels.
The puzzles start out simple, getting you used to how they will usually work and how your character and enemies move. Introducing the mechanic if your grey clone being controllable for a limited time, unless you pick up red pellets, to help in sticky situations. Won't be able to jump back? A grey door blocking your way? Use your clone! This learning period happens during the first act which acts as a tutorial.
As you progress more new gimmicks begin to show up. Bringing in more opportunities to clone, portals, homing missiles, sentries, and more for you to solve. Some needing to be so precise, a second off can make or break it for you. While these puzzles are mostly easy, they get harder as the puzzles get longer. Taking death after death as you try to figure out how to get past it.
After making some progress, bosses will occasionally cross your path. These are straightforward, all using a pattern based attack system that leads to you just needing to survive. Dodge and eventually an attack will go against them or run into something. Using small details to show which stage of damage they are in. Remember the old three times the charm cliché? BOOR uses this so a boss sequence is not too long. A single hit will spell disaster, forcing you to try all over again no matter how close you were to defeating it. This can be very annoying and I do wish there was some leeway with damage when up against bosses.
While this is not voice acted, the opening sequence was done beautifully. Once after, the soundtrack takes over, bringing in a wave of calmness as you travel your way into Eden for the first time. It does change, but it changes very slightly by either changing the speed, tones, or notes. So when you make it inside, the music changes as the stakes become higher. The bosses have a slight change that you can entirely miss, but it does try to have each boss have their own sound.
The sound effects are not unpleasant to the ear, though the dialogue effect can be grating after a while. There were also some areas I thought needed music or some sort of sound effect as it was quiet.
It cannot be helped to think of BOOR's art style adorable. Mostly having a simplistic design with details added when needed. Reds and greys, along with a film grain, to give off the feel of an otherworldly environment; with skulls scattered to show the deaths that has taken place. The humans have a long body, which looks weird by the little girl, and greyish-white eyes.  It is weird that the humans don't have pupils, but it does work with their design. While Boor and it's security bots is represented with eyes that are strangely human-like. Though it does give it the feel of being watched as the pupils follow your every move. One of my favorite moment was a bunch of screens coming down revealing eyes.
BOOR ran pretty well, but I had trouble with the speed of the character. Without changing the settings the character walks pretty slow, but changing seems to make it too fast or fluctuate between the two. Other than this, everything worked fine. Though it is noteworthy to say that you cannot take screenshots.
Taking around two to four hours to complete depending on how fast you can solve puzzles, BOOR can be replayed for multiple reasons. Cogs have been hidden throughout Eden that goes to an unknown device. Finding all the cogs, around 17-ish, does not change anything within the story, but you need at least five cogs to get all achievements.
Another reason is for the arcade games that appear in the middle of BOOR. You can play as long as you can on them, but do not continue if you still want to. Three games are available along with three achievements to go with them. Get 1,000 points in each to get the last batch of keys that is not story related. It starts out slow but quickens as you continue. If you go past to finish the game you will have to restart all over again. I wish there was a way to go back and play the arcades, and if there is one I do not know about it.
+ Adorable art style
+ The use of story telling by character interactions
+ Polished, does what it set out to do
+/- Soundtrack
+/- Unanswered questions
- Difficulty spikes during bosses
While BOOR does nothing original, it does not have to. Using old gimmicks to their advantage and focusing on getting the main aspects right makes this game stand out. While it does have downfalls in some areas, I can still say this is a great game. The price also makes it a safe purchase, not making it too expensive that the length is too small for people. With the open ended ending, I do see a possibility of a dlc or a sequel as many questions remain unanswered.

With how many puzzle platformers that there are on Steam there are two main ways for your game to stand out. Your game could have some unique mechanic that other games haven't used or you can do a great job using the mechanics that your game does have. BOOR falls into the latter category.
When I look at BOOR it doesn't really do anything that I haven't seen done in other puzzle platformers. BOOR does a really good job using the mechanics it does have though to make good puzzles which is what is most important for a puzzle platformer. I found BOOR to be quite enjoyable due to its' clever puzzle design.
While BOOR is good at what it is, it has two problems in my opinion.
First the game is quite easy. Outside of a couple of the later puzzles, I was able to figure out most of the puzzles almost immediately.
The other problem is that the game is kind of short. I think most players should be able to finish the game within 3.5-4.5 hours.
Overall I enjoyed my time with BOOR. If you don't really care for puzzle platformers it probably won't be for you. If you like puzzle platformers and don't really mind that the game is kind of easy I would recommend picking up BOOR.

Alright, so you're thinking of purchasing BOOR but you're not sure if you will get your money's worth. You've stumbled across this review and you need help making this crucial life decision, I'm here to help!
BOOR is a puzzle platformer in the same vein as Super Meat Boy, Braid and Limbo. There are four acts in the game, each with a boss at the end and several levels inbetween. I counted around 85 levels to this game and in the two hours I spent with this game, I think I can safely give a good verdict.
The level designs are fun, with new obstacles and powers being implemented as you progress through the respective areas. You'll start out with some simple puzzles that are easily solveable, but trust me, it gets tougher. Some rooms require precision that will have you being forced to restart levels quite a bit. There are mechanics such as portals which take you to new locations, sentry robots that can shoot blocks, elevation tubes, gravity flippers and my least favourite, homing missile cannons. The missiles must be used to home in on you and break blocks in their path, but the issue is that the missiles fire and move too quickly to give you any leeway. Some stages in the latter half of the game also go on for quite some time and it's irritating when you make it past a tough section in the stage only to fail at the next part, getting yourself sent back to the start of the stage. Some forms of mini-checkpoints would have been great.
On top of the levels themselves, your protagonist has a few key features. One, they can multiply themselves into two entities. While you are split apart, you become a grey form of your character which can move around and interact with the environment as you wish, with a limited timer before you're forced back into your main body. There are these power pellets that reset the timer for your clone though, creating some interesting puzzles.
The main selling point of this game is definitely going to be the art-style and the gameplay. It's a call back to some old games like the Exit Path flash games and you'll certainly enjoy the various environments of Eden you'll play through. The sound design is fairly lacking however, some cutscenes have no sounds to accompany them, making them feel unimportant, while the music during boss encounters doesn't really give me a sense of dread, it barely changes.
The boss encounters are pattern based boss battles where you get attacked by the same attacks with slight changes each phase. This is fine until you die for the fifth time and have to redo everything you've done up until the third phase, which can take roughly 5 minutes. Die enough times and the bosses become a rather horrific time sync. Having an extra health point or a way to make these encounters less tedious would have been more interesting, but as of right now, you can really only brute force your way through them. That being said, I'd say the only disappointing boss was the final boss. And even then, it's still pretty good.
For a simple puzzle platformer, BOOR does a lot of things right and a lot of things wrong, it's not perfect but it is charming in it's own way! Would I recommend this game myself? Yes, I would. It may not be the best game ever, but it's a fun time sink into some fun mechanics. And with the ambigious ending of the story, could we be seeing a BOOR 2 or BOOR DLC? Who knows, this could be the next hit franchise.
Hopefully this review has helped you with your thoughts and hopefully you can see if this game is right for you. I've barely mentioned story and that's because it's fun to experience without knowing too much. Just be aware there are a few moments where the english is slightly broken, but it's minor and not much of an inconvenience.

This game offers some clever / cute voxel / pixel style designs, with great audio design and very simplistic gameplay. The controls of the game consist of left on the keyboard arrow keys or right on the arrow keys. These control which direction your chopper is flying, and alternating between pressing both (simultaneously or not) will affect your height and landing as you drop off rescued infantry or line up your automatically-firing gunfire toward enemy tanks, trucks, and pillboxes.
The sound design of the game is particularly well-done with explosions, rockets, miniguns, and radio chatter all coming through crystal clear while an orchestral, epic-sounding soundtrack makes what's taking place onscreen seem exciting. The game seems to do a decent enough job mixing up the level layout variety, including one where you have to navigate a narrow cavern to emerge from the other side of a hill and rescue stranded infantry, before transporting them back through the cavern and to your home base landing pad, but the missions seem to never break from this repeated formula of 'pick Item X up and drop it off at the base' and it begins to get predictable and kind of tedious quickly with much (all??) of the game's challenges taking place at or near the same general area.
At the end of the day the game is incredibly simplistic and while it functions and delivers mostly what it aims for it's also a title which I can't help but feel like I've already done everything I will be doing throughout the entirety of the game within the first 3 levels. This may fit its 'pick up and play briefly' design, but I found myself getting a bit bored of navigating the same-looking areas to do the same task (pick up infantry and drop them off, or crates in place of infantry) repeatedly. It presents what it does well, but what is present is very simplistic.

There's something I've always found appealing about really simple games with strong gameplay.  Dustoff Heli Rescue checks a lot of boxes on my “Good Indie Game” list by being able to teach me the mechanics in seconds but seriously challenging me with executing them well enough to complete objectives down the line.  Along with that, while it can be completed in a matter of a few hours, it provides a reasonably steady ramp up of difficulty – keeping it from becoming too boring or too hard.
Now if you've been around  for a while, you might be aware that there are quite a few helicopter games out there that have you swooping around picking up friendlies while you blow up enemies.  Choplifter came out in 1982 and there have been tons of sequels, clones, and similar games since, including Dustoff.  You'll be navigating one of your three types of helicopters with a choice of three different weapons as you unlock both through the levels of the game.  Of which there are 25 to complete.  They'll have you battling against tanks, machine guns mounted on trucks and bunkers, and missile launchers of all sorts while you contend with uneven terrain, trees, and scraping your way through narrow tunnels.  One of the most challenging elements of the game is the constantly changing wind featured on some levels, making any sort of precise movement nearly impossible.  Surmounting these obstacles leaves you with one of two main of objectives, picking up allies on the ground by landing or hovering close, or picking up large vehicles with a hook.  Both of which will have you hauling them back to the base to be dropped off.
One of the more interesting parts Dustoff is the control scheme.  Flying involves only two buttons, left and right arrow (by default).  I quickly changed these to A and D because I wouldn't want other keys on my keyboard to get too much work.   Pressing left will make you fly left, pressing right will make you fly right, and pressing both will make you fly up.  Releasing both lets you fall.  What makes this interesting is that if forces the player to really focus on precise tapping and holding of these two keys to maneuver in a way that keeps you alive.  It's immediately intuitive but never easy enough to make the gameplay feel in any way passive.  Not long after the start you're given your first weapon, which by default auto aims and fires.  I found that I had to change this to manual to have any real success, yet it also brings me to one of my issues with the game.
Dustoff has some exceedingly frustrating issues.  The 2.5D (as in not quite 2D or 3D) design has you flying in two dimensions, but enemy targets very often exist slightly in the foreground or background.  When aiming, to hit them you're required to put the cursor directly on the object and hope that the gun orients itself in such a way that it fires to that foreground or background area.  This can be very inconsistent and had me raging several times, especially toward the end of the game as things become more challenging.  Another issue that I encountered is that controls from time to time would not respond as I expected.  I would sometimes end up flying downward instead of to a side or going up much faster than I should have been (seemingly tied to camera movement) and those moments can be devastating – since crashing in to anything usually results in death and requires a full mission restart.  Also, a more minor issue but something I found odd, the game is extremely loud without any internal volume level control.  I had to cut my normal system volume in half to make it tolerable.
Dustoff Heli Rescue provides a few hours of solid entertainment for a small investment (at present the Steam sale has it at 51 cents) and without forcing you to spend much of that time at all learning how to play.  It has a few issues and a repetitive soundtrack, but it was a surprisingly enjoyable experience that got me to complete the whole game rather than give up the moment I found a level too hard.  If you're someone looking for a simple game to eat up some free time for the price of a handful of sold steam trading cards, this is one you should definitely pick up.

I got No Man's Sky late, only with update 1.3 as I was waiting for more content to become available. The game is a "walking simulator" to 30%, resource and inventory management making further 30% with some voluntary fight/crafting/exploration/flight/story elements to add it up to the total.
It is great if you are able to approach it with a mindset of "I have a stressful job, I am happy to spend time strolling around, looking at landscapes, plants and critters and do a bit of quest and gathering and slowly collect the words of the languages". IF you are looking to calm down, decelerate after a long day and enjoy the sceneries I can very much recommend it. It is a game where you make your own goals.
Mine are:
- collect critter pictures (it is like earthly nature, discovering unique ones needs a bit attention to detail and patience but there are MANY really odd creations out there)
- find an earth like lush planet with no or very few aggressive critter but plenty of structures to make a home
- manage to get the portal system running
- find planets for all the special resources that have no insane toxicity and generate the portal ID's for those
- build an extensive greenhouse with all those plant based resources possible
- have a freighter and visit more galaxies
- do the lore stories
- manage to get all the languages fluent
That is plenty to do and I take it slow and enjoy it the same as I enjoy cooking or gardening or even watching fish in an aquarium.
But if you approach it as a premade-content-with-frequent-rewards thing like most story driven games, you will not be happy here...

I don't know why there aren't any reviews for this game, but don't let that fool you. If you are a Broken Sword fan, you should definitely try this one, especially if you liked BS3.
Graphics/Atmosphere: The Angel of Death continues to use the 3D perspective first established in BS3, but it looks much better. With anti-aliasing turned up, some scenes look almost photo-realistic (except for the lower quality character models). As a result, you really feel like you are in the story.
Story: Like any Broken Sword game, there are some parts that are less believable or even boring. Overall though, it was pretty good. I liked how it tied together plot elements from the previous games. The ending left a lot to be desired however.
Puzzles: Maybe I'm just impatient after playing almost nothing but Broken Sword in the past 2 weeks, but I felt like the puzzles were really hard. There were only a handful of major puzzles that I solved all by myself, for the rest I had to use a walkthrough. A couple in particular were really hard because they were logic puzzles, and after looking at a walkthrough I'm not so sure their logic makes sense.
Overall, this is another good addition to the series and is worth playing. It's long, looks really nice, and is full of surprises. So get ready to see what kind of crazy situations George and Nico find themselves in this time.

Almost every death feels like you could avoid it, every situation is a thinking game, and you sometimes wonder how things could have went if you had done them another way. Because time stops when you do, you can look through your entire inventory and pick out the ability or skill that'll save you, and I've never seen it done so well in a modern game.
This game is a huge story of your personal mishaps as you die numerous times, slowly learning how to the game works (while it changes on you every time).
Sometimes I tried to steal from a shopkeeper, and learned not to mess with them when they shot me down. Several playthroughs later, I send my monkey to steal his weapons and kill him in his sleep with poison.
Other times I ran from ogres and sent my pet to his doom to buy me time, and made it out alive.
You can have some really awesome interactions, I recommend playing for about two hours at least to try this game out and see if you like it (definitely give it a few tries and you'll get why it's so good).

In my eyes, the mark of a good rogue-like is how you feel when you die. The best ones will have you feel one of 3 ways, "That death was epic!", "That death was hilarious!", and "Oh my god if I had used [x] I would have survived". Wazhack provides all three.
From exploding gemstones to traps that turn your dog into a goblin, it delivers a thousand different dangerous, unique, and just downright strange situations.
Positives include:
- Every item can be good or bad, blessed or cursed.
- No two runs are the same.
- I've beaten the game and it's still challenging enough to die within the first 100 feet from time to time.
- Items have many different uses and some things that seem useless can be invaluable, for instance a lamp that makes your hands slippery when rubbed can be used to force a cursed weapon to come off.
- Classes are similar enough that it's easy to switch between them but different enough to keep them feeling unique.
- Some things only make sense when your character is on drugs.
Negatives include:
- Multiplayer, though fun, amounts to seeing a persons avatar as you walk the same dungeon in different worlds. You can trade items and give your partner potions, but while they are dead they will drain your health.
- The tutorial doesn't cover things like "What is AC and how does it keep you not dead?"

This game has not recieved the love it deserves.
The unconvential approach demands that the play buy into the premise and approach of the game's design, and I will admit that the game does not really help you do so. Once I took the time to understand its premise, however, I thoroughly enjoyed it.
The most common critique of the game was the inability to save the game. This game is meant to be replayed, repeatedly to use the try new options, explore new paths, and further discover the story and details hiding in the dark corners. The different endings provide different bits of information, and some interestingly pleasantly experiences, should you take the time to see them through.
I know it's hard to come to terms with, but you are not losing anything by the absence absence of a save feature. Each run is a new complete (and brief) experience. Once the map is familiar, speed runs take about 6 minutes (timed), and the world is not terribly large. It may have taken you a couple of hours to make it through the first to your first (non-suicide) ending, but future attempts do not take long at all, once you know the answers.
This game does not follow the format you're used to. Give it some time, expore the many ways to see the story through, and you will likely find this game a delightfully unique experience.

I own hundreds of games on Steam, and Dustoff Heli Rescue is one of my all time favorites.
This game is a side scroller that uses an extremely simple control scheme of only two buttons. Left, right (A,D). The twist about this side scroller is that you are a helicopter, and the game is as much about vertical control as it is about horizontal.
To move straight up you hold A and D. To go left, you let go of D. To go right, you let go of A. Feathering these two buttons is how you achieve fine control of the helicopter. After a few minutes it feels pretty natural.
I suggest using manual fire mode, it's more fun than the auto-aim/fire. If you go with manual fire mode you will aim and fire the gun with mouse/mouse1.
My guess is that most negative reviews are from controllers, because I could see the controls for this game feeling less intuitive on a controller. If I was using a controller I think I'd have left and right controls on the triggers and I'd have fire on the stick click/depress so I could shoot while aiming.

Having not watched the trailer, the biggest surprise for me was that the game is played in 2d rather than 3d. That is to say you control the left/right movement and also up/down (altitude) and that's it, meaning no third dimension to roam in. So it's an on-rails shooter where I was expecting more of a simulator, arcadish but still. Since it's also on smartphones though, it makes plenty of sense the gameplay is such.
The game itself is addictive. I was tempted to complete everything in one sitting, that's how much fun I was having. War is depicted in a cartoonish and nonjudgmental vein that I like very much. There are two control schemes available which provide varying amounts of frustration. The achievements are not hard at all. For people seeking additional replay value there is an (entirely optional) set of collectibles. The 3 weapons are quite distinct from each other - each is best suited to a particular situation so the first one can remain relevant even in the final missions. All in all, this was pure casual bliss.

The original 1996 DR was one of my favorite games that I played on my first ever PC (bought with my own money :-). Obviously it got me very excited to see that a remake was available for free back in 2012. After installation I just couldn't stop playing, even after I had finished upgrading all my cars I kept on driving online until I got to number one in the online kills category. Then I'd realized that this game was dangerously addictive for me and I suddenly stopped playing it after 3 intense months.
A few years (and a failed SSD) later I wanted to see if my record was still there so I re-installed it again and then I got to see all the bad about this game. My saves were nowhere to be found! Even though the online stats (and level times) were there, my reputation level and everything else was back to zero. And when I started to play the new results weren't added to those I achieved a few years back. Hell, I thought, steam kept the game saves on drive C:, and since that SSD had died on me, I lost everything (not only Death Rally, but many other game saves too). But DR is still crazy good, I allowed myself to have a little more fun, did the offline missions again, built up all my cars and even played a little online. But since my new results hadn't showed up as win and kill stats added to the old ones (and for the only achievement missing - reaching level 42 - I had to start all over again and invest my time and energy for months), I just didn't have to heart to continue. But learning from my mistake, I copied my saves to a safe partition to be able to continue eventually to get that illusive achievement. At least that's what I thought.
Now, another year later I've decided to give it another try. But again, even though the offline stats and cars are still there, the fame level is back to zero! Un-f..cking-belivable! I know, probably I should have used the cloud too, but I'm not entirely convinced it would have helped. Why? Because between last time and now, I had no technical issue with my rig that could have influenced my saves and yet they were still missing! So, be warned.
And by the way, playing online usually means playing by yourself against bots. Very rarely I could find anyone to play with.
Pros: Beautiful, good controls, fantastic athmosphere, nice level design that resembles the great original
Cons: Something weird is happenning to the saves, the offline story mode is very short and pointless

I'll freely admit that going into this game my expectations were low. The reviews had been pretty alarmingly negative across the board, primarily for No Man's Sky failing to live up to its hype. I waited for the game to go on sale for around $20 before I finally decided to take the plunge.
And a lot of the criticisms for the game are totally right. The game lacks depth and, after you start exploring your second and third solar system, it starts feeling really repetative. It suffers from one of the worst cases of Daggerfall syndrome since... well, Daggerfall (procedural generation making the game huge, but bland and shallow).  Space combat is extremely wonky and difficult to control. The story is unbelievably difficult to understand, and guidance is inconsistent. Learning alien languages is so slow that the entire system is a joke.
But that aside, I did have fun for the 10+ hours I put into the game. Exploring your homeworld and creating better exploration gear kept me really engaged. The wild creatures were very interesting and the aliens (especially the Gek and the Korvax) were cool to meet. The environments are gorgeous and fun to mess around in. The life support and hazard shielding meters do well to remind you that you are on a hostile planet. The milestones are a good system to help you move in the right direction.
If you can get this game on the cheap, it's definitely worth a try. As near as I can gather, as soon as you get to Atlas, the interesting part of the game is over. So, don't expect to play it for real long.
