Hope Lake is a short almost-adventure with a number of puzzles, regular hidden object scenes and just enough story to create a bit of mystery.
The game makes a number of good decisions that are not always clearly so. For example, you get a map pointing out next-up locations, and puzzles usually indicate when you're on the right track. While this may appear to make the game too easy, not having those helpers may make the game prohibitively hard. The map quickly expands and forgetting where to go next may well take all of the fun out of the game. Similarly, puzzles come with pretty minimal instructions and while well-enough designed some offer a number of combinations that I don't want to brute-force.
Additionally, the game offers to skip puzzles and you can get hints, I guess for the hidden object segments, faster with an easy difficulty mode.
There are a few downsides to the game.
The game starts off with a kidnapping scene that appears to be filmed with a hand camera, clearly nonsense. Either this was filmed by a person, then why not intervene, or there was no person, then what makes the scene/camera shake?
I was disappointed to not be able to jump to any point in game once I finished it. Instead the game offers to start again from the beginning - which I didn't try. A game as close to linear as this should allow for scene selection.
Then there is minor bs where a hidden objects target isn't this clearly visible key/bow/net but that other one you may not yet have found.
And the mayor BS where you constantly loose items that are clearly reusable. You need a bunch of keys (not only those for locks) and, haha, cutting-edge implements throughout the game about 90% of which wouldn't be necessary if the game didn't decide to deprive you of the early-game crowbar and pocket knife.
Despite those narrative shortcomings and the lack of a scene selector I still had a nice time with the game and recommend Hope Lake.

The FF13 series as a whole (FF13, 13-2 and LR) seems to be one of the most heavily disliked FFs, and though I can understand why in some aspects, I would still definitely recommend this game.
PROS
+ Combat is immersive (it deviates from the traditional pick a move then it executes, instead putting you in more of a real time situation) and feels more like an action RPG than a traditional RPG.
+ Customization; you get a wide variety of outfits to equip Lightning with, which affects important stats such as health, ATB (for those unfamiliar to the FF13 series this is similar to a mana or energy bar that recharges when not used). At any time you are able to equip three outfits for Lightning, which substitute as your party members in traditional RPG games (and from FF13 and 13-2). With the wide variety of outfits available, it's very likely that no two players will have the exact same three outfit setup which really allows you to tailor to your playstyle(s).
+ Story is at times dark but overall provides a satisfactory ending to the FF13 series (at least in my opinion); this can be highly subjective but personally I found the game explored many themes (especially philosophically) quite well (life and death being a prominent one, it also plays with the notion of pseudo-immortality and the effect that would have on humanity). Perhaps the game was never meant to invoke these kinds of thoughts of themes, but it did for me and I can say I enjoyed the story very much.
+ Cutscenes were well done and generally a treat but too few far and in between for me personally.
+ Open world element was great for the first 20 hours but gradually became repetitive (a small nitpick).
+ The time limit; an aspect of the game that many dread (at times I also did, I'll touch on that in the cons section), but it provides a sense of urgency as it should in this game's environment.
+ You get to equip Lightning in whatever outfit you please (some to me are over-the-top but it also serves as fanservice).
+ Good optimization and controller support (running on a 960m was no problem at a steady 60fps).
CONS
- Fighting enemies eventually feels dragged out and repetitive; there will be times when you look to avoid engaging enemies altogether. While the combat system is fresh, enemies appear quite often and the sequence is always the same (look for weak points, hit them with combos to stagger, finish them off). This becomes more of a problem on side quests when you're tasked with retrieving items or delivering a message from one place to another, which for a large chunk don't require combat at all.
- Completing side quests and main quests is the only way to "level up" Lightning; there is no experience point system in LR and fighting monsters only nets you gil (gold) and items/abilities. As mentioned already above, this will at times lead one to wish to avoid combat altogether. Side quests include some interesting stories and are varied enough, but for the most part you'll be doing the same things (fighting monsters to collect x items, finding items, delivering messages).
- Character development is on the weak side (Snow, Fang, Vanille and Sazh all have their own sub-stories but these could have been much further developed).
- Hope constantly being in your ear can be quite annoying, to the point where his dialogue constantly gets cut off as you enter into combat or talk to people.
- The time limit, while effective at times, can simply be abused by using an ability to freeze time; while abilities cost an alternate point system called EP, this can be recharged insanely fast by fighting monsters (though it charges slower with weaker monsters).
OTHER COMMENTS
- Characters, their development and impact may not be as strong as in some previous FF games (FFX comes to mind) but is satisfactory and enjoyable overall.
- Moderate replayability as there are a few features that are only unlocked after starting a New Game+.
TL;DR - Overall, the story seems to be hit-or-miss with people (it was a hit for me), but due to that and a fresh combat system, I would definitely recommend this game. I would rate this at least an 8/10.

The basic rundown : You play as Lightning, who has been tasked to save souls from the dying world, and has been given a few godly powers to help. You start the game with 7 days to go until the end of the world, and have to extend the world's remaining lifetime by saving souls. You save souls by completing quests, which convieniently also rewards you with money, stats, and cosmetic items.
The world is divided up into four major areas, and there are 5 main questlines you need to complete in order to buy the world the time it needs. There are also around 60 sidequests and 80 "MMO-type quests" (basically bringing items back to a billboard) to help you get stronger. It is worth noting that the only way to get stronger is through completing quests. You do not level up, and do not earn experience or stats from fighting enemies.
Let's address the elephant in the room now :
.
All throughout the game, a timer ticks down, to remind you that the end of the world is near. Each in-game day lasts 24 real-time minutes. The timer stops during battle, cutscenes and menus, and you start the game with 7 days, and can earn up to 14 by completing quests. You only need to earn 13 days to complete the game. Yet my first playthough took me about 40 hours.
If you're wondering why the math doesn't check out, it's because of a nifty ability called Chronostasis. This ability allows you to stop the doomsday timer for around 90 seconds at the cost of 1 EP, which is a resource you earn by fighting monsters. The cost of chronostasis is so low that you can abuse it to no end. I had completed pretty much every quest in the game, except for a few super-boss related ones by day 5 thanks to Chronostasis, to give you an idea on how generous the game is with it's time limit.

The global timer is a poorly implemented mechanic, simply because the only way Square found to make it tolerable was to add another mechanic which entirely circumvents it.
Now let's talk about the other thing that sets Lightning Returns apart from the ordinary JRPG : The battle system.
You have three "schematas" at your disposition, each schemata being a loadout of 1 armor(called "garbs" by the game,  some garbs are more on the swimsuit than armor side), 2 accessories, 1 weapon, 1 shield and 4 abilities. Abilities are dropped by monsters, or found in chests, and can be upgraded by fusing abilities of the same type together. You can freely switch between your three schematas during battle, and each schemata has it's own ATB bar, independant from the other two's. This gives you an apparent lot of strategic freedom, unfortunately the majority of abilities, garbs and even weapons are garbage, which limits your options. This system also allows you to play dress-up, if that's your thing.
For the actual battle side of things, the combat is extremely action-focused. You control Lightning's every move, have no party members (except at one point in the game, and for a very short time) and must parry enemy attacks with precise timing to avoid being beaten into the ground. Overall I found this system quite enjoyable, although it is a bit of a trudge before you unlock certain abilities, and sometimes an overuse of visual effects and animations by the game makes it hard to tell what's going on, and in turn, hard to parry/time your attacks correctly.
The first game of the trilogy was heavily criticized for it's lack of player freedom and overwhelming linearity. This is not the case in Lightning Returns. You can do any main quest you want first, although some are easier than others, go to any area whenever you want, and generally do things in the order you please. The only task the game asks of you, is to complete the 5 main quests and enough sidequests before your time is up.
This game also features an extinction mechanic for the monsters. For nearly all monsters, after enough of them have been killed, a Last One, basically a way more powerful version of that monster will spawn. After defeating it, that monster type will no longer appear for this playthrough. This can be a bit of a problem since enemy drops get better after day 7 and day 10. If you exterminated a monster which dropped an ability you  wanted the more powerful version of  before day 7 or 10, you're out of luck for this playthrough. Likewise, the amount of gil the the game has a soft limit because of this extinction system (the vas majority of your income will come from monsters, specifically from Cactuars), and buying a weapon on day 9 when the store begins selling a straight upgrade by day 10 for just a bit more gil is a huge slap in the face.
The plot is a mess. There is no other way to put it. You need to have played the first two games in the series to even have a remote chance at understanding what's going on, and even if you have, the plot is very confused and full of inconcistencies. It's not really interesting either, and this is coming from someone who had no trouble understanding the plot of the first two games and found them serviceable. Still, Lightning gets some funny lines here and there, so it's not all bad.
The music is alright. It reuses a lot of tracks from the previous two games, and the new tracks aren't remarkable, except for one or two.
Graphically, the game looks great in some areas, and pretty mediocre in others. It's nothing eye-scorching, but it is a downgrade from the first game, and feels like a downgrade from the second game, tough I'm not certain about that.
Overall, I'd rate this game a 6/10. If you liked the previous two games, and can get past the doomsday timer (which isn't that big of a deal) and monster extinction stuff, you could be in for a fun time, but don't expect anything amazing. The 16€ pricetag isn't too redihibitory either, which works in the game's favor.

Excellent little game altogether.  Dustoff is a simplistic, yet very involved game where you steer a rescue helicopter around authentic looking Vietnam war scenery, picking up stranded troopers and hardware and returning them to base, all the while blazing away at enemy fortifications, boats, and vehicles with your onboard minigun or rockets.
The game is a 2.5D, meaning it's a 3D environment but you can only move to the left or right, and up or down.
The game#s difficulty level is spot on, with a smooth increase in challenge from start to finish, with just one spike early on that settled down afterwards.  This was the "heavy rain" level, which seemed to be placed such that just when you thought you had the controls down, it was there to knock you off your pedestal, and despite there not being a single enemy in the level, it proved to be quite frustrating altogether to try to navigate in the heavy wind and rain.
The helicopter has unlimited fuel, meaning you only need concern yourself with its health and ammo levels.  You can top these up via health or ammo drops from destroyed enemies, or by returning to base.  Which is just as well, as health drops in particular seem in low supply, and you will take a beating from enemy fire, make no mistake about that!
Progression is simplistic, with new helicopters and weaponry being unlocked and made available as you complete missions.  Each helicopter unlocks allows you to pickup more troops at once and have increased health. The "handling" level of the helicopters went down as you progressed but to be honest I found the top level helicopter to be the most responsive of them all.
You can't actually kill any of your own guys in the field that you are trying to rescue which means you can blaze away to your heart's content, provided you have enough ammo.  This is just as well as they are often to be found in areas of the highest enemy concentration.  It did get a little jarring when I was blasting open the wooden cages that some of the guys were locked inwith rockets, but hey, this is a game not a simulation!
The game's controls are based off 2 single buttons, and if done incorrectly, it could have killed the game.  Thankfully, they nailed it.  While strange at first, it soon becomes instinctive.  Left arrow to lift and move to the left, and right arrow to lift and move to the right, and hold both arrow keys to lift maintain your current direction.  After a while you'll find yourself tapping away to steady up your chopper to lift some guys out of a river (you can't land in water), or holding both arrows, and easing off on one to get a bit of extra height.  It all just works.
Background detail was just excellent, from stray explosions going off, to fellow helicopters going to and fro.  The highlight is on the missions where napalm has been deployed, and when you fly over one of the fiery forests, everything dims and you really get a sense of flying through the blackened, smoke-filled air.
The game is quite short and can be completed in a couple of short sessions, but it is well worth the asking price!

Dustoff Heli Rescue is an okay Choplifter clone marred by bad controls.
You get two buttons, left and right.  Left rotates the chopper to the left and also acclerates upwards.  Right does the same but to the right.  Holding both together accelerates straight up.
The problem is that the controls can't be changed to a normal: left, right, up button style because the stages are designed around the current control scheme.  The skill in Dustoff lies in using the controls but they make the game feel artificially difficult.  If they were simplified the game would be stupidly easy.
And already Dustoff is a pretty easy game, with one or two exceptions.  The largest helicopter, the Chinook, controls like a brick.  The camera in the cave flying sections regularly zooms right in on the helicopter which hides the roof of the cave.  Now combine a wonky helicopter with the inability to see and you recipe for disaster.
With only a couple of hours of gameplay and spike of difficulty that seem more like developer laziness rather than designed challenge make it impossible for me to recommend Dustoff Heli Rescue.
Save your money, buy something else.

You CAN race, and try to get into first (while your gun auto fires and damages opponents) but item drops are important, if you get a couple nitros, you're going to do fine, if you don't... well better luck next time.  The controls aren't conducive to racing.  You turn but quite often your car will go where it wants to and often that's into a wall.
But Link, it's DEATH rally.
Ok... so let's try to kill enemies.  Well there's two problems there.  A. You really only have time to kill maybe 3 enemies if you're lucky.  And B. When an enemy is "almost dead" they feel like they get another health bar.   So you're... going to have to still kill them but now don't know how much life is left in them.
The AI isn't exactly that bright.  I've complained a lot about how Drivatars get into too many accident, but they're based on players, the AI in this game isn't... and yet every so often you get in a three to four car pile up.  Great, you can avoid it and get ahead of them?  Sure, but the two cars not in the pile up tend to be farther down the line especially if you have to swerve around a wreck.
But clearly you aren't using the upgrades.
Ok you're kind of right, I haven't used all the weapons and upgrades.  I have two guns (Shotgun and gattling) and mines.  The mines are great, 3 uses if you're in front of someone you can ♥♥♥♥ them up.  The shot gun is near worthless, and the Gatling gun is thirsty, but does .... well really not that much damage.  And the rest of the upgrades?  WEll upgrades in this game is done like this.  You get 1 upgrade per track, it usually is a new car upgrade.  But then there's Guns, an new tracks that each get upgraded one at a time.  You get extra upgrades by killing enemies, but as mentioned, that's hard as hell to get.  You don't get upgrades by winning races.  (though you get more fame that way)   So to get 5 upgrade parts to get the shot gun is annoying, but you can bang it out in a couple races.  Getting 15(!) upgrade parts for the fourth weapon is a LOT.  I can't imagine what's beyond that.
Which brings me to a point I've seen elsewhere.  This originally was an IOS android game.  The controls feel like it, but the grinding progress and weak gameplay almost confirms it.  This isn't "death rally" it's more "grind fest" and to me that makes it a no at any price.  Yeah it's 10 bucks, but you'd be better off saving that money, watch a video of someone losing a race in this game and realize that's about all you're going to see.
That's not to say you can't win races, but it's QUITE random.  This isn't a game based on "Skill" as much grind for stats, that are expensive, and grind for weapons, and then hope you somehow win.  A shame, because the original game was good, but even ignoring that, Death Rally is not a very good game.  In fact it's bad, not because it doesn't try, but because I think they tried to make this game into something it wasn't.  I don't know where they were aiming, but it's neither a racing game, or a car combat game.

I am extremely disappointed, this game is nothing like the original Death Rally. I could beat the old Death Rally with ease at the highest difficulty so I know what I'm talking about when I say that the cars in this game handle terribly. There are so many bad things in this game: unlimited ammo, autofire, endless powerups from every box, unlocking new cars piece by piece etc. You had one job and you failed miserably, keep the original gameplay in tact and give our old game a facelift. That's literally all you had to do and this game would be amazing, but instead you decided to change every little detail of the addictive gameplay that the old game had. New players who never touched the old one may like it but I would rather replay the old game than play this one.

This is not a good game, and it's offensive that it was branded with the Death Rally name. I wanted to like this but somebody involved in the development of this product did not give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about the origianl game. I read the bad reviews and ignored them... and maybe if you never played the original you won't hate this, but if you are looking for something that is as good or better than the original, you will be sorely disapointed. It's not the worst game i've ever played, but there is no effort at all to replicate what worked in the first iteration. It's a cheap money grab and I'm angry that I fell for it.
EDIT: I feel like it is unfair to give a negative review without naming specific concerns.
- The game is terribly repetitive, and this is compared to a game that had like, 5 tracks and extremely limited graphics and content. There is no feeling of reward for upgrading or buying new vehicles. There seems to be no strategic learning curve. All races feel the same. I was bored after about 15 minutes and kept playing hoping it would change. 2.5 hours later, I just feel cheated.
- The game has no "character" whatsoever. They made some effort with the comic-style story treatment early, but it is way too superficial. Either they had a terribly insufficient creative budget that is spread way to thin, or the team behind the game simply missed what worked about the original.
The original really only had two strengths (three if you count the limited but charming graphics), fun, rewarding progression through the vehicles, upgrades and opponents, combined with a funny/clever atmosphere and experience. Both of these are missing and what is left is, simply, boring.
Not at all a decent tribute to the original. No real campaign mode. Controlls and physics feel terrible. Not reccomended.

This is hands down one of my favourite roguelikes that has come about from the commercial resurgence of the genre. A 2d homage to nethack, turn based but with fluid enough controls that you might forget it's turnbased. Which will obviously result in your death.

I find wazhack to be very addictive and extremely uncompromising. This is a proper roguelike with 2d graphics and a decently clean and simple UI. I die.  A lot.  In fact, I've only had a few characters really achieve particularly spectacular results (compared to their predecessors anyway).  Sometimes you need a game that just throws you into the unknown, encourages you to blindly seek out fate while hoping for a merchant or chapel, and then you're pet hound gets killed so you go on a killing spree.
WazHack is a good enough game to encourage "ok, one more try" and can consume many hours of exploration and sudden death.  Despite the repetitive nature of starting over, there's sufficient content in the dungeon combined with random generation to make each go different enough.  Items and gear are curiously varied enough to make you really wish you could save things forward for your next adventurer.  And there are emotional twists and turns as you try to outguess what will be cursed and how long you can hold out without finding something suitable to eat.
All told... worth it.

Darkestville castle is a point and click adventure from
Epic LLama. it features a villian in the main role, who has evil running through his soul, with a dark humor (that will have you giggling).
There is a tim burton influence showing proudly here, i think the game makers must be a fan of his.
You will start the game in Cid’s bedroom at his castle. From there, you’ll be able to hover over items and characters with your mouse and as soon as you see a skull you’ll be able to interact with them. If you think you have missed something, you can use the hint button which will show you where all the skulls are. You can examine, pick up and talk to them. It’s preferable to talk to characters instead of objects, though. Very quickly, you’ll meet Dan Teapot who has managed to lock Cid up in his castle, and even worse, he’s hired the best demon hunter team, the Romero brothers, to capture and to get rid of Cid from Darkestville. Well, that was Dan’s plan which, of course, didn’t work out. Instead, the Romero brothers capture Cid’s cute pet fish, Domingo.
Cid will have to find a way to free his lovely pet and visit colorful locations within Darkestville, but in the process he will accidentally free other demons. The story is full of humor and you’ll definitely have plenty of good laughs all the way through, with great dialogues and fabulous voice overs. The puzzles are very well done and not hard to resolve. I find it very simple to use and combine items within your inventory, which makes this game even more enjoyable.

the many small improvements throughout the update are often subtle and easily missed, but you will appreciate them. One thing I'd like is to be able to assign buttons to individual weapons... cycling through many items is bad, and multiple key presses are often needed otherwise. only the gravity gun and for some reason the "bug-bait" can be mapped.
Overall, this is one of my favourite games. Highly recommended.

is a top-down combat racing game. Arrested for a series of crime and illegal racing, you avoid jail by participating in the Death Rally tournament where you must attract the attention of a murderous driver known as The Adversary.
: This is a remake of a DOS game by the same name. You race against six opponents (always including one champion) through desert canyons, frozen strips and urban centers. Maps are pretty varied, and some races will drive the track in inverse, other times you'll have specific challenges or handicaps that keep each race fresh. The money you make is spent on upgrading your car's speed, handling and armor, while additional car models, weapons and equipment are unlocked by finding loot drops from other drivers' wreckage during races. Each car has a different acceleration and upgrade cap, while each weapon has a different attack pattern, damage rating and ammo capacity. The game looks great, only some textures and occasional close-up will show this was ported from iOS. As for the control, it is smooth and spot-on (at least with a keyboard, which is what I used 20 years ago with the original
). In true tradition of the original game, it has multiple cameos from other games.
: Gaining levels and money for your upgrades will require you to race A LOT, and the level variety only goes so far, you might find a certain repetitiveness only fans of top-down racing games will tolerate. There isn't much weapon variety, and as soon as you equip a better weapon, you no longer have any control over you base machine gun. Until you master each race track (in either direction), you'll find it near impossible to win the hard races, even with the most upgraded car and weapon, so get ready to do hundreds of races before you can really excel and start climbing the level rankings. The story is nothing more than an excuse for the setting, the story-based campaign is something you're unlikely to repeat.
: ★★★★☆ - Next on your list!
I really enjoyed this game. Although a mobile port, it is still one of the most polished top-down racing games out there. This genre isn't everyone's cup of tea, but if it's yours, I urge you to give
a try!

Running With Rifles is a top down shooter where the player must capture objectives, while fighting on the front lines alongside dozens of others. Players will dodge bullets and bombs as they try and uproot the enemy. Death is an inevitability.
Running With Rifles can be played in either quick match, or campaign mode. Campaign mode has the player select one of the 3 nations, each with a unique colour and starting rifle. The campaign levels are played in whatever order. After each level, the players pick a direction on the map to go, for the next level. Once one nation controls all 9 maps, they are victorious. Both the campaign and quick matches can be customized to the players liking. Including but limited to enemy and friendly spawn ratio and accuracy, total number of units, and starting XP.
As players level up, they will unlock various abilities. Players can commander friendly vehicles as long as they are higher ranked, as well as call in air support. Players can call in various artillery strikes, paratroopers, cover deployment and even tanks. As players rank up, they also unlock larger squad sizes. Squads can be commanded and reduced in size to the players content. Players can visit armouries to equity numerious equipment and weapons they have unlocked, each with their own stats and play-styles. Luxury items can be found on body’s and can be traded at armouries for more RP, the currency used to purchase equipment. Luxury items, weapons and equipment can all be stored in stash locations around the map.
The simplistic, almost hand-drawn art style of RWR definitely suits it well, giving fond memory’s of plastic army men. The aiming is surprisingly solid, as players can see if something is blocking their bullet trajectory. RWR plays fairly well, and rarely bugs out, the AI however, isn’t the brightest.
Running With Rifles does a lot right.
- Fast paced and fun
- Variety of weapons and equipment
- Fantastic aiming and bullet mechanics
- Can tailor the match options to your liking
- Steam workshop and fairly easy achievements
- Surprisingly stable and populated multiplayer
Running With Rifles does a few things wrong.
- AI doesn’t like to take orders
- AI doesn’t like to push forward
- Guns are a pain to unlock
- Guns don’t carry over to new campaigns
- Re-spawning may place players far from the front
- May get boring quick
Overall, Running With Rifles is a fairly good game. If players can get past the abysmal AI pathing and actions,  RWR is a stand up game. A great time killer, and an easy 100%, Running With Rifles is a little steep at $16.99CND, however it goes on sale fairly often, and is a steal at under $10. Pick up a copy with some friends.

RUNNING WITH RIFLES is generally a unique game. At first glance it seems like a twin-stick shooter, but that is far from the case. The game puts you in the shoes of a single, ordinary soldier fighting for either the war between the Greenbelts, Graycollars and Brownpants. You start off as a mere private, but as you rise through the ranks you are able to start commanding other soldiers, going from 1 man to a small platoon of 10 soldiers. No matter your rank, you are still a soldier who can die in a single bullet.
The mechanics in RWR are smooth and interesting. The gunplay mostly involves automatic weapons, but there are single shots too. You can access a wide range of weapons each with different roles in mind, from the reliable assault rifle to a minigun if you can get your hands on it. The AI in the game is very good, they will take cover when under fire and move up against the enemy. Some will stay behind their lines as guards (where the stealth element comes in) and they also make pretty decent drivers. It is always entertaining to see them scrambling to frontlines and fight amongst eachother.
Vehicles in the game are powerful but weak. They can dish out lots of damage and provide cover for friendlies, but when charging into the enemy lines against 20 soldiers, you wont last long. The vehicles aren't there just to attack, they fill many roles such as transport, support, combat transport, etc. The game itself has many obectives aside from the main one. You can sneak behind enemy lines and sabotage them, destroying radio towers which in turn disable the enemies communications for a short time and unblock your own communications in that area.
RWR also features progressive elements, too. Your rank will stay with you in the campaign and multiplayer, your XP, weapons and Resource Points do, too. Resource Points are crucial as they can be spent in the armory and radio calls, which can always turn the tide of any battle (which may I add can sometimes last for hours, even days).
I haven't had any experience in multiplayer, since I've played every hour of this game offline, though I have put in a good 150 or so of on and off play. I sure as hell reccommend this to anyone. It's not something I'd play for weeks on end, but it's nice to have your library and good to come back to every now and then. Trust me, you will get hours of entertainment from this game.

It may have only taken me 2 hours to beat the whole thing, but I can safely say this is probably one of my favorite games ever.
It's everything it promises to be - psychadelic, mind-bending, and hallucinogenic, while also being engaging, reasonably challenging and having a solid mechanical foundation and gameplay.
First of all, it does a great job of easing you into the game as it adds new mechanics. It starts out simple to let you learn and ramps up from there. There's really only ever 4 buttons to worry about, too: left and right, hook, and lance. The fact that it is so simple control-wise means it's that much easier to feel immersed in the game and not worry about what your hands are doing.
That's hardly what makes it great, though. Each level feels like a unique audio-visual experience. In order to complete level goals, you have to be constantly looking ahead down the "pipe". As you perform certain actions, the visuals AND audio react accordingly. The fact that you have to be watching in a certain way and processing what is happening visually, all while everything is changing and responding to what you are doing, is what makes this such a psychadelic, engaging experience.
If you're used to arcade-style games where the focus is on precise, responsive controls and clearly defined, easy-to-read game state, you might feel put off by the idea of this game at first. Everything is constantly moving and waving around and oscillating, which you would think would make it hard to keep track of what is happening. As far as I can tell, though, this is intentional and doesn't hurt your ability to start to gain mastery over the game. As the game state changes (for example, as you speed up), the way you need to visually process and respond to the game changes as well, and the visuals and audio respond to keep feeding you the information you need.
The "ending" is a huge treat; an audio-visual dessert which somehow manages to top the psychadelic experience of each of the levels.
Once you've played through the game, there's plenty of replayability playing through individual stages to get to the top of the leaderboards and competing with your friends or the general public, going for trophies, or even just enjoying the remix mode. However, it seems the friends leaderboard isn't functional (at least for me), so I was a little disappointed by that. Also, the leaderboards don't seem to let me scroll to the next page, so I can only ever see the top 20 or so scores in the world. Perhaps this will get fixed later.
Definitely get this game unless you are concerned about the overwhelming visuals causing diziness or something like that (it wasn't a problem for me and I get motion sickness pretty easily).

It's a very deep and strategic game that presents itself simplistically and comically.  It's a permadeath game, so the successes you have and the wealth you build all feel very rewarding.
Every skill and every talent that you can take upon level up is immediately evidenced in the gameplay mechanics.  There is no grind feel that you must burn through useless levels to reach a singular strength.  If you upgrade something, you'll see the difference.
It's also the best use of RNG I think I've ever seen in a game.  There does not seem to be any restriction related to level or location that results in something not being potentially available to you.  It's not a boring wash/rinse/repeat of "this is what to expect at level 1, and this is what to expect at level blah".  You can literally start a game and have an amazing stroke of luck that puts you into a very positive flow.  You can also play very deep into the game and the whole way having felt like every breath may be your last.
This last point means that even the worst deaths that make you think you hate the game will also be the reason why you start anew and get back to it.  The next attempt can quickly outshine your last.
A suggestion for potential new players:  There are online sources (wiki) which can quickly guide you toward big success in the game.  For hardcore players, I recommend you don't use those online sources and first attempt to completely use your imagination when playing through this.  There are incredibly sensible and logical mechanics built into this game that make it very different from the normal dungeon crawler or rpg.

MAKE PERMANENT DEATH OPTIONAL!  This would be my favorite dungeon crawling game were it not for the perma death feature.  I enjoy finding unidentified items.  Using or reading them with unknown consequences is part of the fun of this game.  So why permanent death permanently?  Please modify this game to set perma death as a player-selected option.

I'm a HUGE aviation buff.  Flight sims for three decades now, I take out the club 172 few times a year, I planespot, I take my boy to watch planes at the lakeshore.  I *DESPERATELY* want this game to be complete and released, because it's fun as hell.
There are a lot of really interesting airport layout ideas that work well, and as a manager-style game, you can't ask for more.  "Rimworld or Prison Architect for airports" really is accurate.  The sound and weather are solid and interesting, the ambient sound is great as you zoom in to hear specific zones.  The aircraft selection is fairly realistic and spans a few generations of airframes.  The choice of airlines served adds depth with their different priorities, fleet size, demands, and refueling chances.  The sprites used for all the objects especially seems to have gotten a great deal of care, with gate parking markings for different airframes' nosewheel indicators.
Sadly the bugs really break this as a game, so far.  If you know Early Access and are okay with that, this is a real gem.  But nearly all games are prematurely ended by a save-breaking bug that stops your airport dead in some fashion or another.  Bus blocks the entire road, no more deliveries or passengers or fuel.  Baggage truck bucks out on the tarmac, now that vehicle and it's parent hangar are immovable and can't be erased or destroyed, locking that parcel of land forever.  There are also bugs that set you back a long way without outright ruining your save, such as crew members not loading (causing a plane that won't load any of the 500+ passengers waiting at the gate), taxiway gridlock where aircraft can't decide where to go, and passengers and crew being randomly stuck in invisible tiny prisons, causing your airport reputation to suffer.
I strongly advise anyone interested in this game to buy it, however if you like a game to be Beta rather than Alpha, you should wait a bit.

Welcome to my review of Darkestville Castle!
In A Nutshell:

-Great Voice Acting.
-Retro, ‘90s Style Gameplay.
-Challenging, but fun, Puzzles.
-Obvious LucasArts/Sierra On-Line Influences.
-Witty Dialog.
-Dark Humor.
-Fun Storyline.

-Very Cartoonish (Possible Pro?).
-Some Pixel-Hunting Required (Minor).

This was a difficult review for me, only because I love the genre, the dark humor, and anything obviously inspired by LucasArts circa 1992. As a long-time fan of titles like
and
, there was little chance I wouldn’t fall in love with Darkestville Castle. If you enjoy witty dialog, silly but still twisted evil plots, quality voice acting, and cartoon graphics, you’ll probably love this title. I had very few instances of getting “stuck,” and when I did, the built-in hint guide quickly got me back on track. Usually, I’d just overlooked something in a scene, which meant I needed to be better about “Pixel Hunting” when I was briefly stuck.
Even though Cid is “evil,” there’s really no horror, murder, or legitimately dark themes to this title, so it’s appropriate for younger gamers as well. There is a little bit of “adult” innuendo, but nothing so risqué as to need censoring or a rating warning – it’s just enough that mature players might catch on, snicker, and it can be overlooked by younger folks. All in all, this is a truly worthy addition to any Point-&-Click collection, and we absolutely loved playing and streaming it over on Twitch. Highly recommend!

Darkestville Castle:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Darkestville was once a peaceful place until a boy named Cid came (fell) to town. From an early age, Cid was out late at night performing evil deeds to prank Darkestville residents. And boy, was he good at it! Let’s recap some of his achievements. . .  The explosive park bench (quite deadly if you sit on it), the front door castle trap (the trap door dropping you into a confined cell), and many more evil tricks! The question, my friends, is do you really want to meet Cid from Darkestville Castle? Yeah, you want to - he’s cool!
Darkestville Castle is a point and click adventure game where you play the prankster demon Cid.
You will start the game in Cid’s bedroom at his castle. From there, you’ll be able to hover over items and characters with your mouse and as soon as you see a skull you’ll be able to interact with them. If you think you have missed something, you can use the hint button which will show you where all the skulls are. You can examine, pick up and talk to them. It’s preferable to talk to characters instead of objects, though. Very quickly, you’ll meet Dan Teapot who has managed to lock Cid up in his castle, and even worse, he’s hired the best demon hunter team, the Romero brothers, to capture and to get rid of Cid from Darkestville. Well, that was Dan’s plan which, of course, didn’t work out. Instead, the Romero brothers capture Cid’s cute pet fish, Domingo.
Cid will have to find a way to free his lovely pet and visit colorful locations within Darkestville, but in the process he will accidentally free other demons (which gives him a few headaches). The story is full of humor and you’ll definitely have plenty of good laughs all the way through, with great dialogues and fabulous voice overs. The puzzles are very well done and not hard to resolve. I find it very simple to use and combine items within your inventory, which makes this game even more enjoyable.
Great graphics, the games runs very well and you use your mouse to move Cid around, choose dialogues and pick up or use objects.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Good Graphics
-	Quirky and fun characters
-	Fun story with good dialogues and voice over
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Puzzles could have been harder to figure out
-	No trading cards
It has been a while since I played this type of quirky and fun point and click adventure game. If you enjoy games like Full throttle and others of the same style, you’ll enjoy this one too. This is great fun!
7/10

Okay so right off the bat this isn't a bad game. However...I do feel that it was not worth the full 15$ I think it should've been about 10$ There is a lot of fun in this and some jokes that made me laugh pretty loud. Some of the puzzles are very tedius and hard to figure out and doesn't help when some of the puzzles need some strange logic. I am also dissapointed though with just how little things are explored. (Some spoilers after this point) you meet a guy in the underworld who acts like Cid for the underworld. (maybe swapped for Cid at a young age?) Yet you do nearly nothing with him. You learn no real reason WHY Cid was put in Darkestville, and so many other questions that are left open that bother me.
Now based on the credits this seemed to have a fairly small team compared to a lot of other games which I can use to explain some things. Though for 15$ I wish that more of the game wasn't static. I wished you could see more things in the background happening, or from time to time a silly animation from a static character while waiting. There was some but not a lot of animation when you weren't involved. The Inventory wasn't bad but I feel that it was a bit tricky and wished their were more lines for when you had the wrong item being used because hearing "Nope." "Nu-uh" "I will not use *Item* here" got annoying with how often I had to do trial and error to figure it out.
I noticed the lip movement was odd but I believe that this game isn't originally English so I chock that up to just I'm not playing the native langauge.
I will also note their is a character name "Vigo" and his name throughout the game is pernounced "V-Go" but the narrator calls him "Vi-go" which just sounded weird. It's more a nitpick but I didn't like it.
The game also had a bad habit of red herring hints. There is one character you need to trap and he says something about a Purple Raptor, and another character seems to be that when he sneezes after drinking something Cid had made before he turned into a purple monster. So I spent thirty minutes trying to figure out how to make the thing so he would turn into the monster and could be bait to trap or just lure him away for me. In the end that was a throwaway Line.
I know this has a lot of negativity but the trailer does show the best parts, Cid is a pretty likable character he is "Evil" but not a monster. It started to leave the goofy childish side and get a bit more serious but not enough.
While some of the meta jokes were really funny, others where forced and dissapointing.
What I do hope for though is since Steam says this is like Deponia (good series BTW) that Darkestville Castle fallows in Deponia's footsteps and make a few sequels going on with and improving the story and explaining the backstories of Cid and a few other characters more. I'd love to see Cid do more maybe a level where he is just doing his pranks or so (could've actually been a good tutorial moment) delve into his decisions more, does he stay how he was or does he try to improve himself?
This game in the end I think is at LEAST a 6/10 it's not bad, but it clearly has flaws. The things though that appeals to me the most about it is Cid is a great character, the world is intriguing to me, the humor for the most part is good (every comedy has its bad jokes) but the potential sequels are what I hope for. I want to see more of Cid, maybe a spin off or a section in a sequel/prequel where you play as the Romeros (I feel they needed more screen time).
I am going to keep my eyes open and hope that this becomes a series because Cid the demon of Darkestville deserves love.

How about everyday the only thing you have to do is play a few pranks here and there at the town you reside at? Even better, with little repercussion other than one person trying to lock you in your house. Trying to figure out new pranks once you get tired of the ones you did and perhaps increasing in intensity over time. Would be a dream, especially for those who do regularly prank others.
We play as the short-of bad guy who lives at Darkestville, a demon named Cid. Cid has been at Darkestville since he fell as a falling star as a baby. Not wasting any time to torment the residents at any chance since then. At some point, whether Cid was able to build a castle, took the castle for himself, or the residents just gave it to him so he would not be in anyone’s hair all the time, Cid got possession of a castle that serves as his home. Luckily, away from the town just in case a prank in the making goes haywire while in the planning process.
As you can probably tell, Cid is more like an annoying prankster than a villain. As you talk to other residents, this goes a little more into this as since a lot of people seem to forgive him. Some due to knowing him since he was a child to just not caring as long as Cid pays his debts or goods. With the other major pranks that can cause harm it plays out two ways: the residents get word about it (Cid accidently slipping it out while talking or spread by someone seeing him do it), it goes horribly wrong in Cid’s face, actually benefits Darkestville, or never got off the planning stage.
The day we looked into Cid’s life is the day that someone actually tries to get Cid out. A Dan Teapot decided to phone in demon hunters to rid Darkestville of their one demon. Though Dan seems to not have planned everything out as Cid does manage to evade the demon hunters...only to have his fish, Domingo, to be mistaken as one instead. And, well, perhaps the demon hunters are as well. Not taking any information on how the demon looks like, only what the sender looks like, and not having some way to know if one is a demon. Perhaps the other demons were more aggressive and did not expect Cid to be complacent.
Based on the information we are given, and how Cid acts, I would hope that I was not the only one that thought Cid’s heart was not all into wreaking havoc. I did crave some serious moments, or semi-serious moments, that delved more into how Cid is like and if he felt bad about pranking sometimes. We do get this towards the middle of the game where his motive changes, but I do wish it was more. The ending does suggest that Cid might of went back to his regular pranking schedule, but perhaps not as Cid is not like any demon. There were also some characters that I do wish got some development on, especially one particular one that I wonder happened to him.
I do like how this did not develop as an episodic point and click game, only going as far as making fun of them while instilling fear in the player. Nobody likes waiting on the rest of the story after a huge development in the story even if we know it would be episodic. Or fearing that there never will be another episode due to the lack of sales, like I have seen with some games that I loved and wanted to see conclude. Of course, talking about this will lessen the hold it will have, but it was just too well done just to not talk about it. I do also like the inclusion of prelude chapters for puzzles that will only take place in one area.
The puzzles are decent. The only hard ones you will get stuck on are the ones you have to try an item on everything or having to combine two items that you would not suspect to. Other than that, you will get the idea of what you need by talking to people or looking at the environment. A lot of the conversations you will have will more or less pertain to a puzzle, even if you find out about it before or not, which can cause some confusion. There is a point where you have to get nails and and a hammer to repair a bridge, but you won’t know that unless you go there first. So if you go to where you will be able to get the hammer and talk to the person first, asking for their hammer is weird. And luckily, the items you can pick up are very obvious, with one or two things thin enough to escape your view.
The graphics has a nice hand drawn, cartoon feel that might of existed years ago. I quite liked all of the backgrounds and how Darkestville was laid out, often able to see where an exit will lead to if you were not sent to the overview map. For items you can interact with, they are obvious, and even then you are able to hit a button so you can see what can be interacted with. Being able to grab, look, or talk to anything or anyone. I also loved the painted glass art and the art on the chapter cards. With the character designs, some of them don’t exactly look like they fit in this universe. Some humans will look drastically different from other humans you interacted with.
The audio is well done. There were no different sound quality between any of the characters and all of them kept up whatever sound altering that it went through without jeopardizing much. It is really surprising that a lot of the voices were done by one person, you can certainly tell for one or two but for the others not exactly. If you keep the subtitles on, you will see little to no typos. If there were more than what I have seen they might be more covert, but the one I picked up was when a character said “which” but the subtitles had “witch”. On this note, the soundtrack does top off the areas and keeps the atmosphere of just another light-hearted game throughout.
+ Interesting story
+ Some puzzles are well done
+ Nice graphics
+ Sound quality
+/- Humor is subjective, so jokes might not hit with you
- Some puzzles can have you trying an item on everything
Darkestville Castle is interesting as you play a prankster that Darkestville more or less tolerates. If you love point and click games, you would no doubt love this game. If it wasn’t the visuals that got you interested, it would be the light-hearted tone that is throughout and is very pronounced in their trailers. So if you are looking for more serious themes or moments, this might not satisfy you. Either way, this game was fun and will keep you wanting more till you get to the ending. Perhaps the chapter cards serve as a little guilty pleasure as “just one more” can take place.

I don't typically write reviews that are very descriptive in general but this game has it all-fantastic soundtrack, great voiceacting(I mean it) and a pretty clever writing.
It takes you back to the age when games like these were sprawling and the genre of point and click gained traction through its pretty in depth writing.
The antagonist or depending on your moral values, protagonist pokes fun at almost everything and the game writers have included a humour factor everywhere.
Especially, when you try to use a soap as a lubricant for a chain, it has a special dialogue which other games would have at like "Oh, a chain[object 1 here] cannot be used with a soap[object 2] here", this game has it like "You might think this is a pretty good lubricant but soaps cannot be used as a lubricant for a chain" and it was actually more clever but I forgot the actual dialogue.

Rating: 6.5/10
Genre: Third Person, real-time RPG
The Good:
+ Graphics and presentation.
+ The combat system has been overhauled from previous entries. Combat now plays out in real-time. You can equip up to 3 outfits. Within each outfit you can equip a weapon, shield, accessories and abilities. Within combat you can freely switch between outfits. Like previous entries, how you setup before battle is more important than the actual battle.
+ This is a very non-linear game as you can tackle any main/side quests in any order you prefer.
+ Among the F13 trilogy this is the best optimized game, it does have some problems but compared to the nightmare that was FF13-2 this is a massive improvement.
The Average:
+/- The game features a time limit in which you must accomplish as many main/side quests as possible before the day ends. You are originally given 6 days to complete everything however you can extend this by completing as many quests as you can. You are also given the ability to freeze time for a few short minutes, however you are only given a limited number of uses and must kill enemies to restore how often you can use the ability. Given that the story is about the world ending, it makes sense from a gameplay perspective but the mechanic becomes a bit tiresome after a while.
+/-The story, to no surprise is a convoluted mess. You must play FF13-2 and to a lesser degree FF13 to have any understanding of what is happening. I got the impression the developers had no idea where to take the story after FF13 so they started making things up on the go. The story is held together by strong presentation and voice acting.
+/- You are presented with two difficulty options, easy and normal. Normal is too difficult especially for a first playthrough and easy is very easy outside of optional bosses.
+/- Killing enemies doesn’t reward you with anything other than recharging your meter so that you can use certain abilities and granting you skills to customize your character. Once you have the skills you want there is little incentive to kill enemies.
The Bad:
- You must complete side quests to level up stats. To complete side quests, you must be at the right place at the right time and sometimes meet other conditions. This becomes very problematic because its so easy to miss quests often resulting in using a guide to help you.  Almost every side quest is some variation of a fetch quest and the game gives very little or no helpful advice in how to complete any of them. Given the importance of side quests, a better system really needs to be in place.
Conclusion:
Square finally made a competent final fantasy port and to their credit, are not afraid to try new ideas rather than rehashing the same old things, sadly not every idea is a winner. This game is completely different from the previous games and given the new mechanics this is one of those games where you either love it or hate it.

I don't really have words for how wonky and utterly bizarre a game Lightning Returns is in the landscape of Final Fantasy titles. Utterly incomprehensible in its monolothic culmination of three titles of nonsensical stories, Lightning Return continues Final Fantasy 13's grand legacy, yet fails to match the same gameplay and graphical excellence of previous titles. The Sidequests are so utterly removed from logic that the stories are frequentably laughable and nigh impossible to even take seriously, but it's difficult to match when watching the idiotic movement patterns of NPCs and the constant clipping of gear. There's often fuel for hilarity during the very cutscenes that contain the sidequests and story when wearing costumes made of Moogles, with mustache, tophats, and countless other ridiculous accenting items and costumes, watching as NPCs are jostled and knocked about by the milling patterns of surrounding NPCS, There's a distinct sense that the game didn't have enough time to be developed and that shines through every facet of the design. The very doomsday counter that looms over the player's head is easily ignored when stopping time through a single skill implemented from the start, grinding big  monsters for EP to spend on its usage after abusing gear provided from DLC. This grind continues into the rest of the game, whether it be doing fetch quests, or extincting entire species after felling countless creatures as you traverse an open world fighting monsters. This is all despite having a detailed customization system of costumes and large number of skills ranging from debuffing, blocking, physical attacks, and spells, with room for gear and accessories to add stat bonuses and buffs to the gameplay. Each costume and often has its own buffs and debuffs and a specialized use towards what skills would be best to use with them, some even transforming based on the costume or weapon used. The level of detail can, at times, be staggering and overwhelming. But even with this and a hybrid real time, command-based battle system involving staggering foes, ultimately one doesn't even need to change strategy and consequently battles don't really amount to much, which is likely why the extinction system even exists. The very rare opportunity to need to change costumes and customization settings only comes from the occasional boss and large-scale monsters, leaving the player with a wealth of time otherwise spent grinding and questing as opposed to having challenging gameplay. So, why am I leaving a positive review? In spite of, or perhaps because of these reasons, this game is enthralling. Maybe it's because the game's wonkiness is endearing, whether it be for comedy or for the strangely emotional motivations for the characters. Maybe it's because each costume referencing previous titles, there's always a fun easter egg or two to enjoy while running around and slaying monsters. Maybe it's because playing Final Fantasy 13's game have weakened me. Or maybe it's because it's an absolute joy to play in a Final Fantasy game, customizing, exploring, and operating as I choose in an open world, off the rails that most every Final Fantasy game has kept us on to some extent. Eitherway, I've been enjoying what may easily be the strangest, most unhinged title in the series. So approach with caution and buy on sale.
TLDR: Weird, hilarious, grindy, but unpredictable, with open world, easter eggs, high customization, and player choice for how to utilize their time. Buy on sale and approach with caution, mileage may vary, but can be enjoyable dependant on the person and their taste.

It's fair to say that the initial release of No Man's Sky in August 2016 generated a great deal of controversy, perhaps best summed up in this vid from YouTube:
The initial reveal of No Man's Sky at E3 in 2014 promised a diverse and beautiful universe to explore, but I suppose that given the development timescale and competing demands of graphics, gameplay, storyline (or absence thereof) and need to ensure that NMS would be playable on diverse platforms meant that compromises had to be made, which is justifiably reflected in the Steam user reviews.
However since the first release of NMS, Hello Games' development team have been quietly working towards addressing most of those early criticisms.  We've seen no fewer than three major patches released, which have incrementally improved upon the graphics, user interface, gameplay and have to a large extent given the player more to do than simply gather fuel, travel from planet to almost identical planet and scan lifeforms.
I'm pleased to report that the resulting incarnation of No Man's Sky almost lives up to the initial promise.  I say 'almost', for there are still some criticisms to address which I'll detail later, but for the most part NMS is an involving and a really quite charming game which deserves further investigation.
There are now three game modes, with a permadeath mode being a reasonable challenge to a seasoned gamer.  The Survival and Creative modes respectively offer a greater challenge or an unhindered exploration experience.  All three feature missions, an improved storyline and the welcome addition of base building.  It's now possible to build farms, obtain a rover vehicle to explore planets and to purchase larger freighter spacecraft.  These enhancements are well integrated into the game, without giving the impression that they'd been bolted on as an afterthought.
Planets are now much more diverse than at initial release, with many more types of planet to explore offering some unique challenges.  Despite the procedural generation, quite a few planets are still a little samey, but there's now much more to see and explore.  There's incentives to craft improvements to your suit and multitool, requiring you to find star systems with mineral deposits to convert into better equipment as you go.  Blueprints for upgrades may be purchased at space stations.
Some criticisms still remain, however.  Those of you lucky enough to play NMS in 4K with a sufficiently powerful graphics card will notice considerable framerate slowdown when exploring on foot and some of the textures won't stand up to close scrutiny.  I would venture that there are still optimisation improvements to be made to the graphics engine here.  Nvidia's GeForce experience will give you the best compromise between performance and appearance, but it's still exactly that - a compromise.
Despite the aforementioned procedural generation, lifeforms are a little bit identikit and it's easy to travel between solar systems and encounter seemingly identical lifeforms drawn from a limited range of variables.  At least they're now a lot less awkward and silly than at initial release, but there's room for improvement here.
In summary, despite some lingering criticism, Hello Games have been mostly successful in their efforts to improve No Man's Sky and in doing so have enhanced the character and charm of the game.  I think that it deserves a second look and I hope that Hello Games continue to refine and polish, certainly recent magazine reviews have been quite positive and I would now quite happily recommend No Man's Sky.

The progression curve in this game is rather steep. You will die. A lot.
If you stick with it and manage to rank up enough that you're allowed the privelege of wearing a bit of body armor then you'll find things become a little easier. Just a little, though. Call it the difference between being one-shotted from across the map by an enemy you never even saw and being two- or three-shotted from across the map by an enemy you never even saw. Progress!
That may be slightly unfair, but then this game can also feel pretty unfair at times.
Some bullet points:
*A great, consistent style. From the artwork to the soldier's chatter the game has a good vibe to it. Somewhat cartoonish while also a bit gory and violent. "Whistling past the graveyard" is an expression that fits well here.
*A good sense of scale. You really are just one (very, very expendable) cog in a massive machine. Where you go, how you get there and what you do are entirely up to you. Feel free to embrace life as a R.E.M.F., hanging out by the supply shed and chatting with all those poor souls headed toward the front who have no idea of the hell that's about to be unleashed upon them. Or embrace your inner Rambo, making yourself into the spearpoint of the entire army's thrust into enemy territory, and attempt to do it all by yourself. Let me know how that works out.
(R.E.M.F. = Rear-echelon mother@#%^er)
*A surprisingly effective arsenal of weapons, armor and support gear designed to make spending the hours as the meat in a grinder a little less unpleasant. You'll have to work to have access to all these fun toys, however. And by "work" I mean "die, an awful lot".
(Of note here is that the developers recently removed the loss of XP upon a death. Previously you lost both XP and RP, Rank Points, when you died. Now you only lose the RP, it being the "currency" used to purchase all those goodies like artillery strikes and so on. With that change it's now easier to progress in terms of your soldier's rank, i.e. Private to PFC to Corporal etc., while still being a challenge to obtain RP. Higher rank means access to more powerful equipment and support from the Armory, but you'll still need to put in a fair amount of effort to actually be able to purchase them.)
*My favorite bit: Co-operative multiplayer. PVP is a blast but I personally find there's a distinct shortage of games built around cooperation as opposed to competition. The AI in the game is challenging and unforgiving. It's very satisfying to team up with a couple dozen other players to teach the AI a lesson or two.
Lastly a couple of gripes/disclaimers/pet peeves:
*Line-of-sight is extremely important in RWR, as is distance. The enemy can and will spot you at the extremes of their vision's range, which means you won't have much choice (if you want to live more than a few seconds) but to spend a lot of your time sort of "sweeping" the mouse cursor along the far edges of your screen. This is the only way to see as far as the game allows you to see with whatever weapon you have equipped. It can be annoying at times. It can be dangerous, as well, since looking in one direction obviously limits your sight in other directions. Focus too much on the enemies across the field and you may just miss the enemy about to knife you in the back.
This isn't a criticism of the game. The setup works, and it works well. It's more a heads-up to potential buyers that you'll need to be on your toes at all times, constantly aware of your surroundings, which isn't everyone's idea of a good time.
*Lack of servers. It's true that there really aren't many people playing the game, sadly. A few hundred, perhaps? Even so, the co-op servers only hold 24 human players, and there aren't many of those servers, and only a few of them in the U.S. It's not unusual for me to log on and discover that all the U.S. servers are filled up, and I'm left only with servers in Germany or China or the like to play co-op on.  The whole situation is a bit of a Catch-22.  A small playerbase means less servers needed, or affordable; but on the other hand the game will have difficulty growing and attracting new people if there isn't room for them to play.  I may be overthinking it but I figured it needed to be mentioned in any review. The current playerbase seems friendly, dedicated and knowledgeable, just very very small.
Enough said. It's a really enjoyable game with an unfortunately small playerbase in terms of multiplayer. The single-player campaign will afford you hours of fun and the game is worth the price for that alone, however. Get into some co-op and you can easily lose track of time and find yourself wondering when you last had a shower or slept. Definitely recommended.

I’ll start by admitting that the hand-drawn, cartoonish graphic style in adventure games, is very dear to me. I grew up with LucasArts classics such as Day of the Tentacle, Full Throttle and the Monkey Island series. The third game in that franchise, 1997’s The Curse of Monkey Island is still my go-to template for judging any adventure video game which tries to emulate both those visuals and the rich sense of humor. I’m pleased to say that Epic Llama’s latest Steam project, Darkestville Castle, is just such a game which managed to remind me of times long past for the adventure genre. It’s the developer’s second title to be released on Steam after their 2015 debut, Champions Of Chaos 2. Darkestville is a new genre for the dev team, yet they made next to no mistakes in regards to it. So far, so good.
The lovable rogue in Darkestville Castle is an antihero worthy of Guybrush Threepwood’s legacy. Instead of a “mighty pirate”, players shall now meet Cid, The Demon of Darkestville. A purposely goofy protagonist which almost reminded me of Dark Shadows’ Barnabas Collins, minus the family drama. So a vampire he is not and Cid doesn’t quite fit the image of a demon either. Consider him an avatar of trickery first and foremost. A prankster in the mythological vein of both Loki and Pan.
Cid the Demon has a castle of his own and seems to live a happy life by being left alone to his own devices, which in our case, means employing evil schemes on Darkestville’s citizens. His “nefarious plans” fail everytime so he’s regarded more as a nuisance than a threat. This is by no means a dark tale involving actual demons and that becomes obvious right from the first few minutes in-game, after you’re introduced to the antihero via stained glass images depicting his early life and “exploits”.
The peace and quiet get disrupted one night after Cid’s pet fish, Domingo is kidnapped by a team of equally clumsy demon hunters which mistake him for his owner. All sorts of funny situations shall arise, some of which hover close to black humor, without crossing the line. The story itself is of decent length and it’s divided by a prelude, two interludes and three chapters. Epic Llama did their “homework” and went for a well structured and self-contained storyline instead of an episodic format which seems like the more popular choice in nowadays adventure games. I’ve been waiting for over an year, to play Slap Village’s second chapter which is still nowhere to be seen, so I appreciate any title that can wrap things up nicely and then focus on a sequel without resorting to  cliffhangers.
It’s no surprise that the game’s powered by the Unity Engine. The developers needed a strong framework for their project, while they focused on those skillfully drawn backgrounds and characters. Quality caricatures which visually represent the absurdity of the subplots. Apart from the static assets, the animations were also spot on. From motion to speech patterns, it’s that noticeable effort, that extra mile if you will, which separates a story-driven adventure from a run-of-the-mill Hidden Object Game. Darkestville Castle scaled perfectly to 4K resolution and it never featured a single frame rate drop, nevermind a glitch or crash to desktop.
The English voice acting I opted for, never felt unconvincing and the voice actors were inspired choices. The game felt a bit off in Spanish or Russian, but the options are there if you need them. Same applies to the subtitles and so far I’ve only spotted a single typo in my entire playthrough. In one conversation with an NPC, the misspelling of “which” with “witch”. Slap Village had far more typos so I won’t complain about that or deny the fact that I need to spell check my own reviews, several times after I’ve just published them. Errare humanum est…
The gameplay itself follows the classic guidelines left behind by Darkestville Castle’s many spiritual predecessors. Players control a main character in his direct interaction with NPCs either through dialogue or items. An inventory system allows for the collection and potential combination of several items into a single one. The dialogues have multiple options to choose from and they can lead to the acquisition of new objects or story progression. Cid the Demon doesn’t stray from the norms of previous adventure protagonists and perhaps that’s an issue, if you’re looking for visible character development.
The puzzles involving the aforementioned items are never that hard to figure out and spotting them during new scene backgrounds, is made even easier by the inclusion of a “hint button” in the upper right side of the screen. Some combinations won’t be straightforward so I suggest you experiment at any time, with the items already present in your inventory. Interaction with the objects and NPCs, features three options which range from touch/grab/eat, look and talk. It goes without saying that you need to thoroughly examine each new place you visit. HOG or not, the key to success is always hidden in plain sight.
In the end, my biggest gripe with Darkestville Castle is that its jokes alone, can’t carry the game without the inclusion of some form of replay value. There is very little to do other than chat in a few dialogue lines with each NPC until you figure out how to use an item and where. Curse of Monkey Island and pretty much every other LucasArts adventure game, knew how to place challenging puzzles between (not-so) friendly chats, throw a funny song on occasion and even easter eggs or pop culture references. Anachronistic elements by themselves won’t cut it in the long run.
Darkestville Castle's visual style sets it apart from the conventional 3D graphics that are becoming the rule of thumb for the genre, sadly. I grew up with 2D cartoons, so biased or not, I prefer them. They represent a higher level of dedication and hard work which 3D rendering diluted more often than not. I’m not an expert in animation, I just prefer good ol’ 2D methods. It all boils down to taste in the end, so you’re free to prefer the newer, modern 3D forms of animated expression. Darkestville Castle will surely not disappoint fans of the adventure genre looking for a more light-hearted perspective and puzzles which never force you to seek online solutions.
+ Steam Achievements.
+ Pleasant visuals & sounds.
+ Humorous story and characters.
- No in-game collectibles or incentives for replay value.
- Puzzles are too easy, most of the time.
- No Steam Trading Cards.

Went into this game with high hopes. Intial artwork looked quirky and fun. After playing through the game in its entirety I have a few issues with this game.
First, artwork wise, the design of these characters just didn't go well with eachother. The only way I can describe it is that they were drawn by two different artists with different styles. It was as if some random kickstarters for the game entered their art and had it put in the game as a reward for supporting this games creation.  Cid, the protagonist is well design and clearly the most work went into his character. All other characters in this game however lacked any kind of personality and fell flat.
Second, the puzzles. In the beginning the puzzles were simple enough as expected to get the player used to the logic used in the game. However, towards the end I found myself clicking random things together just to get some kind of hint as to where to go next. Unless I completely missed something, one of the puzzles has you clicking on EVERYTHING just to find a hidden door. The other characters gave random and somewhat misleading information making me believe the puzzle was supposed to lead one direction, when it actually had nothing to do with solving the puzzle or future puzzles.
Then the final puzzle, RIPPED RIGHT OUT OF MONKEY ISLAND.
Basically the whole time I was playing this I felt like I was playing a subpar version of the Monkey Island games. There were so many directions this could have played out story wise that would have made me forgive the abysmal puzzles which where neither overly difficult except when random logic was required, or clever. I never felt rewarded or smart for solving these puzzles, more like "ugh, finally...I can move on". But no, the story end exactly how you expected and just like the narrator says in the begining "dissappointing".
What the creators of this game can learn from this experience is, develop your characters more, supporting and protagonist. You can have the random npc's that give you a hint, but I expect at least a couple of character to have some kind of character development or something interesting about them in the least. Cid is only mildly interesting in the way that he's a "badguy...Or is he?"....trope. And as far as puzzles, don't make me pick up a bunch of random items and then hand them to people who ask for them. That's not puzzle solving, that's fetch questing.
I think I'm only being super harsh on this because of two things. The initial reviews which intially got me interested and thinking this would be fun and the $15 price tag.
If you are still interested in this game, I HIGHLY suggest waiting for a drop in price/sale.
