So, Garou has been a while on steam, but it has been rocking the arcades for years!!!
The last chapter of the fatal fury series introduces us a new main character, Rock Howard. Yes, he is the child Terry picks during his Real Bout ending, and YES!! he is Geese´s son.
Several features have been removed from the old games, now we have a lineal 2D fighting game, you cannot switch tracks anymore. It doesn´t have the double health bar, so no infinite max moves, and last but not least, most of the main character rooster has been removed or replaced.
So, what makes this game awesome??
As every good game, it requires a rich story, which indeed Garou has. We see an older version of Terry Bogard signing up on another tournament held in South Town by the hands of a misterious guy. You will get a variety of characters to play with, each one with a particular "final" bout against his enemy in the game, getting an special pre fight speech wich will reveal insights to the story and the characters reason to, well, be there and fight!
You can play as a Kyokugen karate guy this time! and no, is not Ryo from Art of FIghting, but Butt, his apprentice! and if by any reason you are missing Mai or Andy, you can play as the new Shiranui Martial Arts representative, a shuriken and bomb thrower little kid called Hokutomaru. Kim´s sons (which were 1st portrayed on the Fatal Fury motion picture) now are full grown fellows with awesome fighting skills...and many new characters that complete a very versatile rooster!
Gameplay-wise, it brings 2 new original features to the fighting games at the time it was released. The T.O.P system, which consists of choosing a 1/3rd part of your health bar to be a frame that when reached, the player will start restoring health slowly, and also gain a new extra attack. The "Just Parry!" system its a game breaking feature, it allows the player to block on the very last second, if timed correctly, it will restore health and also allow him to counter his opponent wi.th any move (yes, MAx moves too!).
We get the classic 2 energy bar system, using a max move with 1 bar stored will perform the weak version of the max move and by spending the 2, you will perform the stronger version of the attack.
Is that it? Hell no!!! Garou introduces us the Break system. It allows you to cancel a certain special move, so in case you were blocked the character can stop the motion and prevent a counter, or if the move hits, you can also "break" it to leave your foe on mid air and punish him with a nasty combo!
Last but not least, the characters can perform "fake" motions (down LP+SP) that will make them perform the 1st frames of an special attack, but not performing said attack, just to trick your opponent and some of them are cancelable!
Its an all time classic that truly deserves your attention, and the price its really worth the fun!!

Unlike too many point & clicks (not sure why so many fail developing such simple, time-tested controls/UIs), this one nails the user interface where everything just works as you expect it should work. Searching around for items and interacting with objects is always enjoyable since there's so much uniquely humorous dialog to hear, The writing is very well done - it's clever and amusing with a very cohesive feel. It's not a bad game, necessarily, but not good enough to recommend. The English translation is kind of iffy and often doesn't quite match the narration. The puzzles are interesting and fun, but objects are frequently misnamed, which makes hidden object scenes more difficult than necessary. At one point there was a hidden object scene with two ropes in, and the game asked you to find one rope. It had to be the one specific rope though; the other one had to stay so you could find it again later on down the line.
The graphics are needlessly complicated and it can take a long time to transition from one scene to another, which is a problem when you only need to do one thing in an area and then leave to go elsewhere. Fortunately there's a fast-travel option, which cuts down a little on this.
And the story, while interesting enough, is just kind of jumbled. The opening cutscene makes it clear we're looking for a missing girl. Okay, got it. A few scenes into the game, once the tutorial showing you how to gas up your car and inflate your tires is done, you find a drawing of what appears to be a witch scratched on a table. "What a terrible drawing," the main character says. Okay, looks like atmosphere-building. Sounds good. But if you check your journal it shows you that same drawing along with a caption that says, "This must be how the girls saw Mrs. Braun!" Wait, who's Mrs. Braun? What girls? Are we at the boarding school already?
Nothing is established. I feel like this is the kind of game that needs a better opening cutscene, that rolls down the suspects and victims and actually introduces the characters we're going to be dealing with.
Finally, after I exited out of the game, it just stopped working. Now trying to start it up gives me the black screen-o-death. But nothing is actually dead--task manager says the game is still running, and keyboard shortcuts still work. I still haven't decided if it's worth my time to try and fix it.

I don’t get to write often about projects using RPG Maker assets because frankly, it’s getting hard for me to differentiate between dozens of similarly looking titles using flimsy plotlines filled to the brim with clichés. And then I set my eyes upon Introvert Quest and suddenly I was intrigued. Social commentary in this particular game type? Yes, developer Amaterasu Software has once again released a 2D “classic” JRPG that defies what was once standard for this subgenre. The dev team has some noticeable experience and judging by their previous (and future) Steam projects, they certainly learn from their own mistakes.
You will discover Bryce Han’s story through an increasingly more weird set of missions. They’re actually more like errands and RPGs in general, have made this trope an actual gameplay mechanic. Players have to get used to the game and take it slow, right? Anyway, Bryce is the titular introvert in this case, but after playing his Quest for quite a bit, I find him the most “normal” person within Sky City. Almost makes you wonder if it’s not a dream sequence in fact. Some kind of even more twisted Matrix, filled not with murderous robots, but freaks and caricatures instead. Well, let’s just pretend that everyone else in-game is sane and that Bryce has this shyness problem that he needs to fix if he’s ever to become a “productive member of society”!
Luckly for him, the psychiatrist he’s visiting has just the solution to this issue. Multiple ones, in fact and quite intensive. The errands reminded me of the Postal series, only that you don’t have the option of killing anyone and you shouldn’t either. Peaceful outcomes are the best and Bryce doesn’t lose his tranquility no matter how much he’s being abused (verbally, most of the time) by various NPCs. Yes, non-player characters are everywhere (an introvert’s biggest nightmare is human interaction, of course) and they all seem to berate our troubled protagonist. You’ll have to find out more by actually playing the game. Surely you don’t expect me to spoil Bryce’s adventure?
Nicely detailed and diversified but still RPG Maker standard assets. Truth be told, I haven’t played sufficient titles using this graphics engine, to notice much difference from one iteration to another. I couldn’t complain about Introvert Quest becoming visually repetitive, since Star City is skillfully constructed, both indoors and on the outside. City street, squares, parks and office buildings are all battlefields for someone who’s stepping outside his comfort zone. Couldn’t tell exactly what RPG Maker version is powering Introvert Quest, but I was pleased enough by the visuals to stop caring about specifics.
What really bothered me though, was the fact that I couldn’t take a single screenshot through the Steam Overlay. The imbedded frame rate counter worked (60fps, no surprise since this game could probably be run by pre-smartphone era devices as well) but no option of actually opening the Overlay or taking screenshots I could link to my Steam profile. And that is an issue which few Steam games seem to feature, fortunately. Screenshots are visual aids in my review writing process and also serve as an archive that can highlight certain gameplay aspects to me, even after many years since last playing the game in question. In other words, Steam screenshots are darned important to me.
Sounds offered the right amount of diversity and were pleasant enough. Soundtrack starts off with a few piano songs but later moves on to more modern tunes. No voice acting, but that didn’t come as a surprise given the game’s price tag and JRPG legacy.
If you’re expecting a lot of combat in Introvert Quest, you’ll be disappointed. You need to regard this title as social commentary mixed with satire while the interaction within it, rarely escalates into violence. Dialogues and quests offer multiple choices with entirely different outcomes. That’s the bread & butter in this particular game. There are several “combat scenes” which I suspect are just poking fun at Pokemon. You’ll understand after you play. Overall, I enjoyed the gameplay in Introvert Quest precisely for its unpredictability and quirky set of characters.
Any game that defies the conventions “set in stone” by its predecessors, will have my admiration. You’re not playing a knight in shining armor or a brave ronin in this JRPG satire. You pretty much simulate an average Joe, feeling the pressures of “modern” society. A place in which others have to explain to you what’s normal and what’s not, while being condescending at all times. Haven’t seen it through but I expect a bittersweet ending to this story.
I didn’t wish to rate it any lower because of that screenshot issue which is purely subjective. I’m aware most Steam gamers couldn’t care less for the Overlay or its uses. The story itself warrants a purchase in Introvert Quest’s case. And it’s also decently priced, even though adding some Achievements would draw attention from far more customers and potential players. Food for thought, devs. Just like this game.

+ Interesting storyline and characters.
+ Multiple choices ensure replay value.
- Limited Steam Overlay and no screenshot support.
- No Steam Achievements.

Iv really been hoping for a good space game and was hoping No Mans Sky would be just that game. My 1 hour and 30mins on No Mans Sky was filled with optimization issues and forced me to play on low settings that even then still had issues. After fiddling with that for 20minutes I decided to see what I needed to do to get my ship back up and running since they start you off with a crash landed ship on a random planet. Turns out their hints are pretty much useless and the things you even fix I hardly understood the purpose of. I wasted 12minutes fixing some pod near by my ship I first noticed needed repairs only to work my butt off and the pod doing just nothing other than turning on. I got a distress signal out, but what good that did as no one even heard it nor was coming based on what I knew. Wandering around I was lost on what I needed and what was required to get my ship into the air. It seemed like after fixing one thing and feeling the gratification of success so I could finally leave this one spot only got me a message that another part of the ship needed repairs itself. I ended up dying when I had no idea where plutonium was despite it was over just a tiny cliff where my body no lies. Thanks scanner with the range worth crap.
Dying is not very challanging or a fear either in this game. I died only to see my supplies floating in some odd shape and me spawning right back at my ship, so in short no fear of death in a exploration game, makes it feels a tad pointless. Rolling somehow is placed on the mouse when you move left and right which makes it seem like a drunk pilot is flying your ship. I had to get my sensitivity at 100% in order to feel any bit of control and even then I flew a few feet and landed only to hear my ship demand more plutonium again! Lucky for me I found that red gold and took off again this time off the dam planet. I found a freighter right away flying around a bit and landed only to relaize my 2k worth of money is not worth 187 billion that was required to purchase the strange stick like ship at C rank and so I left and headed for the starbase. God knows how much a S class freighter would cost I thought to myself as I was nearing the starbase. Flying was fun....to a point. Did I mention that I had to change controls along with my sensitivity to I could fly worth crap in this game? Whats with space games and flying mechanics that just seem horrible? Either way even with the mechanics workable I still had issues flying, but no where near what I had once before. Landing in the station I was greeted with strange creatures I had no clue about or what they were saying. Not bad and sorta fun I thought for the first time in this entire game. Thats 80minutes in. The strange tutorial or quest giver told me to get a drive core and just throwing my supplies at a vending machine I had enough to buy the part. So with a few minutes left I sped to a planet the quest log had me go to only to do two things on two different planets. Planet 1, turn on a becon that did nothing. Planet 2, find a log for something and then nothing....its like the tutorial or quest logger or whatever it is sort is half doing its job and half telling you to just do anything. On planet 3 I thought to myself as I was collecting minerals for the new flight blueprint thing I had been asked to build.....this is the game. It's a mining recources game that after you get something you go back and do this all over again. The wilflife I found in the game didnt interest me and felt more fake than real. The plants and everything felt generic and copied and god even with wildlife and plants the planets feel so empty! I feel like the only person to ever set foot on any one of these planets despite finding the generic human bases about the size of a small truck with the same generic look over and over again. I just could not take it and demanded my money back.
So that was my time in No Mans Sky, its a game I was hoping would be better than most space games. Eve online is about deciving and betraying people where all you go after is money and rich people own the game. Elite dangerous asks you to buy dlc constnatly and even then you cant get out of your ship other than going in a rover. Star citizen has been in the works for 5 years and still demands money in buying land and $45 to just buy one ship with no end in sight. No mans sky is sadly something that gave free updates, but requires so much work to feel less empty that at the moment its not even worth $25. Once they fix that maybe....but until then no space game is worth my time or money. Sadly No Mans Sky is no different. Between optimization, emptiness, wonky controls and much much more this game is just no where near feeling as good as it should be. Early Access Review:
This is a very promising game but still has a way to go. The core mechanics are in place but at present there is not yet enough depth or challenge to give this game long term playability. It's a challenge to get a profitable airport initially but once there (and once you learn the game) it's straight forward and the airport is pretty much self sustaining with no challenge left.
There are lots of great sounding ideas planned that could make this a great game - such as First Class meaning something, random events beyond weather blips, etc - but at the moment don't expect a challenging management game. For now this is more like a sandbox game where you can make a big airport and watch it run.
It's worth buying right now IF you're willing to watch the game grow and/or if you want to contribute to the community (including of course supporting the game by buying it!); and this is regularly evolving and being updated by the devs which is great. I've enjoyed the 10 hours I've plugged into the game so far and am glad I bought it. But as with any Early Access, if you're expecting a fully fledged game then you may be disappointed at this stage (Nov 2017). From the road map in 6 months it should hopefully reach a more challenging state, but for now only go for it if you're willing to accept a working Airport sandbox game.

Its the continuation of the previous two FF13 games and the ending of the FF13 series within the Fabula Nova Crystallis timeline of FF games.
Owned 2 of the 3 games on PS3 (don't have a hard copy of 13-2), rebought all 3 on Steam because I like collecting stuff. Unlike the PS3 version, all the DLC is included for free in this game, granted there is one Garb set you can't get here but you get everything else. Not as hallway-like compared to 13 which is what most hardcore FF fans complained about. I have pretty low standards when it comes to gaming anyways so disregard my opinion on anything that involves stories XD I'm no hardcore FF fan but I've been around it for some time, started playing when FF13 came out, Nova Crystallis is my timeline.
One of my favourite things about LRFF13 or as some would refer to it as 13-3, the combat and schemata system. You have 3 primary schemata slots, each with their own outfit, weapons, and attack sets that you choose to your liking. It still uses the attack gauge found in 13/13-2 but when the attack gauge is empty, you simply switch to your other 2 schematas and use those while your primary set recovers its AP. Also you get to dress Lightning up :3
The game IS TIMED, so you can't exactly take your time exploring. I honestly haven't played both the PC and PS3 version in over a year so I can't remember how many in-game days you need to beat the game in, but I believe its like 11 days? 13 days if you manage to complete everything if I remember correctly. If you're not a fan of timed events in any game, chances are you're not gonna enjoy running around doing quests and killing things within a time limit. Its obviously doable, and say you do fail, it'll let you start a "New Game+" which carries over all your garbs, attack moves, weapons, all your Gil(?), character exp/level and you basically get another shot at it, but with everything that you thought you lost.
All in all, I think most can agree that its a vast improvement over "Final Hallway 13" as the hardcore elitist fans would call it. Also because its part of the Fabula Nova Crystallis series and Fabula Nova Crystallis sounds awesome as ♥♥♥♥. If you can't tell, I really like saying Fabula Nova Crystallis.....

Different
The world ends soon and since God only can create things not souls you need to save as many as you can by doing stuff for people. If you break it down to the core you basically do a lot of miniquests under time constraints.
The time limit is prolly one of the major reasons this got♥♥♥♥♥♥on so much. Normally im not a fan either but it works for this game. Theres no intricate schedules for everything like in Majoras Mask, but things change and it creates a sense of urgency and impeding doom the game really wouldnt have otherwise if you could just fart around at leisure. Its quite generous anyway (having some practice from having played this on PS3 i ended up having several days with nothing to do anymore) and in the worst case you get to start over and keep your stuff and stats.
The combat system is different from the usual FF stuff too in that theres no party, you instead can switch anytime between 3 equipment slots with their own ATB Bars. The only thing inherent to Lighting are some special skills otherwise everything from weapons to "armor" to magic and physical attack and defense skills can be freely customized with those slots, you got free reign to make the most garbage and most op setups imaginable.
Another difference is that you dont level, there are no XP Points. You get stat increases from finishing quests. Those can be done more or less anytime in any order you want.  There are the big main ones you have to finish within the time limit to at least not get a game over (Quest chains with a boss and big expensive Final Fantasy cutscene at the end), side quests with either abit of story and background lore attached to em (not all available right away, dependant on which day youre on and somesuch), and plain old dime a dozen Fetch/kill quests from message boards (mostly more unlock the farther youre into the game).
Following the "No XP", how enemies come into play is abit different too. They drop stuff and money like in any other FF but the most important resource from them is probably replenishing your special magic points. Whats so important about the special magic points? One of the special magic abilities is a limited timestop youll have to rely on if you want to get more than the basic minimum of quests done. At the start you fight monsters to get by - In the later stages of the game youre basically a vampire harvesting them to fuel your time juice addiction. Also Monsters can go extinct - the last of its kind will be a supermook dropping good stuff but that also means you risk having places with nothing to feast on if you kill everything indiscriminately.
Think it also got abit of flak for Lighting being kinda sullen all the time. I dont mind - it fits the character and setting and its not like FF has always had the bestest Protagonists ever (Heyo Squall). Plus its really funny having the dumbest quests making you do the stupidest♥♥♥♥♥♥and Lighting delivering a somber monologue about the follies of mankind at the end. Maybe its even intentional at times? :O
The graphics are abit crusty but imo it still looks pretty good with a nice art style. Its a robust port, except the unlimited fps option breaks things.
So now the single low point: The parts of the overarching plot revolving around Lightings former party in the first two main chapters. You can deduct Lighting knows them but otherwise these dudes plop up once or twice, mope about their dead girls for abit then leave.
Then after the bossfight the big expensive cutscenes go into superham FF dramatic mode with sad pianos and Lighting is all like NOOO BELIEVE IN YOURSELF SHE WOULDNT HAVE WANTED THIS all the while im unable to give two ♥♥♥♥♥ because the only thing i know about them is Lighting knows them and now theyve been mopey for 500 years because their girls are dead because they died and its Lightings fault. Maybe id care more if i had played the other two games where they got all their development and backstories, my fault i guess.
In closing, i like this game alot but it might not be for everyone. Maybe if its on sale give it a try :o

As an added bonus, the game still runs perfectly fine on my potato laptop, keeping well over 100 FPS at all times with high graphics!
If you're looking to replay Half-Life 2 (and I imagine many people are, with the Ep3 leak and all.), I definitely sugggest going in fresh with this mod if you want to see HL2 look much nicer, but without sacrificing aesthetics and design as other "improvement" mods [*cough*fakefactory*cough*] will.

I may not have many hours on record for how long I've owned the game, but that comes down more to me obsessing over competitive online games despite myself.
This game is terrific. Absolutely awesome. It can be very unforgiving, and it's incredibly random, but that makes it so much more satisfying when you accomplish something. Some runs you'll essentially die of starvation - others, you'll end up in an otherwise unremarkable fight but that blessed potion was actually a blessed potion of *insert horrible death-causing status effect here*. Maybe you'll be a sliver of health away from losing but come out on top, only to have an egg hatch with an enemy snake to finish you off. Literally anything can and probably at some point WILL kill you.
Now, that doesn't mean that you won't do awesome stuff too! There are 16 different characters (8 different classes, slightly different male / female versions - slight enough not to♥♥♥♥♥♥anyone off, significant enough to make them play differently) which all need to be approached differently in terms of strategy. Choosing the correct skills based on your run, the strategy for the character you're playing, and dealing with the craziness of the RNG with everything being possibly extremely awesome or horribly deadly... It's Very, Very fun :)
I'd recommend to all!

Wazhack is a traditional roguelike (very Nethack-ish) reimagined as a 2D platformer/side-scroller.
The controls and the UI are streamlined, simplified and easy to use, even for people who may be new to the roguelike/dungeon crawling genre. No hotkeys to memorize or confusing menus. The graphics while simple, have their own unique charm. The music/sound is not particularly noteworthy but works well. The sound also serves to provide the player with audio cues.
The gameplay is a rehash of the classic "get to the Xth floor, get the thing" formula but instead of the classic top-down plays more like a side-scrolling platformer. A warning...it's not a platformer. It's a turn-based game.
If you play this game like Mario Bros./Sonic (which you can) you will die more often than you would otherwise. In fact, you have about a 50/50 chance of killing yourself. There are many times when it is wise to stop, evaluate your surroundings, inventory and enemies before making your next move.
Verdict: This game is +1 fun!

The premise is great: classic-classic RPG style adventure through a dungeon with essentially a DnD character.  Lots of cool ideas, perma-death, and ridiculous situations to find yourself in.
The execution however, I decided finally, is pretty bad.  The game has some bugs that can literally be game ending.  Considering every single action and item are generated by RNG, an entire game going haywire on what is FINALLY a good run can be about the most frustrating gaming experience you can have.
Example:  we are in a Co-op game and my friend finds a blessed scroll of remove curse.  This will remove curses from every item in your inventory.  This is during easily the best run we've ever had; 20+ wands and books each, multiple bows and arrows(witch and hunter), I had 3 fireball wands to start, it was great.  I give everything to him in a trade to de-curse, and EVERY SINGLE ITEM DISAPPEARED.  I was left with a blank inventory.  As anyone who plays the game can tell you, catastrophic events happen in game all the time.
Playing a game where one in-game mistake can be catastrophic with bad programming on top was way more frustrating then fun, and it made me angry I wasted hours and hours one the game and researching all it's silly quibbles online.
Future Potential = 9/10, actual current enjoyment easily say -5/10.  =(  Don't buy unless dev gets serious about making this game bug free.

Introvert Quest is story driven comedy rpg set in modern times. You take the role of Bryce, a troubled kid living in the city suburbs. After visiting your psychiatrist, you are put on a 3 day program to integrate you into society. The story is unusual but very intriguing. The game has tons of side content and a whole city to explore which gradually opens up as you become less anti-social. I think it's worth your time, especially considering the low price.

Introvert Quest is a completely different take on the JRPG genre. You play as a creepy introvert who is forced by his shrink to become a normal member of society. Your quests will require of you to go grocery shopping, eat lunch in public and seek employment. There seem to be a ton of sidequest and a whole city to explore. The game is dialogue heavy, but it's genuenly funny and well written. I would definitely recommend this game if you are seeking an RPG that is different from the norm.

Jurassic Island: A Dinosaur Zoo is currently in the Steam Early Access program and it's a tycoon style sim game where you must build and maintain your very own dinosaur theme park (Jurassic World anyone?). It currently has an IndieGoGo campaign going, which has nine days left. Doesn't seem like it's gonna get there.
First thing I want to point out is that this is another mobile port of a game to hit the Steam Early Access landscape. Not that this is a bad thing, but Jurassic Island does exist on mobile platforms for 99c, which when compared to the $5.99 price tag on Steam can be a bit hard to justify the price increase. Also consider that I haven't played the mobile version, so where a game like Minimon is trying to separate itself from its mobile counterpart, I'm not quite sure what the differences, if any, are.
It also seems the developer has made other games using this format of top town sim with a pair of games, The Terminal and The Terminal 2. So in essence this may just be a reskinned version of those games. Currently 'The Terminal 2' sits at a paltry 24% positivity rating on Steam and was released August of 2014 and to not much surprise Jurassic Island seems to be heading in the same direction with a 33%.
During my first look I went searching for a tutorial to get an idea of what we were dealing with and hidden in the settings menu I found "Game Tutorial" which promptly took me to a 2 minute video on YouTube. This isn't an effective way to learn how to play a game. So this didn't start off as a positive experience.
My overall experience can be boiled down into one word, broken. With no tutorial everything is a confusing mess. I was unsure of what to do or how to do it. I gave up on the first look when I hit a point and the game asked me to build an "Egg Mine" and it just wouldn't let me place it, anywhere. I tried to build some roads and the pathing system is impossible to direct because it was made for a touch screen, the same goes for the electric fences to keep your dinosaurs confined. Did I say dinosaurs with an 'S' as in plural, I meant dinosaur. I was only able to hatch one, because I couldn't figure out how to hatch another one, or how to get more eggs.
Overall, Jurassic Island: A Dinosaur Zoo is a broken port of a mobile game, if it worked there may be something here. That's not the case and it seems its bound for extinction(rimshot).

My second favorite game of the XIII trilogy (after XIII itself). The graphics are lackluster compared to XIII but not any worse than XIII-2, the music is better, the combat is better, and the npcs are more relatable. Although there's just as many item fetch quests as there was in XIII-2, LR gives you better motivations to actually go get those items and you feel emotionally rewarded once you complete the quests. The combat system is more fun than that of XIII-2, and on par with that of XIII: while XIII rewards you for good paradigm setups, LR rewards you a bit more for personal mechanics, especially for the final boss fight of the game (perfect guarding oboy). I'm a bit iffy on the doomsday clock - it bothered me a lot during my first playthrough because I'm a completionist but not a confident gamer, but if you just throw away your pride and follow a walkthrough (partially or completely) then you'll have plenty of time left over.
For those who wonder about story and characters - if you liked the characters of Lightning Farron, Hope Estheim and Snow Villiers from the first two games, definitely get this game. I feel like LR's story was mostly written for those three characters. Of course, other characters also return, but I didn't find their storylines in LR to be nearly as compelling.

Final Fantasy is my all time favourite game series, but this is one entry that is difficult for me to recommend. Deep down there is a good Final Fantasy game here, but in my opinion it's the few experimental game mechanics that end up ruining the experience for me.
In a lot of other RPG's I find it's really easy for me to get addicted to grinding through side quests for the sake of being a completionist - but LIGHTNING RETURNS really makes that difficulty. Availability of quests or their completion can be tied to so many different factors like what day it is in the game world, what events have happened, what time of day it is. What it boiled down to for me is that completing side quests just became even more of a chore, and I found myself having trouble completing many of them without the help of a guide.
It wouldn't be so bad if you could just skip over them, but like all games in the FFXIII trilogy I found there was a huge ramp up in difficulty for the final boss, so I would suggest you'll have some trouble beating the game unless you complete a good number of side quests.
I found the main story thread to be fun though, and the different environments you can to learn and explore made for a nice overall structure.
Still some enjoyment to be had if you're a hardcore Final Fantasy fan, but would definitely recommend a guide to help you move through some of the side quests more efficiently so you can enjoy the main story content.

A fun game where you control a Helicopter and either seek out and rescue allied soldiers by landing next to them, or by simply destroying stuff like bunkers, tanks, and sometimes other Helicopters with your mounted Machine gun.
There are various ways to extend game time, such as trying to complete the level in the least amount time possible, finding the Dog tags hidden in levels, and also retying levels with different Helicopters and Guns. There are 3 different Helicopters and 3 different Guns, each behaving a different way.
Along with the basic controls(Up, down, left, right, shoot), there's a "Pro" control scheme for flying, which it behaves more realistically physics wise.
I recommend this game to anyone who likes those Lunar Lander type rescue games, or anyone who likes some 'copter combat.

I think this game is a lot of fun. I want to play more but wonder if there needs to be more balance because I'm getting bored. I'm at a point in the game where in order to expand I need to have an additional runway. This whole game I've been very conservative. I've only hired what I needed. No addt'l workers. I have only 5 stands (2 small, 3 large). Take home ~36k/day. I have to expand to make more money per day, Either I focus on building more inside or stands or building more outside. I've already built all the retail I can. I have a cafe. Tons of news stands, several ATMs. I can't squeeze any more seating, plants or anything else for that matter with the space I have. If I build more stands my rating goes down because I have only 1 runway and I can't add any more to it without constantly causing delays. People get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I lose contracts. So then building a new run way it is. Okay, so a runway is 100k, plus I need lights because my contracts have night flights. So, 25k more. Now I need to get to that run way. Lets see, a taxiway block is 18k per square. I need minimum 9 for the size of the runway and 2 more to connect. So 198k. Alright. Now I need to get to that runway from my current structure. That's at least 4 more taxiway blocks, plus I'll need a turnaround to keep things going. So, lets say 4 more. 144k. So 125k for runway and lights. 342k in taxiway (<-- this seems super unbalanced). So just to get a new runway plus taxiway I need ~$467k. I make 36k a day. It would take about 13 days to get there. I mean if that's what it takes, that's what it takes. I guess I could fire staff to reduce my hourly. But they do stuff now and if I fire them, I risk losing customer satisfaction. I also could focus on fuel delivery, but that opens a whole other can of worms with research, the money and time involved there. Plus the facilities and assets required. I would rather not feel like I have to put the game at full speed and walk away just to make progress due to my perceived monetary restrictions.
From that perspective, the game doesn't suck me in. I've otherwise had a ton a fun playing. The building and staff mechanics remind me a lot of Prison Architect, another favorite of mine.
Future Recommendations:
-What about creating more zones like an executive center, first class dining or first class seating areas?
-Not sure how this would even work, but 2 floors would be cool. Look at software inc. They did multiple stories well IMO.
-Allow for multiple drop off and pick up areas. Having only one in a large airport just doesn't seem right. Passengers should be able to be dropped off at the ticketing center closest to their drop off zone. Maybe this can be a feature that comes with advanced ticketing?
-Build-in mechanics to support construction zones to prevent non-secure areas and freaked out passengers. I get the process of requiring all passengers to go through security if something becomes non-secure. But that leaves at minimum only 2 hours to build without passengers. If you have a full schedule, passengers start arriving at 1:45 AM and last flight is around 10-11pm depending on delays. In order to build foundation (which you guessed it, is also super expensive) you can only do a little at time because of a) monetary restrictions and b) you otherwise risk creating a non-secure environment for passengers, c) the # workers you have and where you build in conjunction to delivery zone depends how fast things build 2 only 2 hours. Even behind the fence when you're constructing they freak out (get stuck) if there's an open wall to the outside. Maybe make it so that as part of the game you have to create construction zones ahead of building, so passengers don't freak out and wouldn't have to empty the whole airport mid-day for a full security check (yea, that happens, and it sucks). In real life there's construction going on at an airport at any given time and passengers aren't affected, generally. Construction zones would force proper planning and restrict passengers from entering, IMHO.

Yes. Running with Rifles is such a good game. It is the perfect blend of Battlefield's massive battles and frantic action and Arma's slower, more tactical gameplay.
PROS
-Campaign is super cool. Instead of being a story, you are put right into a massive battle that spans all maps. It really makes you feel like you are contributing to something, not just put in a random battle
-Great variety of maps
-A unique rank up system where you climb the chain of command on the field, unlocking new guns. new radio calls and squad members
-A good balance between too tactical and action packed
-Good AI. They will actually use the radio and call for air strikes, paratroopers and more. They will sometimes talk to each other on long trips across the battlefield, which really adds to the imersion. AI drivers are smart most of the times. They will preform manuvers like flanking, rushing and retreating to prevent stalemates
-Dynamic inventory. Things that you can pick up will show up as you move close to them in the inventory menu. Very easy to use
-Total non-linear battles. There will always be more then one battle taking place
-All maps can be played in singleplayer, co-op and pvp
-Mod support
-Cheap price
-Stealh feels realistic and satisifying. It's not some AC bullcrap where enemies will stare at you for 5 seconds and then decide they didnt see you. Gunshots are heard when they should be heard.
-Pretty hard. RWR does not try to help you out in any way, which I think is it's strongest point. When you start off, you are a private. A private cannot tell a sergeant to get out of a vehicle if he needs a ride. Absoloutly no hand holding.
-No microtransactions of any kind. No lootcrates or purchasable in-game currency. Just one DLC.
CONS
-Kind of dead. Not much content in the workshop.
-No way to join a friends squad
-Some vehicle physics seem off, like how you will bounce off a rock if going fast enough.
-Not many vehicles. Really only the basics. Tanks, jeeps, ACPs, Hummers, Boats. No air vehicles.
TLDR
Running with Rifles is one of my favourite shooter games. Quite alot of content for 16$. Definitly deserves a spot in any fan of the Battlefield series.
9.5/10

I played roughly two hours of this game and I believe I got a decent handle on its controls and concepts. As it states in the decsription you are simply a single soldier in a big war. The more of the enemy you destroy the more experience you earn and the higher your rank becomes. Increasing your rank unlocks new weapons and allows you to command more soldiers in your squad.
Thats pretty much the game right there. You run around a map in an isometric top-down arena battling decent AI. I'm not recommending this game as it simply doesn't do much and what it does it does poorly.
Gunplay is simple but made difficult due to poor camera angles. The vast majority of the weapons are locked behind an XP wall and require a secondary resource called RP to acquire. RP is a resource you gain by looting bodies of blue items, whiskey, chocolate, ipod shuffles, gameboys etc that you then take back to your base and turn in at the armoury. The issue with this is that it breaks the flow of gameplay and, since everytime you spawn with a custom loadout beyond the basic rifle of your faction, you use RP the resource quickly runs out. Once you level to corporal and acquire a radio you can call in fire missions that also requires RP.
It seems like a major oversight to have a vital resource requiring you, the player, to break off combat/leading your squad, to run around the battlefield (while getting shot at) to loot items then run to the nearest armoury and offload the loot.
The squad based tactics are abysmal. You press page up to order ai infantry to join your squad, as I only made it to corporal before deciding to refund the game I was only able to have one soldier in my squad. There is no way to issue orders to your soldiers, you can't customize their equipment, you cannot use them tactically or order them to bring vehicles/gather blue loot. You just open your squad to random infantry below your rank to join you and then run to the battlefront and just hope the AI can handle it from there.
It's a barebones battle sim. Get it on sale or give it a pass.

This is a fabulous little game (4.5 out of 5), reminding me of a mix of Choplifter, Fort Apocalypse and a little Desert Strike, with bright colors and a nice 2.5D voxel-look. This game is among my current top favorites. It allows for a quick round or two-three trying to complete a map/mission, so is quite inviting for casual play. The controls need a little getting used to, but once you've finished one or two maps they do feel natural and add to the feel of the game (I'm using gamepad controls).
Basically there are two "styles" of play, sometimes mixed in one mission: what I would call "normal flight" where one rescues soldier or brings in equipment while bringing down or avoiding enemy fire, and "fort apocalypse" mode where one navigates the heli through cavernous parts. There are in total 25 maps/missions for now. My favorites are the ones that require a little planning on taking down the enemy in the right order to be able to survive the mission. I care a little less for the "fort apocalypse" parts because I like flying that chopper, not inching forward (although once more practised, one can fly through caves with higher speed).
Completionists can try to finish every mission for silver or gold medals, and collect up to five extra items per mission that give rise to soldier dog tags. I feel the game is fun enough to attempt this.
The game has a cool intro screen by the way, with the heli blades spinning in slomo. Bottom line: recommended!

This game is not a masterpiece but it delivers what you'd expect from a standard HOG.
I liked the narrative. It was intriguing and I kept reading bits and pieces of letters and diary entries to gain more knowledge about the past. I was definitely invested in the story and the only thing I have to criticize is that the player doesn't have to be too bright to solve the "mystery" on his own. From the point I realized this, the game just turned into a puzzle-solving game, although the plot wasn't downright boring.
There are a few mislabelled items and sometimes I had to click EXACTLY at a specific spot to get an item, which can be frustrating. Sometimes I simply missed the spot, assumed I was doing the wrong thing and was stuck even though I could've solved it right then and there.
For me personally that wasn't much of an issue since this is a rather common thing among HOG. But I can understand that for other people this factors into how much they're willing to spend on this game.
The puzzles weren't particularly challenging either, but I suppose it's difficult to find the right balance. What I consider easy, others might find frustrating.
I really liked the map in this game. I got to explore a few places and it never got out of hand. I've played games where new paths open up left and right and you're stuck in a maze and overwhelmed by all the places you can go. This game kept it rather linear and still provided a map to give an overview.
The cut scenes felt a little ridiculous at times, but again, to me that's fine. HOG to me simply mean puzzle solving and a little narrative on the side. If I want a story-driven game with good cutscenes and voice-acting, I'd definitely not choose a HOG.
The graphics were fine too. Not out of this world, but fine.
The only thing I really disliked about this game was the music. It is one track playing on a loop over and over. This irritated me to a point where I simply took off my headphones and only listened during the cut scenes.
This game really could have been longer but given the narrative, it was quite all right to end where it did.
I personally enjoyed it and would recommend it, but I can understand that others would not enjoy it as much - particularly anal people.
It wasn't a GREAT game or anything amazing, but it's fun and relaxing and I like looking for hidden objects and exploring some settings, just a bit of point-and-click for a calm weekend afternoon.

With a flood of HO games (not that I'm complaining), this is one of the better ones if you're looking for something to take up some time without being frustratingly difficult. Clocking in at over three hours, you get a lot of time in with this one and the overall quality is quite good.
The art design is up to par with HO games. Everything is hand painted and looks as good as would be expected. The story is actually pretty good. At its core it's a believable revenge tale that doesn't rely on superstitious hocus pocus like a lot of HO games do. All achievements are story-based, so you'll get all of them during playthrough. Hints are simply that - hints - that don't punish you by denying you achievements because you dared to ask for help. And what little voice acting is in it above par for most HO games.
If there is one big negative it's that this game was clearly not properly translated for the American market. There are many HO items that won't make sense to some Yankees. For example, "electrical tape" became "friction tape". (Both are available in the US but in all of my years of home improvement I've never heard of friction tape before now.) A "frame" was not a picture frame or anything similar but was instead some item that I couldn't identify. Vinyl (as in audio records) was spelled "vinil" (French? Brazillian?) Fretsaws are more likely to be called "hacksaws" in the US. "Fetters" are more likely to be called "shackles". And in irony of ironies, a statue of an American football player is identified as a soccer player! There are a few more examples, but you get the idea. The ending was rather abrupt and some of the backstory wasn't explained, but you can make assumptions from what was presented.
Still, this was one of the better HO games I've played, and I've played a lot. It was straightforward, more logical than a lot of HO games, not very punishing (which can be refreshing), and a decent way to spend a few hours. If you like HO games, buy this.

I remember playing
some time ago - another HOG published by Alawar, yet ended up in the repertoire of RunServer for some reason or the other. That game left me with a bad taste in the mouth, so I wasn't expecting much of a miracle from this one either.
presents a somewhat similar experience with the small developer team Far Mills + MysteryTag, and with a more mystery, less supernatural undertone... ending up quite supernatural anyhow. Sure, it has a better environment mapping and far longer gameplay stored, but it is similarly halfway done. Now that I played the game, it is safe to declare that it is 2/2 miss for games hailing from RunServer catalog.
We are a random lady detective - detective Kelly Wells, if you are awfully curious - invited to investigate the kidnapping of Emily Lynch, a young women recently disappeared near Hope Lake. Why we are to be sent out to the woods by the sheriff of the area, in the middle of the night, without arms or backup to track a kidnapper exceeds me, yet here we are. Apparently, there was an old boarding house run by a mean Mrs. Braun back in its day in the area, and our investigation conveniently leads us to the said boarding house. We are soon to discover the involvement of a well nurtured psychopath in this kidnapping, in an attempt to exact revenge for an old crime. Be warned, supernatural - even though not the richly depicted kind - is yet again the primary element of this half-baked story.
Okay, again for the record, I actually love hidden object games. I'm all in for some mindless entertainment when it comes to sparing an afternoon to fetch some items and solve some basic puzzles with a story undertone. Yet, even I expect a certain quality set within the boundaries of the genre! The story is ridden with countless logic errors, undermining the skill and IQ level of both our detective, and the perpetrator. Every turn we take, we basically stumble upon the mystery perpetrator, and he manages to escape by a neck - 6 times or so - yet he still keeps running about without destroying the evidence, hiding the kidnapped girl or dealing with the detective properly. Oh, come on! It's a single woman with a .38 in an abandoned house in the middle of the woods, which you supposedly spent all your life in! What kind of a bad guy you are? This guy is a dozy, I tell you.
The display is the better part of this game, with decent artwork and somewhat appreciable atmosphere. Voice acting is subpar - do not expect lip-synch or anything - and there is only one soundtrack piece running in the background again, and again, and again... Now, that gets annoying pretty easy. Illustrations are not various, but they are quite alright. One would prefer better cinematic pieces though, considering the tone and the atmosphere.
Gameplay is nothing extraordinary. It is your millionth HOG, with wrongly labelled items on awfully shady environments at every scene. Every single HOG scene that I encountered included a wrongly labelled item or two, so after a while, I started clicking on random items until the scene is done, considering there is no misclick penalty either. Puzzles? They are all really easily and some are only time consuming. Nothing creative or even remotely challenging. Okay, let me state you one favorable factor: there are lots of areas interconnected with a decent map that would present you available action indications. So, there is no backtracking at all - which would be a huge plus in this genre normally. Sadly, it is not enough for me to recommend the game.
For some automatic achievements coming with the game, the full price is a monstrous exaggeration. I highly recommend for you to grab this on a heavy sale, if at all.

This game is a beautifully looking 2d platformer with creative puzzles and an interesting story. It is also however a game plauged with a plethora of problems.
The controls are frustrating and difficult, and although it features control support, the buttons often cease to function throughout the game. The Y button for example fires the bow, but half-way through the game it just stopped work.
Puzzles are vague and convoluted usually featuring jumps that require razor percision timing to complete. Puzzles -are- creative and once you understand what it's actually asking you to do the ingenuity of them is revealed; that's the problem though as the solution to puzzles is often not clear and the level design does not support a clear path to their solution.
Enemies are boring and lack tells, often just running into the player and doing damage with little indication of when they are attacking. Since enemies often come from off screen, it's sometimes unclear of when you can actually hit them. At one point during the final boss fight I became stuck between a big-slam-guy and little minions and was stun-locked into oblivion.
Speaking of boss fights, the final boss fight is single-minded, and a fight that could have otherwise been really cool and exciting is brought down to a level of being mobbed by minions while shooting up.
By the end of the game I just wanted it to be over. Blue Sheep is a wonderfully beauitful game and has some great ideas throughout. It desperately needs a better level designer and systems designer though, and I look forward to their next go.
tl;dr
Completion Time: around 1.5 hours
Graphics 8/10 - animations are lacking, but this is an otherwise beautiful game.
Gameplay 4/10 - Combat is boring, enemies are bland, puzzles are difficult, gameplay is slow
Sound 6/10 - The music is nice.
Story 6/10 - I'm guessing this game is about suicide, but I felt more and more as if I was fighting a nameless evil.

This game's great art direction, beautiful soundtrack, and important story are marred by unresponsive controls, dull AI, and level design on par with bad Little BigPlanet levels.  You get the sense that the designers got too close to it without running it by enough outside testers.  Instead of encouraging you to stop and think or try a different approach, the design is rooted firmly around placing objectives *just* out of reach and timing hazards *just* right so that only a speedrunner would get any satisfaction from it.  A typical player won't enjoy the bang-your-head-against-the-wall repetition.
The game's problems steal your attention from the experience it's trying to share with you, and eventually one too many missed jumps, ignored button presses, spongy attacks, or maddeningly long recovery times leaves Blue Sheep unable to recover.

Blue Sheep is a 2.5D Platformer-Adventure game in which you play as the “Outsider”, a young girl who is experiencing the memories of someone who has opposed “The Beast”. The Beast and The Influence are evil forces that seeks to destroy the people of the land, the beast often manifesting itself as a nightmarish shadowy wolf creature that serves as the games main antagonist. Shortly after leaving her home, the outsider finds herself wandering through a mystical, wondrous world following after the one that stood against the beast and learning what became of him as the story progresses.
The main body of the gameplay in Blue Sheep revolves around platforming puzzles ranging from simple get from point A to point B jumping puzzles to more complicated sequences that require careful use of game mechanics introduced to the player throughout the game in order to be solved. Some puzzles required pushing buttons to open up doorways or using a flower that allows the outsider to float over longer distances than she can normal jump or dash to. One puzzle in particular was quite confusing, involving a series of rooms containing sculpted stone faces on the walls with either all eyes open looking towards one of the two doors out of the room or all eyes closed. Going through a doorway leads to another face room, and the next doorway to another face room, and so on and so on with an occasional enemy. The solution was not very clear, and led to half an hour of trial and error before stumbling upon the exit. Besides that, the puzzles were fun and engaging.
The mechanics of combat are fairly simple as the only weapons available to the player are a wooden sword and a bow. Left click swings the staff and right-click and hold aims an arrow, while releasing fires the arrow. The arrow can be charged up by holding it longer to do more damage. Enemies attack the player a couple at a time, in the movement plane with the rest of the onscreen enemies in the sidelines in either the foreground or background cheering on their buddies in battle against the outsider. As enemies are defeated the others outside of combat will join the fray until all foes are disposed of. There is not much in terms of variety of bad guys to fight, but there is enough to keep things interesting, from bomb toting bullies to hulking beasts that do area of effect damage.
The sound design for Blue Sheep is a great example of how well composed music aids in the story-telling aspects of a game and can really assist in the immersion of a player within the game world. Blue Sheep starts this early by incorporating flowing melodies into the menu, with a little piano tune playing with each click on a menu option or back button each adding to a sort of melody of interaction that makes adjusting something as simple as the game resolution a pleasing activity. Inside the game itself, the musical score captures the adventurous and dream-like aesthetic of the environment and continues to compliment the setting as the environments change throughout the game. Towards the later end of the game, the music does a wonderful job of helping to convey the feelings of the characters and elicit emotion form the player as well. In the environments themselves, little sounds such as the clinking of tiles underneath the outsider’s feet as she hops across rooftops assists in bringing life to the world inside the game. In addition, the game features high-quality voice acting for the narration and story elements of Blue Sheep. One unfortunate sound related issue in Blue Sheep is that the volume controls do not work all the time, as in certain portions of the game the volume was extremely high despite all sound levels being set at minimum.
Visually, Blue Sheep utilizes a warm stylized art style that helps bring depth the game environment, from the lush green hills and trees in the beginning of the game to the stone temples later on. The environmental design is full of small details and accents that add to the beauty of the game, but does not distract from or obscure gameplay elements as the player is making their way through the game. The cinematic style camera following the character around the world of Blue Sheep was a design choice by Noetic as opposed to a traditional player tracking camera that is commonly used in games of this type. This was done to emphasize the narrative/story element of Blue Sheep while giving gameplay a movie-like feel as the outsider travels through the world. The character models used for the main characters and enemies are high-quality and unique in their design. The animations are smooth and varied, and when coupled with the fun and interesting character models, provided personality and a sense of life to each character.
Pros
1.	Highly Detailed, Beautiful Environments
2.	On-Point Sound Design and Musical Score
3.	Appealing Stylized Art Aesthetic
4.	Strong Voice Acting
5.	Unique and Interesting Cast of Characters
6.	Strong Storytelling and Use of Metaphor
7.	Story Contains Emotional Depth
Cons
1.	Combat Gets Dry
2.	Puzzle Solutions Can Be Obscure
3.	Sound Volume Spikes
4.	Can’t Change Settings In Game, Only In Start Menu
5.	Character Controls Not Explained Well
6.	Big Difficulty Spike at Final Boss
At this point it is pertinent to share some background on the developers Gabriel Priske and Ryan Kratt. Gabriel always wanted to make games, teaching himself 3D art at age 13 and eventually using his talent as an environmental artist on Dungeon Defenders 2. Gabriel was diagnosed with a mood disorder that manifested in episodes of depression and anxiety. Ryan Kratt was suffering from heavy depression when he met Gabriel. Soon the two started hanging out together and connected over their shared emotional patterns. During this time, Gabriel suggested that Ryan should focus his efforts into something to help move past his problems as he had done to help overcome his own. Taking this advice, Ryan began learning how to program and moved in with Gabriel to focus even further on his endeavors in programming. Eventually the two came up with a concept for a game that would deal with many of the issues that they themselves dealt with. Through this project and personal work Ryan began to feel better, with support from Gabriel along the way. This project was Blue Sheep. Both Ryan and Gabriel hope that Blue Sheep can make a positive difference in the life of someone who plays the game.
Yes, the games combat gets repetitive after a while and can be frustrating at times, but that is not the point of Blue Sheep. It is a game whose purpose is to share a narrative and explain concepts like depression through metaphor, and in this regard it is spot on. By the end of the game I was choked up, sharing in the emotion that was being played out on screen and echoed by the musical score. This sadness was a good thing, as it was brought about by empathy for the characters and the understanding of the metaphors that had come to a point at the conclusion.
Gameplay:    6/10
Story:	      9/10
Sound:           7/10
Graphics:       8/10
OVERALL       7.5/10
Blue Sheep is a game that is worth playing for the wonderful storytelling and the unique stylized aesthetic that it uses to do it.

Besides those two little problems, Dyad is a really interesting game. It becomes pretty addictive once you really get into it because there are so much things that get added in the gameplay as you play. But I'd like a option to have the game running on "Windowed no borders". It'd be super.
Let's get into things. In Dyad, you basically are a little... non identified thing with kinda tentacles (just what I think, maybe it has a name) and you must grab onto "enemies" being little light orbs. You must make pairs of enemies that are the same colors to boost your speed and get more points. That's basically the base of the game.
But it's not only that. Sometimes, you just need to make pairs and finish the level. Sometimes, it's a race and you need to finish is in less time as possible. Buuut, you can also start to "graze" the enemies by grabbing them. A circle will appear around them and then you just need to pass close to them. This'll build up a "lancing" bar, then you'll be able to "lance" on the enemies. This is like a super boost and you can hit the enemies like that to go faster and make the lancing last longer (I think? I'm not sure about this)
Those are the only things I tried so far. There must be some other modes and special things to do. Also the music and sounds are really great.
Since I always have my game controller plugged, I still haven't figured out how to play with a keyboard. But the experience with the controller is really enjoyable and easy to play. You just need the buttons and left joystick. And fingers. And hands. And eyes. And a brain. You get it.
This is the kind of game you'll want to play a level over and over again to master it and get a high score (at the time I'm writing this I hit the 9th place of a level on the global leaderboards after trying a level a few times). The fact that you can edit the way you play the levels after finishing them once ("remix") is really interesting and I really like it. You can even play a non-ending game just to, like, relax or practice without being scared of a game over or the end of the level. But I don't know what some of the things do though.
If you're epileptic this is not the game you want to play at all. As you play, the colors and lights become more intense. I myself am not someone who's really sensitive to that, but at one point I had to take a break because it was too much. I couldn't even play the damn level anymore (the game reminded me of Super Hexagon. Must take breaks while playing this or you just slowly become crazy). Also I'm someone who tends to change windows a lot when I play (to take breaks and all) and when it's full screen it tends to freeze the game and sometimes make it crash. An option to have the game windowed but without borders would be really cool. I don't want to touch the launching options because I don't know if it works just like TF2.
After this kinda novella I can only say "Yes, I recommend this game".

So I'm new to the whole SNK thing, bare in my that I am coming into this with fresh eyes. This copy was gifted to me by a new friend (Thank you, AGAIN! lol) That said, I promised I'd give a fair review.
I played for over an hour of online matches with another friend who recently bought the game, and let me start by saying that neither of us experienced any of the bugginess or problems that are being claimed by other reviewers on Steam.
We didn't seem to find any frame-skips, input detection errors, frame-rate issues or even the sound problems that some are experiencing in the practice mode. I tried different resolutions and video options to test this and the port was pretty flawless so far.
* People are having compatability issues
* People are trying to run this application on ancient hardware
* Drivers are out of date or lastly, a background app is conflicting with the game (such as an anti-virus program)
* They may need to verify their files via Steam
My system that was used for testing this game is: intel i5 2.0ghz (oc'd to 3.0ghz), 860m gtx 2gb, 8gb ram, Windows 8.1 to give you an idea, the game was steadily running from 58-60fps in 1080p. Some are claiming to only be able to run at 55-58fps with DotEmu ports. That was not the case for me though.
What did I find wrong? Only a few minor things that could have used polish or such. When I first started the game, I wasn't able to use 1080p effictively, I figured out that I needed to go into my hard drive's Steam files and change the compatability properties to adjust them for this. It worked and this is nothing new - many games need this to be done by the consuer, not just DotEmu games.
* The yellow borders are nice, I'd like for them to be added from the very start of the game (on boot up) Melty Blood has their cool borders, why not this?
* It would be nice to get those 2 missing features from the PS4/Vita ports - although they're not needed
* Brightness and contrast settings would be appreciated, the scanlines and the filter tend to darken the game quite a bit
* When I run the game from Steam's Big Picture mode, it reverts to Steam desktop mode
* The controller remapping should be able to map two buttons for one thing (i.e Start and select or select and kick)
Please upvote this review to make people aware of the issues, what needs to be addressed and the fact that not everyone is suffering from the same issues - in fact, it runs perfectly fine for some.
Am I satisfied? Yes and the netcode is actually great, In the 1hr+ that me and my friend played, we only had maybe 3 full seconds worth of stutter which is pretty good considering. So take this review, chew on it. It's up to you if you want to take a chance on the game. If it looks fun to you, then try it, don't let the negative reviews scare you, after all you have the refund button if you have any issue ;)

"Dear Lightning,
How's it going?  Good?  I hope so.  You might not know this, but I've been playing your trilogy for the past seven years if you can believe it.  Yeah, it sounds far-fetched, but I ended up becoming quite attached to this black sheep in a sea of white wool.  As for why, well, that's hard to say.  It could be that I was so enchanted by Hamauzu's themes that guided me down that long hallway, or perhaps it was the various interesting combat systems you had in place.  Ironically, though, and I suppose it's a bit embarrassing as well, but I've never beaten any of your games.  I have several dozen hours in XIII and LR, but for one reason or another I always stopped when I was getting close.
Then Square announced that your games were coming to PC, and with graphical enhancements even, and I was stoked.  And how could I not be?  While they weren't necessarily my favorite games in the series, they were essentially a second chance for me to beat these games that I put on hold back on consoles...
...but I don't think anyone was expecting the ports to be that bad.  Horrid, even.  Poor options menus, frame skipping (even on >recommended specs), crashing and bugs- XIII and XIII-2's ports were nothing short of abysmal and we really only have durante to thank for the fact that people are willing to give them a shot on PC today.  Then Lightning Returns came around.
LR's always been my favorite in the series, Light.  I'm a sucker for Action RPGs after all, and the garb/skill customization was fun as hell.  It was a lot of what I wanted out of ARPGs in a time when none were really willing to the distance, and even now it's pretty easy for me to get sucked back into this game whenever I reinstall and boot it up.  And even better, and shocking even, was that the port of this game blew the other two absolutely out of the water.  Support for Windowless Bordered, 60FPS, built-in options menu (still a bit cheap but leaps and bounds ahead of its predecessors)- it wasn't the perfect point, and the right conditions, such as populated areas or strong particle effects can slow down the game.
But Light, we gotta talk.  We have problems.  And those problems are you.
I liked you in XIII.  Somehow.  That game wasn't exactly written like Shakespeare but I liked it and I liked you.  And in this game, I...tolerated you.  Look, it's neat that your game wants to present these ideas of existentialism, how "good" is subjective and can be easily corroded and corrupted, and a fair amount of other subjects that it liked to preach- that it liked
to preach, but it's done in the least interesting way possible.  Every loading screen is filled with monologs going on about what happened and the nature of why it happened, every happening creates a drawn out ponderance, and while normally I'd just be able to ignore it, this is how the game is supposed to make us bond with you.  You, the one consistent character throughout this entire game outside of Hope, who I can only assume was turned back into a child to fulfill some fan clamoring...somewhere.  There's also Lumina.  She's a thing.
This might all seem a little harsh and the fact that I'm recommending your game even still probably seems insane, as it should, because a lot of the value that this game tries to create in regards to the viewer is emotional.  Largely, it's meant to build on everything that's happened over the course of the last two games and really bring things to a head for the characters found here.  And it doesn't really work.  Admittedly, people who actually were fans of the first two games will find some investment here, moreso if they liked the characters.  But the problem comes with the fact that you're more of an observer than anything else.   Most scenes play out with you gasping as if you...display emotion?  And your performance overall is rather one-note.  This makes these "emotional moments" fall flat because there's no build-up, no climax.  And this really carries over into the side quests, too, despite a fair number of their premises being particularly alright.  Each quest felt like I was doing it because it was there and I gained benefits from it rather than wanting to do it to see the story proceed, even if I was listening to all the dialogue.
That said, the gameplay's pretty great.  Props to the developers for somehow managing to retool the systems that were in place in the predecessors and turning it into a competent, if a little unique, Action RPG that I'd recommend any day.  For someone like me who's always looking for variety in a genre that has no right to be the same, this certainly scratches an itch.  Being able to create your own character builds and the control you're given with which to do so offers enough option that it can be surprisingly engaging, even on replays.
For instance, back on console I generally went for 3 builds that covered all the bases while doing as much damage as possible: one for magic, one for physical damage, and one that was a mix of the two.  When I came to PC I decided to play a bit more with the efficiency game, making a build for each elemental weakness.  What made this fun, though, was that they weren't all the same with simply different elements.  My fire build had an emphasis on dealing as much ranged magic as possible, meanwhile my wind build was evasive and only used ranged magic as a means to chain into my dodges, but otherwise it was focused on using wind-based physical attacks.  Because even though the game could most certainly be wider than it is, the amount of freedom that's here is a hell of a lot of fun to play around with.
Another ball in your court, I actually liked the world here, too.  Some areas were just plain comfy to be in, the scale of others was quite massive and just fun to explore.  While the stories told in these locations weren't always the most interesting, the world and the gameplay made them fun to do, regardless.  And while some may begrudge the time limit, for me it just made it feel as if there was always something to do.  I had zero problems with it myself, I never really felt particularly rushed and finished with all the story content several days ahead of time simply because the timer isn't particularly strict.  And more than that, there are a lot of fun small things here.  Like how, if left unattended, monsters can kill animals/people, and in some cases, people can kill monsters.  And how you can slide on sand (oh I had a field day with that).  And the amount of life that in the more populated parts of the world- but even if you weren't in the city or at a settlement it never really feels lonely because people are always out and about.
It's just a good time.  I've very select things to say about the story but as a fan of XIII up to this point, despite their being disappointing for the most part, I was nonetheless all the way through.  But there's enough here even if I didn't like the other two games that I could still play this and recommend it to most people.  It's a bizarre mix of FFXIII and Majora's Mask but it works better than any sane combination of these two games should.  But it does, Light, and you've got a good product here.  People should buy this, even at full price it's cheap (and a hell of a lot cheaper than it was at launch), but they should get it on sale if they're undecided since it gets pretty low.
Oh, and while you're at it, please tell Square to stop shoving you into every goddamn product.  You're cool and all but I'm pretty sure this counts as abuse.
Anyway, see ya in Dissidia."

I bought into the Delicious series after watching someone play the games online. Prior to playing Message in a Bottle, I played through three other games. Although I was happy to see some of the same elements, there were some differences that made me a little disappointed.
In Message in a Bottle, Emily's father and his brothers learn that their father, Emily's grandfather, is still alive. He was missing for 30 years. Emily's family goes to Italy in order to meet with him again. The meeting is full of disappointment and the impromptu family reunion is called off. Emily and her father go to each brother's house in order to push them back into the family reunion. Each location offers different time management levels that players go through. Challenges are available but not always a part of every level.
Pros:
- Graphics are smooth and cute.
- Gameplay is simple - all mouse controlled.
- Game gets steadily more challenging as time goes on.
- Different locations offer a little variety.
- Goes will with the rest of the franchise.
Cons:
- Emily's family is not the most likeable group of people.
- Story is ridiculous and not always engaging.
- One level has grape squishing noises that are irritating - one entire level is filled with the noise. Turning off the noise during that entire location was necessary for me.
- The last ten levels, which involve Emily's grandfather, are really boring.
- Grinding was necessary in order to perfect the game.
If you're looking into the Delicious franchise, I wouldn't recommend starting here. It's good for people who are familiar with the game and want to continue playing. If you don't care about the story elements of time management games, this might be an okay game for you.

As always, the story, graphics and game play are just as enthralling and enchanting as is now customary to this lovely cooking series of games and the mouse is as frustratingly elusive as ever :) 10/10 throughout.

This is a "diner dash" clone. If you know what that means, the next paragraph is redundant, but I had basically no idea. It's kind of like Cook Serve Delicious, mixed with the 12 labors of Hercules series. Time and resource management: Customers come into your restaurant, and ask for different dishes. Some are ready made, some you have to prepare - the CSD portion of the game. But your avatar is actually rushing across the restaurant, each action taking a bit of precious time and customer patience - the Hercules part.
So you have to prioritize your cooking, serving and cleaning routes for optimal efficiency, making sure you can bake a pizza, grab a bottle of water, dig up some truffles, clean a table, draw water from the well, send a goat to entertain your guests, play the banjo, and finally catch that freaking mouse, all as quickly as possible. A mad mix of reflexive clicking and quick calculations. My reflexes suck, so I found the game to be just challenging enough on the easiest difficulty setting.
I quit CSD due to the tedium of doing the same thing over and over again, and due to my lacking reflexes. This game
without ruining "your perfect day", which is a huge plus. On the easiest difficulty, at least, you can get 3 stars even if a customer or two storm out. Also, you get a new restaurant every 10 levels.  Same basic idea, but different dishes and moderately different mechanics.
Before and after each level you a bit more of the cute story about a family reunion and amnesia hi-jinks.  The story is basically amusing, and takes itself just the right amount of seriously. It suffers from a bit of over-reliance upon 1950's sitcoms "that's our character, ahahahah" freeze frames, but I found myself fairly invested.
Two odd things though - the food in this game is stylized and cartoony enough that it's unappetizing. I got fairly hungry while playing CSD, but not a single dish in this game got me curious enough to google. Also, for a game about the joy of running a family restaurant, the customers are consistently treated as a necessary evil / pests.
