Under 2-hour review:
After watching the newest Star Wars, I wanted to play a game about exploring exotic planets and finding strange creatures. After ignoring most of the inital hype and taking a passive interest on the launch contreversy I decided to give No Man's Sky the 2-hour refund period to peak my interest.
So how was it?
The intial experiance is simply unintuitive. Its hard to tell whats going on. Its obvious the creators of the game are trying to do something deep, philosophical and mysterious with this game, escpecially when they shove some famous quotes about death in your face every time you die. It really just comes off super pretentious.
You need to start by fixing a nearby spaceship. You need certain elements and items to do so. How do you get them? Figure it out. The game isn't gonna ♥♥♥♥in tell you.
Great, so the game is really hands off then. I should just go out and explore on my own then?
Eh... no. Thats a bad idea too.
You see, your starting planet will always be toxic or radioactive, meaning you need to recharge your spacesuit's shields to stay alive. Problem is, you need specific elements to do so. Where are they you may ask? ♥♥♥♥ed if I know. It turns into a time limit/limited distance you can travel from the spaceship before you die and need to run back for your lost items.
The game immediatly demands you go out and explore to figure things out on your own, but immediatly punishs you for it. Theres no time to get your bearings or take a casual stroll on this rugged planet you've awoken on.
This makes it damn near impossible to find what you need because you'll constantly be dying, losing all your stuff, and just being totally frusterated and confused because you have no idea what you need to begin with.
But surely the scenery would make it worhtwhile? Wrong. The starting planet is always ugly. I tried to find a decent one 3 times. Its horrifc to look at, all lumpy, deserty and will always have horrendously clashing color pallate.
But the creatures! Surely the creatures will be worthwhile!
Nope. They are all disproportionate and ugly to look at too. First creature I saw had huge feet and a tiny head, Creature that made me quit had a fish's tail, stegadon spikes, flew around on tiny tiny butterfly wings and had the face of a cat, constantly mewing in pain at its existance.
The point of the game seems to be to go out and explore a vast galaxy full of who knows what, finding things both bueitful and strange! But getting to the point where you can actually explore? Miserable. It might get better later on, hell it probably does. Theres a creative mode too! But I'm just not interested in getting to it. Its enterily unstimulating.
Wheres the lore? Things to discover, people to talk to? Put in voice logs, lost PDAs, whatever, just give me soem damn breadcrumbs to follow so I don't die of boredom from the pointless grind.
I also got Subnatica recently. If you want to explore a strange alien planet with weird, cute and/or beuituful creatures, that game is what you should be looking at.
I also got Elite Dangerous. If you want to cruise that galaxy in your own personal spaceship, thats the game for you.
Like the concept of what No Man's Sky puts on its tin? Try Starbound. Its really good. Lots to explore, the starting planet is pleasent and only a moderate challange instead of tossing you into a sewer of confusion and despair.
ARK and Conan Exiles are good games to feel a paced open-world exploration with breadcrumbs to keep you sane.
Anyhoo, ramble over
TL:DR: Boring game made by prentious people. As many have said, an ocean only an inch deep.

The NADI Project is a short story walking simulator puzzle game with moderately rich but certainly pleasant scenery and easy gameplay mechanics. Created by a small Italian games studio, it has a simple narrative that's been translated for an English-speaking audience. It will probably take you a couple of hours to complete.
Take the opening pop-up very seriously! Only select "Ultra" quality if you truly have an ultra system, otherwise expect your frame rates to be poor in places. (Switch it to "Low", "Medium" or "High" instead. No one's going to know and I won't tell!) That said if you do actually have a great system, this game will look pretty and will hold above 40 fps even at Ultra at the most challenging graphical moments - which is adequate, if not spectacular.
The game had some surprises for me.
Yes, the translated Italian to English spelling is cringeworthy at times. Yes, the textures are sometimes embarassingly misaligned. Yes, the inventory background is a poor choice and the items poorly sized. Yes, some people with lower-end systems are going to complain about mouse movement or frame rates. But you know what? This game is free, and overall it's better quality than some games I've paid for. A pleasant evening's entertainment. Recommended.

"The NADI Project it is a first person graphic adventure, in which you will face various obstacles to escape from your destiny." ––
"A person’s destiny is something you look back at afterwards, not something to be known in advance." ––
Essentially the story is an exploration game where you play in first-person mode as Jeremy, a man who crash lands on a desolate and barren island and starts listening to the voice of a decedent girl who once lived there, called Anna.
You start off on a journey throughout the island where your main objective will be to collect items of value which in turn can be used to explore further i.e. opening doors, safes and lighting up dark places. Your goal is to discover why the girl and her family where living there, though essentially none of your business but nevertheless, you're obliged to try and solve things for the better.
I say it's none of Jeremy's business because this is what I would rather have expected from this game: If Jeremy is stranded on an island and if he is the actual character in turmoil then why bother listening to dead people's voices. I would have liked to see Jeremy play the survival game in order to get of the island safely. Yeah, throwing in a few ghosts along the way could've brought some suspense and mystery to the whole scenario for sure, but Jeremy's hide still had life, vigor and spirit in.
He did manage to get off the island though, with the help of a cookbook and a two-way radio and after he has read Anna's whole life story in another book...
As far as gameplay mechanics, frame rates, mouse movements are concerned there is rather little to be said, but then again, it's a free game, takes about two hours to complete and you'll get nine Steam achievements. That's it. I recommend playing this title.

I'm basing my review without any prior knowledge of the game, the first time I've heard about it was in 2008, so I can't really judge what the closed beta was like. Yes, this game feels old and even for standards in 2008 it would've been antiquated. However, I used to play literal text mmorpgs and I don't have any issues with it feeling old. Not everything has to be an action mmorpg these days. Eventhough you can tell that Otherland MMO tries to appeal to that audience.
Anyway, having gotten that out of the way, the main reason I even have tried this is because as of right now, it stands at 5% positive reviews. The main issues of people are that it feels old, clunky and weapons not damaging enemies instantly (Projectiles have a travel time etc). Not a huge deal to me.
I have to slice up my opinion into two different parts for the game: the tutorial/prologue and the game outside of that. Since it feels like those are entirely different. I was playing the Equalizer class or whatever it is called.
The assets for the prologue are all over the place: You have somewhat decent looking things and then completely muddy objects. They also heavily reuse single models with the same pose over and over. Because the quality is all over the place, it feels like total garbage.
Biggest critique of the prologue though? The design of it. It tries to teach you the advantages of your 3 different weapon types, but ultimatively it feels like it's artifically padding the gameplay. You have enemies that respawn in a matter of 2-3 seconds, while you require 15-20 seconds to kill one of them. Not only that, but they also respawn around some NPCs and quest objects which only adds ontop of the frustration. All you have to do is hold the left mouse button and wait those 20 seconds for mobs to die. You don't gain any exp for them or at best you get 1.
I came out with around 170 mobs killed.
As if the Prologue wasn't already a huge♥♥♥♥♥♥move to the player already in itself, there's a big one waiting at the end of it. In order to escape, you have to enter a portal - which needs to be used in order to progress. Now you might be saying that this isn't a big deal, but it's on a narrow platform that is completely littered with enemies. Around 20 I'd say. You can't use this Portal on your own, you have to wait for players to team up with you who tank all the mobs in order for you to use it, or do it like me and just die infront of it, then mashing F to use it while you're reviving on the spot.
Never ever put hard mobs into your prologue that are aggressive and especially not a ton of them next to objectives or npcs that are required to progress. The only way this whole scenario could even work, is if you have a lot of players rushing through the prologue but I have a feeling most of them just quit before they even get there. I can't write enough how that whole setup is a huge '♥♥♥♥ you' to the player and I don't understand why it's in the game.
I think the only merit the whole thing has is that it tries to tell a story through 3D stills, it's an interresting concept of story telling and points to them if it persists outside of the Prologue. I doubt it though. The whole stuff about NPCs being there and a ton of mobs respawning ontop of them, are a complete disservice to your game. Let the player walk through that in their own pace without the persistent ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mob comming from the corner of the map to slap you while you talk with an npc.
The Prologue actually had me right on the verge of quitting, but right as I got out it (and thrown into the prison) it changed for the better. It teached me the usage of my AMPs in a fun manner and how to interact with things, it was fun because it didn't last a goddamn hour like the Prologue does and not having to kill dumb damagesponges helps a lot. You can already tell that the game feels entirely different than it did and right as you hit Lambda Mall it kinda makes you want to explore more. It's aesthetically pretty and the assets all seem consistent now. I even was tempted to almost just crank it up to 4K and make screenshots. There's even themed bars, such as one that has flying saucers with cows inside their tractor beams. Quite a lot of neon, it really suits the world. You get to hang around a little and get an introduction into customizing your own player housing. It's a decent, lively hub area, albeit devoid of any real players because I don't think any of the 8 people I started out with didn't manage to get through the prologue.
Quickly you get sent to your first island, which is thematically also pretty and nothing like the prologue. There's some annoyance with the collision detection inside caves, though. Quests are your average run of the mill mmorpg quests and you will have to grind a lot I feel. Also be prepared to be teached the same things you've learned in the Prologue again.
There'S also some quirks with the enemy AI that you don't need in other mmorpgs. It made me question whenever this is a bug or if it's there to actually promote switching your weapon (They have advantages and disadvantages depending on the situation)
I don't have much complaints beyond that and it certainly is a hell of a difference beyond the Prologue.  But I can definitely see that this doesn't appeal to many people and you really need a lot of tolerance to go through that prologue. The UI isn't very streamlined, but it's also very reminiscent of older stylized cyberpunk mmorpgs so I got used to it. Sometimes there's also no background music or sounds missing and as many people know, sound, feedback and music make up a huge portion of a game (Try playing Overwatch with music to off). Lack of feedback (Either visual or an audio cue) is also something I feel that leads to a lot of misconceptions and frustration.
Generally I think the game is playable just fine if you get beyond that point - if you're into this kind of theme and gameplay. However, I personally wouldn't continue because Anarchy Online would serve as a better cyberpunk substitute eventhough the aesthetics of Lambda Mall and beyond that are very very tempting. As far I remember, Otherland MMO was announced as a sandbox in 2008 eg. No character levels, open world, all sorts of skills. The way SWG, EQ, UO etc used to be. But now it seems to be just your typical mmorpg experience. Without considering the prologue, I think it'S recommendable even without the whole sandbox aspect, unfortunately.

A non-biased quick look @ the game:
A competent and unique 'Command & Conquer' style strategy game.  NIGHTSIDE is a four races sci-fi base building real time strategy game set on the dark side of an unknown planet where the valuable "green ice" resource can be found. Follow Adam, a human explorer, as he discovers the secrets of this dark world through a story-driven single player campaign, battle online against other players or team up against AI opponents or practice solo against a challenging AI.

Nightside at first brings you to a great, but simplistic soundtrack. It's dark levels feel foreboding, strange, and unwelcoming. It's factions, all diverse, with unique unit designs. Each faction seems to have it's own special unit with it's own special ability, and they all play very differently. Nightside's Hard Campaign is just as intimidating as it's level design, everything is dark and lit up by units with flashlights. You can reveal terrain on the map, but although you can reveal enemy bases once the fog of war kicks back in you'll only have an idea of where your adversaries are.
The Campaign separates itself between several chapters, and each one of them very challenging. My favorite part is the Nova Campaign, where you're put under certain restraints that make the game just hard enough. The Nova campaign isn't forgiving, as they seem to have the lightest/weakest units but have powerful abilities and cheap units. I really like the soundtrack for the Nova's levels, they fit well and add to the game's overall atmosphere.
Nightside has one resource, but it's complexity comes from the dark level design, and each faction's way of grabbing technology and advanced units. Nightside has a lot of charm underneath it's dark aesthetic, the units and buildings themselves bright up the areas around them, an interesting way of creating 'fog of war'. The game itself looks very fun and I've played one MP game, and even though I lost I enjoyed it a lot.
A solid RTS game, that has a challenging Campaign, very fun units, and diverse factions, all with a dark atmosphere, great soundtrack, and an intimidating shroud of darkness.

Man, I must be really bad at this game because I've never finished it, but I can't stop playing it. It's a rogue-like dungeon crawler with an interesting mechanic: Your enemies don't move unless you do, giving you infinite time to figure out what to do. Suddenly get surrounded by enemies? Look through your potions at your leisure to find one to throw at them, or cast a spell you've learned, or zap them with a wand you found. You start with nothing but a bit of gear and a weapon and absolutely no knowledge of anything outside your starting equipment, spells, wands or food, which varies from class to class (there are a ton of them). Each class has a male and female counterpart, but they are in no way exactly the same except for some overlap on stats, skills and armor. For example, the "fighter" class has a male Knight and a female Valkyrie. They both have armor, good strength, decent intelligence, good dexterity, fight mostly melee, start with decent armor, but the Valkyrie has a shield and has skills like sensing the curse/blessing of items while the Knight as things like Courage that make death harder for him. You also don't know what items/loot you find are without getting some knowledge about them first. Usually that means reading scrolls until you figure out which one is the identify scroll (possibly reading the scroll Destroy Armor in the process), chugging potions and hope they don't paralyze you or make you hallucinate, putting on jewelry and hoping you don't get choked, or using a wand and hope it's not cursed and welds itself to your hand. Items do not stay consistent between runs, so that blue potion that gave you health last run is now acid. But the game is super addicting, because you keep hoping for that one "good run" that will get you further than you've gone, give you just the right scrolls or just the right gear so that you can beat it. Apparently there are two "kings" with minions that you can eventually beat, but I usually die before then. You also have to make a lot of tough choices, like when having to decide whether to part with some items when over the weight limit or being unable to jump (like over traps) in the hopes of finding a merchant to sell it to soon. Also: permanent death sucks.
Pros:
+Good skills/skill trees
+Interesting classes and lots of them
+Tons of items, with items geared towards classes
+Lots of choices and you can take your time, so battles are more strategic rather than button-mashing
Cons:
-Permadeath. Make one bad mistake and all your efforts are wasted.
-Have put in 54 hours so far and have yet to come close to finishing it. Each run starts over fresh so any progress you make before dying is wasted.
-Nothing residual from run to run. You do gain more insights, though, but they are generally unhelpful (ex: when you have a ton of unknown scrolls, the one with the most is USUALLY identify scrolls...Gems that have special powers are always a certain color, like red = firestone, but it could also be a worthless piece of red glass...black potions are USUALLY ink and/or oil...etc.)
-Not all skills are available to all classes, so really useful ones (like the ability to sense whether something is cursed when you use it) aren't always available. I end up playing the same two classes regularly, dipping into the two or three others that I like on occasion.
-Some classes are significantly harder to play than others. Ex: Spellcasters are rubbish early-game when you don't know any/very few spells. By the time you get far enough to pick up some wands or spellbooks, you're already dead so it's pointless, so I hardly ever play them. Or, alternately, the druids are amazing once you get your shapeshifting ability, but you're so bad at fighting most of the time that if you're not in another form you're screwed.
Overall:
8/10. I'm going to continue to play this game to death until I finish or get sick of it (with nearly 60 hours already, who knows when that will be). I wish there was something residual from run to run so I can actually improve my performance, rather than waiting on luck or picking up that one good piece of loot early on that will keep me alive.
Edit/Update: After 118 hours, I finally finished it. I couldn't have done it without a lot of help from the WazHack wiki, because wishing is a mechanic that is EXTREMELY necessary to win, but the game doesn't really explain it at all. I went about 60 hours before knowing it actually existed. Same with copying scrolls, which is super useful late game. There are also items (bags) that I never knew were anything but plain bags that are game changers (the midas bag, for one). But seeing as I bought this game for $5 or less, it is TOTALLY worth it for 120 hours or so worth of play, and I can always replay it.

It's difficult to strongly criticize a free game, but this game does have some big flaws.  This game is very much like The Vanishing of Ethan Carter in both gameplay and design--except whereas TVoEC is a gorgeous, well thought out FP adventure game, The NADI Project suffers from mediocre graphics, painfully slow character movement, and an amateurish story that has plot-holes.  The learning curve isn't very difficult, but I had to resort to a walkthrough to crack the inventory system.  Be advised that to cue the narrative and to ultimately unlock the story (which surprisingly isn't required to finishing the game) you're forced to find hidden items strewn about the map and hopefully roll your mouse over the specific spot where they're placed.
So the game can be frustrating, but the developer DID attempt to create a coherent game with an interesting story although there are some noticable failures.  It's short, it runs fairly poorly, has some bugs, the plot doesn't make sense in some places, but it's interesting enough and it's free.  On a scale of 1 to 10, I'd give it a 4, but I'd add 1 because it's free.  If you're patient and like the genre, give it about 15 minutes--at that point you'll either bail or just finish it in one sitting.
If the developer reads this (or anyone who can give an explanation), I'd sure like to know why you bothered to throw a USB item in the game--it makes absolutely ZERO sense, makes the story confusing, and literally has absolutely nothing to do with how it is employed in the game.  It's one of the most non-sensical things I've seen in a game in ages.

SHUT UP HOPE.  STOP TALKING.  IM TIRED OF LISTENING TO YOU.
I loved FFXIII.  I didn't really care for XIII-2, but someone told me Lightning Returns™ was really good.  Great, even.
Well, as it turns out, the only thing I like about the game is playing dress-up.  Didn't see that one coming, that's for sure.  What's there to dislike?  Well, everything.  The combat rewards frantic button mashing and constant role switching to HURRY UP AND STAGGER OH GOD rather than any semblance of planned out, calculated, turn-based combat.  Hit this button (or really, just hold it), then switch, then hit this button, then switch, then hit this button.  And block.  You block sometimes, I guess.
The story?  I don't know, HOPE WONT SHUT UP.  Just kidding.  Lightning is literally the messiah sent by god to save everyone.  I know what you're thinking--"that sounds REALLY stupid".  Well, it sounds stupid because it is stupid.
In between Hope's constant babysitting of lightning (seriously Hope, shut up), you get a whole bunch of fetch quests around bland, uninteresting areas, sort of like a MMO.  The only thing that's different here is that there is no one around besides your buddy, your PAL, your BEST FRIEND WHO DOESN'T STOP TALKING EVER, HOPE.  Oh, and there are no quest markers either, and quest instructions are incredibly vague.  Haha, good luck.
Did I mention that you have to complete these quests to "level up"?  Yeah, sorry, no actual levels or skill spheres or skill system here.  You've gotta do all of these awful, boring, unintuitive fetch quests while Hope talks about his mom, and if you want new items, or new skills, you have to kill the same boring mobs with the same boring AAAAA-BBBBB-XXXXX combat until you get what you want.
All of these super fun fetch quests, and, well, the entire game is given a time limit.  Wanna complete that fetch quest so you can get some fancy new stats because uh, reasons?  Well, sorry, that door is shut and won't be open until tomorrow, and who knows when that NPC is going to show back up.  I sure as hell don't, because I uninstalled the game.
What was my (short) time spent doing in this game?  About 40% was watching cutscenes, 40% running around trying to find things for npc's I don't care about, 15% listening to Hope whine at me, and maybe 5% actually PLAYING the game--you know, actually in fighting mobs.
I hate this game so much.

It's a top-down shooter with a camera that can pan further ahead if you have a weapon and even further if you have one with a scope.
You basically run around and capture territories through hard fought battles that will take you through trenches and trying to gain a foothold there, to fighting from street corner to street corner, and even sometimes a full out assault on an enemy base or airport.
There is a diverse way to play this game be it run and gun, trying to be a sniper, to being a general of the army, to being a full on special operations guy being stealthy and sneaking around stabbing people in the back of the neck while they look at a picture of their family and say, "Two more weeks..."
The only way I can see this game being better is introducing more spawn types for example, if the map is an island you and your teammates should be spawning on a static boat, preferably a carrier, and climb your way down to a boat to ferry you to the shores of said island until you're able to gain a foot hold. OR, as another example, once you get to high enough rank you can parachute in to a temporary spawn point when a teammate calls for paratrooper support. Small things like that would be fantastic.
It's generally a fun and fantastic game and gains a smile of approvement from me.

This game has a great story and great concept.  The combat system throws me off because it seems clunky.  Fix that and you have an amazing game.
***** Added to review - 08-12-2016 ******
Since they migrated to better servers I can actually play the game now.  My button clicks and key trokes register.  Ther are still many bugs and the game still seems clunky.  For instance, Pressing G locks on to a target, but sometimes this doesn't work.  Locking on to a target made the combat tolerable.  I really do want to like this game because it has a great story.
Pros:
1.  Great concept and storyline.
2.  Beautiful art design.  I often find myself staring at the scenery.
3.  Not a WoW clone. Different setting than most MMORPGs. The only other different one is The Secret World.
4.  Not laggy anymore since they migrated servers.
Cons:
1.  Combat system is clunky.  I think they should incorporate an opnional Tab targetting system. There is an option to do this in-game but it doesn't work half the time (G is the default key and I change it to Tab).
2.  Some abilities don't do anything.  For instance, the Self Heal ability doesn't do anything at all even though I'm not at %100 health.
That's pretty much it.  Only 2 Cons, but they throw the gameplay off.  I will even overlook the graphical lag spikes when changing zones if they fix these 2 things.  Overall the game seems unpolished.
But this game is in Early Access, so I will check back again later and give it a 3rd chance in a few months.

TL;DR: A criminally underrated game (due to much hatred for the FF 13 series) that feels fun, fluid and like a breath of fresh air in the stale genre of RPGS and JRPGs, with only few flaws in it's foundation.
Let me first say that this might be a pretty long review. I am a huge fan of the FF 13 series - that is a statement that many people would already gut me for, seeing how saying that you like the 13 series is equal to commiting treason. I never found a reason to dislike it though - but this is a review for the third installment in that series, not an autobiography about my (maybe bad?) taste in video games.
After the events of 13-2, Lightning awakes out of her crystal slumber and finds out that the world succumbed to chaos. She is then tasked by god to save the remaining souls of the world, so that he may build a new world where all the souls she saved are reborn. From then on, Lightning plays the role of the savior, saving souls and people for the sole reason of guiding them to a new world before the current one dies after the 13th day - and the ultimate hope of God keeping his promise, the resurrection of Lightnings sister Serah in return for her work.
I like the story - it keeps you on your toes, has a few twists and turns and, if you played the old FF 13 games, follows old and working conventions. The side quests of the game are very interesting, in my opinion, as most of them have their own lesson to teach you about life, love and the inevitability of death. Time is important, and how you use it even more so - the game runs on a clock which makes you plan your every move ahead of time.
From then on, you run around in 4 open areas, following main quests, meeting old and well-known characters, fulfilling plenty of side quests to save the souls of the inhabitants of the world and battle monsters.
The battle system of FF 13-3: LR is a pretty unique one. You can switch between 3 garbs (think, classes) in battle, slinging spells and attacking the enemy head-on in an active battle system. Before the battle, you create schematas, consisting of a garb, a weapon, a shield, two accessories and 4 spells/attacks, between which you can then change in battle, depending on your needs.
I wish I could review all elements of the game in depth; since my review can't be THAT long, however, I will list my personal pros and cons of this game here and then drop a quick conclusion and rating.
- The battle System feels fun and fluid. You constantly guard from enemy attacks and attack when you have an opening
- Over 80 different garbs with different attributes and basic spells ensure there is a battle style (or three!) for everyone
- Every enemy has different behaviours, stagger requirements (essentially starting a phase where the enemy can't attack and you deal increased damage) and attacks
- The game offers the right amount of challenge
- Beautiful music all throughout the game
- The time mechanic, while not liked by many, actually makes the game so much better. It is lenient - you will have enough time to do everything in the game as long as you aren't too lazy - but keeps you on your toes and makes you plan ahead, which I personally loved
- Interesting story, though if you haven't liked the story of the two previous games, chances are this won't change, but it's unconventional for sure
- The improvement system for weapons and shields is restricted to New Game +, something I don't really understand. Until then, improving your equipment is not possible.
- While many of the garbs look and sound cool, not all of them are equally effective and many of them are downright useless and will never be used by anyone. Some garbs are just objectively better than many others
- Some of the fights require certain stagger strategies; while that is not bad as far as tactics go, it is sometimes unclear why exactly you can't stagger an enemy, even if the enemy menu tells you what you have to do. Some fights rely on staggering too much, which can be annoying (but also makes it a bit more tactical)
- There aren't many enemy varieties in the game - unlike FF 13 which had tons of different enemy models, there are only a handful found in this game, some even recolored; though the models are still very detailed and a joy to look at
- While the voice acting of the main characters is fine as usual (in my opinion), the many side characters can't offer the same level of consistency - they are often just bad or average
- While many quests in the game are at least somewhat interesting, there are also a few that I couldn't bother to care about at all
- If you haven't played the previous two games, chances are you will miss a lot of references and can't connect to the characters as well
Conclusion: If you have played and liked the first two FF 13 games, chances are you will love this as pretty much everything has improved. If you haven't, you should play those first, as otherwise you will miss a lot of connections and references - this game is not a good entry point to the series, even if the datalog tells you information about the history of the characters.
Aside from a few annoyances and flaws, the game is very fun and fluid and will keep you on your toes thanks to the (mostly) fun battle system and (largely) interesting time mechanic.
Personal rating: 9/10 (Amazing)

Cool concept. Very simple gameplay. Roguelike-ish (Die fast. Die often. Start again).
You play in First Person mode.
You have two resources: AIR and FUEL (short boosts).
Newtonian physics apply.
Air supply is counting down...
You are forced to think quickly and find the next AIR or BOOST 'bubble' in space, between structures. If you run out of AIR, you suffocate. If you run out of short boosts or miss your target, you might drift into empty space ... and like George Clooney ... suffocate, eventually.
Training Mode - gives you more Air and Fuel and lets you practice space suit free flight.
Random Scenario Mode - gives you random tasks to accomplish. Feels like an arcade action game. Something for the competitive gamer.
"Main Mission" - There is even a 'story mode' incl. (good) VO. Music and art style add to the atmosphere.
Yes, this small game 'works' for exactly what it is and wants to accomplish. If you want to contemplate about life and death (in space, or in general), here's your Buzz Aldrin experience.
If you just want to chase colored bubbles in space for scoring points - you can do that too.

Lost in deep space, the only chance of survival is making difficult point to point jumps to collect mid air bubbles of fuel and oxygen.  The choice to have a limited UI hurts the overall experience by making the player rely too heavily on pixel perfect clicks and long periods of waiting with nothing to do.

It makes me sad to have to not recommend this. I was honestly excited by the idea of the Death Rally game being remade and hopefully expanded. Instead what we seem to have is essentially a mobile game scaled up that has a lot of the words in common with Death Rally but feels like it misses on a few important cylinders.
Death Rally was a half race and half car-carnage game and it pulled it together well though sometimes a bit cheesy. Fun could be had as the races really felt like skill made a big difference and timing your mines and machine gun fire to destroy opponents in your way was rewarding though not trivial. Through the game, you got money which you needed to restock supplies like ammo or armor, upgrade your car a bit or buy new cars/weapons.
This version feels like the dumbed down iOS port that it really is. Money now only is here to buy upgrades to the car and repair it. The upgrades feel like they make almost no difference in gameplay (except armor which did actually seem to prolong life). But as a racing game, getting better cars or engines did not make me feel like I was going faster. I've read that even the best car with the best engine does not go faster than the initial car an opponent drives in a beginner race. It makes the upgrades feel definitely token.
There is also no real money management. In fact, after a race, the game seems to expect you to just spend all of your money since ammo is restocked at the beginning of a race anyway. New weapons and cars are unlocked after collecting a certain number of pieces scattered on tracked on dropped from destroyed opponents. It feels like progression in this game could be substituted for attrition. I remember in the original sometimes being in a bad place because I took a loan I couldn't pay back. This made decisions feel like they meant something. Also, additional objectives in the original again meant something since money mattered. Here, they are a yes/no box you click periodically and see if it works. It feels sometimes like an Office product had a pop up with the title "Fun" and boxes that just say yes and no appeared with no real context or consequence to the action.
Yes you do advance faster from placing higher, but it still doesn't feel significant enough. After all, winning a race seems to come mostly down to well placed nitro boosts at the end.
The destruction of opponents seems like an area where this could shine. Unfortunately, there are things in the way of allowing you to really get the full enjoyment from the experience. Your base machine gun automatically shoots for you (after you add your 1 additional gun upgrade). This feels annoying at best since you have unlimited ammo and it's not always shooting, but you have no control over it. Even better is in-race bonuses (repair, money, ammo) are in boxes that must be shot... so you have  to hope an opponent is in front of you near a box so you could happen to shoot that (and they not just take your bonus) or you waste some of your limited ammo.
This is a small gripe, but the in level bonuses do need to be shot and all appear at the beginning of the level. Since shooting can be wasteful and feel a bit random, this means that upgrades you need later are hard to get and running into repairs within seconds of the race starting is common. It just feels like a bad decision. The original randomly spawned them on the track, IIRC, and that was fine. This isn't a realistic game; why must we pretend periodically that it is?
Opponents suffer from what a lot of games have with enemies that don't have the same limitations as you. I've mentioned their cars are always fast enough to rival yours no matter what. They also have unlimited ammo in their nicer weapons compared to the 4 shots you get in some of your weapons. This is especially terrible in the deathmatch sections where destroying cars is the goal yet they don't have to worry about ammo limits. Additionally, they have health like you do. When you hit 0%, you explode and are done. When they hit 0%, their health bar flashes... and they continue to race for a while. Some number of shots into them later (or maybe it's time? I couldn't definitively understand the logic but it seemed inconsistant and like I wasted a lot of ammo trying to kill a single target), they will in fact explode. You have no real indicator of when this is going to happen though, so I frequently found myself passing them and hoping to get their drop on the next lap if they happened to blow up. Though they can still shoot you in this state.
Speaking about laps, one of the biggest places this feels like a mobile game is in the race length. I'm not saying I need long races, but I do feel like the fact that most races take <=1 minute to complete takes away from my enjoyment. That could just be a preference, though.
All this is not to say there is no fun to be had. I was entertained for a while. I could see this being more reasonable on a device without a gamepad or keyboard (I never did get my 360 controller to work with this game) like a tablet or phone where simple games are more acceptable. I at least wanted more. I wanted to feel like I had consequences or choices. I wanted to feel like my ability mattered. Instead, I was watching a nice looking (not amazing by any means, but it does look nice enough... if you don't look too closely at the textures) but repetative and short car chase scene from various movies. Things happen, but the ending never seemed to be directly related.
You can get the original for free from Remedy which runs on Windows (re-released in 2009); I feel that is a better use of your time and money

Death Rally will set you back $10 normally, and $5 on a discount sale which is still $3 more in quarters than I would have put into it if it were sitting in an arcade cabinet at the mall. Yes, it's fun in an old school mindless fashion with your little car racing around small repetitive tracks but due to the mechanics and swimmy control input you can't really "race" in any proper fashion so killing the competition is the only choice to get ahead.  Frankly, the controls are weak even when using the must-have gamepad controller.  You're never seriously penalized for coming in second or even last place, you just get less money awarded to you for the purchase of upgrades to your guns and car performance, and you can't carry the money over between rounds to help in purchasing the pricier goodies.  Sadly even when you do upgrade the results don't feel like a significant improvement.  Graphics are passable while the sound quality is merely functional; neither have flair or panache.  The game tries to create some personality in certain key opponents you face off against but they come off as cookie-cutter archetypes and pose little more challenge than the basic racers which ends up making them boring.  Boring and uninspired gameplay is really the biggest drawback to this game.  I played for 3 hours total and during that time I was able to fully upgrade 4 cars and the gatling gun weapon and once I got to that level I realized I wasn't have any fun and none of the other upgrade levels were going to get any more compelling and I called it quits.  Death Rally was a fun diversion but completely forgettable and only worth playing during a free weekend.  Save your time and money and go buy Renegade Ops instead as that game handles this approach to automotive combat a thousand times better.

Came for the Hack; stayed for the Waz.
Is it Nethack?  No.  It's a simpler, sillier game.  And Nethack was pretty silly to begin with.   It appears as a 2D game, but I think it's closer to 1 and half.  The majority of the gameplay happens on levels, with ladders connecting them.  Mobs can follow you up and down the ladders, no stairscumming here, but for the most part it plays like a 1D leveler.  With Nethack rules.
Mostly.  It's indisputable roguelike in its permadeath and its randomly generated items.  It's indisputable hacklike in its choice of items, punishments for testing scrolls and potions, and there are so many elements taken directly from hack it's beyond mistakable for anything else.  However, some of the most defining elements of hack are missing: prayer chiefly among them.  No more turn count, no more hoping your god will uncurse that item, and no more foodless achieves.  The E-Word is also unavailable, as are most of the options that were available from the # menu in hack.
But it isn't Nethack, it's Wazhack.  It's added so many new things, it's got its own flavor.  The cartoony graphics are fun, especially when hallucinating.  The different classes are really different, even the male and female versions of a class have different playstyles.  I've only been playing a short while, but it seems balanced and just the right amount of accessibility.  It's hard, but I don't think it's too hard.  If you play it like an action game, you will lose.  If you play it like a roguelike, you'll have fun.
It's not Nethack.  It's Wazhack, and that's ok.

Hello Sci/Fi ppl.
I'll make this reeeeal easy for you people: What NMS is and what it isn't for me (it will be apparent why i recommend this up front). There's one very important detail to note: I bought this game when the hype was maxed and everyone went batshit crazy when they didn't deliver. For me, this game captures the Zen of cruising in EVE, some fun (and mostly optional) survival elements, and a positive ingame environment.
This game is one big fat positive vibe for me. After the graphics update, it's stunning (and i'm running on some seriously low settings here). The soundtrack is direct opposite mood of Max Richter (sad, dark and gloomy), and a nice track at that. The gameplay is straight forward and soothing - even when it's in your face and the first few hours are a pain to survive on survial (cus i like survival sims, so why not add another good thing). It's exploring a vast universe and being surprised by the awesome worlds and funny creatures (which, luckily, have been improved upon after release). Now, there's also something resembling a story to the universe beyond atlas.
It's not a "get gud and shoot bad animalz all day yaarh"-sim, like everything else is. It's not massive fleet battles, even though there's dog-fighting and actual space combat (though, i've not gotten to that bit yet this time around). It's a game built up around exploring, and that is why it's good when it is. It is serenity.
Yes, this is very odd review, but it is exactly what NMS apparently is; it's very own. Don't buy this if you want to shoot stuff, be an evil space pirate and dominate the galaxy, no. Just turn away (and go play EVE!). Buy this game if you enjoy some "you"-time in a bright and colourful universe, a nice spacy soundtrack and the will to explore new worlds and get gut at that.

This is what an RTS should be. Simple mechanics, easy to use UI, simple resource gathering to allow for the main focus of building armies and wiping out your opponent. This game clearly pays homage to Command and Conquer and Starcraft with it's faster paced gameplay and overall RTS mechanics and that faithfulness to RTS's of yore pays off with a fun and addicting strategy game. With 3 different factions that all function in varying ways and have different strengths and weaknesses, there are plenty of strategies for victory.
Gameplay Footage:
The most unique piece of the game other than the very 'alienesque' worlds and units is the pervasive darkness that blankets every game. It feels like you're playing on that planet from the movie Pitch Black and the only way you can see the map is to move units there. The game also features a very indepth story line that makes extraordinary use of camera angles to provide a low-budget, cinematic experience. This game was a pleasant surprise and I definitely recommend it! I can't wait to see how far the two devs from Omnidream can go from here.

Half Life 2 was the greatest game of its decade.

I never understood what was so special about Half Life, but looking back once I finished the game it was definitely a pleasant experience, especially when compared to a lot of the rushed and not so good games we see being released today.

Overall my opinion of Half-Life: 2 is that it has greatly improved upon the foundation that Half-Life set while also immensely expanding on the mechanics of both regular gameplay and the story. Personally, I felt as though the story in Half-Life was rather lacking and that the gameplay felt pretty dated.
However, in Half Life: 2 this is greatly improved upon and the story has much more depth than previously while also involving the player more than Half-Life, which in my opinion is a big plus. The gameplay feels pretty smooth, but that's not to say it doesn't have it's kinks, but in general I encountered very few bugs.
Half Life: 2 managed to turn my opinion of the series around, so I'm glad I gave it a shot.

One of the better roguelikes I have played. Like many roguelikes, it is turn based. Unlike most roguelikes, there is a time factor going on behind the scenes that make some characters get more "turns". When you are hasted you get more. When you are encumbered, you get less.
Because the turn based nature of the game is somewhat hidden, you get the sense that it is a more action adventure game than it really is. Time flows by smoothly while you act, and it stays completely still while you do nothing. You can stop and ponder your move as long as you need before moving on.
On the downside, Wazhack has a steep learning curve. Perhaps the biggest obstacle to winning is the fact that Wishing is almost a requirement unless you are very lucky, patient, or both. However, the wish system is not transparent at all. Protip? Dip coins in the well. The wiki page on wishing is recommended reading for you. Nothing else, just the wish page.
The magic system and weapon system is involved. Magic falls on two diametrically opposed scales. Light versus Dark and Life versus Death. THere are five levels available on each scale, and you cannot have more than 5 total between each side. Since some spells are Level 4 and need Level 4 to use to full effect, fully mastering all forms of magic is impossible. Weapons work in a similar way; there are only so many 'upgrades' available for your spell and weapon skills, and once you run out that is it. However, weapons have no opposition; each type has 5 levels of skill.
Like a true roguelike, identifying items and figuring out their properties is a huge part of the game. Don't be surprised if you put on a cursed item that won't come off really quick into the game. It happens. Curses can be removed, though so don't despair. Read the scrolls until you find the one that removes curses.
Ah, yes, about that. What color potion has what effect (same for scrolls, wands, types of jewelry) change from one character to the next. The game randomizes it. The only constants I have seen in potions is that potions of oil and ink are always black, and potions of water are always clear. However, there is also one randomized clear and one black potion in the dungeon. Have fun in the dungeon! Or is it the fungeon?
(Overall 8/10, Story 2*/10, Gameplay 9/10, Graphics 6/10, Sound 6/10, Replayability 10/10)
*I don't include story in the final rating of roguelikes

text: I've never really been a fan of MOST RPGs, generally because I don't have an interest in things revolving around knights, magic, princesses, etc. However, RPGs that deal with other subjects and fantasy settings than the standard D&D-esque fare are generally to my liking. This game falls into that category. While I admit I am about 10 years behind in reading the Penny Arcade webcomic, back when I followed it fairly religiously it was great and I enjoyed it. This game is pretty much what you'd expect as far as Penny Arcade humor, personalities, etc. The gameplay is great and the story parodies HP Lovecraft themes as well as has it's own style in that it merges the early teens to thirties Lovecraftian times with a just right pinch of steampunk; pulled off so well that I, as someone who gags at having steampunk genre things forced at me constantly, actually enjoyed the elements of the genre in this game. It just seemed to fit. Overall the game isn't very long, if you didn't take a break you could win it in a day or faster, but it does of course have three other sequels and was meant to be released in 'episodes' so it makes sense and is to be expected. There are plenty of upgrades to attacks as well as weapons for characters, and there are plenty of interesting areas and situations to get into to keep you entertained through your journey. I will say though that I have owned this game for a long time and was not able to actually finish it until yesterday completely because my old desktop's videcard had some sort of critical error glitch at the final boss that prevented me from beating him because not long after starting the battle the game would simply crash. I wish I remembered what videocard I had so that I could warn other users that had it about the glitch, so sorry for that. I of course since I beat it, have had no issues with any glitches or crashes on my newer desktop. Anyways, all in all it's a fun and fairly casual RPG with a good story and I would reccomend it to anyone looking for an RPG that isn't necessarily all swords and scorcerers. Though, there is a bit of dark magic in the game, it all goes along perfectly with the Lovecraftian theme and associated cultists. So no worries there. :P

But probably the most impressive example of their attention to detail has to be in the options panel. These sly characters purposely set the mouse scroll speed so fast it takes a true gamer to master the challenge of actually getting the option controls open. But there is a further easter egg, because you find there is NO SCROLL SPEED CONTROL! Now how perfect is that? Just exactly what you would expect of some 1995 game that came on both 3.5" and 6" floppys in the box!
tl;dr
These guys built a masterpiece of parody, even though they released it in 2010 you would never know. You would think it is much much older.

Heldric - The legend of the shoemaker is a game that has great potential. The king has left your kingdom and you step up to the role of a knight and defend your city. This is a different take on tower defenses, because you have a main character to take control of and wreck the enemy. Build up your city and defend it with your fellow villagers. Place defenses and buildings in between waves of attackers and upgrade those buildings to help you overcome the enemies. Not every level is the same and the enemies get progressively harder, making you have to change your strategy as you progress. I would recommend this game if you have extra cash and you like hack and slash/ tower defense games. You have both a sword as well as a bow/arrow in your arsenal, you will definitely need both to defeat the different types of enemies you face. The only negative comment I have for this are the controls for the main character in battle, it isn't as smooth as I'd want it to be, but it doesn't ruin the game. The more I play it, the more I enjoy it.
tl;dr Try it, I like it, you might too.

I thought it might be nice to add a little more about the units and race trade offs: some of this is related elsewhere, but having it all in one place is helpful.
Nova:
All buildings must be landed before use, but can be moved and relanded.
Three ground units: two attack air and ground, the mid-sized one only attacks ground. The smallest ground units are really fun for harassment of enemy extractors, and are almost invisible.

Three air units, the smallest one only attacks air. The biggest unit for this race is a Flagship, which of course, flies.
There is a special drone which can disable weapons in the opponent's army and also attacks ground.
The big defense for the mothership is a drone release similar to SC2 carriers.
There is a special ability for the probes which releases three small "flashlight" drones, which move in sync with the probe. It has enough range that parking the probes near your enemy and using the drones is effective.
YX:
This is a sort of "Transformer" race, with the most flexibility (everything is built out of the same building blocks "Cells", which are mobile). A not entirely bad option with this race is to build one probe and a ton of cells and then tailor your army once you know what you are facing.

Buildings are not mobile, once built, but can be split back into cells.
I think you have to build ground tech before air, but you have the option of scrapping the building, so it's not as big of a deal as with Nova if you want to go all air.
There is a special ability for one of the midsized units which bumps up how hard adjacent units hit.
The mothership defense is a shockwave with decent area.
The light option for the probes is a scanning ability, which basically gives a really big circle of vision around the probe.
The big unit for this race is a ground unit, so a little easier to counter than the Nova and Human flagships.
The upgrades for YX have more levels than for the other races, not sure if that means they can ultimately hit harder.
Human:
All of the human buildings are mobile, so you can have fun with moving your base around, and the "static" defenders are easier to get into position. The units are more limited for this race in terms of what they can attack (you have all the permutations of "air" or "ground" units that can only attack air or ground, it is sometimes hard to remember), so you need to be careful with what you attack with what. There is a special ability for the second largest air unit which creates a vortex which attracts enemy fire.
The mothership defense is a missile attack, and the probe special ability is the best one in my opinion, which are a series of torches that you can drop and leave. Torches can be destroyed by the enemy, however.
The flagship is a big air unit, which is probably the best unit in the game for killing the opponent's mothership because of the missile attack.
Overall note: with all races, the mothership defense and the flagship special ability are one and the same. All of the races have a unit which repairs others, something which always bothered me about starcraft (they have advanced technology and it Never Breaks? Really?).
Mouse actions:
In general, left click selects units, middle click pans, right click places/initiates actions. To attack move, use left alt plus right click. To select all units of a given type, use Shift plus left click.

I've known it existed for ages, and presumably dismissed it, including when on sale. I picked it up in a recent weekly sale on a whim, and I'm glad I did.
I find there is something charming about the graphics, it reminds me of 90's prerendered 3D sprites or something, and has some cute item physics and corpse ragdoll.
Sound effects are adequate, although the small amount of music quickly led me to turning it off.
The mobile version is also surprisingly good and controls well, and you can play the first few levels for free if you insist on trying it before you buy.
But the most important thing is the gameplay, randomisation and discovery, and that's where it shines as a true rogue-like. At first you have no idea how to deal with all the different items, but with each run you learn a bit more, and discover a little more of the hidden attributes, details and interactions. Sometimes I find this kind of hidden information frustrating, but so far in WazHack the discovery and new possibilities you learn has been really fun.
I'm informed that WazHack takes a lot of inspiration from NetHack, and while I've played various rogue-likes, and a lot of Angband (which I finally beat recently), I never really played NetHack. I like WazHack enough that I'm thinking I probably should have played NetHack more, but for now I expect to enjoy a lot more hours in WazHack.

This game is an awesome surprise if you are looking for a unique RTS and end up getting this one because it is pretty cheap. I'm happy I got this game for a few main reasons and lots of smaller reasons. The main reasons are:
- The game is balanced.
- The game looks great.
- Combat and base building is fun and unique for each of the three races.
The other reasons I like this game are the following:
- The theme behind the game is interesting.
- Resource gathering doesn't feel like a chore, leaving more focus on combat and base building.
- The music and sounds for the game help immerse you into it's theme.
- The game isn't difficult to learn, and still has a good level of complexity.
If you want more information on the types of things you can do in the game before buying it, read below:
- There are three races; Nova, YX, and Human.
- Types of units/buildings for each race include ground units, air units, production buildings, one defensive building, a resource gathering building and research buildings.
- Most units can only attack ground or air, few can attack both, however the defensive building for each race can attack/defend against air and ground.
- There are what feels like three tiers of units/buildings you can build or produce, as well as one really strong unit with a special ability for each race.
- The really strong unit for NOVA is an aircraft/air unit. It can only attack air until you active it's ability to "Launch attack drones" and it then acts similar to a Carrier from Starcraft. While the drones it launches can attack ground (not sure if they can attack air, haven't tested that yet although the aircraft itself can), they only last for a short duration (about 15 seconds or so) and the ability has a cool down that lasts equally as long.
- The strongest unit for the Human race is also an aircraft/air unit. It too can only attack air and has an ability with a somewhat shorter cooldown that the one from the NOVA race, however it's ability is to "Launch missiles" which do severe damage to random(?) nearby targets, including ground units.
- The strongest unit for the YX race is a large ground unit that can only attack ground. It has a shockwave ability which goes out from the unit and does heavy damage to anything in range of it, which is a rather large area. I'm not sure if the shockwave ability can damage air units however the YX race seems to have the most amount of units which can attack both ground and air.
Information reguarding the unique building style of each race:
- Each race starts with it's main building. If it is destroyed you lose the match. Likewise, if you destroy the enemy's main building, you win the match. There is no way to build another.
- The NOVA race has a hovering/mobile "Mothership" as it's main building. This is where the other buildings (and scouts) come from, inculding the resource collecting buildings. Once produced, your buildings are initially airborne/hovering and you select them, click on the "Land" button and then select where it will be placed and you will then be able to utilize that building.
- The YX race has a hovering/mobile "Hive Mind" as it's main building. This building produces "cells", very small circular slow moving units, which individually are cheap and are how you build all your other units and buildings with this race. All units and buildings you can build require a certain number of cells.
- The Human race has a hovering/mobile "Fortress" as it's main building. The Fortress can produce the resource gathering structures and platforms (as well as an air scout and it's strongest unit). The platform is what you construct all your buildings on in the form of "addons" including your unit producing building (there is only one for this race aside from the Fortress), all research buildings and your defensive building for this race.
- The resource collecting structures for each race look different but all act the same. They all hover and can be told to move over any resource spot on the map to begin collecting resources from it.
This information is about the core of the game. Again, I have not played Multiplayer mode or Story mode but I'm 100% positive they are just as fun as the Versus AI mode. To conclude my review, I want to say if you like RTS games in general, you will be nothing but satisfied with this game. It's definitely on a smaller scale than others like Starcraft or Supreme Commander, but that hasn't stopped me from enjoying it just as much if not more as I would any other RTS.
Finally, if you are on the fence about trying this game like I once was, just get it. You will not regret it!
Good luck and have fun!

I’ve played a fine number of the turn-based strategy games provided in it’s small market and I have a deep appreciation for them because of how easy they are to pick up for a casual gamer and how much depth they offer for anyone willing to take the risk of playing with a more hardcore approach. I was curious and slightly amused to say the least about the bold claim that Future Wars was able to “take turn based strategy gaming away from the micromanagement overkill” and “open the game for newcomers while appealing to the hardcore gamer just the same!" So after playing the game I can safely say that Future Wars isn't anything that I expected at all and is actually a very pretentious trainwreck of a game.
Radon labs, the creators of Future Wars, put a lot of effort into advertising it's "easy rock-paper-scissors" combat system being able to attract hordes of gamers with it. Though sadly this claim fell short of the company's expectations or they're probably lying because in all reality the game doesn't have much of a combat system at all. Looking through the game's "Unit Information" you'll discover that the only information your units have are a class type, it's attack range and the number of spaces it can move. In other words, the combat in this game is based off of a random roll of the die. This is no exaggeration either. it got painfully obvious that no matter what units I was using they had no real effect on the tide of battle as soon as I clocked in over 40 minutes on a single mission. In one of the missions, where I was required to capture an enemy base and eliminate all enemy units they would constantly spawn wave after wave of classes from their factory each turn. Eventually when combat actually engaged regardless of what environment I was in (which in theory give you defense boosts) or if the unit I had was “stronger” or “weaker” than the enemy's the damage being clocked in from both sides would be a completely random range of high or low damage.
This completely destroyed any difficulty the game could possibly have and made the entire game unplayable as the game became an endless cycle of build, attack, and rebuild that would never go anywhere because of how little damage would always be dealt and with how many units can be spawned with the constantly endless flow of cash. Future Wars also had little things that could've made the game a little easier to stomach but were totally forgotten. Such as no skip buttons for the very long battles, no indication of who can be moved or not, having to play every unit before ending your turn, or the camera forcing you to pan back to a unit every time they take any sudden movement are only a few of the game's unneeded annoyances. It also doesn’t help that the HUD is nearly impossible to work with. There is little to no information for what each button and symbol in the game’s menus stand for forcing you to take a wild guess with the small and tiny thumbnails sitting by by numbers that had no real meaning to you. Though considering that even environments with high numbers by the shield symbol on the HUD made no difference over how much damage was given they probably don't even really matter anyways.
The game also looks very ugly, the textures of the objects in the game are very smudgy and pixelated even on computers that can meet the game’s mind boggling 3.0ghz processor requirement and the character design looks goofy with everyone dressed up as superheroes and wearing sun visors in dark rooms. Then there's the story, you can't really actually care about anything bad happening to the characters since all the battles are done on computer simulations and have zero real life consequences on the characters even when a "bad guy" is introduced. The dialogue is also very, very nonsensical with a bunch of weird comments made by the characters or looking like it comes out of a 12 year old's stories on her long forgotten Livejournal page. Future Wars simply isn't a a good game, it's not even one that really needs to exist. It tries it's hardest to fix something that was never broken to begin with and fails miserably by not even providing any depth to it's broken core. It's ugly, it's broken, its built off of zero combat direction, and it's story is badly written that even those who received the game in a bundle or got it on sale for less than a dollar will feel like they've been ripped off. The turn based strategy genre is already small as it is and offers far better titles that do so much more that even considering this game is unnecessary.

Lightning Returns is a mixed bag for me. I really like some of the game's’ mechanics. I dig the combat and the timed nature of the game, that forces you to think about what quests to do in what order. The combat is fun, and discovering good builds and combination was imo the best part of the game. However, there are many problems with this game, and I can’t honestly tell if I love or hate it after 120+ hours. I can say I thoroughly enjoyed many hours, and endured some through sheer stubbornness. I’ve only seriously played FF4, FF8 and FF10, so my knowledge about the series as a whole is limited. I played a bit of FF13-1 and FF13-2 but I didn’t at all like their mechanics. Lightning Returns (LR) has better mechanics than both, and I can recommend the game based on that alone, as long as you have low expectations elsewhere. I picked it up because I knew it had majora’s Mask mechanics, which was neat. PC ports are also cheaper than on console!
FF to me means a story well told with a casual fun approach to turn-based combat. LR partially succeeds by merging turn based combat with timed “world time”. I like this idea since it adds urgency to the plot. Speaking of plot,  the story is really poor in its execution, and suffers from its attempt at being open world. As "The Savior", Lightning must save souls by helping people in need, as  sh*tty MMO quests. In the Witcher 3, most of the enjoyment I had was the fun I had was side quests, because the dialog entertaining and (sometimes) had real impact on the main story. Additionally, Gerald provides a service not easily substituted. Lightning, Demigod by trade,  does mundane tasks I’m supposed to believe  literally saves soul from the dying world. Imagine someone doing for you such a favor, that your soul leaves your physical body in salvation because I found your f*cking doll that went missing? Also you go to hell when if it’s the wrong one btw.  This idea does not work well with the majority of the side quests, and many of them could easily have been left out. It is not clear how many side quests are required to not fail on the final day, but the game makes it very clear immediately that you must do  as many side quests as possible. I ended up completing most of them, and they were not worth it.
Honestly, I skipped all cutscenes that didn’t revolve around the main plot. After the first few hours I realized that the background story pretty much is that people are biologically immortal, and therefore bored. Since the world is nearing its end, you’d think people be panicking, and grow continually more unstable as the plot escalates. It would even make sense as the final installment in the FF13 trilogy.  However, the world is open and casual in its mood which just doesn’t fit the urgency it so desperately tries to instill. LR would work as entry in the series where you discover much grander plot at the end, opening for sequels. Ironically, I think FF13-1 with that counter would work better as the series’ conclusion.
This is that one time, where having more grit and sorrow would be useful infuse some humanity into the vacant lot that is my feelings for whatever this game calls a plot. The main story is very short, so while I had little enjoyment, it also didn’t waste much of my time. I wish the LR was more linear and had more playable characters in the party. I didn’t care for any of the characters in the story, because they are so poorly written. I think this is a SE problem rather than LR specifically though. I do appreciate that much of the dialog were voice acted.
The combat is simple and fun, and is where the game shines. 4 abilities can be mapped at once per costume. Lightning can use 3 costumes per battle you can freely switch between. Each costume comes with at least one ability, and some minor stat bonuses. The costumes are class variations that can be collected or bought at in-game stores. The fanservice is pretty obvious, and it doesn’t make much sense that changing to a different bra somehow makes you more tanky and less proficient with weapons. It would be so much simpler if you could switch between 6-8 classes with, where each class has a unique ability. Instead I have to go through minor class variations that only differs slightly.  It's made so you think there is more content than there actually is, and unnecessary since you already have great control over what abilities to use. That said, the best part of the game is making a setup that works for a hard boss, and succeeding with winning combos. This applies to abilities that can be found as monster drops and leveled up my a merchant. He merges your abilities together. While cool in theory, an xp meter would be so much better, as it doesn’t fill your inventory with HUNDREDS of those.
I just went from A to B for the otherwise fun combat and light platforming. As an Jak trilogy player I’m used to platforming, and while it did spice up LR’s gameplay, the platforming elements lacked depth and variety, and was only once or twice the fun of the level.  Besides  missing more unique effects on found equipment, the actual gameplay is rather good, I’m just way to p*ssed off about everything else!
Speaking of p*ssed of, the worst part of LR is how much time you need to spend in the damn menus! About a half the time is spent in menus for the following reasons:
1) Useful stuff, like planning a route that completes the most side quests, changing gear, and setting abilities.
2) You’re stuck in poorly thought-out upgrading loop for abilities that you cannot perform in a batch!
3) Pause to activate the temporary time freeze.
While no. 1) works fine, the overly animated menus take a long time to load, even on a SSD, but I can manage it. No. 3) is really annoying since the time freeze is so short, and I wonder why they didn’t increase the cost and the time so you spend less time in the menus or gave me a shortcut, because it really breaks the flow. While you don't have to freeze time to make it to the end, you do feel incentivized to not waste EP that you gain from battles. This is a lesser issue on higher difficulties.  No. 2) is the worst. It can take a long time to fully level-up an ability, since it can only be done one step at a time, and each step requires enough clicks that I question why I bother with the game when I have to do so. Go watch a video that shows how this is done, I don’t want to bother you with it.
I could go on about the other less important mechanics and features, but they’re honestly not that interesting. Completing battles give you EP which is used for spells (time freeze, escape battle, teleport to map  etc.). There is also a Day/Night cycle influence what quests are active, but it’s more annoying than the immersion is worth. The world in LR is really big, and I wish there were more teleport spots, because lots of traveling on foot/chocobo is needed that also takes time. Lastly, I liked the soundtrack, but I did find it to loop too often.
The end of the world in a finite time as a hard failure state is a nice excuse to force tension, but only if you have a reason  to give a f*ck about the story or the characters, which I don’t, because the characters and plot are boring, predicable and monologuing.  Additionally, LR has an annoying tendency to to force you pause the game to do mundane tasks that I’d wish weren’t to important for my progression to skip.
I like the combat, and the occasional platforming had its moments.
All in all, I’d recommend the game on the basis that if you aren’t bothered by menus, and can play a game solely for its mechanics, you might still have a good time. The story isn’t worth the effort, just skip the cutscenes unrelated to the main story which is also rather short compared to the time spent doing sidequests, which is most of the content.

The combat mechanics are interesting and an improvement over the previous games for the most part. The story is basic and predictable for anyone who played the previous two installments in the FFXIII trilogy, but reads more like a DLC than a full title. I have three main complaints about the gameplay:
1. New Game + (loading the post-credits autosave of a playthrough) is required to unlock equipment upgrading. Hard mode is required in addition to that for tiers 4, 5, and ★ of abilities as well as fully upgrading your stuff.
2. Garb-locked, non-upgradeable abilities mean that late game you're likely either burning an ability slot for a useful passive (Equilibrium+) or selecting a sub-par or nonexistent passive to avoid wasting an ability slot (Stone and Sand). I don't like the design of 90% of them either, but I wasn't a fan of costume design in the other titles either so no surprises there.
3. Time only serves as a speed bump to quest completion. Many people only exist for 4 hours every day, and some must be talked to on up to 4 separate days. The game doesn't tell you when these people are available unless it's for a main quest, and none have an in-game reason to withhold their dialogue for several days.
Overall, it's a decently fun 20 hour game stretched to a questionable 30 hours for a perfect single run and ridiculous hundreds of hours for the completionist (Easy->Normal->Hard->Hard->Hard etc. until all equipment and abilities are fully upgraded). Like many sequels, the reviews improve as the series wears on and loses the less committed fans, but don't let that fool you into thinking this is a good game.

If it wasn't for the active dev team I wouldn't recommend this. However, despite having only purchased it recently, I've read the patch notes going back a few months and they are making continual improvements. Be forewarned - this still puts the early in early access. If you are looking for things like tutorials, missions, a proper game world etc. then you will be disappointed. However, if you want to get to grips with the game before those features arrive, you might still be interested.
With no tutorial it'll take a few attempts before you figure out the optimum placement, or even what everything does, but playing around with terminal designs is quite fun and most importantly the passenger feedback is extremely transparent so your trial and error isn't maddeningly difficult or arbitrary. You'll (hopefully) soon find your way to making a decent profit and expanding, hiring a CFO and COO to help you expand fiscally and physically, and dealing with bigger airlines - and bigger planes - as time goes on.
But time will go on and in the end it doesn't go anywhere: there is no mission complete, there is no goal. Those will come in time. For right now, it's about building, learning and optimizing, as opposed to reaching specific goals. If you're OK with that, this is a fairly basic but still very enjoyable sim that aviation buffs will get a kick out of. It's full of potential - it's up to you if you want to play it in the meantime or wait for it to be realized. For me, it's *just* on the right side of recommend, but I can see it getting way, way better in months to come.

Secondly the game is to easy, after making a fun open world adventure making the game a true survival is definatly a big key, resources should be scarse, or for the current games state, "in existance" and you should have to control your attacks rather than clicking on a single enemy and destroying an entire hoarde of goblins,
Lastly is content, nobody likes a game where you are stuck with the same weapon and only have a couple enemy's to fight and a few buildings to build, we want lots of different weapons to suit our style of play, different enemy's to regularly challenge the player and multiple buildings so that theres an element of choice, much like state of decay for example.
Overall this game has a good concept and ideas but has a long way to come before it is worth the money, so until this game changes this review wont.

To be frank, however, it's a bit more casual, as you don't have to worry about losing lives or anything. Within the first few hours, it's an easy achievement grind for the hunter in all of us... at least for me anyway. If you're a fan of rally games, or have played the original, get this.

Pros: Several weapons, including rockets and a flamethrower. A couple of rulesets, such as Deathmatch.
Cons: Far too little freedom, with no money retained between rounds(it's either spent upgrading your current weapon or discarded), etc. Upgrading feels like grinding, as it barely matters whether you do well in races or not. Once you've completed it once, you'll probably never play it again.
Recommendation: Look for the original, or find a game that was initially developed for actual gaming, and not for playing on iOS/Android.
You can't make or break yourself in the game; no financial aspect is present compared to the original but it's still fun and comes with hell of a final challenge.

None of the mechanics are great or complex, there's not much variety or depth and there's basically nothing in the way of story to really get into - and yet it was still pleasant enough.
If I'd bought it at full price?
