It feels like it was part of a much bigger planned game that got massively cut-back, making things like crafting completely pointless. On that basis: not worth it.
Still, I like to look at the positive and, as I say, for £3.29 I feel I've had a good enough time with it. All I'd say it buyer beware!

I don't know, friends. It positions itself quite nicely as a relaxing exploration game, splitting the difference between a third person shooter and something like No Man's Sky - and it has some elements that help with that. The music fantastically serves this purpose. The art isn't bad. But for me, fixed-location save points are kind of the antithesis of a relaxing game. Nothing wrong with them, intrinsically, but they really seemed at odds with the core gameplay.
For my tastes, if Sky Break isn't relaxing, there's not much left. The gameplay is kind of there, the story really isn't.
Honestly, I can heartily reccomend the game if you're very used to high-stress Save Point games; because this will be a fun, chill experience in comparison. But it didn't do it for me.

I liked
(their previous game), but it was a small game with a limited scope. Sky Break was a dissapointment to me; it's still a rather limited game, maybe more limited in some ways, and I'd hoped for more from a follow-up.
Sky Break probably has better graphics than FarSky, and there are a few elements like the sky lift and clouds that look really nice.
The atmosphere is pretty chilled out much of the time, outside of combat, and while I was still enjoying the game.
But... most of everything else is a dissapointment.
Combat is basic, and while you have robot minions and a couple of abilities, there is not enough variation or progression for it to stay interesting
Exploration is unrewarding because there is nothing unique to find, just the same randomly spread structures on each island.
It has a crafting system, but there is almost nothing to craft, there are no armor or equipment upgrades, and the same 5 resources are found plentifully and uniformly across all three islands.
Loot chests are found scattered across the map, but only ever contain ammunition, making it so plentiful that crafting even that is almost redundant.
The story isn't much, and the game lacks the personality to engage you with what there is.
Your character almost never speaks, and then only through a few small text boxes.
If even just your companion bot had some personality, like Wheatley from
, that would have gone a long way.
Overall I will be voting no to recommending it; If I had been enjoying the game more, the issues and limitations probably would not stand out as much.

If you look at the time i played, you can probably count a few hours less (for all the AFK time) but other than that that's how much time i really spent in the game - i really enjoyed exploring the map.  You can probably finish it much more quickly if you just go from point A to B, doing only things required for you to progress further in main quest.
The main plot consist of finding a cure, repairing your ship and coming back home. To do that you have to explore the map, look for things for your ship and gather plants to make the cure.  The world here is 4 islands (but 1st one is small and just a tutorial island) - all of them are different (e.g. one is a desert and on the other it's snowing) and on each you can find different mecha-animals, more or less - 2 types for each island (+2 subtypes each)+ some can be found on more than one island + mini-bosses (a harder to beat, non-hackable mechas)
To help you on your quest you can hack up to 4 mecha-animals to be your allies, and further upgrade them to be stronger, with fragments you find on other killed mecha-animals. You can upgrade their health/attack/special ability/shield, it depends on the type how much each of these can be upgraded and what abillity it has. As for your character, you can also 'evolve' it  with chips found in some places.
On all islands there is a non-stop threat of a storm that is deadly, you need to constantly look at it's level and either go back to a place safe from it, or use an ionizer if there is one close and once you make a battery for it to run. There are many of them on the island so you can explore but if you forget about the storm you may find yourself dying when you notice you are in place with none nearby and a full storm.
AI of the mecha-animals may be buggy sometimes, as they tend to get stuck in things, but it was nothing to ruin the fun for me, if it was my hacked mecha i was just going further and calling them later, and if it was enemy they were just easier to kill that way.

I bought this game in a bundle, and that's how i recommend it - on a sale, or in a bundle - the full price may be a little too much for the content it has but other than that it's a very enjoyable game i recommend.

I got this on a coupon. I can't even remember what I paid, but it certainly wasn't much. Now, I'm not going to pretend that this is the outright worst game ever made, especially amongst these other reviews, but make no mistake; This is a bad game.
There were some genuinely fun moments, and those were when the game played to its strengths, forcing me to take into account terrain, vehicle strength and driving distance. That's it.
The bad:
The AI doesn't know what to do with itself, choosing to focus on the nearest threat and hammer away, turning most battles into an endurance test where the player must repeat a working technique over and over (17 campaign missions). I wouldn't complain about this, but for strategy games, depth is needed, and there is very little to be had here, so working with a limited number of options (both in game and in the menus) as long as the game can last is just tedious. A few levels into it, I finally activated the option that removed the pointless driving animations, but everything still took so freaking long. Having to watch the enemy cycle through every one of their units, watch battles exponentially slow because health is directly tied to damage output, and having to make "selections" when there is only one option for an available action is just boring.
The campaign story cutscenes are hardly worth mentioning. The characters are vapid, their "personalities" cliché and unrelatable. However, I really shouldn't be criticizing the story, as it seems that it was just developed around the game. There is nothing wrong with that, but it can be done a lot better than this.
Normally, I'd uninstall a game from my computer when I've gotten all the Steam achievements for it. There are none for this game, thank God. Instead, the game offers in-game "achievements" for beating levels under certain conditions, which rewards the player with concept art that can be found in a few minutes on the internet. It's not amazing work, but even being the completionist I am, this gave me little incentive to keep playing. As such, and due to some things mentioned further down, this is going to be one of the few games which I will never touch again.
A bit of replay value can be found outside of the campaign, in the form of simple maps that can just be played to your heart's content... y'know, if that appeals to you. The multiplayer, on the other hand, is outdated and dead, and that needs no further explanation.
Everything else is downright broken. I had to look on the forums for an explanation on how to get it running, which is no biggie. I've had to do that with plenty of other games. Then I opened the level editor, which should be the saving grace of any mediocre grid-based game. It crashed. Worse yet, I couldn't open the game afterward. I'm certain that looking for a solution or just reinstalling would remove that fiasco, but at this point I just don't even feel like doing it. I really do not.
In a term, it's "wasted potential". Most of the game is not worth playing, and the few moments that are worth experiencing can be found in almost any other strategy game.

I found FFXIII to be the best of the trilogy so far but this one is a close second. FFXIII just did a good job of setting up the characters so I would grow to care about them - which is why FFXIII-LR could have a successful story. I really enjoyed how the game went into a bit of a darker direction, showing how characters would change in a declining world and the characters that were rightous and good suddenly turned out to be disillusioned and either desperate or resigned. I do like the world; in this setting, people never age and never die but also no humans are born. There are characters who have been children for centuries; and those ages old people now await the end of the world in a way thats quite... apathetic, honestly. Cities go on existing like they used to. Most people dont seem to bother with changing their routine. At first t felt out of place but when I remembered those people have been alive for centuries with little changes to their situation, well, it made sense.
In some places you team up with other characters - and again, its interesting to see how their lives turned out and what kind of people they became, centuries later after FFXIII and FFXIII-2 - but otherwise you play on your own. I did wish there was at least one character who would join your party permemently though; maybe the white chocobo would be a nice touch since it would save time on transportation.
Speaking of time - people complained about time limit and I admit, at first I disliked it. I dont like feeling limited in any way in games I like taking my time but let me assure you, the time you get is plenty. The main quest and the side missions help to add extra days as well so dont worry if at start it seems like too little. You have an ability to stop time as well and if youre farming monsters, thats really useful and lets you go on for hours and hours of farming. I actually grew to enjoy the time limit as it added a time management element to the game and I found it fun to plan what to do when.
The different outfits and weapons were a really nice touch but on the downside you could be stuck with an outfit you dislike onlybecause its the strongest.
All in all a good conclusion to the FFXIII trilogy and an enjoyable game. You need to play it at least twice to get all the achivements and personally, I wouldnt say the replayability factor is very strong for me but thats apersonal view.

I was very impressed when I bought this game earlier. This is the final series of the entire Final Fantasy XIII series. Unlike the Crystarium system from previous Final Fantasy XIII series, it is gone from the game. Instead there are numerous schematas that have different abilities. Previous Final Fantasy XIII series Lightning garbs are aslo available as a reward (Guardian Corps and Knight of Etro). Main, side quests and Canvas of Prayers is required to strengthen Lightning for more difficult battles. Abilities can be farmed by fighting enemy monsters and they can be upgraded as well. Game ahs 3 difficulty options: Easy, Normal and Hard. Once you select the difficulty, it cannot be changed in the game. Hard mode becomes available once you have compeleted the Main Story on Easy or Normal difficulty. Hard Mode allows you to upgrade your weapons, shields and accessories. 2 optional bosses are also included on the game. I really enjoyed this game a lot and have quite a few hours in it. The only downside of the game is that you will always need a live internet connection if you want to play with it. Also there is no mouse support for the game too. You have to use keyboard buttons for the controls. I would rate it 10/10.

Lightning Returns is a fun game and I certainly liked it more than XIII-2. There are just a few things that I wanted to mention.
-Pros-
Fun combat.
Interesting story.
Great music (mostly reused from the previous titles).
-Cons-
The time limit.
Low quality graphics (It's quite a step down from XIII).
The game has to be played twice to 100% (As far as I can tell).
Don't get me wrong, the time limit doesn't add any difficulty to the game. I just prefer to take my time doing side quests and I feel too limited. Getting 100% isn't very easy and a time limit doesn't help. I probably won't try any time soon.
The graphics seem to be way worse than XIII's. I remember the first time I played XIII. I was amazed at how everything looked so beautiful. In this game, however, I was amazed at how blurry and pixelated everything except for the main characters looked. There's one cutscene in Yusnaan that comes to mind in particular where a door in the background looks like someone drew it on using MS paint.
The last thing that I want to talk about is 100% completion. I am a completionist in most games that I play. Especially Final Fantasy. I 100% completed XIII and XIII-2. It breaks my heart to see that you have to play Lightning Returns twice to complete everything. It's not that I won't play a game more than once mind you. I've played some games 6+ times. I just don't like the idea of playing a game a second time immediately after completing it.
Despite the cons, I actually really enjoyed this game and I recommend the XIII trilogy to most people that I meet. I know it's not very well liked by most people, but I really like all 3.

*edited* games been abandoned, don't waste your time. I uninstalled, was fun while it lasted.
Many reviews are dated to complain about things that have been fixed. Also many reviews have little to no hours played which seem less legitimate IMO. My review has over 500 hours played, and though yes I am a cultist who enjoyed the novels, the game in itself is good too. I won't lie, it isn't perfect but the potential is unmatched in the mmorpg world. I have equated this game to a dusty corvette. It has a small playerbase atm but that also means it's a tight knit community that's very helpful. Moderators are also pretty cool, even one joined us in our multiwebcam tinychat session we had one night. More details are as follows:
Combat: many complain but we've seen improvements over time, such as suggested on the forums sticky modification and crosshair mods too. They have plans to do an overhaul to it, which I am personally not interested in but it seems the majority is.
Storyline: I am biased because I read the books and it makes sense to me, but I have heard those that haven't read them get lost in the plot. The majority of quests you will do are on the main somewhat linear storyline, but there are some sidequests. There is variety to be experienced even if you skip the sidequests.
Player Housing: I love the idea of having pvp like taking over of one's home so that harvesting eDna and putting up NPC guards will protect it. This feature is not implemented yet as far as I know. Decoration could use improvement.
Crafting: It is simple enough for anyone to learn. Sometimes harvesting particular SOMA is repetitive but then again isn't it in all games?
Multiverse: Love this system! It gives an option to put real variety in a game. Rather than those other mmorpgs where you are stuck in one themed environment. This game being VR based gives endless possibilities to the future simulations. Can't wait to see where they go with it.
Graphics: many have said they are stunning and I agree. Some parts seem dated, but with my fav mmorpg ever having been SWG I don't nitpick.
Customization: Every one of my clanmates/friends has a different appearance. Definitely better than the other mmorpgs where it appears clones are running around because so many look exactly alike. *edit* post release customization removed :'(
Clans/Clanwars: most of these features are not implemented yet, the clanspace is pretty sweet though. There are supposed to be themes but it's currently taken out of game. The clanspace is huge.
Classes: yes there are just 4 (for now, but I've seen evidence there are more coming) but there are 2 stances for each giving advanced strategic players a chance to actually use their skills vs. the tab target buttom mashing that some mmorpgs offer.
Business Model: It's FTP with a cashshop that's really unneccessary. Nice to have a non PTW game that could easily be free for life.
System Requirements: This game runs, not optimally but runs, even on my cheapo pawnshop laptop. Which is nice when I am at college away from my leeter gaming desktop.
Difficulty: Soloing is possible, but using good gamer techniques like kiting and strategic pulling is advised.
Staff: used to be extremely attentive devs that actually have put the player's suggestions into the game but now everything seems to have slowed to tumbleweed status.
Bugs: You have to know that maps/servers will go down and need to be restarted. CTDs will happen. And there are a few other bugs unfortunately :/ but to me it's worth it.
Endgame: there are world quests, factions, challenges, dungeons, and pvp. Lack of playerbase makes it less fun though :/

I'm recommending the game because, after all, it's still mostly enjoyable top-down racing BUT please do not misunderstand: if you played and enjoyed the original, like me, this remake is not ANYWHERE near as good.
Let me summarize:
The visuals are effective - not great, but good enough. It's obvious that this game was first released on iOS and you can clearly see that the developers did NOT bother to increase the detail on the models (textures might have been improved, hard to tell, but the polygon count is very visibly low). Cars like the Deliverator definitely don't look as cool as they used to in the original, but that's subjective I guess.
Music and sound effects are bare minimum. Music was never a strong point of Death Rally so I'm not too bothered by the rather generic, boring and colorless rock tracks they put into this new version. The sound effects are okay, nothing to criticize too much here.
The biggest issue, to me, is the way they changed the in-game economy (ie. the shops - everything you did between races). In the original DOS game, you had the (legal) shop and the (illegal) black market. You had money and you would make important decisions what upgrade or car to save money for. This was a big part of playing the game and the separation between the clean shop and the dirty blackmarket (where you'd get all the good, ie. illegal, stuff) also added a very nice and grimy aspect to the game. Well, they removed ALL of this in the 2012 release. Now you don't even really have money anymore. Sure, you collect dollars but then, all they do, is fill up 'upgrade bars'. It was amazing to be able to safe cash to finally get to buy that amazing and mysterious Deliverator in the original - now cars don't even cost money anymore! You just unlock them by collecting parts on the race track! Now you just click on the armor, handling or speed bar and it fills it up automatically with your money. That's it.
The fact that they completely omitted the black market is also indicative of another change they made: the atmosphere, the vibe of the game, is now very typically iOS orientated. This new game is almost family-friendly while the old one was dark and, well, just plain cool. The writing used to be excellent, in my opinion, really putting you into that oil-stained illegal street-racing, loan-sharking, drug-collecting world. The new version you're buying here is bland and clean, almost sterile. The writing is bad (literally: there's a lot of typos and language errors in the game) and colorless. Even the interface is generic in its 'brushed metal' look.
Another annoyance is the length of the races. Once again, there's the iOS influence. The race length is between 30 and 50 secs average. It's often times NOT enough to kill opponents and it's definitely never enough to actually get 'into' a race. This is clearly designed to be played on mobile Apple devices on breaks, in the bus or on the train.
There's definitely more issues that set this 2012 version behind the original DOS release but those are the main points of frustration to me. However, as I said above, after all's been said and done, this is STILL enjoyable. The actual gameplay is, despite some flaws, still the same good old top-down driving, shooting and killing fun. I bought this on sale for less than two Euros and, for that price, it's a no-brainer must-buy, no question, I would however regret my purchase had I payed full price for it.

This mod is excellent. I saw some person gave a negative review, and after playing it I don't understand how anyone could give it a negative review. This is GREAT.
Here's the thing: You're gonna need a better computer to run this than you ran the original on. Me personally, I have a good CPU and a GTX 780 so I had no problems. There were a couple parts of the game where my FPS dropped down to around 60, but my monitor only does 60 anyway so I barely noticed. Its gonna add a little bit of required computational power. Assuming you have actually upgraded your PC between 2004 and now, you shouldn't have any problems. I haven't encountered any bugs, and most of the time I'm getting 200+ FPS.
As for the mod itself, I see people calling these changes "subtle". Sure, if you don't tend to actually look around and notice whether or not the graphics or pretty, it can be subtle. Me personally, I'm a big fan of nice graphics, that's why I have a nice computer. Let me get this straight: all of the lighting effects are DRASTICALLY improved. The high-definition shadows are a massive improvement over the original, along with a bunch of other things (fog, high contrast, light beams, etc). This is not a tiny improvement in my opinion. Its a SERIOUS improvement, enough to make this game look like it came out after 2010. Even my girlfriend, who doesn't play videogames, watched me playing for a bit and said "looks like the graphics have been updated". Pretty far from minor and subtle.
I'm over half-way through the game and I'm loving it. I'll recommend this to anyone playing half-life 2, whether its your first time or not. Personally its my third time and I'm very glad I found out about this. Its made replaying it feel great. I should note I also paired this with some Hi-Res skin and texture packs to further enhance the game. I recommend you do that as well if you know how. Everything put together, it practically looks modern. It's exactly what this masterpiece deserves.

Would it be so repetitive that the initial joy would convert into boredom in a matter of minutes?
First time I have played, it felt good ... but too difficult for me to adjust, most of the times, I would encounter a enemy, kill him and get killed in the next second, pretty much like any FPS war game before. I was lacking the most important thing: planned movement and strategy.
I would not be able to conquer the map by myself, had no allies to follow me as I was just a private. Suddenly I became more efficient to overwatch killzones, staying most of the time prone and waiting the enemie to come into range so I could pin them down and fire my weapon until the last one, in that "wave", had been neutralized.
It didn't take much time until the enemy AI found a way to flank me. Sitting somewhere and firing was not going to take me anywhere. So I have been paying attention in my mistakes, always trying to help my side, advancing not too much, supporting fire for my team, and then it started feeling more strategic then "arcade".
To sum up, this game is awesome, really well made and if you try to understand it, you won't get bored ever.
I have few online battles so far, but I shall explore more of it and perhaps even host my game so friends can join.
Love RWR, will surely buy it's DLC next week.

It was free. Since I didn't have to pay, I shouldn't say too much that's unpleasant about it.
Clearly influenced by Dear Esther (walking simulator, island, lighthouse, radio mast, ghosts), it's very much like the old point-and-click adventure games, but in a 3d environment. You walk around an uninhabited island, examining certain features and picking up certain objects. Some of the objects have to be combined before they're useful. You do this to solve the mystery of the fate of the previous inhabitants.
Positives - It works. I was able to play it all the way through without crashes or serious glitches. The developer has clearly put a lot of work into what I suspect is his first public offering. Although normal progress is slow, there -is- a "run" button that works. Despite the negatives below, I actually quite enjoyed the game, which is why I've given it a positive recommendation.
Negatives - The story is pretty peculiar, and is not helped by a strange English translation. Many of the textures are poor quality, and the lighting has far too much contrast. Some of the scenery elements (particularly rock formations) just don't look believable.
Note - Save often. There are some areas where you can clip through the intended map boundaries, and then you can't get back.
Conclusion - Despite the flaws, it's a creditable first attempt. The developer has a long way to go, but he clearly has some talent. For a free game, it's relatively entertaining.

An interesting little permadeath rogue-like game, it seemed promising at first.  There are over a dozen classes to choose from, each with a skill tree with unique (or at least varied) skills to level up to improve your chosen character.  Along the way I'd run into leprechauns and psychadelic fountains that caused the entirety of my game to look like I was tripping on acid while I did battle with floating shapes and swirling colors.
Unfortunately, the game quickly gets old.  In reality, the characters don't -feel- much different from one another once you're in the dungeon.  Unlike other rogue-likes, where you will die and go, "Oh man!  I should've done <enter alternative course of action here>" and give the game another go, I felt frustrated more than anything with this particular game.  It seemed like all too often my death was unrelated to anything done on my part and more of a roll of the die that resulted in an overpowered monster showing up or a weapon that was cursed that I never had the opportunity to uncurse on that particular run.
In the end, the game isn't -bad- persay.  I might even install it and give it another go in the future when I'm feeling bored.  I don't recommend this game, however, because there are far better rogue-likes out there to play that are more fun and have a much longer longevity to them.  If you do decide to pick this up, get it when it's on sale!

Let me start with this, I have never played this game on the PS3 nor the Xbox 360 because I don't and never will have any consoles because I don't need to, so playing the game on the PC is my first time.
I see people complaining about the time limit, but simply because they think they won't have enough time to finish the game.
Honestly, to me, it's different, I am not a fan of time limit, not because I am scared not to finish everything before the time's up, I'm sure I can do it pretty easily, the thing is, what if i want to play freely after having finishing the game? I'm not totally sure how the game works once you hit the end since i have not played the game a lot, but once it ends, it probably ends, then you have to start a new game plus, at least, we got that.
But still, I'm against the time limit, or i should say, there should be a "sandbox" mode such as the one you can find in Dead Rising 2 Off the Record, now that would be great.
I always hated time limit in games, I paid for that game, I'd like to play it as much as I want without having to restart (even if i still keep my stuff), It's kind of hard to explain but anyway.
Unlike those who hate it just because they think they won't be able to finish it in time, my reasons are valid.
The game is still good.
Gameplay-wise, it's different, it's cool, it's not too hard when you get used to it, it's actually pretty easy, but it can be kind of boring some times.
You have to wait until your action points regenerates.
The evade skill is kind of worthless in this game.
The gameplay's great, but the rest, i'm not a great fan of it, it's different, sure, it's cool, but imagine if it was more like let's say... You can block whenever you want but not against all types of attacks, you can roll/evade using barely any or no action points, but you can not evade every types of attacks either, the action points would still be there, but it would only be used when using special attacks, heavy attacks and magic.
You'd be fighting more enemies this way, it would be even more challenging (how I imagine it at least)
I don't really care about the fighting being separated by the rest of the World, it's Final Fantasy after all.
So in the end, I am not saying that the gameplay itself should be changed (combos, attacks, etc), but the way how it works, imgine something like The Witcher 3/Dark Souls/The Elder Scrolls perhaps?
It's still pretty great, but in my opinion, if the gameplay was like how I imagine it, it would be way better.
The game seems to have an average amount of content from what I've seen.
The DLCs are pretty cool, and they comes with the base game so that's a plus.
There could be more outfits and weapons from other Final Fantasy games but anyway, it still is great.
Would have been cool if they would have bring the characters so they could be playable (only when you replay bosses stages) instead of just having their weapons and costumes for Lightning.
The graphics are fine considering it's a console port, nothing exceptional for the PC but nothing too disgusting to look at either.
So here i'll be giving this game 7.5/10

This must be the most sincere low budget game I've played on Steam so far, why this is laying out in the neutral scoring scapes me. Meaning no bullshot made me impressed nor overstated descriptions, but people complain when it is the other way around.
Here is a WYSIWYG case. There is no voice acting and plot is kinda simple but it works. Nothing special but creativity flows, specially in hacking and puzzles but gun combat lives the sameness. It's just a game, it does what it does, gameplay. Entertainment, killing time. Also, learn the thing about gaming: if there is immersion, the game is alive. It's also a relief at the same time, it means you can create  games, assuming you got the juice even if it isn't enough and make a run for it in such a place as this.
The problem is that good ideas have already been taken so how to manuever? For some this might not be enough, so I'll be just advising those to look away if not, because you need to consider all this to have fun. Some can't, too busy with the obvious.
Creativity is not AAA graphics dependable. Sci-fi has this thing to boost imagination and this game really does it in an interesting way, specially above the skies. For the devs, I'll say they're on the right track.

This is a fun game, but it feels unfinished. Like there should be lots of little extras that make it a more complete experience.
Pros
+Polished graphics.
+Smooth gameplay.
+Fun to explore varied landscapes.
+Ever present threat of the storm adds a feeling of anxiety about ranging too far from your latest base.
Cons (or possible improvements)
-Shallow difficulty curve: once you have a couple of medium buff mechas the challenge is pretty much gone.
-Only one difficulty setting.
-No Achievements: once you have completed the game there is no impetus to go back and max out stats, tame one of every mecha or just find everything.
-Story and voice acting: you could easily expand and deepen the story that is revealed through logbooks. Some voice acting would give this an extra dimension and make us feel more connected to the player character too.
-Add some secret areas (e.g. that can only be accessed by riding a particular mecha).
-Add some more (unique?) boss mechas to be defeated for special items.
-Make the 'find the cure' quest harder. I managed to get the cure without even realising I was doing it.
-Make it possible to obtain the ship booster engine sooner. You get it right near the end, but as there is nothing driving you to go back and find other things you do not end up using the land anywhere ability it provides.
I know that is a lot of "Cons", but I would still recommend this game for what you do get, I just think it could be a whole lot more than it is.

It suffers from the biggest problem with the airport simulator series: the "loop" of the gameplay just isn't that much fun. Getting everything set up is fun, but once you hit play and start going through the daily grind, there's really no reason or incentive to expand the airport.
I would recommend this if you love airports, however, as it does a good job of simulating the actual mechanics of an airport. The developers have done a good job with it. And I have hope it will turn into a game in which the challenge builds over time, or at least a game where the challenge varies from one airport to another. But for now, the grind gets too boring quickly, which perhaps is a flaw of this type of game, and not that of the developer.
Some things I'd like to see:
- Retail leases, including luxury stores once you hit a certain point
- It would be much easier if you could organise objects by zone.
- This is just a fun one, but passengers should have names.

Visually okay, controls are adequate but enough annoyances to remove the fun pretty quick.  Rogue-like perma-death I understand and expected.   But this is a game where the designers exercise arbitrary control over every choice you can make, and it isn't the better for their choices.
The mechanics and the attack/spell visuals for all the different "classes" are the same.  Their starting stats are pretty much all the same.   And limited by the game -why?  If I want to play a wizard with Intelligence 13 and Strength 15, or a barbarian with constitution 9 and wisdom 16 - why stop me?  The character may die faster, but that's my choice.  And it might make starting a new character every 15 minutes a bit more interesting.  Or at least give the illusion of player control.
But when my pet dies from MY attacks (because I have no control over it and it won't attack but also won't move away?)  I get tired of that pretty quickly.   When you pass a side door the game asks "Investigate Yes/No?" but your answer doesn't matter- either way the monsters come out. In large numbers.  Behind you.   Right on top of your pet, if they're still alive.  (Yeah, every time over at least 20 rounds of

When one of my characters dies because a merchant insists I pay for damages from a dwarf attacking ME - and I sell them everything I'd collected, then try to run - and go through every healing I have, a speed potion, all of my attacks,  and even lead the merchant through a trap (which zaps me but doesn't affect the merchant).   And perhaps I wouldn't really mind that if at least it was my character who had broken the merchant's goods!
Was it exciting for two minutes? Yes.   Did I make me want to try again?  No.   That's where this game falls on it's face.
I don't expect a game to be fair, and games can be arbitrary - up to a point.  But if you want my time there has to be something about it that's rewarding to me.   If there is nothing under my control as the player that can change the presentation of the game, the mechanics, or the outcome then why give you my time?

The first installment of the series (obviously). This game sets the stage for a grand tale of corky, funny, weird and outright erratic and bizzare storyline which unfolds quite precariously; one case at the time. It is very comical in its humor and tone, and obviously meant to be taken as a comedic experience, not as a serious story. The art and animation, while slightly outdated, remain very appealing, and maintain a constant vibe of a comic experience - really, as if you're venturing into a comic book.
The game is a third person, turn-based RPG - but its mechanics differ from the "standard" turn based games, by adding a component of time and timing to the attacks, special attacks and the blocking mechanism, as well as a very flexible "enemy-weakness" system which encourages you to be more flexible in your item use, and not just use the bandages and speed buffs exclusively. There is also a weapon upgrading system, which encourages you to complete the map and not avoid fights, and also includes an "overkill" component to the combat which, among other things, encourage you to be a little more... creative, in your comabt, and not rush to victory in a matter of seconds.
If you want a funny and enjoyable RPG experience, this game is definitely for you. Be wary, though - the replayability of this game is not superb. It's probably only meant for you to complete the achievements.
It's like a Majora's Mask for the modern age.

The fact that people cry about the time limit and played the game for less then 5 horus is ridiculous and sad.
Yes there is a clock moving forward , and you can't go back in time. But you can freeze it. And if you are doing it smart, you can almost freeze it indefinetly. On my playthrough I had to skip 2 WHOLE DAYS. Because i literally finished EVERYTHING else.
You have more time then you'll ever need. But you have to plan your day. So before starting a new day, set yourself goals where you wanna be at what time. And if you have "spare" time, get  to new areas, and begin quests there.
Lightning Returns isn't an easy game, unlike XIII-2. It has hard fights, you can definetly run into "overpowered" monsters right from the start. But you'll get stronger. You'll learn the mechanics of the game, which are pretty neat. You'll have hard, yet fun fights, and have to be on your toes even in "easy" fights. And once you really get into it, it plays smooth and rewarding. Soon you realize you can kill every enemy, boss, if you play well, even if they are "overpowered".
You also have to manage a lot- you can't just outlevel enemies. If you don't setup your equipment for a boss, you will have a hard time. It takes thought, and a bit of" trial and error". Mashing "attacks" without blocking will get you killed in about 5 seconds. Same goes for items: you can't carry endless amount of items to cheese yourself through everything.
And even IF u hit a wall: you can do every "part" of the main quest in your order. Can't beat a mid-boss? Go ahead start the MQ in another zone, maybe you'll get a spell that's effective against the boss you are struggleing with.
But this is what makes this game so great. It's not a walk in the park. It forces you to think about your setup and route you go.  If you like a CHALLENGING game, i'll definetly recommend it. It's not unfair by any means, just .. not easy. It's not like most easy games out there nowadays. Some people hate this game for reasons others games are praised...

TLDR  I would recommend it especially as the game (trilogy) seems to go on sale often enough to warrant playing through them for 3 different gaming experiences that are loosely connected together by its characters.  Just remember you should approach this game for the fun/experience rather than the storyline so try your best to do a completely blind play through and ignore that RPG inclination to grind out and play "perfectly" using a strategy guide.
Gameplay is the game's strongest point and yet it doesn't get as much attention among the critics harping on the downsides of the game.  The overworld isn't a hallway like the first game's first half and feels more like an actual world than the disjointed mess accessed through a hub that was the second game.  As you get to the later part of the game you unlock connections to the areas and see how the world fits together.  Enemies run around the overworld, who can mostly be avoided by jumping or sprinting past them.  You can also use your weapon to smack them for a sizable chunk of their hp before the battle even begins but being ambushed unaware will result in you receiving a penalty instead when entering the battle.  Overall it's easy to constantly fight if you need or choose to avoid battles if you don't (except in very few cases or a few enemies types) so I didn't get that RNG frustration from replaying older FF titles.
Let's talk briefly about the "doomsday clock" that people refuse to wrap their head around and immediately toss the game aside.  The Eradia system is the center of the resource management in this game, if you've played other action RPG games like Risen, Witcher or even Dark Souls, then you know how that plays in to the depth.  The battle system doesn't reward any experience for character level ups instead it gives you items/abilities, gil and Eradia points (EP) which you use to freeze the clock. You'll learn quickly that the tougher encounters give more EP and you're hit with a learning curve in either grinding out weaklings until extinct or suck it up and learn the tougher enemies without taking damage (as recovery items are limited) while balancing the tradeoffs of using powerful Eradia abilities in battle. This would be Final Fantasy's take on pushing the Action-RPG aspects in Turnbased combat to its limit with lots of reactions and swapping around.  After the steep learning curve even with its abundance of tutorials will require some practice to get used to and if you're playing on normal or Hard mode (NG+ only), reaction time and keeping track of the enemies' animations play a huge role to success.  Keeping track of where to restock EP and recovery items properly setting up for each battle where even common large enemies feel like minibosses to hunt down EP while staying alert to battle mechanics feels rewarding.
If you're looking for a relatively less taxing experience easy mode is there that gives you passive HP regen and tons of EP that you can help finish every side quest and misc quest without the resource management needed to wander around aimlessly.  Remember that no matter what you do - even if you squander all your time away and ignoring Chronofreeze and the clock, you still retain all items, stat increases, gil and starting over from the beginning of the clock.  You can skip all the cinematic and avoid most battles if you don't need them so it's not frustrating rushing through areas you'll be overleveled for by avoiding all the trash enemies and getting extra gil for later. If you're a completionist then you'll be doing a Hard playthrough afterwards where it unlocks an item upgrade/crafting system and more into the spell leveling system and unlocks more items for the added difficulty.  Having many or all the sidequests complete gives you a sizable boost in stats and more equipment so it helps in reaching the different stagger conditions and launching and floating strategies which aren't explained much outside of experimentation.
The Controls on the PC Steam version is keyboard only as there are no options for using your mouse for moving the camera so you will have to getting used to using both hands on the keyboard for gameplay even after remapping (I would actually recommend a controller with two analog sticks for sure though).  Unfortunately this meant the camera would create some frustrating experiences in a "Gary" designed level based around platforming over time duration floating tiles where you can fall back to the beginning of the dungeon while being slowly poisoned by the dungeon and dealing with hard to avoid fire mages in tight corridors (Yes, I hate the Temple of the Goddess as the culmination of the bad things in this game).
The voice acting is passable (though cringey inducing at times) but there is enough there if you ignore the campy use of Japanese humor and culture.  Lightning Returns is a more than a bit ham-fisted with its religious subtext and the whole Jesus resurrection and Moses leading his people across the Red Sea but I did find myself interested enough in the returning cast to drive on through the narrative even if some events would make me scoff in passing.  The sidequests range from pretty good to extremely pointless drivel with very little inbetween.  The main story arcs don't have any great twists or surprises  which might seem like a negative to others but it was mildly satisfying moving through the light drama without feeling like the rug is being pulled out from beneath you.  It fails to meet expectations if you're here for the story but at least they tried to tie all the loose ends together.
The ending quickly devolves into a slew of anime tropes - just think Gundam, meets Power Rangers, meets the Dragonball Z yet the very final twist was satisfying for me at least because the uncharacteristic vibe from Lightning.  It didn't feel a need to explain the new game plus mechanic outside of one nod of dialogue which is totally fine with me because reasons I stated above in the gameplay section.  It's not exceptional in anyway and much of it is to justify the gameplay and missions involved but it's a step up from the mess that 2nd game was for sure.
The  cinematics live up to the beautiful FMVs reputations and the flashy elaborate choreography is nice to look at especially at the end.  Toriyama takes a page from his X-2 book and invests a lot into his costumes or garbs in this game with Lightning being clad in some ridiculous outfits.  Unfortunately everything else from character models, area textures and battle animations are just recycled from the previous two games.  This means some costumes don't fit Lightning's head model at all.  Not to mention adornments that seem to be floating around her body when she is the only controllable character in this game simply because they wanted to use these adornments on a variety of other NPCs to help their looks.  This could be considered fine in cutting costs for the game in reusing the perfectly workable models but with porting a few but creating even fewer new enemies, this creates a very limited set of new enemies that are just reskinned into 2~3 different versions and boss monsters become common enemies to add to only 35 or so variety of enemies.  The tacted on feel doesn't stop there as you see the same attack animations for a large variety of skills even if they have different effects.  The entire "last ones" quest and even their rewards are just the assets with their texture stripped so they appear weirdly purple/pink rather than bothering to reskin them or giving them an aura of some sort.  Music is all recycled from the previous two games as well - which might be nostalgic for some but I found myself getting all too familiar of the very limited music and sfx variety as well.  I would say the overall visuals and sounds are below average but still passable

After reading a few reviews (the good ones and the bad ones), felt that I should give this a try, being a huge FF fan and all, wouldn't want to leave the story unfinished, since this is the third installment of Final Fantasy XIII.
Having said that, anyone who hasn't played the previous FF13 games, should start from the begining, otherwise it would feel a bit too much, story and character wise.
- It's a solid port from the PS3 console, at the saving screen you can see that they forgot to change that, game runs smoothly, with minimum loading time and without any crashes, at least so far, you can start playing without any delays, good job on their part.
- The biggest pro is the fighting system, it's nice and clean, you have your magic abilities, your psysical abilities, your status ailment abilities and your defensive abilities, some enemies are immune/resistant to one ability group, while vulnerable to the other, and so on. It requires some planning to set up your gear and schemata, to be ready for any situation, as any RPG should require.
You have 3 schemeta slots in your arsenal, with seperate ATB bars, you can fill those slots with garps (something like the job system in previous FF games), each having 4 ability slots and the ability to change between them mid-fight, feels like having a 3-man party in one, although I would prefer having 3 physicaly present members in a party. Well you can't blame them for trying someting different.
- The main story seems interesting enough, feeding you with small bits of information, while hinting you with some potential twists and turns, but since this is Square, great story and big twists are to be expected.
- The side quests are one of the three cons about this game, they tend to get tedious, sometimes simply boring, very out of place, with no real purpose (although side-quests are not supposed to have any real puprose in an RPG, its worse in FF13:LR).
- Another bad thing are the controls, when you start playing the game, unaware of the issue, you will most likely start on the keyboard...then it gets tricky...the controls are all over the keyboard, the game is in dire need of a controller and a few hours to set the controls on the Big Picture mode to match the game controls, if you try to bypass the Big Picture controller settings and go blind, you are quaranteed to have the buttons all messed up with the game commands/actions.
- The biggest con is the time management element, although Final Fantasy 13: Lighting Returns is an open world RPG game, they went and "narrow" your choises, not with the "where", but with the "when". Some may say that there's too much time on your hands, you don't need to worry about the time limit, on the other hand, when you have a clock ticking, while trying to focus on your surroundings for NPCs, that might have side-quests or something to say/give or for treasure boxs or shining things and at the same time Hope pops from time to time to comment on story developments or feelings or whatever bugs him at that current momment...it's more annoying than enjoying. You feel like you want to stop time...guess what, you can, but it's only for 30 in-game minutes and it costs resources.
- Overall is a decent game, if you get the hang of the time management system is actualy enjoyable, and you can expect magnificent battles that only Square can give you.

What can I say about this game?  Well - if you love airlines, love airports or love building and finding the best solutions for things - it's DEFINITELY for you.  I have seldom come across a build-sim game that targets these three areas so beautifully - and with such great open-ended performance.
Now mind you, if you're looking for another SimCity/The Sims/RCT II, please stop now. This is a very specific game for airline people or for people who love to solve unusual or difficult challenges in moving people from A to B to A again.
As the game is in early access, there can be some issues - and that is to be expected. But in some 6 weeks since I purchased the game, I've had a <single> crash - and beyond that, the faults have been very minor. The producers of the game should stand up and take a bow to create something so stable & fun when IT IS STILL IN DEVELOPMENT! Personally, this is astounding in so many ways.
As for game function, it does take a bit of time to figure through the menus - but nothing too complicated that reading the notes on Steam or asking questions in the forum can't solve.
The graphics are quite nice - seeing the planes pull in, the peeps getting off the plane, and heading to baggage claim... then the peeps boarding the plane and it leaves. Combine that with baggage systems and the other basic facets of the airport, and you have something astounding to work with. The possibilities are endless - and you do have a 'sandbox' mode to build your ultra-mega airport without having the funding issues.  It is however a challenge to start with the basic airport - and to grow it from there (very much like the real thing...)
In the future, I look forward to seeing what else they will add into the game - and to help improve the speed and functionality of the game. (Right now, lots of peeps = slower performance... something that can be a little fussy.)
Overall, there is very little that I am unhappy with - and the improvements are getting better by the month.

I like it, i find myself returning, and playing at a slow pace mostly.
It's a game where you will need to set your own goals, among the many the galaxy offers. The first obvious goal is given by the game itself and it's to travel to the center of the galaxy.
At first everything will seem very alien, fresh and different, but as with any procedural generated environment, its all dependent on the seed. And on your way to the center of the galaxy following the Atlas advise (an orb that works as a guide), or moving in the opposite direction at your own will, you'll just explore, system after system, planet after planet, just finding the strangest animals and environments one after another. You'll harvest the goods you need, to build the items you need, to improve you ship and equipment, allowing you to explore even further both on foot and in space, becoming able to survive  increasingly hostile ecosystems and fight tougher enemies. Some loot you'll use to make stuff, some you'll sell for money to buy better ships or mining tools, in a process that tends to be time consuming given how small your whole inventory is.
After a while, the exploration it starts to get samey, all that "strangeness". And you'll find yourself trying to find more tangible goals to do other than just exploring. Maybe build a colony and see it thrive. Maybe buy a massive space carrier to work as a mobile base. Maybe both, why not? The game is enjoyable if you take it for what it is.  A procedural generated galaxy with a somewhat limited but unusual and original seed, with oversaturated colors palette used masterfully all around , and smooth enjoyable mechanics. It certainly has been able to keep me coming back every once in a while.
A final note: Despite all the misshaps and the giant waves of mindless hype(first), and mindless hate(second) that came together with this game, I think it speaks volumes about the developer capacity, the fact that they never gave up on the game or it's community. They endured the good and the bad (and boy there was bad) moments, ducked they're heads when they had to, and crunched on the work to improve on their work. All this time after release, well... haters are always gonna hate, but the game has come a long way. The Atlas story had a massive overhaul is better integrated  in the world,  options to build a colony and expand have been added, there are more and bigger ships available, better economy balance, more NPC's, tons of more stuff to do, and new game modes (hardcore survival, and creative). They've been working non-stop since the game came out, fixing bugs, adding things, and improving others. They made 2 giant updates (Atlas Rises and Path Finder) that were a massive overhaul on the whole game, all of it for free, not as payed DLC. And they are still working on improving it more. Respect.

I'll start by saying that I rarely write reviews on games unless I have a very strong opinion (for better or worse). Otherland is one of those games.
I consider myself a veteran MMO player, as well as a fairly casual gamer. While I appreciate some guidance and instruction, I've played enough to find my way around without having my hand held.
At this point in time, I can't bring myself to recommend this game, and here's why:
Short version:
Pros:
*Interesting concept - worlds with different themes. That's what had attracted me.
*Try classes out before selecting.
(Short list since I'm not through the tutorial yet)
Cons:
*Little to no instruction in the tutorial (except for movement)
*No skills page to learn what your combat moves actually do. This is a deal breaker for me. (Edit: You do get access to this after choosing your class)
*Don't seem to be able to re-arrange the skills in my hotbar to where I want. What is intuitive for someone else might not be for me. Granted, I didn't pay a huge amount of attention to this, but given the only way to access skill tooltips is in the ESC menu, it likely won't work. Another deal breaker. (Edit: found it. CTRL key for anyone interested)
*No traditional account creation. Had to wait for an automated activation email.
*MASSIVE ping rate - 700+ms - and I'm in Europe playing on the EU server -.-
Long version:
Upon starting up Otherland, I found myself confronted with a typical ELUA and a fill-in for my email address. Entering my email informs me that I'll be emailed account activation instructions shortly. OK, that's different. After about 15-20 minutes wait, I finally received the activation email. In I go, and find myself with an androgynous... android? avatar and an NPC with a trophy over his head. No interaction instructions, eh? Fine. Start running the gamut of usual MMO controls and stumble across the action button. Get some basic instruction on movement and a little avatar customization, then away we go to the class training area.
Four portals, one to test out each class before choosing your favorite. Great! No regret for picking one that doesn't suit you later. Unfortunately, there is also absolutely no instruction for combat basics or class descriptions. Not everyone reads player tutorials or class descriptions on websites, guys. Ok, so I try to check out the skills to see which does what. Skills page? Where? No? Had to go into the pause menu to get the cursor and hover over each skill. Really? So far I haven't seen much difference between the four classes. Root grenades for the ... what was it... Energizer? didn't seem to work, and I lost patience before figuring out the Assassin's sneaking. I have yet to actually choose my class and plan to give them another run, but so far I don't see myself playing this much if at all.
The concept of different themes in each world was an intriguing one, and I hope I'll find more intriguing things if I can bring myself to play beyond the tutorial... otherwise Otherland will be one more Early Access regret purchase...
Update: Completed the tutorial and selected my class. Now have access to the skills page, inventory, and all that jazz. Woo. Followed up with the 'Rescue us from the corrupted sim' quest line, then got sent to the area after. Where I was stuck in a loading screen. I wasn't impressed before, and I'm still not that impressed. The four classes feel pretty stale. Your usual shoot'em up or hack'n'slash types, but the ping rate is still so terrible that it makes no difference. I feel like I'm poking mobs with a butter knife... My advice: don't waste your time or money unless there are some major changes since this review.

To be fair, this review is written after only 46 minutes into the game. The reason I didn't get further is the game mostly did not work.
I have been following this game on and off since 2008. Off mainly because I never received any emails about the game for seven years now (same email address). I figured the game had just ceased development. I noticed it on Steam recently and I guess they had some development issues and it changed hands. I thought I'd give it a try.
First of all, I have a pretty decent setup:
Intel i7-2600K, ASRock Extreme 77 motherboard
32GB G-Skill 2566 MHz RAM
500GB SSD
Zotac 6GB 980Ti Amp! Edition graphics
Benq XL2420L 144Hz monitor
Windows 7 64-bit Ultimate
The game is apparently capped at 60Hz, which is what it showed in most of the setup and tutorial areas, except when passing through the portal gate to get to the class testing areas. These don't even appear to be instances. All it seems to do is change your appearance for the class you're trying. FPS dropped to about 3-4 fps for several seconds.
First I tried to change the key binds because I'm left-handed and always do in games. The key bind options did not work. They would appear to change when you selected them (except 'Left Ctrl', which exited the window) but they would not take and went back to the defaults when you closed the window (after pressing 'Apply'). So finally I decided to move on using the default keys. I faired no better.
I went into the Warrior area first and I could use basic swing attackes by left-clicking mouse but none of the skills would reliably function. I occassionally got a couple to work but eventually they just stopped doing anything. I left that area and went to Marksman. My avatar did not change to Marksman but remained a Warrior, but I could not use the sword even. I left the area and came back, still a Warrior. After three or four times exitng and entering, I finally changed to a Marksman. None of the skills worked, not even the basic ones.
I did not try the other classes because, by that time, I could see no point. I realized I was never going to play this. Now people may claim this is happening only to me and there must be a problem with my system, but I assure you there is not. I've played hundreds of games and have never found one I cannot play. After seven years of development, this game should be far beyond this point. I don't know how it got Greenlit.
Another thing that is odd in the design you may want to be prepared for: The VERY FIRST thing you must do in creation of a character is choose their name, which is totally backward. You have no idea what the avatars look like, the classes, the customization options, etc. I don't know about you, but when I play an MMO a lot of the name choice is decided on how the character looks. Every MMO I've ever played saves the naming to the very last. And by the way, the customization is very very limited. I don't know if they plan to improve this but if they don't, everyone will look exactly the same, save for their gender.
I'm sorry, I wanted to like this game and recommend it. But I'm only telling you my experiences. I cannot recommmend Otherland.

After reading a few reviews (the good ones and the bad ones), felt that I should give this a try, being a huge FF fan and all, wouldn't want to leave the story unfinished, since this is the third installment of Final Fantasy XIII.
Having said that, anyone who hasn't played the previous FF13 games, should start from the begining, otherwise it would feel a bit too much, story and character wise.
- It's a solid port from the PS3 console, at the saving screen you can see that they forgot to change that, game runs smoothly, with minimum loading time and without any crashes, at least so far, you can start playing without any delays, good job on their part.
- The biggest pro is the fighting system, it's nice and clean, you have your magic abilities, your psysical abilities, your status ailment abilities and your defensive abilities, some enemies are immune/resistant to one ability group, while vulnerable to the other, and so on. It requires some planning to set up your gear and schemata, to be ready for any situation, as any RPG should require.
You have 3 schemeta slots in your arsenal, with seperate ATB bars, you can fill those slots with garps (something like the job system in previous FF games), each having 4 ability slots and the ability to change between them mid-fight, feels like having a 3-man party in one, although I would prefer having 3 physicaly present members in a party. Well you can't blame them for trying someting different.
- The main story seems interesting enough, feeding you with small bits of information, while hinting you with some potential twists and turns, but since this is Square, great story and big twists are to be expected.
- The side quests are one of the three cons about this game, they tend to get tedious, sometimes simply boring, very out of place, with no real purpose (although side-quests are not supposed to have any real puprose in an RPG, its worse in FF13:LR).
- Another bad thing are the controls, when you start playing the game, unaware of the issue, you will most likely start on the keyboard...then it gets tricky...the controls are all over the keyboard, the game is in dire need of a controller and a few hours to set the controls on the Big Picture mode to match the game controls, if you try to bypass the Big Picture controller settings and go blind, you are quaranteed to have the buttons all messed up with the game commands/actions.
- The biggest con is the time management element, although Final Fantasy 13: Lighting Returns is an open world RPG game, they went and "narrow" your choises, not with the "where", but with the "when". Some may say that there's too much time on your hands, you don't need to worry about the time limit, on the other hand, when you have a clock ticking, while trying to focus on your surroundings for NPCs, that might have side-quests or something to say/give or for treasure boxs or shining things and at the same time Hope pops from time to time to comment on story developments or feelings or whatever bugs him at that current momment...it's more annoying than enjoying. You feel like you want to stop time...guess what, you can, but it's only for 30 in-game minutes and it costs resources.
- Overall is a decent game, if you get the hang of the time management system is actualy enjoyable, and you can expect magnificent battles that only Square can give you.

This game has more style than substance but don't take that to mean I think the game's bad.
So, we'll start with the aesthetics because they're top-notch.  I'd say Square pretty much at its best.  Everything looks good, sounds good, and is pretty much just good.  More importantly, Lightning looks good and sounds good and is good.  Sorry, leave your waifu at the door, there's only room for how beautiful, intelligent, and the Best Lightning is.
Core gameplay revolves around dressing up Lightning in clothing that gives her mechanical benefits or penalties and will pretty much decide how you're playing the game.  Lightning can shift between three costumes in battle and they function more or less similarly to the paradigms from previous games.
Staggering is still around and sometimes the mechanic is not as intuitive as it needs to be considering how important it is towards encounter/monster balance.
The Time Limit is not as bad as you'd think.  I literally spent the last 6 days skipping ahead because I'd already accomplished everything I was going to do.  Also, achieving the True Ending is doable on your first playthrough but is Very Difficult without some of the benefits of New Game+ like Upgrading Weapons and Armor (a design decision I disagree with massively).
The story is batshit insanity.  I'm talking Kingdom Hearts crazy.  It's not that it's complicated, but it's huge in scope and a lot of it is zany.  Also, it sent me into an existential crisis for about 5 minutes, so good job game.
Anyhow, I put about 40 hours into it and I consider that to be worth the 20 bucks I spent on it.

Graphics as mentioned above are a clone of Prison Architect, as is the UI.  That made it a bit easier to find stuff and know how to build, but they copied an old build as zooming into a zone doesn't filter to only show items relevant to that zone. The AI is really poor.  People go around outside zones and ignore sidewalks going directly into the terminal.  Queues are beyond stupid as they pile up in clumps, and the sounds at the security stations are annoying.

Sky Break by Farsky Interactive is a farcry from an openworld survival game. I have to admit, I loved the artwork, and the idea behind it. Man against machine. against nature; now that would have been a survial game! Unfortunately what was seen in early development was completely scraped for the sake of simplicity. I understand the K.I.S.S. motto; however Farsky oversimplified so much that they lost their driving theme. This was supposed to be a hostile world, where the storms raged, the oxygen was thin, and every mecha was out for blood. Before launch you had to fight the gatherer mecha for precious resources to upgrade your sky base. All of that natural conflict, and personal customization gone! Now it's more like a romp in the wilderness to pick flowers with your wee woodland friends.
That said we move on to the story, or lack thereof. The overarching storyline, if one could call it that was reaching at best. It wanted so badly to be a compelling and epic tale of heroism. Save the entire human race. Unfortunately here again Farsky took K.I.S.S. literally. The story was so simple, so unengaging that your left running around this new world wondering why should you bother to save humanity anyway? You have food, the storms aren't that much of a pain thanks to the plethora of ionizing rods littered around the map; and hey if you ever get lonely just go out and hack yourself a new friend.
The coup de gras for this game came in the form of the hover mech. In prelauch this was your only friend, and salvation on a completly hostile and unforgiving planet. It has now become the game's achilles heel. Before the oversimplification you needed that mech to scan and tell you where to find the next station before your oxygen ran out. Now it serves as a laser pointer marking a straight line from point A to B, making game play nearly linear with only the random spawn of mobs and the limited inventory system to skew the challenge curve.
Overall Sky Break is a beautiful world full of wonderfully rendered and imaginitive creatures; but there is where the positives end. Nearly linear gameplay, mixed with an oversimplification of previous mechanics, and a completely underwhelming story line leaves this player scratching his head. Farsky, you made Alchemy work! You had survival gold, and amazingly turned it into lead.

Am very pleasantly surprised by Otherland overall. The creators have done a great job in recreating the world(s) described in the stories. Vibrant, bizarre, and incredibly imaginative. The character customization system is very well implemented, and I like the versatility it offers now,and can only imagine it expanding into the future.
It's also neat "meeting" Renie and !Xabbu in-game, heh.
I don't know what their long-term goal is with Otherland, but a virtual world like this has amazing potential to become something far more than "just a game", and I hope the developer taps into and really makes the most of that potential. Lambda Mall is the perfect social hub, and can become a great place for a strong in-game community to be nurtured and built.
With that in mind, I'm a bit concerned after playing through the first "chunk" of story in the game, where your'e sent to an Asian village. While it's a nice looking area, the amazing unique virtual world I'd experienced, from the opening tutorials, up to that point in Otherland is quickly replaced by the mundane familiarity of linear "fetch and kill" style quests that plague the typical themepark MMO for the last decade.
By the 3rd or 4th quest in, I was already bored with the place, didn't care what was going on, and just wanted to get back to Lambda Mall, to see other interesting places. Every time I'd turn a quest in, I was disappointed to see a new icon pop up. I just wanted to get it over with and was thrilled when I saw that a portal back to Lambda Mall had opened for me.
If any MMO deserves to move beyond that old and done-to-death paradigm, it's this one.
Now, I understand the setting of Otherland involves a multiverse of different areas, and all aren't going to be outlandish and fantastical. That's fine. I'm just talking about the type of content. In my opinion, a game this unique, in a setting this unusual and imaginative deserves something "more"; something that plays into and off of the uniqueness of the setting.
For example, a MMO like "The Secret World" - talking only about how the questing was handled - even if you forget the investigation missions (though it's not a bad idea) did a great job of providing quest content that avoided the typical "kill # of x" or "collect # of y" routine. In TSW, the world was as much a part of the setting as any character you meet, with its various mysteries and secrets and clues playing an important role in completing a given mission. A place like Otherland would fill that capacity perfectly, and in many different ways.
Still, it's early in development, and the developers have an opportunity to make something awesome out of it, yet. I'm just hoping they strive to provide an experience as unique and interesting as the worlds Otherland is set in. I also hope they really push the virtual world/community potential.
All in all, it's fun. It looks amazing. It performs well enough and I've encoutered few bugs that I wouldn't expect to encounter in a fully released game. I can easily recommend checking it out, even in Early Adopter.

It's not bad, but not great either. I like the concept of a virtual multiverse. I think with a little more love from the Devs, this could be a pretty good game. Obviously this is Early Access and the Devs are probably hard at work to fix the issues that the community points out (well, at least I hope they are).
Things I felt needed work:
-The combat felt kind of clunky at times and the targeting system can use a little more work. Switching targets didn't feel fluid and often hindered combat.
- There would be times where I felt the skill buttons were a little unresponsive.
- Your AI friends didn't fell like they helped all that much while the enemy AI were very quick to swarm and overwhelm you.
- Some minor graphical issues that I'm sure future optimization plans the Devs have will fix.
- I had a cutscene not play for me in the 5square(?) area. The part where they were going to have the festival after you gathered all the villagers.
- Character customization could use some work as well. Allowing us to zoom in and out, or turn our characters would be appreciated.
- Some spelling mistakes in the conversations.
- Would be nice if NPCs can be voiced in the future.
Things that I really liked:
- Good amount of customization.
- Good graphics.
- Big Sci-fi and Fantasy MMO fan, so that was really cool to see both mashed up in one game.
- You get a home, and it's customizable!!
- Story seems pretty cool, so far.
Again, it's early access, so I'm sure there will be lots of fixes addressing a lot of the issues I've mentioned and probably once I didn't know about. Honestly, the game has a lot of potential and if they can smooth out the rough edges, this can really turn into something pretty fun to play. My opinion though, if you do plan to buy one of the Editions, stick with the starter or the delux, unless you really want the following DLCs:
Mummy Skin DLC
Cyborg Skin DLC
+12 Inventory Slots DLC
+2 Character Slot DLC
+15000 Bits DLC
+4000 Credits DLC
Collectors Edition Special Bar
Not all that important. The only thing really good that comes out of it are the bits and credits you get. War is good for nothing, but in this game it's for entertainment.
At first glance it appears just like some average top down shooter, however it's a bit more than that. You take on the role as some average soldier fighting for whatever side you choose to fight for. The goal of the game is to rule the world for your faction, the only problem is that two our factions hold pieces of that world; don't expect the two to give you those pieces like gifts for your birthday. You'll have fight, along with many other soldiers, for those pieces.
You start off with the lowest rank, with just a few toys to play with. As you crawl from the dirt you were thrown onto you will stand, and when you stand you will walk, and when you walk you will run all the way to victory. As you fight you will gain exp and in-game currency, allowing you to increase in rank and make purchases of different weapons, equipment, and off map support. As you rise in the ranks many comrades will follow your every actions, fighting by your side either in the narrow trenches, in the open streets, or even in the cold snowy fronts.
There will be times where you'll need to fight alone, and even away from the front-lines to gain victory for your faction. Go in lone wolf with stealth and the shadows as your ally, eliminating and sabotaging the enemy to give your allies in the front-lines the upper hand.
Despite all that's given to you, you'll still be faced with challanges ahead. Battles lasting for hours, commanders who orders do not have proper sense, over-whelming forces that will make you wished you were back home in your mother's arms.
So...do you wish to stay as boys and girls, or do you wish to become strong men and women?

First review, but here we go. I first played Darksiders 2 on console, then later the normal port on PC. But the Deathinitive Edition is the best Possible version of the game and absoluteley worth it if on sale. Common complaints that are leveid at this game by critics is that it's too much of a mash-up or the pacing is jacked up with the combat verus puzzles. Now I've never played a Zelda game (scandalous, I know) and never got on the God of War hype train. But the good far outweighs the bad in this game. I found puzzles to be a pleasant break from the combat, and vice versa. The puzzles themselves, yes they can be tricky but you just have to know what Death is capable of, and how to work that into your favor for solving them. You play the horseman of DEATH by the way, did I mention that? Combat, when executed properly (button mashers beware), is fluid and beautiful to look at. Perfect combos allow you to juggle smaller enemies and toy with larger ones. The devs themselves said something along the lines of "To War, killing was a duty, to Death it's an Artform." The execution moves Death performs are brutal and satisfying, making each opponent an oppurtunity to see somthing awesome, but boss executions are even better. The RPG elements from the first game have been expanded here, giving various weapon and armor drops that improve your preferred playstyle ala Diablo. Be it more of a caster who summons Ghouls and a Murder of Crows, or a more direct approach with a teleport slash and "Bone Storm" skill. (yes you read that right. BOOOOONE STOOOOORM) The thematic elements of it all, being a Horseman of the Apocalypse, exploring the realms of Heaven, Hell, the Makers and even the realm of the Dead and bringing those who rule them to heel, all make this game a joy to explore. The music ties it all together, with excellent ambient and combat themes orchestrated by Jesper Kyd. Death himself talks a lot more than War did, and my god i'm glad he does because Michael Wincott brings so much personality and wit to him. Your first npc encounter with the Crowfather will prove my point. I would say that this game MUST be played with a controller, otherwise it WILL be clunky as all hell. Any controller will work, just use the Big Picture mode and suddenly your PC is a console. So what are you waiting for? The Bell tolls, the bill has come due and the wicked must be punished. Go forth Pale Rider!
TLDR: This game is awesome and totally underrated, just be sure to have a controller handy.
