Let me start by saying that before I played this game, I knew next to nothing about the Final Fantasy XIII trilogy's story and gameplay. I bought this game hoping to play a good action JRPG, since buying Tales of Symphonia wasn't enough. After hearing that this game had a more real-time approach to the series' turn-based combat, I jumped in.
Lightning Returns: Final Fantasy XIII is a JRPG that defies as many genre conventions as it possibly can, featuring non-linear exploration, a singular protagonist as opposed to a team of six or more, and a mission-based structure akin to a Western RPG. I enjoyed this free reign over where I could go and what I could do, even if it was all under a time limit. In fact, I do actually like the time limit because it gives the game a sense of urgency, adding stakes to the whole 'saving people's souls' thing.
The weakest part of Lightning Returns, in my opinion, is the story. I don't have to know anything about the previous games to know that this story is just stupid. The dialogue is convoluted and forced at times, some of the characters make some odd choices over the course of the story, and the story overall lacks a clear sense of focus. I do think Lightning as a protagonist is compelling, if a bit wish-fulfilling. From the very first cutscene, it's pretty clear what kind of story this is supposed to be, and I can't fault it too much if the writers stopped giving a crap halfway through. 'Tis a shame, though. :/
Lightning Returns as a game, however, is better than I expected. Exploration and mission-based structure aside, the battle system is akin to an infusion of the Tales series and Valkyrie Profile in some respects. Being able to select moves and pressing a single button to execute them sounds simplistic, but the game rewards you for thinking about when to strike instead of mashing buttons all the time. Granted, 90% of my battles consisted of a specific pattern (mash a button until ATB is gone, switch schemata, rinse and repeat), which made most encounters predictably easy, but there are monsters that require you to think a bit. Staggering enemies is a little finicky when you don't know exactly how to do it, especially since no one enemy gets staggered by the same thing.
The schemata system is also compelling, not just in how you can optimize your stats but also customize Lightning's apparel. A wide variety of clothing ranging from elegant to skimpy and weapons ranging from swords to spears gives Lightning various stat boosts and abilities. Some are good, some are not so good. If you plan on beating the final boss, you need to figure out what group of schemata works best for you. Lightning can have up to three Schemata at a time, which is pretty much essential to have if you plan on beating any of the bosses in the game. Personally, I made it through most of the game having one schemata for brute force, one for magic and one that balanced the two yet focused on defense more than attack.
The graphics are top-notch, as expected of Square Enix. The few CG cutscenes in the game are quite well-done, although the in-game engine is not too bad either. Every major character and town has a unique look and feel to it, and although the NPCs get a little samey every now and then, that's to be expected. The music ranges from ambient to bombastic, providing a wide variety of tunes both original and recurring in the series. I didn't really expect the music to be this good, but considering I liked a good deal of XIII-2's soundtrack, it makes sense. My favorite tune in this game is the epic title screen theme (and occasional battle theme), Lightning Returns. It makes a big deal out of her appearing from nowhere after hundreds of years in crystal sleep, doesn't it? :D
Speaking as a casual fan of Final Fantasy, if you have any interest in this kind of game at all, give it a shot. It's definitely different from the classic FFs, but it's certainly an enjoyable game. If you've never played any part of the FFXIII games, I'd say it's okay to start here. The game provides a bit of backstory and a glossary of characters and locations in case you don't know what's going on, but there will be some disconnect since it still kind of expects you to know who these characters are in order for some scenes to connect emotionally with the player. It's still a compelling game if you can look past that, and I give it my full recommendation.

This game is not great but not bad either. If you're looking for some turn-based strategy gaming similar to the Advance Wars series, but for your PC, then this is worth your time. There are big similarities but also some differences in the game rules compared to Advance Wars.
To those who know Advance Wars, I list some differences:
There are no naval units
Only helicopters and air transports as air units, there are no bombers or fighters.
All units are produced in factories, there are no airports. All units can heal in cities or factories, in contrast to Advance Wars, where air units only heal while on airports.
If a unit inside any kind of transport has boarded the transport in a previous turn (not the current turn), then after unloading it CAN MOVE AND ATTACK, I love that detail!
Healing does not cost a corresponding fraction of the unit worth's money, like in Advance Wars.
Downsides of this game:
AI is weak
The Campaign is only 16 missions short (and the story is as bad and cheesy as Advance Wars, but also, luckily, irrelevant to the actual gameplay). There are about the same number of additional missions in "Free Play" mode, and the campaign missions can also be played in Free Play mode (selectable side for AI and player, multiplayer options,...)
The Interface is a bit clunky, not as elegant and informative as Advance Wars. But it does the job and doesn't stand in the way.
With some more polish and missions, this would be a great title on PC. As it is, it's only "ok", worth playing if you like Advance Wars and ready to try a similar game on PC. I enjoyed it but probably I won't replay it.

This is a game in the "hardcore platformer" tradition, which here (and typically) means a run-and-jump game with short but hard levels with infinite lives.  Why play these games?  Because you get to:
-immerse yourself in running and jumping, the most humanly-intuitive mechanics of any game
-plot out and slowly learn to execute action sequences to get yourself through a challenging environment
-experience radical improvement and overcome challenge through skill and practice alone
This game delivers the above pleasures, and features
-Visual clarity: always a plus in skill-based games.  Admittedly this comes from simplistic graphics, but I actually prefer this to some platformers, like Rayman or Donkey Kong games, whose slick graphics can get in the way.
-A simple but well-chosen set of mechanics: double-jumps, extra-jumps, gravity-reversers, and lasers with toggle switches.  Double-jump in particular is a fantastic tool to enrich platformers, and is still under-used.
Jumps are height-adjustable and require a skilled touch, but there is no left/right momentum as you'd find in many Mario games.
The core mechanics and level-design ideas show a strong influence from Jumper by Matt Thorson, one of the best freeware platformers (which however is a Windows-only amateur GameMaker game, and can run slow or fail to run on today's PCs).  Frankly, this is a plus.  Too many indie games try to distinguish themselves with a brilliant new mechanic.  Screw those guys---I like running and jumping!
-Some modest amount of puzzle-solving, but with a focus on skilled execution
-A level editor
-A plot which is silly, vague, and impressionistic, yet surprisingly evocative at points, with elements of Hotline Miami-esque psychological horror coming to the fore in a very well-planned scene that I won't spoil.
-Short length and moderate difficulty (for the genre), which could be a plus or minus.  For me right now, as a busy professional who also compulsively buys and completes hardcore platformers, it's a plus :)
A minus is that a couple (but just a couple) of the levels emphasize nit-picky stuff, like aligning the character juuust right for falling thru narrow apertures.  Precision is an important part of the genre, but in that particular situation it's just not fun.  If I were to tweak the game to my taste, I would make length and difficulty both a bit higher (or add a harder second campaign); make the overall plot more coherent; and make the protagonist a bit more pleasant to look at. (He's a square-shaped, unsightly drunkard with an orange nose.  Note, I am not complaining that he's a square, that's a good shape for this type of game!)
But you know, I paid two bucks for the game, and I'm quite satisfied.  Might even go and design some levels.  Overall this is a nice contribution to the hardcore-platformer genre.  Thanks guys!

Precipice of Darkness marks the first of a series of games staring the duo from the popular Penny Arcade web-comics. Verdict, a very satifying start.
Story- you create the lead character and go on a quest for vengence on a giant robot that steps on your house. On the way, you join Gabe and Tycho, two paranormal investigators, in investigating strange phenomenon around town and ultimatly stop a strange cult of mimes from resurrecting an ancient god. The story combines a mix of Lovecraftian mythos with off-color humor and memorable characters (including your own) in a darkly funny story. Though the begining of a saga, the story is quite short and can be beaten in a few hours. A-
Graphics- This is state of the art graphics... as of early release PS2 era. There is really nothing to boast about visually as the whole project was a low buget indie game. Its not ugly to look at but just nothing to write home about. The cinimatics though are in the style of the web-comics and were entertaining enough to look at but all in all, below standard. C-
Sound- Music is nicely done but does not really stand out and the game sound effects work well but are fairly standard. Though I will give props to the only voice actor in the game as performs his role exceptionally well, even making me crack up several times in the game. B-
Gameplay- This game works on a P.O.C. format that works well enough, but feels kinda clunky. The game would benefit well with controller but unfortunatly doesn't come with that option. Also I find that if I click on a spot with some objects in the way, the characters will run into the object and continue to do so for a couple of seconds before giving up, it was kinda annoing. The battle sequences, though, are very fun and provide a fair amount of challenge as you are forced to multi-task between several characters at once. It does take a little getting used to but it provides a less static battle format compared to other popular RPG's. C+
Overall- The game does suffer several flaws such as control issues and short play time among other issues. I found it to be a very enjoyable and entertaining experience worth recommendation. C+

I'll begin by saying I did not complete Lightning Returns and am basing this review only on what I experienced. I had to stop because the story just became too full of itself for me. There are other issues that include the insane amount of fetch quests, the possibly unintended encouragement of massive amounts of saving & loading, and more. The game does have some good parts to it, but they weren’t enough to keep me motivated to push through to the end.
This game has the worst Final Fantasy story I’ve ever experienced. It comes down to the sub-par writing. They tried very hard to have a grand and epic tale only to utterly fail in keeping me invested in what was happening in the story. The situation is dire and Lightning has only 13 days to save as many souls as she can so that she can guide them into the new world before the old dies. She’s able to do all of this because she made a deal to become the chosen savior of Bhunivelze, also known as God, in order to bring back Serah, her dead sister.
The story then becomes a pretentious melodrama that made me roll my eyes and sigh often. Over time, I just grew sick of everything. I couldn’t bring myself to care about the characters anymore due to the awful storytelling. Almost everyone has been tragically suffering for hundreds of years, you’re fighting against fate, the power of love can open doors and save souls inexplicably, Lightning somehow inspires everyone with her eloquence, and frequent conversations take place about God with Hope. It felt like a strange, alternate take on Christianity where Lightning is Jesus and the Chaos that’s killing the world represents Revelations. It could have worked if they just toned down the overdramatic delivery. On the other hand, the regular side-quests had relatively okay writing.
You can find side-quests by talking to people or interacting with the Canvas of Prayers. While the former can sometimes have some writing and voice acting to back it up, mechanically, they’re mostly uninteresting and forgettable fetch quests. You’re going to be collecting X number of ingredients or items, usually with vague instructions or hints because you’re expected to meander around aimlessly. Rarely will you have quest markers to help you out with these boring activities, making them frustrating too. It doesn’t help when time is a precious and limited resource.
You have only 13 days to save as many souls as you can and the in-game timer reflects that and gives the player a sense of urgency. It also serves as a great annoyance. I think it’s completely manageable since the game eventually gives you Chronostasis which allows you to stop the clock for a short amount of time. You do have to spend EP to keep casting it from the menu and more EP can be gained by killing monsters. I think it hurts the pacing of the game since I had to keep on casting it repeatedly when I was exploring or questing. I don’t know why they went with this timer mechanic when they let you stop it. It’s just there to inconvenience you with areas that open and close depending on time of day and the pressure it puts on you in general. I’m not too keen on time management in a game that enjoys being vague.
The timer and the “Normal” difficulty lead to plenty of loading screens since wasted moves or failed battles can lead to a gargantuan loss of time. Being forced to escape from a failed battle means a loss of 1 hour (out of 24) and the game isn’t afraid to throw overwhelming enemies at you from the very beginning. It’s good that the saving and loading process is fairly quick since I would make saves before many encounters depending on health or if I fought it before. I’d also make one before warping to a town at the start of a new day. At least once, I ended up in a town where the quest givers weren’t present yet which meant I couldn’t turn them in, wasting valuable in-game time and real life time (ohoho).
The outfits and costumes are probably the biggest draw of the game. They make zero sense when thinking about the narrative unless Lightning dressed as Cloud is canon now. I enjoyed them for the aesthetics. They also give you access to different abilities. There’s a humongous collection of different outfits, weapons, shields, and head ornaments to wear (it helps that all the DLC items are unlocked from the start). They all make their way into the cutscenes too so you can have some really weird moments depending on what Lightning is wearing. I guess the game isn’t that serious when the main story isn’t involved.

I wasn’t too wild about the combat in this game. It’s completely functional, but I couldn’t perfect guard for the life of me. It’s also not the most entertaining type of combat. You just keep track of weaknesses, hit them with attacks until they stagger, and then deal big damage to kill them. You’d think outfit switching during battle would add much more strategy to the game, but they just allow you to fire off more attacks or tank more attacks depending on your Schemata (the classes you make) arrangement. I’d be fonder of it if I could reliably find abilities, but you have to acquire them through treasure spheres or monster drops. Don’t expect to find any in shops or in a skill tree (there isn’t one). You do gain more EP abilities over time, so at least you have that.
Finally, I just wanted to mention that the framerate frequently dipped down from 60 to as low as 40. It could not stay stable except during battles. For reference, I have Windows 10 64-bit, a GTX 970 (latest drivers), i7 4790K, and 16GB of RAM.
While I enjoyed playing dress up with Lightning, the game’s story drove me away. Otherwise I could’ve kept going despite the timer and the lackluster combat, but unfortunately, the outfits and combat were not strong enough to carry the game by themselves. I usually want a good story with my RPGs, but failing that, you need an immersive world or great gameplay which Lightning Returns can’t exactly provide. What it can do is let you wear a cactuar on your shoulder or even little chocobos. Kweh!

But 2 years ago this Game arrived as the final part of the trilogy on Steam and although I did not like it before I gave it a try as the FFXIII Series is my favourite for a very long time and I am glad I did because I absolutley fell in love with it!
First of all coming over from the other 2 FFXIII Games, this game is not linear at all (which always was a big critic point for FFXIII) but rather open World. You are free to do whatever you would like to do & whenever you would like to do it.
You will have a Main Story, lots of side quests and a Time Limit to it, whilst this at first rather seems stressing and complicated it is not and you will very quickly get the hang of it just by playing.
Once you got the hang of the new open world system you will be introduced into the new Fightning System which is a huge upgrade and alot different then it was in the first 2 Games in the Series or in any previous Final Fantasy.
Unlike before where you watch the Action happen and just stand around and take hits. You can now block and be more envolved with it. You once again have different paradigmas but only 3.
Ravenger (Magic), Commando (Physical) & Sentiel (Deffensive). For those of you that have played the First 2 Games you should already know these Paradigms. But this time it is different. Each Paradigm has its own equipment, because this time you not only equip rings and braclets.
You can actually Equip Lightning fully with different Armour Sets, Swords & Shields. But be wise, dont choose looks over abilities. Another huge Bonus Feature in here is that no matter what Armour you equip, you can change different Parts of it in whatever Colour you like. This Way you can create Lightning as uniqe as you like.
Whilst she has Armour she also comes with the standard Braclets and Rings you can equip just like before. But now there is another difference. You can upgrade your Armour and your sword at a Blacksmith if you have the right Materiels for it, making it easier to overcome big Monster and Hard Challenges.
Also leveling up and becomming Stronger once again has changed from the previous Games. Before you had the Crystarium and had to collect CP (Crystarium Points) to be able to level up. This has been removed now. You can level up by completing Quests (side & main). So if you feel underpowered to do a certain thing in Main Quest, feel free to roam around and do some side Quests to help yourself and others out.
A little Bonus might be that you can change the difficulty from the gat go to easy, previous games only had normal and hard. And you can also replay the Game as they added a New Game Plus (NG+) Mode.
The Story in this Game is very deep as much as it was in Final Fantasy XIII & Final Fantasy XIII-2 if not even deeper. It made me laugh and cry. Truly a Masterpiece and a great addition to the Series.
Although I did not like this Game at first and was very judgmental of it. It surprised me all the way and I fell in love with it. It is honestly one of my favourite Games of all time.
I do recommend this Game to any Final Fantasy, JRPG, RPG & Story Rich Fan. Since it took me 55 Hours on my first Playthrough I do recommend this Game for its full price.

Ok, that had seemed like a very nice atmospheric game that has released at last. I'd really, really wished to like it; it felt so great at the beginning. I was returning several times after closing it in despair. But no.
The good is that rain is really good.
Anything but this I dislike.
First: IT IS NOT A REAL RELEASE. Still, a lot of bugs that people report and I didn't see any developer response. Many ridiculous design solutions (like no hip-fire and limited storage at the sky-base). They appear to be the results of rough cutting off some functionality and content from early access versions with no substitutions or polishing.
Second (the worst!): very, very poor controls. They are literally awful. I land headshots in any shooter easier than I can aim at the body of calmly standing BOSS mecha here. It is the only game I have ever seen in which aiming with the gamepad is easier than by using a mouse!
Third: mechas ruin all atmosphere. I cannot imagine any reason why mechas, that gone rogue, would behave like this. Ok, they can transform into wild animals, why not, but why they behave like stupid bots? They stand at random points doing nothing until you try to pass through. Felines do not hunt birds, birds do not make nests. No mecha has cover for the case when the storm reaches the fourth level of danger. They. Just. Stand. Where are their service depots? Where they come from on isolated island on respawn? I see no signs of that these questions are mysteries that I will reveal exploring the world. It rather seems like "we can make another game like MMORPGs with mobs, just a singleplayer, why not." Also, no chances to distract them or sneak by. Their sensors are superior compared to your technologies - until you hide in bushes, through bushes they can't see.
So - great atmosphere and idea of a planet, completely ruined by the implementation.

Keep in mind that I purchased this game knowing that there has been a lot of hate for it. I knew that there would be a lot of repetitive gameplay in a massive universe. I knew that it would be nearly impossible to encounter a real person in game and that it would be a "lonely" experience. If you can get past those negatives and see the potential that this game has then you could envision how awesome the experience could be in the future. I enjoyed the rich visuals and exploration with the opportunity to opt into missions, unlock achievements, or simply just be a tourist.
I think that if and when there is more character development and easier ways of connecting with other people online for missions, building colonies, team exploration, and battle modes then this game could really rise to the top. From what I've read, the Atlas update really put in perspective that the developers are not giving up and have a vision for how this game can grow so I think there is more to come beyond what we're seeing. I purchased the game after the Atlas update so I didn't experience it before the excitement of the Atlas update.
Overall I've really enjoyed my experience to become an adventurer with the option to choose missions or explore carefree. I wouldn't say spend the retail price tag until they deliver on more rich updates like we saw in Atlas, but if you see a sale I'd say give it a shot while also keeping in mind of the potential that it has.

I won't go into a lengthy review of this (now), but I may in the future.
First off, I wanted to say that I purchased and played the game just recently after several patches so I will not have any biased opinions based on the state of release.
My first impressions is that this game..... is actually very good. It's beautiful, and scary at the same time. The ships fly pretty good, the controls are very simple as well as the smooth and simple UI. The optimization for me is perfectly fine, the only thing slow about it is the 5 minutes it takes to load my save game.
But the progression is pretty awesome, the aliens are interesting enough, and the market is very helpful. One huge thing that helps this game also is the mod support, it's easy to find mods that do so much in the game and it's very easy to install them. Everything about this game is pretty simple, nothing is real complex, so if you want a super complex space sim - you won't like this game. The visuals are beautiful, and each planet can be different in it's own way because you don't know about what resources it'll have, if it has water, what in gods name is in the water - who knows? I know after playing Subnautica, I certainly don't have the balls to explore the water.
The only real negatives to the game though is that I found some bugs where Ancient locations didn't work and you couldn't interact with the Alien word teaching posts, and the pillar/tower itself wasn't able to be interacted with. But this was only one planet. I also had another location which I couldn't interact with (on the same planet), but I got off the planet and things have been working again.
Also... You can build bases. Yep. I know.

First things first - its an EA and hence there are still tons of little bits and pieces that need work/polish, so I dont understand why people get upset about that since thats what that big light blue box in steam with the header EARLY ACESS means.....
aaaanyway lets get to it
2 MAJOR things i had to figure out/ get told by other people (again its EA people should communicate since most likely the problem you have got solved already)
1. GRAFIXX: since I run a nvida on my laptop i had HUGE fps issues to begin with, I am talkin of averaging 8-12fps essentially making it unplayable - workarround: go into your nvidia CONTROL PANEL and manually tell the grfxcard that it has to use all its juice and not just the base chip for this programm - now i run 50-60fps and that in highest setting . This is straight up a retort too all the people complaing about grafix; YES its not the newst grafix engine there is BUT if you max everything out it will actually look really nice and potentially your rig wont even be able to handle it.
2. HOTBARS: now EVERY class has two PRIME skills, those skills are essentially stances. so if u you activate one that certain skills can be used and vice versa - so best solution imho was to put the prime skills on 1 (one) and than you can arrange the encessary skills in the hotbar which will change over. Now the game at this moment doesnt tell you which skill works in which stance so you simple have to try and drag themonto the hotbar and see if stays there or not. Once I had that figured out I acutally had some interessting combos running. BUT - DO NOT TRY TO DO ANYTHING HOTBAR RELATED IN LAMBDA MALL - because thats a nonpvp zone you cant do anything - just like the different stances the game wont tell you that it simply wont work giving you the impression that something is broken when its acutally not. I had a pretty nice conversation with one of the devs ingame bout a week ago point those things out to him and it sounded like the be working on impletmenting basic things to make that more obvious.
So by and large I have to say im quite opptimistic that the game will end up being a good product, the IP is awesome and the story unfolding very much fits into the established OL universe.
BUT we do need a lot more players so get cracking and see you online

A gem from those wacky lads at Penny Arcade, the entire game is awesome so long as you are not completely sane.
Half the game's worth is in the excellent and smooth gameplay which is a turn-based (but active) RPG based in the parody of New Arcadia, a Lovecraftian city which isn't quite so nice. You play a customizable character who joins the party of Tycho and Gabe, the same animated pair from the original Penny Arcade comics, who battle against dark gods and hunt for tainted artefacts (sometimes both, in which case a discount is made).
The other half of the story is usually the player trying not to laugh too hard at the quips and outbursts of all the crazy characters and strange enemies from fruit-violating robots to dark god-worshipping mimes. DEFINATELY RECOMMENDED

Roguelike, fantasy dungeon crawler with multiple classes to choose from, hundreds of items, spells and weapons? Sounds awesome! But WazHack struggled to live up to my expectations. WazHack is a platforming dungeon crawler set in an epic dungeon called WazHack which I suspect was once part of an epic sewer system.
Like old-school dungeon crawlers, when you’re not moving, neither is anything else; items are numerous and often cursed and likewise with the enemies (numerous and cursed that is, since they’re all skeletons). Why didn’t this game hold my attention? It turns out that WazHack is also available as a phone game and the graphics don’t translate well onto 32 inch monitor. The interface is a little clunky. A little more than clunky. While moving around and attacking was easy enough, using, equipping and consuming items was an ordeal of scrolling through menus, reading stats, and on-screen text.
I did not enjoy my time playing this game. Considering the nature of roguelike games is that you die a lot and have to restart, there has to be a huge motivator to compel you to keeping playing. Going lower and lower into  a dungeon is just not enough to compel me.

Short introduction to the game: The game is about a person, Jeremy, becoming stranded on an island due to his plane crashing and waking up to a voice of another person, Anna, speaking to him.
While I was in the plane, I experienced a reflection issue where everything was coloured purple. After spawning on the island, I notice the lighting. It feels unnatural, like being in a room with beach props scattered around. There are also some performance issues, even while playing on the lowest possible graphical setting. There is also no configurable mouse sensitivity.
The cutscenes give you time to think, and lead you to possible points of interest. The story is interesting enough, and easy to follow once you get used to it. Some minor language issues, but nothing major. The enviroment is interesting, but lacking in interactivity. The only objects that are interactable have to do with the story, except for a minor selection. To progress, you only need to look for items, which aren\\\'t hidden and easy to find (according to me), nothing frustrating. There are also achievements, although tied to progression, so if you enjoy achievement collecting, this game would surely fit you. You can also collect 7 rubies and find out the story of Anna, which is the only collectible part of the game. There\'s a part in the game where you are in a cave, and can barely see one meter infront of you even though you have a light source. There are some horror moments here and there, but more psychological, and brief, than jumpscares. (There are no jumpscares, to clarify.) The ending ties of the game and overall, a good game for being a first game of a new game studio.
TL;DR: The game has its quirks and mishaps, but it is a good game for being a first.

Death Rally is yet another indie game that I want to like, but find myself feeling unentertained and even frustrated while forcing myself to play through the campaign. The arcadey driving is overly simple with hand-cramping controls that lack finesse required in good racing games – even arcade racing games. The RPG element is weak but somewhat addictive. The multiplayer is basically uninhabited and limited to random online-only matches; sorry, no beer-fueled buddy matches. The story is trite and drawn out via ridiculous story-mission level requirements. The only reason I put as much time into this game is because of nostalgia, since Death Rally’s gameplay was 100% lifted from the NES classic R.C. Pro-Am. Overall I say avoid buying Death Rally, which is a shame because it only needed a few things to make this a great game, namely: playable multiplayer, better controls, and deeper RPG / customization choices.

What's more fun than looking down on cars murdering each other? Not much! For those that want to indulge, Death Rally delivers. The control is good (with a gamepad), the graphics are full of eye candy and if you can find someone else to play with, it makes for some intense MP racing.
I reviewed the game at Techgage:

Within 15 minutes of playtime it becomes obvious that Death Rally was originally an Ipad/Iphone game. Following the story and having finished the available missions I would think that more tracks/missions would unlock. But that was not the case. There are about 8 tracks, and they are randomized every time you have played a level. The tracks remain the same, the objectives change from time to time though. These objectives range from killing certain boss enemies, racing a few laps, killing everyone in some sort of arena, etc. With the money you make you can upgrade your vehicle and weapons. During races you'll collect random parts of vehicles and weapons as well, and killing enemies always grants a certain part.
But... the game is just so dull. You can tell it was meant for smaller devices. The graphics have been upgraded though, and other control schemes have been implemented as well, so it is a game worth having; just not for the full price.
[Rating: 57/100]

This game is the inverse of FF XIII: Bad story/chracter development, good gameplay.
Good things in this game:
1. Combat is fun, though I don't care for solo combat with just one character; I prefer a full party.
2. Love the costume system, but there's just one problem: Lighting is absolutely the last character who would willingly dress up in goofy or showy costumes, which is a big problem. The thin "plot" veneer used to justify this is just annoying. If the main character were Vanille, things would be different (see better). Have costumes that the character would realisticly wear (based on their character).
3. We get to deal with the characters we actually care about again.
Bad things in this game:
1. Square added yet more unneeded lore to further confuse the mess they made in XIII-2. Seriously Square, stop doing this! You keep throwing more goofy crap in when you really don't need to do so! Stop making everything as stupidly complicated as you can to hide the fact you don't have a good story to tell. Seriously, stop messing with timelines and time travel; this is not the Chrono-verse and you are bad at using time travel in stories now! FF XIII had a good enough world that throwing all that in just destroyed what could have been a good world and a good story. Not everyhting needs a mystery twist to make a good story. I blame XIII-2 for this crap fest.
2. Character development is shelved or reset, which is the cardinal no-no in story telling. This game isn't really about the characters anymore, it's about a really stupid plot thanks to the 2nd game. Remeber my number 2 good thing up there? It's a great example of how this game is shoehorning the characters to fit the game and story, rather than building the game and story around the characters growth and experience.
3. We don't continue the story, we just jump to the end of time and ignore the previous world altogether now. We don't deal with our heroes going back and dealing with being normal people without a fate, and possbly without purpose. Don't get me wrong, having at a bit at the end of time isn't a terrible idea for immortal characters, but at no point have the characters or the story earned the right to go there. As such it's absolutely anti climactic.
This game feels self-indulgent and insubstantial due to having disconnected from what FFXIII was trying to create with their character driven story.

This game is good. Thumbs up. It's simple, and should run quite nicely on low end machines. It's not going to win any awards for best 3rd person/open world/survival of the year, but it's certainly not going to be a waste of $14.99. It's cute, intriguing, and a fresh look at space survival games (something that appears to be suddenly exploding lately). The game's glitches are small and don't ruin the experience, and it's god the foundations for a true AAA worthy game. That said, it still feels Early Access, with some cllipping here and there, some odd bugs and funny moments that you wouldn't expect in a finished game.
I believe that there is only a small amount of work needed to change this game from feeling early access and into a true gem of a game. It feels, to me, a lot like what No Man's Sky should, and perhaps could, have been - at least in the groundplay side of things.

I cannot give this game a glowing enough review. I am going to say this simply: this game knows what makes an adventure game fun. The pacing is spot on, the enemies/allies are differentiated enough to make assembling a team feel like a worthwhile exercise, and leveling feels like a supplement to the gameplay rather than an obligatory chore. It's like the game understands WHY people enjoy these mechanics, and uses them specifically for their intended purposes. Yes, it's kind of on the short side, but better that than recycling assets and shoveling in needless grind. They knew what they had and how to use it well.
On a side note, I adore the way the storm mechanics are handled. The threat of losing your radar and being hounded by deadly lightning and tornados can lend a real sense of tension to exploration sometimes. The maps can be a little small to take *full* advantage of the mechanic, but again, better too short than too long. Also, whoever decided on the cloud grahpics was a genius. What a simple, elegant, and expressive way to give the sky texture and life.
Long story short: Good things come in small packages, and this one's perfect for the price.

I've owned No Man's Sky from launch, and played it for around 45 minutes then before losing interest. It was slow, it was repetitive, and it lacked depth. There was very little to actually DO- I didn't much care for all the drama around the hype; it was disappointing yes, but my main issues were the lack of things to do.
Now that there've been some updates, the game is much, much better! It's still slow, and it's still repeptitive. But if you enjoy a solo experience where you do the grind and get the rewards, it's a good game. It still has some major flaws in my opinion, mostly lost opportunities- all the bases, and space stations look the same with only exceedingly minor differences. There's still only like, 3 people in a space station, and the conversations and interactions are just as shallow as before. The pilots of the ships that dock at trade ports and space stations never get out of their ships- overall, the universe is a lonely feeling place, with just the barest of hints at the life and cultures around you. The overhyped 'random creatures' you find on planets are all still very, very samey, as is all the planets plant life. Supposedly that's been updated as well, but I haven't really traveled very far in the 40 hours I've played since the latest update, and haven't seen anything I hadn't seen the first time around. That's not to say you don't find neat things, and I have for sure, but MOST of the fauna I've encountered have all looked much the same across the planets I've visited.
All around though, it's a better experience. There are minor quests you can do to earn some money and items. There's a new and improved main quest chain to work on, probably the best addition I've noticed, which leads you through building a base, and getting your land rover thingy, as well as upgrades and craftables. There's much more of a goal in mind than 'fly around between planets'. Flying the ships feels good, and every ship feels different in it's maneuverability; space combat feels better as well, provided you've outfitted your ship with weapons and upgrades and own one with decent manueverability. You can also buy the enormous Freighters that warp in near space stations, and keep multiple ships on them, though they're exceedingly expensive and it's a late game prospect. The graphics are great, though there are some stylistic choices that some people don't like. I think they're fine. I'm personally not a huge fan of the menus and UI, but it does the job. Some things are still frustratingly random, like finding upgrades you want, or new multitools, or decent ships.
It's nice that the developers have continued to work on the game- there's still a LOT they could do, and I hope they continue, but they've made a good effort so far and persisted despite the hate train around their game, which is commendable. They've done enough now that I could happily recommend this game to the right person.
So yeah, I'd recommend this game for sure-IF you do proper research and know what you're getting. Don't go into it expecting it to be something that it isn't and get upset about it. Watch some videos and read the RECENT in depth reviews. Know that it's a very time consuming game, that's focused around exploration, and it's slow to play. It rewards time and effort, and you need to know if those rewards are going to be enough payoff for you. It's a gorgeous game and a great experience, but only for the right person!

Upon entering the game (Rooms 0 - 59), it appears to be an innocent looking "childrens" horror game with adventure time like characters and carboard cut-out jumpscares. This is what they use to fool players who don't google this game before they play! This game is NOT what it seems, but in a good way.
After Room 60 it's into the "true scares" where you are chased by the Mansion's inhabitants. Some rooms seem to be the same (but 1000 rooms is alot to make so it doesn't bother me that much) but you cannot see what is ahead. This means that there is lots of tension, and it doesn't help that when you are least expecting it that the carboard cutouts appear AGAIN.
This is a great horror game and is actually surprisingly scary, there was one moment that really made me jump. As much as it may seem like it through images etc. this game is NOT for younger kids... if a young kid does want to play it, only play up to room 59.
I recommend this game for ages 12+ (if you are brave enough!)
TIP: RUN, DON'T LOOK BACK, RUN.

At the beginning game moves us into a new virtual world. Very innovative and interesting  is that we can test every available class before we make a choose. Future Wars < Advance Wars
(seriously, the rest of this is just going to explain that point)
I enjoy the genre that this game is. I mean... is trying to be. The problem is, this game has nothing original in it. Its a copy paste of Advance Wars for the Gameboy Advance... except even more dull. Now before you get harsh on me, I actually ...kinda... like this game. Ive played it, I have tried to enjoy it. I have had people comment on why I enjoy self torture for playing it. So, I have given it a chance.
Problem 1: This game is a multiplayer turn based strategy where the single player slowly teaches you in 16 missions how to play multiplayer. ...There is no real multiplayer to play.. Also, I could probably teach you how to play in like 4 missions.. maybe if I am going slow. For those of us who have the game and have played the genre, we knew by mission 4 or whatever how to use indirect units.. we knew they couldn't move and attack the same turn, we didnt need 2 missions for the different ranges of indirect units.
Problem 2: THIS GAME IS BORING AND SLOW. I have spent hours, playing 1 single mission because the AI refuses to die even when I have 30 tanks and it has maybe 2. Everything has a damage cap of like 35% damage. I could drop a nuke (not actually in this game, but if it was it would suck) and it would do ..meh, on a good day, 50% damage. So if both sides have plenty of units (which all need selected, moved, and attacked with every single turn) it takes.. forever. I turned off the enemy turn animations and the game still takes hours. Its insane.

This genuinely is the only game that I started that I had trouble finishing. Not because it was difficult, but because it was too boring to continue.
Darksiders 2, (And darksiders in general) is obviously inspired by other games, like metroid, god of war, prince of persia and zelda, and there's nothing wrong with that, the problem comes when instead of taking the best part of the games it's inspired from and improving on them, it takes the ♥♥♥♥♥iest parts and runs with them.
For the most part, the game takes after god of war with a bit of prince of persia, but it gets the entire thing wrong.
God of war was composed out of combat arenas that were strung together by some exploration and a little bit of puzzles to give you a break from combat.
Darksiders 2 on the other hand, is composed 90% out of insultingly easy but extremely time consuming  numerous drawn out "puzzles" that are occasionally interrupted by arenas to give you a break from puzzling.
Most of my time playing darksiders 2 I ran around in dungeons trying to figure out where the ♥♥♥♥ I'm supposed to climb to proggress, constantly pushing levers and switches and doing repetitive puzzles in repetitive areas over and over and over and over and over when all I want to do is beat things over the head with a hammer and partake in the actually fun combat.
The puzzles themselves aren't impresive either. I see a massive boulder. I see a massive boulder shaped switch. WHATEVER WILL I DO!?!?!?
90% of the puzzles are variations of this. Find the massive boulder, push it into the hole. Sometimes the boulder is behind a gate, sometimes it's in another room, sometimes there's a big green crystal in the way, with a big glowing green bomb next to it but it's always the same ♥♥♥♥ing thing with little to no variation.
A 3 year old could solve these puzzles.
But what annoys me the most, is that the developers actually sat down and spent time designing them. Why? Instead of wasting so much time padding the game out with stupid puzzles (I shouldn't even call them puzzles, they don't take any brainpower or thinking to solve, they just take patience) why not just replace them with combat arenas? Pad the game out with something that's actually fun.
The combat is FUN, it's ENJOYABLE, I had fun with the combat system, I WANTED to fight more, combat is cathartic, fast, responsibe and animated beautifully, but most of the game is padded out with these stupid ♥♥♥♥ing puzzles that waste your time and insult your intelligence.
Which brings me to another problem, the game is so padded it's litterally unbelievable. You could seriously remove over half of the game and it would be massively improved.
The numerous puzzles are set in the same sets with the same assets, so you don't get variety, it feels like I'm solving the same godamn puzzle over and over again. And the level design while intresting for a while gets ♥♥♥♥ing boring after a few dungeons.
Like I said, I don't mind padding, if the padding is fun. If the padding was cutting my way through hordes of goons I'd happy, but it's not. It's boring repetitive puzzles.
Another thing I should mention before I close is the prince of persia part. For some reason this game also wants to be prince of persia, and there's nothing wrong with that, prince of persia had good platforming and it was really fun.
The problem is that the level designers were insanely uninspired and that heavily ♥♥♥♥ed with both the "puzzles" and the platforming. While prince of persia took you through cities, ruined temples, secret underground cavers, gardens and torture rooms, 90% of the platforming in this game is composed of "Closed room inside ruined temple." Which gets boring incredibly fast.
The point which made write this review was after I spent an hour or so puzzling through a dungeon only upon reaching what I was looking for to be instructed that I needed to puzzle for 3 more hours to find the 3 magic mcguffins and return to activate the thing. Why?
Why not just remove the 3 ♥♥♥♥ing mcguffins and just let me proggress with the story? I've already wasted my time on this dungeon, why do I need to waste even more unessesary time? It's not like the 3 mcguffins will have a different enviroment or tileset, it'll be the same temple, just drawn out 3 times longer than it needs to be.
I don't hate this game, it's obvious work was put into it, but the problem is that the work was put in the wrong place. The developers focused on padding it out with the♥♥♥♥♥♥parts instead of padding it out with the fun parts.
All, I'm saying is, if you plan to buy the this game because it looks fun, be warned of these things first.
I'm probably going to try to finish the game, just for the sake of completing it, but I don't see myself ever fondly reinstalling it.
Bonus point: The game has a loading screen every 5 seconds and each loading screen can last upward of 3 minutes.
My favourite instance was when I spent 5 minutes loading in after a teleport in front of a dungeon, then once I opened the door it was loading for another 5 minutes, and then when I started running into the dungeon it started loading again for 3 minutes.

Otherland is an Unreal-powered Action MMORPG based on the highly acclaimed novels by Tad Williams, being developed by Drago Entertainment.
The game is very much a work in progress; currently in an early release state on STEAM under a 'pay-to-play' model. It offers three levels, or options if you like, with varying numbers of credits which can be spent ingame on costumes and other useful but fairly standard fare like extra inventory slots, character slots, etc.
Graphics - very bright and cheerful. The characters, in spite of the relatively low number of useful customisation (vanity!) options at present, look good and move nicely and there's an amazing variety of shapes and sizes of npc's giving us a lot of hope for future player customisation. Interestingly, the game allows you to change every aspect of your characters appearance pretty much whenever you feel like it.
There's a good variety of weapons and the very welcome ability to use any weapon you find. That means that a ranged character can have a backup melee weapon available and your melee character has the ability to pull mobs with a ranged hit. That's a really nice feature. You can actually slot three weapons, which have various effects, and swap between them at will and you get regular upgrades as you progress through the story.
It's possible to wear any costume/armour item you find. Of course, there's not always much point but being able to do so makes a very nice departure from the standard MMO system where 90% of the drops are useless to you. The npc's offer you quest rewards which are upgrades to your armour as you progress through the story, as they do for the weapons.
There's an attentive and friendly team working on the game which interacts well with the community. They're monitoring, and taking part in, discussions on both STEAM and the official Drago forums. They're open to new ideas and suggestions and doing a great job of keeping people informed of progress with bugs etc. which they are clearing at an impressive rate.
So far at least, a friendly and helpful community seems to be springing up - certainly on the forums, ingame I can't really comment since I've been soloing so far but I've had no negative issues at all with other players.
Combat feels a bit clunky for an MMO. It sometimes feels more like an old FPS model. Maybe a result of using the unreal3 engine...I don't know. It's not bad and I was sitting on the fence a bit, not sure whether to put this in the 'not so good bits' section because it does work quite well. It's just not as fluid as most other MMO's, lets just say it still needs some work.
At present Otherland is a bit short on quests. The ones that exist give you a very linear progression up to about level 35, and quests are where the bulk of the exp comes from so thats pretty much as far as you can get without grinding.
Some confusion over powers, quests, etc. where things aren't explained terribly well and quest markers over npc's heads but not shown on the maps lead to 'additional exploration'. That can be a pain when you're trying to work out what you're supposed to be doing but there's plenty to explore in some areas and it's nice to get around and see what the developers have been creating :)
Character customisation (described as 'from tiny to huge') is a bit limited at the moment. You actually get from slightly larger than average to slightly smaller than average...certainly nowhere near the range of sizes the npc's enjoy. And vanity (costume) items are hidden by the armour rendering them pretty much useless at present unless you plan on standing around Lambda Mall and not doing any fighting!
A long way to go yet, lots of bugs which are being worked on and the character customisation isn't as flexible as some other MMO's but for me it's fun and I'm enjoying playing the game and trying things out.
It's worth saying again that the 'not so good bits' are due mainly to the early state of the game in its development and are being worked on. I've only been playing for a few days and I've seen some major improvements already, the development team really are getting on top of things.
Overall, after having played for nearly 30 hours, I quite like the game. If you can cope with the inevitable issues that exist in all games at this stage of development then I'd recommend giving it a try.

The Otherland book series captivated my father, and it was he who brought this game to my attention. He's actually been keeping me somewhat aware of this MMO adaptation for some time now, which is odd, because he rarely plays games himself. If he was this intrigued by a game that he most likely wouldn't play, then, I thought, the story must be quite interesting, and so I believed this was surely worth a go.
Unfortunately, as you can see by my thorough lack of game time, I'm not particularly able to review the game. I have tried on 3 separate occasions to play, and every time, even in the tutorial area, I am met with ridiculous ping spikes of 500+, shoddy gameplay (perhaps caused by the ping, though who knows), and crashes. For context, I am on the EUW server, living in the U.K., and have no issue with my connection in other games.
As an example of the shoddy gameplay, while trying out the Marksman class in the tutorial (which gives you access to all or most of your abilities), I would fire at an enemy from range. If I tried to kite them, as you'd expect from a ranged class, they would reset back to their original positions, regenerate all of their HP, and evade any attacks while they moved back. Odd, I thought, perhaps they have a specific aggro range. Maybe if I try kiting them around their original spawn point, instead of far back like I did last time, it'll work? No, they still reset. As a ranged class, I have to sit in melee while they whale on me. This would be solved by a tank, of course, but it's still quite ridiculous that I can't kite.
For all I know though, it's only the tutorial enemies that act this way. I have never played for more than 10 minutes in a single session, as I always crash.
I'm not sure yet if I'll request a refund, or simply wait and hope it gets better, but right now, this game is not playable for me. I can't recommend a game that I can't play.

Review for 4 hours in (please bare that in mind as you read)....
Great concept - Yes (rare to see a sci-fi much less a cyber-punk MMO these days)
Graphical apeal - Yes (somewhat stylized but they are quite nice to look at)
Needs some work to be finished properly - absolutely (this devs are saying that although this is being sold as early access it is somewhat in what used to be a CBT. The game is definately playable, but still has a quite a few bugs, and is still in need of some serious polish).
Things that need to be addressed (IMO):
1. Server stability: they are not fully available at this point
2. FPS/Ping: frame-rate and ping are still very bouncy.  I have encountered a LOT of lag spikes and crazy frame-rate fluxuations at all video settings (from fair all the way to ultra I only experience about a 10 fps difference but the spikes are terrible).  Just needs some optimization which will usually come after full release and NVIDIA (or the other graphics cards) get a hold of it to create the patches.
3. Voice acting: so the sound on this game is great, but the literal lack of ANY voice acting from the NPCs is annoying to say the least, and fully takes away from the game.  I am hoping that this will be added with the full release of the game but have not read into the game enough at this point to know for sure (FFXIV ARR had no voice acting all the way through CBT, it is often times the last thing added to a game).
4. Quests: The quests (at least through the first 10 levels and a bit beyond that) are VERY linear.  The devs have stated that this is a BIG game so I am expecting that to change.
5. Skills: also quite linear with little variation as to how you customize your play-style.  More varation would be greatly appreciated, Especially for those that prefer PVP (as it does not really play like a skill based game i.e. FPS, variation is the spice of life).
6. Classes: only 4 classes?!? Hope there is a chance to branch out further down the line.  Once again variation would be greatly appreciated.
All this being said, it is solid MMO with a lot of potential that I plan to keep playing for the near future.  For the $17 price tag and no subscription nor a reliance on a cash shop it is a great bargain!  Keep it up devs; please don't dissapoint!!!

Sky Break
It’s a one trick pony but it’s at least a fun pony
You are stranded on a strange abandoned planet inhabited by hostile robots. A virus is threatening to destroy the human race and the cure lies within the flora of the planet. That’s about all the story you will get besides a few journal logs. But it’s all the story you need to setup the gameplay. Collecting resources and finding repairs to your ship while surviving the harsh environment to return to Earth to save humanity will be your goal in Sky Break.
There’s a straightforwardness in Sky Break’s gameplay. Collect resources to craft items and upgrade your equipment then rinse, repeat, and move to the next area of the game. As more resources are collected new items become available to be crafted such as different types ammo and health packs, but also the ultimate goal of finding the cure is progressed. The longer you are away from a safe spot collecting resources the more dangerous and unwieldy the weather of the planet becomes. Although enemies are easier to fight during these storms, the use of the map becomes unavailable and tornadoes and lightning strikes makes the experience terrifying, exhilarating, and disorientating.
The robot enemies encountered, called mechas, can be hacked and turned into an ally that will fight beside you. Also, they can be upgraded in the sky base to make them more worthy in combat. Mechas have a nice, sleek design each vary differently in look. But ultimately, all the mechas act in the same clunky way. The exception is the “boss” mecha that will pose as a challenge the first time it is fought, but becomes trivial in subsequent encounters. Mecha collection may be one of the shallowest parts of the game, but it’s also one of the most fun.
While there’s many things to craft, I found myself using very little outside basic and heavy ammos for the blaster. The other types of ammos seem expensive and ineffective. Upgrading the ship feels rewarding, but by the time the ship becomes really useful the game is over. The other player upgrades are secondary to the most useful, player damage. There’s not as much choice as it would appear. Crafting ahead of time is pointless as you can craft anywhere and make the things as you need them.
Sky Break has a few things wrong. The UI is a mixed bag. Crafting is easy enough, but using items is slow and clunky. Often times I used the wrong item or ammo by accident. Spawns of resources will be inside of trees and rocks. The AI of the mechas do funky things in combat. The story feels tacked on as an afterthought. And the game is short (about 4-5 hours), but I’m not sure that I would want it any longer as there is a lack in variety to do. The complaints don’t detract from the game too much from the game though.
Sky Break has some problems. I probably won’t be returning to it anytime soon, but it is an enjoyable game. It’s a one trick pony but it’s at least a fun pony. And I would recommend to any survival game enthusiast or anyone who is interested. At price point, Sky Break is a great pickup for game to play over the weekend.

Sky Break is a prime example of why every new game doesn't need to feature life changing storylines, revolutionary mechanics, or enough gameplay to keep you invested for the next six months. This game has none of these things. The combat is simple, the story is paper thin, and it has virtually no replay value. These are not always bad things!
The game has a very strange difficulty curve in that the very beginning of the game you have a limited (and precious) amount of ammunition to secure your first poke---er your first robotic companion and reach what will become your home base. Early on, the struggle of balancing collection and usage of ammuntion to survive will be real, but once that balance is under control, all difficulty in the game vanishes as you mercilessly gun down robodeer and murderstriches standing between you and repairing your space ship to GTFO. It's also worth noting that for a indie title, the environment and weather graphics are very well done and visually pleasing.
TL;DR - Love this game for what it is; simple, forgettable, short, and fun. Don't hate it for what it isn't. Would definitely reccomend for burning up a lazy Saturday at home.

This is a follow-up review to my previous Carmageddon reviews, so I will only refer to what is new here.
Carmageddon TDR 2000 is the third game in the controversial vehicular combat series. Released in 2000 and developed by Torus Games, an Australian developer known for their family-oriented games based on popular licenses.
Stainless Games, the devs behind Carma were not involved and for valid reasons, as SCi had forced them to push C2 out the door only a year after C1 became a hit, which had pushed the small team to exhaustion and is likely the reason why C2 didn't receive an expansion like C1 did in addition to features being cut or not polished. Despite these setbacks C2 was still a hit, and SCi were ordering them to pump out more Carma shortly after to which Stainless told SCi to sod off. But not before SCi was granted the IP in order to have other devs create what would've likely became a series of Carma spinoffs.
Except only one saw the light of day, since after TDR 2000 SCi cancelled Carmageddon TV and failed having the series successfully rebooted until their eventual merge into Eidos Interactive in 2005. In February of 2009 Eidos PLC were bought in a takeover by Square Enix. Then finally in June of 2011 Stainless had bought back the rights to Carmageddon from Square Enix. TDR 2000, or TDR as it will be referred as from this point on is therefore considered a spinoff from Stainless' mainline series and they typically look back upon it with negativity, most likely due to their relationship with SCi and their lack of creative control over the project. The critical reception was also mixed as the gameplay was not a significant advancement over C2, which resulted in lackluster sales and blurred chances of there being a fourth installment. But was it really that bad?
Off the bat TDR is the most story oriented Carma in the series, as demonstrated with three opening intro movies. The setting this time is thought to be set somewhere after the events of C2's final level which involved setting off a nuclear device that ends the world, which would explain the heavy post-apocalyptic themes in TDR. Except this cannot be the case, as each Carma is its own self-contained universe and timeline. C1 was set in the near future whereas C2 was a more contemporary setting (1998), while TDR is straight up Mad Max. C:R/C:MD went back to C1's setting later on.
The story is about a new millennium gone wrong, cities swell with overpopulation and the beaten down police watch as crime spirals out of control. Those suffering the anarchy want the old values, so new towns called subates are created, segregated and tightly policed. The old cities are emptied until all that's left is the poor and the scum. Their hatred of everyone and everything drives them to further lawlessness and they gain control of the cities. Once they begin to threaten the subates an executive decision is taken and nuclear warheads rain down on the cities, killing millions. The survivors, twisted by fallout and mutation are denied help and left to suffer, yet their strength, numbers and hatred grew. The subate bosses build walls around the cities, isolating radiated prisons where criminality is the only way of life. Cops only venture into this hell if they think the gangs are becoming capable of creating weapons or technology that will give them an edge. No one dare crosses between these two worlds. It will take a four-wheeling genius with no morals, a killer instinct and a burning passion to escape. Since the nuking, no such person has existed. Until now. Max Damage, the avatar of prior games, is now a prisoner who participates in a death race to earn his freedom.
The missions from C2 return, which now serve as the game's progression of the story, unlike C2's which acted more like self-contained challenges and only barred you from going onto the next group of races. But while C2 only had a mission after three races, in TDR after each race you will have to do a mission. Each group in TDR contains 3 races and 3 missions, for a total of 24 races and 25 missions spread across 9 groups in total. The environments include a whoppin' three cities, a theme park, a docks, a military base, a desert which has the most blatant usage of the Mad Max license, and the final location is set in the clean and futuristic Police State. The Nosebleed Pack also adds 1920s and Hell levels as bonuses, non-canon to the plot.
There are 49 vehicles to choose from this time around, most of them new to the series, with 10 more added courtesy of the included expansion, making this the beefiest Carma for sheer variety, although there's notably less heavyweight types near the end like there was in Stainless' games. The cops are back from C1, including the mighty Suppressor, but they're all notably easier to waste this time around thanks to the user operable PUPs introduced from C2, especially the redone Afterburner, which is a real beast this time and treats your car like a jet-propelled rocket which can make for great fun. Some peds also make an effort to fight back, annoying you with steel pipes and Molotovs, while the smart ones flatten themselves against walls to make them harder to hit, but overall they're the same as they've always been. Like C2 you can buy your opponents' vehicles but the parts shop from C1 returns as you manually upgrade your APO between events. You start off underpowered and become overpowered before long, especially if it's all you invest your earnings in.
Visually the game is superior to C2 and looks surprisingly good still for an early 00's title, especially launching the game via Hi-Res, which loads the original uncompressed textures. The in-house engine does a great job showing off detail, with improvements across the board. Wheels can be torn off cars now and detachables are commonly seen. Splitting and crushage still exist, although harder to pull off, but vehicles can be made to easily bend and coupled with losing wheels it can render some opponents immobile. Ped gore displays thick clouds of crimson and an eyeball or beating heart if you look close enough, bringing that C1 style of gore back, but actual dismemberment is more limited than it was in C2.
Sound design is excellent, very loud and crunchy for collisions with other cars bringing more of that C1 feel unlike C2's more soft and squishy feel. Peds are appropriately squishy though and everything from engine sounds to collisions with the environment sound intimidating and impactful. The soundtrack consists of 'Plague' and 'Utah Saints' for a total of six songs, which is less than other games. I didn't really care for the music this time around and played my own instead.
Criticisms are more numerous than other games. The timer is the biggest enemy in the game and the strictest timer in the series, only going up to 4 minutes. Peds net a measily 2 seconds per kill, making them nearly worthless to farm for more time. They're harder to kill too (likely from being radiated) so you need to drive very fast to instakill them, making chaining ped combos harder as a result. Checkpoints grant a time bonus, the only time in the series, as Torus likely encouraged the 'racing' aspect more-so in TDR than Stainless did. Memorizing and farming time bonus PUPs and wasting other cars is crucial to stay in the race for any meaningful amount of time. Some missions can be very tricky at first, especially on first time attempts, but as a whole they're not nearly as frustrating as the ones in C2 IMO. Changes to vehicle handling and physics is less realistic, resulting in less chaos and therefore slightly less fun, and player permadeath from C2 is still here too, but at least you can keep the credits you earned, making it not nearly as much of a waste of time.
If considered for what it is I think it's a great game still. If taken as a Carma game it's weaker than most but I like it more than C2. As such I still recommend it. Wasted 'em!

A brilliant, if complex game. It's a rogue-like (no, not rogue-lite) dungeon crawler Basically, you're in a dungeon, you need to fight your way to the bottom. The way you do it will almost always depend on what you find on the way down. With plenty of variety each run can be significantly differnt, even if you play the same character... except the barbarian/vandal. That goes one way; Smash-Smash-Smash-loot-smash!  You're a mage and can't find spell books? then you'd better hope you can find some strong wands or, gods forbid, learn to use a sword. You're a bard and you learn the "wizard lock" spell? then you're not gonna need that storytelling perk this run!
As you may expect, the game gets harder the deeper you go, but you'll usually find enough just assistance, be it loot to sell, a bakery fend off starvation or a prisoner to release (they'll fight alongside you). The stat customisation is just the right balance of freedom to make you own character and being bound by the class you choose. E.g. your strongst White Witch will be far weaker than your weakest knight, but just as much smarter, yet you could still build a melee focused witch or a spellcasting knight.
The biggest strength of the game is the randomization of the items - Any specific potion could be healling one round and acid the next and you won't know until you drink it or learn to identify it. the scrolls, wands, jewelry, musical instruments and spellbooks are similar. Even weapons and armour are only identifiable by style, the Stats could be anything. Anything could also hold a magical effect or be blessed for bonuses or cursed as your pet might tell you, and you can't unequip anthing cursed. You can throw pretty much anything at your enemies as long as it's not cursed (then it just gets stuck to your hand), distance depends on weight and strength.
Stats don't seem to rise as you level (except health and magic) but theres other ways to make you tougher. You can become more skilled in your weapons or magic, or pick a good perk every level, but all in all you just need to play smart to survive
So in summery. A complicated but brilliant game

Pros:
Incredible fun. Excellent war simulator. Intense action. Varied weapons and factions to play with. Vehicles. Line of site combat. Team work wins battles. Ability to build fortifications, mounted guns, etc to help you push forward against overwhelming odds. The satisfaction from finally breaking the enemy out of a position is intense.
Cons:
IMHO they ruined the PVP, and it shows as no one plays it anymore. Originally, it was the same format as PvE, only with lots of players on all sides. Now, they changed it so a player, vehicle, etc., is completely invisible until they're in your line of site.
Now, while they may seem logical, it makes it incredibly difficult to pinpoint enemies, scout locations, etc. Enemy units flicker like phantasms caught between dimensions as you move between cover and buildings. While in real war you wouldn't know exactly where the enemy is, you also wouldn't forget the second you looked away (which IMHO, is the case with the current system). Even something that displays the enemies you saw in a timed fade out (say, you see frozen highlights of enemies/vehicles for 5-10 seconds before you need to scout them again.
The pros far outway the cons, and PvE is a BLAST as the AI can be quite formidable. I've had games full of long term players that we LOST to the AI despite bitter resistance from our part. So, if you feel a lack of PvP is a game breaker, don't. The PvE is extremely satisfying, and while I started my journey in PvP when the game was first released, I come back time and time again for a few hours of PvE fun.
Bottomline: Excellent and cheap top down war simulator. Tons of action and huge, hectic representations of battles. I highly recommend supporting the developer at full price, BUT, if it's onsale just buy it without a second thought. I have seen it as low as $5 before.
Even at full price, I have 50-60 hours into this game, well justifying the cost of entry. These guys put out a sleeper hit that fell under the radar and it's a shame, as only the dedicated remain. However, there is always a huge boost to the population with every sale, keeping the community healthy.
Any time of day, there are a large number of people on all of the PvE servers (be it Euro or USA.)
Just get it and enjoy. It's the type of game that's difficult to master but easy to pick up, so you should know if you want to return it well within 2 hours. My bet is that you'll be too busy loving it to keep track of that time limit :D

This game is very disapointing. It has a lot of potential, but it definitely feels like something that should still be in beta. The biggest problems I have with this game are:
(1) No map system for planetary exploration. There is a (not very user friendly, see #2) map for traveling between star systems, but nothing for the planetary surface. It becomes difficult to remember wherer you have already explored.
(2) Remembering star systems you have traveled to is a pain.There is a confusing teleportation system, but it is never really explained so I can't tell if there are a limited number of places you can travel. Also, different planets have different resources available, but you can't tell what these resources are, unless you are in space near the planets. So unless you write down what type of planets are in each system, you have to travel around and try to remember where you had seen the necessary planetary conditions.
(3) The inventory system is terrible. Some items can stack in certain inventories, but not in others - this makes crafting items challenging, since the suit inventory is generally small. Also, upgrading components takes up invenroty space, so you can improve your shields or weapons, but it will decrease the amount you can carry. I feel like most of my play time is spent reorganizing my inventory so I can collect new items. Also, it is possible to craft (GIANT) storage containers, but despite how massive they are (I don't understand why), they can only hold like 6 different things. Also, the inventories of the ship and exocrafts are accessible when you are in close proximatey, but you have to enter the storage container inventory separately to remove anything - this makes rearranging inventories even more difficult. Everything should be able to stack the same in all inventories, the storage containers should be a more realistic size for the items they are able to hold, and upgrades should have a separate slot.
(4) The story is super confusing. There are no explainations of anything, which I think was done purposely, but also there isn't a real drive to continue playing. I feel like the developers were going for a 'Minecraft-stye' feel, but at least in minecraft you can build things without progressing the story. I feel like anything I want to do requires a hour-long mission so I can obtain a single blueprint for something I can build. In short, the story is boring, and you can't just freely roam unless you play into the boring story.
(5) A couple extra nit-picky things:
i) I think gravity should be different on different planets, it doesn't really make sense that all planets are the same size.
ii) Space combat is extremely difficult so far - I might just be sucky at it, or my ship might not be very advanced, but so far I have had to avoid conflict whenever possible.
iii) So far, I haven't seen any ability to have multiple ships, I have traded a couple ships for upgrades, but is there really no way to have multiple ships? If there is, that should be made clear from the beginning.
Now for the parts of the game I have enjoyed:
(1) I think the procedural generation is very interesting and I enjoy the ability to name the planets, organisms, and minerals I encounter.
(2) The exocraft and ship are pretty easy to control. Overall the controls in the game are very intuitive (other than when dogfighting - I am still trying to figure that out).
(3) I like the realism with regards to weather and climate on planets.
Overall, I am very disappointed. I was expecting something like Mass Effect meets Minecraft, but this definitely needs a lot more work before I can recommend it.

The game's introduction sequence does a very good job of grasping your attention and getting you to ask questions..
Unfortunately, all that awaits is endless MMO inspired fetch-quests, sub-plots that you really couldn't care less about and Time Restrictions that frustratingly get in the way of the plot and characters you actually want to see.
Gameplay is better or worse depending on how you look at it.. combat is smooth, customization is at an all time high but a cast of likeable party members has been removed entirely. It's only Lightning and her amazing cosplay talent so no more group combos like before.
The entire game is governed by a Game Over timer. The timer itself is not an issue, you gain additional time very easily by doing quests. The issue is all of the restrictions that come with it. Numerous zones of the game are locked off at specific times so if you have a quest there then tough luck. You have to report back to HQ everyday at 6AM. Some quests are vague as hell so unless you Youtube it then you will waste valuable time searching every corner. Honestly a lot of the time the game feels like a job and you have to organize each day like you are putting together a college schedule.. it really got under my skin.
