sometimes enemies get flushed out of cover, and they finally become possible to kill.  but the only way you can get that opportunistic kill is if you already had a team ineffectively shooting at them ahead of time (and wasting ammo) or if you're incredibly fast at telling them to start firing before he gets away.  if your squad sees a guy get flushed out and run out of his cover, they will NOT fire and will sit there and watch him run away.  so your choices are either waste ammo, or let him escape.
if you don't explicity tell them when and where to shoot, every time, they'll just stand there and watch an enemy walk up to them and shake their hand.  I'm not sure if there's a "weapons free" mode I missed somewhere that gives them a little more discretion as to when they fire, but right now your squad will sit there with their mouths hanging open while they watch an enemy run across an empty parking lot instead of picking him off.
even when you do tell them where to fire, they only watch a very tiny area.  there is not 360 degree awareness option/formation.  instead of intelligent thinking soldiers it feels like you're commanding a squad of pacifist robots.
if you want a squad-based shooter with suppression and flanking mechanics, just play the Brothers in Arms series

Full Spectrum Warrior is a great game, though it is old, and it clearly shows. I remember playing this game on the origianl Xbox, and I enjoyed it so much that I remember that I ended up writing a report on it, as well as doing some research on it as well. Originally an Army idea to train soldiers, the game gave also saw the rise of another training aid that replaced the game, and created a bit of a controversy.
The game uses the typical Army scenario of a conflict in a made up country, using information from real world areas to make up things like demographics. You end up taking command of a squad, composed of two fireteams that mirror eachother in layout but have some different characters that attempt to give you a connection to the men; sort of giving them life. Going through various missions, you will occasionally pick up a Charlie team to help complete objectives, and utilize the sitrep system to save your progress.
The game can be tough, as it requires you to be a mix of cautious but aggressive. You need to use both teams to effectively move around the mission area, and to obviously complete your objective; this idea will get hammered into your brain fairly often and early on. Teammembers can get wounded, though I do believe the limit is one per team, and anymore then that will cause the mission to fail. If a teammember is wounded you only have so long to get to them before they bleed out, at that point one of your other soldiers must firemen carry, and you need to drop him back off at a CASEVAC/Resupply point; this eliminates another soldier from being combat effective. Though once you pick him up you can take your sweet time.
The game is not an FPS, not a TPS, if you haven't guessed already. Instead it is a real time squad tactics game, with some somewhat lackluster camera angles. However its a good buy that will keep you busy for several hours to say the least, and it has sequal out that adds some cool new features as well; like buddyteams. A fun game, and perhaps it connects more to me since I played it when it came out, and it harks back to those military days. Embrace the suck without actually embracing the suck.

I saw this game on sale ($5.99), and having played the original darksiders game and eventually finishing it, I hoped darksiders 2 would be able to improve apon the first. No.
TLDR
The first game opened with an epic scene & level at the start of the apocalypse, The Chaos and Power your character has draws you in, and when the power is stripped away you have the motivation to grind away to earn it back.
After awhile, the first game became a pretty repeatitive hack & slash / platformer type game, but the story was interesting enough to (barely) keep me playing until the end.
For me, it is the powerful character that got me interested. Feeling like a God and destroying all those who would dare to face you is great fun and gratifying.
The second game opens with you riding a slow lame horse accross an underwelming landscape to an underwelming first encounter with 3 random enemies. Death is ironically bad at killing. You fight like a filthy mortal.
Attack / roll combat, if you are killed you are actually dead / reload last save (how does death die?).
The majority of this first level is platforming. If you fall, a cutscene will show you transform and teleport back to a checkpoint (dont know why this does not happen when you die?).
The first boss is a depection of War, the character of the first game. War will casually walk over to you and perform the some basic moves, but his attacks seem powerful, perhaps mocking just how weak your Death character really is.
Even after this, & unlocking some powers, the game play is still underwelming.
The combat is poor, the platforming is poor. Nothing about this game play seems original or even inspired.
The story of Darksiders 2 seems to long for the depth and intrigue of the first game. It references the first game constantly and the story is focused on the story of the first game (at least to begin with)
Yes I am judging this game by it's first hour, and yes I know that the formula of these games is to build your character up to power, but my point is the whole start of this game is so underwelming that it is off-putting. Especially because the mid to end gameplay is likely to be mind-numblingly boring too.
The start of a game is where you get invested, interested, and excitied to continue playing, and this game completely fails at this. The story might become interesting eventually, or maybe the gameplay with it's poor camera, poor puzzles, & repeative platforming becomes chaming at some point, but it does not grab my attention from the start.
If none of the above is off-putting to you, and you like the idea of the game, go ahead and buy it. It (probably) has an interesting story, the theme is interesting, and it is an easy game to pick-up and play.
Otherwise don't.

Wazhack is an amazing game. From one guy who worked on Nethack, Wazhack is a side-scroll pseudo-version of Nethack. The gameplay is intuitive and simplified. The graphics aren't on par with games like crysis, but I've easily sunk 100 times the play time in this game than I have Crysis because it's FUN! You'll find that the gems of the game aren't right on the surface. Indeed, it is seemingly just a side-scroll roguelike (or roguelite or roguelike-like for people concerned with semantics). But Waz didn't just make a smash monster, grab loot game. There's unique ways of identifying items, unique combinations of item/spell usage, and unique tactics for various situations. Many of the concepts in Wazhack were carried over from Nethack, but it avoids being quite as complex. I found myself engrossed in this game when I had it on tablet (more so than many other roguelikes) and it still makes an excellent PC game (for casual or serious dungeon runs). If you like roguelikes, roguelike-likes, or roguelites, I can't recommend this game enough. Just try the free browser demo on
and see for yourself!

WazHack is a new take on roguelikes, but don't let the graphics fool you, this game has a lot more depth to it than you can imagine.
WazHack is a 2D roguelike heavily inspired by NetHack. If you're a fan of NetHack then you'll immediately find yourself at home as the game mechanics are pretty similar to the old classic. This game is basically a 2D turn based game. Time only passes when you move or take action, so you can take your time and plan ahead to your hearts content.
This game is hard like any other roguelike out there, so if you're not into hard or challenging games, then don't pick it up. You'll have a pretty good time trying to get past that 300 feet mark or to survive the depths without dying of starvation.
The game also features over 300 different items, and every time you die all the items/potions/weapons/armor will be randomly generated and have different stats. There are also several different classes to chose from and both the male and female version of the class start with different equipment. Playing as a wizard can be extremely hard, but it's also a lot more rewarding later on into the game.
WazWaz has been the lone developer of this game for a very long time already and he has done a phenomenal job so far. Some people might be put off by the "grotesque" or "lacking" graphics, but hey, you're playing a roguelike here.
It's not like graphics matter when you are looking at a genre based around depth in gameplay and game mechanics.
Take your time, plan ahead, always carry with you some items which can help you escape (like teleport scrolls or wands) and learn from your mistakes,you'll soon come out victorious!
And remember: dying is part of the "fun".

FSW is a difficult game to rate. It is a SIMULATION of infantry tactics, not strictly a game. Careful deployment of soldiers and proper use of cover and overwatch is what will win the day and bring them back alive at the end of the day, not heroic charge. Despite the look, this is NOT a FPS, but a third-person game where you give commands to your four man team or split the team into two halves and have them coordinate in pausable real-time.
The problem with this game is the commands are clunky, and the campaign is... difficult. The autosave don't seem to kick in at the right time. Being a 2004 game graphics are subpar but good for its days, and each "level" had to be approached like a tactical puzzle. Do you setup watch in this corner? Flank? Do you have enough ammo? Where is the CASEVAC point? Failure to use good infantry tactics will result in massive casualties, and sometimes, even if you did use tactics, sometimes, Murphy's Law applies and you will lose nonetheless.
So should you get this game? IMHO, no. THQ is no more and its assets had been sold off to various bidders who don't really have any more support for it. And I personally think the FPS: Close Combat: First to Fight is a better sim for infantry tactics as its a true FPS with squad ordering, more visceral that way.

I've decided to edit this review for clarity and to discuss some other points that have been brought up.
First, "Is it fair to review an MMO with less than X hours put into it."
My answer, yes.  If you are charging for a product or service then that product or service is open to review.  If you are selling a product it is considered a final product whether it has an "Early Access" stamp or not.  EA is not a promise of fixes or updates, it is a promise of NO PROMISE of fixes or updates.
I will not discuss the following topics as I have no experience with them...
-End game content
-Crafting
-Clans
Now, on to what I have experienced...
-Tutorial-
Beyond WASD the tutorial teaches you basically nothing.  You will discover sooner or later that left and right click have different effects with your weapons.  What are those effects?  Who knows, the game doesn't tell you.  It also does nothing to establish the universe or what is going on.  You will literally have to look up the novels on Wiki or have read them already to know who anyone is or what is going on.
-Graphics-
Passable.  Texture work on most of the NPCs and players is mostly nonexistant as the Simuloids(?) or whatever you are called all mostly have sheer metal bodies.  This isn't a complaint, could very well be a legitimate design choice based on the novels, I don't know for sure.  The different zones I have been to are infact varied and colorful, the hub world is mostly grey, however.  I am also dealing with dropping frame rates in some areas as low as <1FPS but this is not too common.
-Sound-
Background music works fine.  Sound effects however are either very soft or aren't there.  I've noticed footsteps in some areas go away and leave you feeling awkwardly quiet as you travel.  Launch day problems?  Can't say for sure.
-Combat-
The MMO meat and potatoes.  There are 4 classes to choose from.  Melee tank, melee DPS, ranged DPS, healer.  The skill trees are linear so I don't really see how any one ranged DPS will be too different from another once the game is in full swing.  The actual issue with the combat is the "feel".  All of your attacks are weightless.  There is no feedback when performing a skill or ability.  You will go looking for your skill tab to figure out how best to set up a rotation or what abilities do what but you will only find vague explanations like "Damages enemy/Heals party member".  There needs to be some solid data in the tooltips.  Damage dealt, range, etc.  When executing an ability it is hard to tell if you've hit or missed your target, or if the ability has actually gone off, unless it has an over the top animation.  These things matter in an MMO.
-Misc. Thoughts-
I've gone through the menus and found that I could Lock Targets using Caps Lock but this doesn't seem to have any real effect.
Most in game menus are buggy or broken in the scrolling will only work one way, tool tips will stay on screen until I close the menu and reopen it to view a different tool tip, background not appearing making the text in the menu very difficult to read.
Timers in the player housing are all cut off and don't fit their respective frames.  Seems like an easy fix but a strange thing to make it this far into the dev process.
Take it for what you will.  Watch some (recent)youtube videos, check out a Twitch stream or two, and make an informed decision.

I feel really mixed about this game, and while I am refunding it myself (most likely), I will still recommend it to others, and here's why, broken down into a list of Pros and Cons:
PROS:
-Seemingly huge open world
-You can hack mechas and make them your pets for combat, along with upgrading their strength, abilities, and passive
-The environmental weather hazards put a nice twist on the game as you're exploring
-You start with your ship, which is your main base of operations, also where you upgrade your characters' stats
-Pretty solid graphics for a game of this type, not AAA, but still good imo
-The concept of the game is solid, I love the idea of an open-world, pet training and collective RPGish game
-The devs have pushed out updates continuously over the course of months, which surprises me greatly.  There's only 36 reviews at the time of writing this, which probably means maybe over 200 copies sold.  The devs have stood their ground and devoted their time to this project, even with such a tiny following.  As much as I like games like this, I've never heard of this one, or found it on Steam until now.  Even the reviews are outdated which is why I'm writing one.
CONS:
-The gathering and crafting system seems pretty unfinished, and super basic.  You walk up to resources and grab them, which in turn gives you progress towards unlocking other craftable items, but there's only 10 or so things to craft.
-Doesn't seem like you can customize your gear or armor at all, which sort of takes away from the RPG aspect.  You can only put points into your character to upgrade their stats, and there's only 5-6 upgrades to chose from.  No talents, no skills, nothing.
-The storage chest in your ship is broken.  You tell it to place 1 item in the chest and it deposits them all anyway.
-The grammar on the main page may or may not detract people from the game.  It's quite possible that English isn't the devs first language, but you can tell he's at least trying.  Hiring someone or getting a friend to rewrite the main page so the English doesn't sound broken may help attract people.
-Switching weapons/tools is annoying.  You can't just scroll with your mouse, you have to press Q which pauses the game, select your item from a UI, then unpause the game and continue with what you're doing.
(may or may not be a con for some people but)
-This game is not multiplayer, as of this build.  It's 100% solo.  I was under the impression it was a multiplayer game, but it's not, so keep that in mind when considering a purchase.
OVERALL:  The game isn't bad, and like I said in the beginning, I will recommend it to others, it's just not for me.  But kudos to the devs for sticking with their game, even with no publicity and a small following.
6/10

So far this is just an okay game but it has a really good foundation and concept to build on. I'm giving it a 3/5, it's still in early access and a work in progress but I can see it becoming a good game.
Humanity is threatened by a virus and you have to travel to the planet Arcania where some of the flora may be able to save mankind. The planet has been abandoned since the working drones turned against humans. You crash land and have to find the others. During your search you gather plants and resources to do some crafting and improve your station.
Within the last month in a half or so I've seen a couple updates that have fixed things that seriously annoyed me. The lightning was the worst thing EVER! It did not act like lightning and instead followed you in a chain of about 6 lightning strikes. They have changed it to where lightning strikes randomly and not in chains so if you get out of it's way your safe. Thank you, thank you, thank you. They also made the haze in between the tempest and your weather controlled areas thinner and the fog less thick and less blue so you can see where you're going better.
In one of the last updates they changed the drones to look more animal-like which is nice since there's a little more variety in how they look and how they attack. You are also able to tame some of the drones now which is cool. However, they took out the working drones so the story makes less sense.  The story doesn't seem to be complete yet so hopefully that'll become clearer in later updates.
Some of the controls are kinda funky and the interface could use some work. Being able to see the names of items and maybe a short description when you hover over them would be great. Since it's in early access your bound to come across some bugs. Some are kind of amusing, like leaves fluttering through my station above the clouds, and others are annoying, like my equipped items saying their equipped after I collect them off of my dead body but not being visible on my hotbar (Unequipping one item and re-equipping it seems to make all of them visible again). I would recommend getting the game to support the developers or if it's on sale because it looks promising, but it's just not there yet.

As an intro to this review, I will give my experience with the trio of FF13 games. I have played the first 2 twice. Once on xbox, and once on PC. I have completed Lightning Returns on PC only. I personally liked all of them, from story to gameplay. While the previous games in the 13 series have had preformance issues on PC, and the games themselves were very divisive in their gameplay and story, Lightning Returns changes everything. Combat is completely different and the overall experience is so much better.
The pervious games had quite a few preformance problems on PC. Terrible frame rates, small resolutions (which was fixed later), and even game breaking bugs. I myself was a victim of one of those bugs, as well as fps issues, but was able to fix and play them both. On the flip side, I am happy to say that Lightning Returns was not plagued by any of these problems. I installed the game and went right to playing it, with absolutely no problems at all. The game can run at 60 FPS, and though it did dip below that sometimes, it was mostly stable. You also have a decent number of options to improve your own preformance by clicking on the options menu at the top left of the screen. Unfortunately, you can't access that menu with a controller, but that, along with the acual quit button (as opposed to the main menu button) are the only things you will need a mouse for if you wish to use a controller.
Combat from the first two games was very simple, and was mostly just controlling which classes your 3 fightning charaters were at any given time. Switching between these constantly was very important, but otherwise, the only thing you had to do was choose the auto-battle function and let the game choose the abilites to use.
In Lightning Returns, the system is completely different. There are now things known as "Schemata", or outfits with 4 abilities, 2 accessories, and an optional adornment for each. You get to choose every single one of these for youself, and there is a large pool to choose from.
During battle, you now control everything. You have access to 3 Schemata to switch between, which are all very important because each Schemata has its own ATB guage, which is basically a stamina bar. These fill up much more quickly when the Schemata is not being used, so it is important to switch between them often. Guarding has also been introduced, which is very important. During combat, you will need to guard in order to drastically reduce damage taken. Timing your guard perfectly will negate almost all damage, while simply guarding without proper timing will reduce damage by around half. If you are worried about timing, don't be! I'm pretty bad at timing stuff like this, but there were only a few places where I struggled. If you are still worried, you can play on easy, which allows you to regenerate health for free between combat.
There is now a clock in game, which is very important. You have 13 days to complete your ultimate goal, and if you don't make it in time, you will lose the game. If you do fail, you start a new game, keeping all of your old items, excluding quest items. This mechanic scared me a lot at first. I was sure that I would mess something up because I wasn't going by a guide. My fear, however, was misplaced. By the time i was ready for the end of the game, I still had around 4 or 5 days left, with little left to do. The most important thing to remember is to use the chronostasis ability. This freezes time, but also consumes EP. You start with 5 maximum EP, but gain more throughout the game. Chronostasis costs 1 each use, but you can gain EP through combat very easily, so you can do so much more during a single day in game than you otherwise would. The time limit is not something that you have to be scared of. Just explore, use chronostasis, and don't avoid combat. Also, at the beginning of the game you start with less than 13 days left. Through quests (main and side), you gain additional days, as well as stats and money.
Something else of note is that the game is now open world. You can now do whatever you want, with the only exception being time. Some NPCs will only be out at certain times, and some areas will only be open at certain times. This can sometimes be annoying, but there is almost always something else to do in the meantime, so just come back later if something isn't accessible.
In Lightning Returns, you have one controllable character, who has been in both previous games: Lightning. She is now also known as "The Savior", and has been chosen by God to serve him during the world's final 13 days. Along with her, God also chose Hope, another returning character. He will help Lightning from "The Arc", which is a place created by God and unaffected by time. You will meet many different characters throughout the game, some you may recognize if you have played the previous games, while others will be completely new. If you are new to the series, or don't remember everything from the previous 2 games, then don't worry. The cutscenes alone do a decent job of filling you in, but you will also have a datalog with plenty of information to read through, should you wish to know more.
In conclusion, I personally believe this game was great. As you can see, I spent a bit more than 90 hours playing it and I enjoyed every minute. There were 0 technical issues, the graphics were beautiful, and I really enjoyed the new and much more interactive combat. The Schemata were also a very nice addition, as they allowed a lot more variety, both in combat as well as for Lightning's appearance. The story was emotional, but action packed. It was also mysterious, but consistant. By the end of it all, I nearly cried, as the final cutscene just wrapped everything up so much more nicely than I could have imaged. This game is a great pick up and if you are looking for a great story with good combat, then you have found it.

I honestly am not sure why I like this game. I've played a bit of it on 360, and some on PS3. And now I have a Steam copy I'm playing through. I've bought this game four times, for the record. Once on 360, twice on PS3, and this version. It's a mess, but a mess that's greater than the sum of it's messy parts. A sequel to a sequel no-one probably needed or asked for, and one that was pretty much gaffed from day one due to being the third entry in the arguably most maligned entry in the Final Fantasy franchise. With that said, I enjoyed FFXIII, flaws and all (and, let's be clear, there were a lot of flaws).
FFXIII-2 was a weird beast - it introduced more freedom, fixed some problems with the mostly stellar battle-system, gave us a cool cahracter in Noel. Yet it also went off the deep-end even more with its narrative and made us play as Lightning's younger sister who served solely as 'damsel in distress' in the original game. Basically, one step forward, one and a half steps back.
In continuing the steps analogy, LR:FFXIII steps just enough forward to be equal to FFXIII and then sort of steps to the side and goes off on its own. The story is still nonsense, more so than ever in fact. The battle system seems similar but is also radically different. You meet familiar characters but everything is still weird. But you have a world you can explore, and there's pressure from the whole "save the world in 13 days!" stuff.
If you like your games to be a bit rough around the edges, don't care if the plot makes no sense, and just wanna play as Claire "Lightning" Farron again, I think you'll like this?
Also, I have nominated this for a Steam Award - "Villain Most in Need of a Hug". But, honestly? Everyone in this damn game needs a hug.

I finally beat Wazhack for the first time on the steam version! Woohoo!
I feel that give me a good enough perspective to re-write my review of Wazhack.
The first time i beat the game was with a knight decked out with dragon armor and Excalibur.
The second time was with a wizard who could teleport and shoot lightning bolt and had crazy mana regeneration.
this third time I had beat the game was with a rogue who wielded two legendary curved swords and a suit of crystal armor.
Wazhack has filled a role in my game collection as an exceptional side-scrolling adventure game. it can be unforgiving at times but I have always been rewarded by thinking critically and trying to utilize all avenues.
the main game play is great at the beginning there are usually a dozen or so options to dispatch enemies and some even offer some interesting interactions.
the middle of the game sometimes is a bit of a slug fest you really need to make sure your armor class is high and your weapons hit bonus is decent.
the end game is frustratingly simple you need to  ready yourself to face monsters that are directly countered by items found early in the game.
some of the late game monsters can feel really unfair due to luck and their sheer power.
I would like to seem some puzzle elements like codes or ciphers.
a quest giver would be cool. With quests like bring back 3 rubies or the head of a named monster for a ring in return.
More unique items something like the Midas would be really cool. like the Horadric cube or a portal gem that goes somewhere else.

One of the biggest surprises of last year for me and easily one of my games of 2013. Wazhack is an unusual roguelike (like, a real roguelike, not a roguelike-like) because not only does it feature full 3D animated visuals, lighting and physics, it’s also a side-scroller instead of the traditional top-down fare.
Wazhack wasn't one of my games of 2013 just for its unusual appearance for a roguelike though, I loved it so much because it was the source of many an unexpected and grim tale (as roguelikes often are) thanks to its careful, tactical play and many emergent systems and mechanics. Here are a few choice screenshots from my time with the Android version, complete with anecdotal captions:
Wazhack is full of these moments and often ones that aren't so easy to relay in single screenshots.
Granted, the game's graphics are very… particular, and certainly not for everyone (I personally find them really charming and they look tactile as if they've been handmade), but because everything is in 3D the game can afford certain luxuries that a frame-by-frame pixel art roguelike can't, so for example you can see what gear enemies are wearing and wielding at a glance, while your own character’s appearance changes depending on what you equip. When you sell stuff, you also see it populating the shopkeeper’s shelves, racks, pots and busts (which is a really neat touch). And of course the physics and lighting work with the 3D too: loot explodes and tumbles from enemies, their limp bodies slump and slide, amulets around your neck jostle about, lit lamps illuminate your way, arrows ricochet off surfaces (and can be retrieved), capes flap and fall (yes, there are capes in Wazhack). It's just nice to play a roguelike that can be easily read.
Wazhack is absolutely worth your time if you’re wanting something that's meaty and rich that you can play in short (or long) bursts. It's ideal on handheld devices too. The original PC version here looks a lot better and is easier to use with mouse and keyboard, but the Android and iOS versions are portable gems in their own right.
It's also worth mentioning that Waz (the developer) has been improving and adding to Wazhack since it was released back in 2012 and only recently he added another 8 classes and overhauled the talent system!
- Charming, solidly designed, accessible, deceptively deep, surprising, extremely challenging and replayable, funny, tactical and just bags of fun, Wazhack is a bit of a desert island game for me now and one of the genre’s best kept secrets. The game is available on Windows, Linux, Mac, Android, iOS and can even be played (and trialled) in your browser at:

I originally bought this game when it was released on Desura close to 2 years ago, and have put many hours into it.
It's a "pseudo-turn-based" game, where you can run around with the WASD keys like a platformer, but enemies/NPC's only move and attack while your moving and attacking. While you are not doing anything, neither is the enemy. In a way, it's kinda like FTL in that regard. Kinda.
For those familiar with roguelikes, Wazhack, as the name suggests, takes a lot of inspiration from Nethack, to the point where it might be easier to describe it  "2.5D Nethack". You can see it in the items; the way they are identified, cursed, blessed, enchanted, etc..
That's not to say that it's a clone though, Wazhack has MANY of it's own features that I don't want to spoil for everyone, and even has branch dungeons and many different enemy models and spells.
There's even going to be a multiplayer like feature, though not in the traditional sense.
If you like roguelikes, Wazhack is definitely one to pick up.
EDIT: I hadn't played this game for about 5 months, and the game is even better than it was back then. Loads of new content, including items, events and even classes were added. There's also been even more balance changes. The game was far more fair than Nethack ever was, and now even more so. Just the right amount of fairness and challenge.
For beginners, the Barbarian/Vandal is a great class to start with due to their high health, damage, and starting weapon. You'll have trouble finding armor due to their large size, but their high health makes up for it. By the way, you can tell if your Barbarian/Vandal can use armor if the armor in question has something along the lines of 'very large' in parenthesis underneath it's name.
The only thing I really consider bad in this game is the pet AI(every class starts with a pet). While it's certainly leagues better than Nethacks, they're terrible when it comes to running across ladders, though they're better now than the last time I've played. I also wish you could set their aggressiveness like in Torchlight 2. Honestly, they're not all that useful, but they're nice company in that lonely dungeon. I also wish you could choose which pet to take, rather than each class having it's own pet, though I understand the reason behind that.
For those who want to try before buying, go to it's Desura page here:
On that page, click the blue "Free" button next to demo. If you don't want to use Desura, simple click the Free Button and look for the link that says "Download Direct", and you'll be able to download the standalone demo installer.

The most appealing part of this game for me is the smooth transition between action and strategy. You can be running down a hallway and mowing down goblins, then suddenly you're inches away from a giant, sifting through your inventory and trying to decide which item is the most likely to prevent his club from crushing your skull. Do you have a sleeping potion to throw at him? Maybe this unidentified scroll can teleport you to safety? Your wand of polymorphing might turn him into something that can't wield a club...
Looting is another big part of the game that stands out for me. Almost every enemy drops something, often many somethings. My inner hoarder loves when I've finished slaughtering a battallion of gnomes and find myself standing knee-deep in daggers, various wands, and a pile of tiny outfits. You have a fair bit of inventory space, and it's surprising how fast this can fill up with scrolls, potions, books, gems, weapons, rings/amulets, armors, foods, etc. Then you have to decide what you want to identify, sell, drink, read, or keep for emergencies.
Don't get me wrong though, having hundreds of items and unlimited time to think doesn't make the game get any easier as you go further down. Enemies become stronger and spawn more quickly, until you're fighting your way through waves of liches, giants, skeletons and demons. Your stockpile of healing items, wands and scrolls can be quickly depleted if you don't plan ahead or if you just have ♥♥♥♥♥♥ luck. Beating the bosses and making it back to the top is a major accomplishment, one that you'll only experience after you have a good grasp on how things work and what the best ways to approach situations are. Even then it's still a rather rare experience, especially with the most difficult characters.
There are only a few games that I can say I've put hundreds of hours into, and I'm proud to say that this is one of them.
TL;DR - Replayability, looting, inventory-management, strategy.

CONS

I watched with anticipation on before its first release. It promised much, looked pretty and was openworld +. Yep, I'll be having that, I thought. Then I played with the initial release that a mate had bought. Bit disappointed. Pretty enough, but it was a grindathon mining fest with little much else to keep you enthralled. Nah, I'll not buy it, ta. That's not what it was supposed to be.
A year later, after some of the large updates, and a Steam Sale. I bought it and now spent over 100 hours on it.
The good:
It's pretty enough still and the more horrible bugs that plagued the game are ironed out. The tranquil adventuring around planets/space are pretty sweet and being able to set up a base and expand outwards is fine. There's a good, seemingly unending supply of odd animals/plantlife to discover as well as decent ships to bob about it and the planet/moon types do give you a proper sense of "alien-ness". Alienity? Dunno. You get what I mean. Oh, and freighters, if you can get one, do make life really quite excellent within the game.
The bad:
It's only "pretty enough". It could be prettier - the animals, in their procedurally drawn ways, sometimes end up looking...erm...wrong. And there was too little varience in body-types/shapes so things began to run into each other. And odd things happened like a planet I found where a cow-elephant of massive proportions was flying with little butterfly wings...I mean, it was funny and sweet, but y'know...a bit immersion breaking.
The space battles - the ship controls are at times way too laggy. And to change them to suitable for battles, it gets way too jumpy on a planet so you spaff into cliffs/the floor/cow-elephants.
Bases - at time of writing, and I admit I haven't played for a month, you could only set up one base at a time. I'd like to, as a thought, have one home base and be able to set up outposts (not full bases - but a place where I could get my head down in travelling).
Immersion - you can't RPG this one, yet there's nothing known about the character so you could really RPG it up. Can't buy rooms at the space stations, no beds, no need to sleep/eat/break wind in the privacy of your own cockpit. Shame really. I know it's not that sort of game, but wiuth a few simply additions, it could have been all things to all men/women/cow-elephants.
Physics - they're the same regardless of planet/moon size/shape/proximity. Shame, as going to a say a high-grav planet would be a reasonable catalyst for animal changes (flatter cow-elephants, say) or a low grav-moon (which would at least explain flying cow-elephants). It would add challenges to the game - suit alterations required, ship powering, being captured in gravity wells due to poor flying.
Seems like I'm down on it, so why do I recommend it? Well, it could (and I'm placing as much emphasis on "could" as I can in type, short of making it flash red) be the complete game. Quests (not just grinding), RPG for those that want it and not for those that don't, unexplored planets, good ships of different designs, space wars, and odd critters (heck, evenn one as a pet would be cool!). The basics are now all there and the game is so much better than it was, it's playable now.
Basically - they've created a proper, vageuly believable universe and how you can get about in it. Now I think they could tart up the interior and make it swanky, RPG-able, unique and fun. It could do with being more fun.
So yeah, I'd say get it on sale - it's worth a few quid for what it could become. You've got the shell of a world-beating game - it just needs filling with more cow-elephants.

In other similar games, you are a recruit who has undergone serious (secret) training meant to make you a super-soldier, capable of taking on enemy fire-teams to an entire company. All the while taking in bullets without a vest like you're some sort of soldier designed to be a fully-fledged badass.
That is not the case in this game though, apparently.
As said in this game's desc. You are another common soldier who has joined the army like your fellow brothers around you.
"When you come under fire, you don't simply stand shooting at the enemy with courage. Because that's like getting a free-ticket to heaven'r hell. You obviously take the nearest cover, and return fire when you get the chance. When you raid a base, you don't go alone, you never do, you are not rambo in this sh*t, and you probably will never ever get to walk away a certain base with explosions going off of your back without looking back. When you know you're winning, don't get cocky, because everything is going smoothly is exactly the reason you need to watch out. Hell, how do you think i've made it this far? It's because of experience that shaped me to be who I have to be in this bloody war." - Infantry Journal
These are just a few examples of how you should preferrably engage in combat.
"When I first stepped onto my first mission, I was literally just a shooting target. While we were climbing up this certain hill, we suddenly came under fire. I desperately looked around to return fire to any visible contacts, but none. It was at this moment that I knew we ****ed up. The time when I knew that it was the worst possible time and worst possible place to be under fire. A lot of my own friends had their backs down the ground before I even reacted in time. They were dead before I realized we came under fire. What was I thinking? I don't know, I just went prone and pretended to be dead until the hill was bombarded with artillery, that I gained enough courage to stand up once again and continue with the assault. Though I felt remorse towards my fallen brothers and anger towards myself that I haven't been able to avenge them. That's in the past, at least." - Infantry Journal
Terrain is Vital in this game, they can serve as real purpose to cover a certain area from advancing enemy forces, or against your own. Because of the top-down aspect, terrain may be a little tricky to determine (particularly something that isn't easy to discern) but with time, you can get used to it.
"If you thought you won the war, you haven't. But at least you won one of it's battles, for now. So cheers mate, and let's hope to god that we can win another tomorrow." - Infantry Journal
After you win a certain scenario, you are prompted to choose another scenario depending on where you started and how you want to play it. Thus, giving it a nice touch for me at least, which adds more to the open-world aspect. And speaking of open-world.
"Winning a battle is like solving a problem. Say, Math, if you thought there's only one way to solve it, then you thought wrong. There's always multiple ways to win things over. Be it in style, or in secrecy. Be it underhanded or forthright it doesn't matter because really. It only matters who wins." - Infantry Journal
It's not like war is supposed to be fair right? When one calls in an artillery barrage, you do too. If one decides to flank around an objective, you intercept and proceed to do the same. The open-world aspect in this game is really nice as it gives you more than one approach to win battles.
"I don't know if it's just me, but, lately everyone else except me has been improving in their aiming. By quite a lot actually, just yesterday, I heard that our newest recruits turned into Seargents just after a single mission. RECRUITS, I'm writing to y'. Seriously mate, if things go like this for the next few days, i'm gonna fall behind. Well, time to get some PT." - Infantry Journal
AI in this game isn't really that ridiculous, but you can tweak how well they can Aim. While this game can be considered to be a tactical shooter, there is nothing tactical about winning matches. It is a matter of  spamming reinforcements, brute force seems to be the only answer. When the game is played on the higher difficulties, your teammate AI seem labotomize themselves to the point where they will stand in battle and do absolutely nothing leading to you having to always lead in and getting killed in one shot.
Yes, one shot, let's talk about those. Whoever thought the health/damage system in this game was a good idea must not have any knowledge of game design.
How the health system works is that the soldiers do not have a healthbar, rather every gun has a chance to kill someone. Pistols will have a lower chance compared to assault rifles and assault rifles lower to sniper rifles, very simple. But this game of chance leads to situations where a stray bullet will kill you before you even join the battle, some other times, you will flank, shoot multiple rounds into a guy and he will not die, rather he will just turn around, shoot once and you die.
And sometimes, you will one shot them, there is a way to counteract this through the usage of body vests but those cost resource points and when you have to babysit the entire team, resources can run dry.
I'd recommend this game instantly if the health system was changed, I could pretty much ignore a lot of the other problems with that one change but at this rate I doubt it will be changed thus I cannot recommend it.

I just played the trilogy recently.  The 3rd one has problems.
-They changed the control scheme on it.  ...Probably for the better, but still.
-The Eagle doesn't feel quite as powerful in it as it did in the previous ones.  ...Which is again is probably for the better, since you basically never have to swap out the Eagle until late game in them.
-The time limit maxes out at 4 minutes.  And not just "maxes out the display" and keeps rolling, but actually taps out at 4 minutes.  THIS is my biggest complaint with it.  You are basically forced to keep going in it, you never get a chance to really sit back and explore.  I like exploring the levels.  Pedestrians also give you almost no time.
-The missions.  They were every other level here, not every 4th level like in the previous game.  They also... I dunno, mostly were uninspired?  They're not bad, but they seemed to be fairly bland, particularly early on.  They are hit and miss overall.
Two other issues:  This game includes the Nosebleed Pack.  Now, it's nice in that "more cars, more maps, more content!"  However, these vehicles are not well balanced, and are available from the beginning.  And are available in the opponent's pool from the beginning.  And the hovering car can be very, very annoying to deal with.
Another issue is that the game crashes on story missions.  This is a known issue.  There is a workaround.  The workaround is to turn off the mip filter.  HOWEVER, due to another glitch, that being badly coded menus where the content doesn't contain itself to the windows, you can't actually turn off the mip filter in game.
You CAN do it from the setup though.  So open the setup, go to options, video, advance, and where you see "Mip filter", set it to none.  You may also need to disable Pixel Fog (though I didn't need to).  This should fix the problem.
There's a lot to like about the third game though.  The graphics are a big step up.  The final levels in this game really look fantastic.  The story IS there, even if it's annoying at times.
My favorite of the bunch is the second.  The third has problems.  So, why am I giving this a "yes" recommendation, despite all the flaws, including crashes?  Because, at the end of the day, it's still Carmageddon.  And if you need to get your fix, there ya go.

Squirbs is a 2d Puzzle platformer developed by Team Indev and released January 6th 2016. It's a relatively inexpensive indie developed puzzle platformer which will renew your hatred for platformers.
When you boot up the game for the first time, you walk over to a crystal and destroy it, and now you need to go find the parts and put it back together because you're a clumsy oaf and shouldn't be allowed around breakables.
the key "selling" point for Squirbs, or shall we say "what it does differently" is forces you to control two characters at the same time. So it's a multi-taskers dream or nightmare... I say nightmare because I like to feel successful when I multi-task, instead of dying and restarting like I'm playing super meat boy.
you thankfully can skip levels, as you collect shards you unlock additional levels and additional worlds. If you're really looking for a cheap platformer this'll entertain you for a few hours.
Regarding the extra features, I didn't play co-op, but you do need to port forward to play co op
, My controller worked but I felt like controller vs keyboard made little difference on this game, I got my steam card drops, and I'm not going to get the steam achievements.
As a whole, not a bad game, as a whole, not a good game. Steam is full of many developers "first games" and I definitely get that so I don't want to beat up on it too much. I'll let you be the judge of weather you have pocket lint and time to spend on it, or would rather save up for another game which brings more to the table.

Solid and polished foundation for a game that is similiar to other sandboxy games, however providing you with actual goals.  The controls feel tight and responsive, no real bugs and it runs pretty smooth. However there's an infurating stuttering that happens when the world chunks are being loaded and it somewhat persists even if they're loaded into the ram, otherwise the world generally loads really quickly (2 seconds). The combat system has some depth to it that doesn't just make it a simple button smasher, supported by the skill system that lets you put chips into some sort of memory bank that serve as skills that you can execute if you don't lose your combo, including a stealth system to avoid enemies.
The only real "issue" it has, is the lack of content, which should not be a suprise if you're reading the statement on the store page. Otherwise the game pretty much feels complete. You won't see any placeholders and it generally has decently high quality models, sound and music. So all the developers really have to do is add quests, blueprints and enemy variety.

While Sky Break is in an early stage of Early Access, I see a lot of potential in the game.
Most of the main game mechanics appear to be in the game and they work well for the most part. While the combat could use a little more variety, it works well for the most part even though I think the robots are a little too powerful to start the game. The other mechanics work well together and could develop into a good game. The art style/graphics are also quite nice for this stage in Early Access.
The only real issue with the game right now is the lack of story content. Very little of the story appears to be in the game at this time. This means that there isn't much structure to the game. For the most part you just explore the planet looking for materials to craft things with. The game also has quite a bit of grinding right now. Since I had quite a bit of fun with the game, when the developers add more content I think the game will get quite a bit better.
If the concept interests you and you are willing to explore the planet while waiting for new content to be added, I think you can have some fun with the game. Otherwise if you have any interest in the game's concept I would at least keep an eye on the game's development.
Note: I received a free review copy from the developer.

I knew about Fortify before it was released on steam; a few of my friends used it to make bases. However, I didn't want to get into it right then because it looked unpolished and the controls were seemingly unintuitive. Yesterday, I read on Rust's Devblog 99 that this had just been released on steam. I figured it was time to get it, and while it may not be free, there's probably a reason for that. So, after looking at a few screenshots, I decided I could definitely use Fortify as a great tool to further my base designing skills, which is exactly what it's designed to be. I'm a casual/non-casual Rust player, with over 400 hours on it after playing on and off. Ever since Legacy, though, I've struggled with designing bases. I was never able to fully utilize a great base spot with the most efficient base possible. Now, I'm not saying I'm flawless at this now, but with Fortify, nothing can stop me from making the bases I wish I had months and years ago. It's a fabulous tool, very easy to use, and if you know how to build in Rust, getting around the program won't be an issue. At the point of this review I have 1 hour on the game. That was enough time to build the dream base for my friends and me. It's so easy to use, and there's absolutely no hinderance to your game. I think I can safely say the best alternative is drawing bases out by hand because there's no other program (besides Rust) as thought-out and in-depth (as much as you can be with a Rust base building) as Fortify.
Tl;dr: Get the tool. It's not a game, don't go expecting it's a game. It's not Rust creative mode. It's for building bases to your heart's content. Thank you, RTK Entertainment, for an amazing tool to add to the shed.

Disclaimer: I have not played Darksiders II: Deathinitive edition. I have played the original Darksiders II, though. In this review I will assume that the core game did not change much between editions.
- Combat, combat, combat. I’d say the core focus of this game is combat, and Darksiders goes a great job at it. Controls are responsive and it feels great to dish out huge combos. If you are a fan of Devil May Cry -style combat, you will probably like this game too.
- I enjoyed the challenge of some battles. I remember struggling at some points in the game.
- Plenty of drops and equips to choose from, so you can customize your equipment to better suit your playstyle. Different weapons, for example, have different attack speeds, attack patterns, damage, elemental damage, etc. You can also upgrade some of your weapons. I also enjoyed that the equipment (armour, boots, gloves, etc) actually change your in game appearance.
- The world is fairly large: plenty to explore, plenty to do. There are collectibles scattered around, so keep your eyes peeled. Very glad they included a fast travel option.
- Wall running, jumping, and climbing work well. This may be a minor detail, but since there are many segments where you use these abilities, it adds up over time. Their smooth execution really helps with the flow of the game. I especially like that climbing isn’t slow.
- NPCs and lore are interesting. I won’t go into much detail, but it’s nice to see that effort was put into the backstory of Darksiders I and II.
- Nice incorporation of puzzles. I did not find them particularly difficult but if they were excluded, the game would be too focused on killing everything in sight.
- Some puzzles were unnecessarily simple. They didn’t add much to the game, they were just there for the sake of being there.
- Bugs and crashes. In my case, the flying serpent cut scene would not trigger when I reached serpent’s peak. I had to restart the game and backtrack for it finally trigger.
- It’s not always clear what you must do. I found myself wandering aimlessly a few times. But on the other hand, aimlessly exploring helps you find dungeons, items, and other secrets.
- Typical 3rd person frustrations with the camera, however, this was a non-issue most of the time.
Darksiders II shines bright when you are in combat. It is just satisfying to fight creatures much bigger than yourself and combo them to shreds. Everything else was OK to me. The game runs well and there are sufficient hours of gameplay to keep you entertained. I would only recommend this game to those excited by the combat.

2016 game with 1996 controls. And it's a racing game, where controls should be priority #1.
I've played PS1 games with better/authentic controls.
Sadly, I cannot recommend it, due to the fact that the racing part (in a racing game) is done badly, so when you'll race - you won't get the feel that you're rac... well, you got the point.
Controls: the acceleration is on the "Z" button, brakes are on "S", and steering is on "Q" and "D". Funny, huh? There's more.
You cannot change the controls layout. At all. There's no such option.
I know, who steers with a keyboard, anyway. But still, completely removing the option to set the controls to, for example, WASD - it's ridiculous. Using an item in an MMO/RPG on "L" button - it isn't ergonomic, but, if you do it once in a minute (for a quest, for example), it's fine. But it's a racing game, where you'll be using ZSQD controls all the time... =)
And another thing - though the game uses Unreal Engine 4, the overall level of graphical "complexity" meets the HD tablet game, rather than a 2016 PC one.
I love Unreal Engine for its visuals/performance/scalability/ect, but the use of it in that project is nothing more than a ripoff, and doesn't represent what UE is capable of.
If you want a fun racing game, with decent controls/physics - take a look at other acrades, and leave this one be.

Ok. So this would be my first ever review on a videogame. Here goes. (Also, I hate long reviews too but bear with me XD)
No Man's Sky. No game in recent memory I think has had as much controversy as this one. I mean, the blue or gold dress thing had less firestorm than this game. It's like Rush, it seems: either ya hate it or ya love it. And I'm no different, it seems. I won't lie, I love the hell out of this game. But I'm not here to argue or say it's amazing without reason.
The reason I love this game is because it appeals to me. I'm a huge space fanatic, and this game is the closest I can get to planet-hopping (on my current budget, at least.) I love the far-out views, and putting myself in the scene.
You can be a space-pirate, a space-hauler, practically everything you ever wanted in space! This game has more substance than people give it credit for. Your own imagination can be the storyteller. It kind of takes me back to when I was a kid, when I made up stories and games. It's a childhood dream come true.
And so we come to the end of my review for No Man's Sky. My final review is that I would recommend buying this game, but maybe just when it's on sale. (I bought it just before Black Friday XD) but to me, it's money well-spent. Long story short: It's a great game for those who would have it.

Well lets start with a little backstory, imagine me about a decade ago, a teenager pining for the glory days of the original Carmageddon, where peds equal points and racing is for wimps, when lo and behold I found it.  A budget re-release copy of Carmageddon TDR2000, and at less than a fiver! I bought it instantly.  Maybe the fact that it's already a re-release title after a couple of years on the shelves should've had alarm bells ringing in my ears, but I bought it nonetheless, and after playing the first batch of races and missions I realised that this isn't the franchise I know and love, and by about halfway through I was bored and fed up with this game. After I completed it, I never touched it again.
So what made this such a terrible gaming experience?  Lets start with the environments. At best they're mediocre, and the locations at least are as varied as the original game, but they also looked more dreary and washed out, and to be honest, rather uninspired. Also, althogh the game engine itself is fairly solid, I've got stuck on the level geometry enough times for it to be annoying.
As for the pedestrians that inhabit the maps, they would be satisfying to run over if they didn't all have adamantine skeletons.  I swear, unless you are going full pelt at them, you have to reverse back over them at least once in order to kill them (and even then it wasn't a guarantee!) If that wasn't bad enough the game only gives you a pittance of a time bonus for running them over. 2 seconds?! It took about that long to kill them in the first place!!!
And the missions, oh
the missions!  Having one or two to break up the game is fine, but there were missions shoe-horned between every ♥♥♥♥ing race!  I just wanted to cause some carnage.  And if they weren't asinine fetch quests, they were convoluted and tedious, like shooting sharks with a slaughter mortar, which on paper sounds zany and fun, but in a vehicle can be awkward and frustrating to pull off.
Then there are the cars themselves, all the rest
have been forgiven if the cars themselves were fun to drive, but they aren't.  They're♥♥♥♥♥♥  That in itself is a cardinal sin in ANY driving sim, let alone a Carmageddon sequel.
To begin with, the line-up looks like an A-Z from a Poundland toys catalogue, Rangeing from the silly to the uninspired, with things like a motorized wooden hamster wheel, a pallid attempt at a steampunk monster truck, (which looks more like a boiler mounted on a horse cart,) a tank, nothing special, just a tank, and even a man driving a bathtub (really?), none of which fits the game's setting, bar one, Max's own Eagle, which you started with.
Then there are those cars which goes beyond uninspired to just plain lazy: one of the cars is literally called "Sports Sedan", and is just that.  I watched a video of this game about a month ago and I couldn't tell the opponent vehicles from the rest of the traffic milling about on the map.  Needless to say you won't be tempted to drive every vehicle in the game.
As for the handling it's okay for the most part, but a few vehicles refuse to turn from a standing start, some spin out like they have greased tyres, and then theres the novelty vehicles like the hovercar which is almost impossible to control and ends up adding nothing to the table in terms of gameplay.  I could go on about the gripes I have with the cars in this game (the damage modelling, the sounds, the physics...) but those are the biggest and as far as I'm concerned the worst.
Now for the upshot.  Is it worth shelling out for this game? My advice is no.  There are better games (and sequels) out there that are worth paying for.  But what if despite its glaring flaws you still have fond, nostalgic memories from when you first played it, and want to experience it again. My advice is still no.  You can get this game
its two prequels for FREE if you buy Carmageddon: Reincarnation, which in my opinion is a far better investment, especially considering how well Reincarnation itself is already panning out.
Sorry for the wall of text there, (it seemed shorter in my head) but tl;dr: Don't buy this game.

I've never played this Spy Fox game before. Ever. I always wanted to as a kid, but the furthest I got to playing it was in a demo attached to Spy Fox 3. So, there are absoulely no nostalgia-goggles on me for this review.
But, unfortunately, like the first Spy Fox, I didn't enjoy this game either.
As a follow-up to Dry Cereal, this game is a little bit better in a few ways. It doesn't just show the villain and give him screentime at the end. LeRoach is given some fleshing out (though it doesn't make ANY sense, how a kid denied entrance to a fair and getting laughed at would lead him to join an evil organization and want to take over the world). The humor is much better in this game as well. Spy Fox was still annoying as hell with his snide comments, but I enjoyed the other sight gags and the repeating joke where a chatacter would slide into the screen and say, "S.M.E.L.L.Y. Oh yes. Our arch-nemesis," had me laughing several times.
But with those positive comments, comes my slew of negative ones. For one, I think this choice of location is MUCH lazier than Dry Cereal. It's a cool World Fair, but there's so little to it and it's so aesthetically uninteresting that it got boring to me really fast.
Also, similarly to Dry Cereal, the villain's plan seemed really stupid to me. How would relying on precisely 1,000,000 people cranking a turnstile to enter a fair which would crank a giant mechanical dog could possibly work. How would you know if the stadium could hold a million people? How would you know a million people would come? How do you know your robot is durable enough to destroy an entire planet? Doesn\'t world domination require a successful leadership instead of... rampant destruction? In the words of Tony Stark, "Not a good plan."
The whole S.M.E.L.L.Y. plot didn't really go anywhere either. They mention it several times, and it made for some good jokes... but really in the end it's just LeRoach doing his own thing.
However, the whole "ticking clock" plot allowed for a very Pajama Sam-esque plot development influenced by the gameplay itself. It's not as linear as Dry Cereal. Every piece you get to deactivating the robot dog increases the drive for completion. It's much more organic for a player to get involved in the story, and I prefer it to the archetypal Humongous plots.
But, you saw the thumbs down. And because you liked the game and saw I didn't, that means you're going to downvote my review, even though I gave my legitimate points for disliking it. Even worse, you won't leave a comment telling me why you disagree with my review. I'd happily accept arguments, but this is the internet so ho hum.
In spite of everything, Some Assembly Required is a better Spy Fox installment than the last game. But I still personally didn't enjoy it. I'm not saying that you shouldn't enjoy it because I didn't. I'm saying that I didn't for my own reasons. I'm giving Spy Fox 2 a 6/10.

Does not finishing a game invalidate a review of it? Or does the fact that the reviewer didn't finish it speak as a review for itself?
Well neither really and I'd like to go into detail as to why. I'll start with what's good; the art style is pretty sweet and I think anyone who's played overwatch will agree because it's basically what Blizzard went for when they were making Reaper. The combat, moment to moment is satisfying and weighty enough, different combos and weapons for different applications, not overly complicated or challenging but not brain-numbingly stupid either, engaging, I would call it. Death (you, the protagonist) as a character isn't completely one dimensional, his deadpan and sarcasm made me laugh a couple of times, though he does seem awfully clueless about the world he lives in for someone supposedly so important in it. The game also has RPG elements, in that there are two trees of abilities you unlock as the game goes on, they don't do much other than take the edge off in most cases but there are times where you will need certain ones. They flow into gameplay fairly well, and you're not dependent on them so I'd say it's alright. The puzzles aren't terrible either.
Right, not much I realise but let's be honest there's a reason I didn't finish this game. Firstly, it goes on forever with no end in sight; I spent most of the time chasing the same goal through tasks that were only contextualised when I started them to the point where I lost how it connected to the original plot. And what the original plot was and my stake in it. Something about rescuing War, Death's brother after he did....something. I think the term for this is a "spirograph plot" where you keep moving but don't go anywhere in relation to the main goal. You get told 'oh this is how you can achieve it' then when you do it the game pulls a big sign saying 'Psyche' out of it's butt and waves it then runs off another 10 hours into the mess that is it's mythology.
It's very clear that the game is trying very hard to have a deep world with many unique intrigues and factions, but they're introduced and left behind so abruptly and given little context outside of their own little bubbles that it feels like they're just appearing from thin air like sudden fog, and dispersing just as quickly. It's so contrived and confuscated that it's hard to invest in any of it because none of it feels like it has any weight or real bearing on what you're doing. You end up meeting god knows how many allegedly important people, collect 3 things for them, fight a boss maybe and then you're done with it.
As mentioned before, there are RPG elements, and I'd like to mention the complete redundancy of the loot system; every buggering enemy drops some bronze pants or a new weapon or some useless garbage that an enemy in the next area will make redundant within half an hour. Firstly this chokeslams the pacing as you're forced to stop every so often to optimize Death's hairdo or something ridiculous or else suffer for it, secondly it means that any cool, unique or favoured weapon or appearance will be made useless as you progress into the game, and have to change it for something more powerful you find in a bin or whatever, thirdly it means that seeking out secrets in the levels is pointless as well because you know full well that anything you find will be outdone by something that's randomly dropped in the next area. Fourthly it means that Death usually looks like a fashion disaster and whilst that may sound like a shallow complaint; a game is the sum of it's parts and any detraction is still a detraction.
The areas of the game are arranged a bit like that of The Witcher 1 or Grim Dawn, in that they are big, but you can only ever run around one area and the area before it, which you are rarely given reason to return to save for the commute you're oblidged to do between your missions, and the next area is only unlocked once the previous mission is completed and it makes me wonder why the areas are so big, especially since there's rarely anything in them and as I established before there's no reason to put any time into exploring for loot.
The game also breaks one of the golden rules of boss fights by repeatedly spawning in groups of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ enemies to mob you whilst you're trying to kill the boss, and in the case I refer to it's especially egregious because the boss has phases of vulnerability dependent on a contextual action that any damage interrupts, and an earthquake attack that deals a quarter of your health in damage whilst you're trying to fend off the nippers that come out of the woodwork.
The game also flirts with freerunning but it comes across as pretty token as it's almost entirely linear and doesn't really make the game feel any more organic or open.

I wanted to like this game more, really, but the bugs that plague it are far too much of a problem. Most notable is the control lockup that seems to happen at random, leaving Death standing there like an idiot while you potentially get murdered, depending on when it decides to happen. And on the topic of controls, it would help the game a great deal if the lock-on was toggled instead of having to awkwardly hold LT or Shift the entire fight.
The performance isn't any better than the regular version, and the graphical upgrade is marginal at best. It's something you generally won't notice unless you're actively looking for it.
It's not a bad game, barring the problems. But it's also not a great game either.

In short : If you can get this game under 1 $, get it, because it's fun for about 4 hours or so, but with minimal or no replayability.
Game itself is simple, with minimalistic graphics, gameplay elements resembling mobile and browser games.
City building is pretty basic, as all buildings take some resources, must be connected and some buildings give resources, which you can upgrade.
There are two basic units : basic attack robot and mining robot. Fist one is used for cannon fodder, but the second collects crystals or minerals used to get epic robots. Those can be purchased with minerals and there is a lottery which one you will get and they range, from barely useful to very powerful units.
Combat is basic and involves little to no strategy, as you get 1 side to spawn units. The only tactical decisions you can make is to which unit to send first and how to spread out units. But then weird AI comes in to play, as it will attack in specific pathway, and ignore first buildings. This can lead to some unnecessary casualities.
There are many resource types, but some are a "bottleneck"resources, which mean, only this resource will limit your advance.
Multiple missions and boss battles take place and grant you some items, but some missions and bosses can be farmed to get neccesary resources.
Overall it's a simple, fun, finish once game. Don't expect much, and you will find it enjoyable.

I played Kings Bounty when I was a kid on a macintosh. This modern version of the game is fun but in reality its a children's game. If you are looking for a present for young boys and girls I would suggest that this would be a good game to get them.

Remember the sudden emptyness that lurks into your mind and heart when the newfound relationship with great book or amazing game reaches it's end? This is exactly what happened to me when I have finished King's Bounty: The Legend. The game was not perfect, but I have grown fond of her and did not nearly have enough. At that moment I had to have more, so I have taken up on Armored Princess.
After finally finishing the installation and starting the game a feeling of familiarity spreads inside me. However the game is little too familiar. How would it not be when it uses the same engine as The Legend and changes only little. Developers went as far as to using the same models and pieces of artwork as in The Legend. As you have probably guessed, the first impression was not one of the best. However do not let appearences fool you, the important thing is here. New challenges, locations and even few units.
The story continues few years after the happenings from The Legend, where you have (have you?) succesfully saved the World from demon invasion. However peace was soon to fade, after the hero left to seek adventure in other dimensions, demon army have returned with newfound strenght. At this point you take control of princess Amelie and set on a quest to find the old hero and bring him back. Same as in The Legend, story provides nice background to the exploring and fighting, developers follow the example set in The Legend and provide you with plenty of texts and bits of humor.
So should you get the game or not? If you are new to the series I would first grab either The Legend  so that you can follow up on story, but it is not necessary. And if you have played The Legend and liked it, you should definitely get it, because it takes everything that was good on The Legend and adds some polish.

Nominating this game for a steam awards in the 'suspension of disbelief' category. Considering the subject matter, it seemed to fit with the theme. How to describe this game, honestly also thought of 'it's hard to describe' in another category, but at the end of the day, it still has a fairly obvious theme, albeit supernatural in nature. Ah, Samantha Everett...what a strange little heroine for a story. She is in no way completely innocent or good, but her heart is usually in the right place. Let's see she saw a horrible abduction scene before coming to Dr. Style's; she basically lies about being th new secretary. Dr. Styles is a neuroscientist of some kind (the sign said abnormal research) This Frankstein-like manor usually involves him in his experiments, though he at times gets others involved. It's like a more cerebral version of a gothic novel. Still, Dr. Styles can be really senstive towards the memory of his belated wife. He mentioned it's her 33rd birthday, when she jokes in a flashback that he'll probably forget...just the idea that after all that time, that he didn't, he even got her roses, sort of wins him husband of the year award in my book. Yet, it's ironic that the voice actor (while interesting, plays his character so rough and to-the-point, and almost a little harsh). I wasn't sure if Dr. Styles was just a dual-personality type, though I don't mind the accent, I'm just not sure why he's such a harsh person (aside from the accident he had).
Samantha is a street-wise, slightly pathological liar (though still very sweet and straight-forward. She is very amiable, but some of her conclusions are a little strange). It's ironic that at the start, she is on her way to ...I think it was London but ends up in Oxford due to a simple twist of 'fate' about a downturned signed (which is something I loved, that something simple lead to a fortutous event for her. Samantha's unwillingness to tell the truth did frustrate me at times, sometimes you were thinking, why would you lie about something like that, then you realize Dr. Styles could be very obstrusive at times, and maybe asking about her parents and her past was probably very uncomfortable for her. She lies to him, when he asks about her necklace and that his mother had a similar one that was donated to charity (weird I remember this, after so many months), but she lied and said she got it in a junk lot  at some antique store. I don't think he bought it either LOL, nice try Sam. She also lies to the group of students, in order to find out information that Dr. Styles wanted to know, it seems rather harmless, but Sam seems to be a master manipulator. Then again, she does magic tricks and smoke and mirror stuff in her 'off' time, so honestly it's no wonder. I really liked the use of illusion magic to progress things, it was a strange but unique tactic. And yet, there did seem to be a huge supernatural element at play too (as w/ the signs changing, David's dead wife communicating to him via his 'research and tools', and sometimes just a disembodied voice, or a ghost-like image.
I don't think I fully finished this game, but I was fairly sure I was getting close to the end. I think I read somewhere what happened, but the story was very emotive as is, so I don't think that will ever change. I wondered if Sam and David were related in that big reveal where Sam first meets Dr. Styles who looks like a phantom of the opera type (with his half-mask on, but then again he had burn marks, so he was self-conscious, a man who was so stylish, wealthy and attributed to good looks; a good pedigree some might call). There just seemed to be a recognition between the two, but then I look at another scene where David mentioned his wife had a twin sister who disappeared...I immediately thought of Samantha, ven though she has dark hair and his wife had blonde, it wouldn't take much for Sam to dye her hair. So, I didn't finish enough of the story to find out what her connection was with David and his wife, but I knew it was fairly important. The winds of fate wouldn't blow for just anyone would it? It was just one of those stories where David and his wife seemed like good people, with very few skeletons in the closet, and you often wondered why bad things happen to good people (same question mankind's been asking for so long anyway)? But more importantly, was it really an accident?
This game does require you to put your own beliefs aside to fully enjoy the storyline. It does require you to think a little outside the box, and suspend your disbelief into something very different. I joked once in a screen shot, when you get to an ally in Oxford (where all the campuses are), there is a sign with Samantha's name on it, and I joke....'when you see your name on a sign, you know something's going to happen', that did almost break the fourth wall, but it didn't, because it actually made sense, then you meet a sort of Mephistophles character (he's supposedly a magician too, which did kind of make me laugh), but again since I didn't fully finish it, I could only guess what his purpose was in this game. I felt him simply just supplying her magic stuff and giving her a game of riddles, to be far too simple to be believed (he was such a cryptic character). Even though the graphics, is a little dated, I just love the story-line and how well though-out the characters were, and just how things come together, it leaves you guessing at parts, but I think ultimately it sounded like it would make sense in the end.
