Despite the controversy that surrounded the release of this game it is worth a look. Since release the developers have tweaked and patched it, significantly changing the game with new mechanics, objectives and quality-of-life updates. Whilst it is still open for debate whether the game is worth a premium pricetag if it is available for under $30 it will be worth every penny.
For me it is a 'chill-out' game,  I keep going back to it much as I would to a game like minecraft. It is visually appealing, there are a few different objectives to work towards and it has an interesting art-style and narrative theme. The theme of isolation as a traveller in a strange universe whilst discovering the nature of creation and the history of the alien races that occupy it is well executed.
The game has elements of exploration, survival and base-building all of which are competently executed although not without some flaws. Initially the inventory management aspect of the game is too onerous but I found it is worth persevering with as this eases relatively soon and the game improves considerably once it has done so. I cant say if the multi-player element now works as I have had no experience of it and no desire to either.

While surounded by heaps of controversy, the game is indeed making progress.  Whether or not the end result matches up with the promises and expectations we have been lead into is yet to be seen, but so long as they continue moving forward with it I won't write them off just yet, and remain hopeful.

I just refunded my first game, and it was Running with Rifles.  It seems like a game that would be right up my alley.  But I found the tutorial to be very opaque.  I didn't really know what I was doing, how do change the throw range of my grenades? how do backpacks work?  Why is the first thing I see a sign about radios, but my guy says he can't use a radio? How does the cover system work?  What about squad commands? What are RP?  How do I get them, and how are they spent? Do they carry over between games?  All this and more could have been handled in a 5 minute tutorial mission.  None of it is.  And armed with only these questions, and my knowledge of the keybindings from the options menu.  I joined my first story mission, and ran around with rifles and killed a few bad guys, and died a bit.   And repeated that for about 30 minutes.  And was in basically the same state I started the game in.  I don't feel I had any agency, or impact on the overall outcome of the game state.  I gave both the tutorial and the opening campaign mission (this time on casual) another try, and after the same frustrating feelings of not knowing how to have an impact on the game state.  I decided this just wasn't for me. YMMV, but I had an easier time getting Dark Souls than this.

A light-hearted episodic RPG, Precipice is a must-have for any fan of Penny Arcade and their unique brand of humor. Gabe and Tycho fight an army of Fruit F***ers, introduce plenty of Lovecraftian ideas, and some of their own, including cultist clowns. The combat system is light but remains interesting through use of unique run-time events to keep the player focused. The true victory here is the humor, as the Precipice games will keep you laughing, or at least painfully smiling, the entire time you play them. The games are breezy and light, and never threaten to bog down the player in material that the writers don't feel would be as effective.
Slightly twisted humor from the Penny Arcade guys in game form. Can't go wrong if you like old school RPGs witha  bit of WTF added in.

Darksiders 2 is the second installment of the franchise (In case the number two didn't give it away.), and the last one THQ and Vigil Games worked on before filing for bankruptcy. Overall, it's a great game, and definitely an improvement to the first game if you're into that "parkour/Zelda/Prince of Persia" kind of RPG, following puzzles in every dungeon and slashing through every damnation that the game gives to you.
Pros:
+ Great visuals, though I don't see THAT much of an improvement from the vanilla version (It could just be me not playing for awhile.)
+ Fluid combat system. Interesting combos and fast dodges (until the third dodge; I try to avoid it unless necessary).
+ Lots of depth into the skills, as you have some use for puzzles and combat, some require wrath (the game's mana), or even the ultimate Reaper form.
+ Amazing soundtrack. I wish all the tracks were included though. Some are still missing that I would love to have. Other than that, it fits perfectly into the environment and its atmosphere.
+ Dungeons are nuts, you might as well get lost. I have had that moment a few times. They're not so linear as you think.
+ Difficulty is great for beginners and those who want the extra challenge.
Cons:
- Even though it's the "Deathinitive Edition", there's still plenty of bugs. Some even break the game, but it is still possible to complete. It just gets annoying having to restart the game when I have one that ruins the immersion.
- The game feels rushed, especially near the end where you only have 1-2 dungeons compared to the beginning, but I guess that's what happens when you're a dying company that has to push the game's release date further. There's still free DLC for bonus levels if you're up for it (and the data carries over to the story as well.)
- Camera angles can be awkward upon locking. So try to mind your surroundings as best as possible. (Usually, the enemy you're targeted on is the only one that attacks.)
- Not all bosses take advantage of special puzzles. Some are just for slicing. It would be nice to have more with creative ways to kill them.
- Despair (the horse) feels like it's not used much since fast travel beats the purpose of it. The only time you need it is if you're looking for a collectible sidequest out in the overworld or *spoiler alert sorry* one boss.
- Don't be so happy when you find a chest for loot. Most of the time, you're gonna get crappy gear with crappy stats. You'll eventually find that good one that will take the combat to the edge.
Conclusion: Despite these issues, I have still managed to complete the game and not die once. This is on easy mode though to test if they fixed the optimization issues which they really haven't (Though it's funny that times I get from 90 FPS to 2000 FPS). It would also crash a few times if I alt+tab, so players beware. It's still fun and it doesn't really need all these cons fixed so much, but it would make a difference.
I recommend this game on sale (I got the franchise pack from Humble Bundle).
Here's hoping THQ Nordic makes Darksiders 3 really good!

The most overlooked Final Fantasy, mostly for the negative stigma we can all thank the Internet for. By thank I mean try not to think about it.
Long story short this is as close as we are going to get to Valkyrie Profile 3 (this and Exist Archive of course).
Face buttons for various attacks that are fully customizable. Attacks, blocks, dodges, all can have various properties (mobility, elemental, de/buffs etc.) together with the schemata i.e. Job system switchable on the fly at the press of a button. Each weapon and shield having its own 3d model (something I feel dumb for pointing out, but it is NOT something that is standard in action rpgs STILL).
It is easily the best combat system mainline FF has ever seen so far in my humble educated opinion.
Knowing the characters from previous games is helpful but the main story stands on its own almost completely. The setting is easily the most intriguing in recent memory, nihilistic, resigned, and at the twilight of its life, the immortal denizens offer some interesting sub stories and plots to follow.
Music is as we all should be used to by now, absolutely phenomenal. Themes from all three games, various arranges at key moments, dynamic music and cues during battle, all creating an immersive and exciting atmosphere.
Many people have a preconception when it comes to time limits, rest easy for LR gives you many tools how to work around it and it is not a complicated process at all. On my first guide-less playthrough I had 3 or 4 spare days after completing every single side quest.
TL;DR  Amazing combat, robust aesthetic and build customization, decent post game, excellent soundtrack, dual audio (Sakamoto is essential to FF XIII trilogy).
It became my second favorite FF of all time. (Thanks Tri-ace! I know you did most of the work, even though square is taking the credit). Also, haven't you heard? Lightning is Sakamoto.

Fantastic so far. SimAirport is a true simulation and management game. It offers an excellent balance of challenge, efficiency optimisation and player progression.
The developers definitely have an understanding of the economics of running an airport and even if you don't, you will quickly become immersed in the mechanics.
SimAirport gives players a wealth of mechanics to alter and tailor their gameplay experience to their own tempo. Players have the ability to customise their flight schedules, choose which flight contracts to take, what size planes land at the airport and which gate the planes land at amongst many other things.
Different size planes carry more passangers, with more passangers comes greater efficiency challenges which can be overcome through managing your schedules, adding more ticketing desks, optimising your security, adding more service staff to boarding gates etc.
SimAirport has all the functional elements in to be able to run your very own Airport business and will hopefully just get better as Early Access goes on.
If you are familiar with Prison Architect style games you will love this.
Pros:
- Functional base game mechanics. Baggage, flights, passengers, retail system, garbage, storage, offices for staff.
- Queueing system is excellent once you learn how to do it. (You can assign service desks to queues, otherwise customers ignore the queues)
- Excellent, simple schedule interface for managing flights and gates.
- Passengers give visible feedback on things affecting them like "ARGH" when they have missed their flight, "no staff?" when they did not get served at a cafe in time etc.
- Choice of flights and planes that arrive at your airport. Each plan has different passenger capacity.
-Different airlines have different plan visuals, they are neat.
- Lots of efficiency optimisation and progression mechanics which feel fluid and structured without being linear
- Functioning research system, albeit very limited at the moment.
- Simple staff system, you just plop them and they do their jobs without having to micro-manage.
- There is a cost to firing staff, making your business and staffing choices more valuable.
- Immersive sound effects and visuals
- The animation when a gate attaches to a landed plane is radical.
- Warnings and clear signals as to why something isn't working.
Cons:
- No tutorial at the time of review. This will be a barrier to new players to the genre. If you aren't familiar with mechanics of Prison Architect style games you will have trouble getting your head around the game, how to build etc. Also limited fan-made tutorials on youtube/internet as the game is new.
- You will fail your first few airports while learning how everything comes together.
- Only way to deal with larger amounts of passengers is to add lots of boarding/gate desks for each gate which feels a bit clumsy. In order to board an A380 (~550 passengers) you need about 5 boarding desks to board in a decent time frame. This is also the case with cafe's and cash registers. A suggestion would be research to check people on faster or more efficient/higher tiered vewrsions of service desks and gate desks or an "online check-in" research.
- It's Early Access. More features should be on the way. I'd say the price is worth it but a part of that includes an expectation of expanded features. There's no guarentee of that.

With it's charmingly cheesy story, loveable characters, beautiful backgrounds and great music, Gray Matter is one of my favorite adventure games of all time, and a very underrated one.
Some of the puzzles hold the player's hand a bit too much for my taste, such as the magic tricks, which are a great idea but could be implemented better, making the player think, instead of reading too clear instructions.

I get stumped at one point.  There didn't seem to be anything else for me to accomplish, but the story wouldn't advance.  Fortunately this game avoids pixel hunting by allowing the player to toggle hotspots tags on and off.  It's lovely.  I'd like to see all point-and-clickers do this.  Moving on.  I'm stumped.  Despite the hotspot tags, I've gone from one side of the map to the other (again) looking for something I missed.  Eventually (sigh) I bring up a walkthrough.  Seems I'd forgotten to look at a photo in one of the rooms.  Looking at this photo provided no inventory items.  It didn't move the plot forward.  All it did was give me a brief verbal description of what was in the photo.  And suddenly the story advances, and it reminded me of a long-ago frustration from Gabriel Knight 2: The Beast Within, where I got stalled for hours because I forgot to click on one of many paintings in a museum, and clicking on that painting didn't supply inventory, or move the plot.  So I wondered...who made Gray Matter?  And guess what?  Jane Jenson.  And I was simultaneously delighted and annoyed.  I love Jane Jensen games.  Ms. Jensen?  Please stop mechanically insisting that I hoover up every single bit of superfluous flavour.  KK.  Thanks.  Moving on.  This is a well-made point-n-click where you play two characters, but for the most part you're Samantha, a snarky, talented but dead broke stage magician who's running a mostly harmless con in order to keep a roof over her head, and while playing out the lie, becomes embroiled in a mystery with possible supernatural implications.  The gameplay is good, right up until the end, and the story is good until the climax where I felt the narrative collapsed, but that's not uncommon in games, movies and books.  Play this one for the journey, not the destination, and you'll get your time and money's worth.

The story is good, emotional in parts, tragic even. Plenty of suspense and mystery to it all. Characters are nicely written, dialogue didn't bore me at any point, the game paces itself very well.
A quality game, lovingly crafted, with plenty of beautiful art to look at and great music to listen to. Recommended for any point n' click adventure puzzler fans, you'll get 10 hours of enjoyment out of this for sure.

The King's Bounty series is, in every way, a clone of the Heroes of Might and Magic line. Expect the same sort of gameplay, though the King's Bounty series is somewhat mechanistically inferior. Frankly, you'd be better off just sticking with the Heroes Series.

King's Bounty is a suprisingly lavish production: an entire, non-linear world to explore, filled to the brim with vast armies to fight.  Its turn-based gameplay is surprisingly deep and varied, and in between battles you have the freedom to explore the map and hunt for treasure. It has addictive RPG mechanics and dozens of hours of playtime. Its story is grand, although it is told primarily through text. It's beautifully designed and fun to play. There are also drawbacks though. The game doesn't do a good job explaining its systems. Figuring out morale, leadership and stacking can be a challenge. My biggest problem was with the blatant misogyny in the story though. In the world of King's Bounty, women are defined by what men want from them. Quests involve saving women, changing their appearance to make them suitable lovers, giving them gifts and proving their suitor's worth, more than once even convincing women to give their misogynistic stalkers another chance (or optionally, kidnapping them). The relationships in the game are possessive, superficial, and even abusive. The player can not intervene, only support them or choose to remain neutral (which costs you). Even the protagonist, Princess Amelie, has to convince her father to let her save the world by either pouting or throwing a tantrum. After she saves the world from demons, she is effectively told that her primary duty is to marry and have kids. The game does not critique this nor allow the player to critique it. It's even part of the gameplay: female warriors can have the 'beautiful' stat which causes men to miss them, Amelie can wear dresses into battle, and in one of the standalone expansions, you can pick a wife and her babies will give you bonuses. Women in KBAP are shown as shallow, greedy, treacherous and dependent wretches. Those who are supposed to be sympathetic are obedient martyrs. But I guess the cover gives it away: Amelie's 'armor' is obviously designed with something other than battle in mind. So, good game, but so ♥♥♥♥ed up that I'm not going to recommend it. Yes, I think sexism is a bigger concern than whether games are good.

This game (and every other game in this series) seem to be a small view of the great things that could have come with this game. This game had the potential to be an extremely in-depth geopolitical grand strategy game. Instead, it is a hollow game about military conquest and making money, masked by a clutter of interface options all showing stats of little to absolutely no significance.
This game also feels as if the developers were currently working on a feature, and decided "HEY! Lets add this!" and completely forgot about the task at hand, or could not be bothered to finish said task. A prime example would be the environment system. You may think, "Why, there is none!" and you would be mostly right, however with many Society technologies, they all have to do with the environment, and some even have to do with nuclear fallout (another thing that is not to be seen). And some of the techs say, in the "effects" portion of the tech, "Environmental rating +x%". Well, why would they say it has these effects even though most of these techs dont do anything? Well, the answer is simple. The developers were working on environmental effects to your actions and the actions of other nations, and these technologies would help the global environmental situation. And by hints from the technology, nuclear fallout would be an issue too. However, the developers either did one of two things. They either thought "lets put this in, and this, and this" but never went back to the task at hand (as I said earlier) or had a hard time creating these systems (which I imagine would be complicated) and gave up completely. Not even bothering to remove the technologies that talk about environmental impact, blah, blah, blah.
Also, many (probably a majority) of the technologies have literally no impact. It is literally useless fluff put into the game and branded with a sign saying "THIS DOES SOMETHING" however, it doesnt. Yes, I grant you there are also MANY technologies that do a lot, however if you look at the grand strategy games put out by Paradox Interactive, every single technology has a large impact and is essential.
And all in all, this game is largely unfinished. The developers did update it years ago, however they still left behind the game, and left it very hollow indeed. They moved on to create THREE new titles, all as hollow as this, but with a shiny new interface, map, and a better AI (which is TERRIBLE in 2020, by the way).
Sure, this game can be fun to play even now. However the bad practices that Battlegoat has proceeded with for 4 games (Not sure about SR2010) should not go unnoticed. Practices such as, leaving behind an unfinished game, using said unfinished features and leaving them in other titles (environmental impact "modifiers" still implemented in their SR titles to date). I would also rant about how they pulled Supreme Ruler Ultimate from Early Access and "releasing" it in an extremely unfinished state, however I have a review on that game for you already.
All in all, I would not reccoment anybody to support the bad practices Battlegoat has gone through with many times, and I urge you to turn away from this game and have a look at Paradox Interactive's titles instead. They are very finished, always releasing updates, finishing their games, and have many features. I am sorry Battlegoat but I despise games being left unfinished. Especially 4 games in a row. I would be weary when thinking of buying a game from this company in the future.

I know it says I've played 250+ hours of this game, and I've certainly played quite a few, but probably half of that is letting the game run on its own while I was asleep, or having fallen asleep playing it.
The concept behind the game is really great, and I wish it had been implemented in a way that made it fun to play, but it wasn't.
I did play the original (SR2010) and it is certainly an improvement over that version - less buggy, better controls. But the core problems with the franchise remain.
Basic gameplay is excruciatingly slow; the fastest speed is a tenth of where it should be. Virtually every game mechanic is completely opaque, and zero effort is made to explain any of it. The economic model is absurd and way too easily exploited - even playing as Malawi (the poorest, most technologically backwards country in the world)  I can turn it into an economic powerhouse in just a few game years.
Since no effort is made to balance the various countries, conflicts are rather pointless. The AI is terrible no matter how difficult you make the settings. You have to make your own game objectives because the game itself has none.
Then there's the "engineers" problem - if you lack the tech to build a really good infantry unit, engineers are a very strong infantry unit that can be built with no tech. Although very oddly you can't actually research the unit, you need to trade for the design - but anyone will trade it to you for some cash. The engineer has massive advantages - it's cheap, it can cross rivers, it can bridge terrain for other units, it can accelerate production and repair of buildings, and it can beat the tar out of far more advanced units without breaking a sweat. Why a zero-tech engineer can pound the hell out of many types of advanced infantry units is beyond me.
The economy and force distributions aren't the only wildly imbalanced aspects to the game. Research is ridiculous - if you have the cash you can buy and use techs way way way beyond your tech level. Diplomacy is virtually pointless, as is any other form of non-warfare interaction with other countries.
The UN mechanic is also dubious, there are no substantial benefits to being a part of the UN, and a significant economic penalty is attached to being good by them, when it should be the other way around. It's to your advantage to purposely get kicked out, so that you don't have to pay their escalating membership fees - for which you get nothing in return. An example of how trying to stay good by the UN hurts you: it's apparently perfectly acceptable for a neighboring country with whom you are not at war to allow passage of enemy units to attack your territory, but if you attack that neighbor for that act of war the UN will despise you for it.
Your advisors are just as bad as the AI elsewhere; if you trust them to do anything they will mess it up badly. There's a system of implementing priorities for them, but if this has any actually effect on their behavior I haven't been able to detect it.
The only thing this game does well, gameplay-wise, is tactical unit management on the hex map. If you can slog through all the opaque mechanics and the gruelingly long setup time before a typical country can start invading others, that part is reasonably satisfying.
Other mechanics, like the loyalty mechanic, are just stupid and appear to directly contradict the "realism" goal of the game. Either eliminate that mechanic, or do it properly!
Like its predecessor, SR2020 is a great idea that doesn't really work well as implemented.

The story and the writing style is exactly what I expected from Penny Arcade and probably my favorite part of the game. The art is a 3D, cartoony, steampunk style which I was also very into and again is what I expected from Penny Arcade.
The gameplay reminded me of Super Mario RPG. You explore until you run into an enemy and then jump into combat mode, where your party lines up against the enemies. Your main characters can perform their basic attack, special attack, or team up with other characters for 2- or 3-member team attacks. Instead of being turn-based, there’s a warm-up meter on each character that resets on each action.
If you’re looking for an RPG this game may disappoint you, but if you’re a fellow Penny Arcade fan looking for some RPG mixed in with a great story you’ll likely enjoy playing through this once and then letting it sit.

Before you read any more of this, just note that I am a massive fan of the Half-Life series. I've enjoyed playing the original Half-Life games a lot. I imagine that a lot of you will probably rate this review down but nevertheless I'm still inclined to give my experience of this "update."
After getting back into Half-Life again. I found this on the store and decided to play through it just like i did with the original Half-Life 2 for the sense of nostalgia and seeing if it actually did improve on the original.
I was expecting to find a lot of nice textures and lighting effects redone and improved quite a bit. But I was dissapointed to find that a ton of bugs were now introduced and to some new lighting effects and textures not redone at all. Some places still look like they haven't improved. A lot of new architecture somehow feels uneccesary. Bugs that are not game breaking but however are just annoying in game that somehow were not found and fixed. I played the original Half-Life 2 for 82 hours and I didn't come across this many bugs and glitches. It's also incredibly difficult to notice any change in graphical details. I'll even say that some things that were done to the game feel
But I will admit a lot of other lighting effects have been substantially improved by a lot. The community commentary is very interesting and adept at giving you clear speech of what the game was like in development. Although very hard to notice, some graphical detail was added to certain things. I would honestly not really reccomend this to anyone besides beginners or new players to the Half-Life series. But if you've played most of the original and others, I would reccomend this just for the great commentary.

No disrespect to those that have played and loved the lineage of the games, it is upon those recommendations that I made the purchase.
However as a new initiate to this game, the characters, and the intended play style it is just too much for me and frankly, far too difficult to give me the enjoyment I want out of a platformer.
I have always considered myself a good platformer, going right back to the NES days and even well before that on PC and I have played a wide range, so I don't feel my criticisms are all that out of line.
My real objection to this game is that it really requires absolute precision in every input throughout every level.  Memorization is absolutely essential and I found myself completely dazzled and unable to immediately asses each new situation until dying several times every screen.  The graphics are lovely but they do the player no favors in helping quickly figure out what is going on and where you are allowed to go.
After about 30 minutes I realized that I don't want to play a memorization game and a completely unforgiving platformer where there are spikes and other hazards on pretty much every single surface.  I knew right from the get-go that I was in for a rough ride when the first level was a race against time and I died 30 times just acquainting myself with the controls.
I can only go on my personal experience, and I would think that unless you have a history of enjoying the other games in the series take a pass, because it's hard AF and frankly not a forgiving game in any way which for me amounted to mostly frustration.

The long-waited Jane Jensen game, that many wished it was a Gabriel Knight 4. It isn’t, and it is a good thing: Gray Matter is its own game with its own merits. Despite its troubled development, it is one solid title: the story is the game’s strong suit, as expected. The characters are likable and with their own motivations and despite getting close to stereotypes, they manage to avoid it. The background are a little on the static side, but they are gorgeous and do have bits of animation here and there. The music, composed by Robert Holmes as usual (Jane’s husband by the way) is moody and quiet, and there are some lovely pieces like David’s theme that are just a delight. The game isn’t without flaws, but again even the oh-so-great Gabriel Knight games were: sometimes the story comes to a halt and you need to have the initiative; the magic interface is completely unnecessary and there aren’t even animated; and the Daedalus Club area is a pain to navigate. Other than that, all puzzles aren’t too absurd to figure out.
td;dr: great story, fun game. shower fanservice.

(I need to affirm that I got this game for free in a Microids giveaway special event. This does not have any bearing in my opinions about the game.)
It's a different kind of motorcycle racing game and I've played lots of them, from sims to arcade ones, even some of the original Moto Racer games. Moto Racer 4 is a full on arcade racing game with re-imaginated mechanics from the series past, like the wheelie and tricks, which are cool to pull off and give a boost to your ride. There are two types of motors, asphalt and dirt, with obviously different play styles. The asphalt bikes are very fast and they feel glued to the road, I wouldn't call them stiff, though. Fortunately, all the courses are specifically and smartly designed for the type of ride. The handling for the asphalt bikes are kinda straight forward, as in very little difference between the bikes with higher and lower handling rating. The challenge there is in the split second decision, knowing when to boost, and boosting is not optional, but also in the rubberbanding AI, which makes for a cheaty artificial difficulty, but it's an arcade racer, so it's alright. The problem is that you need to grind earlier stages to unlock as many stars and "tokens" for upgrading your bikes, to unlock a different character that might suit your playstyle, until you get good enough to take on new challenges. Every stage has three difficulty modes, awarded with one, two or three stars. Losing a race means "negative stars" rating, although I didn't really get the point to it, since there's no real downside. If you lose a new race, you have to restart it anyway, while losing stars on older races has no consequence, except if you suffer from extreme OCD.
If I have one major problem with the gameplay is how it handles penalties. The higher you aim for a difficulty, the more specific the race becomes, with lesser margins for error than a formula one race. And if you aim for the upgrade token, it requires reaching a certain score gained by performing tricks, boosting, speeding, jumping, stuff like that, while also trying your best to win the race. The problem with this is that you get penalties for so many things, it becomes a challenge in avoiding them, like avoiding the rubberbanding opponent from hitting you from the back, or stepping a second off the track while boosting. In addition, you will unlock skills that are more pain than use, like double boosting, which requires you to boost in a very short margin of time right after your initial boost, which means you have to take the finger off the boost button and press it again quickly after when a time meter appears. There are too many elements to keep track of and, even though they do add to the challenge, it's not fun, just frustrating.
On the bright side, there's a lot to unlock in this game, from a range of cool skills to bike upgrades and characters each with their own pair of bikes and abilities (just like in the old Moto Racer games), and, of course, new stages and very dynamic, gorgeously designed levels to race through. There's not much of a story, but the characters have great personalities, even if only written, and a Career mode consisting of various stages, not unlike many other racing games, but I really enjoy it for it's creative design and frebetic gameplay.

It's a shame that Steam reviews operate on an up/down system, because my opinion of this game is rather mixed.
On the one hand, it's very clunky. The protagonist controls like a tank, very stiffly and awkwardly. If you've played any early 3D adventure games you'll know what I'm talking about. The animations don't always line up and aren't quite all there. The game lacks polish, to put it frankly. Which is fair for something so clearly on a tight budget. The cinematics, while visually striking, also cut a lot of corners, and it's not always clear what's being depicted on screen.
The game does not make for a strong first impression. However, I started to fall in love with the game at chapter 3. While Samantha Everett is the "main character", it's David Styles who steals the show.  I don't want to give away too much, but I found his character and backstory to be very compelling, and I loved the way the game executed all of it. HOWEVER (again), the game fails to wrap up the story in an entirely satisfactory way. Which again may be to a tight budget, but it left me feeling a bit empty.
Overall, Gray Matter is a nice little adventure game that's rough around the edges, but has likeable characters and a somewhat compelling plot (if you can make it to chapter 3). If you have nothing better to do, feel free to give it a go.

No one has ever just jumped into this game and said, "Oh yeah, I totally understand how this game works." I probably logged 50 hours before I truly had a grasp of the core mechanics, and then only with the assistance of a lot of online research/forum reading... TOTALLY WORTH IT!

This is a very underrated game. While it suffers from a difficult learning curve and can be slow as hell once the number of units increases, for long-term Grand Strategy addicts the degree of complexity this game provides is a sheer joy. It's also a few years old, and already some of the "near future" features feel like the past, but this doesn't mar the game as much as increase the entertainment value.
This Gold edition also includes some really excellent mods that expand the game in many ways, including some very good tech tree mods that extend the potential time period by quite a way. The AI is competent enough to challenge the player; not terrifyingly good like AI War, but certainly able to keep up.
All told: an excellent game for fans of vast quantities of detail.

I've played NMS on and off since its disastrous launch, and...it's fine.
Okay, it wasn't fine when it came out - Hello Games had been vague on what would actually be in the game, which I won't get into for fear of extended discussion that gets nowhere, but pretty much everyone agreed that $60 was way too much for a game where you shoot minerals, get into your ship, shoot pirates, get out of your ship, repeat. There were no goals (besides grinding up to the best ship and laser) and there wasn't much variety.
As of the latest major update, Atlas Rises, I can safely recommend this game as something akin to Elite Dangerous - it's very wide, only just deep enough, and filled with things to work towards: capital freighters, personalized bases, and the end of the story campaign. There's also a bit more variety in the grind, with the latest update adding in-game upgrades that give more credits for discovering objects, as well as missions that give more efficient or unique tasks to earn credits, but it's still a grind (albeit less boring and somewhat shorter).
In other words, No Man's Sky is a "podcast game" - something that's fun to play while listening to a show or chatting with friends. I would recommend buying it on sale, since USD$24 is much more reasonable than USD$60 (regardless of the game's quality).
Oh yeah, and they finally added multiplayer. Hooray and all that.

Squirbs is a platformer with an interesting twist:
You control two characters at the same time, which will respond equally to your inputs. So if you jump, both characters jump, and if you move right, both characters move to the right. For each character, there is a crystal shard in each level, and you need to get very close to them with both characters at the same time to finish a level.
The levels can feature some simple puzzle elements like crates or switches, but usually the actual puzzle involves planning a path for both characters, moving one character freely while the other one is blocked by a wall, preventing one character from jumping by pressing <jump> while that character (but not the other one) is in the air, planning when to best switch your focus between both characters, and so on.
Later levels introduce teleporters, surfaces that influence your movement, and other interesting level elements.
The controls are responsive, and you move / stop as soon as you press or release a button or keyboard key. Jump height can be controlled precisely by releasing the <jump> button/key sooner or later. The only thing I don't like here is that you can't jump while holding <down>, but I only remember one level where that became relevant, and I beat it after adapting my strategy.
So, is this a good game?
Well, I greatly enjoyed this game, and would definitely answer that with a 'yes' for me! :)
1) The platforming in this game becomes very technical / difficult starting after world 1 of 4, requiring you to make precise inputs in order to avoid a mistake that means instant death, so it becomes comparable to Super Robot Jump Jump, Super Meat Boy, I Wanna Be The Guy, the bonus levels in the Escape Goat games, or Kaizo Mario World. However, there are no hidden traps, and each level consists of a single screen and takes less than a minute (often only a few seconds) if you don't make any mistakes, so it's still very much doable for ambitious players.
2) The game is a bit unpolished: Gamepads are supported via XInput, but you can't navigate the options menu with a gamepad, or use it to skip a story screen that you will only see once / the intro screen. Also, if you have a smaller resolution (I think the game is designed with 1080p in mind), the downscaling doesn't look as nice as it could, and button icons or numbers are sometimes hard to recognize.
Another thing I noticed is that physics don't seem to be 100% deterministic on a slower PC, so it can happen that one character is a pixel further to the right than the other character after walking half a screen width, despite a symmetrical level layout. However, this was only rarely a cause for failing, so it was mostly negligible for me.
I was also a bit disappointed that there was no ending, but at least there's some satisfaction thanks to the achievements for completing it.
Some other reviewers claim that it becomes just mindless trial and error after some point. I can not confirm this: For example, the wall jump mechanics that can be found later are implemented in a clever way where you vertically jump if you press the jump button (no directional buttons required) while adjacent to a wall. A smart player will make use of the option to wall jump without moving the other character, while a player that relies on mindless trial and error will fail in many situations where such subtleties are relevant for success. So thinking is definitely rewarded. ;)
------------------------------------------
If you like frustratingly hard games and can look past those flaws, or like to try out games with an innovative concept, I think it's definitely worth it.
Also, if you waver because of the high difficulty, you can still consider picking it up and just play world 1 when the game is at a discount that justifies something between 30 minutes and an hour of playtime.

A perennial favorite, FSW has always been dogged by being a game that is difficult to pigeonhole. Is it a third-person cover-based shooter? Is it a strategy game? Is it a puzzle game? It is a unique combination of all three that combined forms a whole greater than its parts. Unfortunately, gamers expecting  a single genre tended to be discouraged by this unusual mix and the game never got the recognition it deserved.
Despite its age - and all the technical difficulties that entails running it on a modern PC - the game's visuals remain surprisingly attractive, and it is not difficult to lose oneself in the fantasy of a fighting through the streets of the war-torn Middle East. There numerous incidental animations - be it a civilian scurrying for shelter, birds scattering as you approach or the laundry flapping in the wind - make the game's world seem alive and keep you on your toes at the same time.
But it's the gameplay that is the real star; leading my two squads through the dangerous, twisting streets of fictional Zekistan felt more realistic and true-to-life than all the Calls of Duty - or even Arma - games combined. Your crew's limited toolset - a handful of movement and attack options - are more than sufficient to engage and defeat the enemy if combined with a bit of cunning. It is almost puzzle like; "If I move fireteam Alpha /here/ and then toss smoke like this, the enemy will react like /that/, allowing me to maneuver fireteam Bravo into position /there/!" Figuring out the optimal method to not only kill the enemies but also do so in a way that minimizes casualties and ammunition use is amazingly  satisfying (fortunately, for those less talented, you can often "brute-force" your way through most challenges). The game's difficulty curve is gradual and never overwhelming.
The AI is not particularly skilled but can at times be gratingly tenacious, and failing to keep your team in cover will often result in the quick loss of several soldiers. Fortunately, the tangos' skill set is even less complex than that of your troops - mostly they just hunker down behind some cover and take potshots at you, although a few do use grenades - but they make up for this deficit with numbers and being well placed. Attempt to maneuver around them and they often - but not always - will seek new shelter, requiring you to trap them between your two teams coming at them from different directions. The occasional heavy weapon (rocket launcher or machine gun), tank or technical adds to the challenge and variety. Unfortunately - and this is the greatest fault of the game - the initial locations of the enemies is hard-coded into each level, which greatly reduces the replayability of the game. Best of all, once the mission is over, you can watch a replay to relive your successes (or failures), and even - should you chose - jump into the action at any point. Would that other games offered this feature!

Full Spectrum Warrior remains one of the forgotten classics of gaming and those willing to go into the experience with an open mind will be well rewarded with a challenging and exciting game.

The U.S. Army is the most powerful ground force in the entire world. The backbone of a ground invasion is the U.S. Army Infantry, and in the midst of combat, their skills, courage, and teamwork are put to the test.
While readiness continues to be the U.S. Army's top priority, how it goes about its business is changing. Full Spectrum Warrior began as a training aid for the U.S. Army to reinforce Army doctrine and team effort within the troops. It is the most realistic portrayal of Infantry-level urban warfare via unique tactical action gameplay. Players become the Squad Leader, commanding Alpha and Bravo squads. There is potential for danger down every alley, behind every window. Watch those angles folks, we've got a job to do here. Hooah!
- Unique combination of tactical and action gameplay.
- Authentic implementation of U.S. Army Infantry doctrine.
- Simple control scheme lets you command eight soldiers in real time.
- Squad equipment reflects real weaponry and equipment currently in use by the U.S. Army.
- Immersive urban environments with danger around every corner.
- 2-player co-op, each player controls one fire team.
- Includes 2 exclusive bonus levels not available on Xbox.

Lightning Returns has to be one of the most slept on titles in the Final Fantasy franchise. With so many people who disliked the cast of the series to even the mechanics from the first and second, it's no wonder this game is so underrated. But over the next paragraph I'll give my opinion as to why this diamond in the rough is good!
From the beggining of the first cinematic I could tell Square Enix had finally decided to fall back to some basics. The opening made me feel like I was getting ready to be a badass which in all honesty is what everyone wants. The tutorial in the game does a quick and effecient job of teaching how to be in fact a badass right from the beggining. Combat is quick and intuitive  and felt completely fluid. Next up is the customization of Lightning. From clothes, to weapons, to even skills the options are practically endless. I can't tell you how many times I've caught myself in the menus customizing or checking out the different styles of outfits and weapons. Side missions seem like less of a hassle than most games considering completeing them just helps you in the long run and keeps you from noticing the possible monotony of running from one side of a map to another. Yet needless to say I'm a little over 6 hours into what I'm assuming will easily be a 30-40 hour experience, and I've not been this excited and intruiged to play a Final Fantasy game in almost 5 years. Kudos Square Enix!
Lightning Returned for this third installment and brought all the thunder that is Final Fantasy!

First of all, please, do not be fooled by my low play time - I bought the game quite some time ago and have played it for hundreds of hours. And I am long standing fan of the series, starting SR2010, now playing SR1936.
To sum it up, my recommendation is positive, but, please, read more as there are few objections and e.g. Bjoern has quite a few valid points. I would not recommend this game to just anyone.
The game is very ambitious, wide in scope and quite complex with sharp learning curve. Of course you can assign some tasks to AI, but why let computer play my game? Especially as decisions of AI advisors are often quite poor. In general, game more or less delivers what it promises - choose any country and run it as you wish in global environment.
However, there is quite a feel of unfinisheness in some aeas. I think the scope of project was too wide to deliver within set  budget and timeframe. Quite a few ideas are implemented only partially or got axed in full (NBC, environment, tourism and business centers... )
Now, to cover aspects of the game:
Research: there are several hundreds of technlogies and units in technology tree, but their effect is very often "research and forget" without any significant effect. Still, quite a few technologis do have very visible effect. As for the units, you can do well enough with lets say 7 units for most of the game (see warfare). Researching hundreds of unit models covered in game is marginally interesting. Tech level is a bit strange concept - it is possible to have tech level of year 1990 and run phaser hover  tanks...
Diplomacy is quite strange (but I fail to recall any 4X game with really working diplomacy model, and I played many of them - Galciv probably got closest). E.g. casus belli is mostly based on active unit production capacity which gives way to many exploits (as AI is unable to control this aspect), but you will always face up "all computer coalition" in the end. However, I find diplomacy no better or worse than in any 4X game.
Economy is based (I believe) on Joseph Stiglitz theories. General idea is the more government spends, the better economy performs. Economy view aside, this leads to not very realistic in game strategies and exploits. It is very easy to start as - e.g. - Madagascar and triple GDP/c in a year. Moreover, there is very nasty bug related to price mechanism which I will cover later. I do feel economy to be somewhat ovrsimplified, but working (but mind you, I am economy geek :) ).
Warfare is acceptable. Building few hundreds of APC (preferably laser ones) and several naval transports is enough to conquer the world. Everything else is just nice to have. Long range AA and fighters helps limit APC loses against air powers, few dozens of stealth srategy bombers (B-2) are great to override entranched aeas. I found very limited use for tanks, and no use for AT, Recon, most naval units, range AA and most of the aircrafts... There is just no real need to build these types of units. AI does its job to provide resistence, but is by no means real oponent.
As for the nasty, game and save breaking bug I mentioned before... Using artifical production buildings (like synth fuel factory) does increase the final product price. This has positive feedback to output price of buildings which use his product as input (e.g. oil power plant), especially, if it the only input. If ANY country manages to create "closed circle" - like most of the oil produced in synth fuel plant, most of the electricity (used in synth fuel plant) produced in oil power plant - prices will get out of any reasonable range. GDP skyrockets and after several weeks treasury of this country will get out of range which game can handle. This destroys world market and after another few weeks, population gets out of control (not sure if by standard game mechanisms or the data just get overwritten). The game is not salveable in this state. There are workarounds (either conquer the country before it gets there - only handful of countires can get into this loop), or casually check the countries and if they start going this way, load one month old save in multiplayer mode and destroy these buildings. BTW, with careful handling this bug can be used as exploit to get unlimited treasury. The most usual culprit is Moscow, by the year 2029. IMHO this bug should not have escaped testing. Apart of this bug, I found game stable, if resouce hungry.
To sum it up, even as I highlighted some negatives, my overall feeling of the game is positive and - as I bought it for 22 euros and now just added to my steam collection for 2.5 - one of the best values for a buck despite its flaws. I would not hesitate to recommend buy for any global 4X games fan, who can handle limits of the game. And I hope Batlegoat will continue to improve the engine as Paradox did with Europe Univrsalis or HoI.

While I wouldn't say I'm one of Rust's hardcore base builders. Foritfy is certainly one of the most useful tools you can get for base planning, for solo players trying out cool new ideas for their starter base and expansions; as well as big clan architects planning intricate base designs for their next wipe.
With the plethora of new features added into Fortify for its paid-for steam release (such as checking stability and the ability to cause real-time damage to your base design to test its stability), Fortify is definitely worth it for its price.
If you ever plan on building a base bigger than a 2x2 in Rust, I wholeheartedly recommend purchasing this application.

FORTIFY is a Rust base builder's best friend. After using FORTIFY for months previous to its official Steam release, I have found it invaluable due to its many utilities. Being able to see exactly how many resources my eight story base will cost, even down to each large chest, allows my group to plan accordingly for the upcoming wipe. Knowing where I can cram in extra beds into my precisely designed loot room has found use in almost all of my bases. Having the ability to count exactly how many C4 it would take to breach into my cupboard's hiding place lets me know if I need more layers of honeycomb. Examples such as these are why I whole heartedly recommend FORTIFY to ANY Rust player that wants to design a competent base for solo play or for a large clan.

Moto Racer 4, a release which seems to have completely slipped under my radar, recieving little to no fanfare even at the time of its release. I have played another game in this series, Moto Racer 2, and as such I'll be comparing my experience with this title to my previous experience in Moto Racer 2.
To begin, its very much an arcade style racer, die-hard racing simulator fans need not apply. However, i'd say that its very much in the spirit of the rest of the series, as MR2 had a distincly arcade style of gameplay. This arcade style of play is quite enjoyable actually and gives the game a very oldshool style of play. There are a few new additions to the gameplay in Moto Racer 4, the TURBO system, whereby a carefully timed press of the A button will give you a boost of speed at the starting line and also a boost of speed when executing a wheelie. As far as variety in the gameplay goes, you have standard races, time trials and other modes such as 'slalom' where you have to weave in and out of traffic, but still arrive at the finish line before time runs out, and an elemination mode where the racer in last place is eliminated every 30 seconds. You also have a variety of road and dirt tracks, utilising superbikes and dirtbikes respectively. This variety has been enough to keep me entertained so far, with both dirt and road tracks providing their own set of unique challenges and quirks. There are also various tricks to pull off when riding a dirtbike, the tricks must be executed by pushing a certain sequence of buttons, this is a welcome addition to the game as in MR2, tricks would occur at random and didn't really have any impact on the gameplay whatsoever.
The graphics are superb in my opinion, I'm not sure what another reviewer was talking about when he said that the graphics look dated. The game is bright with colour, but still easy on the eye. Coupled with the variety of environments this gives the game an increadibly varied colour palette, making for an absolutely stunning game to look at. In terms of graphics options you have the standard options as well as the ability to toggle bloom effects and post processing options.  However, graphics tweeking enthusiats may be sad to find no indepth Anti-Aliasing options, with there being only a simple toggle to switch AA on or off.
There's also a decent level of customisation in the game, firstly you're offered the choice of several unique racers, each with their own distinct motorcyle, emblem and colour schemes. You can however tweak both the colour schemes and emblems of the riders to your own liking. You can choose the colour scheme for the bike, the rider's outfit and even their helmet. Rather dissapointing is the lack of variety for the dirtbikes. By completing races in the main career mode, you will unlock upgrade points, allowing for you to upgrade the stats of your chosen rider's bike. You can alter stats such as handling, acceleration and the power of your Turbo boost. As mentioned, each rider gets their own unique bike, but only for the road stages. On the dirt stages, all racers will use the same model of dirtbike (custom colour schemes are still applied however). This is the only thing that bothers me about the bikes and cheapens the game somewhat. I do hope that in future we get a variety of dirtbikes to choose from. However, similar to MR2, each rider's bike has a unique set of starting stats and a unique upgrade limit. E.g certain riders will have a bike with really high speed, but low turbo boost potential.  Its interesting to see the devs incorporate this feature alongside the newer customisation feature to help each rider retain a sense of uniqueness.
In terms of multiplayer, there's both online and suprisingly enough local splitscreen multiplayer. I sadly haven't played too much of the online mode, so I'm unable to comment too much on whether or not the game's mulitplayer is still populated 8 months after its initial release. Splitscreen however works very much as you'd expect, hook up another controller to your PC and you and a friend can have some wacky fun times fooling around in single races.
The music is sadly somewhat forgettable but is fitting for the game, if that makes any sense? The dirtbike sections are accompanied typically with punk-rock style instrumentals and the superbike sections are accompanied with instrumental electronic tracks. None of them really seem to stick in my mind even though most of the tracks sound decent enough. Sadly, you can't switch music tracks in game from the pause menu (in the same style as MR2) as it seems certain music tracks are locked to particular race courses. For the best experience, put on the MR2 soundtrack or some Eurobeat and you're good to go.
You can play the game from a 1st person viewpoint, which to me is absolutely brilliant, as you could also do this in MR2. The bike detail on the 1st person view is also very good, with each bike featuring a working set of clocks, unlike in MR2 where the clocks were just a set of flat textures.
A custom track creator would have been absolutely great here as an ingame track editor came on both the PC and Playstation versions of MR2. The creator could have made use of the steam workshop function too, possibly allowing for a larger sense of community surrounding the game. However, from what I believe was intended to be a budget title, that might be asking too much.
Finally, the season pass is still not entirely worth it, with the entirity of the game's DLC coming to far below the £19 currently being asked. Whilst the first DLC pack has been released, it simply consists of 2 race courses, 1 road, 1 dirt. In my opinion they're not worth the £2.79 pricetag. If you intend on getting the season pass/Deluxe Editon, then please buy it on sale. Its not worth the £40 you'll be paying otherwise.
In conclusion, this is a fun arcade racer from a long forgotten series that actually feels like a worthy entry to the series and not just a random bike racing game with 'Moto Racer' slapped on it. I'd highly recommend getting this if its on sale.
Edit 15/11/17:
Over a year has passed since the release of this title, the season pass continues to be poor value to this day. The developers of MR4 have recently released another title 'ATV drift & trick' which seems to re-use an awfully large amount of content from MR4. This new title was most likely going to be the missing piece of DLC from the season pass. Still no word from Microids about what this means. For the time being, don't buy the season pass, just get the base game.

If God of War and Legend of Zelda had a baby, it would be this game.
Darksiders II is a unique blend of hack and slash and puzzle solving, and you will find plenty of both as you play. Like Zelda, there are many dungeons you have to explore to advance through the story, and each comes with puzzles that you will have to solve, usually with unique tools that you find as you progress. Unlike most RPGs, the puzzles in this game can be far from straight-forward, and several require you to really think outside the box and consider the limits of your tools and abilities. Personally I enjoyed this aspect of the game, as it was a nice change of pace from the usual fighting, and I got a great deal of satisfaction whenever I solved a difficult puzzle. However, if puzzles aren't your thing and you'd really rather spend your time slicing off heads and limbs, this aspect may be a major annoyance.
That being said, the combat in this game is by no means poor. As Death, you will be able to use a multitude of weapons to defeat your enemies, each with their own combos and characteristics. This gives the player a lot of freedom in choosing their fighting style. There is also a skills tree with several magic and melee abilities to choose from, providing even more options. You will have many chances to test your weapons and skills, as the game is riddled with a variety of enemies and bosses. There is even an arena mode where you can fight through a hundred rounds of different enemies, each round more difficult than the last, perfect for anyone with that hack and slash itch. Something that deserves special mention is the kill moves that you can execute on nearly every enemy and boss, adding a nice touch of style to every fight.
The graphics, sound and music are pretty top-notch. There's also plenty of content, and if you're a completionist like me who absolutely needs to complete every side quest and explore every dungeon, you'll easily put 50 hours into this game.
If I had to point out a flaw in this game, it would be the occasional glitches you'll likely run into. In my playthrough, I noticed that every now and then, the sound would cut out, or my character would freeze. These issues don't occur frequently enough to ruin the gaming experience, but they can be a bit annoying.
Overall, I consider this to be one of the best games I've ever played. I got it on sale for around $2 so for me it was a complete steal, but I wouldn't regret buying it for full price either. Hope you enjoy it as much as I did.

Lightning Returns is about the constant struggle for hope in a world lost and locked in despair before the final stroke hits 13.  It focuses on a central character that has been prominent in Final Fantasy XIII for the last six years, Claire Farron or more commonly referred to as Lightning, Cloud's distant second cousin (I kid, I kid).  It's time that she puts her foot down and save her sister and the people, for this world, or the next.  Nothing will stand in her way.
Graphics: Not bad, basically around XIV graphics regularly.  Funny note though, they basically spent all their CGI budget on the beginning and end of the game. I happen to like it.  15 minutes of beautiful CGI is a rewarding end for some I'd think.
Gameplay: Good, final chapter of the class / stagger system.  It takes a little getting used to but it gets rewarding for the most part later on.  The structure of the quests is debatable.  A few main quests here, bunch of menial side quests there, all under that pressing timeline.  Especially when you don't know what will help give you more time. I think it is the uncertainty that can increase that sense of pressure (the game nearly tells you as much). +Game also is almost worth doing even with a full time job.
Voice Acting: Always good, I would shake their hands if I ever recognized them.
Conclusion: A solid end to an up and down series that seems to take you everywhere and while some patches are rough, you are glad you could be a part of the ride.
Now, for my crazy analysis of the story...
The Plot...
The game starts with the premise that there is no reason to save the world but only the people who seek salvation in it.  You assume the role as savior, the chosen one by celestial powers only known to be God by everyone that sleeps below the clouds.  And by the looks of it, with the end of the world coming, you have some of the common tropes.  You have people who desperately seek a sense of security, purpose, and salvation through faith in the same celestial being.  You have other people who seek to protect themselves and the things they care about.  Lastly, you have the people who are lost in all of it.  The irony is that most of time you seek to liberate people from their dispair so that they may find hope.  It becomes their salvation.  It becomes a consistent theme throughout the game in all shapes and sizes.  The powers to be that could help have long surrended their efforts to the inevitability of the nearing end.

Throughout the game you task is to save as many people as you can.  Your friends and enemies are the most important souls for you to save.  It's nice to see the familiar faces once more.  I was always a fan of Lightning, but to see Fang was a great pleasure (maybe it was that strong femine touch or that austrailian accent, who knows?).  Snow isn't have bad, he and Hope are like wines, awful if inbibed too soon, palatable if taken with age. Even Caius makes a return, what an♥♥♥♥♥he still is.  Even death can't seem to shake the stick loose that seemed to be shoved so far up there.  But still, like the undeniable prick we all seem to come across once in our paths, Caius reveals the same undeniable necessities that we all need and a singular truth that we need to recognize.  Good, bad, or strange, we all have a choice, and more importantly, a part to play in this story.

Another great scene in the story is Lightnings interaction with Noel Kriss (my one standing objection to the writing of this series, they seem to take these random objects or famous figures and reapply them to their characters, like codenames maybe...Hope, Snow, Fang, Lightning(was a code name), oddly the more stable characters generally have realistic names, anyway, interaction with Noel...).  Lightning decides to play along with the role of being an evil harbenger of death which shows a depth of character and manipulation I haven't seen before with Lightning.  It was very enticing to see her play the role of the villian to fulfill Noel's perception of destiny.  Throughout this game, Lightning has become incredibly perceptive if not wise in some ways.  Which leads me to the one new character, Lumina.  She is the thorny prick that you can never seem to find but you know you sat on.  But that is also her undeniable charm.  She keeps you guessing to the very end.

Fast forward through all the minor quests (they offer insights into Lightnings thoughts but overall, there isn't much personal growth except for the few main quests there are).  Final boss (yep, once you are done with the five or so main quests, its the final boss),
God, no biggy.
As Lightning has said and implied (a little 'spark' of glee for me please) over the course of the game, she has been fighting fate for a long time, and she has been getting good at it. She sees through Gods plan and decides humanity should be accepted as a whole for all of its pros and cons.  The new world should be for everyone free from God.  She will take on the roll of death to give people the chance to live.  So, she kills God. To be fair, it was God's failure to empathize but his equal need to be close to human kind that drove him to eventually try to control humanity.  He was an engineer at heart who wanted to understand what love was but since he couldn't he decided to remove it from everyone else, metaphorical downfall.

Love conquers all, yadi ya. But it has a point, one that should resonate with us on some level.  It is through our love for others, our passions, our willingness to coexist, that we contribute and build a future and vision that only we can dream alone.

Back to the story...God is slain. Everyone comes back together, loose ends from 1&2 are wrapped up here as well (it was nice to see actually, considering how depressing XIII-2 was).  Everyone goes towards the light and decides to be reincarnated in the new world, including Lightning.  Caius and the infinite Yuels remain except for the one that loved Noel.  They would watch over the Chaos that doomed the world in the first place, which, let's be fair, they created.  But even so, they did it with effortless humility.  The cycle of life is finally restored.  And the new world is filled with life.
Extra Ending:
Lightning among us?
The new world is awfully similar to the one I take for granted and more than I care to admit (not to mention avoid mostly by playing these games).  Lightning leaving a train in a rural area ready to face the peacful new world with unbridled optimism (her face is adorable) is both joyful and sorrowful (at least for me). It joyful because she can finally be happy, and sorrowful because our time with her is at an end.  The life of the tragically mundane and stable has finally ended our drama on the grand stage.
With that being said, I wonder, her new life is just beginning. Part of me likes to think the possibility exists that Lightning can start a new adventure with this new life.  Hell, why not?  I would like to see what life throws at her next.

I'm probably not the first to say I haven't actually played much of this game. That being said, while I haven't played much, I have had to restart numerous time, due to time constraints.
Now all you avid gamers who hated XIII to begin with may shoot me when I say I loved XIII.  Heck, I love XIII-2 as well, even though it thoroughly confused me (Going from the fall of cocoon into time jumping with Serah and Noel was really confusing). I was super excited when I heard LR was coming out. Open world, updated graphics, and my favorite character all in one nice little package, I had to have it.  If I had realized how frustrating this game was, I would have bought something else.
Do not get this game unless you're used to have time constraints put on your gameplay, you actually WANT to spend most of your play time looking through guides, and don't mind either restarting certain areas of gameplay or restarting your entire game.
The time constraints just suck all the fun out of it. You practically rush through the main story, trying to save as much time as possible, and don't really get a feel for what's going on. I suppose if you've played this type of game before (Majora's Mask comes to mind), it's probably not that bad for you. But I like to take my time with a game. Explore every nook and cranny, watch the story unfold, and all that, but this game just doesn't have that element. While I'm sure this game could possibly be played without a guide, in order to get the most out of it, I'd advise using a guide straight off. And that bites, because, I don't know about anyone else, but I don't like to do my first play through with a guide. I save that for later so I can focus on storyline my first time through.
I also feel the battle system isn't.... well... I don't know what to call it. It has facets from the previous games of the same name, but it does't seem as stream lined. Yes, its really customizable and what not, and that's not a bad thing. But I really would have prefered to keep the XIII system (Yeah I know. I call it Auto-Win for a reason. That's why I chose the option to default the cursor to abilities).
The growth system is also horrendous. Having some growth from quests isn't a bad thing, but having ALL your growth coming from quests is just stupid. At that point, the only thing monster battles are for are to keep your EP up so you can spam Chronostasis and getting items either for synthesis or quests. After that, monster battles are worthless.
***SPOILER ALERT INCOMING***
As I've said before, the story is confusing. This could be a wonderful stand-alone story (if you actually get to see any of it) but with the previous  games, the jump is really, and I mean REALLY confusing. You go from failing to save cocoon, to time jumping with completely differnet characters to save the timeline, then back to Lightning acting as the harbinger of the end of the world and trying to save souls. Not only that, but in two of the games you fail, so it kinda makes me wonder if you fail at this one as well (and I don't just mean you fail to make it to the thirteenth day, game over fail).
All in all, I'd have to say, with how much I've played of it thus far, I would not recommend it to anyone unless they enjoy this kind of thing. I'll admit, the game is beautiful, but the graphics aren't enough to save it. My opinion may change once I get further in, and at that point, I may change my rating, but until then, I wish I'd spent my money on some other game that I might have actually enjoyed playing.
TLDR: If you enjoy slamming your head into a wall and sticking your finger in a pencil sharpener, you might enjoy this game. Otherwise, don't bother.

While "On the Rain-Slick Precipice of Darkness, Episode One" is undoubtedly intended for longtime fans of the comic, those unfamiliar with Penny Arcade will still appreciate the art style and humor behind this action-adventure/role-playing title.

For a $5 RPG, On the Rain-Slick Precipice of Darkness will meet your expectations (at the time of this review, you can get both Penny Arcade games for roughly $10.) This is no award-winning game, nor does it try to be. This is simply a slightly humorous romp through a zany adventure. To be clear, you don't have to like Penny Arcade to enjoy this game; I personally hate the web comics and found myself chuckling every once in a while. Although the general quality is obviously on a shoe string budget, the lack of any voice acting makes it hard to truely appreciate those few really funny jokes. The gameplay is solid, but takes zero risks and I can't remember a single song from the game which means one of two things:
1). The music is mediocre.
2). The music is horrendous.
The graphics are pretty subpar, but one cool addition is that the character you make is shown in every cutscene and doesn't feel like a silent protagonist at all. If you're desperate for a barebones RPG, pick it up.

Gray Matter marked the return of Jane Jensen to the point and click adventure world.  I would mark the return as a success. Much better than her subsequent game, Moebius, but not in the same ballpark as the original Gabriel Knight.
Gray Matter shows the same quality of research as we saw in the Gabriel Knight series, although not to the depths of Gabriel Knight 2.  Here we learn about magic and are shown about real, historical Oxford.  It's a pleasant atmosphere, with the tone and mystery of a gothic romance.  The story holds your interest, and the game introduces a number of archetypal characters that feel like a bit more than caricatures.  The music by Robert Holmes is fantastic and deserves special mention as well.
The puzzles don't feel gratuitous, and the game strikes a nice balance in terms of difficulty (although the game definitely tends toward the easy side in comparison to the tougher Gabriel Knight).  My only complaint with the puzzles is that a good deal of travel is necessary to complete them- e.g. you can't take an object from a magic shop until your character realizes what they need the object, rinse and repeat.  I've seen some complaints about the "magic system", but I found it easy to follow and enjoyable.
On the negative side, Gray Matter exists in that unhappy grey area of gaming- too much budget to make a 2d, hand-painted, low res point and click game (like the original Gabriel Knight), but not enough of a budget to actually work out the kinks of the interface.  The movement, the cutscene art, the inventory system- they're all clunky and just not all that great.  This is a large part that holds the game back from being a great adventure game.  The other issue is a lackluster ending- the story holds interest, but in the end there isn't a twist or any kind of "big impact" at the end.  The comparisons to Gabriel Knight 1 or 2 don't do this game any favors here.
Final verdict: A successful effort by Jensen, with some very strong stuff here.  With the flaws in mind, however, it ends up being a "good not great" adventure.

I will not write a complete review, there are enough of those here. I will not rant, either. I have played the game and I like the concept; the complexity, micro-managing and pace are fine by me (except you either get declared war on by everybody immediately or nothing happens at all). When I started playing it, I had fun.
However, I cannot, in good conscience, recommend this game for a very simple reason: It's incomplete and has several hefty issues with elements that are vital to the gameplay (AI and performance), and thus borders on a scam; at the very least, it reflects poorly on BattleGoat's business ethics.
This game (main game and addon) was supposed to receive additional attention after release, adding several more features (including a fallout/radioactivity and an environmental impact system). The game did indeed receive several content updates and additional features but, sadly, BattleGoat abandoned the game before the addition and/or revision of several critical features, leaving the game with a stupid AI, pretty damn buggy and, worst of all, content incomplete (which shows - there are buildings, designs, research that are completely pointless because the corresponding parts of the game were never implemented).
I therefore recommend that you avoid this game (and other games from BattleGoat) at all cost. This game is basically a polished Alpha and if the devs couldn't be bothered to finish this game, even after people already bought it, they are not worth your attention. Business practices like that should not be condoned or supported, so think twice before you buy from them - There may very well be a better, finished game out there.
