This final entry to the Final Fantasy XIII trilogy can be summarized in one phrase: The combat system. It is the ONLY reason to play the game. In fact it’s so good that I spent over 450 hours to understand it thoroughly. However, the game fails miserably on almost everything else especially on the game design and story.
EXCELLENT AMALGAMATION OF ACTION AND RPG: The addition of the timing mechanic officially turns this FF title into an action RPG. However it plays very differently from run of the mill action RPGs because Lightning Returns had evolved from turn based strategy. And strategy is what most action RPGs lack.
Besides limited equipment slots, popular action RPGs such as the Elder Scrolls and Diablo series have no restrictions on unlocked skills, thus leading to ridiculously overpowered characters by end game. This game however, allow only four skills you can use at a time in battle, forcing you to think hard about the most effective setup against each foe. So the most powerful enemies are challenging even if you are maxed out.
I absolutely loved the addition of a timing mechanic because it rewards your investment into mastering this skill. Once you get this down, fighting enemies even on hard difficulty becomes a breeze with the right strategy. If blocks are timed correctly, damage can be reduced or even negated completely. A well timed attack also increases damage. It usually doubles the damage, but some equipment can triple or even quintuple that.
Combat is equally demanding on both your reflexes as well as your brain. I have never seen such an elegant blending of both strategy and action in any game. Even though I was beyond disappointed with almost everything else in the game, this ONE aspect gives me hope for the future of the franchise.
COMBAT IS REALLY NOT TOO DIFFICULT: A vast majority of the complaints is nothing more than a “too difficult” and therefore it’s bad assertion. This complaint certainly has its merit, but it’s really a poor game design issue.
With the right setup and a basic level of competency on timing blocks and attacks, most enemies are not difficult to defeat, even on hard difficulty. From mid game onwards, it can get really frustrating if you don’t learn how to setup your equipment.
Unfortunately, neither the in-game tutorials nor gameplay scenarios lead you to explore the depth of the thousands of possible customizations on your garbs, equipment and abilities that this game has to offer. Reading a guide to understand combat is almost inevitable.
THE DESPICABLE END OF WORLD TIMER: This is by far the biggest complaint everywhere. After several playthroughs, I realized that there is way more than enough time to finish the game and it’s really not a big deal. But a new player on their first playthrough will NOT know this. So there is no excuse for the game designers to implement such a silly mechanic.
The clock just ends up forcing the player to only focus on completing quests and objectives because he is constantly worried about wasting time. It certainly made me feel like my boss was relentlessly watching me. I thought games are supposed to be relaxing and not feel like going to work.
NORMAL DIFFICULTY IS TOO HARD: The “normal” difficulty is way too hard for a casual gamer. The learning curve climbs way too fast following the combat tutorials in the beginning of the game. It gets frustrating very quickly. My recommendation for a casual gamer is to use the easy setting for the first playthrough. The game designers really should have the current “normal” difficulty set hard while “easy" should be set to normal. Then they should create an even easier difficulty level below that and a nightmare difficulty above hard. This simple design decision alone would have made the game a lot more accessible to casual players.
UNCONVENTIONALY POOR LEVELING MECHANIC: Only completing quests will “level” your character. This leveling mechanic together with the end of world timer gives the player tremendous pressure to focus only on quests and to avoid combat and exploration. It’s another poor design decision. It is so ironic that the game encourages you to avoid using such a well designed combat system.
REQURING TWO PLAYTHROUGHS TO EXPERIENCE THE COMPLETE GAME IS ABSURD: You have to complete the game at least once before weapons can be upgraded and abilities be leveled beyond three. What casual gamer will play a game twice? Every FF title has allowed the player to unlock everything within a single playthrough without requiring a restart. Yet another ridiculous design decision.
LIGHTNING HAS ZERO CHARACTER DEVELOPMENT THROUGHOUT THE ENTIRE TRILOGY: This is THE colossal failure of the entire FFXIII series. There is no central character to hold the story together. It’s no surprise so many players find Lightning un-relatable. That’s just simply because Lightning doesn’t have any character.
There is a meager sampling of scenes that would qualify as character “development” in the first installment of the trilogy. Hope and Lightning briefly traveled together and bonded. She told him she wanted to forget about the past by changing her name from Claire to Lightning. So that’s the reason why she is so cold and distant from other people. That was it. No more information was revealed as to why she made the name change and what she struggled with. These details are necessary for us to connect with Lightning.
The incessant focus on saving and protecting her younger sister, Serah could have worked had it served as a conduit to develop Lightning’s story. Like many reviewers have already pointed out, the whole trilogy never goes beyond superficial statements from Lightning (and also Snow) about how she needs to be saved and protected. The writers need to illustrate the relationship between the two sisters. Show us bonding moments in the past between Serah and Lightning. Make us care about Serah as much as Lightning does. The same could be said for Snow. Furthermore, the writers could have really used the conflict between Snow and Lightning to add more depth to their characters. The plot contains so many opportunities to develop the main characters. But they really failed to capitalize on it. All that melodrama between the main characters will not work if we don’t care about them.
LIGHTNING RETURNS IS A MESSY HODGEPODGE OF DISJOINT STORIES: Each of the five main quests have little to do with the main plotline. They really made me feel that I am just playing a longer side quest. If the game allows skipping to the final quest, you will not miss anything story-wise.
The random philosophical ramblings from Lightning at the end of most quests come across as nothing more than platitudes. These monologues need to be interconnected and build up to a central theme or relate to the main characters for them to be meaningful. After wasting two games with no character development, it is too late for that here. Just focus on plot, tie up the loose ends and get it over with.
THE MUSIC SAVES THE QUESTS FROM BEING A CHORE TO SLUG THROUGH: A lot of these dramatic pieces made this disaster of a story tolerable. The music has stopped me on many occasions from pressing the skip button on the dialogue scenes.
Some of my favorite pieces includes Lightning’s theme that are used throughout the more serious moments in the story. The Ark’s saintly hymn fit me right into my savior role for humanity. Many of the other pieces that included a chorus truly immersed me into my divine undertaking during the final missions.
I care about Final Fantasy a lot. No other game franchise can tell a story better than the early installments released during the previous two decades. Few stories in any medium can match the epic journey of Final Fantasy VII that many of us still revere a dozen or so years later. I want to see the franchise return to its former glory.

This game looks like a bit of a...idunno, cutsey-pustey mini-joke-game you'd pick up for a laugh.
It's not. My analysis is that it is, basically, a top-down, high-speed (but not overly so) cookdown of everything that makes the open-map, military FPS genre fun. Takes a couple minutes to get used to figuring your firelines out in a top-down perspective, but once you do, all your FPS skills become immediately applicable.
Pros:
*Massive maps.
*Dynamic territory control mechanics.
*Solid character controls, including stances from prone to raised-weapon walking.
*Weapons work as their role indicates.
*Deployables like cover and emplaced weapons makes both offense and defense engaging.
*(Ground) Vehicles.
*Multiplayer and/or Singleplayer, with (though optional for MP)...
*BOTS. (Mostly) non-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ bots. A baker's dozen to spice up an MP server? Sure. 400+-bot mega-battles with you as a tiny drop in an ocean of blood? Go nuts.
*Simple but effective squad mechanics, specifically to control your own fist of bots, through a...
*Solid (inherent in a match or campaign) rank and progression system.
*High customizability of settings, difficulty on various spectrums, and scale.
*Surprisingly "realistic" firefights, including most military field-tactics working as they would, light penetration, suppressing fire (which players SHOULD respect, and bots do) and so on.
*Mods. Expanded versions of normal, Starship Troopers, Halo, Zombies, age-of-muskets, ect.
Cons:
*Aiming is good, but not completely "your own", as in a traditional accuracy bracket based on stance and movement. I'd prefer 1-1 point-and-shoot with recoil, but it probably wouldn't work with the mechanics.
*No air-vehicles. Again, probably wouldn't work, but that's one of the few things I'm missing in my war-immersion, gunning around in a Hind or dropping troops in a Huey.
*Large scale battles can often go into a stale-mate deadlock, where you as a player, no matter how Rambo, feel entirely too small to break it out. Can easily be avoided by not running hundreds of bots on a balanced difficulty (or having an excellent+ run in a main battle tank), but you can dedicate a lot of time to a battle before you notice that war, war never changes.
*Could do with a meta-General mode, which seems to already be in the game, only it's the AI doing it. I'd love to field command this game, and it's almost painful that I can't sometimes.
Summary/Conclusion:
This game has become a regular, if infrequent, fallback to my eternal-curse "I don't know what to play, booored" predicament. Half an hour there, two-four hours here.
Quick and accessible, fun in the moment, can maintain that entertainment value for the amount of time you're willing to spend and employs skills from other action games right out of the box.
And mods make it a pretty endless source of action-game variety.
If they ever add high-level command mode and/or air-vehicles I'm slapping it into my personal hall of fame.
8,7/10, a permanent and reliable member of my library, most definitely worth the money.
And on sale it's a pretty sure bet to not be a wasted purchase.

I went into Gray Matter expecting an 'alright' point-and-click adventure with decent puzzles and mechanics; what I got instead was an incredibly well written storytelling experience, albeit with gameplay one would still deem 'alright'. The atmosphere created was very mysterious, with heavy dashes of both gothic and paranormal sensibilities, so fans of those conventions should be quite pleased with the presentation. Because the genre of the game is point-and-click, one shouldn't go in expecting heavy action-  although there were some great build ups to dramatic revelations, and tension in the style of a true tale of mystery, which keeps the player hooked until the end.
Pros:
+ Quality narrative with an interesting mix of characters
+ Excellent voice acting and attention to detail
+ Puzzles in my opinion not overly difficult or easy, but might require a glance or two at a guide
+ In-game graphics were okay, but the cutscene/hand-drawn art were quite nice
+ Great Soundtrack, both ambient and vocalized
+ Samantha Everett and David Styles as dual protagonists were well developed and had intriguing interactions with both each other & side characters
+ You learn a little something about magic tricks and neurology. Think about the last time this happened in a game you played!
Neutrals/Cons:
- Certain areas of the game experienced a HUGE degree of slow down (Ie. Christ Church Exterior)
- No where does it mention (from what I recall?) that you can double click on an area to have the character you are controlling JOG to the spot instead of casually strolling
- Subjectively there was some potential wasted with regards to character development, and the "building up" so to speak did not always feel like it flowed smoothly
- The ending felt a bit abrupt, and again there was a lot of stuff from the story which could have been wrapped up in a more complete manner. Was hoping for a more detailed epilogue due to all the time and effort invested in developing the cast, but alas many questions went unanswered
Overall:
8.5 out of 10
If you're looking for a slower paced game with a page-turner of a story, and either don't mind or enjoy point-and-click mechanics, "Gray Matter" is the game for you.

MotoRacer 4 is an arcade racer. Containing both asphalt and dirt tracks. However I find the asphalt ones much more satisfying. The dirt ones seem like an afterthought.
This feels a little like Mario Kart – Hear me out before you slay me for heresy. I don't know if any of you are familiar with snaking (The act of rocking back and forth between left and right to gain a turbo boost on a drift, specifically snaking refers to drifting and earning a turbo down straightaways) but MotoRacer 4 has something not entirely different as far as timing boosts and doing specific things to gain the boost for an advantage. For instance, since this is not simulation slip-streaming does not just increase your speed by removing air resistance. But rather earns you a short boost, you can also earn boost by landing with both wheels level to the ground which at times does not always seem correct if it were a proper sim racer. Additionally, you have a boost you control yourself that recharges at various speeds depending on the bike you've chosen setup.
There is no mechanic to control the riders weight, so despite occasionally having my instincts chime in and attempting to pre-load the suspension on jumps or lean into beginning of turns and level off coming out – there'll be none of that here.
There is style point system, which is where the PGR/Burnout comparison comes from. Driving into oncoming traffic and having near misses earn you points, as well is doing wheelies (they happen automatically when you boost) landing well to earn boost among other criteria. There is also a fairly simple trick system. (the Kinetica reference)
I really like the aesthetic, it's sort of this cartoonish faux sci-fi.
Now, the game has some texture pop in -- significant pop in – but it's nothing to really worry yourself with. Unless you paid for this.. That's valid.
There is online and split screen multiplayer and a single player campaign. The modes within are fairly robust. From standard lap races, elimination rounds where a timer ticks and the last place is removed, slalom between traffic, keeping in first to start a personal timer (feels vaguely like Oddball mode in Halo, probably a strange comparison) among some other modes that earn you stars to unlock new events and upgrade the bikes you've unlocked. You can bet stars at the start of an event which is an interesting concept but ultimately doesn't change that much as it resets every time you attempt.

This is probably the best game in this trilogy of games. Absolutely tons of content, great combat, satisfying story, and replayability after you finish the first playthrough.
First, the combat. In the other two, the combat is sort of automated for you, and you don't have any control over your own characters movement which can be frustrating when you watch them walk right into a massive attack. In this game, though, you have full movement over Lightning. You can dodge attacks sometimes by moving around. It really helps in a lot of areas.
The combat in general has way more control over what you can do, and what actions you want to perform in the Schemata system. In the other two, you choose between 5 different Paradigms that you set up, and the AI sorta takes over from there (At least with your two party members). In this one, you set up 3 different Schematas and chose 4 different moves for each, and they each have their own ATB bars letting you switch on the fly to block attacks or switch to melee/magic when the enemy staggers much more fluently than the other two.
This game also introduced a new clock system. If you're a completionist like myself, you may not be that thrilled.
, and it can feel very overwhelming trying to complete all the side quests, Canvas of Prayers and monster extinctions within the allotted time. I played about 4 hours before restarting and following a guide just because I wasn't sure I was going to be able to complete everything in time (That was before I decided I was going to give it another playthrough on Hard). You can freeze time, almost as much as you would like, as long as you keep killing monsters. So it isn't all that bad.
You may have also guessed that, yes, the framerate is all over the place in this game like the others. I can maintain 60 fps throughout the open zones, like the Dead Dunes or the Wildlands, but the two Cities I get constant frame drops. Something I got use to over time, but it is just as bad as FF13-2.
The last thing to mention is the story. It is a satisfying ending to the trilogy, and I wasn't at all disappointed with the story or how it ended. I've noticed that a lot of games nowadays just kinda end, and don't really give the closure that I was looking for. This game does not have that problem. It gives the right amount of closure as well as keeping it open ended enough
It does sort of start off weird, I was wondering what the ♥♥♥♥ was even happening at the beginning and why
, but they slowly explained it over the course of the game.
Overall, a pretty great game that receives a lot of flack just because it's in the 13 trilogy, even though the games in it are pretty good. Worth buying.

Despite its linearness, I played through Final Fantasy XIII willingly. The end of it had all the trappings of weirdo cataclysmic killing of gods and universe unravelling and implausible battles, but the story revealed itself in an engaging way, and the characters were interesting and lovable.
Playing through XIII-2 was less pleasurable. A very interesting character that you wanted to know better in XIII is one of two main protagonists. Alas, with only two characters to follow, it got old. There was little to do in battles, once you had a set-up that worked reasonably well you just mashed a button. Worse, however, was a Chrono Trigger-like wandering through time, messing with cause and effect, but without the multitude of characters' stories being intertwined in an engaging plot. Worst of all, if you did manage to tough it out to the end of the main game, you were rewarded with a most displeasing ending where the end-of-the-world scenario you were trying to avoid all game winds up happening anyway. There's a ton of end-game content that becomes unlocked, but I just couldn't care long enough anymore to bother.
Into that bleak and aimless scenario starts Lightning Returns. Because two characters was deemed to be too many, we've now been reduced to just one, and it's another bloody fashion show - the exact reason I never managed to finish FF X-2, despite having loved FF X.
Furthermore, and worst of all, they have set up a system where you are punished for completing objectives by having a time limit on the game. Yes, time acually ticks away as you progress through the game, and if the timer's up, then you've lost. Yep, all that gameplay down the tube and you have to start over again from the beginning. I'm sorry, when I pick up a mainstream RPG I want to take my time and explore every nook and cranny as I make my way through the game. Here, they attempt to force you to run through the game as fast as possible, to see as little as you can as it goes by.
It all hinges on Replay Value. Replay Value should be based on how much fun the game was to play the first time. Here and in XIII-2, it seems they are trying to force you to replay the game. "Didn't like how it ended? Here, try playing it all over again and see if you like it better this time. Still no? Start again from the beginning and make 'different choices' this time." Starting over is not just a core mechanic, it's at the center of the plot. For me, this just tells me I'm wasting my time.
If they want a game to be played and replayed, it has to be interesting. My Skyrim has 1,000 hours in it. FF X probably has around 350.
In the case of XIII-2, I had seen enough the first play through, and all that extra DLC unlocked at the end was left unplayed. For Lightning Returns, it's been just 3.8 hours so far. I may get a Game Over, I may actually get through to the "end" of the game, but I may quit before seeing either ending. Right from the start, I'm told that what I'm going to do doesn't matter because existence is going to end, and I'm having a hard time caring.
I may yet change this review, but so far, not so good. The company that brought us FF Tactics, FF VI and VII and X has lost its way.
Update (10 hours): Though a veteran of all things Final Fantasy, I just cannot understand or like this game. After writing the above review, I chose to start over on Easy - which I never do in this series. I also downloaded a few DLC freebies in game. The idea was that by playing in Easy, I could enjoy the story and the game, and not feel like I was just getting kicked in the shins the whole time.
It worked for a while. Then, I progressed in the story to a point where I go into a graveyard near the end of Day 2. Suddenly, and without explanation, the monsters went from pushovers to "What just happened?" Most of the time, I have no idea how I wind up dead.
A few theories: First, I like strategy games (which this series used to be about). I take my time, plan my moves, and dominate the enemy. From what I can tell, this is far more of a game about timing moves - a game style I tend to stay away from. Even worse, you could call this more of a brawler-type game, a style of game I simply can't stand.
Attacks can be blocked, if you get the timing right. However, the screen is usually so cluttered with effects that I usually have no idea what's going on. Additionally, wIth the Stagger system as it has devolved, you are being continually being pushed to full offense, and so even if you see an attack coming, it's too late and you can't get your shield up in time.
At this point, I think I'm going to save myself the bother and read a synopsis of the story online. For the premium price tag that these FF games take, I feel as though I wasted my money on this one.

Sorry if this review is not formatted well, because I haven't written many reviews. ( I think this is my second in the years I've been on Steam) but I felt it had to be written because of the bad rep Final Fantasy 13 has had. I think it's an incredible series and many would agree the ending to Lightning Returns is probably one of the better game endings out there in terms of wrapping things up.
After playing 6 of the main Final Fantasies I was sure nothing could top Final Fantasy 7. Final Fantasy 13 alone wouldn't top it but the combination of the trilogy was the first time I actually had to think about it. I can't give a definitive answer but that could be nostalgia.
Battle System
Final Fantasy 13 gives a better more controlled real time action battle system over their previous games. It's not perfect for several reasons imo. It's not really made to hop around like a mad person spamming attacks (in fact you'll probably die fairly quickly if you do). I actually wanted to do this since I prefer to enjoy the story and other elements. You do have to pay attention, the Cloud outfit with its raw power can only get you so far (I'd say like a 1/4-1/3 of the game). Anyway, you can eventually equip a dodge,block,heal and even jump if you want. There are one or two difficulty spikes which are crazy hard and mostly requires you to choose a different path and return later. Also I was surprised to find out there's actually a full on crafting system but it doesn't unlock until after you beat the game. I had no idea. Anyway, technique is much more important that your weapons. At higher difficulties, those improved weapons will be detrimental.
Graphics
I've always found Final Fantasy 13 series to be beautiful to look at it and Lightning Returns is no exception. I own the game on both PS3 and PC and I eagerly awaited the pc version when I was 2/3 done with the PS3 version just so I could enjoy 60FPS and I have to say the game delivered. It wasn't perfect at first but after some light patching it is now as far as I know. It runs great on my Laptop with a GeForce 860m (almost max) and of course no problems on my Desktop with a Core i5 and GeForce 980. I never encountered any graphical glitches and I'll say it again, I think the character models are beautiful to look at. The world is not the biggest but PC version does have enhanced textures. I'd say it looks like a smooth PS4 game.
Sound/Music
All Dialog is voiced and well at that. Lightning’s dialog is my favorite part of Lightning Returns. She has really insightful monologs and character conversations. I love how she's not naive she may even be border line cynical sometimes but she has a reason to help people so she goes through with it. All the music especially the main FF13 theme, the battle and boss themes are all pretty damm good. I didn't like it at first but it grew on me big time.
Story
The game wraps up the Final Fantasy 13 series incredibly. I'm going to sound crazy fanboyish but it definitely has one of the best ending's I've ever seen in a video game. It's definitely my most favorite Final Fantasy ending by far past the others. It's not even just the main story, the people you help feel like you're actually helping people. It's not always about fetching something for someone (there are grind quests like that too but as rewarding). I was moved a few times hearing some of the NPC's back stories, I couldn't believe they put this effort and so much emotion into side stories. Some are short and some long quest lines. it's kinda crazy because there are some really interesting ones that don't really pop up anywhere, you just have to stumble on them by being curious of your surroundings. Like I mentioned earlier Lightning may be slightly cynical and because of that, the game for the most part is not campy expect some slightly dark stories, death and even questions of morality. It's a very immersive atmosphere and the game feeling very open world helps this. Anyway, every character you can imagine makes an appearance of some kind and the story definitely goes full circle with everyone’s choices over the years. Like I said before, I couldn't think of many games that would wrap up plot points so well.
-Additional notes
I play the game exclusively with an Xbox 360 controller. I played mostly on my desktop. I own all three games on the ps3 and the first and last on PC. You'll want to spend some time setting up your outfits with their abilities and MAKE SURE you switch outfits at intervals during battles, even short ones. You do spend most of the game fighting on your own which sucks as a FF game but there are places in which you can have a consistent partner. One can even be powered up a lot if you put the work into it and it will reveal some familiar backstory. The game has metaphorical and literal references to God and Noah's ark.

This looks like a fun puzzle game. Sadly, most of the work on this game went into making pretty clay shapes.
The game is really boring (pun not intended). Even with the difficulty ramped up to "genius" (yes, I tried the non-maze levels which were supposed to be harder) it isn't a challenge. Levels are randomized rather than fixed, so it's a stretch to call these puzzles. The first and second sets of maze levels take forever to complete, and it doesn't correctly award you a star once you do, so there isn't any way to open any of the maze levels past the first two sets. And to get all the points for each maze, you have to beat it at least twice! If you beat it four times, you don't even need to collect cheese to get all the stars. Just find the exit four times and you've hit top score.
In essense, the creator took something that looks vaguely like a puzzle game and instead of writing actual puzzles, greated a random generator to do it. They didn't even take the time to generate the puzzles and playtest them individually to see which ones worked. They just generate the puzzles on the fly, which most of the time are solvable (sometimes in multiple ways, and on occasion not at all), and the only "puzzle" part is jumping through hoops to reach the end. Despite a number of game elements that look interesting and do novel things, there isn't any challenge to using them and most of the game elements don't interact with most of the other game elements.
I'm sad that I wasted five bucks on this. If you enjoy puzzles this is not the game for you. I'm not sure who this game is for, to be honest. Maybe young children? I'm not even certain they'd enjoy it.

Giana Sisters : Twisted Rise of the Owlverlord at a glance seems to be everything you could ask in a side-scrolling platformer: Artsy visuals to gawk at, a bipolar catchy soundtrack, a fresh concept (the two sisters are like ying and yang, night and day and that reflects on puzzle-solving and gameplay). Mix in it the preemptive pastiche of the magical ambiance of Rayman forests, even some of the high speed thrills of Sonic the Hedgehog. What more could one ask?
Well, the truth is that platformers to me need to have a quintessential feature: Tight control  scheme. It's a make or break thing. And unfortunately, Giana Sisters is the latter. I tried both gamepad and keyboard defaults and the movement always feels very unprecise. In fact, I've never been so frustrated with a side-scroller controls and I've been a keen fan of them since the 1990s (I played the lot, Super Mario Bros., Alex Kidd, Sonic, Rayman, Kirby, Donkey Kong Country, Crash Bandicoot... you name it.) None feels as broken as this. So it's a no go, if you want my opinion.

This game is a bit of a mixed bag for me. The story is good and the graphics are great so it should make for a great adventure game, shouldn't it? Well ... the game has quite a lot of small annoyances. For a start, the game feels very static - as beautiful as the backdrops are, it all feels rather disconnected as if you're walking through a painting.
The music is great and in the same style of that of previous Jane Jensen games (Gabriel Knight anyone?) but despite this, this is the first Jensen adventure game where I didn't really feel part of the world. Perhaps the mix of 3D and drawn backdrops is the reason.
But, the biggest problem this game has, are the controls. I wondered why they're so clunky compared to the MUCH better controls used in the Gabriel Knight games so I checked to see if it had gotten a console release and guess what? It did. Once again the console version caused the controls of a PC version to go down the drain ... . The inventory is a fiddly mess - move a little bit too much downwards and it will close and clicking & dragging doesn't exist anymore.
On the plus side, the magic tricks do add a unique layer to the game. On the negative side ... they're needlessly fiddly as well. Most of the times you know exactly what needs to be the done but the game makes you go through all the little steps anyway.
All in all, this is a solid adventure game with a poor UI and some other smaller flaws. Recommended but with reservations.

This game was one of the most pleasant surprises in my whole Steam library. I enjoyed Darksiders 1, but I was also ready to be done with it when I finished its campaign. A short while later, I install and start up Darksiders 2 to see how it compared, and I was blown away.
Immediately you notice many familiar elements from Darksiders 1 - the setting, the art style, the Zelda-ish combat and puzzles. However, most of these (except the puzzles) are just done better in the sequel - the art has much more color and beautiful designs, Jesper Kyd weaves a masterful soundtrack that is up with my favorites in gaming history, the voice acting has been raised at least half a notch across the board, the climbing/parkour elements are better, the bosses are bigger, and the fighting is so, so fast and tons of fun.
The combat lends itself well to frantic button-mashing if you prefer, but there is also plenty of depth to build multiple fighting styles. The RPG-lite elements of item collecting, item crafting, and skill trees were simple enough to be quickly understood but had enough depth to allow you investigate various builds and make powerful combinations.
The game sprawls across several large areas with plenty of sidequests and collectibles, as well as a fighting Arena (which I did not complete), so there is easily over 50 hours of content in this game if you are enjoying it, but you could also probably beat the game in 25 hours or less if you bullrush it. I think this is a fantastic content value, especially since I thoroughly enjoyed the many hours I spent with Darksiders 2.
There are a few negatives - the puzzles are not that difficult, and the story is...what it is. It's an interesting setting in a teen edgelord sorta way, but the story is fairly predictable, but you really shouldn't play this game for the story anyways, it's too much fun in the combat and exploring the world. There can be a fair amount of backtracking if you want to do all the sidequests and collectibles, but if you are methodical about talking to people and looking for things your first go-thru of places and dungeons you can greatly alleviate the backtracking.

I may not have many hours on Steam, but I promise you my PS3 version has seen a good 50+ hours.
GENRE: Action Role-Playing Hack and Slash
PROS:
- Very unique art style
- Fluid and beautiful combo strikes
- Overall Balanced
- Mechanics and Design are solid, and well thought through
- Great sense of exploration and adventure without realising its somewhat linear game-progression.
- Unique boss fights
- Challenging experiences
- Optional "Nightmare" difficulty mode: for those who are truly insane
- Random and intuitive loot system
- Can pick up the game on consoles for about $10 AUD
CONS:
- Only sometimes it will feel slightly clunky
- Very "grindy" if you are wanting to power-game
- Limited conversation animation between player and NPC's
- A bit expensive now for PC - $30 USD on Steam - since THQ (creators) went bankrupt in 2012
- Menus are a little tedious for the first few hours of the game, but if played enough, you get used to it.
REVIEW:
This game has got to be one of my favourite hack-and-slash games out there. It is full of story, adventure, and unique combat. There isn't a single enemy with the same attack animation, and yet you (Death, as the player) can always pick up new and exciting powers, combos, and weapons that make you re-think your entire attack strategy. A giant hammer might be more powerful than scythes, but it's quite a bit slower, meaning you have to time your strikes before rushing into combat.
The loot system is very intuitive and thrilling - you never know what you're going to pick up unless you grind the area for 6 hours, which is optional from a game-play/story perspective. Even then, there is a large pool of items that every section of enemies can drop, and on top of that, every item can have a multitude of different buffs: you might pick up 5 claws (like wolverine's) but one might have an increased health pickup, another might have increased wrath pickup, one might have extra critical chance, etc. etc. It makes the game a lot more fun, and if allows you to adapt more to the enemy's AI if you're after a particular set of items that have a particular buff, and have to grind an area for 6 hours. You end up feeling like a hard-hitting ninja by the end of the grind when you are surrounded by enemies but you know to dodge at this time, then swing in with your scythe combo at this time, activate that power, and boom - enemies dead, free loot, didn't lose a lick of health.
On the flip side, the more you progress through the game without grinding, the more challenging and different the AI can become, and you'll constantly find yourself picking up and using health or wrath items wherever, and whenever, you can.
On top of all this, the graphics and artwork are really things that make you look twice when running through a nordic-based location. The art is very unique to most 3D games out there these days, and it all started with one guy writing a comic book.
RATING:
All in all, I'd give this game an 8/10.

Half-way through the game, I was thinking how to justify a "recommended" tag for this game. Since I loved Darksiders 1 and understood that Vigil wasn't exactly in a good spot while developing Darksiders 2, I thought that maybe this game didn't deserve the flak some people gave it.
But after finishing Darksiders 2, I just don't can't in good will recommend this game.
The amount of reviews claiming that most of the bugs in the Deathinitive edition were fixed are complete bs. In my playthrough, I had a number of CTDs in one playthrough, 3 of which were in major points of the story: one after a cutscene where you're supposed to enter a fountain after meeting Archon (which, when looking for a solution, found out it's actually a major bug that's only been fixed in a november 2015 BETA patch which I didn't even want to try) and two in the last boss of the game. Then I had other random CTDs which apparently are due to the devs messing up with the Shadows quality graphics option, which they have been promising to fix since 3 YEARS AGO. There were some fps drops here and there, but they were very rare.
Gameplay-wise, this game is similar to it's predecessor. It borrows a lot of elements from different sources, the most recognizable are it's similarities to Zelda, going through dungeons and solving puzzles to move forward, fighting some enemies in-between.
Virgil games even managed to ♥♥♥♥ that up. Darksiders 1 didn't have extremely complicated puzzles, but they did manage to make you think one in a while. Darksiders 2's puzzles are pretty much "enter room>run there>scale a wall>parkour>push a lever>run down to where you were>go through next room". They didn't even try to hide what to do, they tried to make the puzzles as obnoxious as possible and give them some "complexity" by giving you different tools for mobility. You will no longer run through big halls, carrying keys, figuring out what to do and how to solve the room. You'll only be backtracking through the same stupid rooms and raging every time you make a mistake and fall or die because it means you'll have to do everything over again. Besides that, the came is a bit off when you need it the most for battles where you're fighting at least 3 enemies and the lock-on is completely useless and will hinder you most of the time.
And finally, the worst decision made by Virgil. The dreaded loot system. The "Hey, if Borderlands is successful because of it's loot system, maybe we should try it on our game?" system, where every legendary armament and equipment becomes completely worthless after one mission from early to mid game, where in-game currency is never used to buy equipment and becomes effectively worthless, where the satisfaction of finding unique weaponry is as much as finding a dead rat under your desk; you will look curiously over it for 10 seconds then store it in the trash can where it belongs.
You liked Darksiders story? Buy it on a very good sale. Maybe you'll force yourself to finish this game to see it through like I did.
You never played Darksiders? Buy the first one and play it instead.
I'm sorry defunct Vigil, but you really ♥♥♥♥ed up.

I'm a sucker for top-down twin stick shooters and I love retro graphics. I saw Creekside Creep Invasion and figured it would be right up my alley. Well it is, and actually the game is even better than I expected! This is one of the only really challenging twin stick shooters I have played, I can't seem to make it past the first part, but that's a good thing, most games like this have been a breeze for me. I'm getting a bit better each time I play so the game isn't impossible.
As it's description says, CCI is a rogue-lite, and the gameplay is somewhat similar to Binding of Isaac and Nuclear Throne. Does it play just like those games? no, but if you've played and enjoyed those 2, then you should give CCI a shot. To me CCI is a lot like a game that few people are familar with, which would be a game called "All Zombies Must Die!". CCI is much better than that game, because for one, that game was way too easy for me and I also like the pixel art style of CCI much better!
CCI has a unique system of randomly switching your weapon out every time you run out of bullets. It adds to the challenge and reduces boredom of being stuck with one weapon. The levels layout changes each time you play and enemies are random. You've got permanent unlockables, different power items you can find, power-ups for yourself, like health, speed, etc..., you also have different costumes you can find and unlock which allow you to perform specials, each costume having their own unique special...The game is set during the 80's on Halloween, so you can't get a much better setting than that.
To top it all off, the devs are awesome, I had a slight issue with gamepad aiming, so I brought it up in the forums...The dev not only responded extremely quickly, but actually implemented a fix within minutes, that actually fixed the issue! I cannot say if I've ever experienced this, I might have once before from another awesome indie dev, but it's been rare for me to even get a reply from a dev, let alone a fix the same day. Incredible. Needless to say, I really like this game, but I also really want the devs to be successful, because they know how to treat their customers right. I cannot say enough good things about this dev.
I highly recommend, yes even in EA, Creekside Creep Invasion. I really think a lot of people who like rogue-like/lite will enjoy this game, and those who are huge into twin sticks, like myself, should really enjoy it as well. I really enjoy the music as well, and the game overall reminds me of a beloved NES game or old school computer game from the early 90s. I don't often have time to play video games these days, so don't let my play time fool you.

Moreover and the most ridiculous one, whenever I exit the game, system dialog comes up, saying "SimAirport stopped" like a program crash. Overall, it's UNCOMPLETE and I would NOT recommend this game until these severe bugs and problems are fixed.

I have seen mixed reviews on here. Keep in mind that the purpose of early access, which is almost essentially an open beta, is to be on the lookout for bugs so they can be fixed before final release. The people who can't stand glitches and issues and are giving do not recommend are missing the entire point of the early access.
That said, I would totally recommend buying this game, but only if you are willing to share and report any issues you have to the devs. They do an amazing issue at rectifying issues as best as they can and as quickly as they can. There will be more improvements in the future and more gameplay features. Will there be broken saves and hiccups in the future during early access? Of course. But they will be resolved in time to make SimAirport a complete game whenever it releases officially. The development team is doing an amazing job and they prove that they care about the community. Not every dev team or company can say that these days with the norm often being rushing a bugged product out quickly and patch it later in order to meet a corporate deadline.
I have also seen some concerns with the game becoming laggy. However, if you opt into the experimental betas (right click the game on steam > properties > betas), you will see that the experimental beta has fixed the lag for the most part with AI improvements. The devs release almost daily patches depending on community input to quickly resolve any issues.

I would like say, potential game but not worth the price at this stage.
The most critical issue for the developers is the algorithms they are using.
1. When the number of people in the terminal increases, the whole game became un-playable. Many people says, pls optimize the game, but from my point of view, it is people routing algorithm issue. Let's say if each people need to use make their own decision from origin to destination, then u need to find the shortest path once, if there are other activities, like visit cafe area, rest room, then there are more decisions to make. Btw, shortest path algorithm is resource consuming if solution space is huge, not matter which variations u r using. My suggestion to this is to reduce the solution space, for example, for unboarding people and boarding people, mark the region they can visit. Or instead of tracking each people, use people flow to represent, and randomly generate some actions.
2, vehicle and plane routing and detouring algorithms: for vehicle, easy to get stuck if using two lanes, u can always see vehicles always change lanes. Again, reduce the solution space.
For plane, if two are face to face, then one need to turn back, but if a third one is behind, then turn back again. For this, I think First Come First Serve, and path reservation can be tested. Means whenever a plane occupies the path, then it will move first, the others have to wait at junction.
In short, this game is not just a game, you need to consider it as Simulation and Optimization platform, many articles you may want to search around.

Supreme Ruler 2020 Gold is the combined product of Supreme Ruler 2020 and Global Crisis.
Produced by Battlegoat Studios and published by Paradox Interactive. (R1)
It is the child of the former *Supreme Ruler 2010 and It has expanded on the original game. (R2)
Note, please go to the bottom for a TLDR summary.
1. Introduction
There are 3 game modes.
● Campaign
● Sandbox
● Scenario
Campaign and sandbox are more or less the same.
If you have decided to play a campaign, you are presented with 3 campaigns to pick from World 2020, Global Crisis and Shattered World. (You can mod in more if you wish.)
Once you have selected your campaign you can chose from 182, 184, and 248, respectively.
You can play as the Superpower of the United States or the weakest of minor powers Malawi.
in World 2020 and Global Crisis.
Or
You can play as a state in the former United States or a sec of former Russia in Shattered World.
There are a lot of nations to choose from, just depends on how you wish to play.
Scenario, as its name implies, has a goal to complete within a given deadline.
Now you're given 3 main categories.
● Supreme Ruler 2020
● Global Crisis
● Custom Scenario
Each one has certain scenarios from their own time frame. Of course, Custom Scenario has only custom scenarios.
2. Gameplay
The gameplay is quite unique. I have yet to find a game that does a real-time strategy like this, it's nice.
Let's just say we are playing as South Carolina in the campaign Shattered World.
2.1 Interface
2.1.1 Top
At the top center of the screen we have the following; Treasury amount, nation played as, game menu, GPD/c, pause/play, game speed, time and date.
All of the above are just information except the time and game menu buttons.
2.1.2 Bottom
On the left corner/center of the screen, you have a sidebar with tabs of various areas.
● Land
● Production
● Research
● Finance
● State
● Operations
● Defense
● Unit Command
Once you have selected one of these the left center/corner will show you the tab and the information related to it.
Here you will have the option to change various sliders related to the tab you have selected. Or change the highlighted parts of the map.
On the right center/corner of the screen, you have your minimap and your email (notifications).
You will receive an email if there is anything of importance happening that the game thinks is important to you. You can change the settings for what you find important or not in the options menu.
2.2 Economy
As South Carolina we have to get a production of coal and metal ore. If we don't we will go into a huge deficit as we are import loads of resources to supply our factories. So we have to build some Metal ore/Coal mines till the demand is met.
But, if we are not careful at how many we build we will have to start importing industrial goods, which cost us more money.
That is just one aspect of the economy. Before we go to war, we have to make sure that we have the proper supply coverage is provided, the military goods produced to feed our solders, and the unit of solders themselves are trained.
It's rather detailed and I have only covered the most basic idea behind the economics behind the game.
I don't know the deepest secrets it offers as I have only played around 20 hours of the game.
2.3 Research/Technology
To be able to build a clean energy building or improve your coal power plants must be researched. Even the equipment your solders use and missiles your planes fire must first be researched as well. (Unless the nation you're playing as starts with the technology.)
Researching a technology is simple, it depends on the number of Research Centers you have and if you can afford to pay the employees.
Here is a small list of the main technologies you can research.
● Warfare
● Transportation
● Science
● Technology
● Medical
● Society
Each one is linked to the others in some way. Some are more beneficial than others. It's your job to find out which ones are better for your situation and goals than someone else.
There is also another type of research, Unit Design.
● Army (Ground)
● Naval (Sea bound)
● Air Force (flying units)
● Missiles (ammunition for missile for various land, air, and sea units)
All the categories above have multiple sub tabs in them for example the Army tab has,
● Infantry
● Recon
● Tanks
● Anti-Tank
● Artillery
● Air Defense
● Transport
With all these options you can tailor the Army/Navy/Air Force however you wish.
2.4 Warfare.
Warfare is very limited to how long your economy can support it. And how fast you will win/lose the war depends on the technology you have researched. It requires strong supply lines, some planning, and a bit of luck.
After you go to the State tab you can conduct negotiations with other nations, or just declare war.
Although, just being aggressive will make you get kicked out of the UN and other nations a valid casus belli.
Once you have a valid reason to go to war or you just declared it. You may now order your units to attack and cross the enemy’s borders and slowly moving your nation’s borders over the claimed territory. The map is made of small hexes so it is rather detailed on the terrain you can claim.
Each unit has a condition bar which shows you the state they are in and how much manpower they have. If the bar is red you are likely out of supplies. If it is almost empty the unit will soon be destroyed because of the lack of men in the unit.
Warfare is like Economics, it has some great details to it. I just cannot do justice explaining all of it.
3. Conclusion.
I enjoy the game very much. But, the only thing that I find to be a large drag is the fact time moves so slowly even on the highest speed setting. The highlight of the game is the complexity and details they made for us to conquer the world with.
This is a wonderful game I enjoy that is made by Battlegoat. It’s a great buy, especially for any real-time grand strategy game fans.
4. My Game Scores and Reasons behind them. TLDR; Look here.
Gameplay                7/10
The game play is amazingly depth. Before you can even think about going to war you must first stablise your economy, have a surplus income, and research and produce the units to attack. I believe that this game delivers the "Conquer the world or die trying" idea really well.
Music/Sounds           4/10
Sounds are nice, they go well with it. They just get repetitive after a while of playing. Just like most other games of this category. Music as well, but that can be fixed with anything you want it to be thanks audio players!
Creativity                 8/10
A nice and original idea to the real-time grand strategy games are. The creative depth and research that was put into the game was amazing.

Okay graphics for a game made in 2008. I suppose if they were much better than they are most computers at that time couldn't handle all the calculations the computer has to make.
Replay Value            6/10
The replay value of this game is really dependent on the player, for me it's a good bit. But it's still dependent on my ability to set a goal. So it will be yours as well, as I cannot set goals for you.
Enjoyment               8/10
I enjoy this game and I can see myself coming back to it at least for a hour or 2 each week. Who knows, might even play it for a few hundred hours.
Overall                      6/10
This game has a lot of potential that is only limited to the players' want to conquer the world and how you want to do it. Diplomacy, War, and Economic Supremacy, but at the end of the day, it's still a war game.

I've played the original 1nsane. I played the demo I'd gotten on a CD with a magazine, and then I played the full game as soon as I found it. I loved 1nsane. I played the hell out of 1nsane. This, sir, is not 1nsane.
It's not bad, but Insane 2 isn't as good as the original. But it is a fun little off-road, open-arena racer. Jamboree, Off-Road Racing and Capture the Flag are still around, and they're mostly good (though the cars seem to roll over way to easily with the flag than in the original). And there are new gaming modes as well. Yeah... about those...
I think that Insane 2 suffers more from "sequelitis" than anything else. It's bigger than the first game. It's prettier than the first game. It's a lot more frantic than the first game. And it suffers for it.
The graphics are incredible. 1nsane wasn't ugly, but this is a very pretty game. The cars don't deform as interestingly in Insane 2, but aside from that, the stages are so good looking. The Thunderstorm stage in particular has so much going on... which leads to my main criticism. There's too much going on. And it distracts (and detracts) from the gameplay.
Each race has at least 6 competitors (up from 4 in the original) meaning that there are more cars running around, pushing into you. There's nitro now, which means that everyone is faster, and the racing itself is a lot more frantic (made even more so by the motion blur). On the Thunderstorm stage, your car can be struck by lightning, which looks metal, but if you're trying to play catch-up, and you lose the race because you got hit at the wrong time, it's more than a bit frustrating.
The nitro does add a certain something to the racing, and getting upgrade points does give the game some aspect of strategy. Upgrading also changes the looks of the cars (which is always nice). But it keeps reminding me of 1nsane, and stuff that's no longer around.
Each league had a pool of cars available (and it seemed as though there were a lot more of them). Vehicles had a differential lock. There was a separate button for repair, and a separate one for recovering the car. And one for righting a car if it rolled over. 1nsane was just... better.
Insane 2 introduces a number of new modes. There's Knockout, in which the last competitor through a checkpoint is removed every 30 seconds. Greed is probably the most fun, because you run around the map collecting bronze, silver and gold packages for points (probably a replacement for Demolition, and good riddance to it). And Pursuit, which was invented by the Devil, who laughs maniacally as He forces you to chase His helicopter around through a bumpy, bouncy arena while your competitors keep pushing you off course.
Odd that. I started out this review, thinking I'd just lightly criticize Insane 2 while extolling how much fun it is to play. But really, compared to the original, this is no fun at all.

I unfortunately never had the chance to play the first 1nsane, which I hear was a fantastic experience, and from what I understand the multiplayer is next to nonexistent for this game.
However.
This is perhaps one of the most enjoyable racing games I've played.
There's plenty to unlock in the way of cars and upgrades, and most of the ways to unlock new cars and gain points for cars requires a little effort, but every moment is enjoyable and worth it - by racing and completing objectives on mainly off-road courses against other AI vehicles who are very aggressive in achieving those goals.
The world physics are set to the extreme - this means that your car will often not have more than one or two tires on the road for most of the time you are racing, and drifting on dirt and snow is commonplace. The emergency braking and the boost make it even more entertaining, and add in AI vehicles that are under the same influences... it makes for a crazy fun experience.
There's plenty of various game modes to enjoy, from a more traditional off-road race to Pursuit of following a helicopter and staying under it to Greed, which is a point box drop collect-a-thon. All of them bring their own mayhem, and while often frustrating, it's also adrenaline-pumping and hilarious to see what happens as cars smash into one another and chunks of metal fly off.
Your car can take damage, and you'll see the wear and tear. It doesn't actually impact how your vehicle handles however (which may be a pro or a con depending on your viewpoint), and unlike in the first 1nsane where you could apparently keep driving with a wheel or two missing, your car simply breaks if you lose one and just have to reset your car. Which has a dedicated key, and I've often abused it to give myself an edge in the CTF modes, where the flag actually has a physical impact on how your car handles and can cause it to flip, especially if you're in a smaller buggy or sprinter and not a massive truck.
All of this, and everything looking good while blasting along at insane speeds. Seriously, this game has some great aesthetics - and it won't break your computer while pleasing your eyes.
I'd highly recommend getting this game even on its own, and if you can get some friends to play it online with you, I can imagine there's plenty of laughs and yelling bloody murder at the screen to be had.

The good:
Strong writing that keeps player entertained throughout the entire experience
Interesting magic puzzle mechanics
Nicely rendered backrounds blended seamlessly with wonderfully done 2D art and cutscenes.
Suggestive voiceover and decent music
The bad:
Character models are very dated with animation that is sometimes almost painful to watch. Character portraits that pop up during conversations look like they all had "egg" shaped head as a base model to which different noses, eyes and hair had been plastered into later (think kinda mid 90's fallout style). Full sized models you otherwise interact with resemble these potato men portraits only if you crank up your imagination to the point where you start seeing a white rabbit with a golden watch popping up from under random furniture in your house.
Puzzle design has some rough spots here and there. On several occasions you can come accross objects which you cannot pickup before having perfomed a number of unrelated tasks, forcing a player to back-track for no apparent reason.
Some of the bonus objectives feel pointless and combined with the technical issues mentioned above bear a feeling of project lead used to large budget realizing half-way through production that the actual budget is too small for the projects ambition.

If you're looking for a classic point and click adventure game and haven't played Gray Matter yet, this is one of the games you likely don't want to miss. The gorgeous graphics, interesting story, intelligently designed riddles and a lot of suspense, combined with a masterpiece of a twist at the game's ending, make this game a piece of art.
The main heroine is a introvert goth girl that ends up in a rich doctor's manor during her trip around England. Being the manipulative sociopath we soon get to experience fully throughout the game, she lies her way into becoming his assistant. Most of the gameplay comprises of Samantha forging IDs, putting a plug in someone's phone, manipulating people into helping her and breaking in. The other part of the game is collecting memories and doing menial tasks as doctor David Styles, who lost his wife in a car accident that also left him terribly scarred.
The amount of riddles is amazing and they are neither too easy nor too difficult. I didn't have to find a walkthrough for any of the riddles, which made me like this game even more, but dispite that, I got stuck TWICE. That was because playing as David you can get very frustrated as what to do next. At some point I clicked through almost every available location to make the story progress. I consulted a walkthrough to find out that there is an MRI room in the basement's main room that  has a computer David can operate. Okay, my mistake. I missed the location that was previously inoperable when Sam loitered around it. But then I got stuck again and couldn't get the story to progress, as I've learned where the Deadalus Club was located, yet it didn't show up on the map. I thought that it was a glitch. After I've checked the chapter's walkthrough step by step, it turned out that I didn't print out a file that was among the files in the folder on David's computer, that suddenly became printable in one of the chapters, so I could use it in... the same place I got stuck before. That made the chapter go to 100% and the Deadalus Club location suddenly was showing up on the map after David left the manor. That was actually rather awkward considering that for Sam the Deadalus Club was on the map and she would refuse to go there saying that she has something to do before.
The fact that an errand to-do-list kind of parts of the game require you to click through locations semi-randomly searching for the thing that makes you progress to the next part ruined the game's continuity for me and I was disappointed that I had to look up a solution, because I wanted to figure out the game without help yet I was stuck at trying to figure out what the thing that you're supposed to find at the moment was. It turned out that I could solve every riddle, but I got stuck because there are moments that make you confused as to what you should do - and some parts of thegames were made in a way that there were blatant clues added as what should be done next. The locations re marked with colors ranging from gold through silver to greyed out, showing whether you've done everything in there required for finishing that chapter. This makes me wonder if the people testing Grey Matter requested that to be done, because of the amount of confusion coming from certain actions opening up others in places you've already clicked through a few moments ago and now they suddenly have an NPC that wasn't there before.
This goes only for the short chapters where you get to play as David, and Sam's part is pretty much flawless.
This is a 9.5/10 game for classic point and click adventure game fans.

First, read my Darksiders 1 review because a lot about this game is true from that review.
8/10 Action platformer with puzzle and RPG elements. Liek the first has all the same hallmarks of the genre predecessors.
I liked this game for the most part. Is a parallel story to the first game this time featuring Death trying to save War from what he believes will be his brothers fate. Is much expanded and improved over the first game in many ways, and is much larger. It feels like the difference between the first Soul Reaver game and LoK:Defiance in terms of how much more there is to it and how the mechanics have been expanded.
Story:
Improved a bit over the first title, and fleshes out some of the background of the Riders. It isnt some hugely deep character driven narrative by any stretch but it definitely gives Death some depth and is engaging. Death also is a snide ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ too which at times is quite funny (Doorstop).
Game World:
Big and beautiful in the first map, but it starts to slip until the fourth. In terms of progression there is a definite sense that the end was rushed as the difference in length as the world maps progress is noticeable with maps 3+4 being shorter than map 1.
Gameplay:
Excellent for the most part, a lot of puzzles as with teh first but they didnt seem as difficult mostly, but some were rather ingenious toward the end. Generally the puzzles are catered to the scheme of the Reaper Skill acquired recently (eg. suddenly all puzzles use Voidwalker once the ability is unlocked). The Reaper skills inparticular Deathgrip felt a bit haphazard, and led to some instant deaths when the game suddenl couldnt grip to a fixed hold. I also didnt like the new skill interface, the rotary system where different skills are arrayed around a reticle and control stick direction selected, some angles the xbox controller doesnt like and so selecting core items like the Deathgrip could be annoying.
Questing is part of the game more than the first, with many mini-quests. Unfortunately I did start to feel a bit fatigued by the experience toward the end with the constant series of fetch quests, which even the main quests were.
There are a lot of itemisation improvements over the first game, with the addition of many more weapons and armours as random chest, purchased adn quest rewarded loot. The game has sets that synergise with the newly added skill trees (not to be confused with reaper skills). There are two trees, one melee and one magical. I found the melee tree was my favourite. The skill trees are filled with talents that require skill points you earn along the way through the levelling and quest systems. This gives far more flexibility compared to the first but you will need to pick how you spend points carefully as there is a fairlylow level cap, fortunately you can respec your points.
In terms of combat the game is fast, and the combat has been expanded with Devil May Cry style combos, my only gripe with this is late in the game there are a lot of enemies that float just outside the hit box of many combos meaning there is really only the option for aerial attacks to take them out. Similarly late game there are many enemies that now knock back and stun, and the difference between their appearance and from before is stark with the game having none, and then heaps suddenly. Another minor gripe I found is there are some enemies who persistently juggle with no way out, and given the propensity for group fights, this becomes extraordinarily annoying at Nightmare difficulty and makes those enemies jsut cancer as I note they are extraordinarily tanking in one instance, and the second that sticks out the creature is super mobile and also is one that floats outside the basic hit box (doesnt help that the areas this one appears have A LOT of fall death locations). My final gripe carries over from the first game, field of view, it is not able to be altered and is pretty small and with the lock on system or targetting becomes stupidly unhelpful (eg The Noss creatures). Like the first there is again the suddenly barred path forward till you clear all the enemies stuff, it doesnt happen constantly so its not labourious. The boss battles are more numerous is this, I do note that more are also screen fillers trying to lend "epic" quality to the fights, this doesnt always work with how bad the field of view is, and for some enemies that have huge area smashes that are really hard to avoid at times and can insta-kill on Nightmare if you are unlucky.
Graphics:
Improved a lot over the previous one in many respects and an indicator of a larger budget. Still retains the original comic book style, but the world created and the environments are stunning everywhere except Earth. Nothing to really complain about here, it isnt aiming for true life detail, it knows it's style and it does it well.
Sound:
Massive improvement over the first game, there is a lot more atmospheric music and it is just amazing for the environments. The sounds in this made me sorely nostalgic for a Castlevania game done right by this developer team. The voice acting is great all the way through with a lot of familiar voice actors. Improvement of the sound buigs from teh first game, it does still suddenly cut out completely during and then after cut scenes and need a reload of the game to fix. Very rare compared to the first though.
I would definitely recommend this to anyone wanting a puzzle platforming action game.
Edit 1: Oh, there is fast travel, there is god damn fast travel. It is great and very welcome.

THE MOST UNDERRATED GAME ! Now, the first Darksiders was our introduction to the series, but the second is where it found its identity, I believe. With Jester Kyd at the helm of the soundtrack, he turned it into this sweeping epic. This track starts off by emanating this mysteriously ethereal, poisoned landscape from which no hope can be birthed. Then around the 3 minute mark, you start to believe that Death can bring a hope with it. A hope for a new beginning, righting eternal wrongs.
It's kind of guiding you through the vision the developers had and found. The first game had good mechanics, and good gameplay, if more than a bit derivative of other games in the genre such as Ocarina of Time, or God of War with a dash of WoW thrown in for aesthetics. Then the second took everything about the first, and blew it up. The tight confined spaces of the first game opened into sweeping, grandiose,  huge dungeons and a fully realized open world. I'm glad they ditched boring old earth for the fantastical planes and hellscapes you see in the second. Throw in a robust, gorgeous loot system and crafting, make the movement buttery fluid, and the combat even deeper and you've got a recipe for success. Cribbing off two of the best game genres doesn't hurt, either, taking what's good about Zelda (dungeons and puzzles), God of War(combat, weapon styles) and even a bit of WoW for the loot. It's an underrated gem, and I only hope they eventually make it in Darksiders III <3

Dead Rising Presents: Final Fantasy XIII
Seriously; it's Dead Rising. This game has a timer, just as in Dead Rising, whereby you have to complete the main quests before it runs out. Just as in Dead Rising this game has side quests that are optional and can also be completed within the time frame the game allots you. UNLIKE Dead Rising completing side quests EXTENDS the timer and is integral to the plot. Furthermore you can FREEZE time with an ability that uses EP points (gained from battle). So it's Dead Rising but, generally, easier. Don't let anyone tell you the timer is too harsh; hell if you go ''game the ♥♥♥♥ out of the system'' mode like me you can complete everything in the 4 of the 13 days you are given, so it provides plenty of wiggle room. Granted some sidequests are only open after doing others, and those others might require multiple days past 4, whereas others are opened up in later days. But generally speaking the large ''bulk'' of them can be completed in roughly 4 days (along with mainline quests). The quests afterwards I did without even stopping time since very few 'new ones' showed up.
The devs thought side quests needed even more of an incentive to go through, so they threw JRPG grinding out the window and decided to innovate. See....there's no actual grinding in LR. It's a JRPG but without any experience gained from battle; there's no point behind them other than drops and money. It's almost an anti-JRPG in that sense.
Instead, quest completion itself boosts your stats.
Quest completed
rewards:
+10 strength, +6 magic.
It's actually one of the more ingenious things this game has come up with and it's really impressive. Rather than grind for an upcoming battle you can go complete story content and plotlines. Granted, these sidequests don't have the branching paths and long, thought out storylines of Fallout sidequests, but it's still impressive how they used it as a replacement for a JRPG element that gets criticized. For it's part I thought the game did a good job of variety and giving each quest character and reason. There's one where a path branches and the reward changes depending on what you pick; more of that would've been great.
The story itself is better than the previous games, because it makes sense. All open-world games tend to have simpler plots, I feel, because you don't want to interrupt gameplay with constant cut-scenes and the linearity required to constantly interrupt play with story. So if you didn't know wtf was happening in XIII or XIII-2, don't worry. You don't have to. You get the sparknotes version here.
Worth mentioning are garbs: costumes that affect stats and provide abilities as well as auto abilities. They tied cosmetics to customization and made it as important as weapon choice and shields. Nothing new but worth mentioning, as there are an assload of costumes in-game. ASSLOAD.
As for the battles themselves the ATB system is still here; battles are in real time but most people end up using their ATB gauge in one go and wait for it to refill. They allow you to move during battles which isn't that big a deal, until an ability you can equip comes up; ''ATB Recharge''. The way it works is you recharge ATB quickly for as long as you have ATB recharge pressed, but are vulnerable during and afterwards when you recover from the animation. So it makes positioning in battles actually matter and animations for moves something other than just an animation for a move until your turn is up. Otherwise the game still suffers from some of the constraints of typical RPG turn based battle mechanics in a real time system; waiting for gauge to recharge is really just a slight step up from turn based since you're STILL WAITING; more abilities like ATB recharge would've made it feel more ''real time'' but whatever. Take it or leave it, but it works. So meh.
Verdict? A fantastic end to the XIII series, which had a pathetic start. Love Lightning as a stoic protagonist; really liked how they changed up JRPG elements here, and the ingenuity makes me want to play XV if and when it comes to PC. It's sort of like Majora's Mask in how it did some really cool new things with established formulas, and I wanna see more of it. We finally got to open world, quest based, ingenuity in how levelling up and XP is alloted in FFXIII and it's fan-effin-tastic. I guess the only downside is that if you want to give more 'meaning' to the world and story you gotta play FFXIII lolololololol. And also try to make sense of  XIII-2's plotline lololololol. Even if you don't this game's just so damn good and creative in various aspects.
Oh, and the music is so good that I forgot to even mention it since lol it's expected from the XIII series at this point.

I had mixed thoughts about this game since I started playing it and it was very hard for me to decide whether to give it thumbs up or down. You can obviously see my descision before you read any further but please let me explain how I came to such conclusion about this game
The good:
*I'm a fan of minimalistic esthetics and that's what cought my eye when I first saw this game - it looks great but the coin has two sides and I'll get back to this later
*Interesting mix of puzzle and physics based platforming
*Attractive price
The bad:
*I mentioned looks as one of the good things earlier, but the game has serious design flaws when it comes to visuals. Whenever you play a level you can see a blurred image of the next level in the background and a blurred image of the previous level in the foreground. It seems fine at first but later in the game levels get more busy and complex meaning that very often the foreground is actually blocking your vision and you can't see crucial elements of your current level or even worse - the position of the cube you control. If this is made delibarately to make the game harder then I'm questioning the developers inteligence
*The main mechanic of the game is not properly explained. I had to play through several levels to sort of understand what pressing "space" actually does. That is again very poor design by the developers
*As mentioned before the game has a puzzle aspect to it (it says puzzle in the first sentence of the description). A puzzle normally has a clear goal that you need to achieve. In this games case the goal is to reach the exit from the level, however in almost every level you cannot see the exit or the whole level which means that planning your moves is impossible without trial and error. Yes you can slightly zoom out your view, but that doesn't help at all. Navigating the level is a difficult challenge already so why make it even more difficult and frustrating is beyond me. I would understand this descision if every level was linear but in this case the levels are all over the place (especially the later ones)
The ugly:
*Even though this game is simple and has very few mechanics - it does suffer from bugs. My cube clipped through walls, I ended the level where I was not supposed to and worse of all the controls did not respond as they should have. For example pressing "space" resulted in reseting my cube which happened a few times just near the exit
I think the devs should have given a bit more thought to the game or perhaps asked more people to test it before the release. I really wanted to like it, but the poor design choices ruined it for me. I cannot recommend the game as it is

King's Bounty is a total rip-off of the Heroes of Might and Magic series, but that's not a bad thing.  You play as the princess of the pre-eminent human kingdom of a fantasy world besieged by demons, sent through a dimensional rip to seek aid and to find your mentor, the protagonist of the first King's Bounty game.  You command up to five units of an absurdly varied assortment of troops as you fight against roving armies of monsters, hunt down buried treasure, and fulfill quests to grow in power.  Battles take place on a tactical grid and involves hand-to-hand combat between units, archery, and spells, cast both by you and by many kinds of troops.  Really, my only complaints are having to go and recruit more troops whenever you take significant casualties in battle and that a lot of battles wind up being kind of monotonous, although this is offset by the huge variety of possible opponents and randomized battlefields.  All things considered, I think this game is well worth the price.
